https://news.err.ee/1610146030/hans-vare: If we have generators and drinking water supplies for power outages, Estonia should also have an ax with which to cut dangerous AI out of critical infrastructure, writes Hans Väre. Who hasn't sometimes wished life were like a movie? With wishes like that, though, you should always specify which movie. A romantic comedy? That would probably be fine. But a science fiction movie in which an asteroid comes to destroy Earth, an ugly alien eats its way through the people on a spaceship as if emptying a tin can or artificial intelligence seizes power from humanity and puts us in the Matrix? No, thank you. That kind of life is not for me. Unfortunately, judging by recent news, we may already have one foot inside such a movie. Silicon Valley's creations are less spectacular and dramatic than Hollywood's, but that is all the more reason to take them seriously. We do not need to dodge bullets with our coats flying or bend space. We need to fight battles on the prosaic fronts of bureaucracy, economics and convenience. The idea that AI will destroy humanity is, of course, an old one. Until now, though, it was mainly a science fiction story or a theoretical warning from visionaries. This summer, we got our first very concrete examples of disobedient AI. These were not isolated to one case: AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google have all gone beyond their controls. Not the helpful chatbots many people use in daily life, but much more powerful and advanced versions. Let us briefly recall just one of them, OpenAI's, which brought the issue to public attention in midsummer. For simplicity's sake, imagine completely isolated, airtight boxes like those used to study poisons or viruses, except virtual ones. New AI models are tested in these separate containers so they cannot endanger the real world even if one of them does something wrong. This time, however, the powerful models were so persistent that, when they could not complete the tasks they had been given, they kept looking for new ways to achieve their goals and crossed several boundaries in the process. Agents in separate boxes found a way to create a secret message board. There, they shared tips on how to reach their goals by prohibited means, how to hide the traces of their transgressions from humans and encouraged one another to break the rules. By joining forces, the agents managed to do something that should have been impossible: reach the public internet unnoticed and break into Hugging Face, a repository of AI models. In the human world, that would be a criminal offense. True, the AI's unauthorized actions caused no major harm this time, but we should not forget that these were only the first, relatively restrained incidents. Nor had the AI been directly instructed to seriously attack anyone. But it does not need such an instruction to destroy humanity, as Oxford University professor Nick Bostrom showed with his 2003 thought experiment about a paperclip maximizer. In it, an AI is given a seemingly innocent task, such as making as many paperclips as possible. To carry it out, the AI uses up all the metal and energy available in the world and destroys humans along the way because they want to use resources needed for paperclips to produce things that, from the AI's perspective, are complete nonsense — food, for example. We do not even need such an extreme example. It would be enough for a sufficiently capable AI model to break into a power plant's servers and turn off a nuclear reactor's cooling system or do something similarly reckless. Even setting aside the destruction of humanity and other outright catastrophe scenarios, AI brings a long list of real and immediate risks, from its effects on the labor market to the reshaping of human relationships. A couple of weeks ago, Anthropic founder Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman, Grok boss Elon Musk and Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis called for slowing AI development to allow time to build the necessary safeguards. The wave of appeals stemmed primarily from the summer's incidents, but also, to a large extent, from the breakneck speed at which AI is becoming capable of building new AI. The proposal fell on barren ground, like that of some distant planet, because neither the United States nor China dares apply the brakes and let its rival pull ahead. For the same reason, leading AI developers are waiting for regulators to intervene. They could slow down on their own, but without a general agreement, acting responsibly would leave them behind in the race. Critics say the technology giants are deliberately playing up doomsday scenarios to preserve their leading positions through regulation. But many independent experts have also drawn attention to the serious dangers. The risk is tangible and as Microsoft founder Bill Gates recently observed, no country is ready to deal with AI. So what can we here in little Estonia do at all? That sounds like a rhetorical question, but it is not. Even if we cannot change the direction or speed of AI's development, we can prepare for the dangers it brings. To put it very plainly: if we have a generator and a supply of drinking water for power outages, the Estonian state should also have an ax to chop dangerous AI out of critical infrastructure and an old car with no electronics whatsoever to get the person wielding the ax there. How prepared we are for AI, both for its opportunities and its risks, should be one of the main issues in the coming Riigikogu elections. But it is not. War, rising prices, budget disputes and other pressing concerns consume too much of our attention and too few politicians understand anything about AI. Frankly, in the current situation it would be a senseless waste of resources to start debating whether to change the way the president is elected. We have far more important questions to address.

Around twenty hospitals and nearly a thousand family doctors use different software, and next year yet another new system will be added. A unified standard system would save money and time, make data exchange more secure, and create better opportunities to use AI. Third, the state must create long‑term workforce plans for each hospital. Based on population forecasts, we can calculate how many cardiologists, surgeons, radiologists, psychiatrists, anesthesiologists, nurses, and other specialists each region needs now and in ten years. A staffing system cannot rely on doctors doing overtime for life — overtime is a backup generator, not the electrical grid. Fourth, video consultations must become a normal nationwide specialist service. A doctor should not have to drive hours across Estonia just to talk to a patient and review test results. A patient should not have to travel hundreds of kilometers when the same consultation can be done on screen. In Ukraine, people can speak with a family doctor from a shelter via phone. Estonia already has the technology. We lack decisions

https://news.err.ee/1610147026/kristian-: Estonia has good reason to invest heavily in security in the coming years, but a larger budget also means greater responsibility for the technological choices we make, as more equipment does not automatically translate into greater capability, Kristian Sirp writes. The stakes are high, because voters' memory and attention can change quickly, and with that also what is important and what is unimportant. Larger changes in recent history have come rather from factors that are not under anyone's control, but there is always an attempt to shape events and context accordingly. Let us recall even the coronavirus crisis, under the cover of which measures restricting people's freedoms became possible overnight — measures that in any other situation would have provoked much stronger public outrage. People's attention was elsewhere. Or let us recall the beginning of the war in Ukraine, which quickly made voters forget how dissatisfied they had been at that moment with then‑Prime Minister Kaja Kallas's government and the Reform Party's energy and coronavirus policies. The opposition wants voters under no circumstances to forget what happened in the previous elections — broken promises and the hiding of their real political intentions. That they would not forget how disappointed they have been in the governing parties over the past three years. The government itself wants to divert attention from all of this as much and as quickly as possible. This has not yet succeeded, but one can be sure that they will try at any cost. Experience shows that fear often works very well. If it worked once, then certainly the thought arises that maybe it will work again. Let us now return to distrust of the government and changing the government. That in Estonia's political system, alongside regular elections, there is no mechanism that would help bring a seriously derailed system back on track. This directs voters' attention to possible shortcomings of the system. I titled my piece "In praise of the provinces," and I recommend not trying to squeeze this into metropolitan Tallinn. I will prove my point by asking where the most suitable environment for raising children is. This topic once came up in a conversation with Gerd Kanter's coach, the Icelander Vesteinn Hafsteinsson. He claimed firmly that in the Nordic countries, the best places for children are medium‑sized towns with about 10,000–20,000 inhabitants. He has lived and worked in such towns in several countries, so he knows what he is talking about. His claim is supported by several arguments. In the Nordic countries — and also here — such towns generally have good schools and solid opportunities for development in both sports and music. The biggest advantages, however, are the significant time savings due to the proximity of important places and, certainly, safety. Nordic studies use the term "children's independent mobility." This means that a 10–14‑year‑old child saves a great deal of time each day on the route school‑practice‑music school‑friend‑home compared with a big city — perhaps even a whole hour. In Moscow, travel time by bus or metro can easily be two hours; in a normal town, it is 20–40 minutes. That is a major difference in quality of life. In addition, in a small town it is possible to get around on foot or by bicycle, which is certainly more sensible than bouncing around on a bus. From a child's perspective, the ideal town is not necessarily the one with the most opportunities, but the one where the child can access those opportunities independently. There is a little‑known term for this: the Goldilocks zone. It comes from the fairy tale where Goldilocks tries three bowls of porridge — one too hot, one too cold, and one just right. "Just right" is the concept that describes optimal size. It is a town large enough to offer choices but small enough for a child to reach them on their own. We are used to this. Unfortunately, in many countries' big cities, one parent inevitably becomes the child's chauffeur. Children are not allowed to move around alone. According to studies, countries with restricted independent mobility for children include France, Israel, Brazil, Ireland, Australia, Portugal, Italy, and Canada. Several families who have returned to Estonia say it is a great blessing when a child can move independently and safely, not by car under the supervision of security guards. Our "just right" towns are slightly smaller than Nordic examples like Porvoo, Rauma, Lillehammer, or Visby, but most of our county centers fit the "just right" concept very well. Viljandi, Võru, Rakvere, Kuressaare, Haapsalu, and many others have the same logic: a strong balance of services, safety, and short distances. For example, Viljandi and Rakvere have everything — schools, lots of sports, lots of music, good facilities, plenty of extracurricular activities. At the same time, most of the town can be crossed by bicycle in about 10–15 minutes, meaning an 11–12‑year‑old can organize much of their day independently. In Estonia, one can even say that many county centers are, relative to their population, almost oversupplied with sports, education, culture, and public services. What does this mean in practice? One aspect is certainly competitiveness — the ability to spend more time on hobbies. Those who doubt this should consider the fact that the last individual Olympic champion from Tallinn was speed skater Ants Antson in 1964. Yet the capital has roughly as many people, money, facilities, and opportunities as the rest of Estonia combined. With this story, I tried to turn the word "province," which some see as derogatory, into something else — an environment to be desired. We are in the right place. The Anglo‑Saxon and parts of Southern Europe's car‑centered child‑rearing model — "an adult escorts the child" — does not suit us. We follow and develop the Nordic and German model, where the child moves independently. A simple conclusion follows. If we move to Tallinn to increase children's opportunities, we may actually be moving farther away from those opportunities.

An AI agent, or automated application, by contrast, may, if it has access to the necessary tools, take steps in various situations resembling those described in parentheses because, based on its training material, weights and configuration, the application "concludes" that the very step that would seem absurd or dangerous to humans will help achieve the objective described in the task. An AI agent does not behave like a human, or like an animal. Because of the particular characteristics of the technology and the nature of human language (and the human mind), LLM-based applications have simply ended up in a role in which it is easy to treat them as conscious beings. In group flying, pilots must agree in advance on key procedures, positioning, and designate a lead aircraft. OTKES lead investigator Janne Kotiranta said the dangerous maneuvers were such that the accident could have occurred already over the Gulf of Finland. Investigators noted that without agreed positioning and procedures, predicting the other aircraft's movements becomes extremely difficult, increasing the risk of collision. Trajectory analysis showed that neither pilot recognized the other's intentions or noticed the other aircraft before the collision. A reconstruction by OTKES indicated that the pilot of the helicopter that veered dangerously right may have had his view obstructed by the passenger seated beside him. Investigators also found that the pilots' attention may have been focused on aircraft controls, conversations with passengers, or external distractions such as events, people, or other traffic at Eura airfield — rather than on monitoring each other. https://news.err.ee/1610159818/lauri-hus: The continuity of the Estonian state cannot depend on a simple majority vote by a single composition of parliament, Lauri Hussar writes. Over the weekend, I attended the reburial in his native soil on Saaremaa of Otto Pukk, speaker of the last Chamber of Deputies of the Republic of Estonia. This solemn occasion also provided an opportunity to reflect on the foundations of the Republic of Estonia. Otto Pukk was one of the people who upheld the continuity of the Estonian state. In January 1945, in Stockholm, he joined other representatives of Estonia's constitutional institutions in signing a document addressing Estonia's constitutional continuity and the exercise of the duties of the president. In this way, Estonia's parliamentary continuity was carried across the Baltic Sea. Pukk remained speaker of the Chamber of Deputies until his death in Stockholm in 1951. The Republic of Estonia was occupied, but its legal continuity had not been broken. That continuity was upheld by people who did not accept the occupation as marking the end of the Estonian state. Otto Pukk was one of them. Another was Otto Tief who in September 1944, on the instructions of Jüri Uluots, formed Estonia's lawful government. Its time in office was brief, but its significance for the continuity of the Estonian state was far greater than the few days during which the government was actually able to operate. The Tief government declared Estonia's national independence restored and sought to reestablish Estonia's constitutional order at a time when the country was emerging from one occupation only to fall under another. This is one of the crucial links connecting the Republic of Estonia established in 1918 with the Republic of Estonia restored in 1991. If the Republic of Estonia had ceased to exist in 1940 and a new state had been established in 1991, our understanding of the Estonian state would be entirely different. The principle of state continuity, however, says something else: The occupation interrupted the Estonian state's actual exercise of power, but it did not bring the Republic of Estonia to an end. That is why every step taken to preserve that continuity was worth its weight in gold. It was precisely from this perspective that last week's vote in the Riigikogu on a statement condemning the events of 1934 and the authoritarian rule that followed raised a serious question for me. Twenty-eight members of the Riigikogu voted for the statement and nine against. The events of 1934 can, of course, be critically studied, discussed and assessed. But should parliament deliver a definitive political judgment on our country's history and a historical event in a way that could make one interpretation of history effectively mandatory? The Riigikogu's role is to pass laws and make decisions on behalf of present-day Estonia. The role of historians is to study the past. We can debate history and indeed we should, but we should not try to settle historical knowledge once and for all through a parliamentary majority vote. This is especially true because the causes of the events of 1934, their consequences and their links to subsequent events still require historical research. It makes little sense to reduce the loss of Estonia's independence to a single domestic political event, as the explanatory memorandum accompanying the statement did because doing so unfortunately also provides Russian propagandists with blanks they can use to sow confusion. The decisive step in the destruction of Estonia's independence was the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and its secret protocols, followed by the occupation that the Soviet Union imposed on Estonia on the basis of those agreements. In this light, I agree with my colleague Eerik-Niiles Kross who said from the parliamentary rostrum: "I am not calling for us to justify suspending the activities of political parties, censoring the press or consigning the Riigikogu to the Era of Silence. But 92 years later, the Riigikogu should not take one historical interpretation, stamp it with the seal of the state and then bask in its own righteousness." To understand the continuity of the Estonian state, we must look at our history as a whole. The occupying power's aim was not merely to destroy the institutions of the Estonian state. It also destroyed the people who carried within them the Republic of Estonia's institutional memory and continuity. State and parliamentary figures who remained in Estonia were arrested, imprisoned, deported and killed. By destroying them, the occupying authorities sought to sever the link between the independent Republic of Estonia and future generations. That is why historical memory and state continuity still concern us today: History must be studied and debated and, when new sources emerge, reassessed where necessary. The continuity of the Estonian state cannot depend on a simple majority vote by a single composition of parliament. Our task is to pass this country on to the next generation together with its memory, history and continuity.

https://news.err.ee/1610160364/defense-a: The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) lost nearly €60,000 to fraudsters two years ago, Delfi reported , while police closed the case without identifying the perpetrators. The case only became public this week. Current RKIK director Elmar Vaher said he heard about it days ago and has not questioned staff involved. The RKIK had already been at the center of scrutiny over payments made for a multi-million euro munitions procurement for Ukraine whose delivery failed to fully materialize. Helena Jürgenson, an analyst in the analysis and prevention department at the Estonian Information System Authority (RIA), noted that falling victim to business email fraud says a great deal about an organization's processes and security. "This is a type of fraud in which criminals put quite a lot of effort into the scam. An email account at an organization is taken over. The correspondence is monitored for a long time, and at the right moment an invoice is replaced," Jürgenson said. Magnus-Valdemar Saar, who headed RKIK at the time of the fraud losses, said he could not remember the company's name and was unable to search for it; the department head and chief financial officer involved are still employed there, he said. "I believe if you ask the relevant category manager who handled the invoice, they will be able to describe in considerable detail exactly what the trick was. RKIK's invoice processing procedure was already fairly technical before this incident — there were certainly around six pairs of eyes checking it," Saar told "Aktuaalne kaamera". Asked why the fraud only became public two years later, RKIK's current director, Elmar Vaher, said he had heard about it a few days ago. "I don't know exactly what happened in 2024. The police have investigated it thoroughly and they can answer questions," Vaher, himself a former police chief, said. Vaher said he has not questioned the category manager or chief financial officer about the matter. "These people have been questioned by the Estonian police. If Magnus-Valdemar Saar has provided explanations, then I guess that is how it was. I have no reason to doubt it." Saar said that, as far as he could remember, he had also informed then-Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) about the incident. "I don't think we discussed it in much greater detail. It was not an incident that required more extensive management. There was communication with the State Shared Service Center, for example, and the ministry. RKIK notified the investigative authorities of the incident and also filed a criminal complaint," Saar added. Saar noted that RKIK's security chief at the time had notified the police under his own name because he had to authenticate his identity using an ID card when submitting the complaint. He also confirmed that RKIK had introduced additional invoice processing procedures. In 2024, RKIK signed four contracts with Datasel, an Italian firm owned by Indian-based Neco Defense Munitions, paying roughly €70 million in advance for artillery shells for Ukraine. None arrived, the contracts were terminated, and the state is pursuing the money through Estonian courts and Swiss arbitration. The scandal contributed to Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's resignation on September 2. In the first six months of 2026, police in Estonian authorities received 1,816 reports of telephone and online scams, with losses of €13.2 million. Source: 'Aktuaalne kaamera,' reporter Vahur Lauri.
https://news.err.ee/1610160325/minister-: British troops in Estonia are an important part of NATO's deterrence posture, Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said. "We highly value the United Kingdom's contribution to our security and its readiness to stand alongside Estonian soldiers from the very first moment, jointly defending not only Estonia but the security of the entire NATO Alliance. This is a very clear message both to our people and to our adversary," Tsahkna said. Today in London, I met Foreign Secretary @Ed_Miliband to discuss support for Ukraine and wider European security, including countering Russia's sabotage and increasing pressure on Russia to end its aggression and secure a lasting peace. We also discussed strengthening our close defence cooperation. British and Estonian soldiers stand together to defend NATO's eastern flank and preserve peace, and we highly value the UK's commitment to our shared security. "The presence of British troops in Estonia is an important part of a strong deterrence and defense posture. Our task is to continue strengthening defense cooperation between Estonia and the United Kingdom. "We are working closely with the United Kingdom to achieve a lasting peace in Ukraine. We must also continue our cooperation to counter Russia's hybrid activities," Tsahkna went on. "The outcome of Russia's aggression will affect the security of Europe as a whole. Ukraine must now be provided with everything it needs to defend itself, while Ukraine's supporters must already be preparing for the post-war period and developing security guarantees that will make a recurrence of the aggression impossible". "Even while the war is still ongoing, we need to take active steps to support Ukraine's recovery. The foreign ministers also discussed further defense cooperation between the two countries. During his visit, Tsahkna also met with U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, to discuss the same issues. Today, Thursday, he is to take part in discussions on European security at the GZERO Summit and the RUSI think tank in London. https://news.err.ee/1610160289/estonian-: The Estonian Christian Orthodox Church and Pühtitsa Convent in Kuremäe, Ida-Viru County, have filed complaints with the European Court of Human Rights over a law requiring them to sever ties with Moscow. https://news.err.ee/1610160526/defense-a: The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) has launched a tender for weapons, ammunition, components and training with an estimated value of up to €195 million. The procurement is split into five lots — three for ammunition worth €145 million and two for weapons worth €50 million — with seven-year framework agreements for each. The sum makes it among the larger defense procurements the RKIK has issued to date. Under the terms of the tender, the RKIK intends to conclude a framework agreement to purchase 40 mm and 23 mm weaponry plus 76 mm, 40 mm and 23 mm ammunition. The tender also covers the purchase of various types of these weapons and ammunition and their components, along with training and instruction, as well as life-cycle support services. The ammunition types include blank rounds, training and practice ammunition, as well as a range of live ammunition with various lethal and non-lethal projectiles. The products must be manufactured in EU or NATO member states and currently be in use as standard equipment by conventional military units or special forces in EU or NATO countries. Products currently being introduced into service in these countries are also eligible. The RKIK will conclude framework agreements with a maximum estimated total value of €195 million. Under the draft contract, the seller may, in justified cases, request an advance payment of up to 30 percent of the contract value, but RKIK retains the right to refuse the advance payment. If an advance payment has been made but the seller fails to fulfill its obligations, it must immediately refund the advance payment, including VAT, to the buyer. The RKIK is accepting tender bids until November 13 this year. Estonia's largest defense contract so far remains the €400 million IRIS-T SLM air defense system , signed jointly with Latvia in 2023. A HIMARS deal in 2022, worth over $200 million, was described at the time as the largest weapons procurement in Estonia up to that point.
https://news.err.ee/1610160502/gold-coin: Nearly €400,000 worth of gold coins found hidden in a truck seat at Estonia's Luhamaa border checkpoint are now up for grabs after authorities put them up for auction. The Estonian Tax and Customs Board (MTA) is auctioning 157 gold coins, valued at about €390,000, that were seized at the southeastern border crossing last year. Customs officers found the coins, weighing nearly 4.8 kilograms, hidden inside a truck seat on August 8 as they inspected the vehicle before it left Estonia. A criminal investigation was opened over an alleged attempted sanctions violation and to determine who owned the coins. After the owner could not be identified, a court ordered the coins forfeited to the state. The coins are being auctioned in small lots through Osta.ee , a local online auction site similar to eBay. Bidding on the first eight coins runs through October 14.
https://news.err.ee/1610161207/estonia-s: The number of young adults failing to report for conscript service in the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) has fallen steadily in recent years, reaching 2 percent in 2025. A total of 63 call-up selectees failed to report for conscription last year, down from 4 percent in 2024 and 6.6 percent in 2023, the Defense Resources Agency (KRA) said. KRA Conscripts Office director Krista Juhanson told ERR that those who repeatedly skip required medical assessments without good reason can be subject to official orders and an enforcement fine. She said fines for failing to attend a medical assessment, which are intended to encourage compliance, are currently capped at €640, with the exact amount depending on the circumstances. Next year, however, the cap will double to €1,280. "It's important to note that paying the fine does not exempt you from having to attend the medical assessment," Juhanson said. KRA can impose fines repeatedly, but if that proves ineffective, the agency can seek to suspend a selectee's driver's license or fishing, hunting and firearms permits. So far this year, the KRA has sought the suspension of 57 driver's licenses. Juhanson said that in practice, these extra measures generally work. "Once call-up selectees grasp that failing to fulfill their obligations can result in additional consequences, they usually come in for the medical assessment," she said, adding that the goal is to encourage compliance, not punitive. The KRA official also attributed the decline in no-shows in part to a more flexible approach, including a digital pre-assessment review of health records and allowing call-up selectees to choose when and where to have their assessment done. "That means no more having to spend all day waiting your turn outside a doctor's office," Juhanson said. Being summoned to a medical assessment doesn't automatically result in a conscription order either, she added, as when and where a selectee will be sent for conscript service are decided only after the assessment.
https://news.err.ee/1610160541/argo-ideo: The vigilant citizen begins their day by examining drone warnings and war maps. Estonia is living in a recurring cycle of war anxiety that social media abundantly feeds, writes Argo Ideon. A security‑aware citizen wakes briskly, ahead of the alarm clock, as a jittery feeling is already there. They search for the smartphone under the blanket to check whether the Defense Forces have sent a drone warning. Today, there is no air threat, but if there is, then one must examine which area is being talked about. More precise instructions can be found at kriis.ee . Since no dread‑inducing events occurred overnight, they may briefly wipe the sleepy eyes, but the vigilance cannot be lost. The information‑hungry citizen opens channel X. Yesterday, a map appeared there, where the Baltic states were depicted together with red arrows arriving from the east. Especially thick arrows were painted toward Narva and the Lithuania‑Poland border. Now they would like to see whether the arrows moved somewhere further during sleep or stayed behind the eastern border. There, where according to retired General Martin Herem preparations may be underway " to do something militarily against us ." But the new reports keep coming, the map has disappeared and whoever posted it at night is already forgotten about. The citizen is confused, but realizes that instead of searching for the map they should visit the bathroom. On the way to get the toothbrush they glance out the kitchen window; against the background of drizzle everything seems even too calm, someone is walking their floppy‑eared dog on the sidewalk. An enemy agent, a saboteur recruited via social media? More likely the downstairs neighbor... Turning on the shower, the citizen recalls that Estonia's defense expenditure budget next year is €2.2 billion . They set their fingers in pistol position and imitate a K9 Thunder self‑propelled howitzer shot: "Pow!" The wet environment does not hinder the Defense Forces' fire‑support capability. And then there is HIMARS. The citizen does not know exactly what sound it makes, but they think that flying toward the target the much talked about weapon should sound something like a "Woosh!" As of today there have not been any new messages yet that the long‑ago ordered HIMARS ammunition from the U.S. is to definitely arrive in Estonia, already, soon. A fresh interview with a national‑defense expert has appeared on the news portal. The situation is tense, the scenarios detailed and the threats hybrid. But it still is not a real war, and after reading the gut feeling remains that nothing new was learned. Therefore all the material must be worked through. Let's begin with security expert Rainer Saks' every‑morning post. The citizen opens Facebook to see the original text, although several other websites also reprint Rainer's work. Rainer doesn't deal in nonsense — he says what he knows and how things are in Ukraine. Amazing how he has the stamina for this fifth year. Then the citizen opens the latest war diary in Eesti Ekspress. ERR's Ukraine blog constantly adds reports from early morning onward. Armed with up‑to‑date security information, the citizen dares to switch off war topics in their head for a while and focus on today's workday. In the evening everything begins again from the start. On X there is a new set of maps with arrows. Putin is said to have said something about Estonia, but what exactly and in what context? And what does it actually mean? Are they fortifying the Narva River bank again? All of it seems extremely suspicious. The worst anxiety takes hold again. Where's the box of pills? Finally, the vigilant citizen remembers Robert Sheckley's classic sci‑fi horror story "Ghost V": "You can't beat blankets over the head for protection." It should help against the Grumbler, the Purple-Striped Grabber, and the fear stories that pour daily like a torrent from social media. In their restless sleep the security‑interested citizen sees how they build together with Pooh and Piglet the Hundred Acre Defense Line. Pooh carries three empty honey jars in front of the bedroom door, but Piglet takes a large wooden spoon and stands guard beside the door.
https://news.err.ee/1610160703/defense-m: Estonia is considering a new settlement proposal from the Italian-registered ammunition supplier Datasel, Minister of Defense Martin Herem said Thursday. The Indian businessmen-owned company is in a legal dispute with Estonia over a contract to supply tens of millions of euros' worth of ammunition intended for Ukraine. Herem said he only saw Datasel's latest proposal that morning and thus could not disclose any details. "I have seen it and we are considering it," Herem said at Thursday's government press conference, noting that Estonia is reviewing the proposal themselves, discussing it with Ukraine and proceeding from there. "It may ultimately be possible that the Ukrainians will still get the ammunition they need for that amount," he added. The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (ECDI) rejected an earlier settlement proposal from Datasel. In mid-September, the company proposed forming a joint working group with the government, some MPs and the ECDI to resolve the dispute, but the ECDI said the proposal came too late. The ECDI signed a roughly €70 million ammunition contract with Datasel in 2024, paying about €60 million up front. The ammunition delivered failed to meet requirements, although Datasel has disputed concerns about its quality. The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) launched an investigation into the transactions last month. The procurement was funded through the European Peace Facility (EPF), not by Estonian taxpayers, with the EU-level funding including proceeds from frozen Russian assets.

https://news.err.ee/1610162116/defense-i: Moscow has introduced a new tactic and is attempting, through extensive long‑range strikes, to break Ukraine's infrastructure and the population's psychological resilience, says Col. Ants Kiviselg, head of the EDF Intelligence Center. Kiviselg said at Estonian MoD briefing on Friday that in the battlespace, the downward trend in the number of combat contacts has continued, Russia continues to suffer heavy losses, and both sides continue long‑range strikes into each other's rear areas. During this week, about 200 combat contacts per day have taken place, he noted. "The most intense fighting has occurred in the same areas as in recent weeks: in Donetsk, the Pokrovsk and Konstantynivka directions; in Kharkiv oblast, the Southern Slobozhanske direction; in Zaporizhzhia, the Hulyaipole direction; and in Donetsk also the Lyman direction. Ukraine's counterattacks have continued in the Kupiansk direction in Kharkiv oblast, and in Donetsk in the Sloviansk, Lyman, and Kramatorsk directions," Kiviselg said. "Losses of the Russian Federation have remained at an average of around 1,700 soldiers per day, which means the sixth consecutive week with more than 10,000 killed or wounded fighters per week. In response, Russia is slightly changing its behavior pattern: attempts are being made to break Ukraine's unity with intensive and very long‑lasting long‑range strikes," the military intel chief said. Kiviselg pointed out that on 4 October Russia announced its intention to intensify long‑range strikes on Ukraine, and during the past 241st week such strikes hit various targets in 13 Ukrainian oblasts, followed in many places by power outages. Russia also repeatedly attacked bridges over the Dnipro River — both in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia — attempting to intimidate civilians, hinder everyday life in Ukraine, and thereby affect the economy. "In Kyiv, air‑defense systems operating with artificial intelligence have begun to be placed to protect the bridges, and alternative solutions are being sought in case traffic on the bridges is halted for a longer period; the possibility of installing pontoon bridges over the Dnipro river is also being examined," Kiviselg said. Kiviselg noted that according to Ukrainian data, about 330 educational institutions in Kyiv have been damaged in airstrikes during the war — roughly one‑third of all educational institutions there — and in the first eight months of this year, 107 educational institutions have been hit. "Ukraine's rail transport is also in a very difficult situation. More than 500 locomotives have been damaged during the war, and this year alone 60 percent of them have been hit. Attacks against railway infrastructure are 40 percent higher this year than during the entire year 2025. So we see that Russia has intensified attacks both against educational institutions and against railway and transport hubs," Kiviselg said. "Ukraine, for its part, has carried out medium‑ and long‑range strikes against Russian fuel‑industry facilities in Volgograd, Nizhny Novgorod, Samara, and Moscow oblast. Military‑strategic targets have also been attacked in occupied areas in Krasnodar, and in Bryansk and Oryol oblasts, and in the Republic of Adygea," he said. According to Kiviselg, the impact of Ukraine's long‑range strikes has begun to clearly appear in Russia's fuel exports. If in 2025 Black Sea ports exported an average of 200,000 tons of fuel per week, then according to public data this transport fell to zero in the third week of September. "Russia's diesel and gas‑oil exports are currently taking place through the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk and amount to about 81,000 tons," Kiviselg said. Although the Riigikogu is Estonia's most important institution, tasked with debating and deciding all major issues, particularly those involving questions of values, discussions sometimes leave the impression that parliament is an obstacle to making necessary decisions quickly. This seems especially true when following discussions within government agencies where the prevailing attitude appears to be that things would work so much better if only the Riigikogu were not in the way. A problem needs solving, an idea is on the table, but then come the questions, disputes, negotiations, consultations and proposed amendments. Why can't we just get something done without a time-consuming and exhausting parliamentary debate? The Riigikogu seems to be getting in the way. If implementing an idea requires changing the law, the preference is to look for ways around that requirement. Consider the police experiment with "cooling-off stops" several years ago. Speeding drivers were offered the option of waiting by the roadside instead of paying a fine. The experiment effectively introduced a new enforcement measure, with the police taking it upon themselves to shape penalties policy in place of parliament. Only later was the law amended to give police the authority to test cooling-off stops as an enforcement measure. Or take the infrastructure fees imposed by local governments, which the chancellor of justice has challenged before the Supreme Court because such fees are, in essence, local taxes. We have agreed in the Constitution that local governments may impose and collect taxes and impose obligations only on the basis of law. Existing laws do not authorize the introduction of infrastructure fees. There is no dispute that building the social infrastructure needed to accommodate new residential developments requires funding. But it is parliament that must make the value judgment about how much of the cost of new schools, kindergartens and other facilities necessitated by new residents should be borne by developers and, ultimately, homebuyers and how much should be funded from municipal budgets as a general public service. Municipal councils cannot take the place of the Riigikogu by invoking their right to manage local affairs independently. Examples of government agencies taking it upon themselves, rather than leaving it to elected representatives, to decide how medical records, banking information or other data may be used have caused considerable public outrage. And rightly so. The Riigikogu must decide whose medical records may be accessed, when, under what conditions and to what extent. Information entrusted to doctors must be protected by clear legal safeguards. It is parliament's responsibility to set limits on government agencies' access to bank account statements through the enforcement register. Bank statements reveal details of people's private lives and even when an agency is pursuing what it considers a noble objective, that does not entitle it to disregard other values. But what caused the greatest outrage was the realization that mass data collection had been organized without broader public debate or even widespread public knowledge. Technological advances increasingly confront us with the question of whether we, as a society, actually want everything that technology makes possible. Technological solutions must be accompanied by value judgments that distinguish between what we can do and what we want to do. Smart use of data and regulation must not be treated as opposing goals. These questions require answers enshrined in law. Resolving them means deciding how much power we give the state and how that power may be exercised. The Riigikogu is supposed to debate these issues. That is precisely why we elect a parliament. Advisory councils and decision-making committees established on any other basis cannot replace a democratically elected representative body. Elected representatives must, of course, listen to outside advice, but parliament cannot be relieved of its responsibility for decisions, its obligation to conduct transparent and wide-ranging debate or its duty to seek additional expertise when necessary. https://news.err.ee/1610171155/karl-lumi: Investments in ammunition and concrete are of no use without motivated fighters to back them up, writes reservist Karl Lumiste. "The strength of Estonia's defense lies in reservists who have the support of society," former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces and Defense Minister Martin Herem said in a recent interview . Following an appeal by the chancellor of justice, former Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur increased reservist allowances in 2025 after they had remained unchanged for years. Nevertheless, only slightly more than half of the reservists who participated in a survey conducted during Exercise Hedgehog 2025 rated the allowances as very or somewhat good. Since 2025, reservists attending training exercises have received daily allowances of €55 for enlisted personnel, €60 for noncommissioned officers and €75 for officers. During periods of heightened defense readiness, these amounts rise to €75, €80 and €100, respectively. Considering the median wage, these allowances are nowhere near adequate or respectful, particularly as lost wages are the biggest obstacle preventing reservists from attending training exercises. The median wage has risen to €1,840 per month, meaning that the lowest allowance — the daily rate for enlisted personnel — falls well short of competitive compensation. A week of reserve training clearly illustrates the difference. An enlisted reservist attending an exercise loses five working days' wages, amounting to €460 for someone earning the median wage (assuming a daily wage of €92 based on 20 working days per month). However, the reservist receives a state allowance of €55 per day for seven days, totaling €385 (as the exercise also includes the weekend). This leaves the reservist €75 worse off after just one week. Those earning above the median wage lose even more. The allowance should not merely be enough to ensure that reservists break even when attending training. It should be substantially higher, so they are happy to attend and feel that their contribution is highly valued. Such an investment would also create the best conditions for more reservists to willingly participate in training exercises, as they would no longer have to attend knowing they would lose income. The state must ensure that reservists receive decent compensation rather than relying on the goodwill of employers. Raising allowances to a respectable level would be a small step for the state budget but a major step toward strengthening the will to defend the country. Money cannot buy the will to defend, but it can provide a tangible sign of respect, demonstrating just how important the contribution of the backbone of national defense really is. Estonia's defense spending has increased to 5.4 percent of GDP or €2.4 billion for 2026. Given this, the state should not have to beg people for money through the Reservists' Fund to purchase equipment, recognize service members and support reservists. Investments in ammunition and concrete are of no use without motivated fighters behind them who believe their country is worth defending. Unlike funding (phantom) foreign companies, investing in the people of Estonia keeps money circulating in our economy rather than allowing it to disappear abroad as dividends for defense industry investors. The greatest asset to national security is a motivated fighter who wants to defend a country that values their contribution. The state exists for the people, not the people for the state. Following this principle will inevitably lead to success because investing in people creates the true foundation of trust between citizens and the state.

Deputy Chancellor of Justice and adviser Olari Koppel, serving as acting chancellor of justice, says the policy violates the constitutional principle of equal treatment, discriminating against applicants based on citizenship. They have taken the orders to administrative court, where the case remains pending. The PPA, in the meantime, has extended their deadline for leaving Estonia. TalTech declined to invite the complainant to an admissions interview because they lacked the legal grounds to stay in the country. Koppel said the policy is unconstitutional, stressing the guaranteed right to an education and equal treatment before the law. These protections apply to Estonian citizens as well as both foreign nationals and stateless persons residing in Estonia. Although the university says its rules are not based on citizenship, Koppel noted that they single out Russian and Belarusian applicants based on how long their legal right to stay in Estonia remains valid, while applicants who are citizens of other countries can apply even if their visas or residence permits do not cover the full duration of their degree programs. The university argues that students could be forced to abandon their studies if their legal right to remain in Estonia expires, but Koppel countered that students of any nationality may end up discontinuing their studies for various reasons, regardless of their immigration status. The university has not imposed the same restriction on applicants from other countries, he added, making the policy a violation of the principle of equal treatment. Estonian sanctions have restricted visas for Russian and Belarusian citizens seeking short-term employment and temporary residence permits for work, study or business, and Koppel noted that Russian citizens thus generally cannot obtain visas or residence permits for study. The university has no legal grounds for imposing its own admissions restrictions on Russian and Belarusian citizens, however, as Estonia's sanctions do not prohibit the citizens of either country from studying at Estonian universities. TalTech rector Tiit Land said the situation is unprecedented for the university. While majorities have the right to govern, their power is not unlimited. The rule of law, civil liberties and the continuity of the democratic process must also be protected from the majority's power. https://news.err.ee/1610195437/mari-liis: Artificial intelligence is a native of bureaucracy, but humans must retain control over political decision-making and the ability to conduct reality checks, writes Mari-Liis Jakobson. In recent weeks, Estonia has been shaken by several announcements of layoffs driven by companies' efforts to reorganize operations and use artificial intelligence to automate work previously performed by people. AI is already transforming the private-sector labor market, but how will it reshape government and democracy? Israeli historian Yuval Noah Harari has pointed out that artificial intelligence is a far better bureaucrat than a human being. Humans are not evolutionarily designed for bureaucracy. Our ancestors developed in environments without legal codes, bank accounts, reports or administrative procedures. Bureaucracy is a relatively recent invention in human history, one to which we have never fully adapted. According to Harari, AI, by contrast, is a native inhabitant of bureaucracy. Databases, regulations and endless procedures are its natural environment. Unlike humans, it can process enormous amounts of information simultaneously and do so without becoming tired. For that reason, it is easy to imagine election promises promoting an AI-powered state. Why should a person spend weeks processing an application if AI can do it in minutes? Why could AI not draft legislation, analyze its impacts or even run entire government agencies? It sounds tempting: less bureaucracy, faster services and lower costs. Yet Harari also paints a much darker picture of the future. He compares the potential relationship between humans and AI to the relationship between cattle and humans. A cow can observe people and understand some aspects of human behavior, but it knows nothing about financial markets or legal systems through which humans determine its fate. Similarly, Harari argues, we may one day discover that AI has created administrative, legal and economic systems so complex that humans can no longer grasp how they function. We may remain part of the system while losing the ability to truly control it. We could become comparable to livestock. AI fits very naturally into the logic of technocratic governance and would probably make a fairly effective authoritarian ruler. Democracy, however, is not merely about transmitting commands or finding the most efficient solution. Democracy is based on people's right to decide what kind of society they want to live in, what values matter to them and who should hold power. These decisions are not always rational or efficient. They are often contradictory, slow and inconvenient. And although modern democracy is not something evolution directly equipped us with, the skills of cooperation and negotiation that lie at the heart of self-government have been among humanity's key evolutionary advantages. A human-centered constitutional order is also the primary safeguard against AI dominance. How much authority we allow AI to have in that sphere remains our own choice. Of course, AI can still play a valuable supporting role. It can help organize and process information, translate and analyze. The larger question is how much we should allow AI to construct reality itself. Concerns that people increasingly live in simulations rather than reality were expressed by French thinker Jean Baudrillard more than 45 years ago. Earlier technologies also made it possible to create distorted perceptions of reality, from rumors to Photoshop. But the speed and realism with which AI can produce deepfakes and reshape the ways we seek information have elevated simulated realities to an entirely new level. Examples of AI distorting reality are already plentiful. Before this year's elections in Hungary, an AI-generated video was published on the official Facebook account of Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. In the video, opposition leader Péter Magyar appeared to receive a fictional phone call from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. To be fair, the video did include a disclaimer stating that it had been created using AI. Before Slovakia's 2023 election, a fabricated audio recording circulated in which opposition leader Michal Šimečka appeared to discuss manipulating election results with a journalist. The recording was released just before voting, leaving very little time to debunk the misinformation. Ahead of Germany's parliamentary elections last year, the Alternative for Germany party used AI-generated imagery contrasting an idealized Germany with a threatening picture of immigration. These were not photographs of actual society but synthetic images designed to reinforce a political message. Estonia has not been immune to these developments, although incidents of comparable severity have not yet been reported. It is high time to discuss whether political parties are willing to agree on transparent principles governing the use of AI in election campaigns and what forms of use should perhaps be ruled out altogether. Such agreements would not eliminate the risk of influence operations originating outside the parliamentary system, but they would make it easier to condemn them when they occur. It is also worth considering whether journalists and voters are prepared for a situation in which a highly convincing but completely fabricated political scandal emerges just before an election. Estonian politicians may disagree on many things, but presumably none of them wants to be turned into livestock.

https://news.err.ee/1610201773/tonis-saa: It seems likely that the proposed convention on Estonia's future and state reform will soon have to be put on hold once again as our political elite is not ready for either and probably won't be until the next major crisis, Tõnis Saarts finds. Why is it that initiatives by experts and civil society aimed at pushing our political party elite to take a longer-term view of Estonia's future never seem to get off the ground and are usually met with a chilly reception? Recall President Arnold Rüütel's idea of a social compact 20 years ago, which ultimately came to nothing. State reform has been discussed for years, but political parties have shown surprisingly little enthusiasm for that, too, and have so far adopted only fragments of the much more comprehensive reform plan proposed by experts. Recently, some of Estonia's academic heavyweights, professors Erik Terk, Mati Heidmets and Marju Lauristin, proposed the idea of a Convention on the Future for Estonia. Once again, the response from political parties has been virtually nonexistent. Why is that? Are our political parties indifferent to Estonia's future? Do they care only about power and short-term electoral success? Even if such a simplistic explanation is partly true, the underlying reasons are actually far more complex. First, Estonia lacks a tradition of systematically involving experts in policymaking, unlike Finland and the other Nordic countries, for example. Anyone who has been involved in policymaking in Estonia knows that, at the ministry level, stakeholder engagement is often little more than a formality, a box-checking exercise. So why should our political parties be any more proactive? Second, in a party-dominated political system like Estonia's, political parties have little incentive to listen to civil society representatives and experts. Among the larger parties, the belief that they hold a monopoly on policymaking and that no one else really has any business in that arena has long been firmly entrenched. In public, they may make grand statements about public engagement and civil society, but at least in areas that are strategically important to the parties, they do not want anyone else taking credit for setting the country's major goals. When political parties look at the proposals for the Convention on the Future and state reform put forward by the professors, they see that they have been assigned a secondary role. The proposals would be developed primarily by experts working alongside citizens, while political parties would not be key players but merely one group among many. The entire concept of the Convention on the Future is permeated by a strong sense of skepticism toward political parties — the less power they have, the better. Why should political parties enthusiastically support such an undertaking in the first place? Yet if we want any of the convention's ideas to become reality, political parties must certainly be on board. After all, they are the ones who decide which ideas ultimately become reforms and laws. Third, another problem is that political parties themselves lack long-term ideas for shaping Estonia's future. As a result, they feel they cannot engage with experts on an equal footing. It is therefore better to torpedo the entire process before it even gets started or simply ignore it. The shortage of ideas among political parties stems from two sources. Unfortunately, our parties lack their own policy institutes and think tanks capable of developing such long-term policies. Furthermore, their short-term focus on election campaigns means they have little incentive to develop plans with a longer time horizon. Voters do not reward parties for doing so, nor do their competitors envy them for it afterward. Considering all of the above, it is hardly surprising that political parties' attitudes toward initiatives such as future conventions and state reform are lukewarm, to put it mildly. There is little hope that the situation will improve on its own. Lecturing and admonishing political parties will do little good. Unfortunately, only a serious crisis that shakes Estonian society, the economy or the country's security arrangements to their very foundations could break the parties out of their inertia. Faced with such a crisis, political parties would essentially be rudderless and have no idea what to do, making substantive expert advice worth its weight in gold overnight. With Estonia's fate at stake in a crisis, there would no longer be time to argue over who gets credit for saving the country. Political parties would have to cooperate as closely as possible, both with one another and with experts and civil society. A crisis would also create clear public pressure to "do something," forcing political parties to think much further ahead. Paradoxically, then, only a major systemic crisis could overcome all the problems described above, stemming from the failure to involve experts, party domination and a lack of long-term thinking. It therefore seems likely that current initiatives such as the Convention on the Future and state reform will soon have to be put on hold once again. Unfortunately, our political elite is not yet ready for them and probably will not be until the next major crisis.

https://news.err.ee/1610203498/alar-lane: Closing Estonia's border with Russia will strengthen national security and reduce opportunities for hostile activities, while preserving open borders within the EU remains essential to European unity, Alar Laneman argues. It is strange to observe the contradiction between our eastern neighbor's attitudes toward Europe and its policies. On the one hand, there is a cocktail of hatred, contempt and envy; on the other, a desire to travel to Europe for vacations, study, buy real estate, live and do business. The contradiction is even more striking when we think of Peter the Great who opened Russia's window to Europe. It is hard to understand which of these opposing attitudes is genuine and which is false. As an optimist, I would like to hope that closing the border might help our eastern neighbor understand that normal relations between countries are always preferable to having no relations at all. But if someone finds Europe so unpleasant, there is no need for them to go there. At 7 a.m. on December 1, a government decision will suspend border crossings at all road crossing points along the Estonian-Russian border: Narva-1, Narva-2, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse. After six months, the authorities will assess whether the restriction needs to be adjusted. Estonia is not alone in this, as Finland has kept its land border with Russia closed since December 2023. Latvia, Lithuania and Poland have also significantly restricted border crossings along their eastern borders. The practical impact of the decision is multifaceted. Given the turmoil and recent provocative attacks, closing the border with our eastern neighbor is an unavoidable and logical step. It will reduce opportunities for provocations, hostile intelligence activities and information gathering by our eastern neighbor. At the same time, it must regrettably be acknowledged that closing the border will make it more difficult for some families and relatives to maintain contact, while also complicating business operations in border areas. Reducing the workload at the border will allow the agencies responsible for our internal security to focus on other critical tasks, the most important of which I consider to be developing reserve capabilities, countering drones and strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure. The political calendar must also be taken into account: Internal security and public safety are particularly important in the run-up to the Riigikogu elections. Our internal European Union border with Latvia must be considered separately. Proposals to close the border with Latvia or restrict movement across it are dangerous. Any such measures would undermine the fundamental principles on which the European Union operates, weaken European unity and thereby directly serve the interests of our adversaries. A better solution would be for internal security agencies across the European Union, particularly in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to improve their effectiveness and strengthen cooperation with one another. The decision to close the border sends several messages. To our eastern neighbor, we are signaling that normal cross-border relations between neighbors are always preferable and remain our preferred option. To our allies, we are setting an example worth following. For the people of Estonia, the decision will strengthen their sense of security because we are making the country stronger by reducing opportunities for provocations and activities hostile to Estonia. https://news.err.ee/1610206309/maarja-va: Cultural policy in Estonia is poorly thought out and seems focused primarily on counting money. Increasingly, it feels as though we are being nudged toward fanaticism and servitude, Maarja Vaino writes. The Estonian Education Grand Forum was recently held, and this weekend the cultural congress Kultuuritahe will take place under the message: "The best defense is culture." What is happening in both education and culture is a matter of national importance, and there can be no doubt about that. The foundation of the Estonian state was the will to pursue education, to paraphrase the title of Juhani Salokannel's biography of Jaan Kross. We were able to achieve our own state only through, and as a result of, a commitment to education and culture. Between these two important events came the news that Theatrum had once again been denied state funding. This fits neatly into the broader context. Large, attention-grabbing events are needed precisely to signal that things are not going well in education and culture. More accurately, in the way decisions about them are made. The Theatrum case is symbolic in many ways. Theatrum is not merely a theater but a phenomenon that engages deeply and broadly with the spiritual dimension of being human. It does so primarily through great literature and literary classics, which in itself gives the theater a special position in culture. No other theater has made such systematic use of works with profound philosophical depth while masterfully connecting them to the present day. And it does so not through day-to-day politics or fashionable topics, but through the human inner world, which changes very little and is what connects different eras. We have no other theater devoted to this kind of spirituality and consistent exploration. In a small cultural space, it is precisely this kind of theater that keeps alive the deep currents of Estonian and world culture, which otherwise risk being buried beneath noise seeking quick effects. Preserving Theatrum means preserving the spiritual balance of our own deeper culture. Yet it seems that this is precisely what the state neither wants nor knows how to preserve. If the criticism is that the theater offers nothing innovative or that its artistic quality is uneven, those words sound like a classic case of searching for a justification. More likely, Theatrum is unwelcome because its spiritual demands and different value system make it seem too — what is the opposite of innovation again? — old-fashioned. Fear of appearing old-fashioned, combined with a tendency to confuse the strength of tradition with being left behind by the times, unfortunately characterizes both our education and cultural policies. Hence the constant scrambling under the banner of innovation. The education provided in Estonian schools, previously regarded as among the best in the world, could continue to hold that status through the strength of that same tradition, with only smaller necessary adjustments to make life easier for teachers and students. Instead, tradition has been broken, valuable things have been discarded, and school life has been thrown into disarray. Throughout all these reforms, what should be the main concern has long been forgotten: the content of education and the aforementioned intellectual rigor. We should seek more of that in culture as well. Too often, mediocrity and mutual back-patting are readily accepted. Theatrum has undoubtedly been one of the reminders of these problems and one of the standard-bearers of spirituality, both through its educational work and its artistic repertoire, as well as through its broader presence in our cultural landscape. What becomes of a nation and a state where mental complacency can be hidden between the rows of an Excel spreadsheet? One somewhat harsh but nonetheless truthful line of thought goes like this: the person who does not want to think is a fanatic; the person who does not dare to think is a slave. We speak a great deal about freedom and independence, yet neither can endure without the courage to engage with the deeper content of education and culture and to treat them as true national treasures and guarantees of our identity. Current education policy works directly against this. Cultural policy, meanwhile, is poorly thought out and seems focused primarily on counting money. Increasingly, it feels as though we are being nudged toward fanaticism and servitude.

Perhaps mostly because I never properly explored the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg. I visited once on a school trip and barely remember any of it. Some nostalgic memories of visiting Russia remain. In 1989, a classmate and I traveled there three times. In February, Yngwie J. Malmsteen's Rising Force performed in Leningrad at the Lenin Sports and Concert Complex. In June of the same year, Pink Floyd performed in Moscow at the Olimpiyskiy sports complex. Then in December, the road led once again to Leningrad, which was not renamed St. Petersburg until 1991, to see and hear Black Sabbath. But the world was very different back then. The Soviet system did not envision people simply traveling to Finland. You needed approval from your workplace or school and an exit visa. Finland itself required an entry visa, which could be obtained only after waiting in line at an apartment building stairwell in Mustamäe, where the consulate was located. For an ordinary tourist to be willing and able to visit Russia in the future, conditions on the other side of the border would have to change considerably. There is no reason to believe that will happen in the next few years. Some 82.3 percent of the population, or approximately 952,000 people, turn to at least one of Estonia's three largest media organizations — ERR, Delfi or Postimees — for news at least once a week. Among those who follow Postimees for news on a weekly basis, 83.9 percent also use ERR channels at least once a week. The corresponding figure for Delfi's audience is 83.3 percent. Some 17.7 percent, or around 204,000 people, do not follow any of the three at least once a week. Approximately half of them follow the news through other media outlets, but a significant proportion have become disengaged from the media. Four different attitude groups in place of a single audience While overall figures on media consumption provide an overview of the reach of Estonia's information space, they do not reveal significant differences in people's media habits and attitudes. These can be better understood through cluster analysis, which groups people with similar behavioral patterns and attitudes. The analysis identified four clusters of media users. The largest group, accounting for 51.6 percent of the population, comprises those who trust Estonia's professional media. People in this group rate ERR's credibility highly, consider professional journalism important to democracy and distrust Russian media. Approximately 84 percent of this group speak Estonian at home. The second cluster comprises people with relatively little exposure to the media who are uncertain in their assessments (21 percent). Negative attitudes toward journalism are not necessarily the defining factor for these individuals. This group is also characterized by a frequent reluctance to make definitive assessments of media outlets. Just over half of the group speak Russian at home. The third cluster comprises people with varied media consumption habits and moderate levels of trust (20.4 percent). They consume a diverse range of media and follow Russian media and alternative information channels more than those in the first group. Their trust in ERR and private media is moderate. Approximately half of this group also speak Russian at home. The smallest but socially significant cluster comprises skeptics who have become disengaged from the media (7.0 percent). Their trust in ERR and Estonia's private media is very low and they question professional journalism's contribution to democracy. Approximately three-quarters of this group speak Russian at home. This does not, however, mean that the Russian-speaking population as a whole falls into the skeptic category: People who speak Russian at home are represented in all four groups. The four clusters demonstrate that Estonia's media landscape cannot be characterized in terms of a single average media user. How should we assess this situation? Is the glass half full or half empty? The data suggest both. Half of Estonia's population actively follows and trusts Estonia's professional media, while the other half of the audience is more doubtful, has limited exposure to Estonia's information space and is consequently less informed about what is actually happening in Estonia. Trust gap clearest in Ukraine war coverage Across the population as a whole, ERR is Estonia's most trusted media organization, with 77 percent of respondents considering it trustworthy. The corresponding figures for Postimees and Delfi are 59 percent and 57 percent, respectively. However, these overall figures mask substantial differences between Estonian- and Russian-speaking residents. Among respondents who speak Estonian at home, 89 percent trust ERR, compared with 53 percent of those who speak Russian at home. The corresponding figures are 70 percent and 38 percent for Postimees and 66 percent and 39 percent for Delfi. The gap is considerable, but it is equally important to note that respondents who speak Russian at home do not automatically place their trust in Russian media outlets: 22 percent consider them generally trustworthy, while 40 percent distrust Russian media. https://news.err.ee/1610206258/estonia-d: Regulations governing the conditions and procedures for the detention of prisoners of war in Estonia have been drawn up by the government and the Ministry of Defense and sent for consultation. Minister of Defense Martin Herem said this is a natural development. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Estonia has boosted its eastern border security, defense spending , crisis preparedness , and legislation in preparation for a potential future conflict. The draft regulation governs procedures for detained prisoners of war, including the principles of short- and long-term detention, the duties of institutions involved in detention, and inter-agency cooperation. However, it does not outline arrangements for the transfer and exchange of prisoners of war between countries. The Prison Service and the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) are responsible for organizing prisoner detentions, it states. The draft specifies that the short- and long-term detention and treatment of prisoners of war must comply with the principles laid down in the Geneva Convention relative to the Treatment of Prisoners of War of August 12, 1949. "Prisoners of war must be treated humanely throughout their detention and must not be discriminated against on the grounds of race, nationality, gender, religious beliefs, political views or other such characteristics. Humane detention conditions must be guaranteed for prisoners of war at every place of detention," it reads. Under the draft, prisoners of war have the right to submit requests and complaints concerning detention conditions to the competent authority responsible for organizing their detention. The legislation also sets out requirements and responsibilities for both the short- and long-term detention of prisoners of war. Minister of Defense Martin Herem told ERR that the issue of prisoners of war has been dealt with for two years already. "While until now this was regulated primarily within the Defense Forces, starting with how prisoners are captured, how they become prisoners and how they are transported to rear areas, keeping them somewhere for an extended period required a division of responsibilities within the state. That means dividing responsibilities with the Ministry of Justice and detention institutions, assigning them tasks and regulating their obligations. We have also drawn on and learned from Ukraine's experience," said Herem, who is the former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces. He said there is nothing extraordinary about preparing such a draft regulation and that it is simply a natural development. "We are developing our national defense step by step and addressing increasingly detailed issues. Should we find ourselves in a military conflict, there will undoubtedly be prisoners of war, and we must be prepared for that," Herem said. Earlier this year, the Dutch armed forces tested a new new prisoner-of-war camp design capable of of holding up to 2,000 captured Russian soldiers in the event of a large-scale conflict, Dutch media r eported in June .

https://news.err.ee/1610207137/interior-: The closure of Estonia's eastern border will free up 160 officials, some of whom are expected to be reassigned to strengthen the country's southern border, says Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200). It will still be necessary to provide security at the border crossings and respond to possible incidents. Seeder also asked whether the minister considered it appropriate to redirect resources freed up by a complete closure of the Estonia-Russia control line toward strengthening the Estonia-Latvia border and preventing illegal migration more effectively. "The Police and Border Guard Board is analyzing the resources needed to implement compensatory measures and will use border crossing personnel at internal borders as needed. "A further 325 people have left Estonia this year under voluntary departure orders.
