https://news.err.ee/1610206810/estonia-e: Estonia's Internal Security Service (KAPO) deported a Russian national working at the state-owned Enefit oil plant on Wednesday over suspected intelligence ties. Authorities revoked Anton Zuev's residence permit and imposed on him a 10-year Schengen entry ban, citing national security risks linked to contacts with Russian special services. Enefit's Auvere oil shale comple in Ida-Viru County is just a little over a mile (2 kilometers) from the Russian border, but forms a critical pillar of Estonia's energy security . KAPO stated that Zuev had been deported to prevent and preempt a security threat under Estonia's Aliens Act. KAPO communications director Marta Tuul said: "Zuev was sent back to his home country. He was a citizen of the Russian Federation whose family lives in Russia. Zuev worked periodically in Estonia at the Enefit oil plant." The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) confirmed it had annulled Zuev's Estonian residence permit at KAPO's recommendation, on security grounds. "We expelled him from the country and imposed a 10-year Schengen entry ban on him," the PPA announced Zuev is the fourth Russian citizen KAPO has publicly named in deportation announcements this year ,aimed at countering security threats and hostile intelligence operations. On February 12, authorities expelled Andrei Zhuravlyov on suspicion of planning anti-Estonian activities and gathering intelligence on Russia's behalf. On March 18, Kirill Kudryavtsev had his residence permit revoked and was deported due to his contacts with Russian special services. Estonia had in any case tightened border enforcement and residency vetting since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and following two recent sabotage attacks on Estonian defense industry firms, from next Tuesday, December 1, the border with Russia will be fully closed, the government announced last week. In March this year a chimney at the Auvere power station was damaged after being hit by a stray Ukrainian drone at a time when Ukraine was hitting Russian oil facilities at Ust-Luga.
https://www.lrt.lt/en/news-in-english/19: As Lithuania steps up preparations for potential aerial threats, a new civic initiative is encouraging residents to turn unused Android smartphones into acoustic drone detectors that could help identify low-flying aircraft. The project, called Drone Radar, aims to supplement existing warning systems by creating a network of sensors capable of detecting the sound of approaching drones. Project creator Audrius Zujus said early warning systems alone are not enough and should be complemented by additional tools that can identify threats more quickly. “We allow people to connect old, unused Android phones and, for the first time in the world, create an acoustic radar of this kind,” Zujus said. “The device detects drones by listening for the buzzing sound they produce.” Acoustic sensors are already widely used in Ukraine. They record sounds, which specialised software compares with a database of known audio signatures to determine whether they match drones or other flying objects. Such sensors have already been deployed along Lithuania’s border, and the Defence Ministry is considering expanding the network. Acting Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said acoustic detection systems could complement existing airspace surveillance capabilities but noted that procuring new equipment through official channels takes time. “The procurement process is complicated,” he said. Zujus said citizen-led initiatives can help bridge that gap by providing institutions with additional sources of information. “We are not trying to replace state institutions,” he said. “We are creating a tool they could use when making decisions and receiving additional warnings. But introducing such tools usually takes years, and we see that we may not have that much time.” The initiative comes as Lithuania has recorded an increase in security incidents and air raid alerts in recent months, prompting authorities to place greater emphasis on public preparedness for emergencies. Civil protection training sessions are being held more frequently to teach residents how to recognise potential threats, locate the nearest shelters and assemble emergency evacuation kits. The Lithuanian Red Cross says public interest in such training has grown, with many participants acknowledging they had postponed preparing for emergencies. “I’ve started thinking about how to prepare an emergency bag,” teacher Rasa Bruzgelevičienė said. “I’ve been hearing about it for quite a while, and it feels like I haven’t done enough.” Authorities continue to urge residents to take responsibility for their own preparedness by knowing the location of nearby shelters, following official alerts and maintaining enough essential supplies to be self-sufficient for at least several days.

A series of bomb threats sent by email prompted evacuations at several sites in Vilnius and Kaunas on Friday before police determined the warnings were false. The threats targeted high-tech group Teltonika, an office building and emergency medical services facilities in the two cities. Police said the emails threatened explosions at the locations. At about 11:00, officers received a report of a possible bomb threat at Teltonika’s premises, prompting the evacuation of employees while officers searched the buildings. Similar threatening emails were sent to emergency medical services and another office building. Police said no explosives were found during the searches and that no actual danger was identified. Authorities are collecting evidence to open a pretrial investigation on suspicion of making a false report about a public danger or disaster under Lithuania’s Criminal Code.

The first troops from Germany’s brigade assigned to Lithuania will move into the Rūdninkai military campus this autumn, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Friday as construction officially began on the project’s second phase. Kaunas said work on the first phase of the military base is running ahead of schedule and is expected to be completed 10 months earlier than originally planned. “I want to thank our contractors,” Kaunas said during a ceremony at the construction site. “The first phase will be completed 10 months ahead of schedule, and the first soldiers will move here this autumn. I also thank the contractors responsible for the second phase for a smooth start. I hope we will continue moving forward in the same way.” He said Lithuania has the expertise, resources and sense of urgency needed to complete the project. “This demonstrates our strong commitment to national security and to our German allies,” Kaunas said. “Our common goal is to have all priority infrastructure for the German brigade in Lithuania ready by the end of next year.” The minister said the project was inspired by landmark construction achievements such as New York’s Empire State Building and the Pentagon in the United States. “But we will show that we can do even better. That is our ambition,” he said. Construction of the second phase of the Rūdninkai military campus, valued at about 1.3 billion euros, officially began Friday. The development is being carried out through a public-private partnership and has been divided into three sections. The second phase includes barracks, vehicle garages, maintenance workshops, dining facilities, warehouses, headquarters buildings, fuel stations and parade grounds. Military training facilities will also be built, with some equipped with advanced simulation systems. The 190-hectare Rūdninkai military campus is a key part of Lithuania's preparations to host a permanent German brigade by the end of 2027 as NATO reinforces its eastern flank following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Jan Stoess, state secretary at the German Ministry of Defence, noted that there are already 2,000 German brigade troops and civilian personnel in Lithuania, and that number is expected to reach 5,000 next year. “I believe we are on schedule. [...] There are certain specialists we still need to work on, but we are optimistic that we will reach our goal next year,” said Stoess. His remarks came in response to a question about soldiers’ willingness to serve in Lithuania. German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said during a visit back in June that there are not enough volunteers to join the Lithuania brigade and some will have to be ordered to come. The Germans are satisfied with the infrastructure being built in Rūdninkai, Stoess said: “We just toured the new buildings, and everyone was impressed by the high standards. I believe this will undoubtedly be a success story.” He emphasised that Germany’s commitment to permanently deploy a brigade in Lithuania is firm, and that the soldiers feel welcome. “Germany and Lithuania stand shoulder to shoulder. We can rely on one another, and this military town is powerful proof of that,” said Stoess. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, who attended the ceremony, promised to “personally oversee” the Rūdninkai military campus project. He also confirmed that during a phone call on Thursday, he had invited German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to visit Lithuania.

Archaeologists have begun exhuming the remains of Red Army soldiers buried in the centre of the Lithuanian town of Vievis as part of the country’s efforts to remove Soviet-era memorial sites from public spaces. The burial site is located near St Anne’s Church in Vievis, in Elektrėnai municipality, where a Soviet monument and an eternal flame previously stood. Historical records indicate that 111 Soviet soldiers are buried at the site, although archaeologists said the exact number will be determined during the excavation. The exhumation follows a decision by Lithuania’s so-called Desovietisation Commission – set up under 2023 legislation – which concluded that the memorial violated a law banning the promotion of “totalitarian and authoritarian regimes” in public spaces. The commission said the site promoted the Soviet and modern Russian narrative of the “Great Patriotic War”. It also concluded that the graves were secondary burials because the remains had been relocated from original burial sites in surrounding areas after World War Two. In December 2024, Arūnas Bubnys, director of the Genocide and Resistance Research Centre of Lithuania, said the burial site should be removed in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and their protocols governing the protection of victims of armed conflicts. Elektrėnai municipality said the state has allocated about 130,000 euros for the project. After exhumation, the remains will undergo anthropological examination before being reburied in a cemetery. Earlier this year, Lithuania carried out a similar exhumation of World War Two soldiers’ remains from the centre of the northern town of Šiauliai. Both projects have prompted protests from Russia’s Foreign Ministry. Lithuania’s law banning public symbols that promote totalitarian and authoritarian regimes took effect in May 2023. Under the legislation, monuments and other public objects deemed to glorify such regimes must be removed.

In May, Lithuania declared its first-ever air-raid alert after drones entered the country's airspace, instructing residents to head to their nearest shelter. In the aftermath, it emerged that some shelters were inaccessible when needed - and, perhaps more troublingly, that many people had no idea where to go in the first place. Just over a fifth of Lithuanians know where their nearest air-raid shelter is located, according to a new survey - a gap the country's new interior minister says needs addressing, though he argues residents themselves also bear responsibility for finding out. The findings come from a representative survey conducted by Baltijos tyrimai, a Lithuanian-British market and public opinion research company, between June 19 and 30, 2026. It surveyed 1,010 Lithuanian residents aged 18 and over across 108 locations, with a margin of error of no more than 3.1 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. The poll was carried out via face-to-face interviews in respondents' homes. Only around 22% of those surveyed said they know exactly where to find the shelter nearest their home, in the event of an air-raid alert or other emergency. Four in ten said they thought they knew, but weren't certain. A further 31% said they had no idea where their nearest shelter was - and had never looked into it. Men were more likely than women to know exactly where their nearest shelter was; women were more likely to say they weren't sure, or didn't know at all. By age group, those aged 30-49 were most likely to know the exact location of their nearest shelter, while people over 65 had the weakest awareness. Location made relatively little difference: in rural areas, towns and larger cities alike, more people were unsure or unaware of where to shelter than knew for certain. Exact awareness stood at 21.2% in rural areas, 18.3% in towns, and 24.3% in major cities. Asked about the findings, the new interior minister, Martynas Katelynas, told LRT.lt that Lithuania's shelter system - and the information available about it - is not yet working as it should. The goal, he said, is for every person to know exactly where the shelter nearest their home or workplace is located. "It's clearly complicated - as we saw during the last air-raid alert, when a red-level alert was issued in Vilnius district, people didn't know how to react. Schools also responded inconsistently: some took children to shelters, others took them outside. Some businesses didn't stop work at all," the minister said. He said a common national response standard is needed, but stressed that responsibility does not rest with the interior ministry alone. "This is a shared matter for municipalities, non-governmental organisations, businesses and residents themselves. Let's agree that every resident's safety is, first and foremost, their own priority. People themselves should make more of an effort to find out this information and make decisions for themselves," Katelynas said. Asked what steps are planned to improve public awareness of shelter locations, the minister pointed to public information campaigns on civil defence more broadly. "Civil defence as a topic only really emerged in Lithuania three or four years ago [...] the term likely gained traction after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when we saw that this was genuinely necessary. We learned lessons from Ukraine, and only then did the subject become relevant enough that these questions are still being raised today," Katelynas explained. He said municipalities should be encouraged to share information with residents, and that the interior ministry itself should also run awareness campaigns. "But people themselves also need to understand that this is their concern too. It can be done proactively - there's LT72.lt, there are NGO websites, there are plenty of ideas out there, it's all been prepared, laid out clearly - people just need to make use of it," he said. "Expecting a minister or the government to show up, tell everyone what to do, and have everyone simply follow along - I really don't think that's realistic. We should recognise that residents' own responsibility is not the least important part of this," the interior minister emphasised. Audrius Klišonis, president of the Association of Local Authorities in Lithuania (LSA), told LRT.lt that additional funding is currently available for setting up shelters, and that some municipalities are on so-called "yellow" or "red" priority lists, based on the number of residents their shelters could accommodate. "I think this is one of the key issues. Whether a specific person knows their designated shelter - we have doubts about that, because people are mobile. The whole network needs to be publicised more," said Klišonis, who is also the mayor of Plungė. "Besides, shelter signage is placed on the buildings themselves, and those buildings are often set back from the street, further away. We should be talking about wider signage, so that people - both those living nearby and those simply passing by - would know where to go," he said. Klišonis himself was in Vilnius during the recent air-raid alert, and admitted he only found his way to a shelter by following the crowd around him - not because he knew in advance that it was the designated shelter for the area. He said another recurring problem is that residents are often reluctant to let outsiders into the basements or garages of their own apartment blocks during an alert, meaning that even knowing where a shelter is doesn't guarantee access to it. "People say: this is our building's basement, our shelter, and we won't let others in. We want that attitude to change, because you're not going to drive several kilometres to reach a shelter. We need to work with residents on this," he said. He also noted a bureaucratic hurdle: it was only after the recent drone incidents that the interior ministry approved the inclusion of so-called electronic door locks in shelter procurement list

Lithuania will officially launch construction of the second phase of the Rūdninkai military campus on Friday, advancing a 1.3 billion euro project that will host Germany’s planned permanent brigade deployment in the Baltic country. The second phase of the development, located in the Šalčininkai district near Lithuania’s border with Belarus, is being carried out under public-private partnership agreements. A consortium operating under the name Rudina, managed by Conres, INVL Asset Management and Fegda, was awarded one section of the project in January. Estonian-owned construction company Merko Statyba secured contracts for the remaining two sections. Under 15-year public-private partnership agreements covering construction and maintenance, Rudina will receive 487.61 million euros, including value-added tax, while Merko Statyba will receive 393.25 million euros and 453.5 million euros for its two contracts. Payments will begin after construction is completed. The contracts entered into force in recent weeks. Rudina has secured 200.75 million euros in financing from the European Investment Bank and Swedbank. Merko Statyba has obtained 369 million euros in loans from the European Investment Bank, SEB and Swedbank. Earlier this month, Merko Statyba announced it had transferred a 70% stake in two project companies established for the development to Dutch investment company ELL Real Estate Holding. According to Lithuania’s Ministry of Defence, the second phase will include barracks, vehicle garages, maintenance workshops, dining facilities, warehouses, headquarters buildings, fuel stations and parade grounds. The project also includes military training facilities, some of which will be equipped with advanced simulation systems. The Rūdninkai military campus will cover about 190 hectares and is a key part of Lithuania’s preparations to host a German brigade on a permanent basis by the end of 2027, as NATO strengthens its eastern flank following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Russia is allegedly planning something disruptive in the Baltic states or Poland, though stopping short of full-scale aggression, the Lithuanian president confirmed on Wednesday. We’ve heard similar reports for a while, so here’s the chain of events that will help you straighten out the timeline. Lithuania first announced it was upping security at critical energy infrastructure sites on June 18. Then, the Daily Telegraph reported on July 3 about possible provocations against a Baltic country or Poland to test NATO resolve, citing intelligence sources in Warsaw and one of the three Baltic countries. Then, in an interview published by BNS on Wednesday, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda confirmed there is intelligence on the possibility of attacks. On Thursday, he elaborated during a press conference with his visiting Latvian counterpart, Edgars Rinkēvičs. “I cannot say that we have only just started receiving this kind of intelligence. We have been receiving it over the past two or three months,” said Nausėda. For his part, Rinkēvičs also pointed to Russia’s past assassinations of political dissidents. Naming a series of other attacks, Rinkevičs added: “If we are backed into a corner, we will have to respond as an alliance.” Nausėda concurred: “This planning is taking place at the highest level, effectively in Moscow, and we know that it has not stopped for even a minute.” Recall, Lithuania recently foiled a Russian assassination plot , which would have targeted a pro-Ukraine activist and a Russian opposition figure. In any case, Russia lacks the means to mount anything significant. But analysts have long pointed at something like drone attacks with plausible deniability that would have a “cascading effect”, as Nausėda put it. Think Lithuania–Poland energy link, for example, which is one of the installations where authorities have upped security. The sources quoted by the Daily Telegraph went further, saying there could also be an armed incursion into the so-called Suwalki Gap that links the Baltics with Poland and is flanked on either side by Russia’s Kaliningrad and Belarus. A similar scenario was played out in public wargaming scenarios in the past. They were almost unanimously criticised in the Baltics ( including by myself) for completely ignoring the local military forces and focusing solely on the political paralysis that may – or may not – occur in Brussels or Washington. Moscow, of course, denies all allegations. In other defence-related news, Lithuania has approved a state-level evacuation plan, which foresees around 75 percent of the population leaving in case of a disaster without centralised support. Lithuania's new interior minister has defended giving border guards the right to use firearms against irregular migrants, arguing that officers cannot be expected to protect the country's border without the means to protect themselves, and the state, if the situation demands it. Martynas Katelynas took over as interior minister this week in the newly formed government of Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius. He has previously spoken about the use of lethal force to stop illegal border crossings – remarks he says have been taken out of context. He stressed that he was referring only to exceptional cases where there is a direct threat to the life of border guards, other people, or state security. "If we're asking officers to defend the state, we need to give them the means to do that, and to protect their own lives if necessary. During the migrant crisis, some of those crossing may have been economic migrants - but who can say that among them, during a hybrid attack, there couldn't also be so-called 'little green men'?" he said, using a term that refers to unmarked Russian military personnel, that suddenly appeared during the 2014 annexation of Crimea in Ukraine. "If we want our state border to be secure, we need to give border guards the ability to do that," he added, referencing the use of firearms. He added that officers also need to feel they have political backing. "If an officer finds themselves in a situation where there is a threat to someone else's life or their own, they have the right to use those means. If we expect an officer to do their duty, we have to trust them. If there is abuse, that's for the responsible institutions to assess. But politically, I trust our officers," he said. That question of trust in officers is one Katelynas has faced criticism over before. During the 2021 migrant crisis, he compared Lithuanian officers to OMON, Belarus's much-feared riot police, associated with the violent suppression of pro-democracy protests in Minsk – a remark he has now moved to explain, if not entirely walk back. That year, Lithuania, along with Poland and Latvia, faced a sharp surge in migrants crossing from Belarus, in what the EU described as a state-orchestrated attempt by Minsk to pressure the bloc over sanctions imposed following a crackdown on Belarusian opposition protests. Thousands of migrants, many from the Middle East and Africa, attempted to cross into Lithuania that year, prompting the government to declare a state of emergency and reinforce its border. As part of the response, Lithuanian authorities relocated some migrants to a site near the Rūdninkai military training ground, a decision that triggered protests from local residents who had not been consulted or informed in advance. Police and Lithuania's Public Security Service (a gendarmerie-style force used for public order operations) were deployed to disperse the demonstrations. It was this operation that prompted Katelynas's comparison to OMON at the time. Asked about those earlier remarks, Katelynas said his criticism had apparently never been directed at the rank-and-file officers who dispersed the protest, but at the decisions taken by the interior ministry's leadership at the time. "The situation reached a point where the use of force became unavoidable, and the officers were carrying out an order they had been given. My criticism was aimed at the decisions taken by the ministry's leadership, because in my view, that crisis was mishandled," he said. According to Katelynas, the ministry's biggest failure was not the dispersal of the protest itself, but how the crisis was managed and communicated to the public beforehand. "People should have been spoken to first, and it should have been explained why certain decisions were being made. That didn't happen – residents simply found out that migrants were going to be moved into their community. It's natural that this triggered a reaction, and eventually the Public Security Service had to step in. The officers weren't to blame for that - they were carrying out an order," he said. Migration via Latvia, and possible border controls Asked about a recent rise in secondary migration - migrants entering the EU elsewhere and then moving on through Latvia towards or through Lithuania - Katelynas did not rule out introducing additional controls on the Lithuania-Latvia border if current measures prove insufficient. "At the moment, Lithuania is already helping Latvia deal with illegal migration - we've sent border guards to assist. Let's hope that's enough, but if it isn't, we will certainly need to consider various measures. We cannot become a transit country that anyone can pass through, with a porous border," he said. 'We should learn from other countries' mistakes, not our own' On migration policy more broadly, Katelynas said the priority was to balance economic needs with national security interests. "Migration has to be a tool for Lithuania's prosperity, but without creating threats to national security," he said. He added that highly skilled specialists should not face unnecessary obstacles, but that foreigners planning to stay in Lithuania long-term should integrate into Lithuanian society. "If someone comes to our country and benefits from the security and opportunities it offers, they should respect our rules, culture and traditions. If you're planning to live here for a longer period, learning Lithuanian shouldn't be a problem," he said. He described labour migration as, in principle, a temporary solution to specific labour market shortages. "We need to clearly identify what we're short of, how many workers we need, and which countries we're looking to for them. In my view, we should focus on countries that are culturally closer to us. We can see that France and Germany are facing serious problems as a result of poor decisions made in the past. We should learn from other countries' mistakes, rather than making our own," he said. Latvia will donate SENTINEL radars to Lithuania to strengthen the country’s NASAMS medium-range air defence systems, Lithuania’s Defence Ministry said Thursday. The ministry said Latvia had decided to transfer the radars free of charge after a proposal from the United States. According to the ministry, Latvia uses alternative systems to meet its air defence needs. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas thanked Latvia and the United States for their cooperation in strengthening regional security. “The SENTINEL radars will provide more precise detection and tracking of aerial targets, increasing the effectiveness of our NASAMS air defence systems,” Kaunas said in a statement. The ministry did not specify how many radars would be transferred or when they would be delivered. NASAMS, developed jointly by Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace and the US defence company Raytheon, is one of NATO’s most widely used medium-range air defence systems. Lithuania received its first NASAMS batteries in 2020 and is currently implementing the second phase of its procurement program, according to the ministry.

The European Union’s General Court has dismissed a lawsuit filed by a Lithuanian port operator seeking to overturn sanctions that ended the transit of Belarusian potash fertilisers through Lithuania. The court rejected the remaining claims brought by Klaipėda-based Bulk Cargo Terminal, which is controlled by businessman Igor Udovickij, and ordered the company to pay the legal costs. Bulk Cargo Terminal had sought to compel the Council of the European Union to adopt new rules or exemptions that would have allowed the transit of Belarusian potash through Lithuania despite EU sanctions. However, the court found that the company had lodged its appeal after the applicable deadline and ruled that it had no authority to amend decisions adopted by the Council. The ruling brings an end to the company’s legal challenge. In May 2024, the General Court dismissed another part of Bulk Cargo Terminal’s case challenging the EU’s restrictive measures against Belarus. Proceedings continued only on the remaining claims, which were rejected in Wednesday’s judgment. Lithuania halted the transit of fertilisers produced by Belarusian state-owned potash producer Belaruskali on February 1, 2022, after the European Union imposed sanctions on Belarus following Minsk’s crackdown on domestic opposition and its support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Before the sanctions took effect, Belaruskali products had been transported by rail from Belarus to the Lithuanian port of Klaipėda for export for more than a decade under a contract that had been due to run through the end of 2023.

The Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian chargés  d’affaires in Moscow have lodged a joint diplomatic protest with Russia’s Foreign Ministry, rejecting allegations that the Baltic states had opened their airspace for attacks on targets inside Russia. The diplomats said statements made by Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin on July 4 were false and accused Moscow of continuing to spread disinformation despite repeated denials from the Baltic governments. “Despite the fact that Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania have consistently expressed their official positions at various levels, the Russian side continues to spread false information and escalate tensions. The Baltic states reject Russia’s accusations as completely groundless,” the three countries said in a joint statement. The statement stressed that drone incursions into Baltic airspace are a consequence of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, not the result of any actions by the Baltic states. “It is emphasised that drone incursions into Baltic airspace are a consequence of Russia’s full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine,” the statement said. The chargés d’affaires also rejected other recent statements by Russian Foreign Ministry officials concerning the Baltic countries, saying claims that the rights of residents are not protected in Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are unfounded and part of a deliberate Russian “disinformation campaign”. The three countries reiterated that the rule of law is guaranteed for all residents and said Russia’s assertions are not based on facts. The Baltic states also again called on Russia to end its war against Ukraine and reaffirmed their support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and right to self-defence under the UN Charter.

Lithuania is deploying a fresh team of border guards to help Latvia patrol its frontier with Belarus, as Lithuania's incoming interior minister, Martynas Katelynas, says he has not ruled out reintroducing border controls with Latvia if migrant numbers continue to rise. The moves reflect growing frustration in Vilnius over what officials describe as a steady flow of migrants crossing into Latvia from Belarus and then travelling on into Lithuania and beyond, five years after Minsk was first accused of engineering a migration crisis on the European Union's eastern border. Reinforcements sent to the Belarusian border Nine Lithuanian officers, including two dog handlers, left on Monday for Latvia, the State Border Guard Service said. Drawn from units normally stationed at Pagėgiai and along the Baltic coast, they will take over from a team that has been patrolling high-risk sections of the Latvia-Belarus border since July 1. Working under Latvian command, the guards will focus on surveillance in the areas judged most vulnerable to illegal crossings, as well as other general border security tasks. The deployment is due to run for two weeks, after which Lithuania will decide whether further help is needed depending on conditions on the ground. Lithuanian guards provided similar support to Latvia between 2023 and 2025. The Lithuanian authorities say Latvia has come under considerable strain this year, with close to 7,900 migrants intercepted, detained or turned back at its border with Belarus, roughly nine times the number of attempted crossings recorded on the Lithuanian side, where about 900 people have been stopped so far in 2026. Lithuania says it has now prevented more than 25,500 illegal crossings since the start of what it calls a Belarusian-orchestrated migration crisis. Minister-designate floats border checks with Latvia The renewed assistance comes as Lithuania's incoming interior minister, Martynas Katelynas, said he was keeping open the option of temporarily restoring checks on the Lithuanian-Latvian border, warning that so-called secondary migration – people entering the EU via Latvia and then moving on into Lithuania – had risen sharply. Ministry figures show such movement roughly quadrupled in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, climbing from just over 300 people to more than 1,200. Katelynas compared the possible measure to the temporary controls Poland introduced last year on its borders with Lithuania and Germany in response to a similar rise in migrant numbers, which produced queues of several kilometres at crossing points during busy periods. "If the situation does not change, all possible solutions must be on the table," he said, describing internal border checks as effectively a last resort – a "nuclear" option he said would only be used if other ways of managing the flow, including detaining and returning migrants before they reach Lithuania, proved insufficient. He said the practical burden already fell heavily on Lithuanian border guards even where a returns agreement with Latvia was in place, since each case required paperwork, verification and temporary accommodation for migrants – a process that takes time, resources and can raise human rights concerns. 'Latvians themselves must show initiative' Katelynas argued that Latvia needed to take more responsibility for the problem, pointing to Lithuania's own experience of largely containing the crisis in 2021 and 2022 through a physical barrier along its Belarusian border and the use of pushbacks and returns. He said migrants who cross into Latvia often disappear from view, only for Lithuanian guards to later detain them – sometimes carrying forged documents – on the Riga-Warsaw bus route as they attempt to travel on through Lithuanian territory. He described this situation as unacceptable and said he expected the matter to be raised through diplomatic channels, including between interior ministries or at head-of-government level, while stressing that Lithuania did not intend to stop supporting Latvia's border guards in the meantime. According to the interior ministry, Lithuania detained around 1,200 migrants who had travelled from or through Latvia last year, roughly two and a half times more than the 540 recorded in 2024. Belarus has been accused by Western governments of deliberately funnelling migrants, many from the Middle East and Africa, towards its borders with Lithuania, Latvia and Poland since 2021, in what the EU has called a form of "hybrid warfare" against the bloc in retaliation for sanctions imposed on the regime of Alexander Lukashenko. Lithuania responded by building a border fence and tightening its own controls, and says this has sharply reduced attempted crossings on its territory, even as neighbouring Latvia continues to report high numbers of incidents.

Despite positive announcements about a new air defence mission in the Baltic region, NATO has not fulfilled a three-year-old pledge made in Vilnius to maintain a rotational deployment of air defence systems in the Baltic states, officials and experts say. The delay is largely due to a shortage of air defence capabilities across Europe, with many systems also urgently needed to support Ukraine. Lithuania’s defence officials say the new mission format would allow NATO to deploy air defence assets more quickly when needed and avoid lengthy political discussions. At the 2023 NATO summit in Vilnius, alliance leaders agreed that air defence systems would be deployed to the Baltic states on a rotational basis, meaning the systems would remain available in the region while different allied countries would take turns providing them. A year later, then-Lithuanian Defence Minister Arvydas Anušauskas said preparations were underway. “We are discussing the deployment of specific air defence systems in Lithuania, including Patriot systems. This will happen this year,” Anušauskas said at the time. However, the commitment has not materialised as a permanent arrangement. In 2024, the Netherlands deployed a Patriot system to Lithuania for 10 days, while Italy carried out a short-term deployment in 2025. Similar temporary deployments have taken place in Latvia and Estonia. Rimantas Sinkevičius, chairman of the Lithuanian parliament’s National Security and Defence Committee, said the situation is more complex than publicly acknowledged. “There is more information available in classified channels, and it is not necessarily unfavourable for Lithuania. There are systems available – from allies, not from Lithuania,” he said. Laurynas Kasčiūnas, deputy chairman of the committee, said the current reality does not match expectations for the rotational model. “This is certainly not what we expected from the rotational model,” he said. Experts say the main obstacle is a shortage of air defence systems throughout NATO. “There is an overall shortage of these systems in the alliance. It is a chronic shortage,” said Tomas Jermalavičius, head of studies at the International Centre for Defence and Security in Tallinn. “There have been figures suggesting that the alliance has only about 5% of the capabilities needed to protect the entire eastern flank.” At a recent NATO summit in Ankara, alliance leaders did not revisit the specific rotational deployment pledge but instead approved a broader change: replacing the Baltic air policing mission with an air defence mission. Lithuania’s current Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said the new approach would give NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe greater flexibility to move capabilities where they are most needed without lengthy political negotiations. “It allows NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe to redeploy and adjust plans, moving capabilities where they are needed most while avoiding political debates that sometimes arise,” Kaunas said. He added that the new mission could enable faster deployment of additional air defence assets. “Additional air defence capabilities could be deployed as quickly as possible when needed, avoiding all political debates,” Kaunas said. Kasčiūnas said, however, that the fundamental challenge remains a lack of available systems. “To arrange something, you need to have something to arrange. The physical shortage of air defence systems is the biggest challenge,” he said. Jermalavičius said the shift from air policing to air defence should currently be viewed mainly as a political signal to allies that the Baltic region is a priority. “It is a signal to allies that this is one of the priority regions and that greater attention should be given when making commitments and allocating resources,” he said. The expert also noted differences in how Baltic countries present the mission change. Estonian officials, he said, have focused less on the new mission status and more on changes to fighter pilot engagement rules and operational procedures. Jermalavičius added that national capabilities remain essential. Minister Kaunas acknowledged that Lithuania faces major challenges in strengthening its own air defence. “We are racing against time, trying to speed up processes and acquire radar systems, kinetic capabilities, anti-drone solutions and drone capabilities as quickly as possible,” he said. Lithuania has allocated an additional 800 million euros this year to strengthen air defence. However, Kasčiūnas said current plans remain insufficient. “The plan that has been created is very fragmented and only partially addresses the problem. According to our calculations, about 5 billion euros will be needed for air defence capabilities by 2035,” he said. The Lithuanian government’s program prioritises protecting military and critical infrastructure, while Kaunas said plans also include improving defences against air attacks on major cities.

More than half of Poles oppose reintroducing compulsory military service, according to a new poll, even as the country weighs its defence posture amid regional tensions. The IBRiS survey for daily Rzeczpospolita found 51.1 percent against a return to conscription, with 37.7 percent in favour when asked whether mandatory service should be restored given the current international situation. Support broke down into 15.1 percent answering "definitely yes" and 22.6 percent "rather yes." Opposition was strongest among opposition-party supporters, government voters, and those who do not vote at all, the newspaper noted. Support was far higher, however, for a different idea: compulsory military training for both men and women. Three-quarters of respondents (76.6 percent) backed the proposal, against 17.6 percent opposed. The debate over conscription has run in Poland since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The article was initially published on July 20, 2026, 13:40 (GMT+3)

A Belarusian businessman living in Lithuania, Dmitry Skinderev, claims the Migration Department is planning to revoke his refugee status because of his criticism of Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya and her inner circle. But his colourful past paints a different picture. Skinderev is a controversial figure: he threatened an adviser to opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya in Vilnius, while videos in which he criticises the Belarusian opposition regularly appear on Belarusian propaganda programmes. The businessman, who says he had “no interest in politics” until the mass protests in 2020, was also sentenced to prison in Belarus for extortion. After realising that “the rule of law was weakening in the country”, he said he joined a civic movement in 2020 and later ended up in Lithuania. However, the independent Belarusian outlet Nasha Niva reports that Skinderev did not participate in the protests following the disputed election results. In addition, in spring 2020, he posted a strange video address on his YouTube channel in which he claimed that unknown individuals had offered him the chance to overthrow the regime. “I was offered the chance to organise an armed coup, to organise a Maidan here, as happened in Ukraine. […] I am not a representative of the opposition, I am not a politician,” Skinderev said. In the same video, he said he had reported the incident to Belarusian law-enforcement authorities and included a photograph taken outside an office at a police station. “I believe elections and a change of government should take place democratically. I simply want the rights of businesspeople to be protected,” he continued. According to Nasha Niva, by 2020, Skinderev was deeply in debt, owing about €160,000. This coincided with the beginning of his more active online presence. ‘Extortion as part of an organised group’ At the beginning of the 2010s, Skinderev ended up in a Belarusian prison, where he spent two years. Nasha Niva reports that Skinderev was convicted of “extortion as part of an organised group, or causing serious consequences, or on a large scale”, according to information from BelPol, an association of former Belarusian security officials who joined the opposition. Asked about this at a news conference, the Belarusian became irritated. “I was slandered. I disagree with this and never expected that I could be imprisoned for something I did not do. My goal is, if we manage to change the regime in Belarus, to review my [2002] criminal case,” Skinderev said. Skinderev says he came to Lithuania with a valid visa. According to him, after he applied for a residence permit, he was immediately summoned to Lithuania’s State Security Department (VSD) because he was wanted by Interpol. “I was on Interpol’s wanted list, but I did not know about it. Because of the criminal case, the KGB wanted to bring me back,” Skinderev said. Asked by LRT.lt which specific case had led to him being wanted, the Belarusian replied: “For bribing an official.” He immediately clarified, however, that the case had been fabricated, as Belarusian special services often brought economic charges in order to seek the extradition of political opponents. Such a practice did exist. For example, presidential election candidate Viktar Babaryka was imprisoned after being accused of money laundering and taking bribes. At the time of publication, Skinderev’s name did not appear in Interpol’s wanted persons database. He says that 12 criminal cases have been opened against him in Belarus. His lawyer, Mikhail Parchimovich, said the Migration Department’s notification stated that Skinderev posed a threat to Lithuania’s national security. According to him, the document did not specify the grounds for that claim. Information on whether a person poses a threat to national security is collected by the Lithuanian State Security Department (VSD) and passed on to the Migration Department. In a comment provided to LRT.lt, the VSD said it had acted on the basis of the Intelligence Law and the principle of confidentiality. The VSD also said that the decision in the case would be taken by the Migration Department. “When a decision is made, the foreign national will be able to assess it and, if dissatisfied, appeal to the courts,” the department told BNS in a comment. Skinderev is convinced that the procedure to revoke his asylum is linked to his criticism of Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya and her inner circle. Judging by the news conference he organised earlier in July, this is the issue to which he devotes most attention. The businessman says he came to Lithuania at Tsikhanouskaya’s invitation to work with her team, but became disappointed. Now, he openly criticises her office, focusing primarily on what he claims was the non-transparent distribution of $380m provided by the EU and the US to support Belarus’s democratic forces. He has provided no evidence for this claim. Meanwhile, this winter a video circulated in the Belarusian media showing an aggressive man approaching Tsikhanouskaya’s adviser Dzianis Kuchynski at a cafe in Vilnius and beginning to insult him. It later emerged that the man was Skinderev. When Kuchynski asked Skinderev to leave, the businessman shouted: “I’ll hit you in the head!” Skinderev himself does not consider those words a threat. Organising provocations with Lithuanian MEP Gražulis Another incident took place on the day a group of released Belarusian political prisoners was brought to Lithuania. An asylum centre was set up for them in Vilnius, with Kuchynski coordinating its activities. That day, Skinderev again tried to provoke a conflict. This time, he was accompanied by European Parliament member Petras Gražulis. “They came with Gražulis to the asylum centre, supposedly wanting to meet the released political prisoners. But a provocation against me and everyone present began immediately. As soon as they saw the police, they left. Russian businessman Sergei Shnaider, the owner of the Mere discount retail chain operating in Lithuania and Latvia, has been added to the European Union’s 21st sanctions package. The measures is forcing the chain to close all its supermarkets operating in Lithuania, 15min.lt reported on Friday. According to 15min.lt, several of the Mere shops in Vilnius appeared to be already closed on Friday afternoon. Contacted by BNS, a representative of Mere declined to comment on whether the closures were temporary or if they were linked to the sanctions. “Due to technical issues, we are not operating anywhere in Lithuania,” the representative, who declined to give her name, told BNS. The Ministry of Economy and Innovation confirmed on Friday that the owners of the Svetofor Group – which also owns the Mere stores in Lithuania – are under EU sanctions. As of Thursday, all funds and assets belonging to these individuals within the EU must be frozen, and they are prohibited from receiving funds or other economic resources. Latvia’s Financial Intelligence Unit also reported that the chain’s operators in Latvia will have halt their activities. The Latvian authority said sanctions apply to Latprodukti, which operates the Mere chain in Latvia, and the Latvian branch of Lithuanian company Valiente. Both companies are required to immediately cease operations in compliance with EU sanctions. According to the Financial Intelligence Unit, Shnaider was sanctioned for materially or financially supporting actions that undermine or threaten Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. The agency said Shnaider indirectly owns more than 50% of both Latprodukti and Valiente’s Latvian operations. LRT reported last year that Valiente’s shares had been acquired by Spanish company Vigalight, which is owned by three Russian citizens who previously controlled the Mere retail chain. According to Spain’s corporate register, Shnaider owns 79% of Vigalight, while Andrei Veikulainen holds 15% and Valeriy Yakovlev owns the remaining 6%. Last October, Lithuania’s then Economy Minister Edvinas Grikšas said that Mere could be added to the sanctions list despite changes in its ownership structure. Latprodukti, established in 2020, reported revenue of 31.57 million euros in 2024, up 53% from the previous year, according to company filings. It posted a net loss of 71,800 euros after recording a profit in 2023. Its 2025 financial results have not yet been published. The company is directly owned by Serbia-based SKTrade DOO Beograd, while Shnaider is listed as its ultimate beneficial owner. Mere operates 12 stores in Latvia and around 20 in Lithuania.

Auditor General Irena Segalovičienė argues that Lithuania should commit to spending more than 5% of its gross domestic product on defence beyond 2030 to prevent future governments from cutting the military budget. Segalovičienė proposed enshrining the target in Lithuania's strategic documents, arguing that audits show elevated defence funding will remain necessary well into the next decade to maintain the country’s strengthened security posture. She said the National Security Strategy should require defence spending of more than 5% of GDP until at least 2035. “The state has decided to increase its security and truly elevate the national defence system from one level to another. We must have clear strategic patience so that this does not become a subject of intense political debate,” Segalovičienė said. Her comments come after Lithuania’s State Defence Council, which brings together the country’s political and military leadership, agreed to allocate between 5% and 6% of GDP to defence from 2026 through 2030. The additional funding is intended to finance the development of a national military division, procure new weapons and equipment, and prepare infrastructure for the permanent deployment of a German brigade in Lithuania. Deputy National Defence Minister Karolis Aleksa backed the proposal, saying that reducing defence spending after 2030 would make it difficult to sustain the capabilities currently under development. He said maintaining long-term military spending would require broad political consensus. NATO members agreed at the alliance’s recent summit to increase defence-related spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, responding to pressure from the United States and growing security concerns posed by Russia. Under the NATO agreement, allies are expected to allocate 3.5% of GDP to core defence spending and an additional 1.5% to broader security-related investments, including dual-use infrastructure and cybersecurity. Lithuania plans to spend 5.38% of GDP, or about 4.8 billion euros, on defence this year, making it one of NATO’s highest-spending members relative to the size of its economy.

Lithuanian prosecutors are investigating a Lithuanian citizen suspected of spying for Russia by collecting information on military facilities, equipment and troop movements, the Prosecutor General’s Office said Friday. The Vilnius Regional Prosecutor’s Office launched the pretrial investigation after Lithuania’s State Security Department obtained intelligence indicating that the suspect had been gathering information using methods associated with Russian intelligence and security services. According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, the suspect allegedly established contact through the Telegram messaging app and, acting on instructions relayed by intermediaries linked to Russian intelligence, collected information about military infrastructure and activities in Lithuania. Investigators say court-authorised surveillance found that the suspect photographed and provided information on a Lithuanian Armed Forces battalion, a company manufacturing military radar systems and the movement of military equipment at Vilnius Airport. The suspect also allegedly shared photographs of military hardware and offered to collect similar information while traveling in Belgium. Prosecutors said the evidence gathered so far indicates the suspect acted knowingly to assist a foreign state and understood that the information was being passed to a person potentially representing the Russian Ministry of Defence. Under Lithuania’s Criminal Code, collecting or transmitting state secrets or other information of interest to foreign intelligence services on behalf of another state or its representatives is punishable by six to 15 years in prison. The State Security Department urged the public to remain vigilant against recruitment attempts and provocations, warning that Russian and Belarusian intelligence services actively use social media platforms to identify, recruit and communicate with potential agents.

Lithuania has not yet decided whether to join two newly launched international defence financing initiatives unveiled during this month’s NATO summit, Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said. Speaking to the business daily Verslo Žinios, Valys said Lithuania was closely following both the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank and the British-backed Multilateral Defence Mechanism but had not made any formal decision on participation. According to the minister, Lithuania is paying closer attention to the Multilateral Defence Mechanism because it combines defence financing with cooperation on military procurement. “Lithuania is participating in discussions related to this initiative at the expert level,” Valys said. The two initiatives were announced during the NATO summit in Ankara earlier this month as part of broader efforts to strengthen allied defence capabilities and expand financing for the defence industry. Canada’s Defence, Security and Resilience Bank has already attracted eight participating countries: Latvia, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine. The Multilateral Defence Mechanism, launched by Britain together with Poland, the Netherlands and Finland, is expected to become operational next year. Valys said Lithuania remains engaged in discussions with partners on both initiatives while assessing the potential benefits of participation.

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys on Thursday criticised concessions made to Russia in the energy sector as part of negotiations on the European Union’s latest sanctions package, saying they undermine the bloc’s overall pressure campaign against Moscow. “The new sanctions package significantly increases pressure on the Russian financial sector and further restricts Russia’s access to capital markets. However, negotiations on the 21st package showed that EU sanctions policy decisions are increasingly driven by the economic interests of member states,” Budrys said in a statement. “This dangerous trend not only limits the EU’s ability to increase pressure on Russia but also weakens the impact of sanctions already in place,” he added. The latest sanctions package expands measures against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, adding 41 vessels to the sanctions list and bringing the total number of sanctioned ships to 692. The EU also broadened the criteria for listing vessels and introduced a requirement to report sales of liquefied natural gas tankers. The package further targets Russia’s financial sector, imposing sanctions on more than 80 Russian banks and extending transaction bans to another 33. Restrictions were also applied to four financial institutions operating in third countries and 14 crypto-asset service providers. In the energy sector, however, the EU agreed to suspend a review of the Russian oil price cap until July 15, 2027. Unless member states decide otherwise by that date, the current price cap of $44.10 per barrel will remain in force. The new measures also seek to curb sanctions circumvention through third countries by tightening export restrictions on entities linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex. Two additional Russian ports and four airports were also added to the sanctions list. The package expands import restrictions on a range of revenue-generating goods, including copper, nickel and lead ores, raw zinc, certain chemicals, glassware and automotive parts. It also imposes individual sanctions on 216 additional people and entities. Separately, the EU approved new sanctions against Belarus, including restrictive measures targeting the Mozyr Oil Refinery and the European Trade Company, which sells Belarusian petroleum products in Russia.

Ukraine’s recent changes in military and political leadership could undermine stability during the war with Russia, Lithuania’s former army chief said, arguing that commanders and defence officials should not be replaced so frequently during active hostilities. Retired Lt. Gen. Vytautas Jonas Žukas said President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision to dismiss Ukrainian army chief Oleksandr Syrsky after days of protests in Kyiv and other cities appeared risky because leadership changes require time for new officials to understand battlefield conditions and implement plans. “I am an opponent of such sudden moves,” Žukas said in an interview on LRT TV’s Topic of the Day programme Wednesday night. “When governments, ministers and army commanders are changed at the same time, stability suffers and ongoing programs can be disrupted.” Ukraine appointed Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapaty, a former commander of the Joint Forces, as the new army chief after Syrsky’s dismissal. The change came amid broader political turmoil following Zelensky’s decision to remove Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, a move that sparked public criticism. Analysts believe Fedorov, a popular reformer minister, was dismissed due to his strained relations with Syrsky. The dismissal sparked protests in Kyiv and other cities, leading to Syrsky’s dismissal. Žukas said he did not know the underlying political reasons for the changes but suggested Zelensky may have made a mistake by allowing the dispute to escalate. “In wartime, especially during active fighting, you need to look for compromises,” he said. “The minister and the army commander must understand how serious the situation is and find common solutions.” The former Lithuanian commander said tensions appeared to have centred partly on differences over Ukraine’s military modernisation. He noted that Fedorov had become popular because of efforts to expand drone production and increase drone strikes against targets deep inside Russia. “Many people in Ukraine associate this breakthrough with the new minister’s arrival,” Žukas said. He argued that if the conflict between political and military leaders could not be resolved, Zelensky should have replaced both officials rather than removing only the defence minister initially and later dismissing Syrsky following public pressure. Žukas said the episode marked another instance in which Zelensky had responded to public pressure, referring to earlier protests over changes involving Ukraine’s anti-corruption institutions. “Now dismissing people again and starting everything from the beginning creates instability,” he said.

Lithuanian and Polish border officials are meeting Thursday to discuss ways to make inspections at their shared border more efficient while Poland maintains temporary controls aimed at curbing secondary migration, Lithuania’s interior minister said. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the two countries should seek to streamline inspections by focusing on higher-risk vehicles and cargo while allowing regular travellers to cross more quickly. “Trucks and cargo vans can be inspected, but when we see two people traveling for business, holidays or other purposes, or perhaps a single person, the check could probably be faster,” Katelynas told reporters. The minister said he raised the issue with Polish counterparts during an informal meeting of European Union justice and home affairs ministers in Dublin last week. According to Katelynas, border officials from both countries were due to meet Thursday to discuss practical measures to reduce queues at the crossing. Poland reintroduced temporary border controls with Lithuania and Germany in July 2025, saying the measures were needed to stem secondary irregular migration. Warsaw argues that migrants who enter Latvia from Belarus travel through Lithuania before attempting to reach Poland and continue onward to Western Europe. The number of migrants intercepted after entering Lithuania from Latvia has risen sharply. In the first half of this year, Lithuanian authorities stopped more than 1,200 people arriving from Latvia, compared with just over 300 during the same period last year. Lithuania has responded by sending teams of border guards to assist Latvian authorities, although it has said it will not provide the full contingent of 100 officers requested by Riga. Katelynas has also not ruled out the possibility that Lithuania could temporarily restore controls on its border with Latvia if secondary migration continues to increase. Under European Union rules, countries in the Schengen area may temporarily reintroduce internal border controls only in exceptional circumstances when public policy or internal security is under threat.

Britain is replacing the tanks of its brigade stationed in Estonia with drones, saying it is responding to the changing nature of warfare. “The way of war is changing, and our response must change with it. We know that a more mobile, agile force would have a greater effect against Russia than traditional armour,” the British defence minister at the time, Dan Jarvis, said in Tallinn last week. As part of the move, Britain is increasing the number of troops stationed in Estonia from 800 to 1,200. It will also transform its Armoured Battlegroup in the country into a Mobile Anti-Armour Force equipped with high-tech drones, the UK Ministry of Defence said, adding that the country would also pre-position long-range drones in the Baltics. The lessons of Ukraine show that tanks are becoming less important, according to Tony Lawrence, head of the defence policy and strategy programme at the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Tallinn. “They’re not, of course, redundant. They are vulnerable and have to sit back a bit more in today’s warfare,” Lawrence said. However, the move does not mean the UK is turning its back entirely on traditional armoured vehicles, and some of its decisions are already in line with changes previously implemented in Lithuania. The UK is beginning a large-scale procurement of Boxer infantry fighting vehicles, which Lithuania already operates, Lawrence said. “This is the mobile element that they are talking about in various press releases.” The UK’s move in Estonia also reflects changes in London itself, as well as debates within the NATO alliance. “It’s about the commitment that the UK wants to show to this burden-shifting agenda inside NATO. The UK does not have a good story to tell about defence spending – it’s quite tight. It looks like it will be tight for some years to come,” Lawrence said. Lithuania has previously announced plans to buy tanks, while Germany is also deploying an armoured brigade equipped with tanks to the Baltic country, even as it highlights the brigade’s drone capabilities in its public messaging. “There has been a certain amount of discussion in Estonia, particularly by drone manufacturers who want to make the case that this is the only way to go and that Estonia is far behind,” he said. “But I think it’s been stronger in Vilnius than here.” According to Lawrence, the type of weapons sent to the Baltic states is also influenced by debates within individual NATO countries, while it is important to maintain different capabilities across NATO’s eastern flank “so that different tasks can be carried out”. “You will always have inconsistencies – with Germany heavily emphasising armour and the UK putting more emphasis on drones, you would want to have a more consistent posture across the whole eastern flank. “The fact is that we, the states that provide land forces, are constrained by domestic interests and policies, so you have to rely on NATO as the planning level above that to smooth out force posture,” Lawrence said. Writing in The Daily Telegraph, retired British colonel Hamish de Bretton-Gordon said the changes in Estonia showed that the role of tanks on the battlefield had changed – they must now operate alongside a range of technological solutions, including drones. “Ukraine has fundamentally changed warfare,” Bretton-Gordon wrote.

The European Union is still failing to agree on its 21st package of sanctions against Russia, with Lithuania’s ambassador to the bloc saying signs of European fatigue with pressuring the Kremlin are becoming increasingly apparent. Lithuania is among the few countries backing the toughest possible sanctions against Russia, with ambitions ranging from closing European borders to Russian soldiers to banning the transport of Russian liquefied natural gas. But Lithuania’s ambassador to the EU says Europe is growing tired of punishing the Kremlin. “The argument heard most often is that sanctions should not harm European countries and their economies compared with Russia,” says Lithuania’s ambassador to the EU, Nerijus Aleksiejūnas. As a result, restrictions on Russia’s fishing sector have already been dropped from the sanctions package, while Bulgaria is vetoing sanctions against Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill. France, Italy and Spain are the main opponents of a ban on Russian soldiers entering Europe. They issued the most visas to Russian citizens last year. A compromise appears likely, with the decision postponed until the autumn and handed over to the European Commission, where no member state will be able to veto it. “The best way to solve this problem is through changes to the visa code, where all the rules are set out,” says Aleksiejūnas. The European Commission’s proposal to ban EU countries from transporting Russian gas and selling tankers to Russia has caused the most controversy. Greece, which manufactures specialised liquefied natural gas tankers, opposes the move. “Those ice-class vessels capable of transporting Russian liquefied natural gas are specifically designed for the Arctic, and no other country or company apart from Russia is carrying out projects in the Arctic,” says Petras Katinas, an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI). Having failed to persuade Athens, the EU is considering allowing an exemption. Greece not only supplies tankers to Russia but also transports Russian gas, worth €2bn last year. “The Greeks are the biggest service providers for Russian LNG,” Katinas says. The gas storage facilities that were depleted during the unusually cold winter are also causing problems. As a result, Russian gas is in demand. This year, imports from Russia were almost a fifth higher than last year, with the EU paying Russia nearly €6bn for it. However, imports of Russian gas will be banned from next year. “More gas is being bought ahead of the ban – we saw the same thing before the previous ban,” Katinas says. There is also debate over the price cap on Russian oil. Lithuania’s aim is to keep it frozen at $44 a barrel. If it were recalculated, it would rise to $60, as the EU’s current limit is set at 15% below the market price. Greece, Malta and Cyprus, however, do not want the price cap to remain frozen. “The signal being sent is that they are backing away from their own sanctions,” Katinas says. Lithuanian diplomats say that despite the disagreements, there are also areas of consensus. “The aim is to restrict Russia’s financial market, its access to capital and its access to alternative sources of financing such as cryptocurrencies. Well, there is much more in the package,” Aleksiejūnas says.

Under a new proposal from Lithuania's presidential palace, migrant workers who have lived and worked in the country for two years would be legally required to leave for six months – a rule that not only risks forcing them away but could also block them from family reunification and from ever gaining permanent residency. The following is an opinion piece by Dr. Skirmantas Bikelis, Senior research fellow at Law Institute of Lithuanian Centre for Social Sciences. How well people of different backgrounds live together is a complicated question – as complicated as society itself. Trying to sum up migrant integration and social wellbeing with a single number or percentage is not just imprecise, it can be actively misleading. Yet that is exactly what is happening in Lithuania's current immigration debate, and foreigners living here should understand what is being proposed and why. Earlier this spring, Vilnius mayor Valdas Benkunskas made himself something of a laughing stock among experts by announcing a supposedly scientifically-proven figure. According to him, once migrants reach 10% of a city's population, this marks a "tipping point" leading to the formation of migrant ghettos – and he used this claim to argue for stricter, migrant-unfriendly measures in the capital of Lithuania, where migrants already make up that proportion of the population. Sociologist Karolis Žibas, founder of the NGO Diversity Development Group, dismissed this, saying that Benkunskas' "10% tipping point" argument was plucked out of thin air, with no research to back it up. In reality, according to Žibas, ghettos or segregated neighbourhoods form because of factors like lack of affordable housing, housing discrimination, income inequality, or gaps in education, not because of any specific percentage of foreigners. Still, these are problems worth fixing regardless of how many migrants live in a country. A new figure, this time from the presidential palace Now a new, even smaller number has emerged – this time from the office of President Gitanas Nausėda – being used to justify tightening immigration rules further. Foreigners currently make up 7.5% of Lithuania's population, and the president's chief adviser, Vaidas Augustinavičius, argues this figure already needs to be "managed" and "restricted." At the president's initiative, the National Security Group within the presidential palace has drafted amendments to the Law on the Legal Status of Aliens. If passed, these changes could make it significantly harder for many labour migrants to build a stable life in Lithuania – and could even push existing migrant workers to leave, with little incentive to come back. First, the president is proposing to change how labour migrant quotas are calculated so that they include not only newly arriving migrants but also those continuing to work in Lithuania. This would sharply reduce – essentially by half – the quota available for new arrivals, unless the overall quota were doubled. It is not clear if that's happening any time soon. Secondly, perhaps the single most consequential change in the package: labour migrants would be required to leave Lithuania for at least six months after every two years of work. A presidential adviser, Evelina Gudzinskaitė, has defended this by suggesting it simply gives workers a natural chance to visit family back home, in line with how their work cycles operate anyway. But this framing misses the real impact. Migrant workers can already visit their families whenever they choose - they don't need a forced six-month 'deportation' to do so. Worse still, under current Lithuanian law, migrant workers only gain the right to bring their families to live with them after two continuous years of legal residence. So, a mandatory six-month departure every two years would permanently block that right, meaning workers could never reach the residency threshold needed to bring their spouses or children to Lithuania. It would also prevent them from ever qualifying for permanent residency, which requires five continuous years in the country, and eventually citizenship. Why family reunification matters - and why blocking it backfires EU law on family reunification recognises that living together as a family supports social stability and helps migrants integrate into their host country, which in turn benefits the wider economy and society. When families live together, money spent on housing and living costs stays in Lithuania rather than being sent abroad. Research in criminology also suggests people with family responsibilities are generally more likely to follow the law (as per Robert J Sampson and John H Laub's theory of informal social control). Blocking migrants from settling permanently or reuniting with their families would strip away their motivation to learn Lithuanian, put down roots, or build a long-term future here. As Ivanas Trunovas, a migration researcher at Diversity Development Group, puts it: "There is a worrying trend in Lithuania – rules are being tightened for both those already living here and new arrivals. This reduces their motivation to integrate and build a long-term life in the country. If we don't see newly arrived people as part of our shared future, and don't guarantee them opportunities, protection and access to services, the result will be that Lithuanian residents of foreign origin become less willing to integrate." The explanatory note behind the proposal argues Lithuania has reached its limit on accepting migrants, that the country has not invested enough in integration services, and that a more "flexible" labour market requires higher turnover of foreign workers. This reasoning does not hold up well. Once again, attempting to justify strict anti-immigration measures with a particular figure (7.5%) makes for a rather flimsy argument.
