Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry has proposed expanding national sanctions against Russian and Belarusian citizens, including new restrictions on property purchases near strategic sites and entry bans for individuals who support Russia’s war in Ukraine. The proposed amendments would bar Russian and Belarusian cultural, entertainment and sports figures from working in Lithuania if they support Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, have participated in the war or contribute to “Kremlin propaganda” through their activities, the ministry said. “As a democratic state, Lithuania has a duty to protect its public space from regimes that systematically violate human rights, wage aggression against neighbouring states and use culture and entertainment as instruments of soft power,” the ministry said. Under the proposed amendments to Lithuania's Law on Restrictive Measures Regarding Military Aggression Against Ukraine, Russian and Belarusian individuals and organisations would be denied entry to participate in public activities in education, science, culture, sports, the arts and entertainment if they have operated in Russia-occupied Ukrainian territories or directly or indirectly support the war. The restrictions would also apply to individuals who pursue policies or take actions undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence, as well as those who support human rights abuses or repression against civil society and democratic movements in Russia and Belarus. The ministry also proposes requiring Russian and Belarusian nationals seeking to enter Lithuania for educational, cultural or sporting events to sign a public declaration condemning Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and affirming support for the UN Charter and Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and internationally recognised borders. Those who refuse to sign the declaration would be denied entry. Russian and Belarusian citizens not covered by those provisions could continue participating in such activities in Lithuania, provided they do not represent their home countries and compete or perform as neutral participants. Organisers of public events would be responsible for ensuring compliance with the restrictions. The draft legislation also seeks to tighten restrictions on real estate purchases near strategically important facilities. Under the proposal, Russian and Belarusian citizens holding Lithuanian residence permits would be prohibited from purchasing property near national security facilities or military training grounds. Belarusian citizens without Lithuanian residence permits and Belarusian legal entities would also be barred from acquiring property in those areas. Lithuania has already imposed broader restrictions on property purchases by Russian citizens. The Foreign Ministry has proposed that the amendments take effect on January 1. Similar proposals targeting performers and real estate purchases were previously introduced by the opposition Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats but were not adopted because only the government has the authority to initiate national sanctions legislation. Lithuania’s Law on Restrictive Measures Regarding Military Aggression Against Ukraine has been in force since 2023. It was introduced to demonstrate support for Ukraine and impose restrictions on certain rights of Russian and Belarusian citizens, whose countries Lithuania regards as aggressor states. Lithuania has already barred several performers from entering the country because of their support for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government or performances in Russia or Russia-annexed Crimea.

Lithuania has resumed negotiations with the Taiwanese Representative Office on an economic cooperation action plan following a change in government, the Foreign Ministry said. The talks were temporarily suspended in June as the new Social Democrat-led government restructured the cabinet. The ministry said strengthening economic cooperation with Taiwan remains a long-term foreign policy priority and that Lithuania aims to sign an economic cooperation action plan once negotiations are completed. According to the ministry, the plan is focused on building sustainable economic ties and supporting the development of Lithuania’s high-tech sectors. It declined to disclose specific details while consultations are ongoing. The ministry said Lithuania’s position on Taiwan remains unchanged and that it seeks to deepen practical cooperation in areas of mutual benefit, including trade, business, education, science, culture and people-to-people exchanges. Officials had previously hoped to finalise the action plan by the end of May and sign it in June before the negotiations were paused. Lithuania and Taiwan have sought to deepen economic ties since the Taiwanese Representative Office opened in Vilnius in 2021. At the time, Lithuanian officials expressed hopes that the move would lead to stronger investment and commercial cooperation. More recently, however, some Lithuanian officials have voiced frustration over what they say has been a slower-than-expected pace of Taiwanese investment. The opening of the representative office triggered a sharp deterioration in relations between Lithuania and China. Beijing viewed the decision to allow the office to use the name “Taiwanese” rather than the more common “Taipei” as support for Taiwan’s efforts to assert greater international standing. In most countries, similar offices operate under the name “Taipei”.

Lithuania’s new government is signalling a tougher approach to migration, with President Gitanas Nausėda proposing stricter rules for foreign workers and officials insisting that migration flows could pose economic and security challenges. Under Nausėda’s proposal, foreign workers would receive temporary work permits valid for two years and would then be required to leave Lithuania for at least six months before being allowed to return. Moreover, they would not have the right to family reunification – that is, to bring their families while they work in Lithuania. The plan has drawn criticism from legal experts and business representatives, who warn that tighter restrictions could worsen labour shortages and hurt the economy. At the same time, security officials say migration routes through the region have become part of a broader security challenge linked to Russia and Belarus. Lithuania experienced a major migration crisis in 2021, when thousands of migrants crossed or attempted to cross the border from Belarus in what the European Union described as a state-sponsored pressure campaign. “Lithuania was the first country targeted by this attack. We were the first to have to make decisions in this nonstandard situation,” said conservative MP Agnė Bilotaitė, who served as interior minister from 2020 to 2024. Under her leadership, Lithuania responded by interning several thousand people who had entered the country, allowing authorities to push back migrants attempting to cross from Belarus, and building a fence topped with concertina wire along the border with Belarus. Lithuania’s neighbour Latvia is now facing a similar challenge. Nearly 8,000 migrants have attempted to enter Latvia from Belarus this year, about nine times more than the number recorded in Lithuania, according to Lithuanian officials. Antanas Montvydas, deputy head of Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service, said Latvia’s incomplete infrastructure and gaps in border surveillance systems have contributed to increased pressure. Migrants who enter Latvia often attempt to travel onward through Lithuania toward Western Europe. Lithuanian authorities have stopped about 1,200 people arriving from Latvia over the past six months. Recently appointed Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Lithuania could consider temporarily restoring border checks with Latvia if migration flows become impossible to manage. “Clearly, this would be a ‘nuclear’ option, but if we had no other possibility to control the flows and stop migrants at the border, not on our territory, I think we would have to take it,” Katelynas said earlier this month. However, both Nausėda and Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius oppose restoring internal border controls with Latvia, saying it would undermine the principles of the Schengen free-travel area. “Ninety percent of our problem is not with Latvia. We have no special problems in relations with Latvia, so in my view creating internal borders within the Schengen area would be a defeat and a kind of capitulation to this phenomenon,” Nausėda said. Latvia has asked Lithuania for additional assistance rather than border restrictions. Lithuania recently sent a second team of 10 border officers, while Latvian officials have said they need around 100 additional personnel. Latvian Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava said the main challenges are increased pressure at the border and a shortage of officers. Lithuania’s debate over migration also reflects a growing tension between security concerns and labour market needs. Nausėda’s chief national security adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said the number of foreigners living in Lithuania has reached about 220,000, or 7.7% of the population, placing pressure on integration systems and contributing to social tensions. But legal expert Skirmantas Bikelis criticized what he described as misleading arguments behind the proposed restrictions. He said the number of foreign residents has remained relatively stable and warned against using isolated incidents involving foreigners to justify broader restrictions. Business representatives argue that migrant workers are essential because many sectors face long-term labour shortages. “Employers have needed migrants for 10 years already. There are jobs that Lithuanians cannot be encouraged to take even with high salaries. Migrants are a solution,” Bikelis said. He warned that limiting foreign labour could damage the economy, particularly because work quotas for migrants are often reached before the end of the year. Supporters of stricter migration controls use security concerns as argument. Giedrimas Jeglinskas, a security and defence expert, former chair of the parliamentary National Security and Defence Committee, said every foreign arrival carries risk of possible recruitment by hostile intelligence services, particularly among people arriving from Russia-speaking communities or former Soviet countries. Lithuanian border officials have repeatedly reported cases of Belarusian officers escorting migrants toward the border. Lithuanian authorities have consistently described migration via Belarus as part of a “hybrid attack”. Baltic leaders have also warned of possible new Russian provocations targeting countries that support Ukraine. President Nausėda said critical energy and transport infrastructure could be potential targets because attacks on such facilities could have a wider impact. Officials have warned that possible attacks could include sabotage, cyberattacks, information operations and other actions aimed at weakening public trust and reducing support for Ukraine. “The goal of Russia is to influence society, trust in institutions and reduce support for Ukraine,” Jeglinskas said.

Lithuanian construction company YIT Lietuva has won a 29-million-euro contract to build a Leopard 2A8 tank assembly and repair facility in the Kaunas Free Economic Zone, the company said Monday. YIT Lietuva and Lithuania Defence Services signed the agreement for the project, which will create a 13,000-square-meter plant to support the assembly and maintenance of Leopard 2A8 tanks and other heavy military equipment for the Lithuanian Armed Forces. Lithuania Defence Services is a joint venture between Germany’s KNDS Deutschland and Rheinmetall Landsysteme. “This project is significant not only for our company but for all of Lithuania. It will contribute to strengthening the country’s defence infrastructure and play an important role in ensuring the technical readiness of the Lithuanian military in the future,” YIT Lietuva CEO Kęstutis Vanagas said. Sebastian Dietz, CEO of Lithuania Defence Services, said the facility would provide long-term maintenance capabilities for heavy military equipment. The company will be responsible for tank assembly, technical servicing, repairs and ensuring the combat readiness of equipment in Lithuania. YIT Lietuva will oversee the design and construction of the plant. Construction is scheduled to begin in August and be completed in November 2027. The first tank assembled at the facility is expected to leave the factory in late 2028. The plant will be built on a nearly 10-hectare site and is expected to create up to 100 jobs, including 70 production positions and 30 administrative roles. Lithuania Defence Services announced plans last December to invest about 50 million euros in the facility. State-owned Epso-G Invest is expected to acquire a 25.1% stake in the company. The project is part of Lithuania’s broader effort to expand its defence industry and strengthen military capabilities amid heightened security concerns in the region.

Lithuania’s ruling coalition and opposition remain divided over whether to launch a new parliamentary investigation into an alleged US Central Intelligence Agency detention site after the country suffered another defeat at the European Court of Human Rights. Members of the ruling coalition argue that previous parliamentary and law enforcement inquiries have already examined the allegations, while opposition parties say a new investigation is needed to resolve unanswered questions and protect Lithuania’s reputation. Orinta Leiputė, head of the largest faction of the ruling Social Democratic Party, rejected calls for a new inquiry, saying the issue had already been investigated by the Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence in 2009. The allegations emerged that year after US broadcaster ABC News reported that eight terrorism suspects had allegedly been held at a black site near Vilnius between 2004 and 2005. A parliamentary investigation launched in 2009 did not find any direct evidence of detentions, but concluded that conditions existed were in place for the CIA to operate a black site in Lithuania. The inquiry identified two possible locations in Vilnius and nearby Antaviliai, as well as several CIA-linked flights to Vilnius and Palanga. Lithuanian prosecutors closed their investigation in 2011, saying there was no evidence that the Antaviliai facility had been used as a detention site. The case was reopened after a US Senate committee report on CIA detention and interrogation practices was declassified in 2014. Agnė Širinskienė, head of the Democratic Union “For Lithuania” parliamentary faction, said the group had not formally considered the issue but questioned whether a new investigation would be useful. Aušrinė Norkienė, deputy chair of the Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union, said she had not formed a final position but questioned the need for a probe into events that took place more than two decades ago. Opposition parties have pushed for renewed scrutiny. Laurynas Kasčiūnas, chairman of the Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats, said a new investigation was needed, particularly to clarify the use of unaccounted funds referenced in the US Senate report. He called it a matter of Lithuania’s self-respect. Remigijus Žemaitaitis, leader of the Nemunas Dawn party, said his faction would support reopening the investigation and expressed interest in joining a parliamentary commission to identify those involved in operating the alleged facility. Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen, leader of the opposition Liberal Movement, also backed a new inquiry, saying recent European Court of Human Rights rulings requiring Lithuania to compensate alleged detainees conflict with the official position of Lithuanian institutions and show that the issue remains unresolved. Earlier this month, the ECHR ordered Lithuania to pay 30,000 euros to Saudi national Abd Al-Rahim Hussein Al-Nashiri over his alleged illegal detention at a secret US site in Lithuania. The court also ordered Lithuanian authorities to seek assurances from the United States that he would not face the death penalty. It was the third ECHR ruling against Lithuania over the alleged CIA detention program. Lithuania has maintained before the court that the Antaviliai facility was an intelligence support centre, not a black site, and that flights linked to the site carried communications equipment rather than detainees. However, a 2014 US Senate report on CIA torture at secret detention sites refers to a facility known as “Site Violet” that operated in 2005-2006. Although the report redacted the names of specific countries and officials, human rights groups have argued that the site was located in Antaviliai. President Gitanas Nausėda said earlier this month that he trusted the conclusions of Lithuanian institutions that no CIA prison existed in the country. He said he saw no need to reopen the issue, arguing, inaccurately, that previous investigations had already determined that no CIA detention facility had operated in Lithuania.

Lithuania’s border guards discovered a tunnel leading from Belarus into the country, the State Border Guard Service (VSAT) said in a statement on Monday, adding that the tunnel was likely intended to be used for irregular migration. Officers found the tunnel on Wednesday last week after detecting “vibrations in the ground indicating that an underground tunnel might be being dug from the Belarusian side” in Lithuania’s southeastern Varėna district, VSAT said. Polish officials assisted their Lithuanian counterparts, bringing specialist equipment designed to search for tunnels. After drilling a hole, officers discovered a tunnel which did not yet have an opening into Lithuanian territory. The tunnel, around a metre in diameter, was found at a depth of 1.5 metres below ground, according to VSAT. Tunnels have previously been discovered in Lithuania and Poland, which were used for smuggling goods and people across the border from Belarus.

A tax-free shop serving foreign NATO troops at Lithuania's Rukla military base is being supplied by German company Gebr. Heinemann, which has faced criticism over its trade of luxury goods in Russia and Belarus. Lithuania’s Defence Ministry said it intended to investigate the circumstances of the cooperation between Heinemann and the shop's operator, German firm Gratus. A similar retail outlet is planned for the Rūdninkai military campus, which will host the German brigade. ​ “I would rather not comment at this stage because we first need to gather all the information. Once I'm back at work, we'll look into it,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told BNS. “If an investigation has already been carried out and the institutions responsible for national security found no violations regarding Heinemann's operations at the airports, then, as I understand it, the company can continue operating in Lithuania,” he added. ​ The ministry said such retail points are regulated by international treaties and are standard at NATO military bases abroad. ​ The Rukla shop is restricted to personnel from the Bundeswehr and other NATO nations, offering cigarettes, beverages, gifts, military souvenirs and other items. ​ According to the ministry, the Bundeswehr manages the shop through Gratus Lithuania, which was established in 2017 when the German-led international NATO battalion was deployed to Rukla. Gratus Lithuania is a subsidiary of German company Gratus that cooperates with Heinemann, which operates duty-free shops at Lithuanian airports. ​ Heinemann confirmed it supplies goods to troops in Rukla and provides retail consultancy services. ​ Earlier this year, LRT reported that Gebr. Heinemann supplied luxury goods to shops linked to the regime of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, following previous reports of supplies to Russia. The company said it complies with sanctions against Russia and Belarus, adding that its duty-free operations are separate from its supply activities. ​ Lithuanian authorities have previously assessed Heinemann's activities on several occasions and found no security risks. ​ Lithuanian Airports and the Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence (NSGK) also found no grounds to suspend the company's operations. ​ However, the Defence Ministry said it would now examine the cooperation between Heinemann and the Rukla shop operator and assess whether a new national security compliance review is needed.

Lithuania is detecting dozens of attempts to smuggle migrants via tunnels from Belarus, with the border guard chief saying that the Minsk authorities are most likely involved in the operation. “Recently, we have seen a change in migrants' tactics: they are increasingly using tunnels or caves,” Rustamas Liubajevas, the chief of the State Border Guard Service (VSAT), told 15min in an interview published on Tuesday. He added that the border guards have discovered “tens of places” where tunnels are “almost certainly” being dug. Previously, VSAT said the officers had uncovered a tunnel in southeastern Lithuania, leading from Belarus. “Without logistical support from the Belarusian border guards, this would not be possible. First of all, all of this activity is taking place right next to the border. Then there is the need to supply timber, as the tunnel has wooden supports,” Liubajevas said. “So we have little doubt that the Belarusian authorities are either turning a blind eye or actively helping migrants dig these tunnels. They may not be digging them themselves, but the work is clearly being organised using migrants,” he added. According to Liubajevas, this has become more common this year, although the first such tunnels were discovered last year. He did not provide the exact figures to the 15min reporters. He said migrants had previously used similar methods on the Belarus-Poland border.

Lithuania’s Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius is facing questions over his doctoral dissertation after a complaint alleging possible plagiarism was submitted to the country’s academic ethics watchdog. The complaint, which was forwarded to ISM University of Management and Economics, comes after renewed public attention on Sinkevičius’ 2015 doctoral thesis on factors influencing alcohol consumption. The dissertation was not available online for most of the past decade and was uploaded to the electronic library only after questions were raised about its accessibility. Sinkevičius defended the dissertation while serving as mayor of Jonava and received his doctorate from ISM. He became prime minister years later, bringing renewed scrutiny of his academic work. “I wrote the dissertation myself and defended it publicly,” Sinkevičius said. “Investigations, if they are launched, will not change the fact that the dissertation was prepared, defended and publicly available. I am completely calm that any review will end favourably and that this issue will be closed.” The complaint is being considered by ISM, which said it would decide whether to launch an internal review. The Academic Ethics and Procedures Controller’s Office said it had received the complaint and forwarded it to the university. Some researchers and experts have already analysed the dissertation using artificial intelligence tools and raised questions about similarities between parts of the work and other academic sources. However, ISM officials cautioned that such tools alone cannot replace a formal academic review. “Electronic tools have opened up many possibilities for interpretation,” ISM Rector Dalius Misiūnas said. “Ten years ago, such tools did not exist. Now, with artificial intelligence and a PDF file, any dissertation can be examined in detail.” Misiūnas said the dissertation had gone through the required academic procedures at the time, with a review panel representing four universities. He said he believed the work was completed by the doctoral candidate and publicly defended according to the rules in force at the time. However, he acknowledged one procedural issue: while the hard copy of the dissertation was available, the electronic version was not. “One issue remained – the electronic version of the dissertation was not published immediately after the defence,” Misiūnas said. The dissertation’s supervisor was Vilnius University professor Sigitas Urbonavičius, who is currently unavailable for comment because he is on leave. The defence committee was chaired by ISM professor Ilona Bučiūnienė. Vytautas Nekrošius, president of the Lithuanian Academy of Sciences, said originality and novelty are essential requirements for doctoral work regardless of the institution where a dissertation is defended. “These criteria are assessed by the defence committee – first by the supervisor when reviewing the draft, then by the department, by appointed experts and finally by the defence committee,” Nekrošius said. The controversy comes as other members of Lithuania’s government have also faced scrutiny over academic work. Culture Minister Lukas Alsys postponed the defence of his dissertation earlier this year after reviewers raised concerns about possible plagiarism. Alsys said the issues involved citation errors and that he intended to correct them. “I was told there were inaccuracies in citations, and I will correct them,” Alsys said. “Such things cannot remain in a work of this type.” Agriculture Minister Kęstutis Mažeika also holds a doctorate and said he has no concerns about the quality of his dissertation, which examined breeding boars and sperm quality. The debate has also raised broader questions about whether politicians’ academic records reflect their character and suitability for public office. Nekrošius said a doctoral dissertation provides insight into the person who wrote it because it represents years of sustained work. Ignas Kalpokas, an associate professor at Vytautas Magnus University, said academic integrity is an important measure for public figures. “We expect politicians, especially those holding the highest offices, to be honest and principled – both toward themselves and others,” Kalpokas said. Sinkevičius’ case has also drawn political attention. Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said questions should be directed to ISM, emphasising that universities must ensure the quality of their academic work. “We hear from the leadership that this is a high-quality university and worth studying at and paying money for. It must check what works have been produced and evaluate them,” Olekas said. The controversy comes amid wider criticism of Lithuania’s academic standards. Education Minister Raminta Popovienė said the issue of Sinkevičius’ dissertation should be discussed in a broader context because it concerns the quality of higher education institutions.

Two foreign nationals stand accused of trying to smuggle drug-laced paper to the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, the Prosecutor General’s Office said on Tuesday. W. Sh. and Sw. S. face charges of large-scale drug smuggling and illegal possession of narcotics with intent to distribute, with the case being referred to a court in Vilnius. ​ The pre-trial investigation was launched in September 2025 after an employee at a parcel distribution terminal in Vilnius discovered a hidden compartment in a shipment and alerted police. ​ The packages, handed over to a courier by the defendants, were intended for delivery to the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. ​ During a search of an apartment rented by the suspects, police officers discovered a very large quantity of various psychotropic substances, totalling 1.78 kilogrammes. ​ Investigators allege that the defendants used specialised equipment to impregnate A4 paper sheets with psychotropic substances. To evade customs controls, the sheets were concealed in hidden compartments built into shipping boxes. ​ The defendants are currently in custody. They face up to 18 years in prison for drug smuggling and up to 15 years for possession with intent to distribute.

Lithuania's Office of Intelligence Ombudspersons will not launch an investigation into the alleged CIA secret prison that may have operated in the country two decades ago, the watchdog said in a statement to BNS. "The intelligence ombudspersons consider that there are currently no newly emerged significant factual circumstances that would provide grounds for initiating an investigation," Justas Gaidys, senior adviser at the office, said in a comment to BNS. Gaudys said the decision not to investigate was based primarily on the fact that the parliamentary Committee on National Security and Defence (NSGK) had already carried out an inquiry into the alleged prison more than a decade ago on the instruction of the Seimas. He also noted that the Prosecutor General's Office is continuing a reopened pre-trial investigation and that the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has already delivered three judgments concerning the detention of individuals at alleged CIA facilities in Lithuania. "Recognising that this issue remains significant to the public, the Ombudsperson plans to initiate an inter-agency dialogue with the competent Lithuanian authorities," Gaidys said. "The aim of this dialogue will be to assess the possibilities of obtaining new information, determine whether any additional action falls within the ombudspersons' remit, and build a comprehensive understanding of the situation," he added. Debate over the alleged CIA prison resurfaced after Lithuania lost its third case before the ECHR in July. The Strasbourg court awarded 30,000 euros to Saudi Arabian national Abd Al Rahim Hussein Al-Nashiri over his unlawful detention at a secret CIA prison in Lithuania. The court also ordered the Lithuanian authorities to seek assurances from Washington that the terrorism suspect would not face the death penalty. Allegations that the CIA operated a secret detention facility in Lithuania first emerged in 2009, when US broadcaster ABC News reported that eight terrorism suspects had been held near Vilnius between 2004 and 2005. Later that year, the Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence (NSGK) concluded that it could not establish whether detainees had been transferred to Lithuania, but found that the conditions for such transfers had existed. Earlier this year, the Prosecutor General's Office confirmed that it is continuing its investigation into the alleged unlawful transportation of people across Lithuania's state border. New probe should be led by inter-agency commission – minister Lithuania's Justice Minister Rita Tamašunienė said later on Wednesday the country stood by its position that there was no CIA prison. Any further probe should be handled by an inter-agency commission, she added. "An inter-agency commission should investigate, if we were to form one. [...] We need to decide who actually has the competence to investigate and present arguments in a way that leaves no doubt in the future," Tamašunienė told reporters on Wednesday. The minister said such a commission would ensure the issue was not politicised or perceived as an attempt to conceal information.

Lithuanian border guards have found another unfinished tunnel believed to have been intended for migrants to enter the country from Belarus, the State Border Guard Service (VSAT) said on Wednesday. On Sunday evening, officers from the Kapciamiestis border station of the Varena border district used vibration sensors to detect suspected digging activity near the village of Pertakas in the Lazdijai district. At the site, the border between Belarus and Lithuania is marked by a stream. The border fence is therefore located further inside Lithuanian territory. After spotting the approaching border guards, around 20 foreign nationals fled back into Belarusian territory, VSAT said. The officers then found an unfinished tunnel about 11 metres long. It was designed to pass under the patrol path further into Lithuanian territory. Logs believed to have been intended for structural support, excavated sand and buckets were found at the site. The tunnel was then filled in, VSAT said. This marks a second announcement of a detected tunnel in one week, with the VSAT chief previously saying that migrants are increasingly attempting to dig tunnels to enter the country from Belarus. Rustamas Liubajevas, the VSAT chief, pinned the blame on the Belarusian border guards, saying such an operation cannot take place without their involvement.

Even calls from a close relative should be treated with caution, as AI-powered scams are now taking place in Lithuania. A Vilnius resident, Domantas (his surname is known to LRT but has been withheld), shared his experience with LRT. "My sister called me. Her photo, name and phone number all appeared on my screen. I answered, and I heard my sister asking for help because she was in an accident. It immediately struck me as strange because my sister doesn't drive," he said. Realising the call might be a scam, he ended the conversation and immediately rang his sister. She told him she was at home watching TV and had never called him. After hearing what had happened, she remembered receiving a phone call some time earlier from a company whose name she could no longer recall. The caller had tried to sell her a product or service. The conversation lasted several minutes before she firmly told the salesperson she was not interested. Domantas said he had heard about similar scams before, but until it happened to him, he had assumed they were more myth than reality. He described the trick as highly convincing. Šarūnas Grigaliūnas, head of the Cyber Security Competence Centre at the Kaunas University of Technology (KTU), told LRT that scammers posing as relatives, bank employees, police officers or other trusted figures over the phone was nothing new. "However, generative artificial intelligence has changed one crucial thing: fraudsters no longer have to convincingly imitate a person themselves. They can use a voice that sounds like a real family member. According to Grigaliūnas, this type of scam usually consists of several stages. First, fraudsters gather information about their target in advance, including their name, phone number, family relationships, social media profiles, photographs, videos, comments, workplace, place of residence and other publicly available information. Some of this information comes from social media, some from leaked databases and some from previous scam attempts. He stressed that criminals do not need lengthy recordings or extensive personal information. By publicly sharing relatives' names, birthdays, schools, pets' names and other personal details, people can unknowingly provide material for social engineering attacks. Likewise, a short audio or video clip posted on social media may be enough for criminals to clone someone's voice. "In some cases, fraudsters deliberately call a person, ask a few harmless questions and use the conversation to obtain natural voice samples. "In the simplest scenario, they prepare AI-generated phrases in advance. More sophisticated attacks use real-time voice conversion, where the fraudster's speech is processed so it sounds like someone else's voice. "In even more advanced schemes, AI can be combined with scripted conversations, automated dialogue and personal information about the victim," he said. Grigaliūnas also pointed out that seeing the name of someone you know on your phone does not necessarily mean the call is coming from their device. "If fraudsters spoof the caller ID, your phone may display the contact exactly as it is saved in your address book. The technology itself is not the attack. It simply creates the illusion of trust. "The real mechanism is social engineering: creating a sense of urgency, fear or shame, asking the victim not to tell anyone, urging them to transfer money immediately, hand over a bank card, approve a transaction or reveal a PIN, Smart-ID code or login credentials," he said. He also warned that even if people realise they are speaking to a scammer, they should avoid prolonging the conversation. The goal is not only to avoid losing money, but also to avoid giving away additional personal information. "The longer someone talks, the more the fraudster learns: how they react, the names of family members, the nature of their relationships, which details seem believable and which questions cause stress. A longer conversation also provides more voice samples. "We should not exaggerate and think that a single word is enough to steal someone's identity. But longer, more natural speech helps criminals capture a person's intonation, speaking pace, emotional reactions and characteristic expressions. That information can be used in future attacks," Grigaliūnas said. According to Grigaliūnas, the most important thing to understand is that a familiar voice or recognised phone number is no longer enough to verify someone's identity. Instead, people should assess the situation as a whole. The cybersecurity expert said several warning signs may indicate that the person on the phone is not a loved one but a scammer. Such calls are often unexpected and emotionally charged. The caller, posing as a relative, may claim to have been in a car crash, arrested, admitted to hospital or hit by another emergency. They then urge the victim to transfer money immediately, hand over cash, buy gift cards, provide security codes or open a link. Scammers also frequently insist that the victim keep the conversation secret, avoid contacting the police and not call back to verify the story. They may refuse to provide a family-agreed security phrase and try to keep the victim on the phone. Other clues include inconsistencies in the caller's story. Although the voice may sound familiar, they may phrase sentences differently, get family events wrong, confuse places, names or dates, or display technical oddities such as unnatural pauses, delays, unusual background noise, a monotone voice, overly perfect speech or repetitive phrases. "However, relying solely on technical signs is risky because AI-generated voices are improving rapidly," Grigaliūnas warned. He advised people to verify a caller's identity through an independent channel by finding a trusted phone number themselves and calling back. He also recommended paying close attention to the caller's tone of voice, choice of words and the possibility that AI voice cloning may be involved. Fam

That day, the world's attention was focused on Moscow. On July 30–31, 1991, some 3,000 journalists gathered there to witness one of the defining moments marking the end of the Cold War – the signing of a landmark arms-reduction treaty between the United States and the Soviet Union. At the same time, Lithuania was hosting the Fourth World Lithuanian Games, bringing together more than 6,000 Lithuanians from across the globe. The celebration reunited members of the Lithuanian diaspora with their homeland after decades of separation. Among the participants was future Lithuanian President Valdas Adamkus. Few could have imagined that Adamkus would instead be asked to react to images from Medininkai. "It is horrifying. There are no words in the civilised world to express the feelings, the tragedy that took place this morning," he said. The fatal shots fired on the morning of July 31 killed Vilnius Customs inspectors Antanas Musteikis, Stanislovas Orlavičius and Ričardas Rabavičius, Road Police officers Algirdas Kazlauskas and Juozas Janonis, and members of the ARAS special police response unit, Mindaugas Balavakas and Algimantas Juozakas, who were on duty at the Medininkai border post. The only survivor, customs officer Tomas Šernas, later became a key witness in the Medininkai case. LRT.lt reconstructs the events leading up to and following the Medininkai massacre in July and August 1991, based on material from the LRT archives and the newspapers Vakarinės Naujienos, Respublika, Tiesa and Lietuvos Rytas. The euphoria that followed Lithuania's declaration of independence in March 1990 had, by the summer of 1991, given way to economic hardship, pressure from Moscow, and a campaign of intimidation against the country and its officials. Soviet forces still occupied the Radio and Television Committee buildings – the present-day LRT – and the Press Palace, seized during the January crackdown, while newspapers increasingly questioned the country's chosen path. "Where have we ended up?" asked a reader identified only as A. V. from Šiauliai in a letter to the press. "People hoped for a better life, believed in Sąjūdis [the Rebirth movement] and the deputies it put forward, but so much has been turned upside down." Letters expressing similar frustration appeared almost daily. Attacks were not confined to the border. On one June evening, Soviet troops occupied Vilnius's long-distance telephone exchange for several hours. Such incidents had become part of everyday life. The day before the Medininkai killings, newspapers carried what appeared to be just another routine report from that turbulent period: "On the night of July 28, according to ELTA, five unidentified men in civilian clothes armed with automatic weapons attacked the Saločiai border checkpoint. They forced border guards to lie on the ground, took their belts, money and three portable radios, then set fire to the checkpoint building before driving towards Latvia." By July 1991, Lithuania's independence had been recognised only by Iceland, Denmark, Moldova and Slovenia, itself fighting for independence from Yugoslavia. Most Western governments still regarded developments in Lithuania as an internal Soviet matter. Despite its precarious position, Lithuania continued taking practical steps towards full independence. Temporary vouchers, known as Talonai, were due to enter circulation on August 5, beginning the difficult process of separating the country's economy from the Soviet rouble. Newspapers also celebrated the introduction of Lithuanian-designed police uniforms. Yeltsin and Landsbergis, Bush and Gorbachev Although the Soviet Union was being torn apart by internal political struggles, few realised it was living through its final summer. Only three weeks remained before the failed August coup, and less than five months before the Soviet Union collapsed. While Mikhail Gorbachev remained highly popular in the West, his support at home had steadily eroded. At the end of July, international attention shifted from the war in Yugoslavia back to Moscow, where preparations were underway for a summit between Gorbachev and US President George H W Bush. The two leaders were due to sign the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START I), a landmark agreement widely seen as another milestone marking the end of the Cold War. More than 3,000 journalists travelled to Moscow to cover the summit. Yet the Bush administration's approach to the Baltic states, and its reluctance to press their case, reflected continued support for Gorbachev despite his weakening domestic position. Backing from Washington remained crucial for the Soviet leader. Although Lithuania was not represented at the talks, its parliamentary leader, Vytautas Landsbergis, told reporters that "Lithuania will also be discussed" during the meetings. The events at Medininkai would fulfil that prediction. Even before the high-profile summit, another historic development had dealt a significant blow to the Soviet establishment. On July 29, Landsbergis and Boris Yeltsin, then president of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR), signed a treaty in Moscow recognising each other as sovereign states. Russia also acknowledged the continuity of the Lithuanian state. The RSFSR became the fifth state to grant de facto recognition to Lithuania's independence. The timing of the agreement somewhat overshadowed what had been expected to dominate the international agenda: the Bush-Gorbachev summit, which was due to begin the following day. A few days later, a Vakarinės Naujienos correspondent reflected on the possible motives behind the Medininkai killings: "What was it? Revenge for the treaty signed between the Republic of Lithuania and the Russian Federation? A deliberate attempt to undermine the Bush-Gorbachev talks in Moscow? Simple vandalism? With land routes fortified above ground, Belarusian authorities have apparently decided to take irregular migration underground. Literally. In the past week, Lithuania's border guard service (VSAT) has unearthed at least two unfinished tunnels dug from Belarus, both believed to be intended for irregular migration across the border. VSAT chief Rustamas Liubajevas revealed the finds are far from isolated. According to him, migrants' tactics have shifted toward increasingly using tunnels or caves, and border guards had identified "tens of places" where tunnels are almost certainly being dug. Liubajevas said the trend has intensified this year, though the first tunnels surfaced last year, and noted migrants had already burrowed their way through the same playbook on the Belarus-Poland border before it tunnelled its way into the Lithuanian sector. Lithuanian officials aren't buying that Minsk is in the dark on this. Liubajevas argued the tunnels' proximity to the border, plus the need to supply timber for structural supports, makes it implausible that Belarusian border guards aren't aware – or actively lending a hand – even if migrants themselves are likely doing the digging. Border guards will likely need to shore up their defences with vibration sensors and tunnel-detection gear more commonly associated with conflict zones or drug-smuggling corridors. With two incidents surfacing in under a week, expect this to keep popping up as Vilnius's new government tries to get to the bottom of its migration strategy. Talks have begun following Latvia’s finance minister's announcement that due to financial difficulties, airBaltic will likely need to shrink. The carrier posted a €44.34 million loss last year despite revenue growth, and Fitch has put the airline on negative watch. Meanwhile, Lithuania’s Transport Minister Juras Taminskas is threading the needle – no panic, but no denial either. THE CIA CASE THAT JUST WON’T DIE The country has been accused for nearly 20 years of secretly hosting a CIA prison near Vilnius, where terrorism suspects were held and interrogated between 2004-2006. Lithuania has never officially admitted this happened, but the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) keeps ruling that it did. Each time, Vilnius pays up but insists nothing new needs investigating. After the latest loss, the Justice Ministry said it would fully implement the ruling, but paired that with officials saying no further digging was needed since no such prison ever existed, and the president suggesting even the death-penalty request to the US could look like meddling in another country's affairs. But while the government calls the matter closed, opposition leaders want a new parliamentary probe, arguing three straight ECHR losses can't be squared with the authorities insisting there's nothing to find. At the same time, Lithuania's intelligence ombudsperson also declined to open a fresh investigation, citing the same existing inquiries, while leaving the door open to informal talks between agencies. Lithuania lost on Thursday its first prime minister and a signatory of the Act of the Re-Establishment of the State, Kazimira Danutė Prunskienė. Colleagues recall the diplomatic tour that earned Prunskienė the nickname the Amber Lady, as well as the tears she shed in the days before the fatal events of January 13, 1991. Former Culture and Education Minister Darius Kuolys, who served in Lithuania's first post-independence government, and independence signatory Vytenis Povilas Andriukaitis reflected on her legacy. Andriukaitis, looking back today, what mark did Prunskienė leave on Lithuanian history? Andriukaitis: An enormous one. If we look at the past 130 years of Lithuanian history, she was probably the most outstanding woman of the country's period of social and spiritual revival. Perhaps I could say that Gabrielė Petkevičaitė-Bitė was the defining figure of the first national revival, while Kazimira Prunskienė was the defining figure of the second. Kuolys, the final 14 years of Prunskienė's life were very difficult after her stroke. Yet, according to her family, she continued to follow developments in Lithuania closely. You and other members of the first government visited her regularly. What do you remember? Kuolys: She cared deeply about everything. She reacted passionately to events and, even after her stroke, would still sing together with members of the first government. I would add something to what Vytenis has said. Kazimira Prunskienė had the task of forming the first government of the restored Republic of Lithuania – the government established after March 11, 1990. It was a government led by a woman but made up entirely of men. There was not a single female minister. Looking back, it was probably Lithuania's most professional government – apart from me, the youngest and least experienced minister. The cabinet consisted of academics and professors, and the prime minister herself was a professor. It also brought together people from different political backgrounds. There was Romualdas Ozolas, the deputy prime minister and one of the leaders of the Sąjūdis independence movement, while on the other side there was Algirdas Brazauskas, leader of the Communist Party. Kazimira Prunskienė succeeded in uniting Lithuania at that time. Although she herself came from Sąjūdis [the Rebirth movement], she governed in an unmistakably democratic way. What set Prunskienė apart was that she never tried to impose her own will. It was a cabinet of independent-minded people who listened to one another, debated, argued and searched together for solutions that would benefit Lithuania. Those traditions of democratic government were established by Kazimira Prunskienė from the very first years of independence. Kuolys, did Prunskienė ever explain why she chose you for her government? You have said you were the youngest and least experienced minister, yet you clearly gained her confidence. Kuolys: Only later. It came as a great surprise to Prunskienė when the Sąjūdis leaders proposed me. It was unexpected for me, and it was unexpected for her too. But once we started working together, one thing became very clear. Alongside those democratic traditions, Prunskienė was above all a woman of action, as well as a woman of intellect. She came from academia, but she was also practical and action-oriented. The first government had to operate while Soviet troops were still stationed in Lithuania. It had no independent state budget and no national currency. Yet it was this government that had to lay the economic foundations of an independent state. Prunskienė faced enormous uncertainty. No one knew when Russian tanks might roll in, yet Lithuania still had to be built day by day. She was a woman with remarkable determination, capable both of bringing a team together and of leading it herself. Andriukaitis, when people speak about Prunskienė, they always recall her landmark diplomatic tour of the West, during which she met US President George H W Bush, UK Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President François Mitterrand. It is often said that, after those meetings, Mikhail Gorbachev had little choice but to negotiate with Lithuania. Andriukaitis: Absolutely. First of all, we must remember that from March 11, 1990, until the autumn of that year Lithuania had not yet been internationally recognised. It was very clear that, among the former Soviet republics, only Moldova recognised our independence immediately. It was therefore crucial to understand how the capitals of the world's leading countries viewed Lithuania. Her visit was prepared exceptionally well. And then there was her personal charm. Just imagine – newspapers across the world began calling her the Amber Lady. We still remember that this nickname came from the foreign press. Andriukaitis: Exactly – from the foreign media. It was clearly intended as a counterpart to the Iron Lady. Margaret Thatcher was the Iron Lady, and then this woman from the Baltic states arrived and became the Amber Lady. The word "lady" itself conveyed so much – her charm, her manners, her ease in communicating with people, her broad outlook and her exceptional communication skills. She was nothing like the stereotypical rigid functionary of the Lithuanian or Soviet Communist Party. Her visit came as a genuine surprise, and that is why the international press embraced the name Amber Lady. Kuolys, you have given several interviews today and said that you saw Prunskienė in tears. What made the prime minister cry? Kuolys: It was because of Lithuania. Kazimira Prunskienė was a sensitive person. At the time, we were still preparing for what we hoped would be another visit to Moscow, trying somehow to avert the coming blow. Before the events of January 13 [the Soviet crackdown], we could already see that Moscow was preparing for a decisive strike. Prunskienė returned from a meeting with Mikhail Gorbachev. Italian troops on Friday took over NATO’s Baltic air policing mission, replacing French and Romanian forces that had been carrying out the task. ​The air defence contingent of approximately 200 personnel began its rotation with four Eurofighter Typhoon (EF-2000) fighter jets. This marks Italy's sixth deployment to the Šiauliai airbase in northern Lithuania and its 11th in the Baltic states. ​ The outgoing French Air Force detachment consisted of about 110 personnel, while the Romanian contingent included around 100 troops, comprising pilots, medical staff, support personnel and communications specialists. ​ French forces provided protection with four Rafale aircraft, supported by six F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jets from the Romanian forces. ​ Both the French and Romanian contingents were involved in downing drones that violated Baltic airspace, with Romania doing so in Estonian territory and France in Latvian territory. ​ According to Deputy Defence Minister Bronius Bieliauskas, the actions of the previous contingents in neutralising drone threats demonstrated NATO's ability to respond quickly to airspace violations. ​ Bieliauskas also said the decision made at the NATO summit in Ankara to transition from air policing to air defence would strengthen NATO's integrated air and missile defence, providing greater flexibility and allowing for a more effective response to missiles, drones and other aerial threats. ​ NATO’s air policing mission in the Baltic states is conducted from bases in Lithuania and Estonia.

Western perceptions of Belarus remain clouded in uncertainty, despite its connections to the ongoing war in Ukraine. Understanding the hopes of Belarusian society will prove pivotal to properly engaging with the country when the conflict eventually comes to an end, Viktar Baranau writes for the New Eastern Europe magazine, partners of LRT English. Alaksandar Klacko recalls the first days of Russia’s full-scale invasion without any romanticism. For him, the war began the moment he realised that missiles striking Ukrainian cities were being launched from the territory of his own country. Soon afterwards, he joined the Belarusian volunteers of the Kalinouski Regiment fighting on Ukraine’s side. He was later wounded and now lives in Lithuania. “We understood that we were defending not only Ukraine. We were defending the future of Belarus as well,” he says. His story captures the contradiction that has shaped Belarus since February 2022. On one hand, Belarus became a crucial rear base for Russia’s invasion: Russian troops attacked Kyiv from its territory, Belarusian infrastructure supports Russian logistics, military equipment is repaired there, and Russian soldiers receive treatment in Belarusian hospitals. On the other hand, thousands of Belarusians volunteered to help Ukrainian refugees, hundreds joined Ukrainian military units, and independent surveys consistently showed strong opposition to Belarus entering the war directly. Yet, this distinction has largely disappeared from Western analysis. Belarus is increasingly portrayed as little more than an extension of Russian foreign policy. This reflects an undeniable reality: the Lukashenko regime has become deeply integrated into Russia’s war effort and, under international law, Belarus is complicit in the aggression against Ukraine. But this has also encouraged a broader assumption – that the interests of the regime, the Belarusian state and Belarusian society are essentially the same. That assumption obscures one of the most important political dynamics inside Belarus. While the regime has supported Russia’s invasion, Belarusian society has largely rejected direct participation in the war. Understanding this gap is essential not only for interpreting Lukashenko’s decisions but also for thinking about Belarus’s place in Europe’s future security architecture. Belarus being part of Russia’s war is just one part of the story In recent weeks, the question of Belarus’s role in the war has once again come to the fore. After Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russia was using navigation and communication systems located on Belarusian territory to strike Ukraine, he publicly demanded that Alexander Lukashenko stop their operation, threatening to destroy the facilities otherwise. Although Zelensky later reported that the equipment had been turned off, the situation itself once again returned Belarus to the headlines of international media and revived a familiar question: could Minsk become a direct participant in the war? Such questions have arisen regularly since February 2022. Every time Russia increases military activity or large-scale exercises are held on Belarusian territory, Western analysts again discuss the likelihood of a new offensive from the north of Ukraine. Belarus is perceived primarily as a potential Russian military springboard. This framing is quite understandable. If one judges solely by the actions of the Belarusian state, Belarus has indeed become one of the most important elements of the Russian military campaign. In January and February 2022, under the pretext of joint exercises, about 30,000 Russian servicemen were concentrated on Belarusian territory. It was from there that the advance on Kyiv began – the shortest invasion route on which the Russian command placed special bets. Russian troops used Belarusian airfields in Machulishchi, Baranovichi, and Lida, as well as radar stations and transport infrastructure. According to Ukrainian monitoring, in the first months of the war alone, at least 631 missiles were launched from Belarusian territory at Ukrainian cities. Cooperation was not limited to the first weeks of the invasion. Belarus transferred part of its equipment and ammunition from its stockpiles to Russia, provided enterprises for repairing damaged equipment, provided railway routes for supplying Russian troops, and gradually turned into an important element of the Russian military rear. According to Ukrainian intelligence, today more than five hundred Belarusian enterprises are in one way or another involved in producing goods for the Russian military-industrial complex – from electronics and optics to the repair of weapons and the production of components. Another symbol of this dependence was the deployment of Russian tactical nuclear weapons. For the first time since the collapse of the Soviet Union, Belarus has once again become a country on whose territory Russian nuclear warheads are located. Joint exercises using non-strategic nuclear weapons only cemented this role in Moscow’s strategy of nuclear blackmail. If one looks only at these facts, the conclusion seems obvious – Belarus is one of Russia’s key allies in this war. “Belarus provides its territory, infrastructure, and resources to the Russian army. From the point of view of international law, this means complicity in aggression. There can be no two interpretations,” says the former Belarusian diplomat Pavel Slunkin. But it is precisely here, in his opinion, that Western analysis often takes a further step that is no longer so obvious. Given the Belarusian regime’s participation in the war, the automatic conclusion is drawn that the interests of Moscow and Minsk completely coincide. “This is the most common mistake,” says Slunkin. “Yes, Russia and Belarus are in the same military space. Yes, the regimes support each other. But this does not mean that their interests fully coincide.” This conclusion has not only academic significance. Ind

Russia's partnership with Iran has become one of the most influential strategic partnerships in today's geopolitical landscape. While Moscow and Tehran have stopped short of a formal military alliance, their cooperation in drones, intelligence, sanctions evasion and internal security has deepened since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In an interview with RFE/RL, partners of LRT English, Nicole Grajewski, an expert on Russian-Iranian relations at Sciences Po and the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, explains how the conflicts in Ukraine and the Persian Gulf have become increasingly intertwined – and how far Russia is willing to go to support Iran. As regional strikes and maritime escalation intensify across the Persian Gulf, how is the deepening partnership between Moscow and Tehran reshaping both the war in Ukraine and the broader security crisis in the Middle East? What's fairly apparent with the current war and the war in Ukraine is how intertwined the Russia-Iran relationship is and how it's transformed. For example, Iran provided Russia with the Shahed drones that were used quite extensively in Ukraine. In return, Russia has been providing crucial support to Iran when it comes to satellite imagery, potentially targeting support, as well as training, operational assistance, and data sharing. So there's a kind of synergy that actually derived from the war in Ukraine, and you see it translating into this current war. Additionally, many of the same threats that Ukrainians face on a daily basis are what US Gulf allies are currently facing. During the war, Ukraine reached out to Gulf partners when it came to counter-UAV and counter-drone warfare. There are a lot of connections between these two wars, and I think it's a mistake not to analyse them together because they're inextricably tied through the two actors involved, but also through the same technologies and the sharing of resources. Iran's drone and missile technologies proved critical for Russia's campaign in Ukraine. But as Tehran faces mounting threats in the Gulf, is Moscow returning the favour, or is it holding back its own military resources for the Ukrainian front? It's unclear what Russian technology has been transferred and what has appeared in Iranian UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles). It is very clear, though, that Iran's strategy, tactics, and even operational methods have improved, and they share some similarities with Russia's use of these systems in Ukraine. But we don't see Russia transferring a single major weapon system to Iran. The last reported transfer was the Financial Times report about the Verba MANPADS deal [a reported December 2025 agreement for Iran to acquire Russian-made shoulder-fired air-defence missiles]. Since the war, there hasn't been a direct transfer of a complete weapons system. However, because Iran has – or at least before the war had – a fairly robust defence industry and military-industrial complex, Russia can provide components and subcomponents that allow Iran to iteratively improve its UAVs. From what we know so far in this campaign, there are some indications that this is happening, although there hasn't been a smoking gun identifying exactly which components have been transferred. Tehran has long looked to Moscow for advanced air defences and electronic warfare systems. Given the demands of the war in Ukraine, does Russia still have either the capacity or the political willingness to strengthen Iran's defences? It depends on what we're talking about because Russia excels in producing certain systems more than others. For example, much of Iran's defensive electronic warfare capability comes from Russia, and we don't know whether the Russians have transferred offensive electronic warfare capabilities that simply haven't been reported yet. It's also unclear whether Russia has helped Iran rebuild radar systems that were destroyed, but that's another area where it could provide assistance. The biggest issue – and this is where it really comes back to the war in Ukraine – is air defense systems. Russia is in a difficult position when it comes to providing those because it needs them itself, and Iran also lacks the financial resources to purchase them. But there are other ways Russia can provide incremental improvements to Iranian capabilities. That could include light arms or drone subcomponents. So it's not really accurate to say that Russia is so tied down in Ukraine that it can't provide Iran with anything. If anything, it's still able to support Iran in the areas where Tehran needs it most. You've argued that Russia risks looking like a fair-weather partner after developments in Syria and Venezuela. If Iran were to face an existential military crisis, would Moscow step in – or leave Tehran to fend for itself? That's a really interesting question, and we haven't really seen that with this current war, even though at certain points it appeared that the Islamic Republic of Iran was facing an existential crisis. Iran is very different from Syria for Russia. Iran is largely independent. It has its own capabilities and can challenge American power directly in ways Syria or Venezuela couldn't. It also has a highly bureaucratised and relatively advanced military organisation that is spread across the country. So we haven't seen Russia being necessary in that sense. However, if the situation reached the brink of civil war or widespread chaos, with the regime collapsing and being replaced by something resembling the vacuum we saw in Syria, then I do think Russia would become involved. That could mean special operations forces or potentially private military contractors. I don't think we would see a large Russian military deployment or an air campaign similar to Syria. It would be much more measured, focused on providing operational support to whatever remnants of the Iranian government Russia chose to back. Sergei Smirnov, editor-in-chief of the independent Russian news outlet Mediazona, said he is leaving Lithuania for France, citing what he described as a worsening climate for Russian opposition figures following an unsuccessful attempt to revoke the residence permit of opposition activist Leonid Volkov. Smirnov announced his decision in comments reported on the social media platform X by the independent Russian outlet SOTA. “I think the situation in Lithuania will become increasingly difficult, also because of its proximity to Russia,” Smirnov said. “I want to draw attention to Lithuanian politicians’ comments regarding Leonid Volkov. They all unanimously said everything was very bad and that his residence permit should be revoked. In the end, the authorities refused to do so, but the overall atmosphere is one of pressure and suspicion.” Smirnov did not say when he plans to relocate. His announcement comes about a month after he said Mediazona had lost donations from Russia worth about 10 million rubles (about 108,000 euros) a year, forcing the outlet to rethink its finances. “With Russian donations gone, we once again have to think about survival,” Smirnov said at the time. Founded in 2014 by Maria Alyokhina and Nadezhda Tolokonnikova, members of the feminist protest group Pussy Riot, Mediazona focuses on Russia’s law enforcement, courts and prison system and has become one of the country’s best-known independent media organisations. Volkov, a close ally of the late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, has lived in Lithuania since 2019 after leaving Russia, where authorities opened a criminal case against him. Russia placed him on its wanted list in 2021. In June, Lithuanian authorities granted Volkov a permanent residence permit after reviewing his application, intelligence assessments and other information. The decision came after Lithuania’s State Security Department concluded that Volkov did not pose a threat to national security. Earlier this year, Volkov drew controversy in Lithuania after criticising far-right Russian volunteers fighting on Ukraine’s side. His comments celebrating the reported killing of Denis Kapustin, the commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps, were made in a private exchange of online messages and were published without his knowledge. The comments prompted criticism from Lithuania’s political leaders, with some lawmakers calling on Volkov to leave the country voluntarily. The Migration Department subsequently asked the State Security Department to assess whether Volkov’s remarks posed a threat to Lithuania’s national security. The agency concluded they did not. Volkov later apologised for the message, describing it as “stupid”, emotional and wrong. In March 2024, Volkov was attacked with a hammer while sitting in his car near his home in Vilnius. Lithuanian authorities later linked the assault to individuals acting on behalf of Russian interests.

Lithuania is making progress toward normalising relations with China, Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said after meeting with Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys. Olekas said Lithuania’s goal is to maintain relations with Beijing at the same level as other European Union member states. “This objective is included in the government’s program, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is working to achieve results,” Olekas said, according to a statement from the parliament, Seimas. Budrys said Lithuania’s position on China has remained unchanged, emphasising the need for a unified European approach to Beijing as part of the EU’s common foreign and security policy. The foreign minister said differing policies among EU member states toward bilateral relations with China create opportunities for Beijing to influence individual countries and weaken the bloc’s role as a global actor. “Different approaches among EU countries allow China to manipulate countries and reduce the European Union’s influence,” Budrys said. The ruling coalition has recently stepped up discussions on restoring more normal diplomatic relations with China, though the talks have not yet produced concrete changes. The government’s program commits Lithuania to seeking the normalisation of “diplomatic relations with China to the level of diplomatic representation that exists in other EU member states”. Relations between Vilnius and Beijing deteriorated in 2021 after Lithuania allowed Taiwan to open a representative office in the country under its own name. China responded by downgrading diplomatic ties and taking economic measures against Lithuanian exports. Lithuania has since sought to maintain its support for Taiwan while also exploring ways to improve relations with China in line with the broader EU approach.

A Lithuanian powerlifting volunteer has been banned for life and reported to police after allegedly admitting he deliberately sabotaged a Belgian athlete's world record attempt because he was "a racist". At last month's World Classic Powerlifting Championships in Lithuania, Belgian lifter Sonita Muluh squatted 334.5kg – a weight that would have set a new women's world record. ​ However, her attempt was ruled invalid after the barbell made contact with the leg of Lithuanian spotter Ernestas Kusinas. ​ Initially, Muluh believed the incident had been an accident. But Kusinas later wrote on social media that he had intentionally ruined the lift because he was "racist". ​ Five spotters assist athletes during such lifts – two on each side of the barbell and one behind the lifter. Video footage of Muluh's successful 321.5kg squat shows the same spotters widening their stance as they squat alongside the athlete to avoid interfering with the lift. ​ During the final attempt, however, the weight plate appears to make contact with Kusinas's leg. Instagram users later drew attention to comments allegedly posted by Kusinas, in which he admitted intentionally invalidating the lift because the athlete was Black. ​ Racist comments and neo-Nazi slogan ​ The failed lift attracted wider attention in mid-July after American powerlifter and bodybuilder Joe Sullivan highlighted the incident. ​ On his Instagram account, which has around 150,000 followers, Sullivan shared footage showing the barbell plate hitting the Lithuanian volunteer's leg. ​ Reacting to the video, Sullivan wrote that "this should not have happened" and questioned why the spotters did not know how to protect an athlete properly during a world championship squat. ​ Kusinas himself joined the discussion in the comments. ​ "I'm racist and I did it on purpose because I hate you," Kusinas wrote with further expletives. "No one got stuck except for one monkey relative." He ended the comment with the number 88, which in neo-Nazi circles is widely recognised as a coded reference to the slogan "Heil Hitler". A post shared by Muluh Sonita🦸🏾‍♀️ (@sonita_ml) The comments were later deleted, but users had already taken screenshots. Some of Sullivan's followers wrote that he had inadvertently exposed racism at the championships. ​ Photos also began circulating online from Kusinas' social media accounts, allegedly showing him wearing a Nazi eagle badge on his chest. ​ By the time this article was published, the photos and other content had been removed from his social media profiles. ​ Other athletes also responded. Popular British powerlifter Nathaniel Massiah posted a video on Instagram explaining that he had competed at the same championships in Druskininkai, where Kusinas had also served as his spotter. ​ Although Massiah completed his attempts without incident, he questioned what might have happened had Muluh suffered a serious injury because of an intentionally sabotaged lift. His post generated thousands of comments and hundreds of thousands of reactions. ​ Muluh herself also responded to the racist remarks. A post shared by Muluh Sonita🦸🏾‍♀️ (@sonita_ml) A post shared by IPF Powerlifting (@theipf) The IPF condemned racism, praised the Lithuanian federation's response and said it would consider tightening procedures for recruiting, vetting, accrediting and supervising volunteers at competitions. ​ In Lithuania, police will also assess Kusinas's social media statements. ​ "We contacted the police on Monday and submitted a complaint regarding his statements and alleged public incitement to hatred," Barauskas said. ​ No previous incidents ​ The LJTF president said he had also spoken directly with Kusinas, who claimed his comments had been a reaction to online criticism. ​ "I spoke to him. He explained that he reacted that way because he couldn't cope with the pressure on social media and started saying those kinds of things," Barauskas said. ​ The federation also said it had been unaware of photographs allegedly showing Kusinas with Nazi symbols on his social media accounts. Barauskas added that no similar incidents had occurred previously. ​ "He has volunteered as a spotter at our championships for several years, and it never crossed anyone's mind that something like this could happen or that he held such views. ​ "What's more, we hosted the same World Championships in 2024, and the same Belgian athlete competed. If you watch the footage from then, you'll see him encouraging and supporting her. That's why what happened came as a complete shock to us." ​ LRT.lt contacted Kusinas for comment but received no response. ​ Barauskas said the federation had not yet contacted Muluh because it was awaiting the outcome of the Lithuanian authorities' assessment. ​ Afterwards, it plans to contact its international partners and the athlete to explain what further steps it intends to take. ​ This year's World Championships had originally been scheduled to take place in the United Arab Emirates. However, due to the war in the Middle East, the IPF asked Lithuania to host the event instead, as the country had successfully organised the championships previously. ​ The 2024 World Championships were also held in Druskininkai. ​ MP backs Belgian athlete ​ Olympic champion, Lithuanian MP, and member of the Lithuanian parliament's Youth and Sports Affairs Commission, Laura Asadauskaitė, told LRT.lt that she had not previously heard about the incident in Druskininkai. ​ However, she described the volunteer's alleged conduct as unacceptable and supported the federation's decision to impose a lifetime ban. ​ "This is absolutely unacceptable. I believe the punishment is justified because it was a deeply dishonourable act. It is also very sad that it happened – and that it happened in Lithuania," she said. ​ She also expressed her support for the Belgian athlete. ​ "I fully support the athlete, and I believe many others do too.
