Lithuania’s Defence Ministry and military are pursuing an ambitious plan to integrate mobile phones, surveillance cameras, radars and other sensors into a single artificial intelligence-powered airspace monitoring system, following a series of incidents involving drones and heightened concerns over regional air defence. The initiative comes as officials point to recent security incidents, including a Russian missile that landed in Poland and drones entering or approaching Lithuanian airspace. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said the missile incident underscored the need to strengthen air defense capabilities. Last year, Russian-made Gerbera drones were detected in Lithuania. This year, Ukrainian drones headed toward targets in Russia have also crossed into the Baltic state. In several cases, objects either crashed on their own and were recorded by civilian surveillance cameras or disappeared from radar tracking and were never found. “We have a clear vision and concept for implementing an integrated, rather than fragmented, air defence system,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said. Kaunas said Ukrainian experts had reviewed the concept. “Ukrainians helped us stay on the right path,” he said. The military and the Defence Ministry have now tasked industry with developing the system. “We want to connect all detection capabilities available in Lithuania into a single system. That requires software based on artificial intelligence,” Kaunas said. Industry representatives and defence analysts described the project as highly ambitious. “The project is certainly ambitious. It would be ambitious not only for Lithuania, but globally,” said Vincas Jurgutis, a representative of Lithuania’s Defence and Security Industry Association. Retired Maj. Darius Antanaitis said the proposal envisions integrating a wide range of sensors. “The project is very ambitious. It includes artificial intelligence and various sensors, such as surveillance cameras. Even mobile phone cameras and microphones could potentially be connected,” he said. Experts note that detecting and intercepting small drones remains a challenge not only for Lithuania but for NATO as a whole. Finland, for example, has used airships to help monitor its border with Russia. Antanaitis said a broad sensor network could help identify small aerial targets that conventional radar systems often struggle to detect. “We could see very small targets across a 1-square-kilometer area and at altitudes up to 3,000 meters, where many radars cannot detect them,” he said. Meanwhile, Vilnius Gediminas Technical University is already participating in a related NATO project with US and Ukrainian partners. “We are developing artificial intelligence combined with sensor technologies so the system can identify incoming objects well in advance,” said Mantas Mieželis, a defence and security expert at the university. Analysts say Ukraine’s experience in drone warfare offers valuable lessons, but they caution that Lithuania faces different geographic challenges. “Forty kilometres in Ukraine is nothing, but 40 kilometres in Lithuania is the distance from the Belarusian border to Vilnius,” Antanaitis said. While Kaunas said he hopes to see results within a year, industry representatives and experts warned that deployment could take longer. “We do not yet know exactly what technological tools we will need or which specific sensors will be used,” Mieželis said. “If we are talking about pilot projects and prototypes, those could be developed within a year,” Jurgutis said. Antanaitis said one of the biggest challenges will be integrating existing systems without requiring entirely new infrastructure. The debate comes as Lithuanian troops continue searching for a drone that recently disappeared after entering the country’s airspace. The Defence Ministry has earmarked at least 2 billion euros for air defence over the next four years. Opposition lawmakers argue that significantly more funding is needed. Laurynas Kasčiūnas, a conservative member of parliament and former defence minister, said an additional 4 billion to 4.5 billion euros by 2030 would allow Lithuania to build a layered air defence system capable of protecting critical infrastructure, strategic facilities, cities and residents. “We do not have the billions that have been calculated as necessary, which means we must take a different path,” Kaunas said. Opposition politicians counter that with defence spending at record levels, the issue is one of priorities. The government has identified air defence as one of its three most important defence objectives.

The Ministry of the Interior is set to propose to the government that operations at the ‘Paternieki’ border crossing between Latvia and Belarus be suspended, according to a publicly available draft government decision prepared by the ministry. If the government endorses the ministry’s proposal, this will effectively mean that residents and lorries will no longer be able to enter Belarus from Latvia. At present, ‘Paternieki’ is the only official road border crossing on the Latvian-Belarusian border. At the same time, the ‘Indra’ railway border crossing remains in operation, although it is used exclusively by freight trains. Passengers have been unable to enter Belarus by air for several years now. The draft government decision has now been submitted for approval. It is expected that the Cabinet will consider it as a matter of urgency. The move is necessary to safeguard the integrity of the state, prevent threats to public order, create even more favourable conditions for the State Border Guard Service and other relevant agencies to carry out their duties in preventing the illegal crossing of the state border, and to optimise the resources available to the Border Guard Service in a crisis situation, notes the Ministry of the Interior. The Ministry points out that, in fact, the pressure from irregular migration remains as high as ever and requires significant resources from the border guards and other services. Under the law, when a regime of enhanced border security is declared, the Cabinet of Ministers is authorised to impose one or more measures across the entire border area or part thereof, including the full or partial suspension of operations at specific border crossing points. The Ministry of the Interior notes that Belarus has, for a long time, continued to allow and encourage the uncontrolled, illegal crossing of its state border by third parties, thereby deliberately posing a threat to the security of its neighbouring country, Latvia; this is reflected, amongst other things, in the unjustified administrative burden placed on state resources. Enhanced border security measures have now been put in place along the Latvian-Belarusian border to prevent illegal border crossings, thereby enabling the Border Guard and other agencies involved to prevent such crossings. However, the ‘Paternieki’ border crossing point, established on the motorway – a border control post on the Latvian-Belarusian border – continues to operate under these conditions, thereby maintaining greater scope for conducting a protracted hybrid war against Latvia, as well as serving as an additional tool for exerting pressure, carrying out provocations and conducting intelligence operations, the Ministry of the Interior noted. As previously reported, technical faults were detected in the information systems at the ‘Paternieki’ border control post, as a result of which it has not been possible to carry out border checks since July 31. The State Border Guard Service told journalists that those wishing to cross the border should look for other nearby border crossing points located in Lithuania. The government has extended the enhanced border security regime in the Belarusian border region until the end of this year. It was introduced due to the increased flow of irregular migrants caused by Belarus. Enhanced control measures are in place in Ludza and the parishes of the Ludza district, in Kraslava and the parishes of that district, in the Augšdaugava district, in Daugavpils and the Kaunata parish of the Rēzekne district. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said Monay that Vilnius cannot rule out the possibility that Russia deliberately targeted Lithuania’s embassy in Kyiv when two Russian missiles damaged the diplomatic mission over the weekend. “That possibility cannot be ruled out, although we cannot confirm it at this stage,” Budrys told LRT TV. The minister said there were no significant strategic facilities near the embassy other than a power plant about 1.5 kilometres away that Russia has previously sought to strike. “Everything else there is residential housing, except for our embassy,” Budrys said. “Perhaps the aim was to exert pressure or intimidate us, but it has been completely unsuccessful. Our resolve has only grown stronger.” Two Russian missiles landed about 5 metres and 150 metres from Lithuania’s embassy in Kyiv’s Pechersk district during overnight strikes on Saturday, damaging window frames, shattering glass and causing damage to the roof and solar panels, Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said. No embassy staff were injured. Following the attack, Lithuania summoned a representative of the Russian Embassy in Vilnius to deliver a formal diplomatic protest, saying Moscow’s actions constituted a flagrant violation of the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. Budrys said Russia had offered no apology for the incident. He said the embassy had been struck by Zircon hypersonic missiles, weapons designed primarily to target ships, while adding that Lithuania does not know the intended target of the attack. According to Budrys, the Russian representative argued that Lithuania had been warned of the danger because all of Kyiv had been under threat. “We treat such warnings as a threat,” the minister said. In its diplomatic note, Lithuania said it would seek compensation from Russia for the damage caused to the embassy and reserved the right to take further retaliatory measures. “We have planned measures that we could take in response to Russian actions directed against us,” Budrys said. “I would not like to go into details now, but we have the capabilities, the tools and the will to defend ourselves if necessary.”

Lithuania is seeking to establish production of Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles on its territory under a bilateral defence industry cooperation agreement, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Tuesday. The initiative would be carried out through joint investments under a defence industry cooperation agreement signed by Lithuania and Ukraine in May, Kaunas said. “We have an agreement with Ukraine known as the drone deal,” Kaunas told the business daily Verslo žinios. “Changes are currently being made within the ministry’s team to bring in key personnel who will begin translating that agreement into practical solutions on the ground, so that we can localize Ukrainian drone production in Lithuania.” Kaunas said the drones would be manufactured in Lithuania using technology acquired from Ukraine. According to the minister, the project would benefit both countries by expanding Ukraine’s production capacity while strengthening Lithuania’s defence industry through new manufacturing capabilities, technological advances and opportunities for Lithuanian engineers to work alongside Ukrainian specialists. Elijus Čivilis, chief executive of the investment promotion agency Invest Lithuania, has previously said that several Ukrainian defence industry investors had received approval from Lithuania’s commission reviewing transactions that meet national security interests to begin operating in the country. In June, Kaunas invited Luxembourg-based drone manufacturer Luxuav, which was founded by Ukrainians, to carry out testing in Lithuania.

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys on Monday said NATO should respond more forcefully after a Russian missile landed in eastern Poland last week, arguing that the alliance must reinforce its military presence and adopt a stronger political stance following the incident. “There is a desire to remain calm, but to respond firmly,” Budrys said in an interview on LRT TV. “We have managed to remain calm. But that firm response should follow this incident, first and foremost through military capabilities.” Budrys said previous NATO efforts to bolster forces in the region had helped deter further incidents. “The Eastern Sentinel and Baltic Sentry operations showed that when we increase our military presence in the region – something Russia finds unacceptable – it takes precautionary measures. Incidents involving Poland stopped, and damage to infrastructure in the Baltic Sea also ceased,” he said. He added that this did not necessarily mean every previous incident had been deliberate. “It does not mean that every case was planned or carried out intentionally,” Budrys said. “But after this event, the response should be exactly the same.” Polish authorities said Thursday that a roughly 10-metre-wide crater was discovered in the eastern Lublin region following an explosion during a new wave of Russian missile attacks on Ukraine. Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile manufactured near Moscow. A spokesperson for the Lublin prosecutor’s office said a Ukrainian expert had no doubts about the missile’s origin or model. A spokesperson for Poland’s Foreign Ministry said the Kh-101 missile is used exclusively by Russia’s strategic aviation. NATO confirmed that the object that landed in Poland was a Russian missile, condemned the incident and said it remains in close contact with Warsaw. The alliance also pledged to continue taking all necessary measures to defend the territory of its member states. “If there is a shortage of capabilities, we must increase them because we cannot normalise situations in which missiles enter our airspace,” Budrys said. “Ultimately, the political response from the alliance as an organisation could certainly have been stronger.” The missile landed near the village of Tarnawa Kolonia in eastern Poland, about 80 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, during an overnight Russian attack in which Moscow launched 74 missiles and 284 drones against Ukraine. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian missiles and drones have struck several countries in Eastern Europe, particularly Romania and Moldova.

China has imposed export restrictions on Lithuanian laser manufacturer Ekspla, limiting its ability to purchase dual-use goods and technologies from Chinese suppliers in what appears to be retaliation for the European Union’s latest sanctions against Russia. China’s Ministry of Commerce said the measures, which took effect July 24, place 14 European Union entities on its export control list. Under the restrictions, Chinese exporters must obtain approval before supplying dual-use goods, software or technologies that can be used for both civilian and military purposes. Ekspla is the only Lithuanian company included on the list. Other affected entities include companies and research institutions in Germany, France, Italy, Poland, the Netherlands, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria. The ministry said the decision was made under China’s Export Control Law and dual-use export control regulations to safeguard national security and fulfil international non-proliferation obligations. Ekspla said it had not been formally notified of the reasons for its inclusion and was assessing the practical impact of the restrictions. “We have not been informed separately about the reasons for this decision, so we do not know the specific grounds for our inclusion,” the company said in a statement. “Ekspla does not manufacture, sell or develop military products, nor do we have information that our products are used for military purposes.” The company said components sourced from China account for less than 8% of its total purchases after it diversified its supply chain in recent years. Ekspla said it is still determining which imported components could be classified as dual-use items but expects only a small portion of its Chinese supplies to be affected. It added that it has inventories of some components and is already seeking alternative suppliers outside China. The restrictions are therefore unlikely to affect the technical characteristics, performance or quality of its products, the company said, although delivery times could be extended in some cases during the transition to new suppliers. The measures appear to be China’s response to the European Union’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, adopted on July 23. The package added 51 entities to the bloc’s export control list for allegedly supporting Russia’s military-industrial base, including several Chinese companies. Lithuania’s Economy and Innovation Ministry said it is assessing the potential impact of China’s decision, remains in contact with the European Commission and is gathering information on its consequences for Ekspla and its supply chains. The ministry said it is also working with other relevant institutions to ensure a coordinated response and safeguard Lithuanian business interests. China remains one of Lithuania’s largest import partners. Lithuania imported goods worth 2.26 billion euros from China in 2025, accounting for 4.3% of total imports. Exports to China totalled 238 million euros, or 0.5% of Lithuania’s total exports.

A group of  migrants attacked Lithuanian border guards after entering the country through a tunnel on the border with Belarus, news portal Delfi reported on Wednesday. The incident occurred on July 26 in the area of the Kapciamiestis border station, but the State Border Guard Service had not previously disclosed the incident publicly. According to Delfi, border guards detected a tunnel being dug under the state border and waited for migrants to come through. When the first people emerged from the tunnel, four officers detained them and put them in handcuffs. However, about 20 more migrants then emerged from the tunnel and attacked the officers, forcing them to retreat, according to Delfi. The migrants, including those in handcuffs, fled back into Belarusian territory. The State Border Guard Service (VSAT) previously announced the discovery of a tunnel but did not disclose the attack on its officers. VSAT spokesperson Lina Laurinaityte said on Wednesday that information about the assault would be released once permission was granted by the prosecutor's office leading the pre-trial investigation. According to the official, neither the officers nor the migrants were injured during the incident.

Lithuania has no evidence that Russia deliberately targeted its embassy in Kyiv during missile strikes last week that damaged the diplomatic mission, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said. “No, we do not have such information,” Budrys said in an interview with the business daily Verslo žinios published Wednesday. “Based on what we know at this point, we believe the damage was not accidental in the sense that the missiles struck very close to our premises, but we do not believe the embassy itself was the intended target,” he said. In earlier comments to LRT TV about the incident, Budrys had speculated that the possibility of Russia targeting the Lithuanian embassy deliberately “cannot be ruled out, although we cannot confirm it at this stage”. In the Verslo žinios interview, Budrys said there were no apparent military or other strategic targets near the embassy, although a thermal power plant about 1.5 kilometres away has been repeatedly targeted by Russian forces. “That power plant could have been the intended target, but the strikes landed extremely close to us,” he said. “One crater was only a few meters from our fence, while the other was about 150 meters from our premises.” The minister said Russia remains responsible under international law for ensuring the safety of diplomatic missions and that Lithuania is seeking compensation for the damage. “The damage is obvious. Windows at our embassy were shattered and the roof was damaged,” Budrys said. “We will not leave this as it is. What Russia is doing in Kyiv by attacking sites that have nothing to do with military objectives constitutes crimes.” Two Russian missile strikes during an overnight attack on Kyiv on Saturday damaged the Lithuanian embassy, shattering windows, damaging window frames, the roof and rooftop solar panels. No embassy staff were injured. The attack was condemned by Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry has summoned a Russian diplomatic representative to lodge a formal protest, saying the attack constituted a flagrant violation of the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. The ministry has also demanded that Russia compensate Lithuania for the damage caused to its embassy.

Vilnius City Municipality will no longer accept written requests or complaints submitted in Russian, it said on Tuesday. The changes are presented as part of the capital’s integration plan for foreign residents aimed at strengthening the use of Lithuania’s official language. The municipality also said it has removed Russian from its website and electronic queue management systems. Mayor Valdas Benkunskas said the measures implement a policy adopted earlier this year to reinforce the use of Lithuanian in public services. “We are consistently implementing the decision adopted in the spring to strengthen the use of the state language,” Benkunskas said in a statement. About one tenth of Vilnius’ residents identify as ethnic Russians, according to the 2021 census. According to the mayor, more than 1,000 foreign residents have attended Lithuanian language courses over the past several months, while the number of Russian-language preschool groups in Vilnius has fallen by 40%. The municipality said it is expanding opportunities for foreigners to learn Lithuanian. More than 1,000 people are expected to receive training this year through free language courses and remote learning programs backed by an additional 300,000 euros in municipal funding. Language clubs will open across the capital this autumn, while an independent online Lithuanian language learning platform for foreign residents is expected to become available by the end of the year. The municipality also said the number of Russian-language preschool groups in Vilnius has declined from 181 to 112 over the past three years. It added that primary education for children of non-EU citizens is now conducted exclusively in Lithuanian. According to Lithuania’s Migration Department, about 186,000 people held temporary residence permits in the country as of June, while about 21,000 held permanent residence permits.

A court in Russia’s Kaliningrad region has sentenced a Lithuanian citizen to 13 1/2 years in prison on espionage charges, Russia’s Interfax news agency reported Wednesday. According to the report, the Lithuanian national was found guilty of spying for about 13 years and will serve the sentence in a maximum-security penal colony. Russian authorities did not disclose the person’s identity. Interfax said the court found that the Lithuanian citizen collected and passed on information classified as a state secret while in Russia between 2011 and 2024. The report said authorities confiscated the person’s mobile phone and what they described as specialised equipment allegedly used for espionage. Lithuania’s State Security Department (VSD), the intelligence agency, said it was aware of the case but declined to comment any further. “The VSD is aware of the information published in the media, but we cannot provide any public comments on it. Consular assistance to Lithuanian citizens abroad is provided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” the VSD was quoted by the Elta news agency.

During one of the largest attacks on western Ukraine on July 30, a Russian missile crossed into Polish airspace for the first time before crashing on Polish territory. Yet, Poland's response was restraint – was that a mistake? Warsaw decided not to shoot down the Russian missile while it was in Polish airspace, arguing that it posed no immediate threat. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland had been prepared to intercept it if it had continued farther into the country. ​ Although experts understand the decision from a safety perspective, they warn that failing to respond decisively to an incident of this scale sets a dangerous precedent. In their view, it demonstrates that Russia can exploit NATO airspace for its operations and manoeuvres without facing consequences. ​ "Declarations of 'readiness to shoot down missiles should they advance further' do not solve the problem of the systemic penetration of Russian strike assets deep into territories whose security NATO guarantees," aviation expert Bohdan Dolintse told LRT.lt. ​ Warsaw confirmed that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile entered eastern Poland and exploded there. The missile carried a substantial explosive payload. Fortunately, it landed in an uninhabited area and caused no casualties. ​ "This is one of the most unprecedented incidents on NATO's eastern flank since the start of the war," Dolintse said. ​ Polish officials stressed that Poland itself had not been the intended target. However, at least 12 other missiles flying over western Ukraine that night were also considered capable of posing a threat to Polish airspace. ​ "Russian missile and drone incursions into NATO territory during Russian strikes on Ukraine appear to be a risk the Kremlin has accepted," the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in its assessment of the incident. A dangerous precedent in NATO airspace ​ "Neutralisation would be the right answer in political terms as Russians understand only force when it comes to the confrontation," Piotr Woyke, director of the Brussels-based Eastern Flank Institute, told LRT.lt. ​ The incident exposed shortcomings in Poland's developing layered air defence system, while also highlighting that NATO's decision-making process – from identifying a target to authorising its destruction – remains too slow to deal effectively with low-flying cruise missiles. ​ Experts told LRT.lt that Poland and NATO's eastern flank should now focus on strengthening air defence by building a dense radar network capable of detecting low-flying targets, ensuring real-time radar intelligence sharing between Ukraine and NATO, and creating mobile fire units to counter drones and cruise missiles, drawing on Ukraine's experience. ​ They argue that such measures would reduce the need to use expensive surface-to-air missiles against relatively cheap drones. ​ Warsaw also confirmed that a Ukrainian fighter pilot attempted to intercept the Russian missile that night but had to turn back because he was unable to enter Polish airspace. The restrictions were not only procedural but also reflected the significant risk that Polish fighter jets could mistakenly shoot down a Ukrainian aircraft. ​ The incident has therefore raised questions about whether NATO should rethink the architecture of air defence on its eastern flank, giving Ukraine a far greater role than it currently plays. ​ "NATO may need to consider negotiating possible air defence agreements with Ukraine as a matter of self-defence against Russian drone strikes against NATO countries, regardless of whether the Russian drone incursions are accidental or intentional," the Institute for the Study of War said. ​ Dolintse argued that intercepting missiles over Ukraine before they reach NATO territory would be a logical and practical step, giving NATO countries valuable extra time to detect, track and destroy incoming targets. ​ However, experts stress that such decisions should be taken collectively by the alliance rather than by individual member states. ​ They identify the main obstacle as a lack of political resolve among allies – something Moscow continues to exploit successfully. ​ NATO recently announced that its Baltic Air Policing mission would transition into an air defence mission. However, what this means in practice – and whether it would include authority to shoot down incoming missiles – remains unclear. ​ 'From the Kremlin's perspective we are already part of this conflict' ​Experts argue that every drone incursion, and now this missile entering NATO airspace, should be viewed as part of Russia's standard tactic of reconnaissance by force. ​ By doing so, the Kremlin tests NATO's reaction time, technical capabilities and political resolve. ​ "They are probing where the real 'red lines' actually run, rather than empty political declarations of concern," Dolintse said, explaining Moscow's willingness to take such risks. ​ At the same time, the Kremlin advances broader strategic objectives by attempting to sow doubt about whether NATO countries are able to protect their own airspace, as well as undermine allied unity by fuelling debate over continued support for Ukraine. ​ According to the director of the Eastern Flank Institute, this makes a firm response essential. ​ "One clear signal and it’s not the first time: from the Kremlin's perspective we are already part of this conflict – as nations supporting Ukraine, as NATO and as a collective West. ​ "We can’t show weakness in front of his provocations, because they will only become more and more aggressive," Woyke said.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius sought to reassure the public Thursday after the country’s defence minister warned that Russia could stage “false flag” attacks against critical infrastructure in the Baltic region using Ukrainian drones. Sinkevičius said hybrid threats against Lithuania remain real but stressed that the overall threat level has not changed significantly. “A certain level of threat exists. We have faced various hybrid attacks before, including the use of illegal migrants from Belarus, as well as drones and balloons,” Sinkevičius told reporters. “The threats remain, but I would not say that citizens should be additionally worried.” His comments came after media reports citing Lithuanian military intelligence said Russia is considering attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic states using captured Ukrainian drones to conceal responsibility and deny attacking NATO territory. Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas confirmed earlier Thursday that Lithuanian intelligence has information suggesting Moscow is assessing such scenarios, although he said there was no indication Russia had decided to carry out an attack or that one was imminent. Sinkevičius said any public statements about security threats must be carefully considered to avoid unnecessarily alarming the public. “The state is preparing and doing its work quietly. We do not explain everything because we do not want unfriendly neighbouring states to know too much,” he said. “We monitor the situation, assess it and will always respond appropriately.” “I want to reassure society that the threat level has not changed dramatically. It exists,” the prime minister added. “The war continues in Ukraine, Russian aggression continues, and we are seeing various incidents not only in Lithuania but also in Germany, involving drones and explosives. As wars approach their climax, there is often desperation.” Sinkevičius said “false flag” operations were possible not only in Lithuania but elsewhere in the Baltic region and Poland, although he emphasised that authorities were protecting critical infrastructure. He said he had recently visited the liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipėda and had also received briefings from military commanders and Kaunas on the security of strategic sites, including the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydroelectric Plant, the LitPol Link electricity interconnection with Poland, railway hubs and electricity substations. Lithuania’s armed forces have been assisting the Public Security Service in protecting key energy infrastructure since June 18, including the LNG terminal in Klaipėda, the LitPol Link substation in Alytus, a transformer substation in Alytus district and the Kruonis power plant. Leaders of NATO’s eastern flank have recently said they possess intelligence indicating Russia may be preparing kinetic provocations against alliance members. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda has previously warned that the country’s transport and energy infrastructure could become targets of both conventional attacks and sabotage.

Lithuanian military intelligence says it has information indicating that Russia is considering using Ukrainian-made drones to carry out attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region, with the aim of obscuring responsibility for any strikes, according to a report published Thursday by 15min.lt. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas confirmed the assessment to the outlet. “We have data that Russia is considering conducting unconventional kinetic attacks against critical infrastructure in the Baltic region,” Kaunas was quoted as saying. “It is likely that Russia could use Ukrainian-made drones for this purpose.” The minister did not provide details about potential targets or the timing of any possible attacks. According to the report, Russia could deploy captured Ukrainian drones in an attempt to create uncertainty over the origin of an attack and deny responsibility for striking NATO territory. Military drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Some incidents were attributed to Ukrainian drones that had been diverted or disoriented by Russian electronic warfare. Officials in several countries, however, have claimed that Moscow may be deliberately directing drones into the airspace of Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Poland and Finland. Leaders in several NATO countries on the alliance’s eastern flank have recently said they possess intelligence suggesting Russia is preparing kinetic provocations against their countries. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda has previously warned that the country’s critical transport and energy infrastructure could become targets of both conventional attacks and acts of sabotage. Since June 18, Lithuania’s armed forces have been assisting the Public Security Service in protecting key infrastructure, including the liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipėda, the LitPol Link electricity interconnection with Poland in Alytus, a transformer substation in Alytus district and the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydroelectric Plant. On July 17, Kaunas signed an order extending the military’s support for those security operations through August 19. Under the order, the armed forces are to deploy up to 30 soldiers, transport vehicles and a vessel with its crew to assist in protecting the sites. Moscow has denied allegations that it is planning attacks on NATO member states. Russia has, however, repeatedly accused the Baltic countries of allowing their airspace to be used for Ukrainian attacks, claims that Nausėda has publicly rejected. Possible ‘false flag’ ops but no specific plans Defence Minister Kaunas said Thursday that Lithuanian intelligence has gathered information indicating that Moscow is assessing such scenarios, although there is no evidence that a decision has been made to carry them out. “I want to assure you that Lithuanian intelligence is doing its job, that we are gathering information and see that Russia is considering possible provocations in the Baltic region and the possible use of false flag operations there,” Kaunas told reporters. The minister said security has been reinforced at selected critical infrastructure sites, while the armed forces and other security institutions continue to monitor the situation. “We are monitoring the situation based on the level of alert we have assessed,” he said. Kaunas stressed there was no indication of an imminent threat and that Russia had not decided to launch such an operation. “There is no specific date. We are observing Russia’s planning process, something our NATO allies, including Poland and our Baltic neighbours, are also talking about,” he said. “Other NATO countries have repeatedly made it very clear that they see it, hear it, know about it, and have warned Russia not to do it.” According to Kaunas, one possible scenario would involve Russia using captured Ukrainian drones to attack targets in the Baltic states in an attempt to disguise responsibility for the strikes. “As Ukraine successfully attacks Russia in self-defence, some Ukrainian drones are intercepted and some crash,” he said. “Russia possesses some of those parts and drone fragments and is capable of assembling them into a functioning device. The theoretical possibility that such drones could be used in a false flag operation exists.” The minister emphasised that Lithuania is not facing a conventional military threat and that there are no signs Russia is massing forces near the country’s borders. “We are talking about a false flag operation in which a fake Ukrainian drone could be used,” Kaunas said. “At this point, that is probably the most realistic scenario.”

Lithuania’s embassy in Kyiv suffered significant blast damage during Russia’s overnight missile barrage last weekend, and Vilnius still isn’t fully sure whether it was collateral damage or a message. Two Zircon hypersonic missiles – weapons built mainly to target ships – landed just 5 and 150 metres from the embassy in Kyiv’s Pechersk district, shattering windows and damaging the roof. No staff were hurt, but at least nine people were killed and over 20 injured across the city. Lithuania immediately summoned Russia’s representative in Vilnius in protest. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys’ read on the strike shifted over the following days. Right afterward, he told LRT TV that a deliberate hit “cannot be ruled out”, noting the only notable target nearby was a power plant 1.5 km away – “everything else is residential housing, except for our embassy” (other embassies, including Algeria’s and the UAE’s, sit in the same area). By midweek, though, he’d settled on a firmer line: “we do not believe the embassy itself was the intended target,” again pointing to that power plant as the likelier objective. Russia offered no apology. Its representative argued Lithuania had effectively been “warned”, since all of Kyiv was under threat that night – an explanation Vilnius has formally rejected, protesting the strike as a breach of the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations and demanding compensation. Lithuania’s Ambassador to Ukraine told LRT Radio the embassy has no plans to relocate staff out of Kyiv or Ukraine, arguing it’s better to focus on “strengthening Ukraine’s air defences instead of thinking about evacuating embassies”. Indeed, Ukraine is currently facing a growing shortage of the interceptor missiles that protect its capital, with the BBC reporting that missile interception rates have dropped around 22% over the past month compared with the same period last year, all while Russian attack rates are increasing. Just days after the massive overnight attack that damaged the embassy, Ukraine suffered another one – reportedly failing to intercept a single one of the 28 missiles launched at it. The attack on early Wednesday morning was the deadliest Kyiv and its surrounding area have suffered this year, with 17 people killed by Russian ballistic missiles. The same overnight assault also struck the sole logistics center of Lithuanian-capital retail chain NOVUS, causing “massive damage.” No casualties were reported there, but the facility remains under complete shutdown. And Russian missiles were not constrained to Ukraine last week – one crossed into Poland, landing on its soil during a July 30 strike. Warsaw chose not to shoot it down, responding with restraint since it posed “no threat”, though some experts interviewed by LRT.lt warn that sets a bad precedent – Russian airspace incursions now look like a risk the Kremlin has simply accepted. Lithuania's FM Kęstutis Budrys is pushing for a firmer NATO response, saying the alliance's reaction so far “could certainly have been stronger”. Lithuania’s skies are getting busier, with increasingly urgent questions about how to defend them. Lithuanian military intelligence says Russia may deliberately use captured Ukrainian-made drones to strike Baltic infrastructure because doing so would make it harder to pin blame on Moscow. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas confirmed the assessment, though he wouldn’t say what targets or timing Russia might have in mind – or that it is planning anything concrete. For Vilnius, air defence is now the mot du jour. The Defence Ministry wants to fuse mobile phones, surveillance cameras, radars and other sensors into one AI-powered airspace monitoring system , a project even industry insiders call “ambitious... not only for Lithuania, but globally.” Meanwhile, one of the Baltic airspace’s main existing defenders is also changing hands. NATO's Baltic air policing mission at Šiauliai – which successfully downed multiple drones that violated Baltic airspace during its last rotation – has just been taken over by Italian troops, bringing four Eurofighter Typhoons to swap in for the outgoing French and Romanian units. Speaking of Ukrainian drones, Lithuania is pushing to manufacture Ukrainian-designed drones on its own soil, under a bilateral deal signed in May. Defence Minister Kaunas said the ministry is now staffing up to turn that agreement into working production lines using Ukrainian technology – a partnership meant to boost Ukraine’s output while giving Lithuanian engineers a crash course from people who’ve been building drones under fire for years. Lithuania’s central bank just made homeownership a bit more reachable – first-time buyers who haven’t owned property in the past five years can now put down as little as 10%, down from 15%. Lithuania’s spent over €3 billion on innovation funding since 2022, but a new audit says the money isn’t actually building anything that lasts. The gap shows up nationally too – 45 patent applications per million people in 2024, versus an EU average of 152. Diesel just crossed €2.03 per litre, but the Finance Ministry isn't rushing to intervene. The government says it would only consider relief if Brent crude stayed above $100 a barrel for several days running and it’s currently sitting around $79. China has added Lithuanian laser maker Ekspla to its export control list – the country’s only Lithuanian entry among 14 EU firms hit in what looks like retaliation for Brussels’ 21st sanctions package against Russia. Ekspla says it’s still unsure why it was targeted since it doesn’t make military products. Vilnius is tightening space for the Russian language. The municipality said it will no longer accept written requests in Russian and has removed it from some of its digital systems, part of a policy the mayor claims is to strengthen Lithuanian in public life. Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service has frozen the assets of the local operator of the Russian discount retail chain Mere after the European Union imposed sanctions on the indirect owner of the business. The agency said it froze funds belonging to Valiante, the Lithuanian operator of Mere, along with two other companies linked to Russian businessman Sergey Shnayder: warehousing company Next Logistics and food trading firm Litproduktai. All three companies were added this week to the Financial Crime Investigation Service’s list of sanctioned entities. According to the agency, Shnayder indirectly owns 79% of Valiante and 74.87% of both Litproduktai and Next Logistics. Under EU sanctions rules, the companies’ funds must be frozen because more than half of their shares are controlled by a sanctioned individual. Shnayder was added to the European Union’s 21st package of sanctions on July 23, with the measures extending to operators of the Mere retail chain in Lithuania and several other countries. As a result, the affected companies were required to immediately halt operations in compliance with EU sanctions. The European Union sanctioned Shnayder for allegedly providing material or financial support for actions that undermine or threaten Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. On July 24, Mere stores across Lithuania closed without prior notice, citing what the retailer described as “technical obstacles”. Before the closures, the chain said it operated 26 stores nationwide. Meanwhile, Lithuania’s Ministry of Economy and Innovation has expressed concern that people associated with Mere may be continuing their business through the newly launched Ola retail chain, which has already opened a store in the northern town of Šiauliai.

Germany has invited Poland, the Baltic states, Norway, Denmark and Sweden to security talks following an incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in which an explosive-laden drone was discovered on airport grounds, German news agency dpa reported. The meeting is scheduled for late August and comes after Wednesday’s security scare, which prompted the temporary closure of one of Europe’s most important cargo airports. Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key hub for European freight traffic and military logistics. It also serves as an operational base for Ukrainian cargo carrier Antonov Airlines. The drone carrying explosives was found near several Antonov An-124 cargo aircraft, among the world’s largest transport planes. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the incident as “a new threat scenario” in hybrid warfare and said the involvement of a foreign state could not be ruled out. “For the first time, it was not simply a drone at an airport, but a drone carrying explosives,” Dobrindt told German public broadcaster ARD. Later the same night, a cargo aircraft near Leipzig airport collided with an unidentified object. The aircraft landed safely in Hanover, where an inspection found minor damage. German authorities have not publicly identified who may have been responsible for either incident. The investigation is ongoing.

Vilnius City Council recently announced it will stop accepting requests and complaints from residents in Russian – part of a broader push to reduce the language's role in public life since Russia's invasion of Ukraine. But other state institutions say they have no plans to follow suit just yet. Lithuania, a EU and NATO member bordering Russia's ally Belarus, has a large Russian-speaking minority, a legacy of Soviet rule that ended in 1990. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many Lithuanian institutions have faced growing calls to phase out Russian in official settings. The State Tax Inspectorate (VMI) and the State Social Insurance Fund Board, known as Sodra say they aim to serve people in whatever language is easiest for them, and will continue offering support in Russian. A public clinic in Vilnius, the Šeškinė Clinic, says it matches patients with doctors who speak their preferred language, or asks them to bring an interpreter if none is available. Some patients say they'd struggle without Russian-language service. "There was never a point when I could speak Lithuanian. In institutions, it was Russian. At school, Russian. At work, Russian," one woman told LRT.lt. The clinic's information screens now show only Lithuanian and English, but registration staff still ask patients what language they speak and assign them a doctor accordingly. "The key point is registration. We have to allocate patients appropriately – we know which languages our staff speak, which languages they're willing to use with patients, and we assign patients on that basis," explains Evaldas Pilipavičius, a clinic representative. The clinic adds that patients are sometimes asked to bring an interpreter if no Russian-speaking doctor is available. "The younger generation speaks less Russian, which is why registration matters so much. We've had all sorts of situations, including conflicts, but we try to resolve problems flexibly and find a colleague who can help," Pilipavičius says. The State Tax Inspectorate and Sodra say their priority is serving as many people as possible, and neither has any current plans to drop or reduce the use of Russian. "We've noticed a recent rise in the number of Russian speakers, due to the geopolitical situation as well as an influx from Asia. This year alone, up to July, around 44,000 Russian speakers contacted us by phone with tax queries," notes Martynas Endrijaitis, head of the State Tax Inspectorate. "We follow a customer-focused approach and try to provide services in the language the person is most comfortable with. Our advisers aren't obliged to serve people in anything other than the state language – doing so is simply a goodwill gesture," adds Malgožata Kozič, a Sodra representative. Vilnius City Council announced it would stop accepting residents' requests and complaints in Russian. Information in Russian and other non-EU languages will now only be provided verbally, and only if the specific member of staff involved happens to speak that language. The mayor says this is just one step in a broader effort to reduce the use of Russian in public services across the city. "The aim is clear: in the capital of a democratic state, official languages should be used – Lithuanian first, then other foreign languages. The use of Russian reflects a certain complacency that needs to be addressed," says Vilnius Mayor Valdas Benkunskas. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, however, struck a more cautious note: "I don't have a clear-cut answer as to whether this is necessary or not. If it concerned Russian citizens, my answer would be one thing. But if we're talking about freedom fighters who've fled the Belarusian regime, or Ukrainians, the picture changes." Some services have already dropped Russian entirely: since January, driving tests at Regitra, the state agency that issues driving licences, can no longer be taken in Russian.

As the United States steps up its campaign against the International Criminal Court and urges allies to distance themselves from the tribunal, Lithuanian officials are working with European Union partners on a coordinated response while downplaying suggestions that Washington could force Vilnius to choose between supporting the court and maintaining a US military presence in the country. The diplomatic pressure campaign, launched by Washington in mid-July, argues that the Hague-based court poses what US officials describe as an “unjustified threat” to American sovereignty. In an opinion piece published in The Wall Street Journal, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he could not accept a world in which “US soldiers, police officers, border patrol agents and elected leaders” could be brought before an international court, tried by foreign judges and imprisoned thousands of miles from home. Although the United States is not a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, Washington has pledged to urge foreign governments, particularly those benefiting from US security guarantees, either to withdraw from the treaty or reject what it calls the court’s claimed authority to prosecute American officials and service members. The renewed campaign comes as US military operations against Iran continue alongside Israel, whose Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is the subject of an ICC arrest warrant over alleged war crimes linked to the war in Gaza. Relations between Washington and the court have been strained since President Donald Trump’s first administration, and the United States has imposed sanctions on some ICC judges. Washington also continues to object to the court’s unresolved investigations into alleged torture and war crimes involving US troops and CIA personnel in Afghanistan and secret detention facilities in Europe. Lithuania has already received an informal US diplomatic paper outlining Washington’s position and is reviewing it together with other EU member states. “Lithuania, like other European Union countries, has received the US-prepared non-paper regarding the International Criminal Court and is examining it,” the Foreign Ministry said in a statement. “Coordination is taking place at the EU level to ensure a common position in dialogue with the United States regarding the future of the court, based on the principles of international law.” The ministry reiterated the EU’s support for the “universality, integrity and full implementation” of the Rome Statute system. For Lithuania, the court has particular importance because of its investigations into alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, as well as an ICC investigation opened at Lithuania’s request into alleged crimes by the Belarusian government against members of the Belarusian opposition who fled to Lithuania. The issue comes at a sensitive moment for Vilnius as Washington reviews the future of US troop deployments in Europe. Lithuania has sought to present itself as one of America’s closest and most reliable allies on NATO’s eastern flank. Deividas Matulionis, President Gitanas Nausėda’s chief national security adviser, said Lithuania has received no indication from Washington that the ICC issue could be linked to decisions on US military deployments. “These are completely separate issues,” Matulionis said. “The presence of troops concerns security, which is important not only for Lithuania but for all of Europe and for the United States.” He added that Lithuania has not yet held bilateral discussions with Washington on any specific expectations related to the ICC and stressed that Vilnius would coordinate its position with the broader European Union. Matulionis also noted that bilateral agreements already provide guarantees that US service members stationed in Lithuania will not be transferred to the jurisdiction of third countries or international organisations. Lawmakers from both the governing coalition and the opposition similarly expressed confidence that the dispute would not undermine US-Lithuanian security ties. Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the parliamentary Foreign Affairs Committee, said Lithuania should explain to Washington why remaining a party to the Rome Statute serves its national interests. “We should always engage with our partners and explain why membership is important for Lithuania and why our situation differs from that of the United States,” Motuzas said. “I believe the United States would understand.” He argued that NATO security and the US military presence in Europe are strategic issues that extend well beyond Lithuania. Conservative lawmaker Žygimantas Pavilionis also said he did not believe Lithuania’s continued support for the ICC would automatically jeopardise American backing. However, he warned that maintaining close ties with Washington requires constant effort. “The status quo with America should not be taken for granted,” Pavilionis said, calling for new economic, defence and technology initiatives that would strengthen bilateral ties. He argued that Lithuania should pursue projects in areas such as drones, counter-drone technologies or other strategic sectors rather than weaken international institutions that uphold the rules-based international order. Not everyone is prepared to dismiss the possibility that the ICC debate could influence broader US strategic calculations. Linas Kojala, director of the Geopolitics and Security Studies Centre, said Washington’s scepticism toward the ICC is longstanding, recalling similar disagreements before NATO’s eastern enlargement in the early 2000s, when the United States sought bilateral agreements shielding its personnel from the court’s jurisdiction. The current dispute, however, is broader, he said. “Previously the discussion focused on limiting the court’s jurisdiction over the United States,” Kojala said. “Now there is open discussion about dismantling or fundamentally weak

A Lithuanian man drove through barriers at a closed border checkpoint with Russia and briefly crossed the state border on foot last month before being detained, authorities said Friday. The incident occurred in the morning of July 22, at about 10:50, at the Nida border checkpoint, which has been closed to regular traffic, according to Lina Laurinaitytė, head of the State Border Guard Service’s communications department. Border guards monitoring surveillance cameras saw the driver of an Audi A5 Sportback move a protective fence, return to his vehicle and ram through lifting barriers. The driver then manoeuvred around anti-vehicle concrete fortifications known as “dragon’s teeth”, stopped the car and crossed into Russia on foot. About five minutes later, at approximately 10:55, the man returned to the vehicle and drove away from the checkpoint area. He was soon stopped and detained by Neringa border guard officers. Authorities identified the suspect as T. A., a 40-year-old Lithuanian citizen from the Vilnius district. Tests showed he was sober and not under the influence of narcotic or psychotropic substances. The man was detained in Klaipėda and released the following day after signing a written pledge not to leave the country. Laurinaitytė said the incident was not immediately disclosed publicly after an internal assessment determined that other events at the time were considered more relevant for public communication. “When deciding whether to disclose information, we assess the nature of the event, its relevance and the volume of communication at that time,” she said. “On that day, a decision was made to publicise other events that we considered more relevant to the public.” A pretrial investigation into illegal border crossing has been opened. If convicted, the man could face a fine, arrest or imprisonment of up to two years.

Lithuanian authorities are investigating whether the Russian-owned discount supermarket chain Mere, forced to close following European Union sanctions, has re-emerged under a new brand. The country's Minister of the Economy and Innovation has asked the Financial Crime Investigation Service (FNTT) to determine whether newly opened Ola stores are linked to sanctioned Russian business interests and represent an attempt to circumvent EU sanctions. The investigation follows speculation on social media that Mere has effectively reopened under a different name. Market analysts say such a development would not be unprecedented, pointing to a similar pattern in Poland after sanctions were imposed there. Following the European Union's latest sanctions package, Mere stores ceased trading in both Lithuania and Latvia. The sanctions target the chain's owner, Sergei Shnaider, together with all shareholders of the Svetofor Group, which operates the Mere brand. Before closing, Mere operated nearly 30 stores across Lithuania, employing around 250 people. Customers expressed disappointment at the closures, saying the chain had provided low-cost groceries rather than exclusively Russian products. "We used to come here once a week to do our shopping. Food was a bit cheaper," said customer Petras. People interviewed by LRT said products from Ukraine, Latvia and Lithuania were widely available alongside goods from other countries. Many said they hoped another low-cost retailer would replace Mere. Attention quickly turned to a new discount chain, Ola, which opened a store in Šiauliai shortly before Mere ceased trading. Customers said the product range, prices and overall shopping experience closely resemble those of Mere. In Latvia, Ola stores have also appeared in premises previously occupied by Mere. Perhaps most strikingly, the two retailers use almost identical slogans promoting lower prices. A woman identifying herself to LRT Radio as one of Ola's managers acknowledged that she had previously worked for Mere and admitted the business model was similar. "Yes, they're similar – so what? We're not connected to our former colleagues. We're separate businesses. The model is similar, and we're not hiding that. This is business, not politics. We stepped away from that. When everything began, we realised where it was heading and left. We were employees." Minister of the Economy and Innovation Edvinas Grikšas has asked the FNTT to establish whether the Latvian owner of the Ola store in Šiauliai has links to the sanctioned owners of Mere. He argues that the issue extends beyond ordinary commercial regulation. "There is no place in Lithuania for investment from this kind of capital," he said. "The key question is whether these newly opened Ola stores have links to the owners of Mere," he added, referring to efforts to enforce sanctions. "It's rather like a basketball match between sanctions and sanctions evasion. The challenge is to score more points than those trying to get around the rules." The minister said employees affected by Mere's closure should have little difficulty finding work elsewhere, noting that vacancies in Lithuania's retail sector outnumber the chain's former workforce by around ten to one. Retail analysts say the similarities between the two chains may indicate that contingency plans had been prepared before sanctions came into force. "The products are the same, the suppliers are the same, the prices are the same. They're not reinventing anything," said Arūnas Vizickas, founder of retail analysis platform Pricer.lt. Mindaugas Petrauskas, Head of Financial Crime Prevention at Amlyze, believes advance planning is entirely plausible. "It's entirely possible that preparations were made in advance, anticipating sanctions against this group. New companies and similar stores could have been established with ownership structures designed to conceal any sanctioned individuals." Market specialists note that warehouses, logistics infrastructure and supplier networks linked to Russian operators remain intact, making it easier to launch successor businesses. They also argue that establishing any corporate links should not prove especially difficult. "Investigators can identify the suppliers and ask on what basis they agreed to supply goods. Suppliers don't usually extend trade credit to unknown companies," says Vizickas. Analysts point to Poland as an example of how sanctioned businesses may attempt to continue operating under new identities. After Mere was sanctioned there last year, investigators discovered that the business was operating through several companies using different names. "Businesses directly linked to the Shnaider family, where they were shareholders, were sanctioned immediately. But over time new clones appeared, associated with businessman [Viktor – LRT] Lipin, who has Lithuanian roots, with companies registered in his name. We may now be seeing a similar scenario with Ola, although the ownership structure could be considerably more complex," said Vizickas. Petrauskas says sanctions and attempts to evade them inevitably evolve together. "There will always be attempts to circumvent sanctions. But the longer and more complex those chains become, the more expensive it is for those subject to sanctions." Alongside EU sanctions, Latvia has introduced additional national restrictions, banning books, newspapers, toys, clothing and footwear manufactured in Russia or Belarus. "I believe the impact will be minimal," says Maris Andžans, Director of the Centre for Geopolitical Studies in Riga. A Latvian media investigation found that some shops were still selling Russian-made cocoa, mayonnaise and beer, as well as Belarusian kvass. "It says it's from Russia. Whether it is or isn't doesn't matter to me. What's important is that the product is good." Latvian politicians had considered banning all trade with Russia but ultimately restricted only selected categories of goods. Experts say the tougher rhet

Shortly before she and her boyfriend were brutally beaten on the streets of the Polish city of Wroclaw, a Ukrainian woman named Anastasia Kitsay was inside a shop buying coffee. When another man cut in front of her at the register to buy a beer, Kitsay pointed out there was a line, Kitsay’s mother, Karyna, said. The man responded, “Are you in Ukraine?” and called her a “Ukrainian rag”, as they argued and the man left the store, Karyna told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service. Moments later, the man and two others pummeled and kicked Kitsay’s Ukrainian boyfriend, Maksym, as he stood by his car, while also punching Kitsay. The fight, which took place on July 26, was captured on video and circulated widely in Ukrainian and Polish social media. Both were hospitalised. Two of the men pleaded not guilty to charges of ethnically motivated assault during a July 29 appearance in a Wroclaw court. The city’s mayor condemned the incident: "There is not and will not be tolerance in our city for violence motivated by hatred, xenophobia, or national prejudice." Since the start of Russia’s all-out invasion in February 2022, Poland has taken in more Ukrainian refugees than any other European country except for Germany: nearly 1 million Ukrainians had refugee status in Poland as of April, according to United Nations figures. Both the current government in Warsaw and its predecessor have embraced the defence of neighbouring Ukraine as a national-security priority. The Ukrainian population has also helped jolt Poland’s already humming economy. About 1 million are classified as labour migrants, according to Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland. But Ukrainians report growing tensions and resentment from some Poles, who have questioned the depth and duration of taxpayer-funded support for the refugees. Polish police have reported a 30-percent increase in hate crime attacks on Ukrainians over the past six months, according to the newspaper Rzeczpospolita. Kitsay is not a refugee. She said she's lived in Poland for nearly a decade; her daughter Anastasia moved in 2019. But Natalya Melynk is. After the start of the war, she moved from the western Ukrainian region of Zhytomyr to Plock, a city west of Warsaw. On June 27, she said her 15-year-old son and his Ukrainian friend were returning home on a bus when another passenger heard them speaking Ukrainian. "'Poland’s for Poles,'" she said the man told them. “The children were silent, then he said to my son again: "'You hear me? Poland’s for Poles. Speak Polish in Poland.'" Melnyk said her son speaks Polish well, and he replied that they were speaking Ukrainian because his friend was Ukrainian. "In response, the man started shouting: 'Get off the bus. Get out of the country,'" she told Current Time. After her son said they would get off the bus at his stop, Melnyk said the man lunged at her son, and struck his friend. Another passenger told the yelling man to get off the bus. At the following stop, the man “literally threw the children off the bus”, she said. Police officers investigated but did not classify the attack as a hate crime until Melnyk complained. As of July 29, the man has not been identified, she said. The rise in reported hate crimes comes as public surveys show Poles becoming less supportive of Ukrainian refugees. A survey conducted earlier this month by the Centre for Public Opinion Research found that 52 percent of Poles opposed accepting any more Ukrainian war refugees; 42 percent said they were in favour. That figure is down sharply from 2022, just after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, when 94 percent of Poles said they were in support of accepting Ukrainian war refugees. The survey also showed that a majority of Poles, steeped in memories of the Nazi-Soviet invasion in 1939 and decades of dominance by the Soviet Union, support restricting free access to health care for Ukrainians, who until recently were not required to pay into the national health insurance system. The increase in anti-Ukrainian sentiment also comes at a time of strained relations between Warsaw and Kyiv, over a historical grievance dating back decades. In May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced he would be honouring a military unit battling Russian troops with a designation named after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. Poland says the group massacred some 100,000 Poles during World War Two, in a region that today borders Ukraine. At the time, the region was under German control. Poland has designated the killings the Volhynian Massacre, and the country's parliament has declared it was a genocide. Ukraine rejects that designation, saying Ukrainians faced hatred from Poles as well, and thousands were killed in reprisals. Ukrainians have termed the events the Volyn Tragedy. Many Ukrainians hail the Ukrainian Insurgent Army as freedom fighters – a perception that has widened as the country tries to fight off a Russian invasion 35 years after it won independence from Moscow as the Soviet Union collapsed. Zelensky’s honourific designation kicked off a small firestorm of outrage inside Poland. Polish President Karol Nawrocki, a populist historian who is the former director of a World War Two museum, last month announced he was stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest state honour. Zelensky then returned his award to Poland, as did three of his predecessors as president. "Discussions around the politics of memory […] have once again become a subject of widespread public debate in Poland," said Mateusz Kamionka, a political scientist and expert in Polish-Ukrainian relations at the Jagiellonian University in Krakow. He said economic and social factors are also influencing shifts in public sentiment, including the rising cost of living as well as a belief that public assistance to Ukrainians is too generous and should be more limited. “Speaking Ukrainian (or Russian) on the street is becoming a problem," said Alexei Cheplyansky, a Polish journalist. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform party) has claimed Estonia is spending almost 7 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on defence under NATO's new spending goal. Speaking at this week's NATO Summit in Ankara, Turkey, Michal called on allies to increase their defence expenditure during his opening remarks, saying Estonia is investing "almost 7 percent this year" in defence. Under the goal set at last year's NATO summit, allies agreed to allocate 5 percent of GDP to defence in the coming years. This target is split into two parts: 1) 3.5 percent for core military expenditures, such as personnel, operations, equipment, and maintenance. 2) 1.5 percent for security-related spending, such as cyberdefence, supply chain resilience, critical infrastructure, logistics, and defense innovation. Estonia's Defence Mistry foreign communications adviser Liisa Tagel told the newspaper Postimees that when these two parts are combined, it totals 6.9 percent. A united and stronger NATO benefits every Ally. Estonia already invests 7% of GDP in defence, with more than 5% going to core defence. We hope all Allies will keep increasing defence spending. Defence spending must become capabilities. NATO needs a stronger forward defence, more… pic.twitter.com/QK664gSG5Q "The 5 percent Estonia most often talks about – which is actually 5.4 percent – is, by NATO's definition, spent entirely on hard security, meaning areas related to military security," she said. "Estonia has budgeted 1.5 percent of GDP this year for non-military national defence." At the summit on Wednesday, Lithuanian officials, including the president, foreign and defence ministers, and Estonia's Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) called on other countries to boost their spending and were seen wearing "5% club" badges. Both countries are spending at least 5% of GDP on defence this year. Together with @BudrysKestutis in the 5% Club. The club is open. Join us.
