In recent months, Ukraine has carried out a series of successful drone strikes on Russian oil industry facilities.

Lithuania's armed forces need to expand their capacity to take in and train recruits after a record number of young people expressed interest in mandatory initial military service, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said on Monday. Society has shown us that it is ready, young Lithuanian citizens have shown that they are ready, and now we on the military side must also raise our ambition," Kaunas told LRT. More than 8,100 applications were received this year for voluntary mandatory initial military service, though limited capacity means not all applicants will be able to begin training this year. Nearly 4,400 people volunteered to serve before being called up under the draft, while a further 3,700 already on the conscription lists requested priority enlistment. Kaunas said the plan was to admit around 5,000 young people this year, though he noted the figure could potentially be raised by up to 530 additional conscripts. Selection will be based primarily on health assessments, with military commanders choosing those fit for service. The minister put the surge in interest down to public perceptions of the changing security situation, as well as improving conditions within the armed forces. Watching the war in Ukraine unfold and seeing Russia's increasingly aggressive rhetoric, he said, young people wanted to learn how to defend themselves, their families and their country. Kaunas said interest was also being driven by higher pay, improving military infrastructure, and modernised equipment and weaponry. A volunteer who completes nine months of service with a "very good" evaluation receives around €9,000. He said Lithuania should look to Israel as an example when it comes to military service, pointing to a society prepared to respond to threats and defend itself. Given its proximity to aggressive neighbours, he said, Lithuanian society must be similarly prepared.

Lithuania's Reception and Integration Agency has filled 60% of its accommodation capacity, as secondary migration from Latvia continues to increase, according to the latest figures. The agency runs three main temporary accommodation centres, in Vilnius, Rukla and Pabradė, with a combined capacity of 1,000 people. As of July 13, the centres were housing 628 foreign nationals from a range of countries of origin. The agency said vacant places were still available, meaning there was no immediate need to activate additional infrastructure. However, it said the situation was being monitored continuously, in coordination with the interior ministry, taking into account occupancy levels and migration forecasts. Lina Gediminė, a spokeswoman for the agency, said it was strengthening its capacity as migrant numbers rose, adding that, if necessary, efforts would be made to ensure adequate housing, social and healthcare services, legal aid and translation services. The State Border Guard Service, meanwhile, said its detention facilities were currently at 50% capacity, suggesting no immediate need for expansion. According to the border guard service, secondary migration from Latvia remains volatile and inconsistent. An agreement has been reached with Latvian authorities under which Latvia will take back 58 migrants by next Tuesday. In the first six months of this year, secondary migration flows from Latvia rose sharply to more than 1,200 foreign nationals, compared with just over 300 during the same period last year. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said last week that the state could mobilise additional resources, including setting up container camps, if required. While he did not rule out temporarily reinstating border controls with Latvia, President Gitanas Nausėda voiced scepticism about such a move. Border guard figures show more than 8,000 migrants have attempted to enter Latvia this year, where they were either detained and returned to Belarus or turned back at the border, nearly nine times the number of attempted crossings from Belarus into Lithuania over the same period.

Prosecutors in Lithuania have asked a court to conclude a case against a French national accused of illegally transporting migrants across the country's border, using a simplified procedure known as a penal order. According to the pre-trial investigation, the man picked up 19 foreign nationals with no permanent residence in Lithuania while in Latvia on July 5, loading them into the cargo compartment of a minivan he was driving. Those on board were found to include 11 Iranian nationals, four Pakistani nationals, three Afghan nationals and one person of unestablished nationality. Investigators say the defendant was transporting the migrants to Poland in exchange for a promised payment of €7,000. En route, he crossed into Lithuanian territory the same day, but was stopped by police while driving along the Jurbarkas–Šakiai road. The man has admitted guilt, and the prosecutor leading the investigation has decided to conclude the case through a court penal order rather than a full trial. Under this procedure, prosecutors are asking the court to find him guilty and, after reducing the sentence by a third for his admission of guilt, to impose a fine of €30,000. They are also seeking the forfeiture of €40,000, representing the value of the vehicle used to transport the migrants. The case has been submitted to the Kaunas Regional Court.

A former senior Lithuanian military officer alleges his career was cut short in retaliation for raising concerns over public procurement practices in the armed forces, while the Defence Ministry says the decision not to extend his service was based on personnel needs and disciplinary considerations. News portal Delfi.lt reported Tuesday that Audrius Beinoras, who served in the Lithuanian military for three decades, was forced to leave the armed forces last summer after his professional military service contract was not extended. Beinoras, the former deputy director of the Armed Forces’ Military Conscription and Recruitment Service, now known as the Military Commandant Administration, said the decision was retaliation for questioning procurement procedures and reporting his concerns to the Prosecutor General’s Office. The prosecutor’s office granted Beinoras whistleblower status, which provides legal protections for individuals reporting suspected wrongdoing in the workplace. However, prosecutors declined to open a pretrial investigation into the procurement allegations. Beinoras said he raised concerns in 2024 and 2025 over public tenders related to upgrades of the military’s Karys.lt website, which publishes military conscription lists. According to him, the procurement requirements effectively favoured the company that originally developed the website. He said the tender required bidders to use the proprietary Easy Web4 content management system, which is developed and controlled exclusively by Fresh Media, the company that created the website, making it impossible for competitors to carry out the work. Fresh Media denied the allegation, saying all information necessary to administer the website had been transferred to Lithuania’s defence system. The Defence Ministry told Delfi.lt that the procurement process is ongoing and that although the current version of Karys.lt operates on proprietary software, the new tender requires the website to be migrated to an open-source platform. Beinoras also said he fell out of favour with military leadership after questioning the procurement of souvenirs distributed during some military exercises. The Defence Ministry said that last year the Senior Officers Career Planning Commission assessed the needs of the national defence system and, taking into account recommendations from Beinoras’ immediate and senior supervisors, recommended against extending his professional military service. Then-Defence Minister Dovilė Šakalienė approved the recommendation. The ministry said extending a professional military service contract is a discretionary decision that may be granted by the defence minister or an authorised official based on the needs of the national defence system. It acknowledged that seven requests for service extensions were considered at the time and that Beinoras was the only officer whose request was denied. The ministry also cited disciplinary action against Beinoras after he referred to a subordinate using an insulting Lithuanian term roughly equivalent to “idiot”. Beinoras does not dispute making the remark but says the disciplinary sanction was unjustified and has challenged it in court. Speaking on the radio Žinių Radijas on Tuesday, President Gitanas Nausėda’s chief national security adviser, Deividas Matulionis, declined to comment on the merits of the dispute but stressed the importance of transparency in defence procurement. “Public procurement is a very important area in the national defence system, given that this year’s defence budget is 40% larger than last year’s. Transparent and efficient public procurement is therefore one of the highest priorities,” Matulionis said. “We are also trying to help as much as possible,” he added.

Lithuania’s military has been deployed to help protect the country’s liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipėda and other critical infrastructure following warnings from President Gitanas Nausėda and other regional leaders about potential Russian provocations. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas signed an order on July 17 authorising the deployment. The military will also reinforce security at the LitPol Link electricity interconnection with Poland, including the Alytus switchyard and transformer substation, as well as the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydroelectric Plant. The deployment will run from July 19 through August 19. The armed forces will provide a unit of up to 30 troops with transport assets, along with a vessel or motorboat and its crew. Operational tasks will be coordinated with the Public Security Service, which is responsible for protecting Lithuania’s critical infrastructure. The move follows recent public warnings by leaders of NATO’s eastern flank, who cited intelligence indicating that Russia may be preparing kinetic provocations within their countries. Nausėda said last week that Lithuania’s critical transport and energy infrastructure could become targets of both conventional and nonconventional attacks, including acts of sabotage. On Tuesday, Deividas Matulionis, the president’s chief national security adviser, said NATO allies would deploy additional military capabilities to Lithuania if Russian provocations in the region triggered a critical security situation. He said the alliance was taking the warnings seriously and would be prepared to reinforce Lithuania with additional forces and air defence capabilities if necessary. Lithuania’s increased protection of critical infrastructure does not indicate a higher threat level and is being maintained as a precautionary measure, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Tuesday. “Preventively, we are increasing the protection of critical infrastructure. This was done on June 11 at the request of the Interior Ministry, and we are now extending that decision,” Kaunas told reporters. The threat level has not increased, Kaunas added. “The threat level has not worsened or changed since June 11, when this request and decision were made. We are simply continuing the operation as a precautionary measure,” he said. Kaunas said the enhanced security measures could continue beyond August 19 if necessary.

NATO countries would deploy additional military capabilities to Lithuania if Russian provocations in the region triggered a critical security situation, President Gitanas Nausėda’s chief national security adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said Tuesday. The alliance is taking seriously warnings of an increased risk of Russian provocations in the Baltic region and elsewhere in Europe in the coming months, Matulionis assured. “We have issued warnings and the alliance is taking this very seriously. If all indicators were to show that the situation is critical, I have no doubt that additional forces and air defence capabilities would be allocated,” he said. Leaders of NATO’s eastern flank countries have recently issued public warnings, citing intelligence indicating that Russia is preparing provocations on their territory. In Lithuania, authorities have identified critical transport and energy infrastructure as potential targets and have recently strengthened security measures at those sites. Matulionis said the provocations could take various forms, ranging from so-called false flag operations designed to shift blame onto Ukraine to acts of sabotage similar to those seen across Europe in recent years. He said the threat extends beyond the Baltic states to other countries providing strong support for Ukraine. However, he dismissed the possibility of Russia preparing to invade a NATO member state. “There is certainly no information regarding a troop build-up on our border, so the question of a military invasion is ruled out. The probability here is practically zero,” Matulionis said. He added that Russian attacks can be prevented and said Lithuanian authorities are taking all necessary steps “to ensure such actions are not carried out on our territory”.

Hungary’s OTP Bank, which has agreed to acquire Baltic banking group Luminor, says it has been unable to find a legally, morally and economically acceptable way to exit Russia, where it continues to serve about 2 million customers more than four years after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. OTP announced Monday that it had signed an agreement to acquire Luminor, the Baltic region’s third-largest banking group, from a consortium of private equity funds managed by Blackstone and Norway’s DNB Bank. The transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions. The Budapest-based lender operates in 11 countries, including Russia through its subsidiary JSC OTP Bank. According to the bank, it has about 2 million active customers in Russia, where it holds a roughly 0.3% share of the banking market and operates at about 800 locations. Responding to questions from LRT, OTP said it had explored ways to leave the Russian market after the war began but concluded that no viable solution existed. “As with other Western banks, we have not been able to find a solution that is simultaneously legally, morally and economically acceptable,” the bank said in a statement. OTP argued that selling its Russian business under current conditions would require accepting a price equivalent to only about 5% of its market value, effectively handing valuable assets to the Russian economy. The bank said it has sought to reduce its exposure by halting new capital injections into its Russian subsidiary, ending group financing and repatriating a significant share of capital through dividend payments. It added that it complies with all applicable international sanctions and local legal requirements. OTP also noted that it continues to operate in Ukraine, where it says it remains an important lender and has supported the country’s economy and humanitarian efforts throughout the war. The bank’s continued presence in Russia has previously drawn scrutiny. Its Russian subsidiary has promoted itself as one of the country’s leading employers and has participated in business events, including the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, a flagship gathering backed by Russian President Vladimir Putin. Luminor sought to reassure customers that the ownership change will have no immediate impact. “The transaction will be completed only after the required regulatory approvals are obtained and other closing conditions are met. Until then, Luminor and OTP will continue operating independently,” Luminor Lithuania spokeswoman Birutė Eimontaitė said. She added that customers would see no changes to their banking services, contracts or day-to-day relationship with the lender during the acquisition process. OTP Group serves more than 17.5 million customers across Central and Eastern Europe. The bank said the acquisition would strengthen its position in the region while marking its entry into the Baltic market. Following the deal, eurozone operations are expected to account for about half of the group’s net loan portfolio, up from 42%, while total assets would increase by about 13%, according to the company.

Lithuania’s central bank said Tuesday that Hungarian lender OTP Bank’s continued operations in Russia raise “justified questions” as regulators begin reviewing its proposed acquisition of Baltic banking group Luminor. The Bank of Lithuania said the transaction, announced Monday, is still in its early stages and that it has not yet received the formal documentation needed to begin its assessment. “The fact that the group operates in Russia raises justified questions,” the central bank said in a statement. The proposed acquisition will be assessed by the European Central Bank in coordination with Estonia’s Financial Supervision and Business Restructuring Authority and in consultation with the Bank of Lithuania. The Lithuanian regulator said the review would examine OTP’s reputation, financial strength, corporate governance, risk management, compliance with international sanctions and anti-money laundering requirements, as well as other factors relevant to financial stability. Budapest-based OTP serves about 2 million retail customers in Russia through its subsidiary JSC OTP Bank. The lender has said it explored options to exit the Russian market after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine but concluded that no legally, morally and economically acceptable solution was available. OTP has argued that selling its Russian business under current conditions would yield only about 5% of its market value. The bank says its Russian operations account for only about 0.3% of the country’s banking market. According to the bank’s public disclosures, OTP operates at about 800 locations across Russia and ranks among the country’s 50 largest banks. The lender has also participated as a partner in the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, a flagship business event backed by Russian President Vladimir Putin. Last year, OTP’s Russian operations generated more than 558 million euros, representing nearly one-fifth of the group’s consolidated net profit. Marius Jurgilas, a former member of the Bank of Lithuania’s board and founder of fintech company Axiology, said the key question for Lithuanian regulators would be OTP’s long-term strategy if the acquisition is approved. He said he believes OTP sees Luminor as a platform for expanding across the Baltic region rather than as an investment to be sold later, a strategy that could increase competition in mortgage lending, corporate finance and retail banking. Darius Klimašauskas, managing director of financial advisory firm Talisman, said the European Central Bank would ultimately decide whether to approve the acquisition and would take OTP’s continued presence in Russia into account. OTP announced Monday that it had signed an agreement to acquire Luminor from a consortium led by US private equity firm Blackstone and Norway’s DNB Bank. The deal remains subject to regulatory approvals. OTP Group operates in 11 countries across Central and Eastern Europe, serving about 17.5 million customers and managing more than 130 billion euros in assets. Blackstone has owned an 80% stake in Luminor since 2022, while DNB holds the remaining 20%.

Lithuania’s Port of Klaipėda handled 20.1 million metric tons of cargo in the first six months of 2026, a 6% increase from a year earlier, driven by stronger transit traffic and expanding shipping connections with Asia. Port CEO Algis Latakas said Tuesday that Klaipėda’s diversified cargo base had helped shield it from geopolitical uncertainty and disruptions affecting regional trade. “The Port of Klaipėda is highly diversified, and that is one of the key elements of its success,” Latakas said in a statement. “Despite everything that is happening – not only the war but also its consequences, including sanctions and tariffs – the first half of the year was very good in terms of cargo handling.” He said the current pace suggests the port could handle more than 40 million tons of cargo by the end of the year. Containerised cargo rose 12% to 7.2 million tons during the January-June period, while roll-on/roll-off cargo increased 4% to 3.4 million tons. The port handled nearly 700,000 twenty-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, unchanged from the same period last year. The port authority attributed the overall growth to stronger transit flows, the launch of a new deep-sea shipping service linking Klaipėda with Asia and the expansion of short-sea shipping routes. Transit cargo surged 165% in the first half of the year and now accounts for 19% of the port’s total throughput, Latakas said. Among individual cargo categories, oil products increased 12% to 2.3 million tons, liquefied natural gas volumes climbed 37% to 1.6 million tons and fertiliser shipments rose 14% to 890,000 tons. Scrap metal volumes were unchanged at 560,000 tons. Grain shipments fell 7.1% to 1.3 million tons, while minerals and construction materials declined 6% to 940,000 tons. “Weaker performance in several cargo segments has been offset by strong growth in others, allowing the Port of Klaipėda to maintain a strong competitive position in the Baltic market,” the port authority said. The number of freight vehicles transported through the port rose 2.5% to 173,500, while local shipyards completed repairs on 46 vessels, up 31% from a year earlier. According to the port authority, Klaipėda was the only major Baltic port to report cargo growth in the first half of the year. It said the port accounted for 44% of the Baltic states’ total cargo market, rising to 54% when Lithuania’s Būtingė oil terminal is included. The authority said ports in neighbouring Latvia and Estonia continued to lose cargo volumes because of their historically greater reliance on Russian transit cargo, much of which has disappeared under international sanctions imposed following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Lithuania’s military is conducting exercises in Klaipėda and the Curonian Spit this week to train for the protection of critical infrastructure, with the country’s Rapid Response Forces activated for the drills, the armed forces said Wednesday. The exercises are focused on the rapid redeployment of troops and equipment, the execution of standby and peacetime missions, and the military’s ability to operate alongside other state institutions, the military said in a statement. Personnel from the Navy, Land Forces, Air Force and Military Police are taking part in the training. The exercises are being conducted in cooperation with the Military Command Board and coordinated with the Public Security Service, the Klaipėda State Seaport Authority and other civilian agencies. Training activities are taking place in the territory of the Port of Klaipėda, the port channel and the Curonian Spit. Soldiers, naval vessels, high-speed boats and Air Force helicopters are carrying out tactical tasks aimed at improving rapid-response capabilities, the protection of key facilities and coordination with civilian authorities. The drills come as Lithuania has stepped up security measures around strategic infrastructure amid growing concern about potential threats in the Baltic region.

Russian businessman Sergei Shnaider, the owner of the Mere discount retail chain operating in Lithuania and Latvia, has been added to the European Union’s 21st sanctions package. The measures is forcing the chain to close all its supermarkets operating in Lithuania, 15min.lt reported on Friday. According to 15min.lt, several of the Mere shops in Vilnius appeared to be already closed on Friday afternoon. Contacted by BNS, a representative of Mere declined to comment on whether the closures were temporary or if they were linked to the sanctions. “Due to technical issues, we are not operating anywhere in Lithuania,” the representative, who declined to give her name, told BNS. The Ministry of Economy and Innovation confirmed on Friday that the owners of the Svetofor Group – which also owns the Mere stores in Lithuania – are under EU sanctions. As of Thursday, all funds and assets belonging to these individuals within the EU must be frozen, and they are prohibited from receiving funds or other economic resources. Latvia’s Financial Intelligence Unit also reported that the chain’s operators in Latvia will have halt their activities. The Latvian authority said sanctions apply to Latprodukti, which operates the Mere chain in Latvia, and the Latvian branch of Lithuanian company Valiente. Both companies are required to immediately cease operations in compliance with EU sanctions. According to the Financial Intelligence Unit, Shnaider was sanctioned for materially or financially supporting actions that undermine or threaten Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. The agency said Shnaider indirectly owns more than 50% of both Latprodukti and Valiente’s Latvian operations. LRT reported last year that Valiente’s shares had been acquired by Spanish company Vigalight, which is owned by three Russian citizens who previously controlled the Mere retail chain. According to Spain’s corporate register, Shnaider owns 79% of Vigalight, while Andrei Veikulainen holds 15% and Valeriy Yakovlev owns the remaining 6%. Last October, Lithuania’s then Economy Minister Edvinas Grikšas said that Mere could be added to the sanctions list despite changes in its ownership structure. Latprodukti, established in 2020, reported revenue of 31.57 million euros in 2024, up 53% from the previous year, according to company filings. It posted a net loss of 71,800 euros after recording a profit in 2023. Its 2025 financial results have not yet been published. The company is directly owned by Serbia-based SKTrade DOO Beograd, while Shnaider is listed as its ultimate beneficial owner. Mere operates 12 stores in Latvia and around 20 in Lithuania.

Airspace violations in the Baltic states have stopped as Ukraine has shifted its attacks to targets deeper inside Russia, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Monday. “I think it is good that they are not entering our airspace. Because despite the fact that Ukraine has the right to defend itself and is successfully doing so, our airspace and the safety of our citizens remain our top priority,” Kaunas told LRT RADIO. He said the absence of recent incursions was likely linked to Ukraine targeting locations farther from the Baltic states’ borders. Kaunas also said drones that previously crashed in Lithuania had been Ukrainian aircraft affected by Russian electronic warfare systems. “So far, we have such evidence and confirmation, but that does not guarantee that Russia will not stage a false-flag provocation,” he said. “We are discussing this as well and cooperating with the Ukrainians to gather all possible intelligence, as well as with our NATO partners.” His comments came after Lithuanian media reported last week that the country’s military intelligence had information indicating Russia was considering attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region using captured Ukrainian drones in an attempt to mislead authorities about their origin. Kaunas said Lithuania was steadily strengthening its ability to monitor its airspace. The country has radars, is deploying acoustic sensors and has border surveillance cameras and other detection equipment, but the systems do not yet operate as a single integrated network. “There will be additional procurements in the autumn. We are forming an air defence regiment, and we have also announced that we are considering cooperation with South Korea so that we can obtain the systems we need more quickly,” Kaunas said. Lithuania is also working with local businesses to develop an integrated detection system using artificial intelligence that could be connected to kinetic capabilities, he said. “We have already been communicating and cooperating with Lithuanian businesses, seeking to involve them so that they can help create an integrated detection system in Lithuania, based on artificial intelligence, to which we could connect kinetic capabilities,” Kaunas said. Russia accused the Baltic states in April of allowing Ukraine to use their airspace to launch strikes against Russia. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia rejected the accusations in a joint statement at the time, while Lithuania’s military described the Kremlin’s claims as disinformation. Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine in recent months, including strikes on the capital, Kyiv, using ballistic missiles that are difficult to intercept. Kyiv has also indicated that it faces shortages of air defence systems.

More than five years since the beginning of the migration crisis, Lithuania's accommodation centres are still struggling to provide basic living conditions. According to a report by the Seimas Ombudsmen's Office, some people are also subjected to collective punishment and de facto detentions. "First and foremost, this raises not only issues of dignity but also hygiene and safety," Lithuania's Seimas Ombudsperson and head of the Seimas Ombudsmen's Office, Erika Leonaitė, told LRT.lt. The Seimas Ombudsmen's Office published an almost 100-page report on conditions at the Pabradė Reception Centre, which is run by the Reception and Integration Agency, as well as at the Foreigners Registration Centre operated by the State Border Guard Service (VSAT). The government’s Reception and Integration Agency said the shortcomings identified in the report were already being addressed, although this could not yet be independently verified. The agency rejected LRT’s request to visit the Pabradė centre. According to Leonaitė, the problems in Lithuania's migrant accommodation centres extend beyond living conditions. In her view, many of them stem from much deeper issues rooted in public attitudes. "The main problem is a lack of empathy and a human rights-based approach," the ombudsperson said. "Some people believe that restricting the rights of foreigners somehow increases the rights of others. But human rights do not work that way – once they are undermined in one context, the entire culture of human rights and the rule of law suffers," she added. The ombudspersons expressed particular concern about cases in which all residents had their freedom of movement restricted because of violations committed by individual people. According to the report, the combined effect of these restrictions amounted, in practice, to detention. In some cases, residents were not even allowed to go into the internal courtyard for a walk. According to the centre's administration, 170 people were living in the residential blocks in November 2025. Of these, 103 were migrants who had crossed the border irregularly or were staying in Lithuania without legal grounds and had not applied for asylum. A further 59 were asylum seekers, three were awaiting a decision on whether they would be allowed to enter Lithuania, one person had temporary protection as a Ukrainian citizen, and three had already received final decisions rejecting their asylum applications. Most of the residents came from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen and Eritrea, as well as Russia, Belarus, Uzbekistan and several other countries. As of November 7, 2025, only 26 of the 170 people accommodated at the Pabradė Reception Centre were not subject to restrictions on their movement, the report said. In other words, some form of restriction was imposed on around 85 percent of the centre's residents. Inspectors also found that living conditions varied depending on which floor residents lived on. Those on the ground floor – families, couples and the most vulnerable people – were allowed access only to a small internal courtyard. Men living on the second floor had access to a separate courtyard. Conditions on the third and fourth floors were considerably worse. During one inspection, the doors to the third floor were locked, and there were no staff nearby who could allow residents access to the internal courtyard. Moreover, when inspectors used the internal telephone to contact the duty officer, nobody answered. During a later inspection, the doors were again locked, and residents said they were unable to leave the building independently at all. According to them, they could only go outside when escorted to and from the dining hall or during organised football training sessions. Inspectors were particularly concerned by cases in which individuals were placed in complete isolation. According to the report, some foreigners on the third and fourth floors were locked inside their rooms and deprived entirely of the possibility of leaving them. The restrictions were so severe that they could not even step into the corridor or go for a walk on their own. The report therefore shows that a large proportion of foreigners who are not officially classified as detainees are, in reality, living under conditions resembling closed detention. Seimas Ombudsperson Leonaitė said such practices are incompatible with both international human rights standards and the principles enshrined in Lithuania's Constitution. "International human rights standards, as well as our Constitution – Article 20 of which states that 'Human freedom shall be inviolable' – emphasise that a person's natural state is freedom, and only afterwards, following an individual assessment, may certain restrictions on liberty be imposed. "However, in Lithuania the opposite applies to foreigners: their freedom is restricted first, and only then is it decided whether those restrictions can be eased. Collective punishment cannot be justified under any circumstances," she said. For its part, the Reception and Integration Agency stressed that the ombudspersons' findings relate to a specific period and the circumstances that existed at the time. Agency representatives acknowledged that collective measures had been used in the past but insisted that their purpose was not to punish residents. "These measures were introduced to ensure the safety of staff and other residents, reduce the risk of people leaving the centre without authorisation, and respond to exceptional situations, including the management of infectious diseases," the agency said in a statement to LRT.lt. The agency added that such practices are no longer used. Following publication of the report, it reviewed its procedures in light of the ombudspersons' recommendations. According to the agency, arrangements for outdoor exercise and access to fresh air have also been revised. Residents are now regularly informed about the applicable rules and their opportunities to leave the centre'

The United States has not yet made final decisions about its military presence in Europe, meaning there is also no clarity on the future of US troops in Lithuania, the European Union’s ambassador to the United States said. “I’m not sure that the Americans themselves know and have made the decisions,” EU Ambassador Jovita Neliupšienė told Lithuanian news portal 15min.lt in an interview. “First of all, the Americans themselves need to know what to expect and what the final decisions will be,” she said. Neliupšienė said Europe was not a priority in the US National Security Strategy, making it difficult to expect Washington to devote significant attention to the continent. The strategy first focuses on Latin America and the United States’ immediate neighbourhood, where Washington is concerned with disrupting drug trafficking and cartels and controlling migration, she said. “Another priority – if we look at the strategy, although here it differs from reality – was Asia and Southeast Asia, managing the economic threats posed by China,” Neliupšienė said. “In reality, the second priority could be considered security and stability in the Middle East because of the ongoing military conflict with Iran.” “Only then can we talk about Europe. So if you are the fourth priority in strategic documents, it is probably difficult to expect a great deal of attention,” she said. The United States is currently reviewing the deployment of its forces in Europe. Laurynas Kasčiūnas, deputy chairman of the Lithuanian parliament’s National Security and Defence Committee, said in early August that decisions on the rotation of US troops in Lithuania would be clear by early autumn. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has not confirmed that timeline. He said the United States and other partners had asked Lithuania not to disclose too much information about the issue. More than 1,000 US troops completed a rotation in Lithuania this summer. Kaunas said some US troops remain in the country, but the rotation process “has not yet returned to the standard level”. The United States has regularly deployed battalion-sized units to Lithuania since 2019. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Washington changed the status of its forces in Lithuania to continuous rotational deployments. The reinforced battalions typically consist of 1,000 or more troops and are equipped with a range of combat vehicles and other military equipment. Lithuania has said it is prepared to host up to 1,500 US troops.

Belarusians living in Lithuania gathered in Vilnius on Sunday to mark the sixth anniversary of mass protests against President Alexander Lukashenko’s rule, with participants reaffirming their support for democracy in their country and Ukraine. The commemoration began with a rally in Cathedral Square that drew about 100 people. Former political prisoners, politicians, civil society representatives and supporters of Belarus spoke about the country’s struggle for democracy. Participants carried Belarus’ historical white-red-white flags, chanted “Long Live Belarus!” and sang songs that have become symbols of Belarusian solidarity. Many of the Belarusians attending said they still believe the political situation in their country can change, although their optimism has faded since 2020. “I am not as optimistic as I was six years ago,” said Anatoliy Khinevich, a 32-year-old IT specialist who spent two and a half years in prison for participating in protests. Katsiaryna Kanapliova, a 31-year-old French teacher who moved to Lithuania four years ago, said she still hoped for change. “Of course we have hope; the faith hasn’t died out. Maybe in a few years the situation will change,” Kanapliova said. “Our goal is to preserve our Belarusian identity within ourselves. Even if we live in different countries, we want to keep our identity.” Kanapliova said the commemoration was also intended to remind the world that Belarusians continue to resist Lukashenko’s regime and support Ukraine. Tatyana, a 53-year-old former medical centre administrator, said she continued to hope for change six years after the protests. She attended the rally to remind people that “Lukashenko lost the 2020 elections”. “Today we continue the fight for a free, democratic Belarus. We are doing what the people in Belarus cannot,” she said. “I left to escape criminal prosecution after being detained twice, in 2022 and 2024.” Ilya Mironov, a 44-year-old logistics specialist from Gomel who was previously imprisoned in Belarus, also said he believed political change was possible. “We all remember the Soviet Union – it collapsed literally in six months, and in 1990 no one could imagine it was possible,” Mironov said. “But that Soviet empire fell, and independent republics emerged, including the Baltic states and Belarus. So, everything can change in Belarus too.” Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, who moved from Vilnius to Warsaw this year, said in a statement released Sunday that the struggle for democracy was not over. “We are determined to finish what we started in 2020. I truly believe Belarus can become a success story – a story of transition from dictatorship to democracy,” Tsikhanouskaya said. She called on supporters to push for the release of political prisoners, maintain pressure on the Lukashenko regime and stand with Ukraine. About 48,000 Belarusian citizens hold residence permits in Lithuania, according to the Migration Department. Most arrived after the 2020 protests, primarily as labour migrants. Following the rally, participants marched to the Belarusian Embassy, where they observed a minute of silence for victims of political repression and people killed fighting for Ukraine. The commemoration ended with an acoustic concert by Yuriy Stylski, leader of the Belarusian rock band Dai Darogu!. Mass protests erupted across Belarus in August 2020 after Lukashenko claimed victory in a presidential election widely regarded as fraudulent. Authorities responded with a sweeping crackdown, detaining about 65,000 people. Key opposition figures were jailed or forced into exile, prompting Western countries to impose sanctions on the Lukashenko government.

Lithuania, Poland and other Baltic states are stepping up security around dams, power plants and natural gas infrastructure amid concerns that Russia could stage “false-flag” attacks intended to trigger confusion within NATO, Reuters reported Monday. Lithuania has strengthened protection of critical infrastructure after its military intelligence reportedly obtained information that Russia was considering attacks in the Baltic region using captured Ukrainian drones in an attempt to obscure their origin. NATO’s eastern-flank countries have also publicly warned in recent weeks that they have intelligence indicating Russia could be preparing to carry out provocations using kinetic means. Since June 18, Lithuania’s military has been supporting the Public Security Service in protecting the country’s liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipėda, the LitPol Link electricity interconnection substation with Poland in Alytus, a transformer substation in the Alytus district and the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydroelectric Power Plant. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas signed an order July 17 extending the security support through August 19. The military is authorised to deploy a unit of up to 30 personnel, equipped with vehicles, as well as a vessel or boat with a crew. Kaunas, the Latvian prime minister and four intelligence and corporate officials from across the region shared new details of intelligence assessments and measures being taken to protect infrastructure in interviews with Reuters. “We are increasing the security of our critical infrastructure, we constantly exchange information with our intelligence on what to do next,” Kaunas told Reuters. Latvia has increased security around all critical infrastructure, including a dam on the Daugava River near Riga and the Inčukalns underground natural gas storage facility, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told Reuters. In Poland, energy company Orlen is examining alternative natural gas import routes in case its usual supplies or infrastructure are threatened, a person familiar with the company’s operations told Reuters. Orlen imports about 80% of Poland’s gas through the Świnoujście liquefied natural gas terminal on the Baltic Sea and an undersea pipeline carrying Norwegian gas that comes ashore nearby. Gaz-System, which operates the infrastructure, is working under heightened alert conditions, another person familiar with the matter told Reuters. Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe, the state-owned company developing Poland’s first nuclear power plant, said forged company documents had surfaced in an apparent attempt to mislead stakeholders. The company said the trail led “east of Poland”. The company is investigating the matter with intelligence and law enforcement agencies and monitoring the planned construction site for possible sabotage or other threats, spokesman Marcin Skolimowski said. Poland’s electricity grid operator and a military unit also began increasing security in July around an electricity connection with Ukraine that helps stabilise the war-damaged country’s power grid, which is regularly targeted by Russian attacks.

German investigators have found a DNA trace linking a recent drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport to a Lithuanian investigation into incendiary parcels sent abroad, German tabloid Bild reported Monday. The DNA trace has not been linked to a specific individual but matches evidence collected after an incident at a DHL logistics centre in Leipzig in July 2024, according to the report. At the time, four parcels were sent from Lithuania to Britain and Poland. Two of the packages, which contained incendiary devices, were shipped through DHL. One caught fire at Leipzig airport in Germany and another ignited at a warehouse in Britain. Charges related to the incendiary devices have been brought against Lithuanian citizen Aleksandr Suranov; Ukrainian citizens Vadym Borsuk and Vasyl Kovach; dual Russian-Lithuanian national Daniil Jencius; and Russian citizen Eldar Salmanov. The reported DNA link comes as German authorities investigate a drone carrying explosives that was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4. The incident occurred one day after testimony by Philippe Bauer, DHL’s senior director for security network operations support in Europe, at a Vilnius court in connection with the Lithuanian case. The drone incident was followed by another aviation incident in which an aircraft collided with an unidentified object in midair and sustained minor damage, according to reports. Leipzig/Halle Airport is a base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines and one of Europe’s major cargo hubs. It also plays an important role in military logistics, handling shipments for the German armed forces and NATO allies. Reports have suggested that a bus driver at the airport may have brought down the drone after spotting it flying near the Ukrainian aircraft. The circumstances surrounding the drone and its alleged connection to the earlier parcel incidents remain under investigation. The Wall Street Journal reported last week, citing sources, that US intelligence agencies had linked the Leipzig airport drone to Russia.

A nearly century-old empty sarcophagus in Vilnius Cathedral is waiting for the remains of one of Lithuania’s most revered rulers. This autumn, archaeologists will begin a new search for the remains of Grand Duke Vytautas the Great (c. 1350–1430), as part of a much broader effort to uncover the secrets of the cathedral’s past. The Lithuanian government approved a plan in early July for scientific research aimed at investigating possible locations of Vytautas’ remains. It also approved a wider program of research into Vilnius Cathedral, including archaeological excavations, architectural studies, historical research and the examination of human remains. The work is expected to create a database of people buried in the cathedral over different periods and a comprehensive bioarchive of samples taken from the remains. Historians and archaeologists broadly agree that the research will significantly expand knowledge of the cathedral, where systematic investigations have never been carried out on this scale. But they are divided over whether the long-standing search for Vytautas’ remains will succeed. The stone sarcophagus in the cathedral’s Chapter Crypt was made nearly 100 years ago and remains empty. Its inscription bears the date October 27, 1930, when Lithuania marked the 500th anniversary of Vytautas’ death. Vytautas, who ruled the Grand Duchy of Lithuania from 1392 until his death in 1430, never became king, although he sought a royal crown. He remains one of the most important figures in Lithuanian history. The first serious professional archaeological investigations of the cathedral’s underground crypts began around the 1930 anniversary, when researchers hoped they might find Vytautas’ intact remains, perhaps alongside his insignia or regalia. Instead, they encountered problems from the get-go. “The reality turned out to be much more complicated because of the dampness of the underground spaces, the high groundwater level and flooding in the city,” said Alina Pavasarytė, a historian at the Church Heritage Museum. “The underground spaces are, obviously, underground, and this is the deepest place in the Old Town.” Wooden coffins buried there had largely decomposed, leaving human remains mixed together, she said. The search intensified in recent years as Lithuania approaches the 600th anniversary of Vytautas’ death. It also gained momentum after historical researcher Saulius Poderis, who has been convicted of illegal archaeology, published his theory about where Vytautas’ remains might have been hidden. “I am a supporter of the theory that Vytautas was found during the interwar period,” Poderis said, arguing that systematic excavations at the cathedral at the time uncovered his remains. He points to a letter by 18th-century historian Franciszek Ksawery Bohusz, which he says indicated that Vytautas was buried near Grand Duke Alexander Jagiellon in the cathedral’s crypt. According to the official historical account, the remains of three rulers – Alexander Jagiellon, Barbara Radziwiłł and Elisabeth of Austria – were discovered in the cathedral in 1931. All three are now buried in the royal crypt. Poderis argues that the remains of Vytautas may also have been discovered but deliberately concealed because Vilnius was then under Polish control and relations between Poland and Lithuania were deeply strained. “It was a political decision. It was made on the same day the crypt was discovered,” Poderis said. Vytautas’ remains have long carried significance beyond archaeology. The 500th anniversary of his death in 1930 was one of the most important state events in interwar Lithuania. The country was still building its national identity after declaring independence in 1918, and Vytautas was embraced as a symbol of a powerful and independent Lithuania. With Vilnius under Polish control at the time, his legacy also came to symbolise Lithuania’s historical claim to its capital. “Vytautas is remembered in Lithuanian consciousness and memory as one of the most prominent and successful rulers, a defender of independence and a symbol of Lithuania in the 14th and 15th centuries,” said Antanas Petrilionis, a lecturer at Vilnius University’s Faculty of History. “That image of Vytautas and his remains becomes important because people need a symbol they can see, not just hear about,” he said. Poderis said he has spent 17 years investigating the mystery and remains convinced that Vytautas’ remains were secretly reburied during the interwar period. One of the locations he considers most likely is the western wall of the royal mausoleum. Archaeologists from the Lithuanian Institute of History plan to investigate the site this autumn. “This will be an invasive investigation to check the location indicated by Poderis,” said archaeologist Rytis Jonaitis. “A hole will be drilled through the wall, a probe with a camera will be inserted and we will look at what is inside.” Poderis has identified several other possible locations. But Jonaitis said archaeologists cannot simply drill into every one. “If we drilled into every place, we would turn the cathedral into a sieve,” he said. Ground-penetrating scans and other technologies can reveal whether there is an empty space behind a wall, Jonaitis said, but they cannot determine what is inside it. The search for Vytautas is only one part of the government-backed research program. The government has allocated about 7.5 million euros for a comprehensive investigation of Vilnius Cathedral. Researchers will examine the cathedral’s history and historical documents, study its structure and masonry, conduct archaeological excavations, assess artworks and their value, and analyse human remains. Researchers believe about 800 sets of human remains have already been identified in the cathedral. But identifying Vytautas would require more than finding remains in a plausible location.
