Lithuania’s Social Security and Labour Minister Inga Ruginienė has criticised a decision by the Vilnius city government to stop accepting written requests and complaints in Russian, saying the policy risks promoting social exclusion. “The discussion about Russian-language proficiency is very strange,” Ruginienė told the radio Žinių Radijas on Tuesday. Ruginienė said she supports the use of Lithuanian as the country’s official language but noted that some residents, particularly older people, still communicate primarily in Russian. “To me, this is also a matter of respect,” she said. “Are we fostering exclusion and sorting people into good or bad, those with us or those against us? I do not particularly like this approach.” The Vilnius municipality announced last week that it would no longer accept written applications and complaints from residents in Russian. Information in Russian and other non-European Union languages will only be provided orally only when a municipal employee is able to communicate in the requested language. Russian has also been removed from the municipality’s website and administrative queue management systems. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, a fellow social democrat, also questioned the decision, asking whether it was motivated by political considerations or intended as a communications stunt. Vilnius Mayor Valdas Benkunskas defended the policy as part of the municipality’s “consistent approach” to language use. At the same time, the municipality announced plans to expand Lithuanian-language learning opportunities for foreign residents. More than 1,000 people are expected to take part in free Lithuanian-language courses and remote learning programs this year. The municipality has allocated an additional 300,000 euros for the initiative.

Andrius Blaževičius’ relationship drama How to Divorce During the War, which won an award at the Sundance Film Festival earlier this year and is set for a US theatrical release, has been selected as Lithuania’s submission for consideration in the best international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards. The decision was made by Lithuania’s national selection committee, approved by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, the Lithuanian Film Centre said Tuesday. “One of the main arguments for choosing this film was its relevance and proximity,” said committee chairman and director Ignas Miškinis. “It combines human relationships with geopolitical reality, as the title itself suggests.” The film is set against the backdrop of the Ukraine war and explores anxiety, tension, uncertainty about the future, the collapse of a relationship and its impact on the people around it. Miškinis said those themes are universal and can resonate regardless of a viewer’s country or circumstances. He also praised the film’s simplicity and accessible story, saying its characters are easy to identify with and their motivations are clearly portrayed. Naturalistic performances also contribute to the film’s impact, he said. How to Divorce During the War is Blaževičius’ third feature as director and screenwriter. It stars Žygimantė Elena Jakštaitė, Marius Repšys and Amelija Adomaitytė. The drama follows Marija, an ambitious manager at a major advertising agency, and Vytas, a struggling filmmaker searching for direction. When Marija finally decides to tell Vytas that she wants a divorce, she chooses what turns out to be the worst possible time for the conversation. The film premiered at Sundance, where Blaževičius won the directing award. It has since screened at nearly 20 international festivals and received several special awards. “I’m very happy that the love drama How to Divorce During the War will represent Lithuania in the Oscar race,” Blaževičius said. “I hope this will add even more value to the film internationally, particularly in the US, where it will be released in theatres at the end of August.” The film opens in Lithuanian cinemas September 18. The Lithuanian Film Centre and the Lithuanian Filmmakers Union organise the national Oscar selection. The 2026 committee was chaired by Miškinis and included film critics Rasa Paukštytė and Neringa Kažukauskaitė, director and producer Arturas Jevdokimovas, film distributor Giedrė Krikščiūnaitė, animator Valentas Aškinis, and cinematographer and director Eitvydas Doškus. Lithuania’s previous Oscar contenders include Miškinis’ The Southern Chronicles in 2025, Laurynas Bareiša’s Daughters in 2024, Marija Kavtaradzė’s Slow in 2023, Bareiša’s Pilgrims in 2022 and Jurgis Matulevičius’ “Isaac” in 2021. Being selected as Lithuania’s submission is only the first step in the Oscar process. The Academy will review submissions from countries around the world before selecting a shortlist and then five final nominees in the international feature film category. No Lithuanian film has yet received an Oscar nomination in the international feature film category. The 99th Academy Awards ceremony is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

Vilnius must find a compromise that allows Ukrainians and Belarusians to communicate with city authorities in their native languages, Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas said Wednesday, after the capital stopped accepting written requests and complaints in Russian. “I believe that officially we should use the state language,” Olekas told the radio Žinių Radijas. “However, in such interactions, there are other nations whose languages have become more prevalent in Vilnius.” He said he was primarily referring to Ukrainians and Belarusians, who “should not necessarily be forced to speak Russian”. “It seems a compromise must be found for arriving people; a guest can be received in their own language,” Olekas said. At the same time, people planning to live in Lithuania for an extended period should be encouraged to learn Lithuanian, he said. Olekas also said Lithuania needs to improve access to Lithuanian-language education for foreigners, particularly those who have fled war or authoritarian regimes. The Vilnius municipality announced last week that it would no longer accept written applications and complaints in Russian. Information in Russian and other non-European Union languages will be provided orally only when a municipal employee is proficient in the language. Russian has also been removed from the municipality’s website and its queue management system. The municipality said it was simultaneously expanding opportunities for foreign residents to learn Lithuanian. More than 1,000 people are expected to participate this year in free and remote courses, with an additional 300,000 euros allocated for the program.

Lithuania’s government on Wednesday amended its plan for counter-mobility measures, establishing a new defence zone along the country’s borders with Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region. Under the revised plan, a 20-meter-wide counter-mobility strip will extend from the border patrol road into Lithuanian territory. In areas designated by the military for operations, the strip will be widened to 150 meters. The changes come as Lithuania expands its network of defences intended to slow or prevent the movement of hostile forces and military equipment in the event of an attack. The government has pushed back the deadline for completing engineering equipment parks at designated military sites to the end of 2028, from the original April 2025 target. The Defence Ministry said the extension was necessary because the number of planned parks has increased from 27 to 50. The expanded network will require additional time to implement, while state-owned rail infrastructure company LTG Infra has also been tasked with providing storage facilities for the engineering equipment. The deadline for installing reserve obstacles on national roads and approaches to bridges, as well as fitting bridges with structures for explosives, has also been extended to the end of 2028. The revised plan shifts the focus of some measures from planting tree barriers to creating marshes. Those projects are expected to be completed by the end of 2030. According to the ministry, restoring swamps in selected areas should make them impassable for heavy military equipment within several years. Plans to build defensive drainage ditches and stream networks in the Marijampolė municipality have been dropped. The ministry said more suitable locations for such measures had been identified in the Vilkaviškis and Šakiai districts. The changes could require an additional 50 million euros from Lithuania’s State Defence Fund between 2026 and 2030. The government originally approved its counter-mobility plan in July 2024. Lithuania began developing counter-mobility parks in 2023, drawing on lessons from Russia’s war in Ukraine. Last year, the Defence Ministry introduced a unified three-tier defence line, with defensive measures planned at distances of 3, 20 and 50 kilometres from the country’s border.

Ukrainian defence industry company DEMZ will invest in a new ammunition plant in Lithuania, the Lithuanian Ministry of the Economy and Innovation said Thursday. The ministry said it would sign an investment agreement with the company for the major project. “DEMZ will invest in a new ammunition plant in Lithuania, which will become a regional production and innovation centrr for the company, where new products meeting NATO standards will be developed and tested,” the ministry said in a statement. The Lithuanian Ministry of Defence will also sign a memorandum of understanding with DEMZ, according to the statement. Elijus Čivilis, head of Invest Lithuania, the country’s investment promotion agency, previously told BNS that several Ukrainian defence industry investors had received approval from a government commission responsible for screening strategic transactions to operate in Lithuania. Lithuania is seeking to expand cooperation with Ukraine in the defence industry as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has said Lithuania aims to produce drones for Ukraine. He said the effort would involve joint investments under an agreement signed in May to strengthen cooperation with Ukraine in the defence industry.

Lithuania has completed the exhumation of the remains of Soviet soldiers from a cemetery in the centre of Vievis, a town in in the Elektrenai municipality, local authorities said Wednesday. “Archaeological research at the Vievis Soviet soldiers’ cemetery was successfully concluded this week,” Vievis Mayor Gediminas Ratkevičius said. Archaeologists discovered the remains of 81 people who died during World War Two, he said. The remains are being prepared for transfer to specialists at the Department of Anatomy, Histology and Anthropology at Vilnius University’s Faculty of Medicine for detailed anthropological examination. They will later be reburied at an Orthodox cemetery in Vievis. The Soviet soldiers were buried in the centre of Vievis, near St Anne’s Church. A monument to Soviet soldiers, accompanied by an eternal flame, formerly stood at the site. The decision to remove the burial site followed findings by Lithuania’s so-called De-Sovietisation Commission, which concluded that the site violated a ban on promoting totalitarian and authoritarian regimes and their ideologies in public spaces. The commission said the burial site helped entrench the Soviet-promoted narrative of the “Great Patriotic War”. It also noted that the burials were secondary, with the remains having been moved there from other locations. Earlier this year, Soviet soldiers’ remains were also exhumed from the centre of Šiauliai. Russia’s Foreign Ministry protested both actions, accusing Lithuania of desecrating the remains. Vilnius has rejected Moscow’s allegations. A law banning the promotion of totalitarian and authoritarian regimes and their ideologies in public spaces took effect in Lithuania in May 2023. It requires symbols associated with totalitarianism and authoritarianism to be removed from public areas.

People who have survived drug-facilitated sexual assault in Lithuania say they are being let down by a system with too few specialist services, no reliable way to preserve evidence, and long waits for care. The country's social security ministry says changes are coming, but for now, campaigners say, survivors are often left to navigate the process largely on their own. Ten years ago, comedian and human rights advocate Vita Žiba was sexually assaulted after being drugged. She says it took her a while afterwards to understand what had happened to her. "First of all, you barely remember anything, because those drugs are usually designed specifically to suppress memory. I just remember having one drink, then another, and then – a black screen. The next thing I remember is being in some room, I don't even know where, with some man's hands all over me," she said. When Žiba shared her story on social media, she received an outpouring of support – within a week, roughly 800 women had come forward with their own experiences of sexual violence. But she also faced abuse online. "A lot of older men wrote things like 'you had it coming', 'it's your own fault', or 'you should be grateful someone wanted you'," she said. Campaigners note that the substances used in these assaults aren't limited to spiked drinks – they can also be administered by injection. Cases are likely a fraction of the true total Lithuanian prosecutors opened 13 pre-trial investigations two years ago into suspected sexual assaults involving psychoactive substances; seven were later dropped. "That's the tip of the iceberg. It's very hard to say how many cases there really are, because very often people don't recognise what happened to them, don't come forward, are afraid to seek help, or simply don't remember," said Reda Jureliavičiūtė, co-founder of the organisation Ribologija, which works on the issue. Getting help isn't straightforward, either. Specialist care is currently available at only five hospitals, all in Lithuania's largest cities. "If you live somewhere more rural, you have to get to a hospital, wait an hour to be seen – because sexual offences aren't treated as a priority – then wait again for transport to be arranged to the nearest of those five hospitals. And once you're there, you're back in a general queue," Jureliavičiūtė said. Advocates are calling for a clearer referral pathway that would route survivors directly to the right service, rather than leaving them to find it themselves. "Right now everything is scattered – institutions don't even know where to send you. You go to the police, they say go to a doctor, the doctor sends you somewhere else, and you get lost in the process. Meanwhile, if drugs were used, they clear the body within a limited window," Žiba said. Unlike in some other European countries, forensic samples collected from survivors in Lithuania are not currently retained for any length of time, meaning evidence can be lost even when a case is reported. "We need to be able to collect that evidence first, and hold onto it while the person decides whether to pursue a case. Right now we don't have that, there's no window built in for someone to make that decision," said Dalia Puidokienė, head of the support centre Prabilk (Speak Out). The social security and labour ministry says changes are on the way, including a new helpline and investment in dedicated support centres. "Our starting position is that healthcare providers should be required to notify the relevant support centre within 24 hours, so that someone is assigned to accompany the person through the entire process, from first contact onward," said Deputy Social Security and Labour Minister Rita Grigalienė. In the autumn, the ministry plans to bring amendments to parliament on Lithuania's law on protection against domestic violence, which would introduce a longer-term protection order for perpetrators alongside the existing 15-day emergency order. "The survivor would go to court, supported through that process, with all the necessary documentation prepared by specialist centres. We're still discussing whether the longer-term order should run for two, four or six months," Grigalienė said. If approved by parliament, the changes would take effect from June next year.

NATO allied fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace over the northeastern Balvi region early Friday, Latvia’s armed forces said, prompting a temporary air alert in the country’s eastern regions. An orange airspace alert was issued shortly before 04:00 local time in the municipalities of Augsdaugava, Preili, Rezekne, Balvi and Aluksne. Residents received mobile phone warnings urging them to take immediate precautions and seek shelter. The alert was lifted about an hour later after the drone was shot down. Latvia’s armed forces initially did not provide details about the drone’s origin. They described it as a foreign unmanned aerial vehicle that entered Latvian airspace as a result of Russian electronic warfare, suggesting it may have been a Ukrainian drone. Iveta Bērziņa, a spokeswoman for the Latvian armed forces’ Joint Headquarters, told Latvian Radio that she could not say how close to populated areas the drone was when it was shot down. The incident also prompted Finland to temporarily restrict air and maritime traffic in the eastern part of the Gulf of Finland, according to the information provided by Latvian authorities. It was not immediately clear which NATO fighter jets carried out the interception. NATO allies rotate responsibility for monitoring and protecting the airspace of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. The Turkish air force is currently deployed in Estonia, while Italy leads the NATO air defence mission in Lithuania. Latvia, an EU and NATO member of about 1.9 million people, shares a border with Russia to the east. Both Russia and Ukraine use drones extensively in the war in Ukraine, and several drones have crossed or approached the airspace of NATO countries in the region during the conflict. Lithuanian official: NATO drone interception launched from Šiauliai Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre chief Vilmantas Vitkauskas said Friday that the operation to intercept and destroy the drone over Latvia was carried out by fighter jets scrambled from Šiauliai Air Base in northern Lithuania. Vitkauskas told LRT TV that the incident appeared similar to a drone episode in May, when Russian electronic warfare systems allegedly diverted a Ukrainian drone into NATO airspace. “Based on the information we have so far, the object most likely changed course over Russian territory, or crossed the border from Belarus or Russia – that is still being determined,” Vitkauskas said. “The essence is that this is a very similar episode to the one that occurred in May, when operations were carried out [by Ukraine] against legitimate targets in Russia. Russian electronic warfare systems redirected this object, which then entered NATO territory,” he said. Vitkauskas said there were no reports of damage so far and that a search operation was underway. The incident occurred shortly after 04:00, he said. Fighter jets were scrambled from Šiauliai to identify the object and destroyed it several minutes after making contact, according to Vitkauskas. “We can be pleased that this was a successful air defence operation carried out from Lithuanian territory,” he said. Vitkauskas said Lithuanian radars had not detected a threat over Lithuania during the night. “As far as we know, only that one object was detected in Latvia. It changed course and, instead of heading toward a legitimate target in the Leningrad region, was diverted into NATO territory,” he said. He added that Finland had responded by restricting air and maritime traffic, as it normally does in such situations, while Estonian authorities also tracked the targets and shared information. Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said the origin of the drone remained to be determined. “We are gathering information on what kind of object it was and why it was flying here – that information will be clarified once it has been collected,” Kaunas told reporters on Friday.

A Lithuanian border guard was slightly injured during an incident near the Belarus border in late July when migrants allegedly tried to drag him toward Belarusian territory, the news portal Lrytas.lt reported Friday. The incident occurred in the area covered by the Kapčiamiestis Border Guard Station of the Varėna Border Guard Unit, according to Lrytas.lt. Sources told the portal that the officer is currently on sick leave. Vitalijus Jagminas, chairman of the Vilnius County Trade Union of Pretrial Investigation Institutions, also confirmed to Lrytas.lt that one of the border guards is on sick leave. The State Border Guard Service (VSAT) declined to comment on the circumstances of the incident when contacted by BNS, saying pretrial investigations are underway. Lrytas.lt also reported, citing sources, that VSAT commander Rustamas Liubajevas had allegedly instructed border guards on what to say about the incident. The report did not provide details of the alleged instructions. The incident was first reported last week by Delfi.lt, which said four border guards had set up an ambush after detecting a tunnel being dug underneath the state border in the Kapčiamiestis station’s area in Lazdijai district. According to Delfi.lt, border guards detained several migrants and handcuffed them, but about 20 foreigners then attacked the officers during the detention. The guards were forced to flee, while the migrants, including those who had been handcuffed, escaped into Belarus. VSAT publicly reported finding a tunnel and said migrants had fled but did not initially disclose the alleged attack on the officers. Liubajevas has repeatedly denied reports that border guards were attacked, saying VSAT had been unable to establish that such an incident occurred. Meanwhile, prosecutors last week expanded and reclassified a pretrial investigation launched July 27 into the illegal crossing of Lithuania’s state border in the Kapciamiestis border station area. The investigation was expanded to clarify initial information and examine publicly reported claims about the actions of VSAT officers responsible for organising and carrying out border surveillance, control and protection. Prosecutors said the aim is to establish and impartially assess the facts surrounding the incident and the actions of the officers involved. Border guard chief’s position on the line Lithuania’s interior minister said on Friday that VSAT chief Rustamas Liubajevas could not remain in his post if reports about the injured border guard were confirmed.

Some Lithuanian trade unions are opposing President Gitanas Nausėda’s proposals to tighten restrictions on the employment of foreign workers, saying the measures could encourage migrants to disregard local rules and increase the number of unskilled workers, LNK news reported Thursday. Nausėda has proposed a new system under which economic migrants would be allowed to work in Lithuania for a limited period and would then have to leave the country for at least six months. The president says the measure would help prevent family reunification and a faster increase in the migrant population. Audrius Cuzanauskas, head of the Lithuanian Trade Union Alliance, said requiring workers to leave the country periodically would make their employment less stable and could undermine efforts to ensure they meet labour requirements. “Two months are spent training these workers so they can do the job and at least meet the minimum requirements, even though supposedly skilled workers are being brought in,” Cuzanauskas said. “We already see that they are being brought in with quite a few violations, so it will be even worse then.” Nausėda’s adviser Evelina Gudzinskaitė defended the proposal, arguing that many foreign workers coming to Lithuania do not learn the Lithuanian language, pursue careers or seek to integrate into local culture. “The majority of the workforce currently coming to Lithuania does not seek this and does not even make an effort to do so. They just need to earn money,” she said, without quoting any evidence. Gudzinskaitė also argued that larger foreign communities could become more settled and attract additional migrants. “That means they would become factors attracting even more foreigners, and communities of such foreigners would be established,” she said. Social Security and Labour Minister Inga Ruginienė has previously criticised the proposed changes, saying they would not reduce the number of migrants in Lithuania but could instead increase the number of foreigners who remain illegally and refuse to follow the country’s rules. President Nausėda has proposed establishing a new model of fixed-term work permits for foreign nationals that would speed up the processing of applications while requiring workers to leave Lithuania for at least six months after their two-year work permits expire. The permit would not allow them to bring their families to Lithuania. The Seimas, Lithuania’s parliament, approved the proposals at the consideration stage in mid-July. If lawmakers give final approval, the changes would take effect next year.

Lithuania and Ukrainian defence company Dnipro Electromechanical Plant, or DEMZ, signed a major investment agreement Friday under which the company will establish ammunition production facilities in Lithuania and create up to 450 jobs. Lithuanian Economy Minister Edvinas Grikšas and DEMZ chief Jevhen Muzykin signed the agreement in Vilnius. The total value of the investment was not disclosed. DEMZ plans to build an ammunition assembly plant near Balbieriškis in the Prienai district and manufacture metal shell components at the Alytus Industrial Park. Construction is scheduled to begin this autumn, with production expected to start by the end of 2027. Alytus Mayor Nerijus Cesiulis said after the signing ceremony that DEMZ would invest tens of millions of euros in the city, although he did not provide a precise figure. He previously described the project as the largest investment to date in the Alytus region. Prienai Mayor Alvydas Vaicekauskas confirmed Friday that the new ammunition plant would be built near Balbieriškis. The Ministry of Defence and DEMZ also signed a memorandum of understanding to explore ways to use the company’s Lithuanian production capacity to meet Ukraine’s needs and strengthen resilient defence supply chains in Europe. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius called the project important for both Lithuania’s security and its economy. He said Lithuania would produce NATO-standard defence products using Ukrainian expertise and battlefield experience. Grikšas said the investment would create highly skilled jobs and could help develop a broader ecosystem of Lithuanian defence companies around DEMZ’s facilities. The Economy and Innovation Ministry said products manufactured by DEMZ in Lithuania would meet NATO standards. The Ukrainian armed forces would be the primary market, with allied defence needs serving as a secondary market. Grikšas declined to disclose the exact value of the investment but said it would rank among Lithuania’s largest recent investments. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said the Ukrainian investment would give Lithuania an opportunity to adapt more quickly to developments on the battlefield. “This is a vital innovation process – not only to be able to produce, but also to adapt to the changing situation at the front,” Kaunas said. “If something changes, or if security risks shift, we will have additional capacities for our needs.” The project comes as Lithuania is rapidly expanding its defence industry and seeking to strengthen domestic production capacity amid Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Lithuania’s security threat level remains largely unchanged despite warnings that Russia may be considering attacks on critical infrastructure in the region using Ukrainian-origin drones, the chairman of the parliamentary Committee on National Security and Defence said Friday. “I want to reassure the public that the information presented in this manner has caused unnecessary anxiety. The threat level remains similar,” Rimantas Sinkevičius said after a closed-door committee meeting at the Second Investigation Department, Lithuania’s military intelligence service. Sinkevičius said intelligence agencies had already warned in June of the possibility of various types of incidents, noting that the potential threats were not limited to Lithuania but also concerned other countries in the region. He said Lithuania was strengthening its preparedness by acquiring defensive equipment and improving coordination among state institutions. However, he added that it was impossible to be fully prepared for every possible incident. Reports emerged last week citing Lithuanian military intelligence that Russia might be considering sabotage operations against critical infrastructure in the Baltic region using drones of Ukrainian origin, so called “false flag” operations. The intelligence did not identify specific targets or provide a timeline for any potential attacks. Since June 18, the Lithuanian military has been assisting in the protection of key infrastructure, including the liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipėda, the LitPol Link electricity interconnection in Alytus and the Kruonis pumped-storage hydroelectric plant.

Lithuania’s Ministry of Defence is stepping in to preserve an underground printing press that secretly operated for a decade during Soviet rule, after a military museum decided not to renew an agreement that had allowed the privately owned site to operate as a museum exhibit. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas called the decision bureaucratic and said the government would ensure the historic site remains open to visitors. The underground printing press is located beneath a private property in the village of Saliai, in Kaunas district. A concealed entrance beneath a greenhouse leads to the underground facility. The press was established by Vytautas Andziulis and his associate, Juozas Bacevičius, during the Soviet era. Andziulis’ son, Vykintas, now leads tours of the site. “This is the only entrance and exit to the printing press. Paper was brought in through here,” he said, showing the site. For about 30 years, the printing press operated free of charge as a branch of the Vytautas the Great War Museum under a use agreement. Three members of the Andziulis family worked part time as guides. But the museum decided not to renew the agreement effective August 6 and removed the site from its list of exhibits. The museum’s director, Rita Malinauskienė, said the decision was prompted primarily by concerns about the condition of the building. Cracks were discovered in the ceiling in May, making tours potentially unsafe. She said legal restrictions prevent the museum from using public funds to repair privately owned property. “The biggest problem was the condition of the printing press, and as the head of the institution responsible for fiscal discipline, I could not use money from the printing press’s budget for repairs because it is private property,” Malinauskienė said. The Andziulis family said it did not expect the museum to finance repairs. Vykintas Andziulis said the damaged ceiling had already been repaired by the family. The site attracted about 2,200 visitors last year, free of charge. The family says continued operation at that scale would be difficult without state support. “If we are not suitable as employees, fine, send someone else,” Andziulis said. “We can discuss and negotiate, but there were no negotiations on this issue.” Minister Kaunas travelled to Kaunas district to discuss the situation and said he did not understand the museum’s decision to terminate the arrangement. “The underground printing press was never discovered by Soviet authorities, it was never destroyed, even though it was supposed to operate for only two years. It operated for 10,” Kaunas said. “And now we ourselves want to finish what the Russians failed to do – destroy such an object.” The Defence Ministry currently provides funding through the museum for staff working at the site. About 30,000 euros is allocated annually for the printing press guides’ salaries, while about 13,000 euros has been spent on maintenance services over the past five years. Kaunas said the government could find a way to support the privately owned site, pointing to other cases in which the government purchases services from private organisations. “The state can contribute to private entities and does so – it contributes to private pension funds, purchases services from private schools and private clinics,” he said. “There are precedents and mechanisms, and from the Defence Ministry’s perspective, this site must be protected.” Malinauskienė said the museum was now working with the deputy defence minister to determine what type of use agreement could allow the site to continue operating. The underground press operated from the 1980s until the restoration of Lithuania’s independence in the early 1990s. During that period, it produced nearly 140,000 publications, most of them patriotic and religious literature that was banned or restricted under Soviet rule. The press remained hidden from Soviet authorities throughout its operation and became an important part of Lithuania’s history of underground resistance.

This year, the title of Lithuanian Capital of Culture belongs to Kėdainiai, a historic town once ruled by the powerful Radziwill family and shaped by centuries of encounters between different peoples and faiths. Located in central Lithuania, Kėdainiai is perhaps best known as the country’s “cucumber capital”. But its compact historic centrr offers a richer story, with centuries-old churches and synagogues, distinctive architecture, a forgotten river port and traditional crafts that are still practiced today. The town’s multicultural heritage is particularly visible in its houses of worship. According to Rimantas Žirgulis, director of the Kėdainiai Regional Museum, the town was especially diverse during its period of prosperity in the 17th century, when six ethnic and religious communities lived there. Today, visitors can see an Orthodox church housed in a brick building dating to the second half of the 19th century. The Church of the Transfiguration of Christ retains early 20th-century paintings and valuable icons. Two Catholic churches also form part of Kėdainiai’s architectural heritage. The Gothic Church of St George, built in the 15th century, is one of Lithuania’s oldest churches. It contains notable works of art, late Baroque altars and a relic of Blessed Teofilius Matulionis. The wooden Church of St Joseph, dating to the 18th century, stands with its bell tower near the centre of town. It is known for paintings of St Joseph and the Virgin Mary with the infant Jesus, both featuring ornate metal coverings. “The Church of St George is a unique 15th-century brick church, one of the oldest in Lithuania. The Church of St Joseph is wooden and dates to the 18th century,” Žirgulis told LRT.lt. “It is also unusual that what looks like a village church stood in the middle of what was, for its time, a large town.” Kėdainiai’s religious heritage also reflects its once-powerful Protestant communities. A 17th-century Evangelical Reformed church contains a mausoleum of the Radziwill family and historic pipe organs. The mausoleum was the first restored 17th-century burial site of Lithuanian Grand Duchy nobles in the country. It contains the sarcophagi of several members of the Radziwill family, including Krzysztof I “Perkūnas”, Janusz II, Mikolaj, Jerzy, Stepan and Elzbieta. The church was once the principal Evangelical Reformed church in Samogitia and later became the main church of the Lithuanian Reformed community, Žirgulis said. Another landmark is the 17th-century brick Evangelical Lutheran church, which retains original frescoes depicting the apostles Peter and Paul and the four evangelists. The church reflects the influence of Kėdainiai’s German Lutheran community, Žirgulis said. It stood in Jonušava, then a suburb or separate settlement named after Radziwill nobleman Janusz Radziwill. The town’s Jewish heritage is equally prominent. On Senosios Rinkos Square stands a synagogue complex consisting of the Great Summer Synagogue and the Small Winter Synagogue. The Great Synagogue was rebuilt in the Baroque style after a fire in the 18th century and now houses the Kėdainiai Art School. The 19th-century Neoclassical Small Synagogue houses a multicultural centre with an exhibition about the town’s Jewish community and the Holocaust. The complex is one of only three surviving synagogue complexes in Lithuania. The entire Old Town of Kėdainiai is a major attraction. It is a state-protected urban heritage site and one of just seven such sites in Lithuania. Its compact streets preserve elements of Baroque, Gothic, Renaissance and Neoclassical architecture. Four historic market squares – Senosios Rinkos, Didžiosios Rinkos, Knypavos Rinkos and Janušavos – testify to the town’s role as a regional commercial centre. Among the landmarks is the former 17th-century town hall on Didžiosios Rinkos Square, one of only three surviving historic town halls in Lithuania. The Old Town also preserves houses associated with the Kėdainiai Scottish community, including the Grey House. Another important landmark is Šviesioji Gymnasium, which dates to the middle of the 17th century. The Radziwills planned to develop it into a Protestant institution of higher education, although the ambitious project never came to fruition. Janusz Radziwill had elevated Kėdainiai’s four-grade school to gymnasium status and hoped eventually to turn it into a Protestant academy capable of competing with the Jesuit academy in Vilnius, Žirgulis said. Kėdainiai’s history was also shaped by the Nevėžis River. The site of the former Kėdainiai port, near the present-day Mikalojus Daukša Public Library, recalls the town’s history as a centre of commercial shipping. Flat-bottomed sailing cargo vessels known as vytinės once carried goods along the river. From Kėdainiai, they travelled to Konigsberg, carrying local and Lithuanian raw materials and returning with a variety of goods and luxury products. The town’s history of craftsmanship can still be experienced at the Traditional Crafts Centre, housed in the former Arnet House associated with the Scottish community of Kėdainiai. The centre displays folk art and hosts workshops where visitors can learn traditional crafts that are increasingly rare, Žirgulis said. The building also has a long religious history. From the second half of the 17th century until the end of the 19th century, it served as the residence of the superintendents of the Evangelical Reformed Church in Samogitia – effectively a regional religious centre. Kedainiai was also an important centre of Jewish life in Samogitia, with the region’s chief rabbis living in the town. Traces of that heritage can still be found along Žydų (Jewish) Street, including a surviving house at No. 2 with a wooden annex used for the Jewish festival of Sukkot. The roof of the structure could be opened, allowing residents to pray beneath the sky without leaving the house, Žirgulis explained. As Russia wages war on Ukraine, denying its own history of aggression against its neighbours, a little-known treaty signed 35 years ago is quietly getting in the way of the Kremlin's narrative. In July 1991, five months before the Soviet Union formally dissolved, Russia signed a treaty with Lithuania in which it recognised something Moscow has spent the past two decades trying to erase from the record: that the Soviet Union illegally annexed Lithuania in 1940, and that Lithuania's independence, declared in 1990, was legitimate. That document is still in force. Russia has never torn it up. And that, say Lithuanian officials and legal experts, makes it an awkward loose end for a Kremlin that now insists the Baltic states were never really occupied at all. Under President Vladimir Putin, Russian state doctrine has increasingly leaned on the claim that the Baltic states joined the USSR voluntarily, and that talk of "occupation" is Western-backed revisionism. That framing underpins not only Moscow's rhetoric towards Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia but also, in a broader sense, the ideological justification for its invasion of Ukraine – the idea that the borders and independence of post-Soviet states are negotiable, or fictional. The 1991 treaty directly contradicts that. Dainius Žalimas, a Lithuanian MEP who has studied the treaty closely, argues that its first article, which has no expiry date, remains one of Lithuania's strongest legal cards: it commits both countries to recognising each other as sovereign states with an inalienable right to independence, and bars either from meddling in each other's internal affairs as well as using or threatening force against the other. "All of this essentially refutes every claim made by current official Russian propaganda, and undermines the very foundations of the ideology of 'rashism'. That ideology, which underpins both the aggression against Ukraine and the denial of Baltic statehood, recognises neither the occupation of Lithuania nor the continuity of the Lithuanian state, among much else," said Žalimas. "I think the treaty is very important. We talk about the wavering authority of international law, but it gives Lithuania a solid line of international legal defence, and shows that Russia, for very brief periods in its history, can be different," he added. For example, Lithuania can continue to demand compensation from Russia for the damage caused by occupation, even though few believe this will ever happen in practice. "Just as the treaty of July 12, 1920 formed the basis for all subsequent treaties with the Soviet Union, the same applies here – dozens of Lithuanian-Russian agreements rest on the July 29, 1991 treaty. So the treaty still holds, as long as they haven't broken it," explained Česlovas Vytautas Stankevičius, former deputy chairman of the Supreme Council and head of the negotiating delegation with Russia, highlighting why the treaty still carries weight to this day. The path to the treaty began in secrecy. In May 1990, Vytautas Landsbergis, then chairman of Lithuania's Supreme Council (the country's parliament in the final Soviet years), held a clandestine meeting with Boris Yeltsin, his Russian counterpart, in an empty Moscow school classroom. The two men barely knew each other personally, and the meeting was arranged through informal contacts. Two months later, leaders of the three Baltic states and Russia met in the Latvian town of Jūrmala and agreed to pursue bilateral treaties – partly as a way of applying pressure on Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, who was still trying to hold the union together. That effort was not merely symbolic. The USSR spent 1990 and 1991 trying to force Lithuania, as well as other republics, back into line, including a 75-day economic blockade after its declaration of independence. At the time, it was unclear whether it was better to negotiate with the Soviet leadership or with Russia, which in June 1990 had issued its own declaration of state sovereignty. As a result, negotiations proceeded with both the Soviet authorities and with Yeltsin's Russia, which proved to be a great decision since once the Soviet Union collapsed, Russia became its legal successor. For Lithuania, negotiating and signing the treaty meant securing the backing of the largest Soviet republic for its independence – a powerful argument against the Soviet Union. Meanwhile, Russia's leadership was competing with the central Soviet authorities for control. "The goals of the two states coincided," summarized Stankevičius, who was appointed head of Lithuania's negotiating delegation. Having concluded treaties with Latvia and Estonia, Russia wanted to sign a similar document with Lithuania. But Lithuania's treaty took longer to conclude, largely because Vilnius pushed for tougher language than Moscow wanted to accept. Negotiators clashed over three issues in particular. The first was citizenship. Lithuania wanted to prevent members of the Soviet military and security apparatus – as well as their families – from automatically qualifying for Lithuanian citizenship, while also avoiding a settlement that would let ethnic Russians resident in the country claim dual nationality. A compromise formula eventually restricted citizenship rights to those with ties to Russia who had lived and worked in Lithuania since before November 1989. The second was how to characterise the movement of people under Soviet rule – specifically, how to avoid a formula that would have put Lithuanians deported to Russia by Stalin's regime in the same legal category as Russians who had been resettled into Lithuania as part of Soviet colonisation policy. The two sides eventually agreed on the neutral term "relocating persons" to cover both groups without equating them politically. Medical professionals from Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia returned Sunday from Ukraine after a two-week mission to train and exchange expertise with Ukrainian medical staff working amid the war. The mission was the first joint medical rotation involving all three Baltic states. The specialists trained alongside Ukrainian colleagues working in active combat zones, focusing on mass-casualty response, war trauma, patient evacuations and maintaining hospital operations under constant threat. Marija Jakubauskienė, health aide to the prime minister, described the mission as a testament to the three Baltic nations’ unwavering support for Ukraine. Health Minister Linas Kukuraitis welcomed the returning team and thanked the medical professionals on behalf of the state for their personal contribution to national preparedness. He presented letters of appreciation to each participant. Nine medics took part in the rotation: five from Lithuania, two traumatologists from Latvia and two nurses from Estonia, mission coordinator Vaiva Jankienė said Sunday. “We have a growing group of medical professionals who are capable of taking responsibility and knowing exactly how to act in these situations,” Jankienė told reporters. “More than 100 Lithuanian medics now have experience in Ukraine, which makes us feel much more secure. We have an expanding cohort that will know what to do when the need arises.” Jankienė did not disclose all the locations visited by the team but confirmed that the medics spent time in Dnipro. Medical training rotations in Ukraine will continue, with future missions planned for both existing and new locations. Adomas Kuliavas, head of the emergency department at Marijampolė Hospital, highlighted the resilience of Ukrainian medical staff. “Everyone is smiling, they are pleasant and welcome us as friends. It was an indescribable feeling of hope, I would say,” Kuliavas said. He recalled a poignant plea from a local doctor not to abandon Ukrainian medical staff. Kuliavas also spoke of a Ukrainian traumatologist who has worked at the same hospital since the start of the war, confronting the same harrowing scenes day after day.

Vilnius is tightening the use of Russian in municipal services, a move the capital’s mayor says is part of a consistent effort to strengthen Lithuanian as the country’s official language. However, it only targets Russian and critics warn the policy could hinder the integration of migrants and Russian-speaking residents. The Vilnius municipality will no longer accept written applications and complaints in Russian. Information in Russian and other non-European Union languages will be provided orally – and only when an employee can speaks it. Russian will also be removed from the municipality's website and customer queue-management system. Mayor Valdas Benkunskas said the changes are not an isolated initiative but part of a broader language policy aimed at encouraging foreigners who settle in Lithuania to learn Lithuanian. “When we announced initiatives to prevent children of foreigners from third countries from attending Russian-language schools, that was one message,” Benkunskas told reporters earlier this month. “Then we announced plans to provide opportunities for foreigners to learn Lithuanian if they want to stay and live here longer. The third initiative is what we are consistently doing now: reducing the availability of Russian when it comes to receiving public services.” “This is not politicking,” he added. “These are concrete measures that demonstrate consistency in policy.” Benkunskas insisted that the municipality is not seeking to prohibit the use of Russian in everyday life. “We are not stigmatising the Russian language itself,” he said, adding that residents who do not speak Lithuanian can still receive assistance in Russian if a municipal employee happens to speak the language. But the municipality will not specifically maintain infrastructure for Russian-language services, he said. The policy has prompted criticism from politicians and civic activists who say language requirements should be accompanied by accessible opportunities to learn Lithuanian. Former Interior Minister Vladislav Kondratovič said banning Russian-language services could have the opposite effect from what the policy intends. “Lithuanian must be spoken in Lithuania, and that is not up for debate,” he hedged, but the government must strengthen the official language while providing people with realistic opportunities to learn it. “Real integration takes place when a person learns Lithuanian, participates in public life, understands the state and feels responsible for it,” Kondratovič wrote on social media. He warned that access to public services and people’s dignity should not become tools for politicians to demonstrate that they are tough. Lithuanian-based businessman and civic activist Viktor Vorontsov went further, describing the move as election-oriented politics. Lithuania’s municipal and mayoral elections are scheduled for early 2027. “This is pure politicking, election campaigning and an attempt to rally one’s voters,” Vorontsovas told LRT.lt. He argued that migrants, including Ukrainians, represent an important demographic and economic resource and that authorities should make integration easier rather than create additional barriers. “Our task is to help them integrate, not create additional obstacles,” he said. Vorontsov also argued that Russian remains useful for some migrants from Central and Eastern Europe who may have difficulty communicating in Lithuanian when they first arrive. He suggested that technology could help bridge language gaps, allowing people to submit forms in Russian that could then be automatically translated into Lithuanian. The policy has also received support, notably from the conservative Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats (TS-LKD) party, of which Mayor Benkunskas is a member. TS-LKD leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas called Benkunskas’ decision “right and courageous”. Everyone living in Lithuania should learn Lithuanian and respect its status as the country’s official language, Kasčiūnas insisted. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said the government should assess the consequences of limiting Russian-language services for different groups before introducing similar measures nationwide. The issue affects not only Russian citizens, he said, but also Belarusians who fled political persecution and Ukrainians who may not speak other foreign languages. At the same time, Mayor Benkunskas stresses, Vilnius is expanding opportunities for foreigners to learn Lithuanian. More than 1,000 foreigners are expected to be able to attend free Lithuanian-language courses this year, with an additional 300,000 euros allocated for the program. Language clubs and an online self-study platform are also planned. Demand for Lithuanian classes, however, far outstrip the availability of free courses. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the government should consider requiring foreigners who move to Lithuania to achieve a certain level of Lithuanian within a specified period. But he also pointed to what he says is a broader challenge: Some Lithuanian citizens who have lived in the country for decades still struggle with the language. The debate therefore extends beyond newcomers and migration policy to the question of how Lithuania should balance the protection of its official language with minority rights and the realities of a traditional diverse population. For now, other state institutions are not following Vilnius’ lead. The State Tax Inspectorate and the State Social Insurance Fund Board, known as Sodra, said they would continue providing consultations in Russian. The tax authority said about 44,000 Russian-speaking residents sought telephone consultations during the first seven months of this year. Sodra said foreign-language assistance is provided voluntarily by employees who speak those languages. Medical facilities also continue to accommodate Russian-speaking patients. Lithuania’s defence and interior ministers have been briefed on possible links between a drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany and an ongoing Lithuanian investigation into incendiary parcels sent abroad, but officials have declined to disclose details. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said last week that he expected to receive information related to the incident and reports that “DNA traces also lead through Lithuanian territory”. The Interior Ministry said Monday that Lithuanian authorities were actively cooperating with foreign counterparts to prevent potential acts of sabotage. It declined to provide further details while the investigations are ongoing. Kaunas confirmed that he had received the information but said it was “certainly not for public disclosure”. “This matter clearly falls within the remit of the Ministry of the Interior, so I do not wish to comment on matters outside my department, but all requested information has been received,” Kaunas said Friday. In early August, a drone carrying explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany. Another aircraft suffered minor damage after colliding midair with an unidentified object. The Wall Street Journal reported that US intelligence had linked the incident to Russia. German investigators have since identified a DNA trace that matches evidence collected after an incident at a DHL logistics centre in Leipzig in July 2024. The DNA has not been linked to a specific individual. At the time, four parcels were sent from Lithuania to Britain and Poland. Two of the four packages containing incendiary devices were shipped through DHL. One caught fire at Leipzig airport, while another ignited at a warehouse in Britain. The incendiary-device case is now before the Vilnius Regional Court, where five people face charges. Lithuanian officials have described the defendants as executors and intermediaries, saying the organisers are based in Russia and remain beyond the reach of Lithuanian authorities. Investigators have determined that the operations were organised by the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Russian Armed Forces, known as the GRU, according to Lithuanian officials.

A Moscow court has sentenced Lithuanian citizen Romas Liutkus to seven years in prison in absentia for allegedly damaging the graves of Soviet soldiers in Lithuania, Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office said. The court also imposed a five-year ban on activities related to the administration of websites and telecommunications networks, according to a statement from the prosecutor’s office. Liutkus rejected the charges, saying he removed three Lithuanian-language plaques from the site in September 2024 but did not damage any graves. He said his actions were aimed at removing what he considered propaganda and historically inaccurate inscriptions, rather than targeting the deceased soldiers. Russian prosecutors alleged that Liutkus, motivated by political and ideological hatred of Russia and acting with unidentified accomplices, damaged a burial site for 119 Soviet soldiers killed in 1944 in Krekenava, in central Lithuania’s Panevėžys district. The Moscow court found Liutkus guilty of damaging soldiers’ graves outside Russia and insulting the memory of Soviet soldiers. Liutkus said he handed the undamaged plaques over to the local elder of Krekenava. The incident was investigated by Lithuanian police and the Department of Cultural Heritage, but neither institution found any violations of Lithuanian law, he said. In 2024, Lithuania’s Desovietisation Commission concluded that the monument at the site violated a ban on promoting totalitarian and authoritarian regimes. The monument consisted of an obelisk topped with a star and inscriptions in Lithuanian and Russian reading “Eternal Memory to the Fallen Soviet Soldiers”, along with granite plaques. The Soviet soldiers are buried in a communal cemetery in Krekenava. Liutkus said he learned about the Moscow court’s verdict through public reports and had not received any summonses to court hearings or interrogations. He said he was aware that he could not travel to certain countries where a Russian request for his detention could be enforced. The case comes amid heightened tensions between Lithuania and Russia following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine and Lithuania’s efforts to remove symbols associated with the Soviet Union.

The head of Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service (VSAT), Rustamas Liubajevas, has resigned amid mounting questions over how his agency handled, and reported, a violent incident on the Belarusian border last month, in which migrants allegedly tried to drag one of his officers across the frontier into Belarus. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas announced the resignation at a press conference on Monday, saying Liubajevas had made the decision himself. "No, I certainly didn’t push for it – this was the chief’s own personal decision," the minister told reporters, reading out a statement in which Liubajevas said he did not want to damage the reputation of the service he had led since 2019. "During his time in charge, the service had to withstand a hybrid migration attack orchestrated by the Belarusian regime, strengthen protection of Lithuania’s and the wider EU’s external border, and operate under exceptional geopolitical tension. His experience, professionalism and ability to hold the service together through difficult periods mattered greatly for our country’s security," Katelynas said. "But an institution responsible for guarding the state border needs its leadership to have the full confidence of officers, the public and the political leadership. After the border incident, serious questions arose – not only about whether information had been reported promptly, accurately and in full, but about the circumstances of the incident itself." The minister said he had not asked Liubajevas directly whether he had known about details of the incident that later emerged in the media: "I didn’t ask, but since I was never informed of any additional circumstances throughout, there probably wasn’t much point asking." He said he had not been expecting the resignation before their meeting, and that a deputy would take over on an interim basis while a permanent replacement is considered. He gave no further comment on the incident itself, noting that both a disciplinary inquiry and a separate pre-trial criminal investigation are under way. The incident took place on July 26 near Kapčiamiestis, close to the Belarusian border, when four border guards lay in wait for a group of migrants believed to be digging a tunnel under the frontier. The tunnel was found and several migrants attempting to cross through it were detained – but reporting since has suggested that roughly 20 more people then emerged and attacked the officers on duty. At the time, only the discovery of the tunnel was made public; the attack itself went unreported. Asked about it last week, Liubajevas had described it as "a routine border incident, the kind that genuinely does happen in our service, and will likely keep happening." But the news outlet Lrytas subsequently reported that migrants had not simply attacked the officers – a group had tried to drag one of them back across the border into Belarus. That account was confirmed by Vitalijus Jagminas, head of a trade union representing pre-trial investigation staff, who said the officer had been let go once he managed to break free. "Certain officers did confirm to us that such an incident took place – that officers were attacked, and that yes, one of them was either carried or dragged towards the other side," Jagminas said. He accused VSAT’s leadership of only disclosing information it considered favourable. "Anything that might alarm the public, or point to gaps in the system – they don’t talk about that. All of it gets hidden from the public, and this case shows there was an attempt to conceal the truth. We’ve had signals from people that leadership explicitly ordered staff not to discuss or comment on the incident." The prosecutor’s office initially said it had interviewed everyone involved but held no information about any officer being injured, signed off sick, or dragged across the border. It later reassigned the criminal investigation from VSAT itself – which had originally been investigating the case involving its own officers – to police in the Kaunas region. Some politicians argued responsibility shouldn’t rest with the chief alone. "There’s a chain of people responsible who need to be properly checked – not just asked questions, but examined to see whether the right actions were actually taken, whether the systems in place are not only on paper but actually working, and whether their effectiveness is assessed every time," said Dainius Gaižauskas, a member of parliament’s national security and defence committee. The union’s Jagminas went further: "We want change in this system, and for it to become more transparent. We’re not talking about one individual – this is about teamwork, and the whole team needs to go." Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius had struck a more cautious note before Liubajevas’ resignation, saying it was too early to draw conclusions about individual accountability. "I think, as things stand, the question of responsibility in Liubajevas’ case is premature. We need to wait for the findings of an objective, impartial internal inquiry, and only once we have that in writing should we decide whether any judgements are needed – including about the leadership," he said. Laurynas Kasčiūnas, leader of the opposition conservatives, had urged restraint, pointing to Liubajevas’ role in managing the years-long migration crisis engineered by Belarus. "This is someone who has done a great deal for our country’s security. Even if a mistake was made here, it shouldn’t wipe out everything achieved before it," he said.

Taiwan says its commitment to strengthening economic and trade ties with Lithuania remains unchanged as the two sides resume negotiations on an economic cooperation action plan. “Our determination to work alongside the new Lithuanian government to strengthen economic and trade cooperation remains unchanged,” Eric Huang, director general of the Department of European Affairs at Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said Tuesday. The negotiations were briefly suspended in June as Lithuania’s Social Democrats reshuffled the Cabinet and resumed in late July. Huang said details of the action plan were still being finalised, with the two sides maintaining close contact over the planned cooperation. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry has not disclosed specific details of the plan, citing ongoing consultations. It said the focus was on “building sustainable economic ties that would contribute to the development of the country’s high-tech sectors”. Expectations for closer economic ties with Taiwan grew in 2021 after Taiwan opened its representative office in Vilnius. But Lithuanian officials have more recently expressed frustration over what they consider insufficient Taiwanese investment in Lithuania. The opening of the office triggered a diplomatic dispute between Lithuania and China. Beijing viewed the decision to use “Taiwanese” rather than “Taipei” in the office’s name as support for Taiwan’s efforts to establish itself as an independent state. Taiwan maintains representative offices under the name Taipei in many other countries. Huang’s comments came after US lawmakers urged Lithuanian leaders to continue their “bold path” of maintaining ties with Taipei and not give in to pressure from Beijing. At the same time, Lithuania’s ruling coalition has increasingly discussed normalising relations with China. The government’s program calls for restoring diplomatic representation with Beijing to levels comparable with those maintained by other European Union member states. Lithuania established closer ties with Taiwan under a previous conservative-led government, prompting a sharp deterioration in relations with China. The issue has since remained politically sensitive in Vilnius as successive governments have sought to balance economic interests, relations with Beijing and support for Taiwan.

A Lithuanian executive who previously headed one of Belarus’ largest wood-processing companies was detained and jailed in June, LRT RADIO has learnt from its sources. Vytautas Slankauskas worked as head of internal audit at HS Belacon, an Austrian-owned company operating in Belarus. He previously served as the company’s chief executive for three years. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry confirmed to LRT RADIO that the Lithuanian Embassy in Belarus had been informed of his detention. The ministry declined to provide further details, citing privacy concerns. Slankauskas was recruited by Austrian investors from Timber Group because of his experience overseeing the construction of large industrial plants in Lithuania and Belarus. He previously worked for Western Wood Group and at the Mebelain factory in Belarus, which was built by a Lithuanian company. According to information obtained by LRT RADIO, Slankauskas was accused of supplying defective components to Russia and Belarus. Further details of the allegations were not immediately available. Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has closely overseen the country’s industrial sector, including its wood-processing industry, while the government has taken control of numerous businesses. Political analyst Vytis Jurkonis said Slankauskas was not the first Lithuanian businessperson working in Belarus to be imprisoned and warned that anyone traveling or working there should carefully assess the risks. “This is not the first case, and I am afraid it will not be the last,” Jurkonis said. “It does not matter what kind of capital the company has or what kind of business it is. No one can protect you here because Belarus is not a state governed by the rule of law.” He cited the 2021 forced landing of a Ryanair passenger flight in Minsk and cases involving long-haul truck drivers as examples of the risks faced by Lithuanians in Belarus. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry reiterated its recommendation that Lithuanian citizens not travel to Belarus and urged those currently in the country to leave immediately.

A senior aide to Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda has backed a proposal to tighten controls on Russian citizens transiting Lithuania, saying stricter rules are warranted amid rising violations and a changed security environment. “There is certainly no reason to object,” Marius Česnulevičius, the president’s national security adviser, told the radio Žinių Radijas on Tuesday. Conservative lawmaker Arvydas Anušauskas, of the opposition Homeland Union party, registered amendments this week to Lithuania’s Law on the State Border and its Protection that would introduce a six-hour limit for direct transit through Lithuania, replacing the current 24-hour period. Česnulevičius said six hours should be sufficient to cross the country and would limit opportunities for travellers to move around Lithuania while in transit. Anušauskas has also called on Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys and Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas to tighten Lithuania’s national controls and launch discussions at the European Union level on reviewing the simplified transit regime. According to State Border Guard Service data, nearly 13,000 passenger vehicles registered in Russia crossed Lithuania last year using simplified transit documents. Authorities recorded a sharp increase in violations of the regime, with the number rising more than fourfold, from 360 cases in 2024 to 1,493 in 2025. Česnulevičius said confirmed violations should result in enforcement measures ranging from administrative penalties to the revocation of border-crossing permits or declaring individuals personae non gratae. The special arrangements for transit between mainland Russia and its Kaliningrad exclave were agreed between Moscow, Vilnius and the European Commission before Lithuania’s accession to the European Union. The simplified transit regime allows Lithuania to monitor travel flows and deny entry to people deemed undesirable. Russian citizens traveling to and from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad can use simplified transit documents or simplified rail transit documents. Anušauskas insisted the EU regulation allowing 24-hour transit was adopted in 2003, when the “geopolitical situation” was significantly different. “Today, Russia is waging a war against Ukraine and conducting hybrid operations against the European Union,” he said, without explaining how shorter transit windows would address those threats. Lithuania borders Russia’s Kaliningrad region and Belarus. The country has tightened border controls and security measures since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Plans by a Ukrainian ammunition company to build an assembly plant near the small Lithuanian town of Balbieriškis are being met with a mix of hope and unease, as residents welcome the prospect of new jobs while worrying that the facility could make the area a potential target. The planned plant by Dnipro Electromechanical Plant, or DEMZ, has also raised questions among local community leaders, who say they were not directly consulted before the project was announced. Algis Marcinkevičius, head of the Balbieriškis Juda community group and a member of the Prienai district council, said he first learned about the Ukrainian company’s plans on Thursday afternoon, after reports appeared in the media. “My first reaction was: Why do we know nothing when, so to speak, it has already happened?” Marcinkevičius told BNS. He said he would have preferred direct discussions between residents, government officials and the company before decisions were made. “It is always better when you talk and there is room for discussion,” he said. “Now that the outcome has been determined and is clear, it reminds me of the Kapčiamiestis case. There, everyone admitted that there had been a lack of communication. But now we have a similar facility and a similar problem, so I don’t know where we are going back to.” The government’s decision last year to build a military training ground near the town of Kapčiamiestis on Lithuania’s border with Poland has provoked resistance from the community. Lithuania’s economy minister, Edvinas Grikšas, and DEMZ’s chief executive signed an investment agreement Friday in Vilnius under which the Ukrainian company will produce ammunition and ammunition components in Lithuania. The investment, whose value has not been disclosed, is expected to create up to 450 jobs in Alytus and Prienai district. DEMZ plans to manufacture metal ammunition components at the Alytus industrial park and build a modern ammunition assembly plant on a 30.6-hectare site in the village of Ąžuolai, near Balbieriškis. The site had previously been earmarked for a drone training facility for Lithuania’s Riflemen’s Union. ‘Ammunition factory is not a mayonnaise factory’ Marcinkevičius said he had spoken with several residents since news of the project broke, but there was no clear consensus yet among the community’s 55 members. “Really, nobody knows anything,” he said. “After lunch, messages started appearing that something was happening. [...] I don’t yet feel any political opposition or support because the opinions are not really clear yet.” Marcinkevičius said he would support the project if it served Lithuania’s interests but acknowledged that the lack of information made it harder for him to persuade others of its potential benefits. “I could probably get people to listen to my opinion,” he said. “But my credibility is diminished because I myself feel a little deceived. If I come and say I know nothing and nobody talked to me, the community will probably say, ‘What are you trying to convince us of if you know nothing?’” The plant would be surrounded by agricultural land and would not directly affect many residents, he said. But heavy truck traffic could require improvements to roads leading to the site and stronger road surfaces through Balbieriškis. “That is something they will inevitably have to do,” Marcinkevičius said, adding that the project could also affect nearby farmers and their operations. For local residents, the biggest potential benefit is employment. “If local people could get 40 jobs, that would mean 40 people with families who would not have to send their children to Alytus or Prienai for school, as they do now,” he said. “My dream would be for 40 jobs to go to local people, not only qualified workers.” But he acknowledged the security concerns surrounding an ammunition plant. “In the event of a threat, such a factory could become a target,” he said. “But you can also think that such a factory would have more protection than an ordinary factory, so there are advantages. [...] I see a lot of potential. But I think the biggest question will be security, how much it increases the risk of danger. Of course, this is not a mayonnaise factory.” In Balbieriškis, residents expressed sharply different views about the project. Angelė Mieliauskienė, a sales clerk at the local Darguva store, said she saw little need for the plant. “It’s not necessary. People will live more peacefully,” she said. “Everyone is happy that jobs will be created, but the more of these kinds of things there are, the greater the threat to the people themselves.” She said residents had little say in the decision. “Authorities always speak nicely, but nobody asks us. Nobody,” Mieliauskienė said. “They will do it the way they decide. And it will be quite close to us.” Darius Dirvanauskas, a 49-year-old auto mechanic, took the opposite view. “I don’t object to it,” he said. “It is good for Lithuania’s security, that’s all. I served in the military myself, so I don’t see any problems.” A couple who declined to give their names while walking along the town’s main Vilniaus Street were more sceptical. “It would be a target if Russia launched missiles or something,” the man said. “Making weapons here [...] that’s bad.” At the Loreta guesthouse, 69-year-old cook Ona Blazukienė, who was born and raised in Balbieriškis, welcomed the project. “There will be jobs for people, and that’s a plus,” she said. “There are so many people who don’t work. It will give them motivation to live and earn money.” Blazukienė dismissed concerns that the plant would make the town a target, arguing that Russia would regard Lithuania as a target in any case. Some residents see a potential precedent in Baisogala, where the German defence company Rheinmetall is developing a large ammunition plant.
