Lithuania’s State Security Department will conduct an additional assessment of newly appointed Lithuanian Airports board member Oleksandras Laneckis after concerns were raised about his past links to Russia and Belarus, the Transport Ministry said Wednesday. The move comes after opposition lawmakers have raised concerns about Laneckis’ past business activities and his statements about Russia and Belarus. The Homeland Union–Lithuanian Christian Democrats (TS-LKD) said Wednesday that Laneckis’ appointment may endanger Lithuania’s national security because his company, Friendly Avia Support, used to advise Belarusian state-owned enterprises on aviation matters; and, furthermore, from 2017 to 2023, he served as sales director at the aircraft maintenance company Linetech Aircraft Maintenance, which provided services in Russia and other countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States. According to the TS-LKD, Laneckis also gave interviews and comments to pro-Russian media outlets and published articles there on how to circumvent Western sanctions. “Such comments were recorded in the public sphere even before his appointment to the Lithuanian Airports Board,” the TS-LKD stated in its press release. LRT also reports that Laneckis has previously referred to Russia’s war in Ukraine as a “special military operation”, the Kremlin’s official term for the invasion. He also reportedly described the self-proclaimed Luhansk People’s Republic as a territory of unclear legal status. In May 2021, Laneckis also reportedly offered a neutral assessment of Belarus’ forced diversion of a Ryanair Athens–Vilnius flight to Vilnius to Minsk. The incident, which led to the arrest of Belarusian opposition journalist Raman Pratasevich and his partner, was condemned by Lithuania and its international partners. Transport Minister Juras Taminskas asked the State Security Department to urgently assess newly surfaced information about Laneckis and determine whether it poses any national security concerns. Taminskas said security checks had been conducted on candidates before the appointments and that no adverse findings had been reported at the time. “We will act according to the findings. If the conclusions are negative, we will take a principled stand and such a person will not be able to hold the position,” Taminskas told reporters. Taminskas said he had been unaware of the allegations against Laneckis. Asked whether he felt personally responsible for vetting board members, the minister said he did not follow Russian media or analyse companies associated with them. The State Security Department is expected to complete its additional assessment in the coming days. Laneckis denied wrongdoing and said his previous remarks had been taken out of context. “I am very well known in the Lithuanian business market and people know what I do, who I help and which side I support,” Laneckis told LRT RADIO on Wednesday. “I am open, I have done nothing wrong, I have never done anything wrong.” He said he had never acted against Lithuania’s interests or criticised aid to Ukraine. In a Facebook post, Laneckis said he had provided commentary only to Belarusian and Russian opposition media outlets. He said his company, Friendly Avia Support, ended cooperation with Belarusian partners in spring 2020 and that his and Polish company Linetech’s ties with Russia were severed on the first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Laneckis previously served as vice president for the Russia and Commonwealth of Independent States markets at aviation company Avia Solutions Group, founded by Lithuanian businessman Gediminas Žiemelis. On the Lithuanian Airports board, Laneckis is responsible for strategic planning and the aviation sector. The additional security assessment will determine whether the concerns raised over his past activities affect his eligibility to remain on the board.

Lithuania's government has ruled out offshore oil drilling in the Baltic Sea as part of its commitment to phasing out fossil fuels — even as Russia's Lukoil pumps oil from fields just kilometres from the Lithuanian coast, and geologists warn that domestic onshore reserves will be exhausted within a few years. A quarter of a century ago, Lithuania had a thriving oil industry. Today it is on its last legs, and geologists say what remains onshore will be exhausted within a few years. The question now dividing the industry, politicians and environmentalists is whether Lithuania should look to the Baltic Sea – where Russia is already pumping oil from fields that may, some geologists suspect, connect directly to deposits on the Lithuanian side. The Sakučiai field, one of several operated by Minijos Nafta, one of Lithuania's largest oil producers, has been pumping since 2002. Output has fallen from nearly 600,000 cubic metres at its peak in 2001 to just 26,000 last year. The company can still extract oil from five fields in total, but has shut down two – nearly empty – and was blocked by courts from opening a new site at Kintai. "Explored and exploited onshore deposits are naturally running out, despite the industry's efforts to extract the last drop," said geologist Jonas Satkūnas. The story of Minijos Nafta mirrors the wider arc of Lithuanian oil: a brief boom, a peak, and a long decline. Geologists say the real prize was never onshore. Beneath the Baltic Sea, they argue, lie deposits comparable in scale to those already being exploited on the Russian side – and Russia's Lukoil is making full use of them. The company has been pumping oil from the Baltic seabed near Lithuania for years, from a field roughly 20 kilometres from the Curonian Spit – the narrow strip of land that separates the Baltic sea from the Curonian Lagoon and forms part of Lithuania's coastline. It is now expanding to a new site around 50 kilometres offshore, where one field alone is estimated to hold 20 million tonnes of oil. "There are grounds to believe the Baltic Sea holds oil resources equivalent to – possibly even greater than – what has been found and is being exploited on the Russian side, in the same water, in the same sea," Satkūnas said. Some geologists go further, suggesting the two fields may be connected underground – raising the pointed question of whether Lithuanian oil is already flowing across to the Russian side. Ignas Vaičeliūnas, production director at Minijos Nafta, put it in blunt terms: "If there are half a million tonnes out there, that's a quarter of Lithuania's own annual consumption. If we dared to go offshore, we could have those same volumes." The industry argues that offshore production would cost the state nothing – exploration and extraction costs would fall to private companies – while generating significant tax revenues. It would also reduce the distance oil needs to be transported to the Orlen refinery at Mažeikiai in northern Lithuania, currently the only oil refinery in the Baltic states. But Lithuania's government isn't interested, at least for now. The country has committed to phasing out fossil fuels as part of its green transition, and the environment ministry shows no sign of changing course. "The strategic direction set out in the government programme is oriented towards green transformation, the development of renewable energy and the protection of ecosystems," said deputy environment minister Giedrė Ričkutė. The oil industry points out that fuel consumption in Lithuania is actually rising, not falling, undermining the case for leaving domestic resources untapped on environmental grounds. If the country is going to use the oil anyway, the argument goes, it might as well produce some of it itself. The political sensitivity of offshore drilling is not unique to Lithuania. Last year a Canadian company operating in Poland announced the discovery of what it called one of the largest oil finds in Europe in a decade, in the Baltic Sea near the port city of Świnoujście – a find it described as historic for Poland's energy sector. The announcement was almost immediately followed by protests from German environmental groups opposed to a test drilling operation, and the dispute has been intensifying since. Lithuania's own history with the industry is similarly charged: previous attempts to bring in foreign investment, including a proposal involving US energy giant Chevron, were rejected amid public opposition.

Lithuanian delivery companies report a sharp decline in low-value parcels arriving from outside the European Union since the bloc introduced a new duty on such shipments in July, although logistics firms say it is too early to determine whether the drop will persist. The European Union introduced a 3-euro duty July 1 on imports valued at less than 150 euros from e-commerce platforms such as Temu, AliExpress and Shein. Such parcels had previously been exempt from customs duties. Lithuanian Customs said it was too early to draw firm conclusions from July figures, noting that the month was a transition period during which retailers and consumers were adapting to the new rules. “We are not rushing to draw conclusions from just one month, as July was a period of transition and it took time for retailers to adapt,” the Customs Department said. The measure is scheduled to remain in effect through July 2028, when the EU is expected to consider a permanent system. The impact was immediately visible among Lithuanian delivery companies. Tomas Vaišvila, communications manager at DPD Lietuva, part of French logistics group Geopost, said the company’s parcel volumes had fallen by about 70% since July. Lithuania Post reported a 30% decline in imports from third countries, while Omniva Lithuania said shipments ordered directly from Asia had also decreased. Omniva Lithuania head Tadas Drunga said the initial decline was likely driven by consumers reacting to higher final prices but cautioned against assuming that volumes would continue falling at the same rate. “In the long term, we do not expect a decline of the same magnitude,” Drunga said. Lithuania Post spokesman Lukas Zadarackas said early July figures were also affected by a temporary requirement from Lithuanian Customs for an EORI code when declaring parcels. The requirement was later scrapped. “It is important to consider these temporary administrative changes when evaluating the July data,” Zadarackas said. Lithuanian Customs figures show just how dramatic the change has been. Some 7,200 parcels from China were declared in July, 61.3 times fewer than the 441,300 recorded in July 2025. Declarations of low-value shipments from all countries fell 12.1 times to 41,100. Chinese parcels accounted for 18% of all low-value declarations in July, compared with 91% in January. Logistics companies say the decline in parcel volumes does not necessarily mean consumers have stopped buying goods from Chinese platforms. Olgerdas Janovičius, commercial director at Venipak, said some sellers were adapting by shipping goods in bulk to European warehouses, where they can clear customs before individual orders are delivered to customers. “The market is adapting quickly,” Janovičius said, adding that Chinese parcel flows were falling but that changes in logistics models could partly obscure the true level of consumer demand. Economist Indrė Genytė-Pikčienė of Artea likewise said Chinese companies were likely to respond by routing more goods through European warehouses. The Communications Regulatory Authority said it does not collect specific data on low-value parcels handled by postal operators. The new duty is also expected to change shopping habits. Drunga said consumers may become more selective and place fewer impulsive orders for inexpensive items. “Users will choose more carefully and less frequently add cheap, unplanned items to their baskets just because they are inexpensive,” he said. DPD Lietuva’s Vaišvila expects consumers to consolidate purchases to spread the cost of the duty across more goods. “People might buy in bulk; for instance, instead of three pairs of socks, they might buy 12, so the 3-euro fee has less impact,” he said. Zadarackas said shoppers were increasingly comparing the final price, including delivery costs, before deciding whether an overseas purchase remained worthwhile. Reduced advertising by major e-commerce platforms could also be contributing to the decline, he said. Janovičius said some consumers had brought forward purchases before the duty took effect, while others were checking whether goods were shipped from China or from European warehouses. “The decline is more noticeable among occasional or impulsive buyers,” he said. “Regular shoppers continue to look for ways to avoid or reduce extra costs.” EU seeks to curb surge in Chinese imports The new duty is part of a broader EU effort to address the rapid growth of low-value imports, particularly from China. EU finance ministers agreed in November to end the duty exemption for low-value parcels, arguing that the change would help create a more level playing field for European retailers. Lithuanian Customs has also said the previous exemption encouraged unfair competition and that such shipments could pose health, safety and environmental risks. Nearly 6 billion low-value retail parcels entered the EU last year, up from 4.6 billion in 2024, with most originating in China. The EU is also set to introduce mandatory product-information requirements November 1 as part of efforts to improve tracking and oversight of the growing flow of small parcels.

Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have concluded a five-day joint air force exercise focused on water survival skills, the Lithuanian military said on Friday. This year's Baltic Bikini 2026 drills, organised by the Latvian Air Force, took place in the Baltic Sea. Crews practised evacuating aircraft after an emergency water landing and deploying life-saving equipment – skills that flight personnel are required to refresh every three years. The exercise has been running since 1999, when it was established under a search and rescue cooperation agreement between Lithuania and Denmark, with initial training held in Denmark. Since 2004, the three Baltic states have organised it independently on a rotating basis.

Lithuania's arms and military equipment procurement system is failing to meet the needs of its armed forces despite rapidly rising defence spending, the National Audit Office said on Friday. The findings prompted the defence minister to announce that legislative proposals to overhaul the system will be submitted to parliament this autumn. The audit found that the proportion of failed weapons procurements jumped from 24% in 2023 to 59% in 2025. As a result, some military requirements are being met later than planned. Both internal and external factors are hindering the system's ability to meet military needs on time. Internal causes include funding constraints, shifting procurement priorities, outdated capability development plans, lengthy decision-making processes, a shortage of qualified specialists, insufficient monitoring of procurement efficiency, and fragmented management of key armament projects. The external environment, meanwhile, is shaped by rising international demand for weaponry, limited manufacturing capacity, and long production and delivery lead times – all of which have delayed the fulfilment of various military requirements. "Today, time is as critical a resource in the defence sector as funding. The doubling in the number of failed procurements and months-long coordination of decisions are directly stalling the necessary expansion of the armed forces. We must therefore not only review the legal environment, but also eliminate the other internal causes behind procurement bottlenecks and delayed decisions," said Auditor General Irena Segalovičienė. The procurement process is significantly slowed by coordination: in 42% of cases analysed, internal coordination with ministry departments and advisory groups took between 30 and 374 days, despite recommendations that the maximum duration for an entire international procurement should not exceed 180 to 240 calendar days. Between 2023 and 2025, the Defence Materiel Agency, using exceptions under the Law on Public Procurement in the Fields of Defence and Security, signed 62 contracts for weaponry and military equipment worth nearly €3.4bn. This accounted for 48% of all such contracts and 40% of their total value. The exceptions were applied lawfully. While no fundamental legal violations affecting the outcome of regular public procurements were found, the audit identified serious control deficiencies in 38% of cases, with eight of 21 procurements showing high- or medium-level discrepancies. The report noted that while military capabilities are being strengthened to develop a division, 13 of 16 capability areas related to weapons procurement are still being developed according to outdated plans. The audit found a lack of performance indicators, along with failures to record current capability levels or the timeframes required to reach targets. The National Audit Office stressed the need to strengthen monitoring and project management in arms procurement. Due to fragmented management, some projects lacked implementation plans, while decisions were taken without assessing total project value, including ammunition, infrastructure and lifecycle maintenance costs. The value of the Leopard 2 A8 tank project, for example, increased by 33% once all signed and planned contracts were taken into account – illustrating how a failure to evaluate all project-related expenses makes it difficult to plan funding accurately, manage risk and ensure smooth implementation. The auditor has issued recommendations to the Defence Ministry, the Defence Materiel Agency and the Lithuanian Armed Forces. A key target is to ensure that no more than 730 calendar days pass between the approval of a military requirement and its fulfilment. Further efforts aim to shorten decision coordination to no more than 35 working days and to reduce the share of failed procurements to 20%. The Defence Ministry has pledged to strengthen the management of high-priority procurement projects, while the Lithuanian Armed Forces will update capability development plans and set clear progress indicators. The goal is for 80% of capabilities to have defined target levels, and for 95% to have reached their planned progress by 2030. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas acknowledged the findings, saying the audit "confirmed what has been discussed for years: the procurement system operated without clear deadlines, without separated responsibilities, and without effective monitoring." He said procurement issues had been ignored between 2021 and 2025, but that current reforms were moving in the right direction. Legislative proposals are due in parliament this autumn. A review of public procurement regulations is already under way to accelerate acquisitions. The ministry is also developing a faster procurement mechanism for use in the event of mobilisation or war, improving project management and risk controls, and consolidating procurement data across the national defence system into a single information system. Lithuania's Transport Minister, Juras Taminskas, has removed Oleksandras Laneckis from the board of Lithuanian Airports, following public concern over his alleged ties to Russia and Belarus, as well as contacts with pro-Russian media. Laneckis stepped down from the newly appointed board at his own request, the Transport Ministry said on Thursday. The minister has simultaneously launched a search for two new board members – one independent and one representing the public sector. The minister said Lithuanian Airports manages critical infrastructure, and that all board members are therefore required to maintain an impeccable reputation. "I disagree with the public accusations made against me. I consider them unfounded, untrue, and damaging to both my reputation and that of the company I lead, which has been built over more than a decade of honest work in the Lithuanian aviation sector," Laneckis wrote, describing the allegations as "slander and a politically motivated vendetta." On Tuesday, Taminskas had asked the State Security Department to carry out an urgent additional assessment of whether Laneckis met national security requirements. Laneckis said the department had already screened him and found no discrepancies. The opposition Conservatives had also raised concerns with the authorities, questioning whether his position on the Lithuanian Airports board was compatible with Lithuania's national security interests. They alleged that Laneckis continues to give interviews and commentary to pro-Russian media outlets, and publishes articles there on how Western sanctions are being circumvented. He also faced public criticism over previous comments on the war in Ukraine, and on Belarus's forced landing of a Ryanair flight in Minsk in 2021. Laneckis previously served as a vice-president at Avia Solutions Group (2009-2012), responsible for the Russian and Commonwealth of Independent States markets. On the Lithuanian Airports board, he had been due to oversee strategic planning and the aviation sector. The new board is expected to elect its chairman on August 28.

What would you do to keep a friend? Would you let them use your property to keep and possibly torture their enemies? Would you consider changing your constitution to fit into their long-term military goals? Most importantly, would you cut ties with an international court that just so happens to be investigating your enemies, because it might one day investigate them too? To be fair, the United States is more than just a friend for Lithuania – it is our main security guarantor. But keeping Washington happy and making sure Lithuania stays on the list of countries hosting US troops after the broader review of America’s military presence in Europe, is becoming increasingly complicated. In addition to receiving a Department of Defense questionnaire assessing Lithuania’s, and other NATO states’, alignment with Donald Trump’s foreign policy (quite the business move to outsource this judgment call instead of figuring it out themselves), Lithuania must also rethink its relationship with the International Criminal Court – the ICC. In what appears to be the culmination of decades of US animosity toward the court – officially because Washington views its assertion of jurisdiction over non-member nations as an unlawful violation of sovereignty, and unofficially because it has no interest in seeing its own troops tried over crimes they might commit abroad – the US is pressuring countries to withdraw from the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC. US officials have stopped short of threatening to withhold American troops from Lithuania should it remain an ICC member, but they are likely to seek some form of judicial reassurance that any US troops stationed here would be shielded from the court’s jurisdiction. Withdrawing from the Rome Statute, after all, is quite the unrealistic ask for Lithuania: not only did it refer alleged Russian war crimes to the court, resulting in an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin and that iconic “Putin, The Hague is waiting for you” banner atop the Vilnius City Municipality building, but the ICC has also recently opened an investigation into Belarus over the suspected forced deportation of government opponents – at Lithuania’s own request. Fittingly, our president has assured that Lithuania has no intention of withdrawing from the ICC. But he did say the country is open to exploring the option of forming some bilateral agreements to “avoid a conflict [with Washington]” and “regulate certain things”. Conservative MP Dalia Asanavičiūtė-Gružauskienė has asked the National Security and Defence Committee to examine the Council of Muslim Religious Communities of Lithuania, citing alleged foreign ties and claiming “immigrants” are taking over mosques from the country’s historic Muslim Tartar community – and if the committee agrees, she wants the group deregistered. The complaint follows fellow right-wing MP Vytautas Sinica’s request to the Prosecutor General’s Office to reclaim the Kaunas mosque as state property and return it to the Tatars – gifted to them in the interwar period for their role in Lithuania’s independence struggles, he argues, not to the Pakistani, Uzbek, Kyrgyz and Turkmen nationals who’ve allegedly taken it over since 2019. The mosque’s own mufti disputes this, saying no one is barred on ethnic grounds – what changed in 2019 was the leadership, not who’s welcome inside. One might think that a simpler fix would be building more mosques, but Lithuanian politicians – Vilnius Mayor Valdas Benkunskas chief among them, given the capital is where the shortage bites hardest – are staunchly against it, since “immigrants are supposed to stay in Lithuania only temporarily”. – But not that temporarily. Nausėda’s plan to make migrant workers leave for six months every two years – and drop their right to bring family – is drawing pushback from unions, who say it would make employment less stable and undercut efforts to properly train workers. – VSAT chief Rustamas Liubajevas has resigned amid questions over how his agency handled and reported a violent border incident last month, in which migrants allegedly tried to drag an officer into Belarus, with both a disciplinary and criminal probe now underway. – Lithuania’s top administrative court issued its first ruling under the EU’s new Migration and Asylum Pact, rejecting a North African migrant’s claim that being confined to a registration centre amounted to unlawful detention. – A conservative lawmaker wants to cut the transit window for Russians crossing to and from Kaliningrad from 24 hours down to six, arguing the current rule dates back to 2003 and no longer fits today’s security climate. Following the recent Kaliningrad-train escape scare , no wonder the idea already has backing from the top: Nausėda’s national security adviser says six hours should be plenty to cross the country while cutting down on rule violations along the way. Following last week’s news about two priests accused of child sexual offenses – one who allegedly abused 11 minors over 23 years, and another who faces a child pornography charge – the Apostolic Nunciature in Lithuania says it’s “deeply concerned” about the situation, insisting on “zero-tolerance” while noting that criminal proceedings sit with Lithuanian courts and the canonical probe rests with the Archdiocese of Vilnius. Given that, you’d think a full historical reckoning might be next. Not so fast, says Vilnius Archbishop Gintaras Grušas. Responding to a three-year-old lay Catholic proposal for an independent commission to investigate abuse across the Church, Grušas admitted the idea has logic – given similar inquiries in Australia, the US and elsewhere – but said the Vatican and other bishops’ conferences convinced him a historical dig shouldn’t come first . His priority instead: build a system to protect potential victims now, with a broader look at the past left for later, resources allowing. Empty shop shelves, the hum of generators, beaches devoid of tourists, queues and scuffles at petrol stations, air raid sirens and explosions – this has been life in occupied Crimea since the end of June, when the Ukrainian Defence Forces launched an operation to compel Russia to make peace. At the same time, for the Russian audience, the occupying authorities are trying to paint a different picture – one of enterprises operating smoothly, support for business and a willingness to help the population. How life on the peninsula has actually changed, and how the Russian media are trying to conceal the consequences of these problems – in this report by Suspilne Crimea. Amid power cuts in Crimea, Russian TV channels continue to film reports on life on the peninsula. Local residents have noticed the difference between what is shown on television and what is actually happening. “Over there, people are filming a news report about those who’ve been without power for over 48 hours. I say: ‘Speak up so I can hear all this first-hand.’ But they’re just whispering into their little microphones, and who knows which channel’s showing it,” says the Crimean woman, speaking ironically about the pro-Russian media filming reports in Crimea on so-called state aid for business owners. Residents of the Dzhankoi district are complaining that, when submitting an application, men are required to provide proof that they are registered with the military. The documents must be taken to the local authorities, even though they had previously been promised that the process could be completed via the Russian “Gosuslugi” portal. At the same time, Russian-controlled media outlets are creating the illusion that the occupying authorities “have the situation under control”. Doctors, scientists, sportspeople and factory workers appear in specially filmed videos to assure viewers that the difficulties are temporary. “Yes, these are difficult times, but over the past 12 years we’ve grown accustomed to certain difficulties,” said the doctor. In the video, the young researcher said: “Some of the difficulties currently facing our country motivate me even more to work.” A warehouse worker assured us: “We don’t have any problems.” “There are no problems,” yet field kitchens serving hot meals are being set up in Yalta. Catering establishments are introducing “social lunches” – available to residents based on their place of registration. Another new feature is the “assistance centres”. There, you can charge up to ten mobile phones or use a walkie-talkie. “In the event of a power cut, you can use a walkie-talkie,” says a video about how one such centre operates. At the same time, the occupying authorities are reporting billions of roubles in support. According to their statements, “over four billion” has been channelled into the tourism sector alone. Business owners are being promised rent reductions and loan restructuring. At the same time, Sevastopol’s business owners themselves speak of a deep crisis. “We are business owners in Sevastopol, and we are currently in the midst of a severe crisis. The city has been without electricity for weeks. We are providing our own power. The generator uses ten litres an hour. We have the most expensive petrol and restrictions on refuelling. It costs between one thousand and one thousand two hundred roubles an hour for fuel. And then there’s rent, taxes, loans and staff wages,” the business owners said. Against a backdrop of electricity and fuel shortages, businesses on the peninsula are beginning to close down. A clothes shop in the “Meganom” shopping centre in Simferopol has announced that it is closing down. The “Angarsky Pass” tourist complex had already suspended operations after 30 June. “Due to the difficult fuel situation, many guests are finding it hard to get here, and we cannot operate without guests,” said representatives of the complex. A café belonging to the “Crayfish and Éclairs” chain is closing in Sevastopol. “No one is going to pay off our loans or settle our debts for us. The situation is dire, so we’ve decided to close down,” said representatives of the establishment. Retail in Yalta is also struggling. The owner of a boutique has stated that her business has become unprofitable due to taxes and the general situation in Crimea. Meanwhile, a florist’s in Sevastopol is asking customers to take the goods away at cost price, at the very least. “You all know the situation our city finds itself in. We’ve been left without electricity, internet or mobile coverage. As flowers are perishable goods, we only have a few days to sell them and settle our accounts with suppliers,” the shop said. Amidst business closures, some bloggers continue to show footage of crowded Crimean beaches. But even in such videos, the creators unwittingly admit that there are fewer tourists on the peninsula. Refat Chubarov, Chairman of the Mejlis of the Crimean Tatar People, points out that the true picture can be seen even on the pages of pro-Russian bloggers. “Our colleagues are monitoring around a dozen such bloggers: in Chornomorsk, Alushta, Yalta, Sudak and Feodosiia. And these bloggers generally paint a true picture, particularly in the tourism sector. They show empty beaches; they show not dozens, but hundreds of generators lining the streets of Yalta and Alushta,” Chubarov noted. Occupation officials, on the other hand, are touring enterprises and showcasing production facilities that are “operating as normal”. Following a visit to a greenhouse complex, the occupation speaker of the Crimean parliament, Vladimir Konstantinov, stated that the difficulties relate mainly to logistics. When Zeinab Mamedova arrived in Lithuania at the age of nine, she spoke no Lithuanian whatsoever. Within a few months, she was fluent. This summer, she scored 100% on Lithuania's school-leaving Lithuanian language and literature exam – and won a place to study medicine. Zeinab was born in Almaty, Kazakhstan's largest city, to an Azerbaijani family. Her first language is Russian, the dominant language of Almaty; she also speaks Azerbaijani. Lithuanian was acquired in a classroom, in the small northeastern Lithuanian town of Utena, where she moved with her mother in November 2015. "I didn't know anything about Lithuania," she recalls. "A few days after we arrived, I started school." The school her family chose – Krašuona middle school – had a teacher experienced in working with children who spoke little or no Lithuanian. This was a practical consideration, since nine-year-old Zeinab understood nothing of what was said around her, except in maths lessons. But she was, by her own account, unbothered. "I was a child, so I didn't really worry about it. I just wanted to make friends. And since none of the other children spoke English or Russian, we tried to communicate in Lithuanian. My classmates taught me words – they'd hold up a pencil and say 'pieštukas'. That's how the language slowly stuck." Her very first Lithuanian word, she says, was 'pienas' – milk – learned before she left Kazakhstan, from her stepfather, an Azerbaijani man living in Lithuania. "I didn't even know where Lithuania was at that point. But I asked him how to say 'milk'." She found Lithuanian difficult at first, particularly its complex system of grammatical case endings – Lithuanian is one of the most grammatically intricate languages in Europe, with seven noun cases. "I never liked the locative case," she says, referring to a grammar case that turns the noun into a location. "At home I'd guess at how words should sound. But eventually it just settled in. Lithuanian became very beautiful to me." Reading helped. Zeinab had been a keen reader since childhood, and worked her way through Lithuanian books as her vocabulary expanded. But Zeinab herself believes communicating with others in Lithuanian was most helpful in learning the language. By the time she returned to school after her first summer holiday, she was speaking fluently and without an accent. Her speech therapist, who had been assigned to help her when she first arrived, was astonished. "She told me: 'I think you're very bright, you should become a doctor. My daughter got into medicine, and Lithuania needs good doctors.'" Zeinab laughed it off at the time, saying she would never pick medicine. Ten years later, she changed her mind. Scoring 100% on a national language exam is unusual enough for native speakers. For someone who arrived in the country speaking none of it, it is remarkable. Lithuania's school-leaving exams – taken at the end of secondary school, roughly equivalent to A-levels in the UK – are graded on a national scale, with Lithuanian language and literature among the most demanding. Zeinab sat five exams in total: Lithuanian, history, biology, chemistry and mathematics, plus an earlier international English qualification. Her results across all of them were high enough to secure a place at the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences in Kaunas. But the Lithuanian result came at a cost. The exam requires a written essay based on readings drawn at random from a mandatory syllabus, meaning candidates have no way of knowing in advance which texts will come up, and must work through the entire list for the best result. "In years 11 and 12, I didn't really live a normal life – I mostly just studied. I read every book on the syllabus. I watched every documentary. Even when I was eating, exercising, just walking around, I'd listen to audiobooks. I wanted to go into the exam knowing I'd have something to write about, whatever the question." She even skipped her high school's end-of-year farewell ceremony – a significant occasion in Lithuanian school culture – because the Lithuanian exam was two days later. "I couldn't let myself celebrate, knowing the exam was coming," she said. Though initially hoping to get 100% due to her love for literature, after sitting the paper, she was convinced she'd done badly, and rang her teacher in distress. "She wrote to comfort me. That night I barely slept," Zeinab recalls. When results day came, she was visiting her father and grandparents in Kazakhstan. The results system initially wouldn't load – something she attributes to accessing it from abroad. "After 15 minutes it finally opened and I saw 100. I couldn't believe it. I started screaming, grabbed everyone around me, and said: 'That's it. Thank God.'" Zeinab's family speaks several languages at home – Azerbaijani, Russian and Lithuanian. When her younger brothers were born, the family made a deliberate shift. "We wanted them to learn Lithuanian well, so we started speaking Lithuanian at home too. My mum doesn't really speak it, but she understands a lot." She is matter-of-fact about where her sense of identity now sits. "I think in Lithuanian," she says. "Ten years ago I would never have imagined things would turn out this way. When I arrived as a small child, my mum was even worried I might not learn the language and we'd have to move to Vilnius and put me in a Russian-language school. I'm very glad that didn't happen." She is considering specialising in gynaecology – the field she associates most closely with life itself, she says – though nothing is fixed yet. The Queen Louise Bridge over the Nemunas river has been closed since April 2022, two months after Russia invaded Ukraine. Back then Russia claimed to have shut it for repairs. Four years on, almost no work has been done. The bridge encapsulates the current state of Lithuania-Russia relations in miniature. On the Russian side, the letter Z – the symbol adopted by Russian forces in Ukraine – is painted on a building wall. On the Lithuanian side, the response is a Ukrainian flag flying alongside the Lithuanian one, and a row of anti-tank obstacles known as dragon's teeth blocking the road. And yet every day, about 200 people cross here anyway – on foot, through the narrow pedestrian checkpoint that remains open beside the bridge, in what has become one of the quieter, stranger edges of the war in Europe. The Panemunė crossing point, which faces the Russian town of Sovetsk across the river, is one of only two active border points between Lithuania and Russia. The other, at Kybartai further south, handles vehicle traffic. Three others – at Nida, Rambinas and Ramoniškai – were closed during the Covid pandemic and never reopened after Russia's invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. The busiest crossings are by rail – through Pagėgiai, the small town where Panemunė sits, and through Kybartai – with three or four transit trains running each way per day, carrying up to 300 passengers each. "Most people and freight travel by train. Three or four transit trains run each way per day, each carrying up to 300 passengers, which is more than enough capacity for everyone wishing to travel," said Colonel Rimantas Petrauskas, commander of the Pagėgiai border unit. The 200 or so daily pedestrian crossings at Panemunė are, for the most part, people visiting family. Petrauskas says the largest group travelling into Russia's Kaliningrad exclave – the isolated Russian territory that borders Lithuania and Poland on the Baltic Sea – are Lithuanian and Latvian citizens with relatives there. Others go to tend graves. "A significant proportion are Russian citizens holding Lithuanian or Latvian residence permits, or people with dual nationality – from Germany, France, Israel, among other countries. Some are transiting to Lithuanian airports, finding it easier to fly from here than from Kaliningrad. Only EU citizens can cross without a visa." Crossings increase in January, when Christmas is celebrated in Russia, and rise by 30-40% in summer. Among those crossing on the day LRT visited was a Latvian woman returning from a month in Russia – her first time there. She had flown from Kaliningrad to Vologda, a city north of Moscow, and travelled around villages and small towns with a friend from England. "I haven't processed it yet. I need to get home and think it all through," she said. A woman waiting in the queue to cross into Kaliningrad said she was flying to Moscow to visit her elderly parents. "I live in Lithuania. My husband and four children are Lithuanian. My parents can't come here now. The journey takes so much longer. I find it inhuman – my parents are old, they can't come to see their grandchildren," she said. Another woman, travelling from Latvia to visit her sister in Kaliningrad, said she makes the trip every year. "My son drove me here and is waiting. My sister and her husband can't travel anymore because of their age. Her husband was a military officer – they were posted here before he retired. They used to live in Central Asia, all over the place. They live like everyone else lives now. I'll stay a month," she said. Crossing on foot does not mean crossing freely. Border officers ask arriving travellers about their purpose, check for valid visas and residence permits, and verify that they have sufficient funds. Since September 2022, Russian citizens have been barred from entering Lithuania except in specific circumstances: diplomats, dissidents, employees of haulage companies, and family members of EU citizens. "In other words, entry is only permitted on humanitarian grounds. For example, if someone is attending a funeral and presents a death certificate, we can issue a single-entry visa on the spot, valid for a few days," officers explained. Customs controls are equally tight. Twenty-four categories of goods are banned from import into Lithuania from Russia, covering most foodstuffs: meat, fish, dairy, eggs, honey, fruit, vegetables, cereals, coffee, tea, alcohol, tobacco and more. "Almost nothing can be brought in from Russia. We do sometimes see full bags of food, but we only allow what someone might reasonably eat on the journey itself. And only goods that are neither Russian nor Belarusian in origin," a customs officer said. Even a single packet of cigarettes from Russia cannot be brought through; Lithuanian cigarettes, however, are fine. Export from Lithuania to Russia is not entirely banned, but is subject to an extensive EU sanctions and export control regime covering military and dual-use goods, electronics and luxury items. Undeclared cash is a recurring problem in both directions – exporting EU currency to Russia is prohibited – and officers say such violations are common. The crossing operates around the clock, with shifts of 12 hours and four to five border officers plus a similar number of customs staff on duty at any given time. The requirement to cross on foot has largely eliminated conventional smuggling. "I can hardly imagine anyone managing to smuggle cigarettes, medicines or other goods through here on their person. The main thing we deal with these days is cash smuggling. Electronics and other goods are very rare, exceptional cases," Petrauskas said. Most of those crossing are regulars, he added, who know exactly what is and isn't permitted. "They don't usually try to bring prohibited items or deceive our officers. At Kybartai, cigarette smuggling has been recorded in recent years, but vehicles cross there." Petrauskas, who has served in the border guard since 2005, says the wider Pagėgiai

Thirty-five years ago, Ukraine chose freedom, but for twelve of those years, Ukrainians have been forced to shed their blood to fight against Russian aggression and its imperial vision of the world, says Ukrainian Ambassador Olha Nikitchenko in an interview with LRT.lt. Ukrainians never sought to become heroes, she argues, they simply had no other choice: “If we stop fighting, then we stop existing.” Ukraine is bringing war closer to Russia, Russian people with long-range strikes into its territory. Even Vladimir Putin acknowledged that there is some damage, but still it looks like he has a firm hold on power in Russia. Do you think these attacks are actually changing his calculations with, for example, negotiations? Definitely, because these attacks and these long strikes, we call them the long-range sanctions, they are definitely making all of the difference. We are bringing the war actually into Russia. It's not even closer Russia, but into Russia. <…> And it makes all the difference because Putin can acknowledge this or he may not, but it doesn't change the truth that economically Russia is very much into decline right now. Sanctions are working, long-range strikes are working. So whatever he or his allies are telling themselves, this is definitely working. <…>. But as they say, winter is coming, and there are very serious warnings about another very difficult winter for Ukraine, particularly as Russia is still targeting energy infrastructure, which is not repaired. What worries you the most about this upcoming winter in Ukraine? What we've seen last winter was the most hard and terrible winter for Ukraine, and I hope it stays this way. I do hope we will have it easier. But if you look at what is happening, it certainly does not seem so because we are in for a very hard period. <…> Basically, I would say that the two things that worry us the most. The first is the air defense, because Russia targets energy infrastructure, and energy sector in terms of generators, transformers, energy capacity. So these two priorities are interlinked. So we do very much need more stronger air defenses, anti-ballistic missiles for the Patriot systems, the IRIS-Ts, the NASAMS, and everything along these lines. So it still remains very much essential. There is also the new “Freya” initiative, the anti-ballistic initiative launched by Ukraine, and it is ongoing now, but it still requires time to create that. Ukrainian Energy Support Fund has mobilized more than two billion euros so far, but we are still short 500 million euros to live through the winter. I would actually say that the challenge is broader than the energy, because Ukraine has still to keep schools and hospitals running. It has to finance its defense, maintain macroeconomic stability. That gives us a little more of a broader perspective on how we should go through winter, because as of now 68% of the Ukrainian budget goes into the defense priorities, and it is extremely important for us to continue having the international budgetary support to keep the state actually running and to keep our people living. You have to spend a lot of time explaining Ukraine’s situation and what support it needs. What is the most frustrating or difficult thing that you still need to explain to people about the support that Ukraine needs? When I was just posted in Lithuania, I was preparing for all my meetings, for the first meeting with the president, the prime minister, I was making notes, and I had a very big list of the arguments of why they should be helping Ukraine and why it is important. But I found myself that in every meeting when I just started saying all this everybody would just stop me and say, “Ambassador, yeah, we know that. Like, tell us what you need.” We do share a very special bond, and it's not just because I'm the ambassador here, but because of our common history, common values. Because Lithuania understands very much what the Russians are and what “Russkiy Mir” brings to people. So I'm not explaining here why it is needed, I'm just saying what we need. And Lithuanians never hesitate and say, “Oh, well, that might be too difficult” and “That is impossible.” They just say, “Let us see what we can do”. And we are extremely grateful for that. All of my meetings, all of my speeches here start with a thank you: “Ačiū labai”. Because even in Ukraine, if you would stop a random person on the on the street, and if you would ask to tell what countries are most helping Ukraine, I am sure that you would get Lithuania in the top three. There have been recently warnings, particularly for Baltic states and Poland, that Russia might start false-flag operation, perhaps even with Ukrainian drones. What do you think Lithuania is doing right while preparing for this scenario? I can say that you are doing a great job actually. I also would like to say that we're already helping you with sharing experience that we had learned very painful way. And while we share it, we certainly hope you would never have to use it. <…> You have a great concept of total defense, which includes the civil defense, defence of energy objects, military defense. We're sharing with you processes of how to keep the state functioning during wartime. All of our institutions are in deep connection about the sharing of knowledge and experience at any point should, I wouldn't say the big word invasion but should any of these circumstances occur here. And what do you think Lithuania could do better? It's not what you could do better, but it is kind of also learning on our case and on our mistakes, is that if Russia tells you that it wants to kill you, believe it. So that just maybe be more vigilant. I'm not saying that they will come here tomorrow, but being more aware of that this is an actual threat. This is not something potential. This is not something that might happen. Before the 2022 and before 2014 nobody believed that there could be such an offensive in Europe, that Russia would act

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda travelled to Kyiv on Sunday for Ukraine's National Flag Day, telling the country that only a Ukrainian victory can bring lasting peace and stability to Europe, as Ukraine marked the 35th anniversary of its independence from the Soviet Union on Monday. “I believe that we will soon be able to celebrate victory over darkness together. A victory that will belong not only to Ukraine but to the whole of free Europe,” Nausėda said, pledging that Lithuania would continue to support Ukraine, refuse to recognise the occupation of its territories, and increase pressure on Russia and its allies. He also promised that Lithuania would help rebuild destroyed schools, hospitals and power plants once the war ends, and would continue backing Ukraine’s bids to join the EU and NATO. The ceremony was also attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and leaders from the Nordic and Baltic states. Over the following two days, Nausėda is due to take part in events marking the independence anniversary and a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing – a grouping of countries providing military support to Ukraine – as well as hold separate talks with Zelensky. Lithuania’s first lady, Diana Nausėdienė, is following a parallel programme focused on social resilience and the war’s impact on civilians, including a summit of first ladies and gentlemen organised by her Ukrainian counterpart. The visit comes as Russia has intensified its bombardment of Ukrainian cities. The United Nations says civilian casualties in 2026 have reached their highest level since the war began, and Ukraine is currently facing a shortage of ammunition for its air defence systems. Marking the anniversary itself, Nausėda said in a message to Zelensky and the Ukrainian people that “the determination of the Ukrainian nation to defend its country and fight against Russian aggression gives this day a special significance.” He reaffirmed Lithuania’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity, and said Vilnius would never recognise the occupation or annexation of Ukrainian territory, arguing that respect for a rules-based international order is the only guarantee of a peaceful future. “Ukraine’s fight is also our fight for freedom,” he said. “Lithuania will support Ukraine until its victory.” Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, in a separate message issued from Vilnius, said the anniversary was a reminder that “the principles of freedom, sovereignty and national self-determination cannot be taken for granted and must be cherished.” He said Lithuania’s support for Ukraine remained unwavering, with continued political, military, economic and humanitarian assistance, alongside a role in the country’s reconstruction, stressing that Ukraine’s defence is critical to European security and stability. Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas added his own message on Saturday, stressing the importance of maintaining unity within Europe and the international community in support of Ukraine. “Ukraine is an integral part of the European and Euro-Atlantic family. Even under the extraordinary hardships of war, it continues to implement reforms and move toward the European Union. Lithuania will remain steadfast in supporting Ukraine’s EU membership and its chosen European and Euro-Atlantic future,” he said, describing the courage and sacrifice of the Ukrainian people as an inspiring example of resilience for the rest of Europe. He expressed hope that the anniversary would serve as a reminder “that freedom is stronger than aggression and a nation’s will outweighs any attempt to break it.” Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union on August 24, 1991, following the collapse of a coup attempt in Moscow.

Lithuania’s government has approved €56.6 million to build and renovate schools in Vilnius and Kaunas for the children of German troops stationed in the country. Plans include a new school for around 500-600 pupils on Drujos Street in Vilnius, and the reconstruction of an existing school on Verkių Street in Kaunas to accommodate roughly 200 pupils. The Vilnius project has been allocated €45.87 million, with a further €10.75 million earmarked for Kaunas. Both will be funded through the state budget and government borrowing, covering design, construction, equipment and other costs. The Kaunas school is expected to open in September 2028, with the new Vilnius facility due for completion no later than 2032. The investment follows a defence cooperation agreement between Lithuania and Germany, under which Lithuania committed to providing educational infrastructure for the children of German personnel and their families. Germany plans to station between 4,000 and 5,000 troops in Lithuania by the end of 2027, with some soldiers from the brigade already arrived or preparing to arrive with their families.

The United States plans to provide Lithuania with nearly €11 million worth of AN/PVS-14 night vision devices, Lithuania's defence ministry has confirmed. The US government has signed a $12.78 million (€10.94 million) contract for the equipment with American company Nightline Inc, with delivery required by December 31, 2030. According to Lithuania’s Defence Ministry, no funds from the national defence budget are being used for the purchase, as the contract has been signed and its implementation is being administered directly by the United States.

Eighty-five years after Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union signed a secret pact to carve up central and northern Europe between them, Russian state-aligned media are still fighting over how history remembers it – and a new study suggests the propaganda campaign has shifted focus this year, with Poland increasingly recast as an aggressor rather than a victim. The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, signed on August 23, 1939, was a non-aggression treaty between the two totalitarian powers. Its secret protocols, which divided Poland, the Baltic states, Finland and Romania into German and Soviet “spheres of influence,” were not revealed publicly until decades later. For countries like Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Poland, the pact is remembered as the mechanism that set the stage for their occupation. In Russia, however, it remains a subject of active historical dispute, and pro-Kremlin outlets devote significant attention each year to reframing it. According to a study released on Monday by Debunk.org, a Lithuanian disinformation research centre, pro-Kremlin media published 192 items about the pact this year, of which 169 presented it in a positive light. That marks a sharp fall from 2025, when 481 items were recorded, 403 of them positive. Debunk.org’s chief analyst, Algirdas Kazlauskas, attributes the decline largely to the calendar: 2025 marked the 80th anniversary of Victory in Europe Day, which drove unusually high interest in the Second World War generally. This year, by contrast, Russian state media have concentrated on the 85th anniversary of the outbreak of the war between Germany and the Soviet Union in 1941 – an event they present as the conflict’s true starting point, in what Kazlauskas describes as an attempt to draw attention away from the earlier pact and its secret protocols. Where the pact is discussed, the dominant narrative this year presents it as a reluctant, defensive move – the claim being that the Soviet Union only signed it because Western powers and Poland had refused to form a united front against Hitler beforehand. “This is an attempt to transform the Soviet Union from an aggressor into a victim of war,” Kazlauskas said. A second narrative uses the 1939 agreement as a template to justify Russia’s present-day conduct, with commentators drawing parallels to both the war in Ukraine and current Russia-US diplomacy. “The past is being turned into an alibi for the present,” Kazlauskas said. “The pact is no longer evaluated as a historical fact; it has become an example supposedly proving the success of a chosen strategy. Today’s actions by Russia are explained using this very example.” The starkest shift identified by the study concerns Poland – one of the pact’s principal victims, invaded from the west by Germany and from the east by the Soviet Union within weeks of each other. Pro-Kremlin media are increasingly recasting Poland instead as an aggressor, part of a wider pattern of Russian messaging that has grown more hostile toward Warsaw as it plays an increasingly prominent role in supporting Ukraine and hosting NATO forces. The Baltic states remain targets too, though the tactics used against them are more familiar. Lithuania’s incorporation into the Soviet Union is being denied through two recurring claims: that Soviet leader Joseph Stalin returned the Vilnius and Klaipėda regions to Lithuania as an act of goodwill, rather than as territorial adjustments serving Soviet strategic interests, and that alleged Baltic collaboration with Nazi occupiers should overshadow the memory of the preceding and subsequent Soviet occupation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky awarded Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda the Order of Liberty on Monday as he attended ceremonies in Kyiv marking Ukraine’s 35th Independence Day. Nausėda said the award belonged to all the people of Lithuania for their unwavering and tireless support for Ukraine. "Ukraine's struggle is the fight of all of us for freedom, which is why Lithuania has been, is, and will remain with Ukraine until its victory," Nauseda said. He emphasised that the independence anniversary carries special significance as the country continues to fight against Kremlin aggression. Nausėda noted that the resistance of the Ukrainian people is not only a defence of their own state, but a battle for a rules-based international order where national borders cannot be changed by force. The Lithuanian leader also stressed the need to ensure continuous military, humanitarian and financial support for Ukraine. Nausėda is also scheduled to attend a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing on Monday, which will be co-chaired by the leaders of the United Kingdom, France and Germany.

NATO fighter jets patrolling the airspace of the Baltic states will carry out pre-planned training flights over northern Lithuania on Monday, the country's air force has said, warning residents that they could hear loud bangs resembling explosions caused by aircraft breaking the sound barrier. The flights are part of NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission, under which allied fighter jets patrol the skies over Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – none of which operate their own fighter aircraft – from bases in Lithuania and Estonia. The mission has taken on added significance since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, as NATO has stepped up its presence along its eastern flank.

Growing fears about a potential attack against the Baltic states or Poland benefit Russia, which seeks to reduce Western support for Ukraine, Baltic experts told LRT.lt. In early August, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robert Kaunas warned that Russia was considering possible provocations in the Baltic region, including so-called false-flag operations targeting the region’s critical infrastructure using Ukrainian drones and blaming Kyiv for the attacks. Poland’s Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has repeatedly warned of an identical scenario in his country. The warnings should be viewed in the broader context of Russia’s efforts to reduce Western support for Ukraine, according to Erkki Tori, Director of the National Security and Defence Coordination at the Estonian Government Office. “Since the beginning of this year, the Russians have been looking for ways to tip the balance back in their favour. One of the things they have been working on – and they have been trying to do this since 2022 – is reducing Western support for Ukraine,” Tori told LRT.lt. In his assessment, the Russian threat should not be understood simply as a conflict between Moscow and the Baltic states. “It is actually Russia against the West as a whole. Russia against NATO, Russia against the European Union, because the goal is to divide us so that we are not as determined to continue supporting Ukraine,” the Estonian official said. NATO has reportedly drawn up detailed plans for countering missile attacks, stopping Russian forces at the border and disrupting supply routes deep inside Russian territory. The latest warnings also do not indicate a change in the overall security outlook, according to Marek Kohv, head of the Security and Resilience Programme at the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Estonia. “I think there is actually nothing new in these warnings, and people sometimes overestimate the new assessments, saying that Russia might do something in the hybrid sphere. But we have to realise that Russia has already been attacking us for years in the hybrid domain, so there is nothing new,” Kohv told LRT.lt. Cyberattacks against critical infrastructure have already become a persistent problem in Europe, he added. According to Kohv, Moscow benefits from amplifying fear of possible escalation in Western societies, meaning that the new warnings ultimately work to Russia’s advantage. US intelligence warnings are taken seriously in Estonia, but the country’s national security assessment has not changed. “All the possibilities described in those assessments are relevant today. Russia could use Ukrainian drones if it has them. But from our perspective, the security assessment has not changed since the beginning of the year. At the moment, we [in Estonia] do not have the same concerns that Lithuania or Poland have publicly expressed,” he said. Moscow could intensify information operations, especially ahead of upcoming elections, Kohv said. “I think we will see intensifying disinformation campaigns, particularly against Latvia and, next year, against Estonia as well, because we have elections coming up. Russia has always regarded elections as one of its targets in an effort to change the political situation,” he added. Estonian intelligence continues to assess that conventional military operations against the Baltic states are unlikely as long as Russian forces remain focused on the war in Ukraine. “Instead, we are primarily thinking about various forms of hybrid activity: sabotage, cyberattacks or information campaigns,” said Tori from the Estonian Government’s Office. “You cannot rule out a miscalculation from Russia. This is a lesson that we in the Baltic and Nordic countries have already learned,” he added. The threat from Moscow has existed since1995, which was when Soviet troops withdrew from their territory and returned to Russia, according to Sandis Šraders, a researcher at the Latvian Institute of International Affairs (LIIA) and the National Defence Academy of Latvia. “Russian bases are close to the Latvian and Estonian borders. We have a direct border with the Russian Federation. In Lithuania’s case, Kaliningrad is a heavily militarised region, so the threat has always existed,” he told LRT.lt. Šraders stresses that Russia had been projecting aggressive military capabilities towards the Baltic region long before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since the invasion began, manifestations of Russian aggression in the Baltic states – airspace violations, military exercises and attacks on critical infrastructure – have become increasingly brazen. “In the Baltic states, violations of our airspace have already become a routine occurrence, something both the public and military structures are almost becoming bored of – all those instances when fighter jets have to be scrambled from the Šiauliai Air Base or, for example, from Ämari Air Base in Estonia,” Šraders said. Following Russia’s aggression against Ukraine in 2014, the Baltic states are also aware of the so-called “little green men” scenario. “We know that similar military exercises and incidents have also been recorded along the Estonian border, for example near Narva,” Šraders notes. Speaking about warnings of a possible Russian false-flag operation involving Ukrainian drones, the Latvian defence expert says he feels safer knowing that intelligence officials are already aware of such plans by Moscow. Warnings about possible Russian provocations in the Baltic states and Poland have intensified as Russia faces growing pressure in Ukraine. Kyiv’s attacks in Russia itself represent a significant blow not only to Russia’s economy and military logistics, but also to President Vladimir Putin’s domestic image.
