Lithuania made progress in several areas of human rights in 2025, but many issues remain unresolved because existing laws often fail to translate into practical improvements in people’s daily lives, the country’s parliamentary ombudsmen said Tuesday. “Progress in human rights must be measured by the results for the individual – whether a person actually manages to cross the bridge from formally existing laws to everyday reality without having to fight for it,” Ombudsperson Erika Leonaitė said during the presentation of the 2025 human rights monitoring report. The report found no significant change in the prevalence of violence, with overall trends remaining similar to previous years. Authorities received 55,900 reports of domestic violence last year, about 1,500 more than in 2024, while 4,300 related criminal acts were registered. Women accounted for 75% of domestic violence victims. More than half, 54%, of domestic violence protection orders were issued repeatedly, highlighting concerns about repeat offenses and the effectiveness of existing safeguards. The ombudsmen identified the absence of a legal definition of systemic violence, a lack of long-term protection mechanisms for victims facing repeat abuse and the growing prevalence of cyber and sexual violence as key challenges. On reproductive rights, the report highlighted several developments, including the launch of home-visiting services for families in May and a Constitutional Court ruling concerning access to assisted reproduction. However, access to contraception and medical abortion remains problematic, as do sexual and reproductive health education and issues related to personal autonomy. Foreign nationals accounted for about 7.5% of Lithuania’s population, a proportion that remained stable. The report noted improvements in integration systems, including better access to information for vulnerable and ethnic groups, the introduction of new tools and translation services, and improved procedures for assessing vulnerability. The report also found progress in disability rights. Refusing to provide reasonable accommodation is now recognised as discrimination. However, community-based services remain limited, institutional care remains widespread and opportunities for employment and independent decision-making are restricted. Only 31.5% of working-age people with disabilities were employed last year, while 10,600 people were declared legally incapacitated in certain areas, according to the report. Conditions in Lithuania’s prisons have improved in some respects, but a planned new prison project remains stalled. The ombudsmen said incremental changes have not produced the broader reforms needed to bring prisoners’ rights in line with international standards. Among the main concerns are dormitory-style housing, shortages of prison staff and psychologists, violence, criminal subcultures, a lack of confidential channels for reporting abuse and insufficient rehabilitation and parole opportunities. The report also found that legal developments concerning LGBTIQ+ rights have not been matched by broader policy changes. Courts considered 27 cases involving same-sex partnerships last year and granted 18 requests. However, Lithuania still lacks a comprehensive legal framework regulating same-sex partnerships, the ombudsmen said. Reported violations involving violence and harassment prevention increased 48% in 2025. Such violations were most frequently reported in manufacturing, education, construction and transportation. Of claims involving psychological violence, 42% were rejected last year, 31% ended in settlements and only 1.5% resulted in full or partial satisfaction of the claims, according to the report. Religious minorities also continue to face intolerance. The report found that 32% of Lithuanians said they would not want to work with Muslims, while negative attitudes toward other religious minorities persist. Religious groups were the most frequent targets of reported hate crimes. The parliamentary ombudsmen concluded that monitoring public attitudes in Lithuania remains inconsistent and insufficient, making it harder to assess changes in social tolerance and human rights conditions.

The Lithuanian Armed Forces have deployed a medium-range NASAMS air defence system on the outskirts of Vilnius, replacing the previous short-range systems that have been deployed there since the first drone incursions from Belarus last year. “Speaking about the qualitative change, as planned and promised, we have already replaced our short-range RBS-70 system with NASAMS, and today the approaches to Vilnius are being protected much more effectively and powerfully, with a greater range,” Chief of Defence Raimundas Vaikšnoras told BNS. He did not say when the system was deployed. “Critics may say that NASAMS is not the system you want to use to shoot down a cheap drone with an expensive missile, but until we have other capabilities, it is probably the most flexible option. “It is similar to the missiles used by the fighter jets involved in Baltic air policing. They are actually expensive, but at present they are the most effective means because you can intercept and destroy a drone anywhere over Lithuanian territory. So NASAMS gives us speed, range and accuracy,” the general said. The move comes amid repeated drone incursions into NATO airspace in the alliance's eastern member states. The most recent drone incursion into Lithuania took place in May. A similar incident was recorded in Latvia earlier in August. The unmanned aircraft was shot down by a NATO fighter jet that took off from Šiauliai Air Base in Lithuania. Lithuania currently has two NASAMS batteries, with a third expected to arrive in 2028.

Vilnius City Council approved a 1-million-euro funding package Wednesday to improve the accessibility and preparedness of emergency shelters across the capital. The funding, allocated from the municipal budget, will support three measures: improving access to shelters, installing window protection, and helping applicants prepare documents for shelter development programs financed by the Interior Ministry. Apartment building associations, as well as state and municipal institutions and agencies in Vilnius whose facilities are included in or eligible for the official shelter list, will be able to apply for funding. Educational institutions that do not have officially designated shelters will also be eligible for funding for window protection. Funding will be available only for shelters that remain accessible to residents 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Any barriers to entry must be removable within five minutes, while facilities must also have an alternative means of entry and several people designated as responsible for access. Žygimantas Solovjovas, head of the municipality’s Civil Protection Division, said the initial focus would be on about 12% to 13% of the city’s shelters, most of which are located in municipally owned buildings. Applicants may receive up to 20,000 euros per funding call, according to the municipality. The city will cover up to 95% of the cost of installing automatic or remote unlocking systems, capped at 5,000 euros. Other access improvements will be reimbursed at up to 40% of installation costs, with a maximum of 1,000 euros. Up to 15,200 euros may be allocated per facility for window protection, covering as much as 80% of eligible costs. Protective measures such as window films, shutters and shields may be installed directly in shelters or on the lowest floor of a building if the facility has no shelter or its existing shelter is too small. The third funding measure will provide full reimbursement for preparing technical projects and other documentation required to apply for the Interior Ministry’s shelter infrastructure development programs. The municipality will also cover up to 80% of the cost of additional technical work deemed necessary. Funding will be provided only to facilities that meet the Interior Ministry’s requirements for emergency shelters once the work is completed.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Wednesday he had been informed about CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow but declined to discuss the substance of the meeting. “We knew about the meeting,” Nausėda said. “I would not want to discuss its content because, first of all, that is a matter for the parties to the meeting.” Lithuania had been informed by its partners that details about the meeting, including its purpose and content, would be shared with Vilnius promptly, Nausėda said. “We were informed by our partners that information about this meeting, its objectives and content would be provided to us immediately – probably next week,” he said. Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow Tuesday, becoming one of the few senior US officials to travel to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The CIA and White House have not commented on the purpose of the visit. The Kremlin said Wednesday that Ratcliffe had “contacts” with Russian intelligence services during his visit to Moscow, without providing further details. Nausėda said he believed the meeting was intended to help reduce geopolitical tensions in the region. The last CIA director to visit Moscow was William Burns, who travelled to the Russian capital in November 2021 and warned Russian officials against sending troops into Ukraine. Several months later, Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

The unannounced visit by the director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) to Moscow this week was to deliver a warning to Russia not to attack NATO countries, people briefed on the visit told the Wall Street Journal. Later on Thursday, Politico reported that the “meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states”, citing a person familiar with the matter. The visit followed earlier US warnings that Russia could stage a limited attack against Poland or the Baltic states to test NATO’s resolve. The White House has oﬀered little clarity about the trip, WSJ reported on Thursday, with President Donald Trump publicly downplaying its significance. The last such visit by a CIA director to Moscow took place in November 2021, warning Vladimir Putin not to attack Ukraine.

Renouncing Russian citizenship has become several times more expensive since August. Interior Minister Igor Taro said it is too early to assess whether the price increase will also lead to a decline in the number of applicants. Former Russian citizen Andrei Malaškin began the process of applying for Estonian citizenship in 2022. He said the entire process took nearly three and a half years and was only completed last year. “When the war started, I began to think that Russian citizenship was no longer convenient for me,” Malaškin said. According to Malaškin, renouncing his Russian citizenship took the most time. “I remember I was in the queue for the Russian consulate for about four months. Then I went there and some of my supporting documents had expired, so I had to get back in line and that took another three months or so,” Malaškin said. At the time, renouncing his Russian citizenship cost him just over €300. Since August this year, the same procedure in Estonia has cost €2,376. “I've heard about it. I didn't believe it was true. People can't spend that much money on a document,” Malaškin said. Interior Minister Igor Taro said the price increase is due to the difficult situation in Russia. “I think Russia doesn't have the money to maintain its foreign missions. Secondly, the number of people renouncing their citizenship has probably increased and they don't have enough staff to handle it properly. Under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, no one may take measures to prevent people from renouncing their citizenship. Looking at that general principle, Russia is currently violating the declaration to some extent,” Taro said. Taro said it is still too early to assess whether the high fee will reduce the number of applicants. “Unfortunately, when it comes to Russian state fees, the Estonian state can't do anything about them. The amount is certainly large, but if someone really has a strong need to renounce their citizenship, I think they can find the money,” Taro said. Interest among Russian citizens in obtaining Estonian citizenship has remained high in recent years. A total of 465 applications were submitted to the Police and Border Guard Board last year. As of July this year, 217 applications had been submitted. An article initially published on August 22, 2026, 07:56 (CEST).

Residents of Kapčiamiestis and surrounding villages in southern Lithuania have begun receiving information leaflets about plans for a new military training area. For some, the notices have brought little new information – and little reassurance. The planned training area is already changing the face of the small Lazdijai district town. Roads and streets are being upgraded, a former school building is being prepared for military use, and a former children’s care centre is set to be renovated to house local municipal institutions. But for residents whose homes fall within the planned training area, the changes carry a much higher price. Marija Janulevičienė, who lives in the village of Zmirklės during the warmer months, received an information leaflet about three weeks ago. Earlier this year, she was told in a letter that she would eventually have to leave her homestead and would receive compensation for the loss. Janulevičienė said all the information she has received so far has come in writing. No officials have visited to discuss the plans with her in person, she said, and the leaflet offered little she did not already know. “Nothing. The same thing they wrote in that letter – that they are thinking about building a shooting range here and that residents will be relocated,” she said. The information has not convinced her to leave. “I’m not going to do anything. I’ll just sit here like this and I’m not moving anywhere,” she said. “If they need it, let them move me. I’m not moving anything.” Janulevičienė inherited the homestead from her parents together with her sister and brother. Her family spends the summers there, growing vegetables and picking mushrooms and berries. The other heirs visit on weekends. “They’re unhappy, too,” she said of her relatives. “They say, ‘We won’t have anywhere to come and pick mushrooms.’ It’s so nice here. There are old-growth forests, nature reserves, all kinds of birds, and bison grazing in the meadows.” The Defence Ministry has distributed information about the planned training area to residents throughout the local administrative district. For Tauras Mekas, who spends his summers at a homestead in the planned military training territory, the changes are something he will have to adapt to. “It took me 27 years to build this house, and I don’t have another 27 years to build a new one,” said Mekas, who lives in Menciškė. “I look around and see all the neighbours building and improving their homes. At first, it was depressing, but then I thought, well, this too shall pass.” Other residents who will not have to leave their homes are more concerned about how military activity could affect daily life. “It doesn’t affect me. I live here, not in the area where everything will take place, so I’m not particularly concerned,” said Kapčiamiestis resident Romas Baranauskas. “I say, if they shoot loudly, there will be inconveniences. When the Belarusians conduct shooting exercises, the range is about 18 kilometres from us. If they shoot loudly, our windows shake.” Although the military training area is still largely at the planning stage, residents are already seeing changes linked to the project. The Defence Ministry has allocated nearly 1.5 million euros for improvements to roads and streets in the area. Lazdijai Mayor Ausma Miškinienė said investments promised in connection with the planned training area were already turning into visible improvements. “Essentially, both the quality of life and the appearance of the town will change,” she said. “And I believe people will see and appreciate that. We are seeing concrete results and concrete investments in culture, health, business and tourism.” The former school building has been transferred to the Defence Ministry and is being prepared for military use. The building will provide offices and administrative space for the military, while some areas will be adapted for sports and leisure activities that will also be available to Kapčiamiestis residents, Miškinienė said. A long-vacant former children’s care centre is also due for renovation. The building is expected to house the local library and museum. Kapčiamiestis administrative head Virginijus Golekas said the new premises would provide considerably more space, particularly for the Pliaterytė Museum. The investment is expected to extend beyond the immediate area of the planned training site. Next year, Lazdijai municipality is set to receive nearly 3 million euros from the defence budget for road infrastructure, attracting investment and strengthening health services.

A letter seen by RFE/RL, partners of LRT English, reveals growing concern about Russian aggression in the Baltic states, speaking of a "deteriorating security environment" amid an "increased frequency of airspace violations and drone incursions". The letter was sent to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and signed by the three Baltic European commissioners, Kaja Kallas, Andrius Kubilius, and Valdis Dombrovskis, as well as the Polish and Finnish commissioners. Dated July 30, the letter was one of a series of alarm bells sounded about Russian aggression over the course of the summer that culminated in CIA Director John Ratcliffe's surprise visit to Moscow on August 25. Ratcliffe flew to Moscow to urge the Kremlin against escalating with US allies -- particularly Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania -- sources briefed about the visit confirmed to RFE/RL on August 26. This follows reporting by The Wall Street Journal on August 6 that cited US intelligence stating that Russia may test NATO resolve with a limited incursion as early as this fall. Baltic diplomats who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity confirmed that there was additional intelligence during the summer of Russian false flag operations but no indication about an imminent conventional attack. They were also keen to point out that such operations might not be limited to the Baltics, a concern reinforced by recent cases of alleged or suspected Russian involvement in assassination attempts, fires, and drone incursions in several NATO countries, including Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. At first glance, the three Baltic states – Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia – seem ideally placed to counter any type of Russian attack. They have long warned about and planned for various forms of Russian malign activity. All three have reached or will soon reach NATO’s 2035 target of spending 5 percent of GDP on defense. On top of that, the EU has pledged and begun channeling roughly $14 billion of loans for defense and security investment in the region. And apart from conventional defense preparations, they are also at the forefront of cutting-edge technology -- notably Estonia. Take DefSecIntel Solutions, an Estonian company whose artificial-intelligence software analyzes captured images and and presents all the information on a single screen. “We decided to stand by our Ukrainian colleagues; since autumn 2022, we've been on the front lines with them. And our technologies are being used there. This has certainly given us a major boost," Jaan Hein, the company’s vice president, told Current Time. He said the company's product is being used to protect the borders of Estonia as well as a dozen other countries. Or take the Estonian start-up Wayren, which has developed software installed on smartphones, tablets, and other devices on the battlefield to protect data exchange from outside interference. "Estonia is unique in some ways: as a small country with a relatively small industry, we specialize in cutting-edge technologies. Not so much in large platforms like tanks or ships, as larger countries do, but in smart and innovative solutions that can be integrated into such systems, thereby gaining an advantage” company co-founder Henri Harm told Current Time. But look closer and cracks start to appear. Negotiations on the next seven-year EU budget have started with a European Commission proposal for a $145-billion pot for security and defense investments. But several net contributors, including the largest, Germany, have made it clear that they want a smaller EU budget going forward. Many EU officials fear that defense could very likely be one of the areas cut and this fear is apparent in the leaked letter. Some of its proposals are symbolic, like the entire European Commission “urgently” visiting one of the frontline countries this autumn “as we all see the escalation of threats against the Baltic states”. The main demand, however, is for further funding, with the letter calling for some $115 billion to bolster the business and investment environment in the frontline states. Pointing to growing drone and other activity from Russia, it says “these incidents are already having a negative impact on the region's business environment and public confidence in security. To prevent further deterioration and reinforce deterrence, visible and timely action is required.” Among the actions outlined are “rapid response capacity to disruptions in energy supply and towards critical electricity and gas infrastructure, setting up regional stockpiles for essential goods and civil protection assets, shelters and evacuation infrastructure, and preparedness to respond to hybrid, cyber, sabotage, electronic, and information threats.” Conspicuously absent from the text – and from most EU communications recently – is the “drone wall,” – a proposed project widely discussed last year that the bloc considered funding. The idea was to equip the EU's entire eastern flank with sensors and capabilities to detect and shoot down unfriendly drones. Not much has happened in this regard. As one Baltic official put it to RFE/RL: “It’s easier to talk about the drone wall than to build one. But let’s be frank, nobody has this wall yet, not even the Ukrainians.” The problems are financial, technical, and legal. There is no clarity over who should pay for such an expensive system; key components, including sensors, radars, and an effective command-and-control system, are not yet fully developed; and there is still debate over whether the whole thing should be fully automated or overseen by humans. Then there is Rail Baltica, another EU-funded project that isn’t going as planned. Launched in 2015, it was supposed to connect the the Baltic states, whose rail networks still largely use Soviet-era rail gauges, with Poland and the rest of the EU. The original goal of opening the line this year has long been abandoned, while the revised target of 2030 is also in doubt amid spiraling costs

A record 170 cadets are set to begin studies at Lithuania’s General Jonas Žemaitis Military Academy this year, as growing numbers of young people seek careers as military officers, the academy said Thursday. Last year, 143 students enrolled at the academy, up from 98 in 2024. Nearly 500 applicants registered for motivational interviews this year, with about 280 candidates shortlisted following the selection process. “Given the record-high number of young people wishing to serve their homeland, we have increased the first-year admission quota from 150 to 170 places,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said. For the first time, the academy’s defence studies program also ranked among the 10 most popular programs receiving state-funded university placements. Col. Ričardas Dumbliauskas, commandant of the Military Academy of Lithuania, said the figures reflected the growing prestige of the military officer profession and young people’s increasing willingness to serve their country. The General Jonas Žemaitis Military Academy is Lithuania’s main institution for training officers for the armed forces. Cadets receive both university-level education and military training as part of their studies.

The chairman of Lithuania’s parliamentary Foreign Affairs Committee said Thursday that CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow was useful for Lithuania but did not indicate an increased threat to the Baltic country. “I think this visit is, I won’t hide the word, useful to Lithuania in a certain sense,” Remigijus Motuzas told reporters. He cited recent warnings about possible attacks on critical infrastructure as a reason for Lithuania to pay closer attention to potential threats. “I don’t think the danger to Lithuania has increased, but the visit is another signal that we need to be concerned about our critical infrastructure and devote even more attention to it,” Motuzas said. “I think there is no direct military threat in the near future.” The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported that Ratcliffe sought during his Moscow visit to deter Russia from attacking NATO members, citing US intelligence assessments that Moscow could seek to test the alliance. Officials and intelligence agencies have previously warned that Russia could consider attacks on critical infrastructure in NATO’s eastern-flank countries using drones from Ukraine. Motuzas said he believed the main subject of Ratcliffe’s talks was Russia’s war against Ukraine. “Russia is now in a defensive position,” he said, citing damage to Russian infrastructure, public concerns about security and mobilisation, and a weakening economy. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC), said there was no solid evidence that Ratcliffe had delivered a warning to Moscow about a possible attack on the Baltic states. “We have no firm data that such a signal was sent to Moscow,” Vitkauskas told reporters. “And if it was, then I think we need to look at the consequences – what the Russian side’s reaction would be and so on.” He cautioned against speculation about the substance of the talks, saying there was currently only interpretation and no firm information. Vitkauskas said Lithuania had seen no significant changes in its security environment in recent weeks or months but was maintaining a heightened level of vigilance. “There has really been no change in recent months or weeks,” he said. “The level of vigilance that has been raised in Lithuania for quite some time remains the same, and this is certainly not the time or place to relax.” Meanwhile, opposition conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas said he would seek a meeting of the parliament’s National Security and Defence Committee to brief lawmakers on the purpose and outcome of Ratcliffe’s visit. “I plan to ask for a meeting of the National Security and Defence Committee soon so that lawmakers working in the security field have a certain level of knowledge: what happened, why he went, what the reactions were and what scenarios we are talking about,” Kasčiūnas said. He said it was a positive sign that President Gitanas Nausėda had been informed about the visit in advance. “I think consultations should take place in the coming days to clarify what was discussed and what Russia’s response was,” Kasčiūnas said. The fact that the CIA director travelled to Russia to deliver a message showed that the United States remained committed to the security of its allies, he said. “The Americans are still the ones who are primarily concerned with our security,” Kasčiūnas said. “It is a good sign that the Americans are not going anywhere. If they did not care, they would not fly [to Moscow]. But now everything needs to be done to achieve real deterrence.” Ratcliffe is among the highest-ranking US officials to visit Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. President Nausėda said earlier that Lithuania had been informed about Ratcliffe’s visit and that its allies were expected to provide information about its purpose and content next week.

The unannounced visit by the director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) to Moscow this week was to deliver a warning to Russia not to attack NATO countries, people briefed on the visit told the Wall Street Journal. Later on Thursday, Politico reported that the “meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states”, citing a person familiar with the matter. The visit followed earlier US warnings that Russia could stage a limited attack against Poland or the Baltic states to test NATO’s resolve. The White House has oﬀered little clarity about the trip, WSJ reported on Thursday, with President Donald Trump publicly downplaying its significance. The last such visit by a CIA director to Moscow took place in November 2021, warning Vladimir Putin not to attack Ukraine.

Renouncing Russian citizenship has become several times more expensive since August. Interior Minister Igor Taro said it is too early to assess whether the price increase will also lead to a decline in the number of applicants. Former Russian citizen Andrei Malaškin began the process of applying for Estonian citizenship in 2022. He said the entire process took nearly three and a half years and was only completed last year. “When the war started, I began to think that Russian citizenship was no longer convenient for me,” Malaškin said. According to Malaškin, renouncing his Russian citizenship took the most time. “I remember I was in the queue for the Russian consulate for about four months. Then I went there and some of my supporting documents had expired, so I had to get back in line and that took another three months or so,” Malaškin said. At the time, renouncing his Russian citizenship cost him just over €300. Since August this year, the same procedure in Estonia has cost €2,376. “I've heard about it. I didn't believe it was true. People can't spend that much money on a document,” Malaškin said. Interior Minister Igor Taro said the price increase is due to the difficult situation in Russia. “I think Russia doesn't have the money to maintain its foreign missions. Secondly, the number of people renouncing their citizenship has probably increased and they don't have enough staff to handle it properly. Under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, no one may take measures to prevent people from renouncing their citizenship. Looking at that general principle, Russia is currently violating the declaration to some extent,” Taro said. Taro said it is still too early to assess whether the high fee will reduce the number of applicants. “Unfortunately, when it comes to Russian state fees, the Estonian state can't do anything about them. The amount is certainly large, but if someone really has a strong need to renounce their citizenship, I think they can find the money,” Taro said. Polish border guards detained nine people, including two Lithuanian citizens, on Friday on suspicion of smuggling cigarettes from Belarus into Poland using weather balloons. During the operation, authorities seized more than 3,900 cartons of cigarettes with a total value of more than 621,000 Polish zloty (over 143,000 euros). The detained suspects also include three Polish and four Belarusian nationals. The border guard service said the investigation was ongoing to identify other people involved in the criminal activity. So far this year, Polish Border Guard officials have detained 40 people suspected of smuggling cigarettes from Belarus into Poland using weather balloons.

Nearly 80% of Lithuania’s population supports introducing universal military conscription, with most respondents favouring mandatory service for men, according to a survey commissioned by the Universal Defence Association. The poll found that 76.3% of respondents support universal conscription. More than 40% said only men should be drafted, while nearly 19% favoured conscription for both men and women. More than 23% preferred Lithuania’s current partial conscription system, while 14.5% said the country should have a fully professional military without conscripts. More than half of those surveyed said universal conscription should be introduced as soon as possible, while 25% said it should be implemented by 2030. About 12% opposed introducing universal conscription altogether. “The conclusion is that people are ready and expect decision-makers to transition to universal conscription in the coming years,” said Tomas Godliauskas, head of the Universal Defence Association. “We see that public favourability for a faster implementation of the universal conscription model is indeed high.” The survey showed significant support for expanding military service opportunities for women, although views differed on whether their service should be mandatory. More than half of respondents said they would support including women if military service were voluntary and offered more diverse forms. Nearly 13% favoured drafting women under the same rules as men, while 35% opposed conscription for women. Support for universal conscription for women was higher among men, at 55%, than among women, at 48%. “We can say very clearly – the majority of Lithuanian society across all groups and age categories supports universal conscription by 2030,” said Edmundas Jakilaitis, head of the Strong Together civic movement. Respondents said they would be more likely to support universal conscription if alternative forms of service were expanded, including roles in civil defence, medicine and cybersecurity. More than 38% backed such options. Modern military training, including technology and drone operation, was cited by 35% as a factor that would increase support for universal conscription. Nearly 29% said the ability to serve in their home region would make the system more attractive. Fair compensation and equal conditions for different social groups were each cited by more than 23% of respondents, while nearly 21% pointed to preferential treatment in university admissions or during studies. “Universal conscription is compromised by randomness, lotteries, exemptions and various other limits that may appear non-transparent to society,” Jakilaitis said. He argued that a system in which everyone eligible serves, regardless of wealth, social status or public profile, could increase public support. Jakilaitis said Lithuania’s current nine-month mandatory service should remain in place, while additional forms of service should be introduced to allow more people to serve. The survey comes as Lithuania continues to strengthen its armed forces amid heightened security concerns in the region following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Lithuania’s chief of defence, Gen. Raimundas Vaikšnoras, has said the current number of male conscripts is sufficient to meet the military’s needs. He has previously said the armed forces aim to draft “almost everyone willing and able” by 2030, with 7,000 to 8,000 conscripts serving through various forms of military training. About 5,000 conscripts are expected to be called up in 2026. Conscripts currently serve for nine months, although options introduced this year allow service lasting three, six or nine months. Young men ages 18 to 22 are drafted after completing school, with the number expected to increase annually. Some politicians have described the expansion as a step toward universal conscription. President Gitanas Nausėda has said that once Lithuania’s national division is formed, it will be only a matter of time before the country moves to universal conscription. Former Defence Minister Laurynas Kasčiūnas has also said Lithuania is moving toward universal conscription, but that ensuring high-quality military preparation should come first. The survey of 1,501 people was conducted in August by Norstat through telephone and online interviews. Its margin of error was up to 3 percentage points. The findings are due to be presented at the Universal Defence Forum in September.

Relatives have identified two climbers, a Lithuanian and a Belarusian, who died on Mount Korumdu in Kyrgyzstan, local news outlet 24.kg reported Thursday. The victims were identified as 37-year-old Lithuanian citizen Sergej Rubcov and 43-year-old Belarusian citizen Maxim Polianski, according to the Interior Ministry’s department for Osh region. Their bodies are currently at a morgue in Osh and are expected to be repatriated to their home countries. A third member of the group, 60-year-old Belarusian citizen Nikolai Sviridov, remains missing. Polianski, Sviridov and Rubcov began climbing Mount Korumdu in the Trans-Alay Range on August 2. The group was expected to descend to its base camp several days later, but rescuers were unable to establish contact with them at the scheduled time. Kyrgyzstan’s Emergency Situations Ministry and volunteers subsequently launched a search operation. Lithuania’s Embassy in Kazakhstan has been in contact with Rubcov’s relatives in Lithuania, while the embassy and Lithuania’s honorary consul in Kyrgyzstan have been working with Kyrgyz authorities, including rescue services.

Lithuania is considering the possibility of hosting more US troops, but no decision has been made on how many additional service members could be deployed, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Friday. “It is currently at the consideration stage; there are discussions, and we are answering questions,” Kaunas told LRT RADIO. “From the questions, we can see that various options are being considered.” The United States is reviewing its military presence in Europe. More than 1,000 US troops completed a rotation in Lithuania this summer, although some remained in the country. The United States has regularly deployed battalion-size contingents to Lithuania since 2019. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Washington shifted to a continuous rotational deployment of US forces in Lithuania. The reinforced battalions have typically included 1,000 or more troops along with various combat vehicles and equipment. Lithuania has said it is prepared to host up to 1,500 US troops. Kaunas said Lithuania has the infrastructure and capacity to accommodate additional US forces, but final decisions will depend on military planning and NATO leadership. “We should not become attached to a specific number,” Kaunas said. “The fundamental position is that the United States sees Lithuania as one of its most reliable allies and recognises that Lithuania has done all the necessary homework.” “We are reliable allies, the US recognises that, and discussions are taking place at the technical level,” he said. “The final decisions, whatever they may be, will be announced when that can be done.” Darius Jauniškis, Lithuania’s ambassador to NATO, said Vilnius had received positive signals from Washington about maintaining US troops in the country. “The Americans are definitely not pulling back, and I think we can be confident that we will have troops,” Jauniškis said. “They see both the possibility and the need to have them in Lithuania. The question is really about the details and what numbers we will be talking about.” During a visit to NATO headquarters in Brussels on Thursday, US Deputy Defense Secretary Elbridge Colby urged NATO allies to explain how they plan to meet Washington’s demands for greater responsibility for Europe’s defence. Earlier in August, the United States sent European allies a questionnaire asking them to demonstrate how they were progressing toward taking the lead in defending the continent after NATO members agreed to sharply increase defence spending. Jauniškis said the United States had not imposed any additional demands on Lithuania Thursday. He also said efforts by Lithuania and other NATO members to strengthen their defences should not be viewed as competition for US troops. “I don’t see any competition,” Jauniškis said. “We simply need to be concerned about how we will defend ourselves against future Russian aggression. There is no competition here; we just need to work and do our homework.” Lithuania has budgeted 5.38% of GDP, or about 4.8 billion euros, for the military this year. Lithuanian officials have said the share of GDP allocated to defence next year should also be at least 5%.

Europe wants nuclear back but Lithuania is still haunted by ghosts of its atomic past. Victoria Becker reports for Euractiv, partners of LRT English. As nuclear energy experiences a renaissance in Europe, Lithuania is instead dismantling its atomic legacy at Ignalina, one of the world’s most powerful Soviet-era nuclear plants. “For the next few hours, we will travel to the past,” Ina Daukšienė, who works as a senior communications specialist at the plant, told a group of 16 visitors gathered in the entrance hall of Lithuania’s only nuclear power plant. Ignalina, in north-eastern Lithuania near the borders with Belarus and Latvia, began operating its two Soviet-built RBMK-1500 reactors in the 1980s and supplied around 70% of Lithuania’s electricity. But Lithuania’s path into the EU also ended its nuclear era. It shut down the first reactor in 2004 and the second in 2009. Decommissioning, the process of dismantling a nuclear power plant and managing the radioactive waste left behind, has been under way since 2010 and is scheduled to be finalised by 2050. While Europe bets on new nuclear power, with the EU backing small modular reactors and Poland planning its first-ever nuclear power plants, Lithuania is a test case for the costs, waste and technical headaches that can outlast a reactor by decades. Stepping into the nuclear past means passing through a number of turnstiles requiring a code and badge scans, as well as changing clothes and putting on protective gear. Daukšienė, who has worked in the plant’s communications department for 30 years, hands out masks “for later” and clips on her personalised dosimeter – a portable, card-like device that measures radiation exposure. “We used to be around 5000 people working here; now that number stands at about 1500,” she said, walking down a long hallway. Many of them live in the nearby town of Visaginas, dubbed Lithuania’s youngest city, built during the 1970s to house plant workers. From above, the town resembles half a butterfly, Daukšienė said. But the city never expanded to add the butterfly’s second half. Neither did Ignalina’s plans for a third and fourth reactor, which were abandoned in the aftermath of the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, just three years after the site began operations. Decommissioning is now entering its most difficult phase: dismantling the reactor cores, something never before attempted on this type of reactor. Reaching the reactor hall means following a 600-metre windowless corridor and climbing an ageing stairwell with doors of varying heights. Standing next to the reactor, Daukšienė holds up a replica of a uranium fuel pellet, about the size of two dice. “This can produce energy equivalent to 1000 tonnes of coal,” she explained. The uranium fuel was packed into rods, grouped into fuel assemblies, and inserted into channels running through the reactor core. “There are more than 2,000 channels inside the reactor,” Daukšienė said. “Most of them, 1,661, contained nuclear fuel. The others were used for control, protection and cooling.” As part of the dismantling, workers have already removed the fuel from both the reactor and the cooling pools and moved it to secure storage nearby. But removing the fuel, she adds, does not mean the reactor itself is no longer radioactive. Decades of operation have left parts of the reactor structure and equipment contaminated or radioactive through radiation exposure. That is why much of the work on the core will have to be carried out remotely, using robotic equipment to cut, handle and remove radioactive material. The EU covers around 86% of the eligible decommissioning costs of the Ignalina power plant, while Lithuania and other sources, such as donors or international bodies, cover the rest. Leaving the reactor hall, the group enters the control room. Thousands of buttons, gauges and screens still line the walls, marked with the Russian alphabet. “Each reactor unit has its own control room,” Daukšienė said, adding that only a few people had access to it. When the plant was still operating, five people would monitor the panel at all times. Today, only one person remains on duty. “The control room operators were the only ones in the entire power plant who had food brought to them because they could not leave the control room to go to the canteen. They could even work out, ” she said, pointing to two old-fashioned gym machines in the corner of the room and laughing. So far, around 46% of the plant has been taken apart – more than 83,000 tonnes of the 180,000 tonnes of equipment and materials. Time to put on the masks, Daukšienė said, as the long turbine hall opens up. It resembles a gigantic scrap yard where workers cut apart metals and other materials, decontaminate, clean and assess them for reuse. Altra, the state-owned company overseeing the decommissioning, said that 78% of dismantled equipment and as much as 94% of reinforced concrete have been “released from radiation control and can be transferred to the secondary raw materials market”. “Some of the material is sold at auction or gets recycled,” she said. The dismantled parts which cannot be released are treated as radioactive waste. A site for a deep geological repository will be sought for spent nuclear fuel and long-lived radioactive waste. Other European countries, including France, Sweden and Germany, are also looking for permanent storage options, awaiting licensing, or have started building repositories. In early August, Finland’s Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority deemed the country’s deep repository built into granite safe for operation. This marks the first time that a final disposal facility for spent nuclear fuel has entered the operating licence phase. Daukšienė leads the group back to the changing room, where they remove protective clothing, wash their hands, and each visitor steps onto a radiation monitor, waiting for the screen to flash “clean”. Thousands lost mobile communications after a major storm. Experts say the biggest lesson may have little to do with mobile networks themselves – and much more to do with the electricity grid. The storm that swept across Lithuania at the weekend did more than knock down trees and cut power. For tens of thousands of people, it also cut one of the most important links to the outside world: their mobile phone connection. Some residents were left without electricity or water. Fallen trees blocked roads and, in some places, people could not leave their homes. With mobile networks also disrupted, contacting relatives, emergency services or anyone else became difficult or impossible. The disruption has raised a broader question for Lithuania, a country on NATO’s eastern flank and increasingly exposed to both extreme weather and security threats: how long would the country’s communications networks remain operational during a major emergency? Telecoms operators reported that around 66,000 customers were affected by the storm. By Wednesday, roughly 50 mobile base stations operated by each major provider were still out of service. The worst disruption was recorded in northern, central and southern parts of the country. But experts say the storm did not reveal a fundamental failure of Lithuania’s mobile network. Instead, it highlighted how dependent communications are on another critical system: the electricity grid. Lithuania has around 6,000 mobile base stations – the towers and other sites that connect mobile phones to the wider network. Around 800 stations were temporarily out of service at the height of the storm. That sounds significant, but experts point out that most were in relatively remote areas. Artūras Medeišis, a telecommunications specialist with three decades of experience and dean of the Faculty of Electronics at Vilnius Gediminas Technical University, said only around 2% of Lithuania’s population was directly affected by the mobile outages. He described the network’s performance as broadly satisfactory, noting that the number of affected users was relatively small compared with the number of base stations that lost service. Vitas Grimaila, a researcher at Kaunas University of Technology made a similar assessment. “The critical elements and nodes of the mobile network held up,” he said. The key point, Grimaila added, was that the core or “backbone” of each operator’s network continued to function. The stations that failed were largely part of the access network rather than the critical core infrastructure. That distinction matters. It meant Lithuania’s telecommunications system was not brought down as a whole, even though some communities lost mobile coverage for several days. According to experts and telecoms operators, the main reason mobile services failed was not physical damage to the communications equipment. Mobile base stations have backup batteries designed to keep them running when the power goes out. Depending on the site, those batteries can maintain services for between two and 12 hours. But the storm caused power outages that lasted much longer. Once the batteries ran out, individual base stations shut down. Nearby stations that still had electricity then had to handle more users. Some became overloaded, while others were too far away to provide adequate coverage. Repair teams also faced another problem: they had difficulty reaching damaged infrastructure because roads were blocked by fallen trees or otherwise impassable. According to Modestas Ropė, director of next-generation networks at Bitė Lietuva, the mobile network proved considerably more resilient than the electricity network during the storm. Around 200,000 people lost electricity, compared with roughly four times fewer people experiencing mobile communications problems. But that does not mean there is nothing to improve. For people who live in rural areas, or who happen to be in a location where mobile coverage is already weak, losing a single nearby base station can make a major difference. And in an emergency, that can become a serious problem. Should Lithuania build more mobile towers? The storm has also reignited a debate about where Lithuania should focus its investment. One priority is improving mobile coverage in so-called “white spots” – areas where reliable mobile service is still unavailable under normal conditions. Another is making existing infrastructure more resistant to major disruptions. Medeišis says that having more base stations in an area reduces the risk that a single power failure will cut off a large number of people. Grimaila makes a similar argument: Lithuania should eliminate coverage gaps before focusing more heavily on strengthening the resilience and quality of the existing network. “If a major incident occurred in an area that was a so-called white spot and residents were unable to call the emergency services, people would then be asking whether network coverage was being expanded too slowly,” Grimaila said. At the same time, simply building more towers is not enough. The network needs to be able to keep operating when electricity, roads or other infrastructure fail. One obvious solution would be to give every mobile base station its own permanent generator. But installing a generator at each of around 6,000 base stations in Lithuania, many of which are located on rooftops, water towers or other hardly accessible sites, would be impractical and extremely expensive, since installing and maintaining a diesel generator in each location would be very difficult. Furthermore, a typical generator can consume up to 10 litres of fuel an hour. A 500-litre tank would therefore last for roughly 48 hours. During the recent storm, more than 130 base stations operated by each provider were without electricity for much longer than that. That could mean having to deliver hundreds of litres of fuel to hundreds of locations – while roads are blocked and repair crews are already stretched. As a resu

Some of the artworks that make up Kaunas’ renowned Courtyard Gallery could disappear under a new layer of plaster and paint as renovation work begins on the building that houses them. The gallery, located on Ožeškienės Street in central Kaunas, was launched 14 years ago by artist Vytenis Jakas. Its murals tell the story of the Jewish community that lived in the courtyard before World War Two. Scaffolding now surrounds one of the gallery’s walls as preparations begin to renovate the building. Under the current plan, the murals will be covered. “This is a heritage site that cannot be destroyed. This would be outright vandalism,” Jakas said. The dispute escalated even before renovation work began. Police are investigating possible vandalism after witnesses reported seeing a resident of the building damaging the artworks with a hammer. Kaunas resident Darius Pečiulionis said he saw a man striking the wall with a chisel and hammer. “I approached him and asked, ‘Why did you do that?’ He said in broken Lithuanian, ‘I am a resident. I don’t like this. The renovation has to be done here,’” Pečiulionis said. One of the damaged features was a QR code that provided information about the history depicted in the artwork in Lithuanian and English, Jakas said. The Courtyard Gallery is one of Kaunas’ most visited attractions. Tour guide Nomeda Balasevičiūtė said visitors are often struck by the artwork. “They are amazed. Everyone falls silent when they walk through here. They say they take photos, even people who don’t usually take photos in this courtyard,” she said. Residents may be bothered by constant tourist flows taking snapshots, but numerous signs warn them to be quiet and respect people’s right to peace. By now, most of the locals have become accustomed to tourists visiting the courtyard and viewing the artworks. Jakas says he has proposed a solution that would allow the renovation to proceed while preserving the murals. He offered to repair the lower section of the wall with murals himself, at no cost to the building's residents. “I want to repair the entire lower part myself. We wouldn't take a single euro from them; they would save money,” he said. The building is located in a cultural heritage zone, and the Kaunas municipality is helping finance part of the renovation. But the artworks on the building’s wall were never formally authorised, and the owners did not give their consent for them to be installed. That leaves municipal officials with limited legal means to prevent their removal. “We are all hostages of this situation. The paintings were installed without asking anyone, on the artist's initiative, so somehow we don’t have the instruments to protect them,” said Saulius Rimas, head of the Kaunas municipality's Heritage Protection Division. At the same time, the municipality has acknowledged the value of the artworks. “We have said that we see the meaning in these artworks. They are not bad,” Rimas said. The municipality and the building’s administrator have suggested alternatives that would allow both the facade to be renovated and the artworks to be preserved. But the building’s owners have so far rejected them. Two-thirds of the 13 owners have voted to renovate the entire wall, according to the building administrator. “If there were other decisions, there would be other solutions. As things stand today, the solution is to repair the building’s facade without preserving the art installations,” said Marijus Zaborskas, head of Kaunas Butų Ūkis, the building administrator. The renovation plan could still be changed if the residents approve an alternative, Zaborskas said. But time is running short: Work on the building’s facade and roof is scheduled to be completed in September.

Lithuania on Monday marks the 33rd anniversary of the withdrawal of Soviet troops from its territory, a milestone that completed the departure of the former occupying forces following the restoration of the country’s independence. The commemoration in Vilnius includes a march by the Lithuanian Armed Forces Orchestra, the Honour Guard Company and soldiers from Cathedral Square along Gedimino Avenue to Lukiškių Square. A flag-raising ceremony and orchestral concert will follow at the square. At Vilnius railway station, an installation titled Towards Unconditional Freedom will open, featuring archival photographs, texts about Freedom Day and posters created by members of the public. The opening will be followed by a discussion titled Freedom Talks. Lithuania declared its independence on March 11, 1990. At the time, about five divisions of the Soviet occupying army remained stationed in the country, comprising approximately 34,600 troops, 1,000 tanks, about 180 aircraft and 1,901 armoured vehicles. Negotiations on the withdrawal of Soviet forces began after Lithuania declared independence. The last military echelon of the Russian army left Lithuania on August 31, 1993, at 23:46, passing through the Kena railway station. The withdrawal marked the end of the Soviet and Russian military presence in Lithuania and is commemorated annually as Freedom Day.

What Vasily Mitrokhin brought to Vilnius in 1992 was never meant to leave the KGB’s most secret archives. ‘He is one of the most important spies of the Cold War, because he revealed to the world what the KGB had been up to everywhere,’ in an interview with LRT.lt says British journalist and writer Gordon Corera. Understanding this solitary man with a difficult personality, who, for many years, kept his dangerous mission hidden even from his family, is a complex task. However, in ‘The Spy in the Archive’, British journalist and writer Gordon Corera takes on this challenge. Drawing on various sources and people who knew Mitrokhin personally, the author unravels the extraordinary personality of a man who made it his life’s mission to kill the Soviet Committee for State Security, better known as the KGB. Born in 1922 in Yurasovo, Ryazan Oblast, Mitrokhin felt happiest in the Russian countryside, where he could tend his garden, fish, and hunt. That is why, as Corera notes, it was perhaps only by chance that, in the early years of the Cold War, he was recruited by the KGB as a foreign intelligence officer. However, several failed operations soon revealed that Mitrokhin was not a natural spy. A reserved and introverted man, he found it difficult to navigate different social circles, and he was ultimately exiled to the place that best suited his personality: the archives. According to the book’s author, this decision by the KGB sowed a seed of resentment within him. Over the years, as he gained a deeper understanding of the atrocities committed by Soviet institutions, this resentment grew into an obsession that came to dominate his thoughts. Corera believes that apart from personal bitterness, two things in particular fueled his desire to destroy the KGB. First and foremost, the archivist was shaken by the realization of just how extensively the KGB had acted against the Russians themselves – dissidents, critics of the regime and even allies whom they suspected of posing a threat to the Communist Party’s rule. But the turning point for him was the brutal suppression of the Prague Spring in 1968. It was then that his – and those of others within the system – hopes that communism might still be reformed proved to be in vain. ‘He definitely saw himself as a patriot, not as a traitor to his country. He really did see his enemy as like a creature, a beast. It sounds strange, but he saw it as a beast with three heads: one was the KGB, another was the Communist Party, and third was the nomenclature, the elite, – Corera explains. – He saw this creature like a parasite or kind of awful thing which had occupied his country. And he saw himself like a peasant hero in a folk story who was going to battle this beast and try to defeat it.’ The opportunity arose four years after the events in Prague. In 1972, the KGB decided to move their headquarters from the Lubyanka – menacing building in the center of Moscow – to a new building in Yasenevo. Mitrokhin, who until then had had access to only a part of the archives, was assigned an unexpected task – to oversee the relocation of all KGB documents. This gave him access to all the carefully guarded secrets dating back as far as 1918. ‘So he takes a great risk by writing it down on tiny bits of paper, stuffing it in his shoe and walking out of KGB headquarters and then writing it up at home in his dacha on the weekend. He does this for years without even a clear plan of what he's going to do with it,’ the book author notes. The archivist transcribed thousands of documents by hand, revealing the scope of Soviet intelligence operations around the world during the Cold War. Possessing an exceptional memory, he compiled data on the activities of Soviet spies in the West, Africa, India, Latin America, and Asia; he gathered information on the legendary illegals – Soviet spies living in other countries under stolen identities. The archive he compiled revealed how the Soviet Union used violence, sabotage, influence and interference operations to secure its control and advance the regime’s ambitions. For twelve years, Mitrokhin secretly copied material from the KGB archives, continuing this work until his retirement. He then organized the documents at his dacha and waited for an opportunity to reveal – first to the Russian people and then to the wider world – what the KGB had long kept hidden. That opportunity came at a moment of historic upheaval: the collapse of the Soviet Union. Determined to expose the truth, the former archivist packed a suitcase with clothes and food, concealing a selection of documents beneath them, and set out to offer the material to Western intelligence agencies. This is where Lithuania finds itself at the center of this incredible story. The collapse of the Soviet Union opened up the Baltic states, to which the West quickly sent its diplomats. Some embassies initially operated out of hotel rooms, and Soviet spies, officials, and even imposters, who claimed to have valuable information, began flooding in, looking for opportunities. ‘I'm sure it was very exciting in many ways for people in Lithuania, but also very productive for British intelligence and others, because suddenly here is this new place, which had once been not just part of the Eastern Bloc, but part of the Soviet Union, which they can access and talk to people and meet people in, – says Corera. – In espionage terms, it's a very interesting time and place in this period in the 90s.’ In 1992, Mitrokhin came up with a plan to hand over the archive materials to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) through the U.S. Embassy, making several attempts to do so in both Riga and Vilnius. However, the Americans were skeptical of the shabby dressed elderly man who appeared with a collection of handwritten documents and dismissed him. Only later U.S. intelligence finally realise the extraordinary value of his archive. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) eventually described Mitrokhin’s coll

Leaders of Lithuania’s ruling parties said Monday they had yet to determine the exact military budget for next year but pledged to keep defence spending at or above 5% of GDP. Lithuania allocated 5.38% of GDP to defence in this year’s budget, one of the highest shares among NATO members. “Our defence and our defence funding will allow us to remain in the five percent club. What the exact number will be, and what will follow the decimal point, cannot be answered at this time,” Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told reporters after a government meeting with leaders of the two junior coalition partners: Democrats “For Lithuania” and the Farmers and Greens Union. Virginijus Sinkevičius, leader of the Democrats “For Lithuania”, said the country must maintain defence spending of at least 5% of GDP but stopped short of saying whether the figure should be higher. “What follows the decimal point can be decided once we have the full budget picture,” he said. “The priority must remain staying in the 5% club, and any ‘race after the decimal point’ must primarily be linked to the needs of the military and ongoing projects.” Chief of Defence Raimundas Vaikšnoras said earlier this month that maintaining the current pace of military capability development would require the same or higher levels of funding in next year’s budget. Aurelijus Veryga, chairman of the Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union, said 5% of GDP would be sufficient given Lithuania’s economic growth. “I believe 5% is a truly sufficient commitment,” Veryga said. “Let’s keep in mind that as gross domestic product grows, the figures do not decrease in absolute terms.” Lithuania has sharply increased military spending in response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and growing security concerns in the region. The country borders Russia’s Kaliningrad region and Belarus, a close Russian ally. The government has made strengthening national defence and military capabilities a key budget priority, including plans to expand the armed forces and acquire additional military equipment.

Lithuania’s security situation has not changed following a visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, President Gitanas Nausėda said Monday, adding that he hoped the talks would help reduce tensions in the region. US media reported last week that Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow for meetings with Russian officials. The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported that his goal was to persuade Russia not to attack NATO members, citing US intelligence assessments that Moscow could seek to test the alliance. The CIA declined to comment on the trip. Nausėda told reporters Monday that Lithuania had no reason to be concerned about the visit. “Our allies are informing all of us about the content of the conversation, and we were also informed that the meeting in Moscow would take place,” Nausėda said. He added that Lithuania was respecting Washington’s decision not to publicly disclose details of the meeting. “At this moment, I can say that the meeting addressed the goals that had been set. The meeting was aimed at reducing tensions in the region. I very much hope that this message reached the Kremlin regime at the right time,” he said. Nausėda said the visit did not change Lithuania’s preparations for potential threats. “I generally think that a little too much attention is being paid to this meeting,” he said. The president acknowledged that the meeting was significant and that such contacts were rare, but said it had not altered the broader security situation. “The overall security situation is tense, and nobody intends to deny that. Has it increased dramatically recently? I would disagree with that,” Nausėda said. He said the situation had remained tense since Ukraine started striking targets deep inside Russian territory. “That, in a sense, is pushing the Kremlin regime into a corner,” Nausėda said. “As you know, a person – or any actor – cornered can always try to strike back and create an additional threat.” “That is what NATO and the United States are for: so that together we can first and foremost prevent that threat,” he said.

Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry on Monday reiterated its warning against travel to Belarus after a Lithuanian travel organiser was reportedly sentenced to prison there on an extremism charge. Independent Belarusian news outlet Nasha Niva reported Sunday that 27-year-old Lithuanian citizen Deividas Stanulevičius was convicted of inciting people to engage in extremist activities after being detained by Belarusian authorities at the border. The details of the charges have not been made public, as is common in Belarus in politically related criminal cases, according to the news outlet. Media reports say Stanulevičius had organised tourist trips in recent years, including visits to the part of the Chernobyl exclusion zone controlled by Belarus. He last advertised such a trip in late February, saying another excursion was planned for March 6. He is believed to have been detained shortly afterward. “The Embassy of the Republic of Lithuania in Belarus was informed about the detention of a Lithuanian citizen,” the Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Monday afternoon. The ministry said it could not provide information about specific individuals or the circumstances of an incident without their consent, citing privacy considerations. “The Foreign Ministry once again strongly recommends that Lithuanian citizens do not travel to the Republic of Belarus, and those who are currently there should leave immediately,” it said. The ministry also warned that consular assistance in countries assigned the highest travel-risk level may be available only to a very limited extent or not at all.

Latvia and Estonia issued airspace warnings overnight after drones linked to Russia’s war against Ukraine approached or entered their airspace, prompting NATO fighter jets to scramble, authorities said Tuesday. A warning about a potential threat in Latvian airspace was issued overnight in the Alūksne municipality in northeastern Latvia. Latvia’s National Armed Forces said a potential threat had been detected over the municipality, prompting the NATO Baltic air-policing mission to scramble fighter jets. Residents of the area were advised to remain indoors, follow the “two-wall principle” by putting two walls between themselves and the potential threat, and close windows and doors. They were told to call the emergency number 112 if they spotted a low-flying, suspicious or dangerous object. The warning was lifted at 04:17 in the morning. About 90 minutes earlier, a lower-level yellow warning over a potential airspace threat had been issued in Latvia’s Ludza municipality. It was later cancelled. The incidents come after repeated airspace warnings in Latvia’s Latgale and Vidzeme regions this summer. Foreign drones have also crashed and exploded in Latvia, with NATO fighter jets shooting down some of them. The incidents were believed to involve drones used in the Russia-Ukraine war that approached or entered Latvian airspace. In neighbouring Estonia, Russian-launched drones briefly approached the town of Narva and one crossed into Estonian airspace in the country’s southeast, according to Estonian public broadcaster ERR. Estonian Air Force commander Brig. Gen. Riivo Valge said about 10 drones were detected near the border at around 02:00 local time as Ukraine was carrying out a large-scale drone attack against Russia. At about 03:00, one drone turned toward Narva, prompting authorities to issue a public warning and activate ground-based air defences. Fighter jets subsequently took off from Amari Air Base. The drone later turned back toward Russia and did not enter Estonian airspace. About 30 minutes later, another drone crossed into southeastern Estonia and flew for a time in the border area, Valge said. Its behaviour was unpredictable, and more drones were detected just across the border in Russia. The drone eventually left Estonian airspace without crashing, and the Estonian fighter jets did not have to open fire, Valge said. The warning was lifted after the situation across the border calmed around 05:00. Valge said the situation was calm Tuesday and urged Estonians to focus on the start of the school year.

Russia continues to devastate Ukraine’s cultural heritage. Attacks on the book market, already under threat from the war, have intensified recently – over the summer, a third of Ukrainian publishers’ annual output, including a large proportion of textbooks, was destroyed in warehouses or printing works. Industry representatives are warning of a collapse of the sector, which would deprive Ukraine of the right to speak with its own voice. “The whole world should know what has happened here,” said Viktor Kruhlov, director of the Ranok publishing house, which specialises in children’s and educational literature, to RFI. The Russians attacked the company’s largest warehouse in Kharkiv on August 1. “It was a deliberately planned attack on the bookshop,” noted Kruhlov, according to Reuters. “Two explosions followed one after the other, a few minutes apart. There were about fifty employees on the premises at the time, and it is a miracle that no one died. Everything melted as a result of the heat following both explosions,” RFI quoted him as saying. It was the biggest blow to the Ukrainian publishing industry since the start of the war. In a 10,000-square-metre warehouse, where not only Ranok but also the KnyhoLand chain stored books, eight million books were destroyed in the fire caused by the attack. Around a million of these were textbooks; Ranok prints roughly a third of the total number of these in Ukraine. Although the company has other warehouses, the one in Kharkiv was the largest and housed the majority of its output. “We learnt that during the Second World War, the Nazis burnt thousands of books. Now the Russians are routinely destroying millions of Ukrainian books. It is a deliberate strategy to undermine Ukrainian culture and identity, because Russia refuses to accept a prosperous Ukraine,” added Kruhlov. Russia is systematically targeting the Ukrainian publishing industry. It carried out its first such attacks as early as spring 2022, specifically in Kharkiv. Further attacks followed, which intensified significantly in 2024. In May of that year, Moscow destroyed the Faktor-Druk printing works in Kharkiv, killing seven workers who were printing children’s books. The facility produced around a third of all books in Ukraine, according to the Ukrainian Publishers’ Association. Last year, Russia extended its strikes to include warehouses in Kyiv and Dnipro, and its attacks on Ukrainian books reached their peak this summer. In July, it struck, amongst other targets, a warehouse belonging to the BookChef publishing house, destroying 800,000 copies – the majority of its stock. In the same month, it also destroyed two other warehouses, the office of a publishing house and a printing works in the capital. The attack on Ranok in Kharkiv in early August was followed by further strikes; for example, in the middle of the month in Kyiv, several warehouses belonging to various companies were targeted once again, including BookChef’s backup warehouse, where 100,000 copies were reduced to ashes. The Počajna open-air book market in Kyiv was also targeted. A third of the annual output was destroyed by fire The attacks mentioned above are among the largest, but by no means an exhaustive list. The attacks over the last two months have caused losses to dozens of publishing houses and bookshops – whether through direct destruction or indirect consequences. In July, the Russians destroyed 1.5 million copies and in August ten million, which represents roughly a third of Ukraine’s annual book production, reported Ukrayinska Pravda (UP). The Ukrainian Publishers’ Association reports as many as thirteen million books destroyed over the summer and direct losses amounting to 1.2 billion hryvnias (roughly six hundred million korunas) – though, according to the association, the actual losses are significantly higher. The Ukrainian Book Institute estimates them to be in the billions of hryvnias. The Ukrainian book market as a whole is, however, relatively small; according to the publishers’ association, its annual turnover is around seven to eight billion hryvnias, which is comparable to the turnover of a small shopping centre. Hundreds of schools have also been affected, as nine per cent of new textbooks were destroyed shortly before the start of the school term. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Education, this amounts to more than 1.2 million copies. In the case of some subjects, Russia has even destroyed the entire print run for the 2026–2027 academic year, according to Serhiy Babak, chair of the parliamentary committee on education, as reported by UP. As well as book warehouses, printing works, bookshops and publishers’ offices, Moscow is also destroying Ukrainian libraries. The Ukrainian Ministry of Culture reports that, since the start of full-scale war, 228 libraries have been destroyed and 678 damaged as a result of Russian attacks. The actual damage, however, is likely to be greater, as the figures do not include damage in the occupied territories. Attacks on libraries and book publishing in general form part of a wider Russian campaign aimed at destroying Ukrainian monuments and cultural heritage. The Ukrainian Ministry of Culture has recorded – in the unoccupied territories alone – thousands of such cases. Ukrainian Minister of Education Andriy Butenko described the Russian attacks on bookshops and printing houses as an attempt to destroy the Ukrainian language, history and memory, “everything from which our children’s identity grows”. Similarly, Oleksandra Matviychuk, director of the human rights organisation Centre for Civil Liberties, which was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022, described the destruction of Ukrainian books as “part of Russia’s broader genocidal policy”. “We know from history that the burning of libraries has accompanied genocides for centuries – as a means of erasing someone else’s identity.
