Lithuania’s annual quota for employing foreign workers has already been exhausted, prompting business groups to call for changes to the system, while the government says there is no reason to increase the quota next year and may consider reducing it. Lithuania set this year’s quota at 24,700 foreign workers, but business representatives say it was exceeded in July. Social Security and Labour Minister Inga Ruginienė said, however, that only about 10,000 new workers actually entered Lithuania this year, suggesting the quota system may be allowing the same worker to account for multiple quota places. “About 10,000 new workers have actually entered this year, so we need to look at why businesses have already run out of the quota,” Ruginienė said. “Perhaps we need some adjustments. If we fixed this system, we would see that a much smaller quota would be needed next year.” The International Transport and Logistics Alliance said reducing the quota would hurt not only the transport sector but the wider economy. About 80,000 third-country nationals work in the sector and pay more than 700 million euros in taxes annually through Lithuania’s State Tax Inspectorate and Social Insurance Fund, according to alliance head Povilas Drižas. “If it is not possible to employ at least another 5,000 to 6,000 workers, we can calculate that the state will again lose about 40 million euros in tax revenue,” Drižas said. Some workers are already being employed through companies established abroad, he insisted, potentially reducing Lithuania’s tax revenue further if the quota is cut. The Business Confederation has urged the government to review the quota, arguing that the current system does not reflect labour market needs and that existing legislation allows a higher quota than the one set this year. “There is room to increase the quota,” said Ineta Rizgelė, the confederation’s director general. She argued businesses facing higher taxes and other economic pressures needed government support as the quota had been exhausted unusually early. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas opposes an increase, arguing that businesses should make greater use of Lithuania’s domestic workforce. “Unskilled labour from third countries is a form of social dumping,” Katelynas said, arguing that some employers prefer foreign workers because they can pay lower wages. The quota does not apply to workers whose employers pay them more than 1,750 euros net per month, he said, questioning whether some companies are addressing genuine labour shortages or simply seeking cheaper workers. Rita Karavaitienė, head of communications at the Employment Service, said Lithuania nonetheless faces significant labour shortages because of its aging population and demographic trends. More than 168,000 third-country nationals currently work in Lithuania. About half are employed in transport, one-fifth in construction and one-tenth in manufacturing. Ukrainians and Belarusians make up the largest groups, followed by citizens of Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and India. The number of workers arriving from the Philippines is growing particularly rapidly. About 80% of third-country nationals working in Lithuania are classified as medium-skilled workers.

Russia has no reason, plans or need to attack NATO countries, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko said Tuesday, specifically referring to the Baltic states. “Why should Russia attack NATO, why? The Soviet Union recognised the independence of the Baltic states. And they left peacefully. Why attack them now?” Grushko told the Interfax news agency on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum. He was responding to statements by European officials about possible Russian plans to attack a NATO member. “There is no reason and no plans, none at all, to attack,” Grushko insisted. Western and Baltic officials and intelligence agencies have warned that Moscow could be considering military action against NATO countries. The Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – joined the alliance in 2004. The statements come amid heightened security concerns across the Baltic region following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Baltic officials have repeatedly insisted that Russia poses a long-term security threat to NATO’s eastern flank. Asked whether EU representatives had approached Moscow to discuss their concerns, Grushko said that “there is no real sentiment or desire on the part of Europeans that would be politically expressed as a political desire”, according to Interfax.

Lithuania’s system for controlling exports of high-priority goods to third countries remains stalled a year after it was proposed, as a Belarusian investigative centre has published new evidence that Teltonika devices continue to be traded in Russia. The issue dates back to late 2024, when Lithuania introduced restrictions on the export by air to most third countries of telemetry equipment, internet routers and other goods with potential dual-use applications. The measure was introduced by the conservative government of Prime Minister Ingrida Šimonytė. Teltonika founder Arvydas Paukštys publicly criticised the rules. The subsequent social democratic government of Prime Minister Gintautas Paluckas amended them in January 2025 and only land exports of dual-use goods to third countries remained restricted. Exporters were also required to include clauses prohibiting the re-export of goods to Russia in contracts with buyers and provide customs authorities with written confirmation that recipients had been informed about possible physical inspections. The latest allegations concern a supply chain traced by the Belarus Investigative Center (BIC), an independent research organization operating in exile, in cooperation with the Lithuanian investigative journalism centre Siena. The BIC said Western-made products continue to reach Russia and Belarus despite European Union restrictions. It traced one supply route involving GPS tracking devices made by the Lithuanian technology group Teltonika. According to the investigation, Russian company Laboratoriya Interneta Veshchei (Laboratory of Internet of Things) supplied Teltonika equipment to Belarusian company BelTransSputnik, partly sourcing the products through Hong Kong-based Sinalex. BelTransSputnik then sold Teltonika tracking devices to Russian company Evrosvyaz. The investigation examined trade data from February 2023 through March 2025 and said BelTransSputnik sold 345 Teltonika GPS controllers and vehicle trackers worth more than USD 100,000. In a comment to LRT.lt, Teltonika said it does not tolerate violations of sanctions or export controls and has ended commercial relationships with customers in Russia and Belarus. The company also said it had responded to the BIC’s questions before publication and offered to review the documents underlying the report’s conclusions, which it said contained factual inaccuracies and assumptions. Teltonika said no follow-up request or opportunity to review the documents was provided. The controversy comes as Lithuania’s planned system for tighter control of high-priority exports remains unresolved. The Economy and Innovation Ministry was tasked last year with assessing exported goods and determining which should be subject to licensing. It initially proposed an exporter self-declaration system instead of licensing all high-priority goods. A new proposal registered in February would establish a system under which commissions assess exporters’ applications and recommend whether licenses should be required for specific goods. The proposal has drawn objections from several institutions. The Defence Ministry and State Security Department called for a simpler system with a single commission, while the Lithuanian Business Confederation opposed the new national controls as excessive and disproportionate. The Economy and Innovation Ministry said in late June that the legislation should be finalised within two weeks after consultation with government institutions and the public. However, the cabinet had not considered the proposal as of Tuesday. The ministry estimates licensing all conventional high-priority goods would cost the state about 5 million euros annually. Its proposed system would cost about 60,000 euros per year, mainly for two additional positions.

The Seimas board on Wednesday rejected a request by lawmakers Ignas Vėgėlė and Rimas Jonas Jankūnas to travel to Brussels for meetings with Chinese representatives. “I believe there is a general consensus to reject this trip as an official mission,” Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas said, expressing the board’s position. News portal Delfi.lt reported in early August that six lawmakers belonging to a temporary parliamentary group called “For the Normalisation of Diplomatic Relations with China to the Level of European Union Member States” planned to visit Brussels in early September to meet officials from China’s Mission to the European Union. Vėgėlė and Jankūnas had requested that half of their travel expenses be covered through official mission funding, with the remainder paid from parliamentary funds. Rasa Budbergytė, a member of the Seimas board, said the proposed trip should first be coordinated with the parliamentary Committee on Foreign Affairs and the Foreign Ministry. Olekas said he could not confirm whether such coordination had taken place. “I believe this is a move against Lithuania’s interests,” Conservative lawmaker Radvilė Morkūnaitė-Mikulėnienė said. The parliamentary group was established in December with the stated aim of identifying and removing obstacles to restoring diplomatic relations with Beijing. Its goal is to bring Lithuania-China relations back to a level comparable with those maintained by most European Union member states. Members of Lithuania’s ruling coalition have recently stepped up calls for normalising relations with China, although the efforts have so far produced few results. After meeting with Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys in early August, Olekas said he saw progress on the issue. Lithuania’s relations with China deteriorated sharply in 2021 after Vilnius allowed Taiwan to open a representative office under its own name. Beijing viewed the decision as a violation of its “One China” policy and subsequently downgraded diplomatic relations with Lithuania.

Poland will extend border controls on its borders with Lithuania and Germany for another six months, through April 2, 2027, the Interior Ministry said. The controls were reinstated in July 2025 as part of efforts to curb irregular migration within the visa-free Schengen area. The current extension is due to expire October 1. The Interior Ministry said the decision was prompted by the continued migration route through Belarus and the Baltic states. Poland is seeking to prevent secondary irregular migration, in which people who enter the European Union from Belarus travel through Lithuania into Poland. According to the ministry, since the controls were introduced, nearly 2,300 people have been denied entry, more than 1,300 have been returned under readmission procedures, and 130 people have been detained on suspicion of helping others cross the border illegally. Under Schengen rules, an EU member state may temporarily reintroduce controls at its internal borders when there is a foreseeable and serious threat to public order or internal security. Such controls may initially be imposed for up to six months. If the threat persists, controls can be extended for additional periods of up to six months, for a maximum of two years in total. Poland has not ruled out lifting the controls earlier if the migration situation improves.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Wednesday he expects Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys to return from an upcoming visit to Washington with “good news” about the continued deployment of US troops in Lithuania. “Certain decisions have apparently already been made, but their announcement is being held until coordinated with our partners,” Sinkevičius told the radio Žinių Radijas. “I believe those answers should be positive.” Budrys is due to travel to the United States in September for talks with a “very substantial agenda”, the prime minister said, without specifying the dates of the visit. Sinkevičius said Lithuania had been informed about decisions concerning the US military presence but would not comment on behalf of Washington before the details are coordinated with allies. The United States is reviewing its military presence in Europe as Washington seeks greater contributions from European allies to the continent’s defence. More than 1,000 US troops completed their latest rotation in Lithuania over the summer, although some American forces remain in the country. Lithuania’s Ambassador to NATO Darius Jauniškis said last week that Vilnius had received positive signals from Washington about maintaining a US troop presence in Lithuania. US battalions have rotated through Lithuania regularly since 2019. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the United States shifted its forces in Lithuania to a continuous rotational deployment, strengthening NATO’s eastern flank.

As Lithuania invests in tanks, the debate is often framed as a simple choice: would the money be better spent on drones? But experts say the bigger question is whether Lithuania is adapting quickly enough to the technological changes transforming modern warfare. Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the former commander-in-chief of Ukraine's armed forces, wrote in 2023, comparing the war in Ukraine to the stalemate in the First World War, when new technology met outdated doctrine. Artūras Plokšto, a lecturer at the Military Academy of Lithuania, made a similar comparison during a “Būtent” discussion, Tanks or drones?. “In the 1904 Russo-Japanese War, we saw machine guns, trenches, howitzers and radio communications. In Europe, the great generals said there are some ‘savages’ fighting there, things will be different for us, and our cavalry will solve the whole thing by Christmas. “Then the First World War began, and it turned out it was not funny at all. Eleven million soldiers and 13 million civilians were killed,” he said. For years, the growing use of drones was sometimes dismissed by Lithuanian officers as a feature of less-developed militaries, particularly in Ukraine. That view is now harder to sustain. Drones are changing warfare around the world – Iran has used relatively cheap drones to strike expensive US bases and infrastructure. In Lebanon, Iran-backed groups have used FPV drones to inflict damage on the Israeli military. “Israel saw itself for a long time as the most technologically advanced military in the world and perhaps became a little complacent,” Plokšto said. “When people, including lieutenant colonels, began being killed, there was a scandal: why don't we have anything to stop it?” “Turns out, they had written everything down and carried out the studies, but hardly anyone responded. The situation is clearly similar here in Lithuania, but the response is too slow,” he said. Ernestas, a Lithuanian volunteer serving in Ukraine as both an infantryman and a drone pilot, also shared his experience from the frontline. “The level of the Lithuanian military has certainly improved. [...] But at squad and platoon level, the understanding is still simply a ‘meat grinder’,” he said. “I don't know what new doctrine is being developed by the Lithuanian Armed Forces, but the basic understanding is this: you simply cannot have large numbers of people and equipment in a forest or field because of the obvious threat from drones. “All those nice pictures from Lithuanian military exercises are just nice pictures. They do not reflect modern warfare,” he added. Plokšto again pointed to the First World War as a warning. “There was a famous saying: ‘Red trousers – that is France.’ The French entered the First World War wearing red trousers. “Only after they saw the enormous casualties, because the trousers were clearly visible through rifle sights, did they start changing things,” he said. In May, the Lithuanian Armed Forces announced the creation of a drone unit under the historic ANBO acronym. It brings together different military units working with drone technologies. Plokšto said the key was the speed at which the military could adapt. “It all comes down to the speed of innovation and the speed of the armed forces. We have to be faster than the enemy; otherwise, the enemy will destroy us, including with the precision weapons it also has,” he said. He said Lithuania was already changing, but not quickly enough. “The problem is that everyone around us can see it, and the diffusion of ideas upwards is happening too slowly. Sooner or later, I imagine, it will reach the top,” he said. Ovidijus Kuzminas, commander of the Antanas Gustaitis 1031st Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Company of the Lithuanian Riflemen's Union, says bureaucracy remains a major obstacle. “We have put a bureaucratic burden on our heads. We are operating entirely under peacetime conditions and are not trying to make these processes different. “We are not trying to change certain legal provisions or laws that would unlock this and allow things to move faster,” he said. Gintaras Ažubalis, a retired colonel and military consultant at SCALEWOLF, agrees. “What slows everything down most is not the people working in military headquarters, developing concepts and trying to implement procurement projects. It is bureaucracy in the broadest sense,” he said. “[The country] is still operating under the same peacetime procedures, despite the fact that the commander of the armed forces has repeatedly [...] highlighted the bureaucratic processes that are killing everything,” Ažubalis added. “We are constantly told the same story: manufacturers cannot deliver, or cannot deliver as quickly as we would like. That is not true,” Ažubalis said, pointing out that Lithuanian manufacturers already produce equipment that is being used successfully in Ukraine. “There are plenty of ideas. It's not as if the people serving are stupid. We have elite officers, but their hands are tied. What do we need? We need a clear leader with the political will to sort out all this paperwork mess,” he said. “That is where I would like to see some progress, a breakthrough. Vilnius is like Kharkiv [in Ukraine] – right next to the border. We have to do something,” he added. Kuzminas also pointed to a lack of leadership. “We are missing those officer standard-bearers who would get this moving. They exist, but there aren't many of them – they are a minority. “What I fear most is that these people will eventually hit a wall and become disillusioned, and the issue will go nowhere,” he said. Romas Judinas, an analyst at the Locked N' Loaded Centre for Civil Defence and Security think tank, recalled how Lithuania responded to concerns about drones at the beginning of the war in Ukraine. “We can remember the notorious cases when the Lithuanian Armed Forces denied existing problems with drone procurement and capability development. “It was like shooting ourselves in the foot, and that was probably th

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys called on the European Union on Wednesday to resume discussions on using frozen Russian assets to help finance Ukraine’s military and civilian needs. “We had the interim solution with the financing the military needs. But now with the new demands and the new situation in Ukraine, we see that we need more finances and a longer-term vision, not only for military needs but also for civilian needs,” Budrys told reporters ahead of an EU foreign affairs council meeting. “So yes, this is the reason why this topic must be on the table.” The call comes as discussions have resurfaced over whether the EU should use about 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to help finance Ukraine. The EU is also considering plans to add about 1,600 companies and individuals to its already extensive sanctions list targeting Russia over its war against Ukraine. “We first have to prolong, without any political delay, individual sanctions and expand them to all the other sectors that we were leaving behind,” Budrys said. “And, of course, we have to target the prime energy companies.” Budrys also said Russia does not perceive a sufficient political cost for its hybrid activities against EU and NATO member states. “For them, it is a cheap way to cause tension in our society,” he said. “So our goal is to show that this activity will neither intimidate us nor prevent us from supporting Ukraine and maintaining pressure on Russia.” Since Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU has frozen around 210 billion euros in Russian central bank assets. Most of the assets, about 185 billion euros, are held by the Brussels-based central securities depository Euroclear. Belgium opposed an EU proposal in December 2025 to use Russian cash as collateral for a loan to Ukraine. The country sought guarantees from other EU countries that they would share legal responsibility in the likely event of Russia challenging the move in courts. Failing to secure the guarantees, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever shot down the effort led by Germany and the European Commission to use the Russian assets to give a loan to Kyiv which would only be repaid if Russia agreed to pay reparations. Last week, Sweden, Poland, the Netherlands and Spain once again called on the European Commission to explore new ways to use the immobilised Russian assets to support Ukraine. The call was rejected by the Belgian defence minister. “This is non-negotiable, the door is closed,” Theo Francken told Terzaken, on Flemish TV channel VRT, on Friday night. “Our prime minister will stand firm,” he added. He singled out the Baltic states, among the strongest supporters of the reparations loan, for refusing to drop the issue. “They should also be careful about constantly bringing this issue up again and putting us in a corner. I don’t think that is wise,” Francken said, pointing out that Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia receive a lot of support from Belgium. Russia’s central bank sued Euroclear in a Moscow arbitration court last December, seeking damages over the freezing of Russian assets under EU sanctions. In May, the Moscow court ruled that Euroclear must pay roughly 220 billion euros in damages, according to Euroclear’s lawyers. Euroclear then sued the Russian central bank in a Belgian civil court in June to block enforcement of the Russian judgment, according to Reuters. Euroclear says it froze the assets in compliance with EU rules.

Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya warned that Russia could use Belarusian territory to escalate tensions and provoke NATO member states. In an interview published Thursday by 15min.lt, Tsikhanouskaya said Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko remains willing to provide territory and infrastructure for potential Russian offensive or intimidation operations against the alliance. Based in Warsaw, Tsikhanouskaya said she had received reports that new military infrastructure was being built in Belarus near the Ukrainian border as well as along the country’s borders with European Union member states. “We must be very cautious – we see that the infrastructure for Oreshnik missiles is deployed in Belarus; they are threatening and blackmailing with nuclear weapons,” Tsikhanouskaya argued. Russia has deployed its Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile system in Belarus, which Moscow and Minsk have presented as part of efforts to strengthen their joint security. Tsikhanouskaya also said Russia and Belarus were already conducting hybrid attacks against NATO countries, specifically targeting Lithuania, Poland and Latvia. Her comments come amid heightened concerns in the Baltic region over potential Russian military activity and hybrid threats, including cyberattacks, disinformation and the use of drones.

One person was killed, and over 250,000 people were left without electricity – some are still living through the blackout. This time it was a storm – but what if it was an armed conflict or a drone attack? “We need to change our mindset that the state will come and bring us something. Every family needs to have its own defence plan and the equipment it would need,” says Laurynas Kasčiūnas, deputy chairman of the Seimas National Security and Defence Committee (NSGK) The municipality of Kazlų Rūda in western Lithuania was hit hard by the storm. Its outpatient clinic, like surrounding institutions and residents, was left without internet access. That meant no e-health services and handwritten prescriptions “As a society, we are not prepared for such disruptions. We do not have generators and rely on a single source. This is something we need to pay attention to,” said Renaldas Radvila, head of Lithuania’s electricity distribution operator, ESO. To prevent such blackouts, ESO needs †ø move 6,000 kilometres of cables underground, at a cost of half a billion euros. For now, ESO offered generators, according to the Kazlų Rūda mayor. “If 270,000 consumers are without electricity, what difference do 200 generators make? Other municipalities refused this so-called support because it would have turned people against each other. “There would have been countless theories about why some people got generators, and others did not,” said Mantas Varaška, the mayor. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, experts and officials repeatedly said that everyone should be prepared to survive for three days. However, shortages of water, food and medicines were reported in various municipalities after just a few days following the storm. “All residents of Lithuania received warning messages that a storm was coming and that there would be strong winds. They had time to prepare and could have done so. But did each of us?” said Paulius Rinkevičius, an expert with the Civil Protection Board of the Fire and Rescue Department “Did we park our cars away from trees or secure objects that could be blown out of our yards? Did we make sure we had alternative energy sources or generators? I think we all know the answer for ourselves,” he added. Some institutions were prepared, according to Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC). Some hospitals, he said, used the opportunity to hold real-life exercises and test their contingency plans. For example, the radios used by some public security officials did not work because of problems with telecommunications operators, which ran out of backup power supplies days after the storm. Vitkauskas said natural disasters cannot really be compared with armed conflict, but electricity infrastructure was, and will remain, a target. “We certainly see the risk, and we felt the threat even before the war in Ukraine. We always want greater speed and clearer priorities, but I think we are moving in the right direction,” said Vitkauskas. Meanwhile, critics said this showed that the preparedness for crises, including a military attack, looks good on paper only. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said the immediate priority was to deal with the aftermath of the storm, after which the authorities would examine what failed and why. “Everyone probably understands that storms are unavoidable in the future,” said Sinkevičius.

Lithuania should continue seeking ways to communicate with Belarusian authorities despite strained relations, Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas said Thursday, while stressing that sanctions against Minsk should be strengthened rather than eased. “We won’t perform any miracles here, but we need to seek out different paths and contacts,” Olekas told reporters after meeting with Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya. “We cannot simply separate ourselves and claim we will change everything and things will improve, but our goal is to seek opportunities to deliver our message.” Olekas said Lithuanian authorities maintain regular contacts with the Minsk government at technical and certain ministerial levels, with such contacts periodically renewed. At the same time, he said Lithuania should continue pushing for stronger sanctions against Belarus. Lithuania first imposed sanctions targeting Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko’s government in 2020 following a crackdown on mass protests after a disputed presidential election. Since February 2022, Lithuania has suspended the transit of Belarusian potash fertilisers. The European Union extended its sanctions on Belarusian fertilisers for another year in February. The decision came despite the United States lifting its own sanctions on some Belarusian fertiliser exports this year and subsequently approaching Lithuania and other countries in the region about potentially resuming transit. Conservative MP Žygimantas Pavilionis, deputy chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee who attended Thursday’s meeting, suggested that Lithuanian officials visit Washington before the next extension of the sanctions to coordinate with US officials and ensure the measures remain in place. Pavilionis said the biggest challenge could arise during Lithuania’s presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027, when decisions on extending sanctions are expected to coincide with the presidency. “Knowing that pressure exists and such a threat is approaching, we need to act very actively now, not in February or after February when it will be too late,” Pavilionis said.

For almost two years, Lithuania’s government has been maintaining a goal of normalising relations with Beijing that went sour under the previous conservative leadership over the Taiwanese representative office in Vilnius. So far, there is little perceivable progress – and some politicians are becoming impatient. Lithuanian lawmaker Ignas Vėgėlė, who sits with the non-attached group in the Seimas, said he will travel to Brussels at his own expense to meet Chinese diplomatic representatives after the Seimas board rejected a request to cover part of the trip with parliamentary funds. Vėgėlė and fellow lawmaker Rimas Jonas Jankūnas, members of a temporary parliamentary group seeking to normalise relations with China, are frustrated with the progress on the issue that is part of the government’s official program but has so far seemed stuck. So Vėgėlė and Jankūnas were planning to meet Chinese representatives in Brussels themselves. The Seimas board rejected the request to authorise and pay for the trip, citing both the use of parliamentary funds and concerns that the planned meetings had not been coordinated with the Foreign Ministry. “The decision does not change our decision and agreement to meet high-ranking diplomatic representatives in Brussels,” Vėgėlė said. He argued that Lithuanian lawmakers had previously travelled to Taiwan using parliamentary funds and said they would now have to correct what he described as the consequences of that decision by financing their own trip. The government has tasked Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys with working to restore Lithuania-China relations to the level maintained by other European Union member states. At the moment, Vilnius and Beijing do not even host each other’s ambassadors. “I will wait for the result. I hope we will see some progress in restoring diplomatic relations before our presidency,” Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said this week, referring to Lithuania’s upcoming presidency of the EU Council in the first half of 2027. Rasa Budbergytė, a member of the Seimas board and the ruling Social Democratic faction, said lawmakers needed to coordinate their activities carefully with the Foreign Ministry. “We need to act very carefully, especially since the current government and parliamentary majority are seeking to improve relations with China,” Budbergytė said. “China is a very serious international player, and we cannot simply go there, talk, return and not understand what we talked about.” Vėgėlė defended the planned meetings, saying Estonia’s foreign minister had been able to meet with senior Chinese officials while Lithuania’s chief diplomat had failed to do so for two years. “Our visit already shows attention to this problem and allows us to talk about warming relations,” he said. The details of the government’s ongoing discussions with Beijing have not been made public. Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas has said Foreign Minister Budrys is moving in the right direction, while President Gitanas Nausėda said he expects progress soon. “I hope that, if not the final results of an improvement, then at least some interim results and indications will show that our relations are gradually being restored,” Nausėda said. But not all groups in the parliament are enthusiastic about the goal of restoring ties with Beijing. Conservative lawmaker Radvilė Morkūnaitė-Mikulėnienė criticised the effort itself, insisting that China is enabling Russia’s war against Ukraine. “How can we cooperate – when its not a cooperation of critical importance – with a country that supports aggression? Not to mention about domestic problems with human rights, democracy and other things,” she argued. Vėgėlė and the parliamentary group backing closer ties with China have argued that Budrys’ efforts are insufficient and that progress toward normalising relations has been too slow.

The European Union’s top court ruled Thursday that the EU or an individual member state cannot sanction an EU-based company solely because it is indirectly owned by the Russian state. The ruling came in a dispute between Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service (FNTT), and Inter RAO Lietuva, an electricity supplier controlled by Russian energy giant Inter RAO. The European Court of Justice said the control of a company by a person subject to EU restrictive measures must be established through objective and sufficiently strong evidence. “The autocratic nature of the Russian political regime is not, in itself, sufficiently strong evidence capable of establishing that the Russian president controls a company,” the court said in a statement. The case was referred to the EU court by Lithuania’s Supreme Administrative Court, which suspended proceedings last year while seeking clarification on how EU sanctions rules should be applied. Lithuanian authorities had argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin could influence decisions at Inter RAO Lietuva even without direct ownership or capital links to the company. The European court rejected the argument that the autocratic and oligarchic nature of Russia’s political system was sufficient on its own to establish such control. Lithuania’s Supreme Administrative Court will now have to issue a final ruling in the dispute, taking the EU court’s interpretation into account. Inter RAO Lietuva is 51% owned by Finland-based RAO Nordic, which is controlled by Inter RAO. The Russian energy company’s board is headed by Igor Sechin, a Russian oligarch who is under Western sanctions over his ties to the Kremlin. FNTT restricted Inter RAO Lietuva’s ability to conduct banking transactions in March 2022, citing its links to Sechin. In May of that year, the agency said it had frozen the company’s funds, shares and real estate. The measures were subsequently linked to Putin rather than Sechin. The ruling could affect how Lithuanian authorities assess sanctions involving companies with indirect ownership or alleged links to sanctioned Russian individuals and entities.

Lithuania is tightening inspections of Russian grain moving through the port of Klaipėda after some stevedoring companies resumed handling the cargo, Agriculture Minister Kęstutis Mažeika said. Mažeika said he had instructed the State Food and Veterinary Service to inspect food grain of Russian origin transiting Lithuania, a procedure that had not previously been required. The service has already taken samples from a grain shipment at a customs warehouse in Klaipėda for laboratory testing in France to verify its origin. Results are expected in two to three weeks. Aistė Prielgauskaitė, a service spokeswoman, said authorities were investigating whether the grain, declared as Russian, could instead have originated in Ukraine and been transported through Russia’s Kaliningrad region. “The issue is whether the Russian grain being presented is of Ukrainian origin,” she said. “It might not be Russian as declared. It could be stolen.” Prielgauskaitė said the investigation could involve not only inaccurate declarations but also the possible misappropriation of Ukrainian grain, making the issue politically sensitive. Mažeika said Russia could be attempting to export Ukrainian grain through Latvian and Lithuanian ports. “I had a remote meeting with the Ukrainian minister yesterday, and he informed me that according to their intelligence, Russia will try to export about 1.5 million tonnes of grain through Latvia,” Mažeika said. Some of the grain is already in Latvian ports and could potentially be moved through Lithuanian infrastructure, he said. Mažeika did not confirm or deny reports that the shipment under investigation was loaded onto the Liberia-flagged vessel Donatello. He said the grain arrived from the Kaliningrad region and that samples were taken at the Bega terminal. The minister also ordered inspections of all food grain transported through Lithuania, saying feed grain had already been subject to checks but food grain had not. “If we see that stricter measures are needed, we are ready to take them,” Mažeika said. Klaipėda port chief Algis Latakas confirmed Thursday that grain declared as Russian is being handled at the port. About 47,000 tons had been handled in the first eight months of the year, he said. Latakas said the cargo comes from the Kaliningrad region, rather than mainland Russia, and consists mostly of corn. Because the products are not currently subject to sanctions, authorities have no legal basis to block them, he said. Transport Minister Juras Taminskas said Russian grain should not be exported through Lithuanian infrastructure, calling the practice politically and morally unacceptable while Russia’s war against Ukraine continues. Mažeika said he would consult with Taminskas on ways to prevent grain from “aggressor states” from transiting Lithuania. Bega spokesman Gediminas Gudavičius denied that the Donatello was carrying Russian grain. He said the 38,000 tons of wheat loaded by Bega were of Lithuanian origin and had certificates to prove it. According to customs data, the wheat was brought by rail from Kaliningrad and declared as Lithuanian origin. Mažeika and Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius are due to visit Klaipėda port next Wednesday to assess the situation and discuss measures to prevent similar cases. The Lithuanian Association of Grain Processors and Traders urged the government to block Russian grain transit, saying Russian exporters were increasingly using Baltic ports after shipping in the Black Sea became more difficult because of the war. Association President Karolis Simas said Russian grain was being offered to buyers at substantially lower prices, putting Lithuanian traders at a competitive disadvantage. He called for tighter origin controls, including checks aimed at determining whether grain was produced in occupied Ukrainian territories, and warned that failing to act could damage both the Lithuanian and Latvian economies

Lithuanian intelligence currently sees no increased threat from Belarus, Deividas Matulionis, President Gitanas Nausėda’s chief national security adviser, said Thursday. “I specifically made additional inquiries today, and our services have no such information. As of today, we do not see an increased threat from the Belarusian side,” Matulionis told LRT RADIO. He said that while Russian military installations are present in Belarus, Lithuanian intelligence has not detected new manoeuvre units that would pose a direct threat to Lithuania, Latvia or Poland. Matulionis’ comments followed warnings by Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, who was visiting Lithuania and said she had received information about new military infrastructure being built in Belarus, including near the border with Ukraine and along its borders with European Union countries. Matulionis said Lithuanian intelligence was closely monitoring developments in Belarus. A significant buildup of Russian troops would be a clear signal requiring action at both the national and NATO levels, he said. However, Lithuanian intelligence services currently cannot confirm Tsikhanouskaya’s warnings, he said. According to Matulionis, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko is also not interested in becoming directly involved in Russia’s war against Ukraine and is seeking to improve relations with the West and the United States. Matulionis said Lithuania should not restore political relations with Lukashenko’s government but should maintain communication channels with Minsk to help prevent a potential escalation during a crisis. Following a meeting with Tsikhanouskaya, Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas said Belarusian railways could potentially be used to transport Russian troops and weapons. He said Lithuanian authorities were monitoring and controlling infrastructure being built in Belarus. Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has said Moscow may be considering attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region using Ukrainian drones as a way of testing NATO’s cohesion. He did not specify how concrete the plans were. Lithuania has maintained a hostile approach toward Belarus since Lukashenko launched a crackdown on the opposition following the disputed 2020 presidential election. Vilnius has also advocated for European Union sanctions against Belarus.

The severe storm that swept across Lithuania last month is likely to go down in the country’s weather history, according to Donatas Valiukas, head of the Climate and Research Division at Lithuania’s Hydrometeorological Service. While powerful storms are relatively uncommon in Lithuania, the country has experienced several destructive events over the past decades – some causing deaths, widespread power outages and major damage to infrastructure. One of the most severe struck October 17-18, 1967, when hurricane-force winds battered western Lithuania. In Klaipėda, winds reached 40 metres per second, while individual gusts may have reached 55 metres per second, according to the Hydrometeorological Service. The storm, known as Lena in Sweden, destroyed the Palanga pier, damaged dunes and flooded parts of Klaipėda. Some 3 million to 4 million cubic meters of timber were blown down across the Samogitia region. Another major storm, Anatol, hit Lithuania in December 1999. Wind gusts reached 40 meters per second in some areas and produced waves up to 6 metres high. A Norwegian vessel, the Seines, was washed ashore near Palanga and was not pulled back into the sea until April 2000. In January 2005, Storm Erwin brought winds of up to 35 metres per second to the coast. Dunes and forests were damaged, the Danė River flooded parts of Klaipėda, and about 150,000 to 180,000 people lost electricity. Repairs took six days. Summer storms have also proved deadly. A powerful squall in August 2010 killed four people after unusually strong winds swept across several municipalities. Another major squall struck central and eastern Lithuania in June 2016. More recently, Lithuania has experienced severe summer storms associated with cyclones moving north from southern Europe. A storm in July 2024 left about 160,000 people without electricity. Last month’s storm affected about 268,000 customers at its peak and also caused fatalities. Valiukas said climate change could increase the likelihood and intensity of such events. “As the climate changes, the air warms, holds more moisture and potentially has more destructive power,” he said. He added that Lithuania’s relative lack of frequent severe storms can leave residents less prepared than people in hurricane-prone regions.

Lithuania’s State Security Department (VSD) said Monday that 22 Belarusian citizens who worked for a technology company in the country had been declared threats to national security and expelled. The individuals were expelled from Lithuania and barred from returning. All 22 have also been banned from entering the Schengen area for five years, according to the VSD. The Belarusian citizens worked for a company that participated in a project for the European Union Agency for the Space Programme, or EUSPA, and fraudulently obtained nearly 500,000 euros. An investigation led by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office and carried out by Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service in cooperation with the VSD found that the company had concealed links to the Russian and Belarusian military industries. BNS reported last week that the Vilnius Regional Court convicted two Belarusian citizens of fraud involving nearly 500,000 euros. The project was intended to develop high-precision satellite navigation receivers capable of using the Galileo High Accuracy Service for agricultural applications, including controlling farm machinery and supporting precision farming operations. The project had a total budget of more than 1 million euros, with more than 745,000 euros financed by EUSPA. The company actually received 447,272 euros.

People began entering the EU from Belarus in the summer of 2021. They were soon routinely subjected to pushbacks – and that has continued ever since. Swedish journalist Thord Eriksson travelled to Lithuania, where the interior minister wants border guards to be allowed to open fire on people crossing the border. The gravel road runs between rolling fields before disappearing into dense forest. It could have been out in the countryside somewhere in the Stockholm region, if it weren’t for the fence. It glints in the August sun, topped with thick coils of razor wire. With only a few gaps, the four-metre-high structure runs the entire 1,250-kilometre stretch that separates the EU from Belarus, from Latvia in the north to Poland in the south, with Lithuania in between. Recently, right-wing populists across Europe like Italy’s neo-fascist prime minister Giorgia Meloni, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, and AfD chair Alice Weidel in Germany held up Spain as a threat to the EU and to freedom of movement. Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk held up his own country’s border regime – essentially identical to Lithuania’s – as a model, saying Spain must follow Poland’s example if Schengen is to survive. Exactly what Tusk’s example means in practice is not something the countries along the border are eager to show. No one – not even journalists or aid organisations – is allowed near the fence without a permit. In Lithuania the restricted zone is five kilometres wide, in Latvia two kilometres, and in Poland up to four kilometres. Anyone who defies the ban risks a fine. “You’d better take over, they tend to be more cooperative when a woman is driving,” says Mantautas Šulskus, braking his worn Mitsubishi to a stop. He is the field coordinator of the organisation Sienos Grupė, the Border Group, which he also helped found in 2021 in response to the humanitarian crisis. Now he swaps places with 24-year-old volunteer Vaiva Vinskaitė, a graphic designer who describes herself as a full-time refugee activist. The purpose of the trip into the restricted zone is to see the places associated with 32-year-old Samrin from Sri Lanka, one of the border’s victims. “There are cameras everywhere, so there’s no doubt the border guards already know we’re in the area.” After a while Vaiva parks by the roadside and we walk across a field to a steep slope above the river Neris. It was on the riverbank below that Samrin was found dead in August 2022. Five days earlier, Lithuanian border guards had subjected him to a so-called pushback, forcing him out of the country and into Belarus. Lithuania was the first country along the Belarus border to see people entering from its eastern neighbour, in the summer of 2021. They came through the forests and crossed a border then marked only by posts stuck in the ground. The same development soon followed in Latvia and Poland. There was talk of instrumentalised migration, invasion and hybrid war – the same terms now being used about those who entered Ceuta. It is speculated that the incident in the Spanish exclave was staged by Morocco. The parallels were easier to see in 2021: Alexander Lukashenko, who has ruled Belarus with an iron grip for nearly three decades, had already threatened to let migrants through to the border. The trigger was the sanctions the EU imposed after the country’s rigged 2020 presidential election and the brutal violence inflicted on those who dared to protest. The method was simple: start granting visas to people who would not normally be granted them. From the capital, Minsk, to Lithuania – the nearest stretch of the EU border – was then just a 150-kilometre trip. A border guard has told Politico what happened to those who, for whatever reason, changed their minds and wanted to go back to Minsk: “If they chose to return, they were detained by the Belarusian side and treated like animals. Anyone who tried to return was dragged back to the border – and they were beaten.” The situation initially drew extensive media attention. Reporting teams from around the world travelled to Lithuania, Latvia and Poland. Since then, media interest has faded, not least after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but people are still making it across the border. According to official statistics, Lithuania has so far this year forced nearly 1,100 people to return to Belarus, and since 2021 the total has reached just over 25,000. The figures should be treated with caution, however, since most people have made several attempts to enter Lithuania and are therefore counted more than once. The “invasion” is consequently smaller than Lithuania, Latvia and Poland make it out to be. Since 2021, the three countries have described their actions as self-defence against an outside attack. But it is not Lukashenko who feels the resistance – it is the people who have seized the chance to avoid the deadly crossing of the Mediterranean in order to enter the EU. Among Šulskus and others critical of the country’s pushbacks, the name Ylva Johansson carries a particular weight, he explains. In 2021, the former Swedish Social Democratic minister and member of parliament was the EU’s commissioner for home affairs, which included responsibility for migration. And since Lithuania was the first to notice the border crossings, that is where she travelled in early August of that year. “It doesn’t seem to be people in need of protection, but rather other kinds of migrants,” she told TT news agency . Until then, people who made it into the country had been stopped and placed in accommodation centres that were often makeshift and full, but they at least had a roof over their heads, food, and had their asylum claims investigated. After that, the practice that still applies today became established: anyone who crosses the border is forced straight back out and given no opportunity to seek asylum. “People may not remember Ylva Johansson’s name, but they do remember that the EU commissioner was here and that she was

Lithuania’s agriculture minister has ordered checks on the origin of all grain transported from Russia and Belarus through the country to prevent the possible transit of grain stolen from Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine, the Agriculture Ministry said. Agriculture Minister Kęstutis Mažeika formally asked the State Food and Veterinary Service to immediately investigate the origin of all grain transported in transit from Russia and Belarus, including both feed and food-grade grain. “Uniform checks must be applied to all consignments of grain transported from Russia and Belarus, regardless of their intended use,” Mažeika said in a statement. “We must do everything to ensure that our country’s infrastructure is not used for the transit of stolen Ukrainian grain.” Since May last year, Lithuania, Ukraine and the United Kingdom have been implementing the Grain Verification Scheme, under which mandatory laboratory testing is conducted on feed grain held in customs warehouses, according to the ministry. But changes in monitored traffic flows indicate that some shipments may be moving under simplified direct-transit procedures or being declared as food-grade grain to avoid inspections, the ministry said. Mažeika called for closer cooperation between the State Food and Veterinary Service and the Customs Department to ensure timely information on transit flows and identify and inspect high-risk shipments before they leave Lithuania. The State Food and Veterinary Service last week took samples from a grain shipment at the port of Klaipėda and will have them analysed at a laboratory in France to establish their country of origin, the service said. Aistė Prielgauskaitė, a spokeswoman for the service, said authorities suspect the grain may have originated in Ukraine rather than Russia, as stated in the accompanying documents. If confirmed, the grain could have been stolen from Ukraine and transported through the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, she said. Prielgauskaitė told BNS that grain samples were taken Thursday from a customs warehouse in Klaipėda. The laboratory analysis is expected to take two to three weeks. Mažeika previously told BNS that Russia might seek to export Ukrainian grain through ports in Latvia and Lithuania.

Lithuania is discussing a joint response with Latvia and Estonia to efforts to transit Russian and Belarusian grain through the Baltic states, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Tuesday. Sinkevičius said he discussed the issue by phone with his Latvian counterpart Monday, amid reports that grain allegedly stolen from Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories could be transported through the Baltic countries. The shipments will not be allowed to pass through Lithuania’s Klaipėda port “unchecked”, Sinkevičius told reporters in Klaipėda. “The issue concerns not just Lithuania as a state; in this case, we are talking about three states – Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania,” he said. “We will, of course, carry out checks, monitor the situation and will not allow such cargo to pass unchecked.” Lithuania supports Ukraine and does not want its port and rail infrastructure used to facilitate Russian grain shipments, Sinkevičius said. “We will certainly not allow our port infrastructure and railways to be used in such a way that doubts might arise later, as our partners in Ukraine are watching to see how we behave,” he said. The Lithuanian Agriculture Ministry on Monday asked the State Food and Veterinary Service to immediately investigate the origin of all grain transiting from Russia and Belarus, including both feed and food-grade grain. The service last week took samples from one grain shipment at the port of Klaipėda and plans to have their origin determined at a foreign laboratory. It confirmed Monday that no additional samples had been taken. Sinkevičius said authorities want shipments to undergo genetic testing to establish their origin, although the volumes involved are relatively small by Lithuanian standards. Agriculture Minister Kęstutis Mažeika said the three Baltic states should verify the origin of both feed and food-grade grain arriving from Russia and Belarus. Mažeika said Lithuania was considering requiring inspections at the border with Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region rather than at the Klaipėda port. That would allow the port to prioritise exports of Lithuanian grain, he said. “Our priority is to free up the port for Lithuanian grain from Lithuanian farmers so that as much of it as possible can be exported,” Mažeika said. Authorities are also considering extending mandatory origin testing to other food products, including edible oil, he said. Mažeika said Lithuania would seek a European Union consensus on applying such checks to food products, which currently benefit from an EU exception covering both raw and processed food. The issue has gained attention following reports that grain allegedly stolen from Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia could be entering European markets through the Baltic states. The Lithuanian president’s chief foreign policy adviser Asta Skaisgirytė on Tuesday called for measures to prevent Russia from exploiting ports in Lithuania and other EU countries to export grain.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday she hoped US negotiators who visited Kyiv over the weekend had seen for themselves that Russia is not genuinely interested in ending its war against Ukraine. “I’m happy to see that for the first time the special envoys have also visited Kyiv,” Kallas told reporters in Vilnius. “What it meant for the Ukrainians was three days without bombing of civilians. I think that’s the positive side of this visit.” “I hope that they also heard what the situation on the ground is and Ukrainians also showed them that Russia is not really interested in peace – the opposite,” she said. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over the weekend in a renewed effort to end the fighting. Moscow and Kyiv agreed to suspend strikes while the negotiations were taking place. Witkoff on Monday praised the weekend discussions in Moscow and Kyiv and suggested they could lead to a schedule for new three-way peace talks. The Kremlin also said Monday that it had not ruled out three-way negotiations involving the United States and Ukraine. The talks remain complicated by disagreements over Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, parts of which Russia does not control but which Moscow has demanded as part of a potential peace settlement. Kallas said Europe cannot serve as a neutral mediator between Russia and Ukraine because it is directly affected by the conflict. “In the end, when there is going to be a peace agreement, there are also a lot of asks for Europe to be very clear that these are not some things that we are giving without getting anything in return,” she said. During her visit to Vilnius, Kallas also warned that political parties in Europe that downplay the threat posed by Russia are gaining support. Her comments followed an election victory by Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, in a state election Sunday. Following a meeting with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, Kallas said sabotage and other security threats were moving closer to Europe. “At the same time, the parties that are sort of blind to this threat and say that we should not do anything with this because it’s not our concern, are gaining ground,” she said. “I’m just afraid that we might wake up in a situation where we haven’t done enough to be able to deter the threats and defend ourselves,” Kallas added. “But of course it’s up to the German people, as a democratic country, to make their choices.” Sinkevičius said victories by far-right parties should serve as a warning to mainstream political forces that they are failing to meet voters’ expectations adequately. “I would hope that such cases do not recur and that this does not become a new trend across European countries,” he said. But he said the AfD’s victory in one German state would not affect relations between Germany and Lithuania. “Germany has remained and will remain Lithuania’s most important strategic partner,” Sinkevičius said. Correction on Sep 8, 15:25. The headline was changed to more accurately reflect Kaja Kallas’ statements.

Lithuania’s cost of managing its government debt is set to top 1 billion euros for the first time next year, an increasingly visible burden for a country whose debt remains relatively low by European standards but is moving steadily higher. The figure alone does not signal a debt crisis, says Živilė Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė, an economist at the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists. But the trajectory is becoming more important, she said, as Lithuania moves closer to the 60% of gross domestic product threshold that constrains its room for additional spending. Lithuania’s general government debt stood at 33.3 billion euros at the end of 2025, or 39.5% of GDP, according to the State Data Agency. That remains among the lowest debt ratios in the European Union. Greece had the highest at 146.1% of GDP, followed by Italy at 137.1%, France at 115.6%, Belgium at 107.9% and Spain at 100.7%. Estonia, Luxembourg, Denmark and Bulgaria had the lowest ratios, at 24.1%, 26.5%, 27.9% and 29.9%, respectively. The contrast is even sharper with the United States, the world’s largest economy, where government debt this year reached 122.7% of GDP. In 1980, the US ratio was 34.7%, close to Lithuania’s current level. That does not mean Lithuania is destined to follow the path of the United States or heavily indebted European economies, Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė notes. The European Commission forecasts Lithuania’s debt will rise to 48.4% of GDP in 2027, while the International Monetary Fund estimates that, without additional fiscal measures, it could reach about 60% around 2033. “The more important issue than the 100% threshold itself is the direction and speed of debt growth,” Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė says. “Over a relatively short period, we are moving from around 40% toward 50%, and over the longer term potentially toward 60% of GDP.” Higher debt leaves the government with less fiscal room to respond to an economic, financial or geopolitical crisis and forces it to devote a growing share of its budget to interest payments, she explains. “The main question today is not whether Lithuania will ever reach the symbolic 100% threshold, but at what debt level it will be stabilised and how to ensure that its current growth does not become a permanent trend.” The Finance Ministry also pointed to the 60% threshold. Assuming fiscal rules are followed, the government’s debt-to-GDP ratio should stabilise over the long term and remain below 60%, ministry officials told LRT.lt. Once that level is reached, spending growth limits are set so that the debt ratio either reliably declines over the medium term or remains at a prudent level below the threshold. The cost of servicing Lithuania’s debt has risen sharply in recent years. The state budget allocated 554.3 million euros for debt management costs in 2025. That figure is to rise to 753.8 million euros this year and 1.03 billion euros in 2027. Under the current plan, debt management costs will reach 1.15 billion euros in 2028, including 1.14 billion euros in interest payments. The IMF estimates that government interest expenses will rise from about 0.9% of GDP in 2025 to 1.3% in 2027 and could reach 1.7% by 2030, Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė says. The concern is not simply the size of the annual bill. It is what those payments mean for other government priorities. “Every additional 100 million euros spent servicing debt is 100 million euros that can no longer be spent on education, health care, defence, investment or reducing the tax burden,” she said. Rather than focusing on the symbolic 1 billion euro mark, Lithuania should address the structural growth in debt, she argues, by ensuring sustainable revenues for recurring spending, using public money more efficiently and directing borrowing toward investments that strengthen national security, productivity and the economy’s long-term potential. At the same time, Lithuania’s borrowing costs have been rising. According to the Finance Ministry, the weighted yield on a government bond maturing in August 2028 was 2.684% in January. By August, it had risen to 3.098%. Borrowing costs have also been climbing in the United States, major European economies and Japan. SEB Bank said last week that the yield on US 10-year Treasury bonds had risen to 4.75%, while the 30-year yield reached 5.27%. Ten-year yields on French and German bonds rose to 3.32% and 4.18%, respectively. The French yield was at its highest level since 2008, while the German yield was the highest since 2011. Japan’s 10-year yield approached 3%, a level last seen in 1996. Expectations for future European Central Bank interest-rate increases are one factor behind higher borrowing costs. But for Lithuania, economists at the Bank of Lithuania say other factors affecting the country’s risk premium may be even more important. Expectations of tighter ECB monetary policy tend to push up risk-free eurozone interest rates, which in turn increases government bond yields. But yields on many government bonds have risen by more than eurozone risk-free rates as investors have priced in additional risks, according to Bank of Lithuania economists Vaidotas Tuzikas, Rokas Kaminskas and Linas Jurkšas. For Lithuania, those risks include the size and expected trajectory of government debt and the budget deficit, economic growth prospects, credit ratings, the size and liquidity of the bond market, investor perceptions of risk and the geopolitical environment, they say. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 sharply increased geopolitical uncertainty across the region. At the same time, soaring energy and commodity prices hurt inflation and economic prospects. Those pressures were particularly significant for the Baltic states and Poland because of their geographic position and greater exposure to the economic shock caused by the war.
