Two Lithuanian lawmakers met with Chinese diplomats in Brussels to discuss ways of improving relations between Lithuania and China, drawing criticism from some members of the European Parliament. Ignas Vėgėlė and Rimas Jonas Jankūnas, members of Lithuania’s mixed parliamentary group, said Tuesday that their main goal was to assess the state of bilateral relations and hear China’s position. “The main goal is to find out what the situation really is. To listen more than to speak,” Vėgėlė said. The lawmakers said they wanted Lithuania’s diplomatic relationship with China to be comparable to those maintained by other European Union countries. The visit was organised and financed by the lawmakers themselves after the Seimas board rejected their request for official travel funding. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda’s chief foreign policy adviser, Asta Skaisgirytė, said the lawmakers did not represent Lithuania, its parliament or its government in the talks. Jankūnas rejected that criticism, saying the lawmakers represented a large share of Lithuanian voters as well as a parliamentary group seeking to normalise relations with China. “Without representing the government, we represent the government’s program,” he said, referencing the government’s declared goal of working towards normalising ties with Beijing. The talks come as the EU is reassessing its relationship with China and seeking ways to reduce its economic dependence with the world’s second biggest economy. European Parliament member Petras Auštrevičius, a liberal, urged caution, describing the lawmakers’ visit as “people’s diplomacy” and saying Lithuania should avoid rushing into moves on relations with China. “We need to know how to wait and wait wisely,” Auštrevičius said. “In relations with China, sensible patience is no less important than quick, difficult-to-explain actions.” He suggested the visit was orchestrated by the Chinese government. Another European Parliament member, social democrat Vytenis Andriukaitis, said he did not expect the visit to change Lithuania’s official policy toward China. “Seimas members are free to engage in politics,” Andriukaitis said. “But as for how much this can change the government’s or the parliament’s program – clearly, it cannot.” Meanwhile, another European Parliament member Petras Gražulis, of the right-wing People and Justice Union group, welcomed the initiative. “It certainly won’t make things worse,” Gražulis said, adding that official talks involving the president, foreign minister or the parliament would be preferable. The meeting lasted about two hours and was hosted at the highest diplomatic level, according to the Lithuanian lawmakers, who said they were received by China’s ambassador. Vėgėlė described the talks as warm and sincere and said the delegation had discussed a wide range of issues and taken extensive notes. He declined to disclose what “homework” China had given the Lithuanian side, saying such tasks are handled quietly in diplomacy. Vėgėlė said he would bring the information gathered in Brussels back to Lithuania and share it with the country’s senior officials. Whether another meeting will be held remains unclear.

The Vilnius Regional Court on Wednesday extended the detention of Mukhamad Ali Nurkulov, a Kyrgyz national accused of financing or supporting terrorism, by a further three months. Nurkulov is on trial for transferring small sums of money to the Al Qassem Brigades, the military wing of the Palestinian Islamist organisation Hamas. The defendant maintains, however, that he did not know the Al Qassem Brigades were listed as a terrorist group in the European Union and believed the money would be used for food and other humanitarian aid. Nurkulov’s detention term was due to expire on September 21. Consequently, Prosecutor Rimas Juodis asked the court last week to extend his detention for the maximum period of three months. “The defendant no longer holds a residence permit in Lithuania, so if released, he would have to leave the country immediately. Furthermore, the offence he is charged with carries a mandatory prison sentence,” Juodis said. The prosecutor told BNS that Nurkulov had arrived in Lithuania by plane just as his temporary residence permit was due to expire. He was detained at the airport in March, so he was unable to renew his permit, and it was automatically revoked. Closing statements were due to be delivered in this case last week, but they had to be postponed when it emerged that some documents had been translated from Russian and Arabic not by a translator – who had been warned of the consequences of providing an inaccurate translation – but by a translation app. It was therefore decided that the translations of the aforementioned documents, which will be carried out in accordance with the law, should be submitted at the next hearing.

The government on Wednesday decided to allocate a plot of land in the Varėna municipality in southeastern Lithuania to the country’s Riflemen's Union (LŠS) for drone training. The 51.97-hectare area will be used to train drone operators, develop drone capabilities and anti-drone systems, the Defence Ministry said in a statement. The territory may also be used to establish a long-range shooting range of up to 800 metres and set up a drone competence centre. The decision replaces a resolution adopted in November 2024, under which the LŠS was due to be given a 30.61-hectare plot in Ąžuolų village, Balbieriškis eldership, under a trust arrangement. The decision was changed after it emerged that the plot had been included on a list of state-owned land reserved for investment and was needed by the Ministry of Economy and Innovation for an investment project. Ukraine's Dnipro Electromechanical Plant (DEMZ) plans to build an ammunition assembly workshop there. The Lithuanian Riflemen's Union is a voluntary paramilitary organisation, controlled by the government, and currently has nearly 20,000 members.

Police received an anonymous report Thursday morning threatening explosions at several schools in Vilnius, including the Adomas Mickevičius Lyceum and the Užupis, Žvėrynas, Veiksmo, Pažinimo Medžio and Abraomas Kulvietis gymnasia. The threats said the explosions would take place at 10:00. A private security company also received a report claiming that the Žvėrynas Gymnasium had been booby-trapped, prompting the evacuation of students from the building. No explosions occurred at the threatened time. Police said the threatening emails, which were sent to several government institutions, contained numerous grammatical and logical errors. Officers contacted all the schools named in the threats and sent patrols to the locations. Police said they were checking and analysing the information and that, at this stage, they had found no indication of a real threat. Authorities advised schools to remain vigilant but continue the educational process. Police also recommended that those responsible for school security inspect their premises and immediately call the emergency number 112 if they find any suspicious objects.

Lithuania’s parliament, the Seimas, is opening its autumn session Thursday, with lawmakers set to review a draft agenda containing more than 550 legislative proposals and focus on security, defence and demographic challenges. The session will run through December 23 and include 46 sittings, three of which will be dedicated to the agendas of opposition parliamentary groups. Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas said security, defence and national resilience would be among the session’s main priorities, along with measures addressing demographic challenges. “We intend to focus most of our attention on security, defence and resilience,” Olekas said. “The second theme is tackling demographic challenges, encompassing measures to boost the birth rate, as well as the return of the diaspora to Lithuania and managed migration.” The draft agenda includes more than 330 initiatives submitted by lawmakers. The cabinet has proposed 127 draft laws for consideration. Among the key issues, lawmakers are expected to consider removing from the Constitution a provision banning the deployment of nuclear weapons in Lithuania and approve an updated National Security Strategy. The parliament is also expected Thursday to consider a proposal to hold the next mayoral and municipal council elections on March 7, 2027. Lawmakers are also due to consider legislation establishing a public register of sex offenders. The 2027 state budget will be approved during the session. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has said the government’s priorities centre on “a safe person in a safe state”. A family policy package is scheduled to be presented Thursday. It is aimed at boosting the birth rate, improving the child care allowance system and helping young families buy homes. Other planned measures include increasing the number of conscripts, introducing universal free school meals for primary school students and raising scientists’ salaries. Lawmakers are also expected to consider proposals to establish a free economic zone in Visaginas, limit the frequency of fuel price increases, and streamline public procurement and civil service regulations. President Gitanas Nausėda has submitted 10 proposals for consideration during the session. The Lithuanian parliament convenes for two regular sessions each year, in spring and autumn.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius appointed Germany’s Lieutenant General Jürgen-Joachim von Sandrart as his defence adviser, the government said on Friday. "His knowledge and practical experience in strengthening the defence of the alliance’s eastern flank are particularly valuable to Lithuania. I believe his experience will help us make the decisions needed to strengthen Lithuania’s defence more quickly," Sinkevičius said in a statement. Until 2024, von Sandrart headed NATO’s Multinational Corps Northeast, responsible for planning and coordinating land operations in a region covering Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia. The retired general will advise the prime minister on an unpaid basis, focusing on strengthening Lithuania’s defence capabilities, military transformation, interoperability with NATO allies, particularly Germany, and other strategic defence issues. Von Sandrart served in the German Bundeswehr for more than four decades. During his military career, he held various senior positions within NATO and German structures, including the commander’s position at one of the Bundeswehr’s main land formations, Germany’s 1st Panzer Division.

The United States is currently behind schedule in delivering HIMARS artillery systems to Lithuania, Raimundas Vaikšnoras, the country’s military chief, said on Thursday, adding that identical systems could be brought to Lithuania temporarily if needed. "The HIMARS delivery has been pushed back. I can't say now by how much or for how long. That's entirely on the American side, probably related to their industry. But our crews have already completed their training and firing exercises, so we're waiting for the systems to arrive," Vaikšnoras told LRT TV in an interview on Thursday. Lithuania signed a $495m contract with the US at the end of 2022 to acquire eight HIMARS multiple-launch rocket systems. In April this year, Vilnius signed an amendment to purchase a second HIMARS battery for an additional $280m. "I would also like to emphasise to the public that there is no need to be overly concerned, because we have agreements in place allowing us, while there are delays for various reasons, to temporarily bring identical systems to Lithuania. They could fill certain capability gaps," Vaikšnoras said. According to the military chief, the military has reached an agreement with the Michigan National Guard on the possible temporary deployment of such systems. "They have the same systems and can come to our exercises," he said. The US had previously been expected to deliver the HIMARS systems to Lithuania by the end of this year. Responding to opposition Conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, who said Lithuania's national division might not reach full operational capability by 2030 as planned, Vaikšnoras said the risks were being managed. "To achieve the division's full capability, at least three elements are needed: weapons and equipment, which need to be purchased and delivered on schedule; infrastructure to store that equipment and weaponry; and training areas, military ranges and trained personnel capable of operating the equipment and weapons. "So I can say today that there are no major delays or risks, because I can only speak for my area of responsibility – the training of soldiers," he said. "At the moment, I believe everything is under control. The risks are being managed, so I have nothing further to comment on," Vaikšnoras said when asked whether he saw any obstacles to the division reaching its target. Defence Minister Robert Kaunas said on Thursday that some infrastructure needed for the national division could be delayed, but that there was no significant threat to achieving full operational capability by 2030. Over the past three years, Lithuania has bought around €2bn worth of weapons and equipment from the US.

Guess what – we have more controversy surrounding the Nemunas Dawn party. Officers from the anti-corruption watchdog (STT) and the financial crimes agency (FNTT) raided five of the party’s 11 board members who are also MPs. The party’s leader, Remigijus Žemaitaitis, played down the importance of the raids: “The evidence must be fully collected – if there is evidence, there is evidence; if there isn’t, there isn’t,” he told LRT on Tuesday. The raids centred on a probe after it was found that Žemaitaitis, as well as another party member, rented their own cars to the party. Previously, the election watchdog reported on another potential corruption scheme involving a campaigning laundromat. The scheme was simple enough: people close to the party would bring cash into their bank accounts before transferring the said (and unaccounted for) funds to the party as donations. MAKING BABIES The government is at it again, hoping to offset the looming demographic crisis by proposing an 800-million-euro package of baby-making incentives. The proposal includes free school lunches, more paid leave, payouts for returning diaspora, nanny subsidies, and more (and no – no more talk of state-funded discos to get you mingling). KALLAS IN TOWN Kaja Kallas, the Estonian head of the European Commission’s foreign service, was in Vilnius earlier this week, where she met with the president, the prime minister, and various other heads of institutions; she also made a trip to the border with Belarus. Her message echoed what the Baltics tend to repeat publicly about the threat from Russia – it’s not going anywhere. TRASH CRISIS LRT’s Investigation Team dug up documents showing that the Vilnius authorities knew about the brewing trash dilemma, but decided to risk it anyway. The misplaced optimism backfired, as the head of the administration admitted on record. Unrelated to the latter scandal, the Special Investigations Service (STT) also said it finished its investigation into systemic corruption surrounding waste management in Vilnius. MORE POWER The government will consider next week establishing a reserve of electricity generators after a storm left close to 270,000 consumers without power. There were some generators already made available, infrastructure managers say, but it wasn’t nearly enough. The head of Lithuania’s electricity distribution operator ESO is also set to lose his position as the CEO for the seemingly slow response, as hundreds of consumers still remain without electricity almost three weeks later. In any case, the storm last month is set to go down in Lithuania’s history, meteorologists say . EDITOR’S PICKS – Another weekly update on the skyrocketing cost of living: rental prices in Lithuania keep going up, with no sign of respite. – Here’s how the “weaponisation of migration” definition is going EU-wide. – A group of Belarusian tech workers were kicked out of the country for getting EU funds while working for a company with links to the Belarusian and Russian military industries. – Lithuania’s budget deficit is growing , as expected. – Have you heard of the New Baltic Cuisine ? – The Baltics are not happy about Russia's grain transit. – Researchers are on the trail of elusive remains of Grand Duke Vytautas. h – US Envoy warns against building a conference centre over a former Jewish cemetery. – Finally, some good news in education: Lithuanian students are doing alright. Written by Benas Gerdžiūnas Edited by Justinas Šuliokas

Prosecutor Redas Savickas on Friday made sentencing recommendations to the Vilnius Regional Court hearing the case of Erika Švenčionienė, Valery Ivanov, and Kazimieras Juraitis, accused of aiding another state in actions against Lithuania and of publicly denying Soviet crimes. The prosecutor recommended a two-year prison sentence for Švenčionienė, an 18-month prison sentence for Juraitis, and a fine of 15,000 euros for Ivanov. In his closing argument, the prosecutor stated that the defendants acted in the interests of Russia and Belarus. ​ Švenčionienė and Ivanov, the former leader of the pro-Soviet organisation Yedinstvo, are accused of denying Soviet crimes, while Švenčionienė and Juraitis are accused of aiding another state in actions against Lithuania. ​ Before the hearing began, Švenčionienė spoke about friendship with Belarus and “vatniks”, recited a poem about Vytautas Landsbergis, and claimed that the September 11 terrorist attack in the United States was orchestrated by the American government. ​ “This is a crime against Lithuania’s statehood and sovereignty,” Prosecutor Savickas said in his closing argument regarding the charges against Švenčionienė and Juraitis for aiding another state in actions against Lithuania. ​ According to him, the defendants repeatedly disseminated false and defamatory information about Lithuania and Ukraine when appearing in Russian and Belarusian propaganda broadcasts. ​ Švenčionienė sought out individuals willing to fight on Russia’s side in Ukraine. The defendants’ ties to Belarusian authorities and the KGB were confirmed by data from the State Security Department (VSD) included in the case file. ​ According to Savickas, the defendants aided Russia’s information war against Lithuania. ​ When appearing in Russian television propaganda broadcasts, Švenčionienė urged the Russians to defeat Ukraine as quickly as possible and "rid it of Nazis". She also claimed that Lithuania intended to attack Russia and stated that “your victory is our victory”. ​ In his closing argument, the prosecutor also mentioned public statements by Ivanov and Švenčionienė in which they denied Soviet crimes committed during the January 1991 events. This case has been pending in court for nearly three years. The proceedings have been prolonged due to Švenčionienė’s recurring illnesses and the defendants’ endless motions, which the court is required to consider. ​ During the trial, the defendants claimed that there had been no occupation of Lithuania, that it was not Soviet soldiers who killed people on January 13, and that Loreta Asanaviciute was not run over by a tank. ​ The Prosecutor General's Office said in December 2023 that the pre-trial investigation had gathered evidence proving that Švenčionienė and Juraitis, acting in a group of accomplices, helped Russia and Belarus and their organisations act against Lithuania on more than one occasion in 2022. ​ Švenčionienė and Juraitis are members of the International Forum of Good Neighbourhood – a now-dissolved organization founded by Algirdas Paleckis, a controversial former politician and diplomat convicted of spying for Russia. ​ Under the Criminal Code, a conviction for aiding a foreign state in acting against Lithuania carries a prison sentence of two to seven years. ​ Denial or gross trivialisation of Soviet crimes is punishable by community service, a fine, restriction of liberty, arrest, or imprisonment for up to two years. ​ Last June, Švenčionienė was convicted in another case, which saw her sentenced to 1.5 years of restriction of liberty for publicly denying Soviet crimes. ​ To date, Juraitis has been convicted twice, and Ivanov – four times. ​ In 2023, Ivanov, a Russian citizen, had his residence permit in Lithuania revoked. Once the guilty verdict is announced and takes effect, he will be required to leave Lithuania.

It was early morning in the US. President Valdas Adamkus, who was visiting Washington, was hurried to a secure shelter, while in Vilnius, senior officials gathered for an unscheduled meeting to discuss the country’s security situation. Based on archive reports from Panorama, this article reconstructs the issues that dominated life in Lithuania in September 2001, the country’s response to the terrorist attacks and how Lithuanians assessed the situation. "It was like a science-fiction film about Armageddon. But this was really happening, in the very heart of the democratic world’s financial centre, next to Wall Street,” Vykintas Pugačiauskas said as he began his dramatic report on September 11, 2001. “As panic-stricken people tried to escape the area around the World Trade Centre, oil and gold prices rose around the world, while the dollar fell," he added. The terrorist attacks also caused concern in Lithuania. That same day, Lithuanian officials and heads of the country’s security and law-enforcement institutions gathered for an unscheduled meeting with then Prime Minister Algirdas Mykolas Brazauskas. Although it was decided not to declare a state of emergency in Lithuania, then parliamentary speaker Artūras Paulauskas told journalists there was "some worrying information", but declined to elaborate. Prime Minister Brazauskas said at the time that the situation was not dangerous, but additional measures would be taken. Following the meeting, security at strategic sites was increased. The biggest security operation was at the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant: access to the surrounding area was restricted without special permits, while armed officers carried out regular patrols. Increased attention was also given to the Port of Klaipėda and the international ferry terminal, while ships patrolled the waters. Following the attacks, additional security measures were also introduced at Vilnius Airport. The terrorist attacks brought transatlantic air travel to a halt both in Lithuania and around the world. As a result, large numbers of passengers were stranded at airports. Lithuania was no exception – at the time, an average of about 50 people travelled to the US every day on connecting flights. The terrorist attacks also pushed up fuel prices. According to the report, the price of petrol rose by five cents. A petrol station representative said fuel sales had increased by 25%. However, no major economic shocks were observed in the first few days. Banks also saw increased demand for European Union currencies and, somewhat surprisingly, the Lithuanian litas. During this period, people were exchanging US dollars for litas. In 2001, Lithuania was making major efforts to join NATO. It was therefore not surprising that visits by the country's leaders to the US were frequent. Before the trip, President Valdas Adamkus said he expected his visit to Washington to be one of the most challenging of his entire presidency. That morning, Adamkus and the Lithuanian delegation attended a working breakfast with representatives of American Jewish organisations, where the threat of terrorism was also discussed. It was during this breakfast that news of the attacks first broke. The presidential delegation was taken to a shelter in the basement of the hotel. Later, the entire delegation moved to the Lithuanian embassy in Washington, which was considered a safer location. Because of the situation, the planned visit was cut short by four days. Interestingly, the delegation was also among the first passengers to be allowed to board a transatlantic flight from the US after the attacks. The delegation became passengers on the first transatlantic flight after the terrorist attacks. The US authorities also provided a military aircraft to fly the delegation to Reykjavik. From there, they transferred to a Lithuanian Airlines aircraft and reached Vilnius Airport at 04:00 on September 13. After returning to Lithuania, Adamkus said the attacks would not make Lithuania’s path to NATO more difficult and could, on the contrary, make it easier. The day after his return to Lithuania, the president issued a special address in which he spoke about the events of September 11 and their significance for Lithuania. The president also expressed his full support for US action and spoke about changes in international politics. "September 11 shook and changed the world. We, the people of Lithuania, also need to fully understand these changes. In a single day, our world became more fragile and vulnerable, as even the most powerful country in the world proved to be vulnerable," Adamkus said in his address to the nation on September 14. The speech prompted a range of reactions. People interviewed in the streets of Lithuanian cities disagreed with the position expressed by the president and pointed to the theme of revenge in his speech. Many of those interviewed also referred to Lithuania’s small size and limited influence. "I would say we should refrain from that. We are a small country, and no one will defend us. We will exhaust our own strength for the sake of others, and there will be nothing left for us," one woman told reporters. Opinions and assessments varied. It is important to remember that at the time, Lithuania’s prospects of joining NATO and the European Union were viewed in very different ways. While some saw membership as Lithuania’s steady return to the West, others associated it with an increased threat. Nevertheless, the government at the time continued the integration process and supported the implementation of Article 5 of the Washington Treaty. But it was the possibility of further attacks that caused the greatest concern. As reports spread about the possible use of biological weapons, Panorama journalists looked into the situation in Lithuania’s laboratories. What was Lithuania living through before the attacks? Lithuania’s authorities have issued an all-clear (code white) following an earlier air alert warning over a potential drone sighting, which later turned out to be a flock of birds. “The Lithuanian Armed Forces inform: AIR ALERT IS OVER (WHITE). You may leave safe places or shelters,” the authorities said in an emergency message on Sunday afternoon. The yellow air alert over a potential drone sighting was issued on Sunday at around 13:00 local time in Vilnius and the surrounding region, as well as the Trakai and Elektrėnai regions. Flights at Vilnius Airport were temporarily suspended. The yellow alert meant there was no danger yet, but people were advised to locate their nearest shelter in case the threat level was elevated to code red. The authorities later clarified that NATO jets confirmed the radar sighting was a flock of birds.

Ukraine and Poland, two Central and Eastern European states whose regional influence has often been underestimated, illustrate how middle powers can shape outcomes once reserved for great powers, Maksym Khylko and Adam Reichard write for the New Eastern Europe Magazine, partners of LRT English. In January 2026, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney used the podium of the World Economic Forum in Davos to warn that the world was living through “a rupture, not a transition” in the international order, in which great powers increasingly treat economic interdependence, tariffs and supply chains as instruments of coercion. His central claim – that middle powers are not powerless but must act together or risk being “on the menu” rather than at the table – has become a reference point for a broader debate about the future of democracies in the changing world order. Scholars and analysts from Central and Eastern Europe have converged on a similar diagnosis. In a special 2026 edition of New Eastern Europe dedicated to this new disorder, Andreas Umland argues that the world as we know it is nearing its end and is increasingly being displaced by a system that presents itself openly as non-liberal, if not outright anti-liberal, reflecting the shifting preferences of powerful leaders. Wojciech Michnik links this trend to the fate of European security, arguing that the sense of Europe adrift in the emerging order stems from both external shocks and internal shortcomings: on the one side, the United States is signalling that Europe is no longer the central theatre of American strategy; on the other, Europeans themselves remain divided over how far they are willing to go in assuming strategic autonomy. Paul Bell frames the resulting predicament starkly, describing Europe as sandwiched between autocrats who, for their own distinct purposes, are each working to weaken it, undermine European policy and democratic values. The case for European strategic autonomy rests on a structural observation: no single EU member state, and arguably not the Union as a whole in its current institutional configuration, possesses the sovereign capability to guarantee its security, prosperity or technological relevance if the assumptions underlying transatlantic and global economic integration continue to erode. Discussing EU strategic autonomy as independence (disengagement from external dependence), as responsibility (binding more closely with like-minded partners to jointly resist coercion), and as hedging (preserving room for manoeuvre between rival powers), Daniel Fiott argues that the EU’s ability to resist being wedged apart by Washington or Beijing depends less on a top-down Brussels-led strategy than on internal binding efforts among member states. When considering the role of middle powers in this context, the Central and Eastern European states play key roles: Ukraine’s resistance to the Russian invasion has served as the external shock that pushed EU member states towards a more responsibility-oriented posture, while Poland has played an important role in anchoring the Union’s defence posture around this model of autonomy, particularly at the initial stage of providing assistance to Ukraine and, in parallel, unprecedented investments in its own defence. Ukraine, Poland, and the EU: middle powers in practice The concept of the middle power has a long lineage in international relations theory, dating to debates at the founding of the United Nations, when Canadian and Australian diplomats sought recognition for states that, while lacking great-power capability, made disproportionate contributions to the war effort and collective security architecture. A middle power is generally understood as a state occupying an intermediate position in the international hierarchy: it lacks the capacity of a great power to determine systemic outcomes unilaterally, but possesses sufficient economic, military, diplomatic or normative resources to shape outcomes within a region or issue-area, typically through coalition-building and multilateralism rather than coercion. Eduard Jordaan’s influential distinction between “traditional” middle powers – wealthy and stable democratic states, which tend to legitimise the existing order – and “emerging” middle powers, which are often semi-peripheral, more assertive regionally, and less committed to defending a status quo that historically marginalised them, remains analytically useful today. This distinction helps to comprehend the phenomenon of the rise of authoritarian and illiberal middle powers, in particular in the Middle East and Asia, which combine regional assertiveness with a transactional, sovereigntist posture toward international institutions. Thus, the challenge facing the EU is not simply that great powers behave without constraint, but that the “middle tier” of the international system, once assumed to be a natural constituency for a rules-based order, is itself becoming ideologically heterogeneous and, in some cases, corrosive of that order. Against this backdrop, it is in the EU’s vital interest to support the development and cooperation of democratically-oriented middle powers. Ukraine and Poland are critical cases in this regard. Over the last four-plus years, Ukraine has offered a vivid illustration that a middle power can confront a far greater one and avoid defeat. Despite Russia’s overwhelming advantages in population, military-industrial capacity and nuclear status, Ukraine has not only resisted conquest since February 2022, but has imposed disproportionate costs on the aggressor, including long-range strikes deep inside Russian territory that have unsettled Moscow’s calculations and prompted the previously sceptical Donald Trump to change his stance on Kyiv’s chances. While Ukraine’s resilience has depended on external support, its agency in whole-of-society mobilisation, drone-warfare innovation, and asymmetric strategy has been decisive. Lithuanian authorities are investigating an unidentified object, likely a stray drone, that crossed 60 to 70 kilometres through the country’s airspace early Sunday. Meanwhile, an air alert that was issued Sunday afternoon in eastern areas of the country was probably triggered by birds. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre, said several scenarios were being considered and that investigators could have more information as early as Monday. “A stray drone is probably one of the possible scenarios, as we’ve seen before,” Vitkauskas told reporters Sunday. “Another possibility is that it could be related to smuggling [...] smugglers’ aircraft do occur as well. It could be a hostile reconnaissance flight.” “There are various versions, certainly a great many,” he added. Lithuanian military radars detected the object at about 04:05 Sunday morning near Varėna in southern Lithuania. The military said the object travelled across Lithuanian territory before entering the airspace of Russia’s Kaliningrad region and likely came from Belarus. Vitkauskas told LRT RADIO that morning that the object was most likely a drone. The Lithuanian Armed Forces said available data was insufficient to establish exactly what the object was. No immediate threat to residents or property was identified. Authorities were analysing radar data and other parameters to determine how the object operated before, during and after its incursion into Lithuanian airspace, Vitkauskas said. Lithuania has previously recorded several incursions by Ukrainian drones carrying explosives that authorities said may have been diverted or disoriented by Russian electronic warfare. Seven such drones have entered Lithuanian airspace in recent years. Afternoon air alert was triggered by birds A separate air threat alert issued Sunday afternoon in Vilnius and surrounding areas turned out to be a false alarm after the detected objects were identified as a flock of birds. The yellow-level alert lasted about 38 minutes, from 12:59 to 13:37, in Vilnius and Vilnius district, as well as the districts of Trakai and Elektrėnai. NATO fighter jets were scrambled in response. Vitkauskas said the rapid response demonstrated that Lithuania’s procedures for dealing with potential air threats were working. “The defence mission activated from Šiauliai; there was a rapid response, and the objects were identified,” he said. He expressed regret that authorities were unable to establish sooner that the objects were birds rather than a potential threat. “To sum up, I think we did a good job of issuing the alerts,” Vitkauskas said. “Of course, it’s a pity that we weren’t able to identify even sooner that it was a bird and not some object posing a threat.” Emergency notifications about both the alert and its cancellation were sent to residents’ mobile phones within minutes, he said. The incident also provided an opportunity to test emergency information procedures involving mobile alerts, radio and television. “I think this system worked quite well,” Vitkauskas said, adding that residents responded calmly and authorities saw no crowds or panic. Vilnius Airport temporarily suspended operations during the alert, affecting three flights. Defence minister critical of military’s response Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas says he is not satisfied with the explanations provided by armed forces representatives as to why the public were not informed about a possible air threat detected by radar Sunday morning. “This morning I was provided with information regarding a possible airspace violation in Lithuania [Sunday] morning. I was not satisfied with that information; it does not answer all the questions, and there are certainly still questions remaining,” Kaunas told journalists on Monday. “I have asked for a working group of experts to be set up, comprising both the Deputy Minister overseeing the working group and representatives from the General Inspectorate and the Lithuanian Armed Forces, so that by tomorrow evening an analysis and a chronology can be provided detailing exactly what happened, how it happened, and why certain decisions were taken,” he said. According to him, the working group’s conclusions will show whether the algorithm for responding to potential air threats needs to be improved, and how specifically this should be done.

Some politicians are proposing a gradual shift away from Russian-language instruction in schools serving the country’s Russian-speaking minority, with a proposal to teach all subjects in Lithuanian except the students’ native language by 2030. The Education Ministry says it supports increasing the use of Lithuanian in minority schools to promote better integration into Lithuanian society. The proposed changes, however, would not apply to schools where instruction is conducted exclusively in Polish. Under the proposal, put forward by the opposition conservative Homeland Union (TS-LKD), social studies subjects including history, geography and civic education would be taught exclusively in Lithuanian at Russian-language schools beginning in 2028. Two years later, all subjects except the native language would be taught in Lithuanian. The proposal is justified by pointing to significantly weaker results among minority-language students on Lithuania’s state Lithuanian-language school-leaving examination. Students who fail the state-level Lithuanian exam face barriers to pursuing higher education. Education expert Arūnas Šileris said many minority students currently choose a lower-level B exam, which has a higher pass rate but does not provide eligibility for higher education. “We care about the child and their future in Lithuania, so that they can successfully move forward in life and establish themselves, regardless of whether they belong to a national minority,” said Laurynas Kasčiūnas, chairman of the TS-LKD. At the Konstanty Parczewski High School in Nemenčinė, in the Vilnius district, instruction is provided in both Polish and Russian. Sixty-five students, including 10 Ukrainians, study in Russian. Principal Renata Krasowska said Russian-speaking students take only their native-language classes in Russian, while other subjects are taught together with Polish-speaking students. At Aitvaras High School in Klaipėda, mixed classes are taught in Russian and Lithuanian. Beginning this school year, life skills, ethics and physical education have been taught in Lithuanian. History and geography are also taught in Lithuanian, as required by education law. Principal Marina Ustinova said the proposed changes could create better conditions for students to learn the state language but warned that implementing the full model by 2030 would be a major challenge for education policymakers. The ruling Social Democratic Party says the goal is justified but questions whether the education system has enough teachers, textbooks and updated curricula to implement the changes. “We will need to assess whether Lithuanian-language teachers are prepared and what will happen with children who started under the previous model,” said lawmaker Jurgita Šukevičienė. Krasowska said her school would implement any changes adopted at the national level. The Education, Science and Sports Ministry will consider the proposal to phase out Russian-language instruction. Deputy Education Minister Jonas Petkevičius said the ministry believes students from national minorities should receive more instruction in Lithuanian to improve their integration into Lithuanian society. The government is also considering a requirement that children of foreign nationals study only in Lithuanian and attend Lithuanian-language schools and kindergartens. Kasčiūnas said the proposal specifically targets Russian-language institutions and does not extend to Polish-language schools, citing Lithuania’s treaty with Poland regarding the Polish minority. He also argues that Polish being an official EU language justifies Lithuania treating its Polish- and Russian-speaking minorities differently. Russians are Lithuania’s second-biggest ethnic minority comprising just over 5% of the population, according to the 2021 census.

Heavy alcohol consumption has increased in Lithuania over the past five years, while tobacco use has also risen slightly, according to a government study released Monday. The study by Lithuania’s Department of Drug, Tobacco and Alcohol Control found that 11.2% of respondents said they consume six or more standard alcoholic drinks at least once a week. That compares with 7.1% in 2021. “Compared with 2021, this indicator has increased slightly this year, and we also see that men are more likely to consume alcohol excessively than women,” Aura Rutkauskė, a senior specialist at the department’s monitoring and analysis division, said at a conference presenting the findings. At the same time, the share of Lithuanians who drink alcohol more moderately has declined. Nearly three-quarters of respondents said they had consumed alcohol during the previous 12 months, compared with 84.4% in 2021. The share who had consumed alcohol during the previous 30 days fell to 57.5% from 62.8%. The study defines excessive drinking as consuming six or more standard alcohol units on a single occasion. One standard unit contains roughly the amount of pure alcohol found in 200 millilitres of beer, 100 millilitres of wine or 25 millilitres of spirits. Beer and cider remained the most popular alcoholic drinks. Some 2.9% of respondents said they consumed them at least four times a week, 9.6% two or three times a week and 17.6% two to four times a month. Tobacco use has also increased slightly. The proportion of respondents who had tried tobacco at least once in their lives rose to 73.3% this year from 65.2% in 2021. Respondents reported smoking an average of 12 cigarettes a day, up marginally from 11.9 in 2021. Men reported smoking more cigarettes per day than women. Traditional tobacco products, including cigarettes, cigars and pipes, remained the most widely used nicotine products, with 60.7% saying they had tried them. Electronic cigarettes ranked second, with 31.3% having tried them. E-cigarette use was particularly common among younger respondents. Among those ages 15 to 34, 51.4% said they had tried electronic cigarettes at least once. The average age at which respondents began smoking was 18, up from 17 in 2021. The survey, funded by the European Union Drugs Agency, was conducted from January 21 to March 29 among 4,670 permanent residents ages 15 to 64. It is Lithuania’s sixth nationally representative study on psychoactive substance use since 2004.

The device was discovered and safely recovered by military personnel in the village of Rusinowo in the West Pomeranian province, near the coastal town of Jaroslawiec, according to the minister. TVP World has reported the discovery. “Military personnel detected and pulled a DRONE from the Baltic Sea in the beach area of Rusinowo, near Jaroslawiec,” Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X. ‼️W rejonie plaży w miejscowości Rusinowo koło Jarosławca wojsko zlokalizowało i podjęło z morza Bałtyckiego DRONA. Wstępne oględziny wskazują, że to bezzałogowiec wojskowy pochodzący z Rosji. Na miejscu służby realizują czynności związane z zabezpieczeniem miejsca zdarzenia i… He said an initial examination indicated that the aircraft was of Russian military origin. “An initial examination shows that it is a Russian-made military unmanned aircraft,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said, adding that security personnel were securing the scene and the recovered equipment.

US President Donald Trump’s special envoy for Belarus, John Coale, is visiting Lithuania on Monday and met with Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys, Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said. Budrys thanked the Trump administration for its continued efforts to secure the release of political prisoners held by Belarusian authorities. “The release of political prisoners is an extremely important humanitarian goal,” Budrys said in a statement. “We value the leadership of the United States and its efforts to restore freedom to people who have been unlawfully imprisoned because of their views and civic activities.” Budrys said Lithuania would continue providing necessary support for US humanitarian efforts and for political prisoners who are released. He welcomed each release but said the overall number of political prisoners in Belarus remains high and repression of civil society continues. Budrys also said Belarus remains closely integrated into Russia’s military and security structures, continues to support Russia’s war against Ukraine and contributes to military pressure on the West. The two officials also discussed challenges posed by irregular migration from Belarus. Budrys said that after a temporary decline at the beginning of the summer, the flow of migrants has begun increasing again, while the scale of secondary migration through Latvia is also growing. Coale last visited Minsk in March, when Belarus released 250 political prisoners. After that visit, the US envoy urged Lithuania to restore the transit of Belarusian fertilisers and hold a high-level meeting with Minsk. Independent Belarusian news outlet Zerkalo reported that Coale’s visits this week are aimed at securing the release of another group of prisoners, potentially numbering several hundred people.

Vilnius International Airport temporarily suspended operations around 11:00 Tuesday after an unidentified object was detected on radar, Lithuanian authorities said. Traffic was resumed about 30 minutes later. Darius Buta, a spokesman for the National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC), told the BNS news agency that fighter jets participating in NATO’s air policing mission were scrambled in response to the detection. He later said no danger was detected “No dangerous objects have been found. The fighter jets [from the NATO Air Defence Mission] are returning to base. The risks have been properly assessed; no warnings have been issued to the public.” Lithuanian Airports (LTOU) has confirmed to LRT.lt that traffic was suspended at Vilnius Airport. Information on the Vilnius Airport website indicates that a flight from Catania, Italy, operated by Wizz Air, was cancelled. The plane was scheduled to land at 12:25.

Residents of a Lithuanian village where NATO air policing fighters shot down a drone in the early hours of Tuesday described a tense night of explosions, aircraft and flashing lights that left some fearing the worst. The drone was destroyed near the village of Pratkūnai in the Kaišiadorys district early Tuesday. Residents told LRT.lt they heard the drone and military aircraft before and after it was intercepted. Vitalija, a local resident, said she heard the sound of the drone flying overhead. “It was a strong sound, as if a war had started. There was also a light,” she said. Another resident, Virginija, said she was anxious despite having received similar warnings before. “We’re already used to it. But we really don’t want things to be frightening,” she said Tuesday morning. Kazys, who lives about 2 to 3 kilometres from where the drone was brought down, said an explosion woke him. He said it felt as though his house had shaken. “I could hear a military helicopter flying. I could clearly see it,” Kazys said. He described experiencing intense fear during the night. “You can’t imagine it. You can’t put it into words. It wasn’t thunder, it wasn’t something else – it felt like the end of the world. I was terribly frightened. I’ve never been so scared in my life,” he said. Kazys said he also spoke with police during the night and told officers where he thought pieces of the drone might have fallen. He questioned why it took so long for the air-threat warning to reach residents. “It exploded, and 50 minutes later they announced an air threat. What kind of system is that? It’s ridiculous,” he said. At first, he thought two aircraft might have collided because of what he saw in the sky. “There was so much fire, so many sparks and the smell of gunpowder,” he said. Marytė, another resident, said she immediately understood what had happened when she heard a heavy thud. “A dull bang, and that was it. Everything was over. The windows didn’t shake. There was a roar, but not like an airplane. I live in the centre,” she said. “What is there to be afraid of? I’ve lived my life,” she added. Saša, who lives near the cordoned-off area, also heard the explosion. “I heard an explosion at night, around midnight, maybe a little after. Something whooshed, then there was a big explosion,” he said. He received alerts on his phone and saw that a yellow warning had been issued. “We felt uneasy. Then another message came saying the air threat warning had been lifted, and we went back to sleep. It’s unsettling. Something bad is happening,” Saša said. He said the windows did not shake, but the noise was unmistakable. “The sound was quite loud. I could hear it clearly. I thought maybe something in the forest had hit a tree,” he said, adding that military police had already arrived by the time he got up for work early Tuesday. “It’s unpleasant, there’s no question about it. Now you think, ‘Just don’t let it happen to you’, and then it happens right here – especially with a strategic facility nearby,” said Alvydas, another resident, referring to the Kruonis Pumped-Storage Power Plant located several kilometres from where the drone was downed. Not everyone heard the incident. Svajūnas said he slept through the explosion and was awakened only by the emergency alert on his phone. “It’s strange, but I didn’t hear anything,” he said. “The signal came to our phone and woke us up. It had been raining, and I heard what sounded like a roar, but then everything stopped.” The incident marked the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuanian territory. Authorities believe the drone entered Lithuania from neighbouring Belarus.

Global oil prices have surged toward $110 a barrel after Saudi Arabia shut a major oil pipeline following an attack by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, adding to pressure on already high fuel prices in Lithuania. Diesel in Lithuania has cost more than 2 euros a litre since August, while gasoline prices have also continued to rise. The government is preparing measures to ease the burden on households and businesses but has not yet disclosed the details. For drivers, the rising prices are increasingly painful. “There’s no mortal pain, but there’s not much pleasure either. I’d like prices to go back down,” Vytautas, a driver interviewed by LRT TV, said. Another driver criticised the government for failing to act after previously saying that €2 a litre would be a threshold for intervention. “The government has been saying for a long time that €2 would be the limit, and then they would do something. Now it’s already €2.30, I saw diesel at that price. It’s terrible for people,” he said. Energy Minister Lukas Savickas said one possible trigger for reducing fuel taxes could be a sustained increase in the average diesel price. “One element is an average diesel price of €2.20 for at least five consecutive days. That could be a reference point for when we could begin activating a policy of reducing excise duties,” Savickas said. He said the Finance Ministry was preparing the main proposal, but the ministry has not commented publicly on the measures. Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said last week that the government had promised to consider action if oil prices remained at $100 a barrel for at least five days. “That’s only the second day, so let’s wait five days, and then we can talk about what we have mentioned more than once,” Valys told lawmakers. But Brent crude has remained above $100 a barrel since last Wednesday. The average price of gasoline in Lithuania is now slightly above €1.90 a litre, while diesel averages about €2.18. “We already have 20 consecutive days when diesel has averaged more than €2, but gasoline is rapidly catching up,” said Agnė Bagočiūtė, director of the Lithuanian Energy Agency. “That makes us think that other measures may also need to be applied.” Oil prices have risen in response to the closure of a major east-west oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia after it was attacked Friday by Houthi rebels from Yemen. The pipeline has become an important alternative route as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains restricted. Crude transported through the Saudi pipeline is also purchased by Orlen Lietuva, a major oil refinery operating in Lithuania. Savickas said Lithuania was not facing an immediate fuel supply shortage despite the price increases. “It is very important to distinguish between two issues: supply security and prices,” Savickas said. “We have no supply challenges. The Orlen group says it is not experiencing and does not expect any challenges to supply security. But the issue of prices is separate.”

NATO air policing fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight Tuesday, authorities said, prompting temporary warnings of a possible air threat in several municipalities. The defence minister confirmed on Tuesday afternoon that the drone was equipped with an explosive device. The drone was brought down near the village of Pratkūnai in the Kaišiadorys district, about 60 miles west of Vilnius and near the Kaunas Reservoir, the National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC) said. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, NKVC head, told LRT RADIO that the drone most likely entered Lithuania from neighbouring Belarus. It remained in Lithuanian airspace for about half an hour, flying along the outskirts of populated areas before being intercepted. The drone was shot down by Italian troops stationed at the NATO air base in Šiauliai using Eurofighter jets. Military police, regular police and other emergency services were dispatched to the crash site, where they recovered debris overnight, the Lithuanian military said. “The site has been cordoned off and is being guarded, and military and Lithuanian police forces are currently working there,” the military said in a Facebook post. Authorities said they would not draw conclusions about the drone before an investigation was completed. Vitkauskas said officials were collecting the wreckage and had activated Operation Skydas (Shield), a procedure normally used at sites where there is a risk of an explosion. He said there was a high probability the drone carried an explosive charge, although it was not immediately clear whether it was a combat drone. Warnings of a possible air threat were initially sent to residents of Vilnius and the surrounding district, as well as the Trakai and Elektrėnai districts. The warning was later extended to the Kaunas region as the drone continued westward. The alerts were subsequently cancelled. President Gitanas Nausėda thanked NATO allies for their response, saying the readiness of regional defences was vital as Russia intensifies its aggression against Ukraine. “Together with our NATO allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace,” Nausėda said on X. Lithuanian army commander Gen. Raimundas Vaikšnoras said such incidents were linked to Russia’s war against Ukraine. Lithuania has issued several warnings of possible air threats in recent months as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine continues, but Tuesday’s incident marked the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuanian territory. On Sunday, authorities issued a similar warning to residents in southeastern Lithuania after radar operators detected what was later determined to be a flock of birds. Earlier that day, authorities near Varėna detected another object crossing Lithuanian airspace and entering Russia’s Kaliningrad region. It was also believed to have come from Belarus, but officials did not issue an air-threat warning, citing insufficient information.

The US Department of Justice on Tuesday charged five people with organising attacks and killings around the world, including in the United States and Lithuania, as part of a global network prosecutors say has operated on behalf of Russian intelligence services since at least 2024. The network most recently sought to recruit people in the United States to surveil and kill Russian dissidents at the direction of the Kremlin, according to an indictment released by the department. Prosecutors also allege that members of the network recruited and paid others to carry out or attempt terrorist attacks against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries supporting Ukraine. Three of the defendants are alleged to be senior members of the Russian intelligence network: former Russian intelligence Col. Yuri Khrameyev; his son, Kirill Khrameyev, an officer with Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB; and Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a Cuban citizen living in Russia. The other two defendants, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro, are alleged recruiters based in the United States who worked for the Russian spy network. In one case, prosecutors allege that this summer Delgado Suarez and Castro recruited a person living in the United States to surveil a prominent Russian dissident. The person was initially offered between $1,000 and $1,500 for surveillance, followed by an offer of $40,000 to “eliminate” or make the target “disappear”, according to the indictment. The Khrameyevs also allegedly tried in 2025 to recruit a US citizen to kill a person in Lithuania whom they accused of “spreading lies about Russia”. After the US citizen rejected an offer of about $25,000 to carry out the killing, Yuri Khrameyev allegedly proposed what he described as “easier work”, including setting fire to a warehouse or attacking an electrical substation. Khrameyev said the targets were “all countries helping Ukraine” and offered “serious money for serious work”, according to the indictment. Durruthy is accused of coordinating attacks in the Czech Republic and Lithuania in 2024. “These defendants allegedly acted as part of a global murder-for-hire network that reached the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreign nationals to carry out murders at the direction of the Kremlin,” said John Eisenberg, the Justice Department’s assistant attorney general for national security. The charges include conspiracy to provide material support for terrorism, which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. Khrameyev, Delgado Suarez and Castro also face charges of conspiracy to commit murder for hire, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years. US officials said the alleged activities pose a threat to national security. Russia has intensified what Western governments describe as hybrid operations against countries supporting Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. Suspected Russian agents have been accused of espionage, sabotage and attempted assassinations in the United States, Europe and other Western countries. Lithuania’s State Security Department said the US charges illustrate concerns outlined in its national security threat assessments. Lithuanian intelligence has warned that hostile regimes use unconventional methods to influence public opinion, create a sense of insecurity and pressure societies to make decisions beneficial to those regimes. The department said the case also demonstrated the importance of close and consistent cooperation among international partners in responding to hostile countries.

The United States will lift sanctions on two Belarusian companies after Belarus agreed to release 25 political prisoners, US President Donald Trump’s special envoy for Belarus, John Coale, said after talks in Minsk. Coale said the agreement was reached during negotiations with Belarusian officials and described the prisoner releases as a goodwill gesture, according to the independent Belarusian news outlet Zerkalo. “As a goodwill gesture, Belarus will release 25 people. In return, the United States will lift sanctions on two Belarusian companies, Lakokraska and Bellesbumprom,” Coale was quoted as saying by the Telegram channel Pul Pervogo, which is linked to Belarusian authoritarian President Alexander Lukashenko. Coale also said the US delegation had completed its work in Belarus. The two sides discussed international issues, bilateral matters and other issues of mutual importance, and reached an interim agreement, he said. “The parties will continue working to resolve the remaining issues,” Coale said. “When all the issues are resolved and agreed upon by both sides, additional people will be released and sanctions on Belarusian companies will be lifted.” The announcement comes as Washington has sought to improve relations with Minsk while pressing for the release of political prisoners held by Lukashenko’s government. Belarus has faced extensive Western sanctions over its crackdown on political opposition and civil society, as well as its support for Russia’s war against Ukraine.

A Russian-made Gerbera drone shot down over central Lithuania early Tuesday was apparently headed for Ukraine but veered off course after being affected by Ukrainian electronic warfare, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Wednesday. “Based on the information currently available, it was a Gerbera-type drone,” Nausėda told reporters after a meeting of Lithuania’s State Defence Council. The president said the incident was most likely not a deliberate attack against Lithuania. “Most likely, it was a Russian drone intended for Ukraine that was diverted from its course by Ukrainian electronic warfare measures and entered our territory, where it was shot down,” Nausėda said. The drone entered Lithuania from Belarus and was shot down in the Kaišiadorys district, near the Kruonis pumped-storage hydropower plant, by Italian fighter jets stationed at NATO’s air base in Šiauliai, according to Lithuanian officials. Residents in the Vilnius and Kaunas regions received alerts warning of a possible air threat as the drone crossed Lithuanian territory. Nausėda warned that similar incidents could happen again and said Lithuania needed to improve its ability to identify drones and other airborne objects approaching from abroad. “Vilnius is close to the border, and, undoubtedly, once we identify and detect them, we could and should have the means to destroy drones or other flying objects,” he said. But the president said Lithuania also needed alternative ways of bringing down drones because using fighter jets was not an efficient solution. The incident was the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuanian territory as Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues. Similar incidents have previously occurred in Latvia and Estonia. Lithuania has issued several air-threat alerts in recent months. On Sunday, residents in parts of southeastern Lithuania received an alert about a possible air threat, but authorities later determined that radar systems had detected a flock of birds. Earlier Sunday, authorities near Varėna, in southern Lithuania, also detected an unidentified object crossing Lithuanian airspace and possibly entering Russia’s Kaliningrad region. The object was believed to have come from Belarus. No air-threat alert was issued because authorities said they lacked sufficient information about the object.

An investigation into a drone shot down by NATO fighter jets after it entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus will take time as authorities work to identify the aircraft and determine its flight path and possible launch site, Lithuania’s defence minister said Wednesday. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said specialists needed to thoroughly examine the recovered debris before drawing conclusions about the drone’s origin. “The investigation will take some time, as the recovered debris must be thoroughly analysed,” Kaunas told LRT RADIO. He noted that drones of different types can be made from similar materials, making it necessary to examine their engines and other technical components. Equipment will also be needed to reconstruct the drone’s flight path and determine where it may have been launched, he said. “The engine is important, as are other engineering and technical components, so that our specialists can accurately assess all the circumstances,” Kaunas said. The minister also said Lithuania had agreed to cooperate and exchange information with Poland, which reported finding a crashed drone of unknown origin on its Baltic Sea coast on Monday. Kaunas declined to confirm speculation that the drone shot down in Lithuania was Russian, saying there was not yet enough evidence to support that conclusion. “Russia is carrying out provocations in NATO countries,” he said, adding that some countries, including Germany, have publicly attributed provocations on their territory to Russia. “Once we receive precise data on all incidents, we will state just as clearly who is behind them,” Kaunas said. “We simply do not want to speculate; we want to investigate this very precisely and present all the information backed by evidence.” The drone entered Lithuania early Tuesday from Belarus and was shot down in the Kaišiadorys district of central Lithuania by Italian fighter jets stationed at the NATO air base in Šiauliai. Lithuanian bomb disposal experts later defused an explosive charge carried by the unmanned aircraft. Lithuanian authorities have repeatedly issued alerts about potential air threats in recent months as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues. Tuesday’s incident, however, was the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuanian territory. NATO fighter jets shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May, marking the first interception of a foreign drone by NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. In June, French fighter jets participating in the mission shot down a drone over Latvia, the first such incident in Latvian airspace.

NATO will not be intimidated by Russia, Germany’s foreign minister said Tuesday after Italian fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, speaking during a visit to the United Nations headquarters in Geneva, said the incident again demonstrated what he described as Russia’s hostility toward NATO allies. “We have once again seen Russia’s hostility toward NATO allies,” Wadephul said, according to German news agency dpa. “This once again proves what Russia is trying to do: It wants to divide us and create confusion, and it must not succeed in achieving either of these goals,” he added. “We will not be intimidated,” Wadephul said, adding that NATO had demonstrated it could repel such attacks. The comments came after a drone that flew into Lithuania from Belarus was shot down by Italian fighter jets stationed at an air base in Šiauliai, northern Lithuania, early Tuesday. The drone was brought down in the Kaišiadorys district, near the Kruonis pumped-storage power plant. As the drone flew through Lithuanian territory, residents in the Vilnius and Kaunas regions received emergency alerts warning of a possible air threat. No damage or injuries were reported. Authorities are investigating the drone debris. The NATO operation was coordinated from the Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany, Allied Air Command said.

Two years ago, a Cuban man living in Russia allegedly helped organise a terrorist attack in Lithuania on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, an international investigation has uncovered. Oemis Romagoza Durruthy was behind the attempted arson of a Šiauliai company’s yard, where equipment designed to detect drones was being stored for delivery to Ukraine. Information gathered by an international team of journalists now indicates that Romagoza Durruthy may also have organised at least three other attacks in European countries through a wider network of Latin Americans recruited online. As Russia’s threats toward Western Europe have intensified, the investigation has uncovered how a Cuban salsa teacher who built a family in Russia allegedly used social media to recruit people looking for work and draw them into a terrorist network. This investigation is a cooperation of LRT (Lithuania), Deutsche Welle (Germany), the investigative journalists of the Czech public broadcaster, and the EBU Investigative Journalism Network. Lithuania has detained seven people suspected of terrorist activity. International arrest warrants have been issued for three others, including Romagoza Durruthy. One of the wanted suspects, a Cuban woman, was detained in Panama this year. The investigation, which lasted more than a year, was conducted by an international group of investigative journalists. Lithuanian law enforcement agencies have not commented on investigations involving terrorist attacks in Europe allegedly coordinated by Russian intelligence services. The journalists, however, have pieced together details of the alleged GRU operation. In Panemunė, a small Lithuanian border town connected by a bridge across the Nemunas River to the road from Russia’s Kaliningrad region, several taxi drivers wait beside their cars. During two hours of filming, not a single customer appeared. Only a handful of people crossed the bridge on foot from the Russian town of Sovetsk into Lithuania. Such a quiet day is more the exception than the rule. More than 40,000 travellers from Russia entered Lithuania through the Panemunė border crossing in 2024 and 2025. Most were Russian citizens, but they were not the only people using the crossing. Taxi drivers wait for all kinds of customers, both people who happen to need a ride and those who book cars in advance. From the remote border town, a taxi is often virtually the only way to travel onward. One driver, identified as Romas, had two advance bookings exactly two years ago, in September 2024. Late on September 8, his taxi was used by Mayra Eukaris de la Lastra Nistal, a Cuban woman living in Russia. Two weeks later, around noon on September 23, another woman, Yexenia Lopez Cabrera, also booked a taxi. Romas drove both women along the same route: to Šiauliai and the premises of TVC Solutions. Between those two journeys, on September 17 and September 22, attempts were made to set fire to newly manufactured mobile radio-frequency spectrum-analysis stations stored at the company’s property. The equipment, which can also be used to detect drones, was intended for Ukraine. TVC Solutions had already completed more than half of its order, according to company director Ramūnas Dirmeikis, 18 of 30 stations. Law enforcement documents put their value at more than 1.5 million euros. A potentially much more serious incident was prevented only because the flammable liquid burned out and the fire went out immediately next to the equipment without spreading to it. The perpetrators had already left the property. “They saw that the flames were burning and did not wait,” Artūras Urbelis, deputy prosecutor general, said at a news conference. “They filmed themselves by the fire and dispersed. Thank God that nature and other circumstances helped us.” The people who arrived from Russia and Europe According to law enforcement documents, the two Cuban women brought to Šiauliai by Romas had been recruited into a criminal group. One of them managed to leave Lithuania and was placed on an international wanted list. According to the latest information, she was detained in Panama this year. Lopez Cabrera did not escape. She remains in Šiauliai prison while her trial proceeds. She is being tried alongside five other alleged members of the international saboteur network: Cuban citizen Andres Felipe Diaz Rivas, Spanish citizen Jose Lopez Aguilar, Belarusian citizen Mark Burda, Russian citizen Yevgeny Omeichenko Velchenko, and Gonzalo de Jesus Ramos Santos, who was recently extradited to Lithuania from Colombia and also holds Russian citizenship. Another suspect, Colombian citizen Carlos Alberto Legarda Devia, is also being held at Šiauliai prison awaiting trial. Authorities believe he was one of the founders of the organised group operating in the interests of Russian special services. The two principal figures alleged to have organised the attack in Šiauliai – Cuban citizens Alexeis Pecora and Oemis Romagoza Durruthy – are being sought internationally. Lithuanian law enforcement authorities have publicly identified Russia’s GRU as being behind the organised group. An international journalistic investigation found that, from May through September 2024, Romagoza Durruthy coordinated and commissioned attacks in the Czech Republic, Poland, Romania and Lithuania. His social media accounts targeted mainly Latin Americans who had the right to travel within the Schengen area. The investigation found that the network generally recruited operatives through social media groups, particularly on Telegram and Facebook. Lithuanian authorities have said that TVC Solutions’ yard and the equipment intended for Ukraine were targeted twice, on September 17 and September 22, 2024. Dirmeikis confirmed that police had warned the company before the attacks that authorities were interested in activity around its property.
