A drone was found Wednesday in a forest in northern Lithuania, likely crashed months ago, prompting authorities to activate a bomb-response plan and send bomb disposal experts to the site, police said. The police later specified the drone appeared to have been used for smuggling and did not carry any explosives. The drone was discovered at about 13:06 in a forest near Keneliai village in Pasvalys district, according to the Police Department. Police said the drone was overgrown with grass and preliminary information indicated it had fallen several months ago. The military and bomb disposal specialists from the police’s Aras anti-terrorist operations unit were dispatched to the site. Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC) said the drone did not resemble Russian Shahed or Gerbera military drones. Police spokesman Ramūnas Matonis told BNS that a photograph sent by officers showed the drone appeared to be intact rather than crashed or heavily damaged. It was found by a forester. Police said the drone is about 2 metres long, with a wingspan of about 2.5 metres. Authorities said more details about the drone would be provided after the site is examined. Giedrius Bronušas, head of the Panevėžys regional branch of the State Forest Service, explained that foresters were clearing areas with fallen trees when they discovered a drone approximately three metres wide. “It’s a forest there. We were carrying out our usual work after the storm: we’d surveyed the areas, were preparing to clear windthrow and were preparing timber for felling. Whilst doing this work, a forester walked over and spotted the drone in the grass. Whether it had become overgrown or had landed in the grass as it fell, I do not know, but in any case it was found in the forest in the grass. According to the forester, it is about three metres wide and shaped like an aeroplane,” Bronušas told LRT.lt. “The area is now cordoned off by the police; officers are on guard, the Military Police have arrived, and no civilians are being allowed into the area. But the drone looked more or less intact; it has retained its shape, with clearly defined wings and a distinct fuselage,” he added. Ieva Petrauskaitė, head of Pumpėnai Eldership, thus described the are where the drone was discovered: “It’s a rather remote spot, with just a few residents and a couple of farmsteads; the rest is woodland and farmland.”

Twenty-five political prisoners released from Belarus with US mediation arrived in Lithuania on Wednesday, Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said. None of those released are Lithuanian citizens, the ministry said. Lithuanian authorities assisted with border-crossing procedures and are ensuring the prisoners’ safe travel from the border to their accommodation, the ministry said. Some of those released did not have identity documents. Medical personnel were also on standby to provide assistance if needed. Among those released are independent Belarusian journalists and other public figures, including Liudmila Chekina, the former general director of independent news outlet Tut.by; Pavel Belavus, founder of Art Siadziba and Symbal.by, a store selling national symbols and souvenirs; journalist and media executive Andrei Aliaksandrav; political scientist Tatsiana Kuzina; and Dzmitry Navazhylau, director of the BelaPAN news agency. The release was agreed during a visit to Belarus by John Coale, US President Donald Trump’s special envoy to Belarus, according to Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya’s adviser Dzianis Kuchynski. As part of the agreement, Washington will lift sanctions on Belarusian paint manufacturer Lakokraska and forestry conglomerate Bellesbumprom. Hundreds of people remain imprisoned in Belarus after authoritarian President Alexander Lukashenko, who has been in power since 1994, suppressed mass protests following his disputed re-election in 2020. Washington has renewed dialogue with Minsk and eased some sanctions since Trump returned to the White House. Dozens of political prisoners have been released following Coale’s visits to Belarus. Viasna, an independent Belarusian human rights organisation that monitors arrests in the country, says 912 people are currently recognised as political prisoners. They include protesters and other civilians, journalists, trade union representatives and people linked to the political opposition. Human rights defenders and activists have warned that while the authorities have released some prisoners, others continue to be arrested and jailed. Before traveling to Belarus this week, Coale visited Lithuania and met with Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys. Coale last visited Minsk in March, when Belarus released 250 political prisoners. After that visit, the US envoy urged Lithuania to restore the transit of Belarusian fertilisers and called for a deputy-minister-level meeting between Lithuania and Belarus.

Lithuanian drone maker RSI Europe plans to invest up to 50 million euros in a new factory in central Lithuania, shifting its focus from developing defence technology to industrial-scale production, the company’s chief executive said Thursday. RSI Europe and Lithuania’s Ministry of Economy and Innovation signed an investment agreement for the facility, which will develop and manufacture defence systems in Panevėžys district. “This is a major step for RSI Europe from technology development toward industrialisation and rapid capacity expansion,” CEO Tomas Milašauskas said at the signing ceremony. The factory is expected to create up to 40 jobs, with about 35% of them for highly qualified engineering and technical specialists, Economy Minister Edvinas Grikšas said. The facility is expected to begin construction early next year, with most of the work completed by the end of 2027, Milašauskas said. “The war in Ukraine has shown that armies need not only the best technologies, but also mass production, industrial scale and, above all, secure supply chains,” he said. The factory will produce complete attack drone systems, including first-person-view, or FPV, drones and about 20 different system elements, according to Milašauskas. RSI Europe already operates a factory in Vilnius with annual production capacity of about 120,000 drone systems. The new facility will not increase that overall capacity, but will allow the company to manufacture more components in Lithuania. The company currently uses more than 400 components and subcomponents in its systems and manufactures only some of them domestically. It imports components from more than 30 countries. “Our total capacity will remain at 120,000, but the range of what we supply will expand,” Milašauskas said. The equipment will meet the needs of the Lithuanian military, although most production will be exported, he said. Current commercial contracts and production plans are primarily based on demand from foreign buyers, while demand in Lithuania is also developing. Milašauskas said speed is critical in the defence industry: “Those defence companies that can quickly make decisions, turn decisions into projects and projects into production are the ones that succeed.” The Panevėžys district site was selected because military manufacturing requires large safety zones, he said. The precise location has not been disclosed. Šarūnas Genys, head of Invest Lithuania’s manufacturing team, said the factory will be built on a state-owned plot reserved for investment. Four such plots, ranging from 42 to 125 hectares, are currently reserved in Panevėžys and Upytė municipalities.

Lithuania’s foreign minister, currently on a visit to the US, said Thursday that he received assurances from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that a reduction in the number of American troops stationed in Lithuania will not last long. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys made the comments after meeting with Rubio in Washington. “We received assurances that this gap, when we have a reduction in US troops, will not last long,” Budrys said in comments distributed by the Foreign Ministry in response to questions from LRT. “All decisions are being coordinated with the Department of War [Department of Defense], the Pentagon, but we expect to hear about them in the near future.” He later said the decision may come within days. “We’re probably talking about days, perhaps the coming weeks; I won’t speculate – they [the US] will make the announcement, but work is proceeding at a rapid pace,” Budrys said on the LRT TV programme Topic of the Day (Dienos tema). Security issues dominated the meeting, Budrys said, but the two officials also discussed the broader regional situation and the war in Ukraine. “We talked about the situation in the region, about US efforts to achieve peace in the war against Ukraine, and about Russia’s intentions and capabilities in the near future,” he said. They also discussed “hybrid” and “kinetic” attacks and incidents in the region, as well as the conditions Lithuania has provided for US troops and decisions expected about their future deployment, Budrys said. The United States is currently reviewing its military presence in Europe. More than 1,000 American troops completed a rotation in Lithuania this summer. While some US personnel remained in the country, Lithuania has not received a clear decision on the arrival of a new rotation. The US has regularly deployed battalion-sized units to Lithuania since 2019. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Washington shifted its military presence in Lithuania to continuous rotational deployments. The reinforced US battalions typically include 1,000 or more troops along with various types of combat equipment. Lithuania has said it is prepared to host as many as 1,500 Americans. During the meeting, Budrys and Rubio signed a bilateral framework agreement on cooperation in the field of critical minerals. “We already hold a huge share of the US market for femtosecond lasers, and we can expand it significantly. And what Secretary Rubio described today – that Lithuania is a ‘photon superpower’ – is something we could be and must be. And this is where we will play a major role in future technological developments in the United States,” said Budrys in a video comment released by the Foreign Ministry. According to the ministry, the agreement aims to strengthen cooperation between the two countries by ensuring a secure and diversified supply of critical raw materials, promoting investment in their extraction and processing, increasing the resilience of supply chains and reducing strategic dependencies. Lithuania intends to contribute to the agreement’s objectives by leveraging its expertise in high-tech manufacturing, advanced technologies, the processing of critical materials and logistics, according to the ministry.

Lithuanian border guards on Thursday evening returned to Russia a 68-year-old Russian citizen who had arrived by the Nemunas River from the Kaliningrad region earlier that day, authorities said. The man was detained in the Pagėgiai municipality at about 13:50 after arriving from Russia and was questioned by officers, State Border Guard Service spokesman Giedrius Mišutis told BNS. “There was no pretrial investigation at that time,” Mišutis said. The man asked for political asylum, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said in a written response to Lrytas.lt, which first reported the incident. However, Lithuanian authorities decided to refuse him entry and return him to Russia. “He is now considered a person who was not admitted to Lithuania and has been returned to Russia under the same procedures as people who are refused entry from Belarus,” Mišutis told BNS. The man was returned through the Panemunė border checkpoint after 19:00. Mišutis said authorities had no information indicating that the man faced a threat in Russia or had any special status that could warrant his admission to the European Union. He was also not considered a member of a vulnerable group, he said. “There was no information about threats to him or any special status and possible admission to the European Union. He was not included in the category of vulnerable persons,” Mišutis said. “A decision was made not to admit this person.” Border guards also took steps to ensure the man’s health after his river crossing, including making sure he had dry clothes, Mišutis said.

What a week it has been! On Sunday afternoon, people in and around Vilnius received air alert warnings about a possible drone sighting. Well, that turned out to be just a flock of birds. However, it turned out that an actual drone had flown across southern Lithuania a little earlier. No alert was issued in that case (the military said the drone posed no immediate danger – and perhaps the sighting occurring at the ungodly hour of 4 AM made them conclude the alert would not be appreciated), which gave the defence minister occasion to voice concerns about public safety and security alert protocols. He later said he was satisfied with the military’s reasoning for not sending out the alert. But then came Tuesday and, right after midnight, another drone was spotted flying from Belarus westwards. NATO fighter jets were scrambled from the air base near Šiauliai to shoot it down just south-east of Kaunas, the first such case in Lithuania (it happened in Latvia this summer). No one was hurt and no property was damaged, although nearby residents reported being seriously frightened . What was the drone and what was its target? Russia hawks issued the predictable “ we will not be intimidated ” statements and calls to up the ante , while the defence minister cautioned that it might take some time before investigators can give reliable answers. Still, the president came forward after a State Defence Council meeting to say it was probably a Russian Gerbera launched towards Ukraine but knocked off course by Ukrainian electronic warfare. As if that was not enough dronefare, Vilnius Airport suspended traffic for half an hour on Tuesday over a suspicious airborne object and foresters discovered a crashed drone in the woods of northern Lithuania. This one, however, appeared to have been used by smugglers and fallen down several months ago. Last Friday, several biker groups decided to show Lithuania’s Muslims – many of them recent migrants – that they are not welcome. They disturbed prayers at a mosque in Kaunas with loud music, revving their bikes, chanting nationalist slogans – and even displaying a pig’s head. The incident brought to the fore developments that have been brewing for quite some time. Besides the usual anti-migrant sentiment, there have been tensions within Lithuania’s Muslim community: the country’s indigenous Muslims, mostly of Tatar descent, have been feeling outnumbered and overwhelmed by the newcomers (this has been used by some right-wing politicians to present their positions as defence of historic Muslims rather than Islamophobia). Moreover, residents around the Kaunas mosque have complained about traffic problems during prayers – a point that has also been invoked in discussions about the bikers’ action. Relatively few political leaders have censured the incident as hate speech, although on Wednesday, around sixty public figures and former politicians published a letter condemning it. Reportedly, police officers were present during the action but refrained from interfering. Under some public pressure, the police have opened an investigation into possible incitement of hatred – having initially treated it as simply an unsanctioned rally. So it’s been an eventful week for Kaunas. On Saturday, it held its second-ever Pride March (the first one happened in 2021), attracting around 500 participants who demanded legal regulation of same-sex partnerships, trans-inclusive healthcare, and LGBTQ+ representation in school curricula. Moreover, Palestinian flags featured prominently at Kaunas Pride, with many participants chanting “no pride in genocide”. This has led to accusations, even from within the LGBTQ­+ community, that the organisers veered too far from the traditional focus of pride events and might have alienated parts of the community. This week, US President Donald Trump’s special envoy for Belarus John Coale made another trip to Minsk – with a stop in Vilnius – brokering a deal exchanging political prisoners for sanctions relief. This time, 25 prisoners were brought to Lithuania on Wednesday, while the US lifted sanctions on two Belarusian companies. This is a significantly smaller batch than before – in March, a similar deal saw the release of ten times as many political prisoners – but Coale said he hoped another one will be concluded soon. Lithuanian leaders, who are notoriously sceptical about any sanctions relief for Belarus, nevertheless thanked Coale for his efforts – while making clear they still didn’t like Lukashenko. This week, Lithuania’s anti-fraud agency carried out several high-profile searches at the National Paying Agency, the main body that disburses the EU’s generous agricultural subsidies. According to reports, the investigation extents to the agency’s director and his deputy, the latter already facing charges of directing EU funds towards his relations. – A Cuban dance teacher allegedly helped organise a terrorist attack in Lithuania on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence agency. LRT Investigation Team reports . – Art unites, art divides. This time, it’s two gilded skulls representing a sixteenth-century love story between the King of Poland and his Lithuanian wife. – The UK’s University of Cambridge is considering establishing a professorship in Lithuanian studies . – Is Lithuania losing its grip on the national sport, basketball ? – Kaunas may beat Vilnius to (re)introducing a new mode of public transit, the tram .

The documentary Letters from the Silenced Country depicts the ongoing repression under the authoritarian regime. Director Andrei Kutsila talked to DW ahead of the film’s Venice premiere. When Belarusians took to the streets in 2020 to protest against the disputed results of the presidential election, hopes were high that the regime of autocratic ruler Alexander Lukashenko would end and Belarusian society would find freedom. But authorities responded with an unprecedented campaign of repression that continues to this day. All forms of dissent have essentially been silenced. In this context, filmmaker Andrei Kutsila directed a new documentary that depicts the state’s system of repression. His film, Letters from the Silenced Country, was co-produced by DW and premieres at the Venice Film Festival on September 9. Like the 300,000 to 500,000 Belarusians who now live in exile, Kutsila realised that he had to leave his home country amid the state’s crackdown on free speech. While he was completing his previous film – the award-winning When Flowers Are Not Silent (2021) on the state’s brutal suppression of demonstrations – different colleagues around him were arrested, he says. Many of them have since been released, “but at the same time, new prisoners are found to keep filling the cells. The situation is not changing; it’s even worse now,” Kutsila tells DW. As the film points out in a postscript card, the human rights organisation Viasna has documented at least 65,000 politically motivated arrests and detentions in Belarus since the 2020 protests. “From the outside, people live their normal lives, but the streets have become quiet, and conversations are reduced to whispers,” says Kutsila. Those who remain in the country can be arrested and sent to prison simply for posting Belarusian symbols of freedom and resistance online, notes the filmmaker. That was one of the reasons that motivated him to make Letters from the Silenced Country. Returning to Belarus to meet and film protagonists in person was not an option, so he looked for an alternative way to portray their situation after the protests. Letters to prisoners became the starting point for Kutsila’s film project. “I read thousands of them,” he says. He then picked stories of individuals – political prisoners, exiles and underground activists – who embodied different aspects of the situation. Belarusian opposition activist and environmental campaigner Vitold Ashurak is one of the film’s protagonists. Sentenced to five years in prison for participating in the protests, Ashurak’s fate is portrayed through his correspondence with friends and family during his imprisonment. Letters from a friend include meticulously selected photographs. Ashurak finds brief moments of mental freedom in these pictures, while the same images are also poetically embedded in the film. But CCTV footage showing prison guards beating inmates brings viewers back to the brutal reality: Vitold Ashurak died under suspicious circumstances while in custody. His name is remembered as a symbol of the state’s repression. The film also includes animated sequences based on drawings by young student Kasia Budzko, who was sentenced to two and a half years in prison for participating in protests. Another protagonist in the film is Andrei Ostapovich, a former criminal investigator. In August 2020, he left his position, writing a letter of resignation in which he denounced the police officers’ brutality against protesters. As one of the first security officials who publicly and categorically opposed the Belarusian regime, Ostapovich fled the country – facing many perilous detours. In one scene of Letters from the Silenced Country, Ostapovich is asked if, after everything he’s been through and witnessed, he still believes in a free Belarus. After much hesitation, his only response is a sigh of resignation. Filmmaker Andrei Kutsila shares this ambivalence: “Of course, it’s in a way my perspective too, as I tried to express my feelings through my protagonists.” But Kutsila focuses on long-term progress, adding: “History is the foundation on which we can build a free country.” “You know, 200 years ago Belarus didn’t even exist on a map,” he points out. There have been struggles to free the country ever since: “So from this long-term perspective, there is a lot of hope.” “No matter how awful the situation is, the only thing that can empower and give us hope is solidarity, connection between people and love. So these are the things giving us hope,” notes Kutsila. “And the film, I think, shows this.”

Deep in the forests of central Lithuania, along the banks of the Lietava River, stands an ornate wooden church that seems almost out of place in the wilderness. There are no houses around it. No permanent residents. The road leading to the site winds through remote forest and is difficult to navigate. Yet the church remains – carefully maintained, its carved wooden details preserved, its cemetery tended. This is Perelozai, a former village of Pomor Old Believers whose community disappeared during the second half of the 20th century. Today, the church and cemetery are the only visible reminders of a settlement that once was home to hundreds of people. The Lietava River itself has an unusual place in Lithuanian history. Some historians have suggested that the name Lithuania may have originated from the river's name, although the etymology remains debated. For centuries, Perelozai was part of a much larger story: the migration of Russian Old Believers to the lands of the former Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, where they sought refuge from religious persecution. The history of Old Believers in Lithuania dates to 1679, when some of those fleeing persecution settled in what is now Lithuania. Their flight followed a major religious rupture in 17th-century Russia. Patriarch Nikon, backed by Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich, introduced reforms intended to bring Russian Orthodox religious practices closer to those of the Greek Orthodox Church. Some of the changes may appear minor today. Worshippers were instructed to make the sign of the cross with three fingers rather than two. The singing of “Alleluia” changed from two repetitions to three. Processions around churches were to move in the opposite direction, the number of bows during prayers was reduced, and changes were made to chanting, the shape of the cross and the spelling of Jesus’ name in icons and religious texts. For many believers and priests, however, these were not minor changes. They viewed them as a betrayal of the faith and refused to abandon established traditions. The resulting split in the Russian Orthodox Church became permanent. The church authorities condemned the old rituals and books as erroneous and heretical at the 1666-67 Moscow Church Council, and those who rejected the reforms were excommunicated. The anathema was formally lifted only in 1971. The Old Believers who resisted the reforms faced persecution, torture and executions. Under Peter the Great, economic pressure was added to religious repression. Old Believers could be subjected to double taxation and a separate beard tax. Old Believers began settling in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in the second half of the 17th century, often choosing remote, heavily forested areas far from major roads. Their arrival coincided with a period when large parts of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania had been devastated by wars and plague epidemics. Local landowners were willing to accept newcomers who were regarded as hardworking, sober and skilled in different trades. The settlers were given land and various concessions. Many learned Polish and Lithuanian and became established members of their communities. By 1772, an estimated 180,000 Old Believers lived in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. In Lithuania, large concentrations developed around Zarasai, with significant communities also in the areas of Rokiškis, Jonava, Kupiškis, Biržai and Seinai. Their villages were often tucked away in forests. Over generations, Lithuanian Old Believers preserved distinctive traditions, including their style of religious singing, icon painting and bronze casting. Their religious books were published and copied, while elements of older Russian vocabulary survived in their language. Old Believers arrived in Perelozai during a second wave of migration in the second half of the 18th century, during the reign of Catherine the Great. Her policies toward Old Believers fluctuated, with periods of renewed repression followed by greater tolerance. The Perelozai settlement is believed to have been established near the end of the 18th century, when its first church was also built. By the middle of the 19th century, about 150 Old Believers lived in the village. Around 1870, lightning struck the church and its roof burned down. The impoverished priestless community could not afford to rebuild it, and worshippers used a temporary prayer house for years. The Russian authorities continued to restrict Old Believers, particularly during the reign of Tsar Nicholas I. They sought to pressure or persuade them to join the official Orthodox Church and restricted the construction and repair of Old Believer churches. After the 1905 Russian Revolution, those restrictions were eased. Nicholas II was forced to grant Old Believers greater civil rights, including the right to build and repair houses of worship. A new church was built in Perelozai on the stone foundations of the earlier one. Its construction was financed by wealthy Vilnius Old Believers, including members of the Pimonov family, a prominent family of real estate magnates. Professional craftsmen were hired and building materials purchased. The community also acquired religious items, icons made according to the old canon, religious books and silver liturgical vessels. The church was repaired and reinforced during the interwar period, giving it essentially the appearance it retains today. During World War Two, German forces took away both of its bells. Perelozai was once more than a religious settlement. A school and community centre operated there in the 19th century. At the beginning of the 20th century, about 500 believers belonged to the parish. A ferry operated across the nearby Neris River from the mid-19th century until the postwar period. With few bridges in the area and forests and wetlands making travel difficult, the crossing was important to local residents and loggers. It was also used by smugglers and postwar partisans. Moscow is planning more decisive action against NATO, which could range from missile and drone attacks to a limited ground incursion, European spy chiefs told the British daily Guardian, adding that a panicked reaction risked helping the Kremlin. Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently warned that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch drones or missiles on NATO territory to show that collective defence works in theory only. Amid other recent reports, Baltic and Polish leaders also acknowledged US warnings of potential Russian operations against European countries. Michal Koudelka, the head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, told the Guardian that a small-scale invasion of NATO territory that bordered Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. ​ “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said. ​ Koudelka said this could happen in a matter of “months, not years”, adding that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”. ​ The Guardian said officials in Baltic countries have been more cautious, urging against panic and citing Moscow’s stretched resources in Ukraine. ​ “We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, told The Guardian, adding that it was an “open question” whether Moscow had concrete plans. Mežviets said Russia was moving from random attacks to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. ​ “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said.

Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas is beginning a week-long visit to the United States on Monday, where he will discuss the security situation, bilateral defence co-operation and the presence of US troops in Lithuania with American officials. According to the Defence Ministry, Kaunas will meet US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, as well as members of Congress Patty Murray and Roger F Wicker. During the visit, the minister also plans to meet representatives of US defence companies Lockheed Martin, Palantir, Northrop Grumman, Mach Industries and Epirus Inc. According to the ministry, over the past three years Lithuania has purchased around €2bn worth of weapons and equipment from the US. These purchases include Javelin anti-tank missile systems, JLTV armoured vehicles, Black Hawk helicopters, HIMARS multiple-launch rocket systems and AMRAAM missiles for NASAMS air defence systems. Kaunas will also visit the Pennsylvania National Guard and meet its commander, Major General John Pippy. The Pennsylvania National Guard has co-operated with Lithuania since 1993 under the State Partnership Programme. According to the ministry, the co-operation covers the development of a division in Lithuania’s military, training for Black Hawk helicopter pilots and technicians, joint exercises and the exchange of experience in crisis management.

For Marija, a recent drone incident over Lithuania was a reminder that emergency preparedness could no longer be something to think about later. The Vilnius resident had long considered putting together a go-bag with essential supplies. But after a drone flew into Lithuanian airspace from Belarus last week and was shot down, she decided it was time to act. “I had been thinking about packing a bag for a long time, and the latest incident with the downed drone made me think about how prepared my family really is,” Marija told LRT.lt. “In reality, we are almost completely unprepared.” Her bag now contains medicine, water, canned food, a Lithuanian first-aid kit, a battery-powered radio, a flashlight, spare batteries, a thermal blanket, a raincoat and other essentials. She had begun buying canned and other nonperishable food after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but had done little else to prepare for an emergency. “I decided to buy a ready-made go-bag and supplement it with personal items,” she said. Marija is not alone. Businesses selling emergency go-bags say demand has increased following a series of drone incidents and other high-profile events in Lithuania. The latest incident occurred overnight last Monday into Tuesday, when a drone entered Lithuania from Belarus. After midnight, residents in Vilnius, Trakai and Elektrėnai, and later in Kaunas region, received alerts from the military advising them to identify a safe place. The drone was eventually shot down over Lithuania. President Gitanas Nausėda said it was likely a Russian-made Gerbera drone intended to attack Ukraine but had deviated from its course. It was not the first time drones have entered Lithuanian airspace, adding to concerns among some residents about how they would respond during a crisis. Manvydas Poškus, head of the company 72h.lt, which sells emergency go-bags, said interest in preparedness has risen sharply after high-profile incidents. “We especially feel this after high-profile events, including those of recent days – sales really increase sometimes by several times or even dozens of times,” Poškus told LRT.lt. The company’s preassembled bags cost between 159 and 199 euros, while a family package costs 249 euros. Poškus said family-sized kits have attracted particularly strong interest. He stressed, however, that a ready-made bag should be viewed as a starting point rather than a complete solution. “Our goal is that people don’t have to think from scratch about dozens of different categories of items,” Poškus said. “The essentials are already prepared, and the rest can easily be adapted to each family.” Another retailer, Militar.lt, also reported increased demand. Representative Mantas Niuniavas said sales tripled after an earlier drone incident before returning to normal, but demand has risen again following the latest event. Companies have also begun purchasing go-bags in larger quantities for their employees, Niuniavas said. The bags sold by Militar.lt cost between 155 and 205 euros, depending on their contents. The most popular option is the more expensive version, which includes a long-lasting dry food ration, he said. Dovydas Petrauskas, director of go-bag retailer Pasirengęs, said the growing interest reflects a broader understanding among residents of the importance of being prepared for emergencies. “In our assessment, this is a positive trend, showing that the go-bag is increasingly less of an impulsive or emotional purchase prompted by a specific incident,” Petrauskas told LRT.lt. His company’s kits range from 189 to 279 euros. But simply buying a bag and leaving it at home is not enough, Petrauskas said. People should familiarise themselves with what is inside, know where each item is and understand how to use it because an emergency may require them to act quickly. He recommended adding items suited to individual or family needs, including clothing, additional food and water, documents, regularly used medicines, cash and other personal necessities. A go-bag does not have to be purchased ready-made. It is possible to assemble one themselves using items available at home. The bag should be kept somewhere easily accessible and checked at least twice a year. Expired food and other products should be replaced, electronic devices tested and clothing updated for the season. The rule of thumb is that, in case of an emergency that may involve disruptions to essential services – such as electricity and water supply – one has to be prepared to take care of oneself and one’s dependents for up to 72 hours. Even people who intend to remain at home during a crisis are advised to keep a go-bag ready. If circumstances change and an evacuation becomes necessary, having essential belongings gathered in one place can save valuable time.

A Vilnius district court on Monday sentenced Antanas Kandrotas, known by his nickname Celofanas, to 60 days in detention for disturbing public order after punching Valdas Bartkevičius, a prominent pro-Ukraine activist, during a protest in December last year. Kandrotas had a verbal altercation with Bartkevičius, who then spat at him. Kandrotas then punched the pro-Ukraine activist. Kandrotas, who grew to prominence for his anti-Covid, anti-LGBT and, later, anti-Ukraine activism, is currently hiding in Belarus. When the latest sentence is combined with sentences he has yet to serve, his final time in prison amounts to four years, seven months and 10 days. On June 11, the Lithuanian Court of Appeal upheld a conviction against Kandrotas in a financial crimes case, reducing his prison sentence to two and a half years. The ruling took effect immediately. However, Kandrotas went into hiding, with authorities being criticised for allowing him to flee to Belarus. Last week, the Vilnius Regional Court rejected an appeal and upheld a sentence of four years in prison for organising riots outside the Seimas, Lithuania’s parliament, in 2021. The prison term will begin to run from the date of Kandrotas’ actual arrest.

Lithuania does not recognise the results of Russia’s State Duma election, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said on X on Monday. "Russia’s State Duma so-called elections were neither free nor fair. Opposition silenced, independent voices suppressed, #OSCE observers barred. Holding sham votes in occupied territories of #Ukraine is a blatant violation of international law. We will never recognise these results," Budrys said on X. He was speaking after preliminary results showed Russian President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party had won a record 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma. With almost all votes counted after an election in which parties critical of Putin did not take part, his political force will have a larger supermajority in the lower house of parliament than it did in 2016, when it also set a record by winning 343 seats.

A new rotation of US troops is on its way to Lithuania, President Gitanas Nausėda said on Tuesday. "Great news for Lithuania – US troops will continue to be stationed in our country. We are grateful to President Donald Trump and the US administration for this decision, which is important not only for Lithuania’s security but for the security of the entire region," Nausėda said in a statement issued by the presidential office on Tuesday. New US troop rotation on its way to Lithuania, says president A new rotation of US troops is on its way to Lithuania, President Gitanas Nausėda said on Tuesday. "Great news for Lithuania – US troops will continue to be stationed in our country. We are grateful to President Donald Trump and the US administration for this decision, which is important not only for Lithuania’s security but for the security of the entire region," Nausėda said in a statement issued by the presidential office on Tuesday. According to the president, the exact number of US troops has not yet been confirmed, but it will not be lower than previously. Presidential adviser Deividas Matulionis told LRT RADIO that he did not have the information on Tuesday morning, but official confirmation about the US troops had reached him by lunchtime. "It has been confirmed that the troop rotation is on its way, already on trains, and is expected to arrive in Lithuania in the near future," the presidential adviser said. He also confirmed that the number of US troops would definitely not be lower than the previous deployment. "I cannot say exactly because the Americans have not yet given us the number. The only thing I can say is that it will not be lower than before," Matulionis said. Discussing the deployment of US troops to Lithuania, Matulionis said Washington had not imposed any conditions on Lithuania concerning fertiliser exports from Belarus and that Lithuania had been among the first countries to respond to a US questionnaire on defence commitments. "No, definitely not, there were no conditions," the adviser said. The US is currently reviewing the deployment of its forces in Europe. More than 1,000 US troops completed their rotation in Lithuania this summer. The US has regularly deployed battalion-sized units to Lithuania since 2019. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Washington changed the status of its forces in Lithuania to continuous rotational deployments. These reinforced battalions have typically consisted of 1,000 or more troops, along with various types of combat equipment. Lithuania has previously said it is prepared to host up to 1,500 US troops. In August, the US sent a questionnaire asking European countries to demonstrate progress toward taking primary responsibility for the defence of the continent, following an agreement to increase defence spending.

Lithuania has not yet received a request from the United States to allow the transit of Belarus fertilisers through the country’s territory, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said on Tuesday following Washington’s announcement of major fertiliser purchases from Minsk. ​“There has been no such request,” Sinkevičius told reporters in Kaunas on Tuesday. ​ US President Trump said Monday Washington was working on a "massive" deal to buy fertilisers from Belarus. ​ "The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus," Trump said on his Truth Social network, adding that this would enable US companies to pay “substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada”. ​ According to him, President Trump’s claims regarding fertiliser trade with Belarus are most likely related to trade tensions with Canada, which is currently the main supplier of potash fertiliser to the United States. ​ The prime minister reiterated that Lithuania knows nothing about any such agreement: “Perhaps the US is looking for alternative ways to supply its farmers, [...] but it’s likely the content of discussions between the US and Belarus, and it is unknown to us.” ​ “So far, Lithuania has not been informed of any such agreements, if they even exist,” he added. “At the moment, it’s all been limited to Trump’s tweet, but this may just be an indication, or perhaps a way of applying pressure.” ​ Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said earlier on Tuesday that no European Union country could currently be part of a deal reportedly being negotiated by the US for the imports of Belarusian fertilisers. ​ The US imports the vast majority of its potash – a chemical salt used to manufacture fertiliser. Prices soared after the Ukraine war. ​ In 2024, 79 percent came from Canada, 11 percent from Russia and 4 percent from Belarus, according to the US Geological Survey. ​ This year, the US administration has lifted sanctions on Belarusian fertilisers that had been imposed at the beginning of this decade, but the US has been unable to import them due to restrictions on the transit of goods from Belarus.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda criticised a new United Nations political world map after Russian-occupied Crimea was depicted separately from Ukraine, the presidential office said Monday. Nausėda raised Lithuania’s concerns during a meeting of the Baltic states’ leaders with UN Secretary-General António Guterres in New York, where the Lithuanian president said maps used by the United Nations must comply with international law and respect countries’ sovereignty, territorial integrity and recognised borders. Lithuania supports efforts to make the world’s cartographic representation more accurate and equitable, Nausėda said, but stressed that the UN should consistently apply its policy of not recognising Russia’s annexation of Crimea and other Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia. Nausėda also said Russia remains the main long-term threat to European and transatlantic security and that the threat extends beyond Ukraine. “Russia’s threat is not limited to Ukraine,” the presidential office quoted Nausėda as saying. “Lithuania and other European countries are also facing violations of their borders.” The UN General Assembly approved a resolution in September supporting a new world map designed to provide a more accurate representation of the relative land areas of continents. The resolution was backed by 164 countries, while the United States voted against it and six countries – Ukraine, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Serbia – abstained. The new map enlarges Africa while reducing the apparent size of North America and Europe. It replaces the traditional Mercator projection, which makes areas farther from the equator appear disproportionately large, with a projection intended to better represent the actual relative sizes of land masses. Crimea is shown in grey on the new map. Its colour differs from both Russia and Ukraine.

Vilnius International Airport temporarily imposed airspace restrictions due to the threat of smuggling balloons from Belarus, the airport reported on Tuesday. ​The restrictions were in effect from 23:25 local time on Monday until 02:40 on Tuesday. ​ Operations at Vilnius Airport were disrupted by the smuggling balloons after a several-month break. The previous such incident was recorded in June. ​ Approximately 20 flights were affected during that period. ​ Passengers whose flights were disrupted due to the restrictions or cancelled are asked to contact their airlines directly. ​ This year, operations at the capital’s airport have been disrupted about ten times due to the threat of smuggling balloons. ​ Lithuanian officials view such incursions as a hybrid attack by the Minsk regime.

Lithuania has not been informed about a potential major US deal to buy fertiliser from Belarus and will not change its position toward Minsk, the chairman of the Lithuanian parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee said Monday. US President Donald Trump said Monday that Washington was working on a “massive” deal to purchase potash fertiliser from Belarus at prices substantially lower than those currently paid to Canada. The volume and timing of a potential agreement have not been disclosed. “We have no reason today to lift sanctions on Belarus. This is the common position not only of Lithuania but also of the European Union,” Remigijus Motuzas, a Social Democrat who heads the Foreign Affairs Committee, told BNS. “We cannot influence the decision or agreement of the United States regarding the purchase of fertiliser from Belarus. Time will show how the United States will manage to reach an agreement on the purchase of fertiliser from Belarus,” he said. Motuzas said Lithuania continued to regard Belarus as an undemocratic state and maintained its position toward the government of President Alexander Lukashenko. “Although political prisoners are being released, nothing is changing in Belarus,” he said, citing continued restrictions on the opposition and the imprisonment of people who are active in public life or on social media. He also pointed to Belarus’ continued support for Russia’s war against Ukraine and what he described as ongoing hybrid attacks against Lithuania and other neighbouring countries. Motuzas said it was too early to comment in detail on how a potential US-Belarus fertiliser agreement might work, noting that recent announcements by the Trump administration had sometimes concerned longer-term plans. The potential deal has drawn criticism in Lithuania. Žygimantas Pavilionis, a conservative lawmaker and deputy chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee, said such an agreement would undermine solidarity with Ukraine, the European Union and Canada. Pavilionis said the United States itself had previously imposed sanctions on Belarusian fertiliser and argued that the situation in Belarus had deteriorated since then, citing Lukashenko’s support for Russia and continued repression. The United States has eased some sanctions on Belarus as part of negotiations with Minsk that have included the release of political prisoners. On September 16, US envoy John Coale said Belarus had released 25 prisoners, while Washington lifted sanctions on two Belarusian companies. The Trump administration has also previously eased restrictions on Belarusian potash producers. Reuters reported Monday that the United States obtains the vast majority of its potash from Canada, while Belarus is a major global producer. Before US sanctions were imposed, Belarusian fertiliser was transported through Lithuania’s Klaipėda port. Lithuanian officials have remained sceptical about restoring the transit, citing European Union sanctions and concerns about providing a source of revenue for companies linked to the Belarusian government. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said last week that Lithuania’s and the United States’ positions differed on easing sanctions against Belarus, although he did not specifically mention fertiliser. Foreign media have previously reported that US officials were seeking the removal of sanctions on Belarusian potash to enable its transit through Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine.

Germany is struggling to fill its brigade in Lithuania with volunteers, as originally intended. Still, German officials assure that the Lithuanian brigade will be fully operational by the end of 2027, as planned. The German Defence Ministry has said Defence Minister Boris Pistorius plans to order some soldiers to be transferred to the German armoured brigade being established in Lithuania. About 80% of the brigade’s positions have so far been filled by volunteers, according to the ministry. “Imagine yourself in their position. You have never lived abroad before. Your wife or partner has a job. Your children go to school. I think it’s a serious step, and we have to give them some time,” German Ambassador Cornelius Zimmermann said. “But be assured – we will fill the gaps, because this is a matter of national interest,” he said. Lithuania and Germany signed an action plan in December 2023 outlining the deployment of the brigade, which is expected to reach full operational capability by the end of 2027. “Our commitment to transfer a brigade with full operational capability to Lithuania no later than the end of 2027 is set in stone,” Zimmermann said. “We are particularly looking for specialists, in information technology and other fields, and they are not so easy to find.” Germany has already transferred about 1,700 brigade personnel to Lithuania, with the number expected to reach about 2,000 by the end of the year. The full deployment is expected to eventually include about 5,000 German troops and personnel. Fausta Šimaitytė, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Lithuania, said linking the brigade’s success to voluntary transfers may have created unrealistic expectations. “Perhaps it was a mistake to link the brigade’s success to the principle of volunteering, because expectations were raised and that became the measure of the brigade’s success,” she said. “From the first day, it should have been clear that this is a Bundeswehr military task, not a volunteer project.” Šimaitytė said radical political parties in Germany were seeking to use Pistorius’ plans to transfer some soldiers compulsorily to Lithuania to promote a narrative that young Germans would be sent to the eastern front. She also emphasised the importance of the brigade to Germany’s broader security role in Europe. “Germany is taking on greater commitments in European security, and this is an expression of Germany’s increased ambitions – that Germany really can take on this role,” she said. Lithuanian Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said he had no doubts Germany would fulfil its commitment. “Whatever form it takes, whatever actions they take there, I truly believe” they will deliver, Olekas said. Lithuania is also building infrastructure to accommodate the German brigade at a military town in Rūdninkai, south of Vilnius. Construction is being carried out in three stages, with the first expected to be completed soon. “We are going to Germany in October to report that construction is nearing completion and that the first stage will be finished,” Lithuanian Vice Minister of Defence Bronius Bieliauskas said. “From February, the Germans will gradually be able to move in with their equipment.” The second stage of construction began this summer. It includes housing, garages, workshops, dining facilities, warehouses and training facilities. “The conditions that have already been created today are good. The Germans themselves acknowledge this. Sometimes they say our conditions are much better than those in Germany,” Bieliauskas said. The facilities are being designed to allow German troops to live in Lithuania with their families. They will have access to housing, rental and travel compensation, education opportunities for children and language courses. Germany will cover part of these expenses. The permanent German brigade is part of Lithuania’s efforts to strengthen its defences and NATO’s eastern flank following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Lithuania’s parliament on Tuesday backed a proposal to remove from the constitution a ban on stationing weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on the country’s territory, opening the way for a potential future deployment of NATO nuclear weapons. The proposal received 99 votes in favour, 13 against and five abstentions during its consideration in the Seimas. The vote advances the constitutional amendment but does not itself authorise the deployment of nuclear weapons in Lithuania. The Constitution’s Article 137 currently states that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory. Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said the first vote on adopting the constitutional amendment is scheduled for October 6, with the final vote planned for January 12, 2027. Constitutional amendments require two votes separated by at least three months, with at least 94 of the 141 lawmakers required to approve the measure at each final stage. Remigijus Žemaitaitis, leader of the Nemunas Dawn party, opposed the proposal, arguing that Russia and Belarus could use it for propaganda purposes. He also said nuclear-armed states would be able to use nuclear weapons to defend Lithuania if necessary without removing the constitutional provision. He argued that the relevant constitutional article should only be changed through a referendum. Ignas Vėgėlė, a member of the parliament’s mixed group, questioned why the proposal would remove the entire provision rather than only the restriction on weapons of mass destruction. The article also prohibits foreign military bases. “Why are we deleting this part of the sentence as well? Are we planning to hand over Lithuanian territory to military bases that we will not control or manage?” Vėgėlė asked. He noted that Lithuania’s Constitutional Court has ruled that allied foreign military bases can operate in Lithuania if they are established by allies and remain under Lithuanian control. He argued that a similar principle should apply to weapons of mass destruction. Laurynas Kasčiūnas, parliamentary leader of the opposition Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats, said nuclear weapons are a key component of deterrence. He said nuclear deterrence helped prevent the Cold War from becoming a direct military conflict and argued that Lithuania should not maintain restrictions that do not apply to some of its NATO allies. “We are the only country in the region that has this restriction. Latvia does not have it, Estonia does not have it, Poland does not have it, Finland has just removed it,” Kasčiūnas said. He cited a hypothetical scenario in which a US allied ship carrying nuclear weapons or a nuclear-capable aircraft might need to pass through Lithuanian territory for deterrence purposes. Kasčiūnas stressed that removing the ban would not mean Lithuania had decided to station nuclear weapons there, but said eliminating the constitutional restriction would give the country more options as part of NATO’s deterrence arrangements. Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee and a Social Democrat, also said Lithuania should not create obstacles to NATO’s nuclear deterrence or become the weaker link in the alliance’s regional security posture. “Lithuania must clearly show our allies and adversaries that we will defend our independence by all means,” Motuzas said. “We cannot be less protected than other NATO countries.” He said changing the constitution would send a strong signal intended to reduce the risk of military aggression. Liberal Movement leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen said deterrence should not be viewed as an escalation of war. “Today’s vote is about ensuring that we are not weaker,” she said. The proposal comes amid broader discussions in Europe about nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron has promoted the idea of developing a European nuclear deterrence framework under which partner countries could potentially host French strategic aircraft equipped with nuclear weapons. The Financial Times reported in June that the United States was considering deploying nuclear weapons in additional NATO countries in Europe, although no such deployment in Lithuania has been announced.

It’s unrealistic to protect Lithuania’s airspace completely, Deividas Matulionis, chief national security adviser to the president, said on Tuesday, adding that it was necessary to focus on protecting key sites. “Covering the entire territory is truly unrealistic. No country in the world – perhaps Israel has some capabilities – is able to fully protect its airspace,” he told the Žinių Radijas radio. He said the goal was to protect “cities, critical infrastructure facilities, and our border”, saying the measures should include “anti-drone defences along the border”. Among other things, the presidential adviser emphasised that while air defence is a priority, the development of ground forces is also very important. ​ “We shouldn’t go from one extreme to the other. The development of our ground forces is just as important a priority,” he said. According to Matulionis, drone detection and drone destruction – kinetic measures – should go hand in hand and be integrated as early as next year. ​ “We said that if there really is a shortage of funds, the members of the State Defence Council will certainly agree to reallocate some funds in favour of air defence – if there isn’t enough, so that this becomes a priority and we can protect our airspace,” the adviser said. ​ “Detection is one thing; destroying them is another. That is why it should be combined with so-called kinetic systems – whether they are interceptor drones or some other systems that would instantly transmit information, allowing the operator to make the appropriate decision,” he added. ​ Last week, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that had flown into Lithuania’s airspace from Belarus. The unmanned aircraft was downed in Kaišiadorys District, central Lithuania, near the Kruonis Pumped-Storage Power Station. ​ As Russia’s invasion of Ukraine continues, potential air threat alerts have been issued repeatedly in Lithuania over the past few months. However, the incident last Tuesday marked the first time a drone had been shot down in the country’s airspace. ​ A NATO fighter shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May, in what was the first interception of a foreign drone. In June, French fighter jets participating in NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission downed a drone over Latvia. ​ Previously, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said that a larger portion of next year’s defence budget should be allocated to air defence. Lithuania spent 524 million euros this year on beefing up air defences.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Wednesday he had no information indicating that members of the country’s Muslim community posed a threat to national security, as a parliamentary committee prepared to examine the activities of a Muslim religious organisation. “I have no information that there are individuals who pose any threat to our national security,” Sinkevičius told reporters. He said migration policy must balance businesses’ need for workers with national security considerations. The Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence was due to examine the activities of the Council of Lithuanian Muslim Religious Communities, also known as the second muftiate, including its alleged links with other Islamist organisations and any potential security risks. The meeting was scheduled as a closed session, according to the committee’s agenda. The issue was raised by conservative lawmaker Dalia Asanavičiūtė-Gružauskienė, who in August asked the committee to investigate the organisation. She said its establishment, approved by the Justice Ministry in 2019, had divided Lithuania’s Muslim community and alleged that it had sought to take control of houses of worship through aggressive actions. She also raised questions about the organisation’s international partners and whether any had been accused of financing terrorism or promoting radicalisation. Committee Vice Chairman Laurynas Kasčiūnas said lawmakers would consider whether the organisation posed a national security risk, whether it had links with Islamist organisations and whether there was a risk of radicalisation. Officials from the State Security Department, Justice Ministry and Interior Ministry were expected to participate. The muftiate has rejected suggestions that the Muslim community poses a security threat. Mufti Aleksandras Beganskas has said Muslims in Lithuania do not feel safe and that he has personally received threats. Tensions have risen following an incident near a mosque in Kaunas on September 11, when a group of bikers gathered during Muslim prayers, made noise, chanted nationalist slogans and brought a pig’s head. Police later launched a pretrial investigation into the incident. Beganskas said the demonstration was directed against Muslims and called on authorities to ensure the community’s safety. The muftiate has also urged Muslims to remain calm and not respond to provocations. Intelligence agency sees no security threats Lithuanian intelligence has no information suggesting members of the country’s Muslim community pose a threat to national security, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Wednesday. He attended a closed meeting of the parliamentary Committee on National Security and Defence, which examined the activities of the Council of Lithuanian Muslim Religious Communities. Representatives of the State Security Department, Lithuania’s main intelligence agency, also attended the meeting. “According to data from the State Security Department, there are no extremist threats of any kind to national security,” Katelynas told reporters after the session. This was later confirmed by Giedrius Krupauskas, deputy director of the State Security Department, who declined to comment further to reporters. Meanwhile, Rimantas Sinkevičius, Chairman of the National Security and Defence Committee (NSGK), argued that although intelligence agencies have no information about a threat posed by a second muftiate, growing migration are cause for concern because it can spur radicalisation among local Lithuanians. “The agencies do not observe any radicalisation within the Muslim community or any significant changes. On the contrary, they note a certain tendency among their leaders to prevent political involvement and radicalisation. But the other side is becoming radicalised – Lithuanians, our community, are becoming radicalised. I’m talking about the biker club, about a young man who burned the Quran, and so on,” said Sinkevičius. “Our society’s intolerance or simple ignorance could also provoke radicalisation of the other religious community, the Muslim side, which is not the case today. The question is how to manage this process so that this does not happen, because religious conflict is very dangerous for social stability,” he argued.

Any breach of European Union sanctions to facilitate a potential US deal to buy Belarusian potash fertiliser would amount to a “moral humiliation”, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda’s national security adviser said Wednesday. “Any violation of EU sanctions would have a moral aspect – as well as a legal and financial one. [...] It would be a kind of moral humiliation,” Deividas Matulionis told LRT RADIO. US President Donald Trump said Monday that Washington was working on a major deal to buy Belarusian fertiliser, potentially allowing US companies to obtain it at lower prices. The proposed deal has raised questions about how the fertiliser could reach international markets while EU restrictions on Belarusian goods remain in place. Matulionis stressed that any Belarusian fertiliser would not necessarily transit Lithuania or the port of Klaipėda, as it did before sanctions were imposed. “This is an issue between the US and Belarus,” he said. “If there were transit, it would not necessarily have to be through Lithuanian territory, so why should we specifically be informed?” He also rejected suggestions that Washington was pressuring Lithuania to facilitate the transit. “We know that America is interested in cheap Belarusian fertiliser and this has been discussed,” Matulionis said. “It is not the case that someone is imposing conditions or putting pressure on us.” Matulionis said the issue had been discussed both previously and last week with US special envoy for Belarus John Coale during his visit to Vilnius. “I want to assure you that it was not a form of pressure,” he said. “It was a statement that it would be useful for America, and a question about how we would react.” The US is also discussing the issue with other countries in the region, Matulionis said, adding that Lithuania and its neighbours have so far maintained a common position. “We would not want the Americans to transport potash through Russia, because that would provide additional revenue for Russia’s war machine,” he said. “The Americans are talking not only with us, but also with other countries in the region, but so far we are all holding together, and I see no concessions either from us or from other neighbouring countries.” Lithuania has previously said it does not want to resume the transit of Belarusian potash through its territory while EU sanctions remain in force. Before sanctions, Belarusian fertiliser was transported through Lithuania to the port of Klaipėda. The United States has separately sought ways to obtain Belarusian potash after lifting its own sanctions on the sector, while EU restrictions remain in place. Matulionis also pointed to comments by Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko that Minsk currently does not have enough available potash to export large quantities to the United States. “Lukashenko himself said that he does not have the capacity,” Matulionis said. He suggested that if serious negotiations were underway, they might not have become public, adding that Russia could have warned Belarus against pursuing closer ties with Washington. Matulionis said Lithuania would welcome any US effort that could reduce Belarus’ dependence on Russia, although he cautioned that such a shift would be difficult after more than three decades of Lukashenko’s rule. “If the Americans succeeded in pulling Belarus away from Russia, that would, of course, be a fundamental change, and we wish them success,” he said. “But we see that it is difficult.” He noted that EU sanctions on Belarusian fertiliser are due to expire at the end of February unless renewed, potentially changing the situation in the coming months. Matulionis also dismissed speculation that the return of US troops to Lithuania was linked to the possible resumption of Belarusian potash transit. Instead, he said, Washington’s decision to send a new rotation of troops to Lithuania before completing a broader review of US forces in Europe reflected Lithuania’s commitment to developing transatlantic relations. The United States announced this week that a new troop rotation was heading to Lithuania, with Nausėda saying it would likely involve about 1,000 soldiers. The latest US-Belarus discussions have also focused on the release of political prisoners. Coale visited Belarus last week, after which 25 prisoners were released and the United States lifted sanctions on two Belarusian companies. Lithuanian officials have stressed that Washington’s approach to Belarus differs from that of the EU, while maintaining that regional allies should coordinate their policies toward Minsk. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said Coale’s September visit to Vilnius focused on political prisoners and regional security.

Lithuania will impose national sanctions on Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman after the European Union agreed to remove them from its sanctions list, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Tuesday. “Oligarchs are part of Russia’s war machine. The regime’s ‘wallets’ must not be allowed to feel at ease in Europe while Ukrainians are being killed,” Sinkevičius wrote on X. “I have instructed the relevant authorities to initiate the process for imposing national restrictive measures on Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman,” he said. The EU agreed Tuesday to extend sanctions against about 3,000 Russian individuals and entities for three years but remove Usmanov and Fridman from the list. The measures, which include asset freezes and travel restrictions, had previously been renewed every six months. Latvia had opposed the deal but ultimately abstained, allowing the agreement to proceed. Estonia also said it would impose national sanctions on the two businessmen after opposing their removal from the EU list. Ukraine criticised the decision, urging EU countries to maintain pressure on Russia rather than ease restrictions on prominent Russian business figures. France had pushed for Usmanov’s removal, citing national security concerns without providing details. European media reports have linked the move to diplomatic efforts involving French citizens detained in Azerbaijan, although Paris has not publicly confirmed such a connection. Fridman’s removal followed pressure from Luxembourg and Slovakia, according to diplomats cited by European media. Fridman has filed a multibillion-dollar legal claim against Luxembourg over assets frozen under EU sanctions. The EU imposed sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman in 2022 following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Their removal means the two men will no longer be subject to the EU-wide asset freezes and travel restrictions associated with the sanctions list. Lithuania’s move follows similar action announced by Estonia and Latvia, which said they would seek to maintain restrictions against the two businessmen at the national level.

Poland would help evacuate civilians from Lithuania in case of an attack by Russia, Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Tuesday. "Poland will help. Poles will help, state institutions will help," he answered a question from reporters during his visit to the Polish-Ukrainian border. He pointed to Poland’s experience of taking in Ukrainian refugees following the February 2022 invasion. ​ "If any of the Baltic states, such as Lithuania, Latvia or Estonia, were attacked, we would call for Article 5 to be invoked," he said, referring to NATO’s collective defence clause. Lithuania approved an evacuation plan in case of an emergency in July, with Vilnius having such a plan in place from 2025. Baltic officials maintain there’s no immediate threat of a military conflict. However, recent intelligence reports, released publicly, show an increased threat of Russia launching more sabotage or other attacks as it is increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.

A new rotation of US troops is on its way to Lithuania and will likely involve about 1,000 soldiers, President Gitanas Nausėda said Tuesday, as Washington reviews its military presence in Europe. “I think we can talk about that,” Nausėda said in a video response to questions from LRT. He said the number would likely be similar to the previous rotation and “will likely not be smaller”. “A hundred more or less doesn’t make a significant difference. The most important thing is that this is an extremely important deterrent in this geopolitical context,” he said. Nausėda had announced earlier Tuesday that a new US troop rotation was heading to Lithuania, after uncertainty over the future of the American military presence in the country. He said he could not yet provide details about how long the new rotation would remain because the arrangements were still being coordinated. But he said he had been told that “the rotation will return” and that the decision had been approved in principle. “I was simply told that the logistics are moving forward,” Nausėda said. “I think this is substantial enough evidence that we are entering the final stage of this entire process, which will have a positive and successful outcome.” Nausėda said several factors had contributed to the decision, including his appeal to US President Donald Trump regarding Lithuania’s host-nation support package, Lithuania’s commitment to spend 5.4% of GDP on defence, cooperation on issues involving the Strait of Hormuz, a readiness to send a mine-clearing mission, and broader energy and economic cooperation. The president also said he had discussed defence industry cooperation with the head of Lockheed Martin, focusing on expanding the company’s operations in Lithuania, integrating Lithuanian companies into its supply chains, localising production of certain components and developing maintenance capabilities in the country. Nausėda said he believed the discussions had helped reinforce Lithuania’s image in Washington as a reliable strategic partner. The United States is currently reviewing the deployment of its forces in Europe. More than 1,000 US troops completed their previous rotation in Lithuania this summer, although some American personnel remained in the country. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said last week that he had received assurances from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the reduction in American troops in Lithuania would not last long. The US has regularly deployed military battalions to Lithuania since 2019. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Washington changed the status of its forces in Lithuania to a continuous rotational deployment. The reinforced battalions have typically consisted of 1,000 or more troops equipped with combat vehicles. Lithuania has said it is prepared to host up to 1,500 Americans.

The burning of a Quran in central Vilnius and a confrontation outside a mosque in Kaunas have intensified a debate in Lithuania over immigration, integration and who is responsible for rising social tensions. A video showing a Quran, Islam’s holy book, being burned in central Vilnius was published over the weekend. Police said the incident itself had taken place earlier, on September 13. The episode followed an incident outside a mosque in Kaunas, where bikers brought a pig’s head and shouted and sang during Muslim prayers. The incident also included reported threats against members of the Muslim community. Mufti Aleksandras Beganskas said he had heard threats that included promises to burn the mosque and harm him and his family. The incidents have prompted politicians to offer sharply different explanations for what is driving tensions in Lithuanian society. Some say political rhetoric is contributing to the problem. “There are specific names – I won’t name them – five names that are inciting discord in society,” said MP Tomas Tomilinas, a member of the Democratic Union “For Lithuania” parliamentary faction. Others argue that immigration itself is contributing to social tensions and are calling for tighter limits on the number of foreign workers allowed into Lithuania. “It is time to send a message to society that we are reducing the immigrant quota,” conservative Homeland Union party leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas said. Under Lithuanian law, the annual quota for foreign workers can reach 1.4% of the country’s population, or about 40,000 people. The quota for this year was set at 0.9%, equivalent to nearly 25,000 workers. Kasčiūnas is proposing to cut the quota to 0.4%, which would allow roughly 10,000 foreign workers to enter the country each year, with exemptions for highly skilled professionals. He has also called for greater scrutiny of the countries from which migrants are recruited. “The State Security Department should assess which direction is more compatible with our values,” Kasčiūnas said. He suggested that Lithuania could look more closely to Latin America, describing its predominantly Catholic countries as culturally closer to Lithuania. He added jokingly that the region also “plays football well”. The proposal has drawn criticism from politicians who warn that sharply reducing immigration could have economic consequences. Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen, leader of the Liberal Movement, said reducing the quota could increase unemployment. “Unemployment in Lithuania would likely increase further, and it is already twice as high as in Poland,” she said. “I would say we need a discussion involving society and an explanation of what the consequences would be.” Tomilinas said Lithuanian companies had become heavily reliant on foreign workers. “I think we should try to ensure that a Lithuanian is employed in every job – even long-haul truck drivers,” he said. “But unfortunately, 70% to 80% are foreigners. Our businesses are operating ‘on foreigners’. That's the situation.” The government itself is divided over whether the current system needs to be changed. The Social Security and Labour Ministry is responsible for setting the annual quota and is currently calculating how many foreign workers Lithuania will need next year. “We are definitely calculating it. So far, I don't see very serious arguments for increasing it. We will calculate it for next year and see whether there is an opportunity to reduce it,” Social Security Minister Inga Ruginienė said. Ruginienė said the current system was strict and functioning. “The strict system we have today works, and we believe it will continue to work,” she said. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas takes a different view. “I have to admit that the quota system is not working. We need to think about changes, and I am already thinking about them. A model is being prepared,” he said. Katelynas has said Lithuania’s immigration policy will become stricter and that he plans to prepare a new migration policy model within several months. The annual quota of how many foreign workers companies can bring into the country was exhausted in early September, adding pressure to a debate that businesses say needs a clearer long-term direction. Andrius Romanovskis, president of the Lithuanian Business Confederation, said the absence of a consistent migration policy was allowing the issue to become increasingly political. “The lack of migration policy is also what leads to everyone having their own opinion and recipe,” he said. “We see that this issue has become completely political, with politicians competing with each other over who can propose stricter regulation as they begin their election campaigns.” The debate comes as the number of foreigners living in Lithuania has grown.
