According to the Migration Department, arrivals from predominantly Muslim countries have increased since 2024, particularly from Uzbekistan, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Overall, about 220,000 foreigners live in Lithuania, accounting for nearly 8% of the country’s population. Most of them, however, come from Ukraine and Belarus.

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have asked the European Commission for 500 million euros in emergency funding to strengthen their defences against drones, citing a growing threat from Russia, according to Finnish media reports. The three Baltic defence ministers sent a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday, Finnish newspaper Iltalehti reported. The letter was also reported by Estonian publication Postimees. The letter was signed by Estonian Defence Minister Martin Herem, Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis and Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, according to the reports. The sources said von der Leyen had received the letter. The Baltic states are seeking additional EU funding because of what they describe as an increased Russian threat in recent months. They hope the money can be provided this year and that the European Commission will respond within several weeks, according to Iltalehti sources.

Lithuania will close external service centres in several Muslim countries in Central Asia and Europe, citing potential national security and terrorism risks, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Wednesday. “I have made the decision to close the branches of the external service provider in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Katelynas said in a Facebook post. The centres process applications for residence permits and initiate migration procedures for foreigners seeking to come to Lithuania. Katelynas said an assessment of security risks and the threat of terrorism found no justification for continuing their operations. “When the State Security Department warns of potential terrorism risks and has already identified individuals from Central Asia with radical views or links to terrorism, the state cannot wait for a risk to become an incident,” Katelynas said. He said Lithuania did not plan to open new external service centres in other countries following the closures. The decision comes as Lithuania has tightened controls on labour migration from Central Asia. Migration Department Director Indrė Gasperė said Tuesday that the number of workers arriving from the region had increased in recent years, but applications from Central Asian citizens seeking to enter Lithuania for employment are currently no longer being accepted. The department said the external service centres had been suspended after receiving very large numbers of employment-related applications. Lithuania’s 2026 quota for foreign workers is 24,706. Once the quota is exhausted, temporary residence permits for employment can generally be issued only when additional statutory conditions are met, including higher salary thresholds or employment in certain high-value, shortage occupations. The closures will also affect Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Lithuania opened an external service provider centre in October 2025 as part of a broader restructuring of the countries in which foreigners could apply for Lithuanian residence permits and national visas. As of September 1, nearly 227,000 foreign nationals held valid residence permits in Lithuania, according to Migration Department data. Ukrainians accounted for about 80,000, followed by nearly 48,000 Belarusians and about 13,000 Russian citizens. Uzbekistan had about 12,600 citizens with valid permits, while India and Tajikistan accounted for about 9,400 and 7,500, respectively. The number of Central Asian nationals living in Lithuania has grown significantly in recent years. Official data show that the number of Uzbek citizens holding valid residence permits rose from about 10,500 at the beginning of 2026 to more than 12,600 by September 1, while the number of Tajik citizens increased to about 7,500.

Two US Army battalions will arrive in Lithuania in late October as part of a regular troop rotation, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Wednesday. “The preparation process and logistical arrangements are currently underway, and two battalions will arrive in Lithuania at the end of October,” Kaunas said. The number of US troops will remain similar to previous rotations, at around 1,000 personnel, he said. One unit will be a heavy battalion equipped with heavy weaponry, including Abrams tanks. The other will be an engineering battalion tasked with supporting the development of Lithuania’s division, border protection and defence-related projects. The US troops will remain in Lithuania for nine months. Kaunas discussed the deployment with US Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defence Elbridge Colby during a visit to the Pentagon on Wednesday. The Lithuanian minister also proposed considering the possibility of establishing a permanent US military base in Lithuania, although he said no decisions had been made. More than 1,000 US troops completed their previous rotation in Lithuania this summer. The United States has regularly deployed battalions to Lithuania since 2019. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Washington changed the status of its forces in Lithuania to a continuous rotational deployment. Lithuania has previously said it is prepared to host up to 1,500 US troops.

Lithuania’s Defence Ministry spent nearly 48,000 euros on a celebration for employees returning from summer holidays, prompting criticism from President Gitanas Nausėda and a demand for an explanation from Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius. The September 10 “Defence Ministry community meeting” at Vilnius’ Bokšto Square was attended by about 200 people, including Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas himself. The final cost was 47,559 euros, of which 44,994 euros was covered by the ministry and the remainder by participants, according to reports by Lrytas and the Reporter news program. The initial estimate was 50,364 euros, but the ministry’s Budget and Finance Department urged organisers to reduce the cost. The event included catering, venue rental, technical and event services, live music, a DJ and an illusionist. Employees also paid 15 euros each for two alcoholic drinks. The ministry said the gathering was intended to strengthen relationships and cooperation among employees and foster a sense of community. It described the event as its only gathering of this kind for staff during the year. Kaunas defended the event as normal practice for an organisation but said he would review how it was planned and whether the spending had been objectively assessed. “Since I was not involved in the direct planning process, we will look into whether everything is truly objective,” Kaunas told LRT. He said such gatherings could help employees work toward common goals and improve cooperation. “I think we should stop pretending that people working at the ministry are not people, that civil servants are robots,” Kaunas said, adding that the ministry wanted to attract specialists from the private sector and provide good working conditions. He later admitted that the cost could have been excessive. President Nausėda said the spending risked undermining public confidence in defence funding. “Such things compromise and discredit all defence funding,” the president said through his adviser Frederikas Jansonas. He called for a principled response and said Kaunas should ensure defence funds were used “sensibly and transparently”. Prime Minister Sinkevičius said he had demanded that Kaunas explain why the event had been organised. “Every organisation has events for its staff, but this time the price is surprising,” the prime minister said through his adviser Gedas Salyga. According to Lrytas, the celebration was not held last year, when the ministry was led by Social Democrat Dovilė Šakalienė. Under previous conservative-led administrations, similar gatherings were held on ministry premises and cost several times less. The scrutiny comes as Lithuania is devoting an unprecedented share of its budget to military spending. The 2026 budget allocates 5.38% of GDP, or about 4.8 billion euros, to defence.

Kaunas plans to begin designing its first modern tram line, which would also be the first one in the country. Before the ambition could be implemented, the city will need to iron out funding – and overcome scepticism from even some Kaunas residents. The city council last week approved an updated sustainable mobility plan, clearing the way for the tram project. City officials say they will seek European Union funding, while the estimated cost remains uncertain. Kaunas Deputy Mayor Andrius Palionis said the main goal was to develop environmentally friendly public transportation that would be less vulnerable to traffic congestion. “We will begin the procurement of design work for this particular route,” Palionis said. “A project and an idea of this scale are never realised overnight. Cities can implement such projects based on the experience of other European Union cities, but only with European funding.” The proposed first route would run along Savanorių and Šiaurės avenues. Palionis said the streets were selected in part because their existing infrastructure is sufficiently wide to accommodate tram tracks. “Naturally, trams need tracks, but the route was chosen as the first one that could be implemented because the existing street infrastructure is sufficiently wide,” he said. The city has not yet determined the final cost of the project. Palionis said an initial estimate of 150 million euros had been included in the sustainable mobility plan based on an analysis, but stressed that the figure was only theoretical and could change substantially. Kaunas residents have expressed mixed views about the proposal. Some said a tram could improve public transportation and help reduce congestion. One resident told LRT RADIOo that she had spent one and a half hours traveling from the Saulėtekis area to Giraitė because of traffic congestion. “Traveling by tram would be faster,” she said. Another resident welcomed the proposal, saying improved public transportation could benefit the city. A representative of the blind community also said the project could be worthwhile if accessibility needs were considered. “I think it could be a good thing,” she said. “We haven’t had anything like this here before. [...] If the needs of blind people are also taken into account, so that people from our community could use the tram to travel from one place to another, then why not?” Others questioned the need for a new form of public transportation and said the money could be better spent elsewhere. “We should refrain from such extravagance,” one resident said. Another said existing buses were no longer as crowded as they once were and that spending money on a tram would be wasteful. A third resident said the city should instead invest in more trolleybuses and buses, particularly because of congestion during rush hour on Savanorių Avenue. The proposal has also drawn criticism from the opposition in the city council. Vaida Pranarauskaitė, head of the Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union faction, said the project raised questions about both financial responsibility and long-term strategy. “Expensive design work has no firm guarantees regarding a source of funding,” Pranarauskaitė said. “If European Union or government funding is not secured, this project will simply end up in a drawer.” She also said the proposal disregarded findings from feasibility studies commissioned by the municipality and questioned the need to replace or supplement the existing trolleybus and bus network on Savanorių Avenue. Transport Minister Juras Taminskas, however, welcomed Kaunas’ plans and said he hoped the city would become the first in Lithuania to introduce a modern tram system. “Excellent plans, and I believe Kaunas will overtake Vilnius,” Taminskas said. “If we have opportunities in the next EU funding period, starting in 2028, we will certainly support this and look for every possible way to include the project in potential funding lines.” He cautioned that it was too early to say whether Lithuania’s state budget could contribute because public finances were under pressure. Taminskas said legislation adopted in 2018 on the development of metropolitan transportation systems provides a legal basis for municipalities, including Kaunas, to develop tram projects. He said some legislation might need to be amended before construction could begin. Potential changes could involve traffic rules and legislation governing construction and environmental impact assessments, as well as possibly the Roads Law, he said. Kaunas would be the first Lithuanian city to introduce a modern tram system if the project proceeds. The city currently relies primarily on buses and trolleybuses for public transportation.

Moscow could launch a military attack against a NATO country in the coming months, the Danish intelligence service said on Thursday. “There is a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia,” the Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said in a statement on Thursday. “A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia’s part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months,” it said, adding that DDIS outlined that the scenario could include strikes on infrastructure, with Moscow saying they took place because of Ukraine’s jamming, as well as a similar, troops without insignia, scenario as seen in Ukraine in 2014. “However, ahead of such a deployment, Russia would likely first build up regular forces near the border in order to be able to counter a potential NATO response,” DDIS said. ​ Such a scenario, as well as the “highly unlikely” scenario of a full invasion, would take months to prepare and would be difficult to conceal. This marks the most blunt public warning of potential Russian aggression against a NATO country. Previously, the Baltic states and Poland acknowledged they had received warnings from the United States of potential Russian attacks.

Belarusian citizens will be able to apply for temporary residence permits in Lithuania through external service provider offices in Armenia and Georgia starting in November, Lithuania’s Interior Ministry said Thursday. The measure is intended to allow Lithuanian employers to continue recruiting workers from Belarus after changes to the country’s immigration law take effect November 1. “To ensure that employers continue to have the opportunity to bring in workers from Belarus where there are labour shortages, Belarusian citizens will be able to submit applications for temporary residence permits at external service provider offices in Armenia and Georgia,” the ministry said. Without the new arrangement, Belarusian citizens would no longer be able to enter Lithuania for employment purposes after the law changes take effect, the ministry said. The decision follows Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas’ announcement Wednesday that Lithuania would close external service provider offices in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Bosnia and Herzegovina because of “security concerns”. Applications for Lithuanian temporary residence permits will no longer be accepted at those offices from November 1. The number of countries with external service providers will consequently fall from 31 to 27. According to the Interior Ministry, applications for residence permits on the basis of employment will be possible in 21 of those countries. In five countries – India, Cambodia, Ghana, Azerbaijan and Mongolia – employment-based applications are not available. Applicants there are limited to priority categories, including study, highly qualified employment, academic and scientific work, family reunification, intra-company transfers and certain investment-based cases. The ministry said Belarus currently has no external service provider office authorised to accept applications for Lithuanian residence permits. Belarusian citizens seeking permits for employment therefore currently apply in Lithuania through the Migration Department while legally present in the country. From November 1, however, foreigners, including Belarusian citizens, generally will no longer be able to submit residence permit applications from within Lithuania, except in specified cases. That would otherwise leave Belarusian citizens unable to apply either in Lithuania or abroad, the ministry said. The new option in Armenia and Georgia is intended to close that gap. The Interior Ministry notes that the Migration Department must consider national security interests, foreign policy priorities, labour market needs and institutional capacity when selecting countries where external service providers can operate. It must also consult the State Security Department, the State Border Guard Service and police. The possibility for foreigners to submit temporary residence permit applications abroad through external service providers was introduced in January 2023. As of September 1, nearly 227,000 foreigners held valid residence permits in Lithuania, according to Migration Department data. They included about 80,000 Ukrainian citizens, nearly 48,000 Belarusians, 13,000 Russians, a similar number of Uzbek citizens, 9,400 Indians and 7,400 Tajiks.

The European Commission is “carefully assessing” a request from the Baltic states for 500 million euros to strengthen defences against drones, saying it understands the security concerns facing Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania and takes them “very seriously”. LRT.lt received the commission’s response Thursday evening after the defence ministers of the three Baltic states sent a letter to Brussels on Monday requesting urgent funding to strengthen the region’s defences against the growing threat from Russia. “We understand the concerns of our member states and take them very seriously,” the European Commission said in its response, confirming that it had received the letter and was carefully examining it. The letter requesting funds was signed by Estonian Defence Minister Martin Herem, Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis and Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas. It is classified, but Kaunas has disclosed some details of the Baltic proposal. According to Kaunas, the three countries want to develop a counter-drone air defence system that could eventually serve as a model for other EU countries. “Air defence and counter-drone solutions are relevant not only to our region but to the whole of Europe,” Kaunas told LRT. “Lithuania has taken the lead in creating a counter-drone air defence system, which means combining detection with artificial intelligence and connecting it to kinetic capabilities, that is, the same interceptors.” Kaunas said the plan has already been discussed several times. The ministers also argued in their letter that the Baltic states form a frontline barrier protecting the rest of Europe and therefore warrant additional EU investment. “We are the barrier, the wall that protects the rest of Europe,” Kaunas said. “So naturally, Europe should take this into account and invest additional funds both in European security and in our security.” Finnish newspaper Iltalehti, which first reported on the letter, said the Baltic states expected a response within several weeks and hoped the European Commission could provide additional funding for regional drone defences this year. The request comes amid a series of warnings about possible Russian provocations against NATO countries. In Latvia, residents of the Krāslava municipality were warned of a possible air threat overnight Monday into Tuesday, prompting NATO fighter jets to take to the air. Last week, a NATO fighter jet based in Šiauliai shot down a stray drone that had entered Lithuania from Belarus. Politico reported Friday that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is considering new measures to protect against sabotage and cyberattacks. Major EU capitals, including Paris and Berlin, are reportedly opposed to attempts by Brussels to acquire greater powers in the security field. EU defence ministers are due to meet in Brussels on Monday, when Russia’s hybrid threats are expected to receive particular attention.

Lithuania on Friday launched its largest annual national mobilisation exercise, Vyčio Skliautas 2026 (Vytis Vault 2026), testing how the country would respond to a deteriorating security situation and transition to a wartime mobilisation regime. The exercise, which will run through October 3, combines tabletop scenarios with practical tasks involving about 3,000 civil servants, officials, municipal and institutional representatives, businesses and nongovernmental organisations, as well as about 1,000 volunteers, the Government Chancellery said. The fictional scenario is based on current security threats and includes disruptions to energy and communications systems, the reception of allied forces, ensuring continuity of critical services and maintaining government operations under extraordinary conditions. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC), said the exercise would test the continuity of state governance and how institutions make and prioritise decisions under pressure. September 29 and October 3 will be the two key exercise days. On September 29, authorities will test public warning systems, including sirens, emergency messages sent to mobile phones and the LT72 emergency preparedness app. The exercises will also include evacuation drills involving residents of Vilnius and municipalities near the Belarusian border in a scenario involving a potential military incursion from Belarus. In Lazdijai district, the Lithuanian Riflemen’s Union will hold a parallel exercise, Tvirtas Dzūkas 2026, focused on protecting critical infrastructure, supporting local authorities and maintaining public order. Participants will also conduct surveillance, reconnaissance, target detection and casualty evacuation drills. Polish officials will observe the exercises as part of an international cooperation component, Vitkauskas said. According to Vitkauskas, procedures, logistics, and infrastructure capacity are currently being assessed with colleagues in Poland, while the plan itself should be drawn up once the two countries reach an agreement. “We have an international evacuation dimension: what would happen if it became necessary to evacuate a certain number of people from Lithuania, as well as from neighbouring Latvia and Estonia, across the border? “In situations where we are already facing a war threat, […] border controls would be introduced to ensure mobilisation and prevent people in certain key positions from leaving the country, so that they remain here and carry out their duties,” Vitkauskas told journalists on Friday. He said that in such a situation, a large flow of evacuees could build up at the border. “We need to assess all the procedures very clearly with our Polish colleagues, and that is the main task. There is a large delegation – about 20 people from different institutions in Poland. We will look at all the procedural shortcomings, document them, and then a plan will emerge that will be drawn up jointly, following an agreement between the two countries,” Vitkauskas said. “There is a national plan, while the international one is being developed now,” Vitkauskas added. “We need to establish one-way traffic flows for departures and arrivals, and there are infrastructure issues related to reinforcing bridges. There are many technical details that need to be assessed and documented, and then we can move forward with infrastructure development and the investments that will also be needed,” he said. According to Vitkauskas, the Suwałki Gap is particularly important in this process, “both militarily and logistically”. “We are extremely grateful to [Polish colleagues] for getting involved and for the strong interest they have shown. […] Poland’s participation takes us to another level,” Vitkauskas said. Lithuania will activate the state reserve for the first time, with food supplies stored as part of the reserve to be delivered to designated locations. “During these exercises, the state reserve will also be activated for the first time. This means that food supplies will be activated and delivered to designated locations. Food will be prepared from these supplies and provided to exercise participants as an essential provision,” Aurimas Guščius from the NKVC told reporters. He said hospitals would also take part in the exercise and activate mass-casualty incident protocols. In a tabletop exercise, the evacuation of hospitals and preparations to receive a larger number of casualties will be simulated. “Of course, an exercise like this would not be possible without our non-governmental organisations. Humanitarian assistance will be provided by NGOs. This year, we have as many as nine of them taking part. This is also the largest number in the history of the exercise,” Guščius added. Civilian reserve to number 100,000 people The civilian mobilisation personnel reserve is expected to include about 100,000 people, said Vitkauskas, head of the NKVC. “This is a list of people and positions that enable us to ensure the provision of services and the performance of functions. The plan is to have about 100,000 people – that is the target. People who currently perform these functions in peacetime […] will be, or already are, included on these lists, and these people must continue their work, because continuity ensures that vital functions are maintained and carried out,” Vitkauskas said. “The most important thing is for people to be clear about their positions, so that they are not assigned to other essential tasks, but instead focus specifically on ensuring continuity in their work,” he stressed. The reserve includes civil servants, municipal employees, doctors, engineers, IT specialists, energy-sector workers, logistics planners, police officers and representatives of other professions.

Lithuania’s economy and defence ministers have signed a cooperation agreement with US defence technology company Mach Industries to support the firm’s expansion in Lithuania, the Economy Ministry said Friday. The agreement, signed during the ministers’ visit to the United States, provides for cooperation on establishing a local subsidiary and developing capabilities for the assembly, integration and production of advanced systems and their components. Economy Minister Lukas Grikšas said the agreement would create new opportunities for Lithuanian engineers and suppliers while strengthening the defence capabilities of Lithuania and NATO’s eastern flank. US foreign direct investment in Lithuania currently totals nearly 2.8 billion euros, with manufacturing accounting for 72% of the total, according to the ministry. Mach Industries develops unmanned aviation, space and defence systems, as well as infrastructure for their mass production. The company has already demonstrated its Viper autonomous vertical takeoff and landing platform in Lithuania during exercises at the Rūdninkai military training ground. A separate memorandum was also signed during the visit between Lithuanian company INTA and US-based UVTON Inc. to cooperate on the development of ultraviolet light-emitting diode, or UV LED, applications and products. The partnership will draw on the expertise and intellectual property of Remigijus Gaska, a US-based scientist and pioneer in UV LED technology, for joint projects involving disinfection, diagnostics, sensors and environmental monitoring. The long-term goal is to establish a full UV LED value chain in Lithuania, covering technology development and patents as well as prototyping, certification and production.

American troops are coming back to Lithuania following prolonged discussions over their future in the Baltic states. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda told Fox News he personally pleaded with his American counterpart, Donald Trump, to keep troops in the Baltics. The announcement comes amid a spike in activity about the allegedly impending doom in the Baltics. The Danish intelligence services issued the bluntest warning yet, saying there was a low but growing risk of Russia moving troops into a NATO country along the lines of the earlier little-green-men scenario in Ukraine. Interestingly, Baltic officials have been more careful in their warnings after spending much of the past decade calling out the growing threat from Russia. Their caution against panic is increasingly contrasting with the growing alarmism in the West, with Baltic officials saying panic would play into the Kremlin’s hands. There’s also nothing to suggest an immediate apocalypse anyway, they say. For example, much of the international media found out about Lithuania’s wartime plan to evacuate vulnerable civilians (published in July), causing a flurry of reports. Vilnius also had such a plan in place from 2025. In any case, the Polish defence minister responded to a journalist’s question about it, confirming that Warsaw would help with evacuation if need be. POTASH IS BACK? Next to the announcement of two American battalions headed to Lithuania (and more troops to Estonia) came Trump’s message of a US deal to buy fertiliser from Belarus. Visibly, it caught Vilnius off guard, with officials saying they had no prior knowledge of any such deal and reminded of the existing EU sanctions that ban the transit of Belarusian potash via Lithuania. Recall, the US envoy to Belarus previously called on Lithuania to renew the transit of fertilisers – a cash cow for the regime – that travelled via Klaipėda. Lithuanian officials maintain that nothing has changed in Belarus that would warrant a sanctions rethink. For example, smuggling balloons forced a brief closure of the Vilnius airport, again . DRONE DEFENCES Baltic states are seeking 500 million euros from Brussels to help with drone defences, saying the eastern EU members bear the brunt of Russia’s drone threats. Even as individual countries are footing the bill for beefing up defences, they need more to shield the skies over Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania – even if it’s naive to think that an airspace can be fully protected , one official said. The drone incidents are also prompting more Lithuanians to stock up on emergency go-bags. MIGRATION, ISLAM, POPULISM Intelligence services said there was no sign of the Muslim community posing a threat, but the migration topic is becoming increasingly politicised, with questions posed over the future of Lithuania’s growing muslim immigrant community. This is prompting politicians to react as politicians do. The social democrat interior minister, who was formerly a member of a far-right party, announced Lithuania would be closing migration centres in some Muslim countries over an alleged terrorism threat. Granted, other officials said, Lithuania needs to review its migration approach, with the country living through a period of increased immigration after decades of outward migration and even depopulation. The rising immigration, as well as the populism in response, is driving fears of radicalisation in society as a whole. A case in point: a Quran was burned on a Vilnius street. EDITOR’S PICKS: – Lithuania’s local elections have been confirmed for March 7, 2027. – Lithuania mulls cutting public transport costs to address rising fuel prices. – Politicians are having to defend against criticism for holding a 50,000-euro party at the Defence Ministry. – Lithuania’s EU presidency begins in 100 days (ish). – Lithuania will not boycott Eurovision over the Israel question. – LRT back on agenda: the supervisory and politicised council issued a warning to the general director over an earlier decision that was backed by the very same council. If the director receives another warning, she’s out. Written by Benas Gerdžiūnas Edited by Justinas Šuliokas

Lithuania’s Interior Ministry said Friday that its information system was targeted in a cyberattack and that it had referred the incident to law enforcement. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas was informed Thursday evening of an attack against a system administered by the Information Technology and Communications Department, or IRD. The ministry said newly installed security measures allowed the attack to be detected and prevented from spreading further. Authorities determined that hackers had gained unauthorised access to the EPEKIS information system, which provided public services related to issuing personal and other documents and consultations for Lithuanian citizens and foreigners. EPEKIS has not been actively used since 2018 and currently operates as an archival system. It contains archived data on foreigners who have applied for Lithuanian citizenship. Most of the data consists of foreign citizens’ names and surnames without personal identification numbers. The IRD told the minister that unauthorised access was immediately blocked. The ministry said data sets had been created after the breach, but there was currently no evidence that the data had been downloaded. The incident was reported to the Criminal Police Bureau and the State Data Protection Inspectorate, while the National Cyber Security Centre was notified. Katelynas ordered an assessment of the security of all information systems and databases administered by the ministry. He said double authentication and enhanced monitoring measures had already been introduced following an earlier incident at the state-owned Registers Centre. The minister said authorities could not rule out the use of an artificial intelligence platform in the latest attack. In May, the Prosecutor General’s Office said it was investigating unauthorised access to more than 600,000 Real Estate Register records, including personal identification numbers. The access was carried out using compromised accounts of Migration Department employees, according to law enforcement.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has urged commercial banks to ensure payment systems are ready to operate during a national mobilisation, particularly so people can continue buying medicine and fuel, the government press office said. “We must prepare for domestic payments during a mobilisation regime,” Sinkevičius said after meeting with representatives of the Association of Lithuanian Banks and Gediminas Šimkus, chairman of the Bank of Lithuania’s board. “It is essential to work with banks and retailers so that residents can purchase basic necessities even if stores lose their connection with banks. We are primarily talking about medicine and fuel,” he said. The meeting also focused on ensuring access to cash during crises. Under existing mobilisation plans, selected ATMs would have guaranteed power supplies and regular cash replenishment, according to the government. Association of Lithuanian Banks President Eivilė Čipkutė said banks were prepared to operate in emergencies even if internet or electricity services were disrupted. “On the banking side, institutions are properly prepared in accordance with Lithuanian law,” Čipkutė told reporters. Major banks have agreements with the Bank of Lithuania and have adapted their systems to operate in an offline mode, she said. “If there is no internet, card payments will still be possible, and all cards have been adapted for this,” she said, adding that the financial sector had completed its work in this area. Lithuania is already developing a card payment system for use during mobilisation if internet connectivity is lost. In June, the Seimas approved amendments to the Law on Payments allowing people to purchase essential food, hygiene products, medicine and fuel during communications disruptions. The transactions will require specially configured cards and payment terminals, with spending limits set on existing cards. People will not need to replace their cards, as banks will record the limits on their current cards. Sinkevičius also said the government was prepared to work with banks to improve public financial literacy, including saving and investing. The meeting additionally covered service accessibility in the regions and the government’s planned national strategy to combat digital fraud. As part of the strategy, the Centre of Excellence in Anti-Money Laundering is developing an information-sharing platform for payment institutions. The Association of Lithuanian Banks has said the platform should be implemented by the state.

Europe has so far avoided accusing Moscow of committing acts of war, writes Charles Cohen for Euractiv, partners of LRT English. Hybrid threats from Moscow are intensifying in pace and scope, but Europeans don’t seem to agree on how to label them. Numerous examples illustrate this looming threat. Last week, Belarus held a four-day military drill along the Polish-Lithuanian border as Ukraine reported that Russia was using Belarusian relay stations to guide drone attacks on targets in western Ukraine. That same week, NATO assets shot down a drone coming from Belarus outside the Lithuanian city of Kaunas. Earlier this month, Germany stated that Russia was behind a drone attack targeting Ukrainian cargo planes at the Leipzig/Halle airport in August. “We are not at war, but we are the target of hybrid warfare every day,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said. The EU so far has trodden a careful line, referring to these events as “hybrid”, and not direct acts of war. Hybrid threats differ from armed conflict or hostilities in that they typically remain below the threshold of conventional warfare, a European Commission’s spokesperson said to Euractiv in writing, pointing to a combination of coercive, subversive, cyber, informational, economic or other non-kinetic and, at times, limited kinetic means in a coordinated manner. The goal, the Commission said, is to exploit states’ vulnerabilities, “without necessarily triggering a formal state of war”. “We should be under no illusions about what is happening here: hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said during her September address to MEPs in Strasbourg. The recent acts of sabotage and drone incursions are leading some leaders to harden their discourse. Earlier this month, EU High Representative Kaja Kalla said the Leipzig/Halle attack had “all the characteristics of state-sponsored terrorism”. Last Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told national lawmakers Russia could strike countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland, using drones and missiles and pass them off as accidents. A day later, French President Emmanuel Macron said the “nature of Russian aggression and the threats in Europe are changing”, after briefing party leaders and presidential candidates on national security ahead of the 2027 elections. NATO defines hybrid threats as a combination of military and non-military, as well as covert and overt, means, including disinformation, cyberattacks, economic pressure, deployment of irregular armed groups and use of regular forces. Shortly after von der Leyen’s speech, MEPs endorsed a report calling for a coordinated EU response mechanism against “hybrid threats”. “I don’t like this title,” Rasa Juknevičienė, the European People’s Party MEP who initiated the report, told Euractiv, pointing to a lack of a better alternative. “It does not exactly reflect the reality on the ground, because it looks like it’s not a real war.” “We named those hybrid attacks or hybrid warfare as acts that are not related to each other, but the war that is conducted by Russia involves very concrete people and institutions,” the former Lithuanian defence minister added. Russia has so far targeted European countries within what some experts call a “grey zone”, below the threshold that would trigger a conventional response. For some countries, clearly labelling the state of the threat encourages Russia to go further. “The mere fact that we label it under threshold helps push the boundary of what is acceptable or not,” an Eastern flank official told Euractiv. The source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said their country was differentiating between Russia’s hybrid or sabotage activities and its military threats towards NATO’s Eastern flank. To better address the Kremlin’s strategy against EU countries, von der Leyen last week proposed a “counter-hybrid playbook” as part of the highly anticipated European Security Strategy. The mechanism will help capitals react to “incidents” that fall “below armed conflict but clearly threaten our national security”, the Commission chief said, adding it would resemble NATO’s Article 4. But some argue that too much clarity could serve the Kremlin. For Jamie Shea, a former NATO deputy assistant secretary-general, “being too clear about levels of response takes away the ambiguity which is key to deterrence, keeping your opponent guessing”. The aggressor could then continue provoking and disrupting up to a certain level without worrying about the response, he added. Carlo Masala, director of the Centre for Intelligence and Security Studies at the German Armed Forces University in Munich, told Euractiv he would rather “call it shadow war”. “From the Russian perspective, this is a real war,” Masala said. If one is the daily target of warfare activities, then one is at war even if one is not responding to those attacks, the US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) concluded in a September report on “the Russian military campaign against Europe”. While some experts say escalatory war rhetoric could fuel Moscow’s escalation, the ISW argues Europe’s current language constrains Western responses and signals tolerance to Moscow. The multiplication of incidents is also testing the efficiency of Europe’s current deterrence and carries the risk of “unintended escalation”, Linas Kojala, the head of the Vilnius-based Geopolitics and Security Studies Centre, said. “Changing the narrative from hybrid would not mean we change the type of threat we are facing, because it depends on Russia’s understanding of the effectiveness of Western deterrence,” he added. Using “shadow war” instead, Masala said, would not change the threshold but would make it clearer to Europeans that this is “an orchestrated campaign that is similar to a war”, but with no troops.
