Lithuania’s Interior Ministry is proposing to restore police and other law enforcement officers’ ability to fire warning shots and ease some restrictions on when they can use their firearms, saying the changes would strengthen officers’ protection. The proposals have drawn scepticism from police unions, which say they were not consulted during their preparation and question whether warning shots should be brought back. Under current rules, an officer may use a firearm when there is an unavoidable danger and an unavoidable necessity. The Interior Ministry wants to remove those specific requirements. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the current wording relies too heavily on subjective assessments, which can be difficult for an officer to make in a rapidly developing situation. “These are statements of an evaluative nature. If the state asks an officer to do their job and the officer has 1 to 10 seconds to make a decision, can they assess whether there is an unavoidable danger?” Katelynas said. He stressed that firearms would remain a last resort under the proposed rules. “The firearm is used in a way that causes as little harm as possible, while the safeguards are being further strengthened,” said Darius Domarkas, head of the ministry’s Public Security Group. The ministry also wants to restore the option of firing a warning shot into the air as an additional means of de-escalating a situation. “There was no possibility of firing a warning shot into the air as an additional warning when a situation is escalating and needs to be de-escalated,” Domarkas said. “There was only a verbal warning.” Warning shots were abolished in Lithuania about a decade ago. Former police officer and instructor Dalius Mackela said there were good reasons for removing them. “If we fire those 9 grams into the air, they don't just disappear,” Mackela said, referring to the approximate weight of a bullet. “If, God forbid, that 9-gram bullet comes back down and finds an object, someone will be hurt. Who will stand up for the officers then?” Mackela also questioned whether the proposed changes were necessary, saying existing legislation already clearly establishes when police may use firearms. The debate over firearms use intensified this summer after a group of irregular migrants attacked border guards. Under the ministry’s proposals, border guards would have more flexibility to use firearms against equipment used to cross the border. “They could act against equipment used for illegal border crossings, such as ladders or tunnels,” Katelynas said. The minister also said officers who fire at a suspect would be guaranteed legal and psychological assistance. Police unions, however, say changes to firearms rules alone would not address their concerns. “The whole complicated situation is being turned into a show, with the emphasis being placed where it shouldn’t be,” said Ineta Kursevičienė, head of the Federation of Police Trade Unions. Roma Katinienė, chairwoman of the Police Trade Union, said law enforcement agencies needed an agreement on procedures following the use of firearms or special measures. “What is needed is a common agreement among law enforcement institutions on simplified procedures when a firearm or special measures are used, so that officers do not become hostages to three or five years of litigation,” Katinienė said. The unions pointed to several lengthy cases involving officers. In May, a court acquitted police officer Darius Šerpytis, who had been charged with causing a death by exceeding his powers. The investigation and court proceedings lasted three years. A separate case involving border guard Karolis Ilgevičius has been ongoing for two years. He is accused of shooting at the tire of a fleeing suspected smuggler’s vehicle and killing the driver. The unions also criticised the Interior Ministry for failing to consult them before preparing the proposed changes. “Unfortunately, with the current interior minister, as a trade union, we have not had a single meeting,” the Police Trade Union chairwoman said. Katelynas said the unions would now have an opportunity to give their views on the proposals. He said Lithuania’s security environment had changed and that law enforcement officers therefore needed rules adapted to the new circumstances.

Lithuania began imposing national sanctions on Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman last Friday. ​Vilnius made the decision earlier this month after the European Union removed them from its blacklists. The Lithuanian ban preventing Usmanov and Fridman from entering the country will remain in force for five years and may later be reviewed and extended. ​ "Following a submission by the foreign minister, the interior minister adopted a decision regarding the inclusion of Usmanov and Fridman in the list of persona non grata. As soon as the minister's decision was received, the Migration Department immediately entered both foreigners into the aforementioned list," Rokas Pukinskas, a representative of the Migration Department, said on Monday. ​ Latvia and Estonia also intend to apply national sanctions to the two businessmen. ​ EU sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman were lifted at the demand of several member states. ​ France, which requested the removal of Usmanov, cited national security interests but provided no details. The Financial Times reported that this might have been related to a potential agreement concerning the release of French citizens held in Azerbaijan. ​ Luxembourg, according to diplomats, demanded the lifting of sanctions against Fridman because he sued the country for 15 billion euros in damages over his assets frozen under EU sanctions. ​ According to data from the Latvian government, Usmanov is a Russian businessman with ties to Vladimir Putin and the main shareholder of USM Holdings, while Fridman is described as a businessman close to Putin and the main shareholder of Alfa Group. ​ Meanwhile, EU member states agreed last week to extend sanctions for three years against nearly 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russian aggression.

The number of Lithuanian school students learning Russian as a second foreign language has fallen by more than 40 percent since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while the number studying German has risen by 50 percent. During the 2021–2022 academic year, more than 110,000 students studied Russian as a second foreign language, compared with 65,700 this year. Meanwhile, 39,000 students are learning German as a second foreign language this year, up from 25,000 at the start of the war. The number of French language learners rose from 10,000 to 15,000, while the largest increase was recorded for Spanish, from 766 to about 15,000 students. About 1,000 more students chose English this year, while 279 chose Polish. The ministry emphasised that the data from the beginning of the school year are preliminary. Education, Science and Sport Minister Raminta Popovienė said the ministry is currently focusing heavily on strengthening German language teaching. She said the popularity of Russian will likely continue to decline, but it is not yet possible to abandon it completely due to a shortage of teachers for other foreign languages. The minister predicted that the process should settle over the next five to six years. Starting this September, schools have allowed Spanish to be chosen as a first foreign language, alongside English, French and German. The ministry has also created more opportunities for native speakers and individuals highly proficient in a foreign language to work as European Union language teachers, provided they obtain pedagogical qualifications within two years. The ministry said some schools have already stopped teaching Russian, with 51 schools dropping it during the last academic year. However, municipalities still face a shortage of foreign language teachers, especially in smaller district schools. The ministry has included French and German among priority pedagogical specialisations. Students in these specialisations are eligible for monthly scholarships of 481 euros, while those who sign a contract with a school and commit to working there under set conditions receive 814 euros. Opportunities are also available for those who already have pedagogical qualifications to acquire competencies in another subject. In the 2023–2024 academic year, 48 Russian language teachers participated in a European Union-funded project for free retraining. Half of them chose European Union foreign languages, mostly German.

The ambassadors of Canada, Norway, and Ukraine to Lithuania have co-authored an open letter, announcing their shared effort to bring back home every deported child, detained civilian, and prisoner of war. Across cities in Ukraine, loudspeakers normally used to warn of incoming Russian air strikes broadcast the steady tick of a clock. This is Ukraine’s daily moment of silence, a nationwide act of remembrance for those killed in Russia’s illegal war. In workplaces, homes, schools, markets and on highways, Ukrainians pause to honour those who gave their lives defending their country’s sovereignty and freedom, and remember the thousands of civilians whose lives have been lost to Russia’s aggression. The silence also mirrors the absence felt by thousands of families whose loved ones have yet to come home. Among them are the thousands of Ukrainian children who have been forcibly transferred and unlawfully deported by Russia over the course of its war. Separated from their families and communities, many have had parts of their core identity stripped away: their language, their culture, and even their names. Others are civilians unlawfully detained in territories temporarily occupied by Russia. Many have suffered consequences for teaching their language, practising their culture, speaking out against occupation, or sharing the truth about what they have witnessed. Some have been transferred to detention facilities in Russia, where they are held without due process, denied contact with loved ones, deprived of adequate medical care, and shielded from independent monitoring. For Ukrainian prisoners of war in Russian custody, conditions remain similarly concerning. Returnees have reported harsh treatment, while independent bodies have documented widespread abuse, including torture and sexual violence. These are not side effects of Russia’s war. Russia’s actions are repeated and well-documented violations of international law, carried out at scale, in an attempt to bend the will of the Ukrainian people. Behind every case is a human story: a parent waiting for a child, a spouse waiting for a phone call, a family waiting for someone to come home. We know that the true measure of peace is found in these human-centred stories. It is found in a child returned to their family, a civilian released from unlawful detention, a prisoner of war reunited with loved ones, and a community given the chance to heal and rebuild. The scope of this issue is immense, and no country or organisation can address it alone. Success requires sustained cooperation among governments, international organisations, humanitarian actors, and civil society. This is why Canada, Norway, and Ukraine will convene foreign ministers and international partners in Toronto on September 28 and 29 for Pathways to Peace: Second International Conference on Returning Ukrainian Children, Detained Civilians, and Prisoners of War. Building on the progress made at the Ministerial Conference on the same topic, hosted by our three countries in Canada in 2024, the conference will bring international partners together to support Ukraine’s efforts to return, rehabilitate and reintegrate Ukrainian deported children, detained civilians, and prisoners of war. Their return is a humanitarian imperative and critical to any peace process, helping to build trust and lay the groundwork of a just, lasting and dignified peace. Every person returned reunites a family. Every family reunited strengthens a community. And every community prospering helps rebuild Ukraine. Each morning, millions of Ukrainians pause to remember those who are gone and those who have yet to return. In their remembrance and with extraordinary courage and ingenuity, they also repair what Russia has damaged, care for one another, and strengthen the communities that Russian aggression has sought to tear apart. It is our hope that Pathways to Peace will mobilise the international community not only to pause with Ukraine in remembrance, but to act alongside it to help bring home every deported child, detained civilian, and prisoner of war. Co-authors: Ambassador of Canada Jeanette Sautner Ambassador of Ukraine Olga Nikitčenko Ambassador of Norway Atle Konta Midttun

Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs disagrees with the mounting calls and reports that Russia may attack NATO or the European Union in the coming months in an attempt to weaken their support for Ukraine. He says they've already started. "We are not talking about a conventional war. We are talking about all kinds of provocations, all kinds of acts of sabotage, all kinds of tests, and definitely this is something that is already happening as we speak," the Latvian leader told RFE/RL in an interview at United Nations headquarters on September 21. European intelligence officials, the CIA, and even French President Emmanuel Macron and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk have all warned in recent days of assessments that Moscow may go as far as to launch an air attack in some form on NATO territory in the coming months to show the military alliance's Article 5 common defence pledge is little more than a few words on a piece of paper. Instances of attacks in recent months attributed to Russia – what the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) calls a "coordinated series of kinetic campaigns" – include arson, assassination plans, and the sabotage of infrastructure, such as railway vandalism and electronic interference. Moscow consistently denies any involvement in the sabotage operations attributed to it by European governments, but officials from NATO and EU capitals have ramped up efforts to draw up contingency plans and measures to counteract. One such scenario is the so-called Narva scenario, which describes a hypothetical military scenario in which Russia would attack a NATO country using hybrid warfare tactics similar to the initial phase of the actual 2014 Russian invasion of Ukraine's Crimea. Narva is a small city with a sizeable Russian population on the Estonian side of the border with Russia. Analysts have said that such a move from Russia could be taken as a means to test NATO's willingness to risk a direct confrontation over strategically insignificant territory. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna warned of growing Russian hybrid attacks across Europe in an interview with RFE/RL this week, saying there are lots of rumours that Putin is going to wage a full-scale military operation against the Baltic states or Poland. But, he added, "our intelligence doesn’t see any serious military movements on the other side of our borders because Russia is stuck in Ukraine". Analysts at the ISW, however, said on September 21 that while Estonia and Latvia have both said that they have yet to observe any evidence of a buildup of Russian forces near their borders that would be necessary for a full-scale invasion of their countries, "scenarios for Russian action have not received the detailed analysis they deserve and require". RFE/RL contacted several diplomats with knowledge of EU and NATO preparedness planning, but none would give concrete examples of what is in the works saying the information was classified. One Central European official acknowledged that there are informal discussions on a working level on what to do logistically in case the Baltics and Poland are attacked, but added there are no official guidelines and real preparations in place. A NATO official said the alliance has the national defence plans of members, "which are top secret but essentially spell out what we do in all types of war scenarios". Rinkēvičs said calling the current wave of Russian attacks "hybrid" may also be stifling the urgency needed among European officials to address the situation. "I think that when we use the word "hybrid," then it somehow sounds less, let's say, dangerous, kind of more innocent terminology than actually those acts per se," he said. "I think that the most dangerous scenario would be if Russia gets reckless, if we do not respond in an efficient manner and there are real casualties happening. [...] Our part of Europe is trying to be as ready as possible. But look, if Russia launches a missile attack, then it is absolutely clear this is Article 5, and then it's absolutely clear that there is going to be a response." The increased tensions have caught the attention of Washington, which has been looking at its European troop deployments, basing arrangements, status-of-forces agreements, and general host-nation negotiations. Last week, US President Donald Trump says Washington and Warsaw are making "major progress" toward establishing a permanent US Army base in Poland, potentially expanding the American military presence on NATO's eastern flank. The move came a day after Polish authorities temporarily closed airports in Lublin and Rzeszów as Russian strikes targeted parts of Ukraine near the Polish border, according to Polish officials. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has also warned that Russia could seek to conduct drone or missile attacks against NATO countries supporting Ukraine while presenting them as accidents. He too said such incidents could be intended to test NATO's response and undermine allied unity. The assessment was based on intelligence from NATO, Ukraine, and the United States, according to Tusk. Similarly, the Baltics were rattled last year when three Russian jet fighters violated Estonia’s airspace for 12 minutes. According to Estonian officials, the Russian pilots acknowledged but disregarded communication from two Italian pilots in F-35 fighter jets, which had been scrambled from NATO’s Baltic Air Policing Mission in Ämari Air Base in Estonia, before ultimately being escorted into international skies. Tsahkna pointed out in his interview with RFE/RL that Russia is already attacking Europe. In response to the incursion, which Russia denies, Estonian called for Article 4 consultations under NATO's constitution, which are just below invoking the collective defence clause in Article 5. "We must be ready to act united," Tsahkna said. Russian President Vladimir Putin is showing no signs that he "really would like to have a meaningful peace and a just and lasting peace" with Ukr

Britain’s top navy general Gwyn Jenkins visited Lithuania and the Baltic states last week as the UK continues to build the 10-nation Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) as a coalition of the willing that would speed up decision-making in case of a Russian attack. “I'm not being alarmist. Nobody is catastrophising what could happen in the Baltics”, he said, adding that Russia will continue “to probe for weaknesses” unless NATO countries show strength. ​ In an exclusive interview with LRT.lt, General Jenkins spoke about the importance of the Klaipėda seaport, the British-led JEF as a coalition of the willing, and the growing risk of Russia “doing something stupid” in the Baltics. You mentioned the word alarmism. I'm seeing a lot of that now, especially in international media. From your perspective, are there any signs we're seeing that would require more vigilance than before? ​ I'm a military strategist by profession. Our job is to be prepared, and that means we take all our threats, all the threats that we see in front of us, very seriously, but that isn't an excuse for making the Russians out, out to be more than they are. ​ [...] Russia is bleeding in Ukraine. It has made a massive strategic mistake in picking an egregious illegal war with a sovereign state on European soil that we are all supporting. ​ While the war goes on, I don't believe Russia has the capacity to take the more alarmist courses of action that some people talk about. It recognises that we are a phenomenal force if it was stupid enough to pick an Article 5-type scenario. ​ But the concerns are of something happening below that threshold? If I have a concern about Russia, it is that I don't think they're very professional. I think their ability to miscalculate is huge. When I see it in the Baltic, and I see it in the North Sea, and I see it around the British Isles and elsewhere, unprofessional behaviour has the potential to escalate certain scenarios. ​ Our management of that and our ability to contain something– if they do something silly, stupid, illegal, egregious – that is where the concerns lie. And that's not the same as a pre-planned massive invasion of Europe. ​ This threat is very serious. I am worried and concerned about Russian behaviour and what they might do either during the war or once the war in Ukraine is finished [and] what happens to the Russian state after that point. [...] If I wind back 15 years, I was in the military staff college education, right round about the G8 in Northern Ireland when Vladimir Putin was there. I actually met him because I was the military assistant to the prime minister. At the time, in all of our war games and exercises at that point, the precursor to war was what we’re living through at the moment [in Europe]. If you'd asked the 15-years-ago me what the condition-setting would look like for confrontation with NATO, we're in all of that. That is not to predict a war, but it is to say that we can't be complacent. ​ What do you remember of Putin? ​ He's very short in a way that his images don't necessarily portray. He’s very intense, not very engaging as an individual with anyone. But I didn't spend a lot of time with him. The Suwalki Gap question receives a lot of attention. What can you comment from the naval, or from the British, perspective? Land resupply is obviously crucial to both your nation and all the Baltic states and all our forward land forces – the UK forward land forces in Estonia, the Germans here. If military strategy and history teach me anything, it's don't depend on just one line. The sea lines of communication and our ability to resupply across the Baltic Sea is really important. I think you have some of the best port facilities in the Baltic states; they are really important infrastructure that we should make sure that we can protect. Is that what you talked about during your meetings here? ​ Yeah, I have, because we have learnt a lot from Ukraine in terms of their ability to protect their port infrastructure and the challenges they've had. I think we've seen a lot from the conflict in the Gulf recently in terms of how you protect port infrastructure from a range of possible attack options. ​ I'm really keen that we continue to talk about how that can be done here, how we support each other in that, because it's important to all of us. It's been a key part of my, some of my discussions here. ​ For people who don’t know about the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), which also includes Lithuania, is this a fail-safe for below-Article 5 crises? So the most important thing I think about JEF is it is a complement to NATO. We are working hand in glove through the JEF with the NATO planners on how the JEF can support NATO plans. The advantage of the JEF is there's 10 of us, and we don't need consensus to act. Is it a coalition of the willing, essentially? ​ Basically. As the scenario evolves, the flexibility of the JEF means any of us can contribute [in a way] that is really supportive of the NATO plans. ​ When you look at the way the NATO plans are set up now, as NATO is developing consensus and trying to understand what has happened and is deciding what its response is, we have the ability as JEF nations to act quite quickly in support of each other. ​ I know that politically you're quite keen to stress that JEF is not competing with NATO. But I think for many people in the Baltics, saying that we have some form of a regional alliance where nations can act quickly in case there's a danger would be a reassurance factor. ​ It should be reassuring, because JEF has been a really useful construct for all of us. It will span the Baltic to the high north [and] all the navies that we're talking with and all the nations are really enthusiastic about it. So what’s Lithuania's role? Protect Klaipėda at all costs? ​ I think there is definitely a view of, as we work through the JEF plans, where the critical bits of infrastructure are on which we both nationally de

Lithuania's Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas apologised over a party for ministry employees that cost nearly 48,000 euros and said a new system for motivating staff and building a sense of community would be created.

A Lithuanian presidential aide dismissed a new Russian threat to NATO countries over the Kaliningrad region, the 15min news website reported on Tuesday. "We are informed about the new Russian threats, which are completely baseless and seen as a measure of psychological pressure," Deividas Matulionis, national security aide to President Gitanas Nausėda, told 15min. Matulionis spoke after the Russian embassy in Belgium announced that Moscow was allegedly ready to use its entire weapons arsenal if NATO countries attempted to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country. "We are deeply concerned about provocative statements and actions by the North Atlantic Alliance's leadership and NATO member states concerning the Kaliningrad region, which is an integral part of the Russian Federation," the Russian embassy said in a statement. "We have stressed that Russia has the necessary means to repel possible aggression and is prepared to use its entire available arsenal of weapons to defend its territory if NATO countries attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of our country," the Russian embassy in Belgium said. NATO confirmed to LRT.lt that it had received an "informal document" (non-paper) from the Russian embassy in Belgium warning about Kaliningrad. "We strongly condemn threats to use force, including any irresponsible rhetoric concerning nuclear weapons. We call on Russia to end its unjustified war against Ukraine," NATO spokeswoman Allison Hart said. This is not the first time this year that Moscow's propaganda has accused NATO or alliance countries of plans to blockade or occupy Kaliningrad.

Russia is seeking to spread fear and divide Lithuanian society, but Lithuania is preparing by investing in its defence capabilities, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkecičius said on Tuesday. He also stressed that while the risk of Russian attacks against NATO remains, the threat level has neither significantly increased nor decreased. ​ "Russia seeks to spread fear, to bring division among our societies. But it will not succeed. We're not shaking. We're doing what is meant to be done," Sinkevičius told reporters in Brussels on Tuesday. ​ "We're investing hugely in our military capabilities, in our defence capabilities. And we'll be continuing," the prime minister added. ​ Siinkevičius spoke after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. ​ "We're investing. We're getting ready. We're getting prepared. We're working with the societies, calming down the societies. ​ “I think it's a must to say if the threat is there for the society, but you can't exaggerate and say: 'Oh, something is happening in upcoming months or weeks.' But what I was addressing also Secretary General: is there any proof, real proof? Are intelligence services providing something on the table that Russia is getting ready for something? ​ “And there is actually none, so I mean the risk remains, but it did not fluctuate, or is it increasing or decreasing. So, I think we have to, in this sense, calmly do our work, and we're doing that," Sinkevičius said. ​ Rutte said that NATO has a response to grey zone incidents, such as drone incursions, acts of sabotage or cyber attacks. ​ "We have all the response options we need. You will not always see them publicly. They will not always be symmetric. It will not always be tit for tat. But we have the response options we need," the NATO chief said. ​ "More generally speaking, I would urge some calm because we are investing in our defence. Russia is not in a good place. Their economy is not in a good place. [...] So, some calm is in place here, but also carry on. Carry on with the investments like the Lithuanian government is doing and the rest of NATO is doing at the moment," Rutte said. ​ In recent months, European countries have faced more acts of sabotage attributed to Russia, while Russian drones have been violating the airspace of eastern NATO states.

Estonia on Tuesday accused Russia of sabotage following an arson attack in August on a defence firm, Milrem Robotics. "We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... in Tallinn was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote on X. ​ Tsahkna said that the perpetrators had been apprehended and "no longer pose a threat", and that Estonia had summoned the Russian ambassador. ​ "This act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine," he wrote. ​ The Kremlin dismissed Estonia's accusation, the AFP news wire said.

Lithuania wants the US to maintain a permanent troop presence in the country and is ready to pay for it, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told in an interview with Bloomberg on Tuesday. "We would certainly agree to it if they [the Americans] are ready," Sinkevičius said. According to him, Lithuania is ready to cover the costs of a permanent US troop deployment. ​ The prime minister said he discussed the issue with US Special Envoy for Minsk John Coale, who visited Vilnius in September. ​ Currently, US troops are deployed in Lithuania on a rotational basis. Two US troop battalions, totalling about 1,000 soldiers, will arrive in Lithuania at the end of October, along with Abrams tanks. They will serve in Lithuania for nine months. ​ American troops have been regularly deployed in Lithuania since 2019. Following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Washington changed their status to an uninterrupted rotational deployment. ​ Lithuania has previously indicated it is ready to host up to 1,500 US troops.

Czechia would send two mechanised brigades in case of a Russian attack against the Baltic states, the country’s Prime Minister Andrej Babiš told a local news website on Tuesday. "Of course we are preparing. If, God forbid, Russia were to attack a Baltic state, then, under Article 5, we have to send two of our mechanised brigades," he said. Babis’ government, which includes a pro-Russian anti-immigrant party, previously halted Czech contributions to military aid for Ukraine, Reuters reported. He was also previously criticised for saying he would not send Czech soldiers to fight for allies, according to Reuters. "The ​fact we do not talk about it and journalists don't get fodder ​for their articles does not mean we don't address it," Babis said. "Of course we would ​be active and ​we talk about ⁠it, but I don't see a reason to share classified information." There have been repeated warnings voiced by European leaders, as well as security services, about a potential Russian attack. Baltic leaders, however, have played down fears of military action by Moscow, instead saying the Kremlin is intensifying its sabotage and disinformation campaign against Europe.

Lithuania plans to activate its state reserve for the first time during the Vytis Vault 2026 mobilisation exercise, using stocks of oil, groats and flour to feed some participants. This will test procedures for supplying food from the state reserve, as well as its coordination, management, and interaction with economic entities involved in the process, the Agriculture Ministry said. Justas Jaskonis, an aide to the agriculture minister, said the government will decide on the proposal at its meeting on Wednesday. ​ The Lithuanian Riflemen's Union exercise Strong Dzūkas 2026 will also take place in the Lazdijai district, with training focused on protecting important sites, maintaining public order, setting up transport control posts and conducting defensive operations. ​ Vytis Vault 2026 is Lithuania's largest annual exercise of its kind. It began last Friday and will continue until October 3. ​ The state reserve is used during emergencies or crises, when mobilisation is declared, or when a state of emergency or martial law is introduced. It consists of food, medical supplies, other material resources and funds.

As European leaders warn of possible Russian attacks and hybrid provocations, experts and officials agree that there are no signs of a new escalation. “In my view, the situation remains as it was. The point is that the Russians certainly have not stopped, so talk of possible provocations is nothing new,” military expert and Vilnius University Institute of International Relations and Political Science (VU TSPMI) associate professor Deividas Šlekys told the ELTA news wire. In his assessment, large-scale military operations are less likely than specific provocations aimed at spreading panic among the public and exerting political pressure. “Nobody is preparing to conquer us at the moment – neither right now nor this year. In this case, some kind of specific, highly precise attacks or provocations are more likely, aimed not so much at causing physical damage as at sowing serious panic in people’s minds,” Šlekys said. According to him, Russia could use such provocations to divide Lithuanian society and undermine unity among NATO countries. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC), said Russia’s hybrid pressure on Lithuania and other European countries is “not a new phenomenon”. “Since 2024, Lithuania alone has recorded a number of attacks or provocations involving acts of sabotage, as well as cyber and information operations,” Vitkauskas told ELTA. He said warnings and preparedness measures by neighbouring and allied countries were a responsible response to the current security environment. “Early warning, institutional preparedness and informing the public reduce the impact of provocations and strengthen NATO’s overall resilience,” the NKVC head said. When assessing specific incidents, Vitkauskas urged people to distinguish confirmed facts from speculation and rely on information provided by official institutions. “Based on the official information published so far, there is no evidence that the drones that entered Lithuanian airspace were targeting sites in Lithuania,” Vitkauskas said. He noted that Lithuania has strengthened the protection of strategic infrastructure, while the NKVC, together with intelligence and other responsible institutions, has issued recommendations to companies and institutions that may face the risk of sabotage or acts of subversion. Vitkauskas also urged the public to remain vigilant and not spread unverified information, as kinetic incidents or provocations may be accompanied by information operations aimed at causing fear and undermining trust in institutions. Martinaitis: threat level remains unchanged Meanwhile, Tomas Martinaitis, a Social Democrat and member of the parliamentary National Security and Defence Committee (NSDK), says the level of the Russian threat remains unchanged. Meanwhile, Moscow’s messaging about possible retaliatory actions against NATO and EU countries may be intended to cause anxiety and undermine public confidence. "If we assess the situation as a whole, I would say that the level of the threat, as intelligence officials have also confirmed, has not changed. Russia's unpredictability remains. The tactics may be changing slightly, with different types of actions emerging, but the essence remains unchanged," Martinaitis told ELTA. A similar sentiment was repeated by the Lithuanian prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, as well as the secretary-general of NATO, Mark Rutte, in Brussels on Tuesday. In recent weeks, the leaders of several European countries have spoken about the threat of possible Russian provocations. In early September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that, based on intelligence assessments, Russia could be preparing hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine, and urged the public to be prepared for various scenarios. Meanwhile, Finnish President Alexander Stubb also urged people to prepare for possible drone attacks and other hybrid attacks.

Lithuania’s government on Wednesday approved a draft legislation banning Russian and Belarusian nationals from purchasing property in areas located near strategic sites, even if they hold residence permits. Belarusian nationals without residence permits would also be barred from buying property, while Russians were banned from doing so in a previous bill. The restrictions would not apply where ownership is acquired through inheritance. ​ If approved by the Seimas, the amendments would come into force on January 1 next year. Latvia and Finland previosuly banned Belarusian and Russian nationals from purchasing property, with exceptions for those who hold residence permits in the respective countries. Estonia is now planning to introduce a similar ban.

Lithuania’s government on Wednesday approved a proposal to ban Belarusian and Russian artists and other cultural figures from performing in the country if they had worked in occupied or annexed Ukrainian territories. The ban would also extend to people who have directly or indirectly supported Russia’s war against Ukraine. The government is yet to outline the specific criteria, with the amendment still to be approved by the parliament. The restrictions would not apply to people who have "clearly acted against aggression, occupation or annexation, publicly demonstrated their opposition to these actions and whose activities objectively did not contribute to the implementation of the interests of the occupying authorities". ​ The Foreign Ministry proposed that artists and cultural figures would be required to sign a publicly available declaration condemning Russia's aggression against Ukraine and expressing support for Ukraine's territorial integrity. ​ Refusing to sign the document would prevent them from carrying out activities in the country. ​ If approved by the Seimas, the amendments would come into force on January 1 next year. So far, Lithuania has taken individual decisions to bar several performers who support Vladimir Putin's regime and have performed in Russia or Crimea from entering the country.

Construction of a Leopard 2A8 tank assembly and repair plant officially began in the Kaunas Free Economic Zone on Thursday. ​The 13,000-square-metre plant will assemble and service Leopard 2A8 tanks and other heavy equipment of the Lithuanian Armed Forces. ​ The plant is being built on behalf of Lithuania Defence Services, a joint venture company established in 2022 by two German arms manufacturers, Rheinmetall and Krauss-Maffei Wegmann. YIT Lietuva, a construction company, is carrying out the work for 29 million euros, with the project scheduled to be completed in November 2027. The first tank assembled in Lithuania is expected to roll out of the plant at the end of 2028. Thirty-eight of the 44 Leopard 2A8 tanks bought by Lithuania will be assembled in the plant, while six or more will be manufactured in Germany. ​ "We are also ready to support an additional assembly line for new clients in the Baltic region," Lithuania Defence Services board chairman Markus Franz Schmidt told reporters. A share transfer agreement for Lithuania Defence Services was also signed at the event, under which KNDS Deutschland and Rheinmetall Landsysteme will transfer part of their shares to Lithuania’s state-owned EPSO-G Invest. ​ Economy and Innovation Minister Edvinas Griksas confirmed to reporters that under the agreement, Lithuania became a partner in the project. ​ "The state naturally contributes and becomes a shareholder in important projects like this one. As I mentioned in my speech, I cannot wait to hear the roaring Leopards assembled here in Lithuania," he said. EPSO-G Invest head Tomas Varneckas later indicated that under the agreement, the company will own 25.1 percent of Lithuania Defense Services, while KNDS Deutschland and Rheinmetall Landsysteme will each hold 37.45 percent. The transaction is expected to be completed within the next six months. ​ The plant is expected to create up to 100 jobs. Lithuania Defence Services plans to invest about 50 million euros in the project.

Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev on Thursday praised Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius’ comments that there is no evidence Russia is preparing an attack on NATO, calling the remarks “unusually wise”. “The unusually wise words from a Lithuanian PM who openly says that the ‘scare with Russia’ EU hysteria is not based on ANY facts,” Dmitriev wrote on X. He said EU officials were using Russia as a “bogeyman” to divert attention from what he described as failures over migration, the economy, “woke” policies and what he called warmongering. The administration of US President Donald Trump has not invited several key allies, including the Baltic states, to next month’s NATO meeting, Politico reports. The administration has previously threatened to create a “list of good and bad countries” that would include governments that do not align with the US president’s priorities. According to six diplomats familiar with the preparations for the meeting, the gathering in Poland – organised at the initiative of Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby – will essentially serve as a working group on NATO’s future. However, the meeting may exclude countries like the United Kingdom, France, and the Baltics that allocate significant funds to military spending and have supported US foreign policy. Their diplomats question why these nations have been left out. “We’re doing everything we’re being asked to do. We’re trying to understand what the criteria are and what the purpose of these meetings is. So far, we’ve been given little information,” an official from one of the excluded allied countries told Politico. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the situation, and the Pentagon declined to comment. President Gitanas Nausėda said on Thursday that overemphasising the situation created artificial hype. He stressed that this was a meeting of the so-called Bergen Group, to which Lithuania did not belong. The format includes the US, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Germany and the Netherlands. "NATO has more than 30 members, and in this case only six are participating [excluding the US]. This seems to me a bit like creating some sort of artificial hype," Nausėda told reporters on Thursday. He said Lithuania and other countries could be invited to the format in the future if it expands.

After a six-month break, US troops are set to return to Lithuania, with about 1,000 soldiers expected to deploy under a new rotation. Lithuanian officials and defence experts say the return sends a strong deterrence message to Russia, while Vilnius is also seeking a permanent US military presence. The Americans are familiar with the forests around Pabradė, where their presence in Lithuania grew steadily over the past decade – from several hundred troops to more than 1,000 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. But the continuous US mission ended in June as Washington reassessed its military role in Europe. A newly built facility in Lithuania stood empty for six months. Within a month, however, it is expected to house American troops again. The new rotation will include a heavy battalion equipped with Abrams tanks, as before, while an artillery battalion will be replaced by an engineering unit, President Gitanas Nausėda said. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said the deployment would contribute significantly to the development of Lithuania’s national division and strengthen the protection of defensive lines along the border. The engineering capability is particularly important because Lithuania’s own engineering regiment in Kaunas is still being developed and lacks much of the equipment needed for heavy units, said retired Col. Gintaras Ažubalis. Former military commanders said Lithuania is developing its own artillery capabilities, making the US engineering deployment a useful complement to the country’s existing forces. “The artillery unit means fire support; now we have an engineering unit, which means logistical support, so that the tank battalion can operate effectively,” said Lt. Gen. Jonas Vytautas Žukas, who served as Lithuania’s military chief from 2014 to 2019. The Americans will also bring specialised equipment and machinery that Lithuania does not have, said Lt. Gen. Arvydas Pocius, who served as military chief from 2009 to 2014. The number of US troops is expected to remain around 1,000, although it is not yet clear whether the rotation will continue without another break after nine months. “I doubt this nine-month rotation would have happened if there were no plan to continue the rotation afterward,” Žukas said. Pocius agreed, saying there had been no indication that the deployment would be a one-time arrangement. Estonia has also secured the temporary return of US troops. “That is good news, because American troops on the eastern flank are very important for our security, and it is a very clear message to President Putin: There is no point even thinking about aggression against NATO’s eastern flank,” Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said. It is not yet clear where the US troops returning to Lithuania will come from. They could be drawn from US units already stationed in Poland, Ažubalis said, arguing that the source of the troops would not change the strategic significance of the deployment. Former MP, security and defence expert Giedrimas Jeglinskas said the deployment was linked to US forces in Poland and Washington’s plans for a permanent base there. US President Donald Trump has said progress has been made toward establishing a permanent American base in Poland, where negotiations have been underway for about six months. Experts say such a move would fit into a broader strengthening of NATO’s eastern flank. The precise form of the US presence in Poland remains unclear. It could involve a permanent deployment sought by Warsaw, potentially involving about 5,000 additional troops, or strengthened rotational forces numbering around 10,000, said Gerlinde Niehus, a former deputy director of NATO’s defence policy and planning division. “Whatever form it takes, the overall direction is clear – strengthening the eastern flank,” she said. Lithuania is also seeking a permanent US base. “Since we are compensating for the presence of US troops in Lithuania, I proposed establishing a permanent US military base,” Kaunas said. Whether Lithuania’s existing military infrastructure will be enough to persuade Washington to establish permanent bases in both Poland and Lithuania remains uncertain. Retired officers say NATO and the United States view Poland and the Baltic states as part of a single strategic region. “All of this is part of the security of our common region. I have no doubt that these groups will not be separated,” Žukas said. He nevertheless argued that Lithuania should first focus on completing the establishment of the German brigade. Germany’s brigade remains Lithuania’s priority By the end of next year, Lithuania expects the German brigade to number about 5,000 troops – roughly five times the planned US deployment. But Germany has faced difficulties recruiting enough personnel, particularly specialists. “Our commitment to transfer a full-capability brigade to Lithuania no later than the end of 2027 is carved in stone,” German Ambassador to Lithuania Cornelius Zimmermann said. “We are particularly looking for specialists in information technology and other fields, and they are not so easy to find.” Fausta Šimaitytė, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Lithuania, said the brigade should be viewed as a military commitment rather than a voluntary project. Germany’s domestic politics could also affect the broader environment in which the brigade is established, with the Alternative for Germany party continuing to gain support. “Germans keep their word, especially the military. Of course, much will depend on political decisions and who comes to power,” Pocius said. Nausėda sought to reassure those concerned about the German commitment. “I see that various messages are being spread again. Rest assured, the German brigade will be in Lithuania at full strength,” he said. Lithuania is testing a Ukrainian-developed airspace monitoring system designed to detect low-flying drones and other threats by analysing acoustic and radio signals, the Defence Ministry said Friday. The pilot deployment of the SkyFortress system is intended to strengthen the first stage of Lithuania’s air defene network – detecting and tracking potential threats before they can be intercepted. “Air threats are changing rapidly, so we are adapting our solutions accordingly,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said in a statement. “Instead of developing everything from scratch, we are adapting systems that are already operating in Ukraine.” SkyFortress uses artificial intelligence to detect and track low-flying drones and cruise missiles based on acoustic or electromagnetic signatures, the ministry said. The system can classify detected objects in real time. Under a contract signed this summer, the project also includes processing data collected by the system’s sensors, using libraries of digital acoustic and radio-frequency signatures based on unclassified data, and training personnel, according to the ministry. Testing will assess the system’s ability to detect and identify low-flying unmanned aircraft in Lithuania. The deployment comes as Lithuania and its Baltic neighbours have strengthened airspace security amid Russia’s war against Ukraine and an increase in reports of potential air threats in the region. A drone that entered Lithuania from Belarus was shot down over Lithuanian territory in September by Italian fighter jets stationed in Šiauliai. It was the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuania. Similar incidents had previously occurred in Latvia and Estonia. The Defence Ministry said SkyFortress will contribute to strengthening Lithuania’s broader air defence capabilities, from surveillance and identification to the interception and neutralisation of aerial threats.

European Union interior ministers discussed tougher measures to combat irregular migration Thursday, including plans to establish return centres in third countries. Lithuania says it supports an initiative by several EU countries but does not currently plan to join it. The ministers meeting in Luxembourg were also expected to give final approval to new EU rules that would expand authorities’ powers to detain people facing removal and allow the creation of so-called return centres outside the bloc. The initiative is being promoted by a group of five countries: Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands. Rwanda and Uganda are among the main candidates to host such centres. The centres could serve as destinations or transit points for people being removed from the EU, including those whose asylum applications have been rejected. Supporters say they could facilitate repatriation and deter people from attempting to enter the EU irregularly. Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas, who represented Lithuania at the meeting, said Lithuania did not face a large enough migration problem to participate in the initiative at present. “Lithuania does not have a problem of such a scale that we need to participate in this format, but we support the efforts of other European countries to solve this issue,” Katelynas told LRT. “If there is a need, we will certainly support the initiative. And if at some point in the future we need it ourselves, we would certainly join.” Katelynas said EU countries currently implement only about one-third of decisions ordering migrants to be deported. He said irregular migration at Lithuania’s external border was currently under control, although the country had faced an increase in secondary migration earlier this summer. “There are currently about 200 irregular migrants at Lithuania’s Foreigners Registration Centre, most of whom should be returned to Latvia or other Schengen countries,” Katelynas said. The proposal for return centres has drawn criticism from human rights advocates and some politicians. European Parliament members Anna Strolenberg and Tineke Strik of the Greens group held an online news conference Wednesday following a visit to Uganda and Rwanda. They questioned whether the two countries were appropriate locations for EU return centres, citing concerns about human rights, conditions in the proposed facilities and their potential impact on local communities. They also argued that the centres would not address the causes of irregular migration and could become costly. EU ministers in Luxembourg were also due to discuss proposed changes to asylum rules that would apply during emergency situations, including circumstances in which migration is considered to be used as a tool of political pressure. The debate follows a reported surge of migrants at Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta this summer, when about 80,000 people were reported to have attempted to enter the territory. Some right-wing politicians and EU countries have argued that the right to seek asylum should be restricted in situations where migration is considered to be “instrumentalised”. Swedish and Estonian ministers also arrived in Luxembourg seeking details from the European Commission on possible restrictions on Schengen visas for Russian citizens. Lithuania supports that initiative as well.

Raccoons are being counted and monitored on the Curonian Spit as authorities prepare a management plan for the invasive species. The animals are likely to start being trapped and hunted as early as next spring. "The impression is that there are quite a lot of them here, but it is difficult to say exactly how many. I would estimate there could be between 50 and 100 individuals," says Saulius Rumbutis, an employee of the Tadas Ivanauskas Zoological Museum. Raccoons are nocturnal animals and usually hide during the day. "They often choose large natural tree hollows or simply a broken-off section of a pine tree. They climb up such a pine and can spend the day there sleeping, then go out at night to look for food," Rumbutis says. Most raccoons are being observed in Juodkrantė. The omnivorous animals stay close to settlements, where there is plenty of food. "They crack open mollusc shells and feed on them, find a bird's nest on the ground or in a tree and eat the chicks or eggs. If they find a pizza slice discarded by a tourist in a bin, they will certainly eat that too," says Rumbutis. On the mainland, only the occasional raccoon is spotted, but they have to face deadly predators, including wolves. On the Curonian Spit, raccoons usually die only after being hit by cars. "They would run across the road at night while we were driving through the forest. I've seen them," one local woman says. "They become uncontrollable, and that's the problem. Then they destroy some of our native animals," another woman adds. The Environment Ministry is preparing a plan to manage raccoons because the problems will increase if nothing is done, according to scientists. Raccoons are likely to start being hunted as early as next year. "They can be caught using live traps. They smell the bait, go into the traps and get caught. The problem is that if the traps have not been specially modified, raccoons can easily use their nimble front paws to open the doors of traps and escape," says Rumbutis. Raccoons may have spread on the Curonian Spit after someone released animals that had been kept in captivity.

Lithuania’s authorities have issued an all-clear (code white) following an earlier air alert. “The Lithuanian Armed Forces inform: AIR ALERT IS OVER (WHITE). You may leave safe places or shelters,” the authorities said in an emergency message. Previously, at around 09:50, a possible air raid alert (yellow) was issued, indicating that a possibly dangerous object had crossed into Lithuania's airspace. The warning affected Vilnius County in the east of the country. The alert was called off around 50 minutes later. “It was confirmed that there was no air threat, as the object posed no danger. Whether it was birds or some other object, I cannot say at this time,” NKVC Director Vilmantas Vitkauskas told LRT RADIO on Saturday. According to the National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC), fighter jets have been scrambled. The controlled airspace around Vilnius Airport has been temporarily closed due to the activity of unidentified flying objects. “The object has not yet been fully identified; fighter jets have been scrambled and are carrying out that procedure. We are receiving reports from residents that they are observing a possible object already outside the Vilnius area, moving toward Jonava. But we cannot confirm this, as these are reports from residents,” NKVC Director Vilmantas Vitkauskas told LRT RADIO. He said it is likely that an alert could also be issued in the Kaunas district. According to him, the speed of the object is relatively slow so it cannot be ruled out that it could be just a flock of birds. On the one hand, living from one day to the next and worrying about their homeland; on the other, looking for ways to obtain permanent residence in the EU after March 2028. This is precisely how women who fled Ukraine for EU countries at the start of the war described their experiences of living under temporary protection to Suspilne. This summer, the European Union and Switzerland extended temporary protection for Ukrainians already living there until 4 March 2028. For new arrivals, however, the rules have changed: applicants must now prove that they have been exempted from military service in Ukraine and left the country legally. Meanwhile, for many Ukrainians who have been living in the EU for several years, temporary protection means ever-deeper integration into the lives of the countries that have taken them in. According to Eurostat, there are currently over 4.4 million Ukrainians living in the EU who were previously granted temporary protection. With every month of the war, the number of those returning to Ukraine is decreasing, believes Ella Libanova, director of the Institute of Demography and Social Studies at the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine. At the same time, in her view, it is most likely that women aged over 25 with a higher education will return. After all, back home they have significantly better prospects for professional development. Suspilne spoke to Ukrainian women who were granted temporary protection in Poland, Germany and Ireland during the early years of Russia’s full-scale invasion. It also sought to find out the views of men who have moved to the EU and hold this status. Poland: Ukrainians are needed, but attitudes are deteriorating Inna Bezroda has been living in Poland since 2022: she moved there from Kyiv with her two children after the full-scale war began. Inna has cancer, so her husband joined her a year later after leaving Ukraine legally. Because of her illness, Inna is unable to work, so her husband provides for the family. The family rents a flat in Warsaw. Apart from child benefit, to which working parents are entitled in Poland, the family receives no other social benefits. Thanks to her husband’s job, Inna is entitled to health insurance and free cancer treatment. If she were living in Poland on her own, she would have lost her right to access healthcare from March 2026 onwards – due to new changes to the law. These changes have deprived those who are not in work of free access to medical care. Vulnerable groups – pensioners and people with disabilities – are the hardest hit by this. The Temporary Protection Mechanism in the EU was introduced specifically for Ukrainian refugees on 4 March 2022 in response to Russian aggression. It grants the right to reside and work legally in the EU. Ukrainians are granted this status without lengthy bureaucratic procedures. As part of this scheme, in addition to the legalisation of their status, they were granted access to state healthcare and assistance with renting accommodation. However, year after year, individual countries review various aspects of the temporary protection arrangements for Ukrainians within the framework set by the European Union. This applies both to access to healthcare and to the provision of accommodation. Furthermore, such protection will come to an end once the EU recognises that it is safe to return to Ukraine. At the same time, Ukrainians are sometimes helped by charitable organisations or individuals outside this formal framework. “I lived in Warsaw for three years in a flat with my children for free; it was given to us by a Polish man, a complete stranger,” says Inna. “I recently went on a rehabilitation programme for cancer patients, where I was the only Ukrainian. I was worried about how people would treat me. But everything went brilliantly; I made friends with the Polish women. We talked about politics, and I admitted to them that I’d been afraid to come v and I felt a lot of support. They said: "If you ever hear that we Poles have a negative attitude towards Ukrainians, just think of our faces.” However, Inna acknowledges that attitudes towards Ukrainians in Polish society as a whole have deteriorated compared with 2022. Although her command of Polish is limited, Inna avoids speaking Ukrainian on public transport so as not to cause offence. "We used to joke about it in the family: if Poland comes up with anything else [regarding Ukrainians], we’ll get in the car, pack our bags and head further west." Poland is home to over 970,000 Ukrainians under the temporary protection scheme, the second-highest figure in the EU after Germany. Most of them (68 per cent, according to the UN Refugee Agency) are in work, as the country provides virtually no social support. Many Ukrainians are in jobs below their qualifications, whilst a significant number are still working remotely for Ukrainian employers or running their own businesses. Ukrainians’ contribution to Poland’s budget exceeds the cost of supporting them: in 2024, the country’s GDP grew by 2.7 per cent thanks to refugees. Warsaw therefore has a financial interest in keeping Ukrainians in the country – despite the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of politicians. According to Inna, her family isn’t particularly concerned about how long the EU’s temporary protection programme will last. After all, Poland has already introduced a scheme allowing Ukrainians to switch to a different, more permanent status known as CUKR. This new status is not dependent on having a job or a certain level of income, which is particularly important to Inna. Ukrainians who held temporary protection status in Poland as of June 4, 2025, and whose status remains valid at the time of application may apply for the Temporary Residence Permit (TRP). TPR status will be temporary (three years – Ed.), but the time spent under this status will count toward the period required to obtain long-term EU resident status. Latvia’s defense minister has played down any immediate danger after Russia’s latest nuclear warning to NATO over Kaliningrad. “I don’t see an imminent threat at this point,” Raivis Melnis told RFE/RL in an interview in Washington on September 30, echoing NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who said he did not take the Russian warning "that seriously". Russia warned NATO this week that it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, its heavily militarised Baltic exclave wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. In a diplomatic memo circulated to NATO member states, Moscow said it had information that the alliance was preparing an “air and naval blockade” of the territory. The warning prompted Rutte to call on Russia to “stop the nuclear threats”, saying NATO is a defensive alliance and that “this is absolutely not called for and not helpful”. He added that Russian President Vladimir Putin knows that he cannot win in a direct confrontation with NATO. Melnis said Russia had repeatedly resorted to nuclear threats since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, arguing that Moscow uses such rhetoric to frighten Western populations, weaken support for Kyiv, and test the cohesion of the NATO alliance. “Russia will use any means to threaten us, to bring fear to our people, to support Ukraine, and also to break our unity, cohesion, to support and just test where are those limits,” he said. The Russian warning has nevertheless raised concern among arms-control and security specialists, particularly because of Kaliningrad’s strategic position and Russia’s evolving nuclear doctrine. Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, a nonpartisan Washington based nonprofit, told RFE/RL that the Russian threat should be taken seriously and condemned as unacceptable. He said Moscow’s language reflected what he described as a careless approach to the dangers of nuclear weapons use. Kimball noted that NATO does not appear to be preparing military action to isolate Kaliningrad. Even if such a confrontation were contemplated, he said, using nuclear weapons in a conflict involving another nuclear-armed state or alliance could trigger retaliation, escalation, and potentially catastrophic consequences. He argued that Moscow should instead address its concerns with NATO through diplomatic channels, saying that “rather than threatening nuclear attack, the Kremlin should reach out to NATO capitals to clarify whatever concerns Russia might have and to address those concerns diplomatically and responsibly.” Lynn Rusten, a senior fellow at the Centre for European Policy Analysis and a former senior White House National Security Council official responsible for arms control and nonproliferation, told RFE/RL that Russia’s latest nuclear rhetoric appeared “unhinged and hyperbolic” from a Western perspective. But Rusten also warned of a dangerous combination of factors: Russian threats and provocative hybrid warfare, NATO and Russian forces operating in close proximity, continued Western support for Ukraine, and a lack of meaningful dialogue. She said those conditions could increase the risk of dangerous miscalculation, particularly as Russia and NATO assert competing red lines while channels for managing tensions remain limited. “The lack of meaningful dialogue and the growing divide in security perceptions carries a grave risk of further and potentially unintended escalation and expansion of this conflict,” Rusten said. Sylvia Mishra, nuclear policy director at the Institute for Security and Technology, said nuclear brinkmanship was not new for Moscow but should nonetheless be treated seriously. Kaliningrad, she noted, is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet and is strategically important but geographically vulnerable, surrounded by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia. Mishra said reported NATO air operations around the exclave in mid-August, which included aircraft with capabilities to disrupt communications, radar, and navigation systems, could have heightened Moscow’s sense of vulnerability. She also pointed to Russia’s 2024 revised nuclear doctrine, which formally lowered the threshold described by Moscow for potential nuclear use. Mishra said the latest warning appeared to be the first instance of Russia issuing a written diplomatic note explicitly warning that it was prepared to use nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad. For Melnis, however, the more immediate threat is neither nuclear nor a large-scale Russian conventional military assault on NATO, but an expanding campaign of hybrid activity – hostile actions short of open warfare, including cyberattacks, sabotage, and the weaponisation of migration. He said Latvia and its allies are continuously reassessing the threat, monitoring Russia’s military capabilities, losses in Ukraine, force generation, and activities such as suspected attacks on military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure. “We are monitoring and we are working closely with Ukrainian partners or with our NATO partners,” Melnis said, adding that Latvia’s threat assessment is a continuous process and that hybrid activity is increasing. Melnis said he did not believe Russia currently had the capacity to launch a conventional offensive against a NATO country while sustaining its war in Ukraine. “Russia stopped in Ukraine, they are not achieving the goals,” he said, pointing to Ukrainian counteroffensive operations and arguing that Moscow would face major difficulties trying to conduct two large-scale military operations simultaneously. He described cyberattacks, pressure through migration from Belarus – which Minsk has been accused of facilitating to destabilise its neighbours – and other hostile activities as part of the new security environment confronting Latvia and its allies.
