Lithuania’s Defence Ministry plans to spend 25,000 euros to develop a mobile game called Baltic Defence Line. "In the game, users could practically test how engineering obstacles are planned, how they affect enemy movement, and learn how different defence measures interact with each other. The player, having limited resources, would have to make decisions on how to organise defence as effectively as possible," the ministry said. ​ The ministry says the game is intended to increase public awareness of the state's readiness for defence and encourage interest in national security issues. ​ During Lithuania's presidency of the European Union, the project also aims to draw attention to strengthening the protection of the EU’s eastern border and the defence of the Baltic region ​ The game is planned to be adapted for Android and iOS devices and distributed via Google Play and the Apple App Store. ​ According to public procurement data, the project's value is 24,800 euros. Proposals are accepted until October 26.

Construction of residential blocks for German soldiers at Lithuania’s Rūdninkai training area has been completed, and the country’s defence minister said Monday that infrastructure for the planned deployment of a German brigade remains on schedule. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said construction of the next phase was progressing quickly and Lithuania would complete the necessary infrastructure in time for the brigade’s full deployment. “We will definitely make it in time,” Kaunas told journalists. “We see that the second stage of construction is underway, and it is progressing particularly fast.” German officials regularly visit the site and inspect the construction, Kaunas said, adding that they had not raised any significant concerns. Under an agreement between Lithuania and Germany, Berlin plans to deploy a brigade of about 5,000 troops to Lithuania by the end of 2027. Most of the brigade will be based at the Rūdninkai training area. About 2,000 military personnel and civilian employees are expected to be serving under the brigade’s command in Lithuania by the end of this year. Questions have been raised about whether Germany can meet the deployment timeline after it failed to attract enough soldiers willing to volunteer for service in Lithuania. Kaunas said most positions in the brigade had already been filled by volunteers, while the remaining personnel would be assigned to the unit. He said he hoped more German soldiers would volunteer after seeing the living and training conditions being prepared for them in Lithuania. Kaunas also said he saw no indication that the growing popularity of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD, party could affect the brigade’s deployment to Lithuania. The German brigade is intended to become a key component of Lithuania’s defence and NATO’s eastern flank as the Baltic country strengthens its military capabilities in response to Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Germany risks becoming directly involved in a violent conflict with Russia as Moscow’s confrontation with the West takes on a more dangerous form, the head of Germany’s federal intelligence service warned Monday. Martin Jäger, head of the Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, told a public hearing of the Bundestag’s parliamentary oversight committee that Russia currently poses the most direct and comprehensive threat to Germany of any country, German daily Die Welt reported. “The confrontation we are in with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous form: Germany is at risk of becoming involved in a violent conflict with Russia,” Jäger said. He cited an incident involving a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig Airport as one example of the threats facing Germany. Russian intelligence services are operating “very professionally and ruthlessly”, he said. “The threat of attacks against targets in Germany remains real and acute. We must counter it,” Jäger said. He described Moscow’s activities as a “shadow war” aimed at ensuring that Berlin and other European capitals do not make political decisions directed against Russia in the future. Jäger said Russia’s main objective is to undermine European political support for Ukraine and warned that Moscow could again resort to nuclear threats as part of its efforts. At the same time, the BND currently sees no indications that Russia is preparing a large-scale attack on NATO territory. However, Jäger warned that “low-intensity Russian military actions” could occur, particularly in the Baltic states. “We did not seek this confrontation; Russia is imposing it on us, seeing us as its main adversary,” Jäger said. “Because we are resisting Russia’s attempts to intimidate our allies in the Baltic states and elsewhere in Europe.” Germany has become a key obstacle to Russia’s efforts to project hegemonic power in Europe and has consequently become a target of Russian actions, he said. “Those who do not submit become an adversary: That is Moscow’s interpretation,” Jäger said. He also warned that Russia’s war in Ukraine, where Moscow is carrying out increasingly brutal attacks, is entering a highly dangerous new phase. Russian President Vladimir Putin has already crossed a threshold beyond which he could no longer simply halt pressure on Ukraine without risking the foundations of his domestic power, Jäger said. “He has to achieve a success in Ukraine that, from Russia’s perspective, would justify the enormous sacrifices made so far. This forces him to take action,” he said. Despite the pressure, Jäger said there were no signs of panic within the Russian leadership. Moscow is aware of the limits of its military and economic resources, he said.

A project by Baltic Metal Foundry, the Lithuanian subsidiary of Ukrainian defence company Dnipro Electromechanical Plant (DEMZ), to manufacture ammunition and munitions components in Lithuania is being proposed for special status. The Economy and Innovation Ministry has drafted a government resolution that would designate the project as meeting urgent state security and defence needs. The status would allow the company to benefit from special investment and business conditions beyond those provided under Lithuania’s Investment Law. The ministry said the decision would contribute to improving the business environment and increasing investment. Baltic Metal Foundry signed an investment agreement with the ministry in mid-August. Under the agreement, the company plans to manufacture ammunition and munitions components in Alytus and the Prienai district, with the project expected to create up to 450 jobs. The value of the investment was not disclosed when the agreement was signed. Alytus Mayor Nerijus Cesiulis said at the time that the Ukrainian company planned to invest tens of millions of euros in the town. Lithuania’s list of major investment projects shows that the company has committed to investing at least 93.3 million euros in the project. An ammunition assembly plant is planned for the Prienai district, while existing infrastructure at the Alytus industrial park will be used to manufacture metal munitions components. Construction of the plant near Balbieriškis was expected to begin this autumn, with production scheduled to start late next year or in the autumn of 2027. The facility is planned on a 30.6-hectare site in the village of Ąžuolai. The company has said its products will meet NATO standards. Its primary market will be the Ukrainian armed forces, while production will also serve the defence needs of allied countries. DEMZ is a major supplier of defence products to Ukraine’s military. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the company shifted its operations from civilian to military production. It has branches across Ukraine and employs about 4,000 people. Baltic Metal Foundry was registered in Vilnius just over a year ago and currently has one employee, according to Lithuania’s State Social Insurance Fund, Sodra. Data from the Centre of Registers shows that the company’s beneficiaries include two Polish citizens and one Ukrainian citizen.

Lithuania’s parliament voted Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment that would remove a ban on weapons of mass destruction from the country’s constitution, potentially opening the way for allied nuclear weapons to be stationed in Lithuania. The amendment passed its first reading with 106 lawmakers voting in favour, 18 against and six abstaining. A final vote cannot be held until at least three months after Tuesday’s vote. The amendment will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of the Seimas to pass. Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas has said the final vote is scheduled for January 12. Olekas said before the vote that removing the ban would strengthen Lithuania’s resilience and deterrence capabilities. He said eliminating the restriction would also remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other European Union and NATO countries. “We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us,” Olekas said. “By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal.” Opposition conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas urged lawmakers to support the amendment, saying neighbouring countries do not have similar restrictions. He argued that the existing constitutional provision prevents NATO allies from fully including Lithuania in the alliance’s nuclear deterrence planning. “With the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans,” Kasčiūnas said. “Since nuclear deterrence is the queen of deterrence as a whole, this decision is strategically important.” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas also stressed the importance of deterrence, saying politicians should provide the country with every available tool to ensure its security. Kaunas said Lithuania is surrounded by countries with strategic weapons, pointing to Russia’s Kaliningrad region and Belarus. He described the proposed constitutional change as a response to Moscow’s actions. “We are responding to Russia’s aggression,” Kaunas said. “If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions we are having today.” Article 137 of Lithuania’s Constitution currently states that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment would remove that provision. The amendment faced its strongest opposition from lawmakers in the opposition Nemunas Dawn party. Fourteen party members voted against it and two abstained. Aidas Gedvilas of Nemunas Dawn said he was surprised that parliament considered itself empowered to make such a fundamental change and called for a referendum. “There are certainly alternatives to this constitutional provision. We could resolve this through a referendum,” Gedvilas said. Three members of the mixed parliamentary group and one lawmaker from the Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance also voted against the amendment. The debate comes amid broader discussions in Europe about strengthening nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron presented an idea in March for a new European nuclear deterrence framework under which partner countries could temporarily host France’s nuclear-capable strategic air forces. The Financial Times reported in June that the United States was considering deploying nuclear weapons in several additional NATO countries in Europe. Lithuanian military analysts have said Russian media has taken an interest in Lithuania’s plans to remove the constitutional ban. In early September, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned that Lithuania could become a target for Russia if it allowed allies to deploy nuclear weapons on its territory. The Kremlin warned Tuesday that the deployment of nuclear weapons or a permanent US military base in Lithuania would constitute an escalation and force Russia to take measures to protect its security. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian state media. “A military base is part of military infrastructure. If someone’s military infrastructure – in fact, that of a major NATO member – is approaching our borders, of course, this can only be viewed as a step toward escalation,” Peskov said at a news conference. “The same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighbouring country,” he added. Peskov was asked how Moscow would respond if Lithuania moved to lift its constitutional ban on deploying nuclear weapons while the United States considered establishing a permanent base there. “All this will not help ensure stability and predictability on the European continent,” Peskov said. “On the contrary, to our regret, it would be another very significant escalation.” “As for Russia, of course, Russia will have to take all necessary measures to guarantee its security,” he said. Lithuanian officials have stressed that there are currently no plans to deploy nuclear weapons in the country. They say removing the constitutional restriction is intended to ensure that Lithuania does not face legal obstacles to participating in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements.

Lithuania and Poland have identified alternative border crossing points in case of a potential crisis, with international evacuation plans to be drawn up “as soon as possible”, Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said on Monday. “Following the exercise held by our friends in Lithuania, we already have an agenda and an action plan in place,” he told reporters at the Budzisko border crossing with Lithuania on Monday. Mass evacuations were part of Vytis Vault (Vyčio Skliautas) 2026, the largest annual exercise testing Lithuania’s mobilisation system. Around 20 Polish representatives also took part. Following the exercises, Lithuania and Poland are beginning “intensive work” on international evacuation plans, Kierwinski said, adding that Poland has assigned tasks to institutions including the governor of the Podlaskie Voivodeship located next to Lithuania and the Border Guard. “In the event of any crisis, Lithuania becomes a natural route for the citizens of the Baltic states to move towards the European Union, so we must be prepared for such a scenario. “We also discussed population protection and civil defence issues with the minister [Martynas Katelynas] – this is an ongoing process for which we are constantly preparing,” the Polish interior minister said. His Lithuanian counterpart, Katelynas, said “the Suwałki Corridor would become the route through which one million or more people would move” during a crisis. “If the threat were at such a level that people naturally began moving towards the heart of Europe, Estonians, Latvians and Lithuanians would have a single corridor,” the minister said. “Essentially, cooperation between the Baltic states and Poland in the field of civil defence and security needs to be strengthened. And this is happening – Polish experts took part in our exercise, providing their insights and observations,” Katelynas said. As part of the drills, the Polish side identified the need for alternative evacuation routes and border crossing points.

US President Donald Trump said Monday that he would consider establishing a permanent US military base in Lithuania, responding to a question from an LRT correspondent in Washington. “We will certainly look at it. I know so many people in Lithuania. They are great people,” Trump said, according to Reuters. The comments came after Lithuania invited the United States to consider establishing a permanent military base in the Baltic country, which borders Russia and Belarus. Q: Lithuania has invited the U.S. to establish a permanent U.S. base in Lithuania.

Trump: We will certainly look at it. I know so many people in Lithuania. They are great people. https://t.co/dPamjteoiq Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Tuesday that Lithuania was prepared to cover the costs associated with a permanent US military presence. He said he welcomed Trump’s response and described US troops in Lithuania as a “critically important deterrent and security guarantee”. “I am glad that this idea is being taken seriously. We value the contribution of our allies to our security,” Sinkevičius said. Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas also welcomed Trump’s comments and said he would work to advance the proposal. “I really want to thank US President Trump for his truly rational and objective approach to Lithuania and to our efforts to ensure not only Lithuania’s security, but also the security of the region,” Kaunas told LRT RADIO. Kaunas said Trump’s remarks showed that the US president was aware of Lithuania’s investments in defence and its determination to strengthen regional security. “I think this is a sign of good, close cooperation, that the president knows Lithuania, knows our investments, knows our determination to build security and appreciates it,” Kaunas said. Kaunas said he had personally raised the possibility of a permanent US base in Lithuania during a visit to the United States in late September, when he met with Elbridge Colby, the US undersecretary of defense for policy. “We will make every effort to ensure that the idea is seriously considered and that decisions are made,” Kaunas said. He stressed, however, that Trump’s statement was a positive signal and that no decision had yet been made. “We are on the way, everyone is focused,” Kaunas said. The proposal comes as Lithuania continues to strengthen its defence capabilities and deepen military cooperation with the United States and other NATO allies. Kaunas said in late September that two US Army battalions were expected to arrive in Lithuania in late October. The existing rotation system, under which US troops serve in Lithuania for nine months, is expected to continue for now. Lithuania hosts rotating US forces as part of NATO’s efforts to strengthen the alliance’s eastern flank amid Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Lithuania’s authorities said on Tuesday there was no increased risk following reports of a woman dying of pneumonic plague in Russia, adding that institutions were monitoring the situation. ​"There is currently no data indicating that this event poses an increased risk of plague infection to Lithuanian residents. There is also no data on secondary cases or long-term human-to-human transmission. Therefore, Lithuanian residents do not need to take any additional preventive measures at this time," Lithuania's National Public Health Centre (NKVC) said on Tuesday. ​ "If a threat arises due to the potential spread of an infectious disease, countries are ready to respond in a coordinated manner at the EU level according to the mechanisms provided in the European Health Union regulations," it added. ​ A 28-year-old woman, who worked at the plague research institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, may have been infected when a test tube broke. ​ Russian media also reported a possible laboratory incident and a quarantine of about 200 people who may have had contact with the woman. ​ Plague has not been registered in Europe for more than 50 years, according to data provided by NKVC. Other forms of plague, transmitted by animals, still occur in the Americas, Africa and Asia. ​ No plague cases have been recorded in Lithuania for over 200 years.

Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry on Wednesday condemned a Moscow court decision labelling 13 people from the Baltic states and several organisations as “accomplices of Nazi Germany”, calling the ruling a falsification of history aimed at smearing Baltic resistance fighters. “This is not the first time Russia has falsified history to smear the Baltic states and our freedom fighters, thus trying to divert attention from its war crimes and other atrocities in Ukraine,” the ministry said. The Moscow court this week said it had recognised the individuals and organisations as “accomplices of Nazi Germany in committing war crimes and crimes against humanity against the Soviets during the Second World War”. Among those named were Juozas Ambrazevičius-Brazaitis, head of Lithuania’s 1941 provisional government; partisan commander Juozas Lukša; writer Bronius Krivickas, who was killed while fighting in the postwar resistance; the Lithuanian Activist Front; and the Lithuanian Nationalist Union. The court said it based its decision on archival documents from various Russian state agencies and explanations concerning the alleged “criminal actions” of the individuals and organisations from Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said Russia was distorting historical facts by relying on biased archival material while ignoring crimes committed by Soviet repressive institutions. The ministry said the campaign was primarily aimed at a domestic Russian audience and was intended to indirectly justify Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. In a separate development, a memorial to Lithuanian and Polish deportees in the Siberian city of Yakutsk was reportedly replaced in September with a monument honouring Russian soldiers killed in the war in Ukraine. Lithuania’s military has repeatedly said Russia uses historical issues as part of its propaganda efforts, particularly to portray the Baltic states and their resistance to Soviet rule in a negative light. Historians generally agree that the 1941 provisional government of Lithuania, headed by Juozas Ambrazevičius-Brazaitis, collaborated with Nazi Germany that attacked the Soviet Union and pushed its forces out of Lithuania in June 1941. The provisional government, however, was soon disbanded by the Nazis. The provisional government was established by the Lithuanian Activist Front which was notoriously anti-Semitic, pledging in its manifesto “to carry out an immediate and fundamental purging of the Lithuanian nation and its land of Jews”.

Lithuania could restrict the transit of Russian citizens through the country if reports of pneumonic plague in Russia are confirmed and the disease poses a threat to Lithuania, Health Minister Linas Kukuraitis said Wednesday. Kukuraitis told LRT RADIO that any such measures would be coordinated with the European Union, which has established procedures for restricting movement during public health emergencies since the Covid-19 pandemic. “If we saw even the slightest threat, this issue would be raised by us, and decisions would then be made jointly,” Kukuraitis said. He said he met Tuesday with the country’s main institutions responsible for managing such an outbreak. Lithuania has established response procedures and sufficient reserves of medication, he said. Kukuraitis stressed that reports of a pneumonic plague case in Russia have not been independently confirmed. “It is both a worrying situation, and we would like to reassure the public,” he said, adding that information coming from Russia is being treated cautiously because it is a “warring, hostile country”. Lithuania, other European countries and the United States are closely monitoring the situation, he said. Lithuania’s National Public Health Centre said there is currently no increased risk of plague infection for people in Lithuania. It said available information is limited and there is no way to independently confirm that the reported case involved pneumonic plague. Reports emerged Friday that 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in Russia’s Irkutsk region, had died of pneumonic plague. Some reports said special restrictions had subsequently been imposed. The Russian news outlet Lyudi Baikala, citing unnamed sources close to regional security services, reported that Shipilova may have contracted the disease after a test tube broke. Other media reports linked her death to a possible laboratory incident. Lyudi Baikala also reported that about 200 people who may have had contact with her were under quarantine. Russian officials, however, have said tests conducted after her death did not detect the disease. US President Donald Trump said Monday that his administration was closely monitoring the situation. Pneumonic plague is a rare infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It can spread through respiratory droplets, generally requiring close and prolonged contact with a person showing symptoms. The incubation period is one to four days. The disease can cause fever, headache, weakness, cough, chest pain and rapidly worsening breathing difficulties. When diagnosed promptly, it can be successfully treated with antibiotics, which are readily available in Europe and Lithuania.

The Lithuanian military is being deployed to help guard the country’s border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said on Wednesday. He stressed that the situation at the border was currently calm and that “the deployment of troops is a preventive measure”. According to Katelynas, the decision to deploy the army was made following an incident on the Latvian border, after an assessment of the overall security situation in the region and reports that Russia could announce a mobilisation. Latvia’s National Armed Forces said that earlier this week a group of at least 20 migrants, escorted by masked and armed individuals, had attempted to cross the Latvian-Belarusian border. The armed individuals threatened soldiers and actively urged and pushed the group of migrants towards Latvia. Several hours after the incident, masked individuals entered Latvian territory, damaged an electricity distribution panel and stole CCTV cameras. Earlier on Wednesday, Katelynas said such incidents were concerning but that Lithuania was prepared to respond to them.

Lithuania’s government has extended temporary protection for Ukrainians fleeing Russia’s war through March 2028, while introducing a new requirement for some people subject to military service in Ukraine. Under the new rules, Ukrainians subject to military service will have to provide proof that they have fulfilled their military obligations to qualify for temporary protection. Acceptable proof will include evidence of a lawful departure from Ukraine, an exit stamp in a passport, or an official document showing that the person is exempt from military service or has completed it. The requirement will not apply to people who were granted temporary protection in any European Union country before August 4, or who had applied for temporary protection in Lithuania by that date but had not yet received a decision. Under the previous rules, temporary protection in Lithuania was due to expire March 4 next year. The government has now extended it for another year, through March 2028. The Interior Ministry said about 52,000 people currently hold valid Lithuanian temporary residence permits based on temporary protection. The EU activated temporary protection for Ukrainians after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, allowing those fleeing the war to live, work and receive social benefits in the 27-member bloc. This year, following a request from Kyiv for help with personnel needed for the war effort, the EU said temporary protection would no longer apply to people arriving in the bloc who are subject to military service in Ukraine. Under Ukraine’s wartime laws, men ages 23 to 60 are generally prohibited from leaving the country. About 4.4 million Ukrainians currently live in the EU under temporary protection, according to EU data. Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic host the largest Ukrainian communities. Adult men account for about 27% of Ukrainians currently receiving temporary protection in the EU, while women account for 43% and minors for 30%. The EU said last year that it wanted to move away from the current temporary protection system by offering Ukrainians options for longer-term legal residence in the bloc or assistance to those who wish to return home when conditions allow.

A 68-year-old Russian man who came to Lithuania by boat from Russia’s Kaliningrad region last month and was denied asylum has been sentenced in Russia to six years in prison, Lithuanian media reported Wednesday. The man, identified as Igor Odintsov, was sentenced to a strict-regime penal colony over social media posts criticising Russia’s war in Ukraine, according to the Lithuanian news portal Lrytas, which cited Russian media outlet Ruwest. Russian authorities reportedly convicted Odintsov of making “public calls to carry out terrorist activities”. Lrytas reported that Odintsov was the same man who came to Lithuania via the Nemunas River from Kaliningrad on September 17. Lithuanian border guards returned him back to Russia. The connection was also confirmed by Sigitas Šamborskis, chairman of the Lithuanian community in Kaliningrad. Šamborskis described Lithuania’s decision to return the man to Russia as an “ordinary betrayal”. Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service, however, said it was unclear whether Odintsov had formally requested asylum because of doubts over whether his statements, which were not clearly or explicitly expressed, could be considered a request for international protection. According to Lithuania’s Border Guard Service, officers returned the man to Russia on September 17 after he arrived by river from the Kaliningrad region. Lrytas was the first Lithuanian outlet to report the incident. At the time, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas told the portal that the man had requested political asylum but was nevertheless sent back to Russia. The Border Guard Service said there was no information indicating that the man faced threats or had special status that could have led to his admission to the European Union. It also said he was not considered a vulnerable person, leading authorities to decide not to admit him to Lithuania. The agency said officers also took steps to ensure his well-being before returning him, including providing medical care and dry clothing after his journey on the river.

Lithuania will propose that the European Union ban the transit of Russian grain through the bloc and impose sanctions on Russian agricultural oligarchs who support the war in Ukraine, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said. The EU currently does not prohibit international trade in Russian agricultural and food products, including grain, with third countries. In 2024, the bloc imposed tariffs on Russian and Belarusian grain products, but those measures did not completely prevent their transit through the EU to third countries. Sinkevičius said Russia was using EU infrastructure while intensifying attacks on Ukraine, including on its ports and grain ships, and exporting grain allegedly taken from occupied Ukrainian territories. “We will not allow the Russian war machine to profit by using our infrastructure as a gateway to world markets,” he said. Lithuania has stepped up checks on grain transiting the country from Russia and Belarus. Since the beginning of September, the State Food and Veterinary Service has taken five samples from two shipments whose origins were unclear, with the samples being tested at foreign laboratories. Sinkevičius said the transit of Russian grain was a common concern for the Baltic states and that Lithuania and Latvia had similar positions. Estonia banned the transit of Russian- and Belarusian-origin grain through its territory on October 1. Latvia has also called for closer cooperation among the Baltic states on border controls and inspections of Russian grain shipments. The issue has gained prominence after Russian grain began appearing in Baltic transport flows. Lithuanian officials have said the country’s infrastructure should not be used to facilitate Russian grain exports. According to the State Food and Veterinary Service, no shipments of feed grain from Russia, Belarus or other countries considered unreliable have arrived at the Port of Klaipėda since 2024.

Lithuania’s foreign ministry, as well as Canada and the EU external action service, withdrew support from a disinformation conference in Vilnius after being pressured by the US administration, Politico reported Thursday. The reported pressure came after organisers announced sessions discussing US role in spreading disinformation. The #Disinfo2026 conference is being held Wednesday and Thursday in Vilnius. Its program initially included sessions examining the United States as an actor in foreign information manipulation and interference, or FIMI, which reportedly angered the Trump administration. According to Politico , the US State Department asked American embassies in several European countries and the EU to express Washington’s concerns and determine whether governments participating in the conference agreed with characterising the United States as a FIMI actor. One session, titled “USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back”, featured two American researchers and a former CIA official and examined how the United States had become a disinformation threat to Europe. Another, titled “Under attack: How the counter-disinformation community is dealing with US government pressure”, asked lawyers to assess the threat posed by US government entry bans targeting European figures. Canada and Lithuania asked organisers Monday to remove their ministries’ logos from conference materials, according to a conference participant cited by Politico. The European External Action Service, the EU’s diplomatic service, followed suit Tuesday. Asked to comment on the report, the State Department said it could not discuss diplomatic conversations but that it should not be surprising that countries distanced themselves from the conference after learning that it characterised the United States as a “FIMI threat”. “While we are unable to comment on the details of diplomatic conversations, it should not be a surprise that countries would disaffiliate from this conference upon learning that it labeled the U.S. a ‘FIMI threat’,” the State Department said in a statement, according to Politico. Following discussions with US officials, Canada and Lithuania withdrew their support for the conference, meaning they are no longer participating in discussions or featured in conference materials. The European External Action Service was also removed from the official program. Photographs reviewed by Politico showed conference displays with the logos of the Canadian, Lithuanian and EU diplomatic services covered up. France remained the only major sponsor listed. Representatives of the European External Action Service and Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said they withdrew because parts of the conference program did not correspond with their official positions, but they did not specify which parts. Lithuania’s ministry won’t comment on US pressure Approached by BNS for comment, Lithuania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has not confirmed whether it withdrew from the conference because of pressure from the US, saying instead the program did not align with Lithuania’s national interests. “The Foreign Ministry withdrew from participating in the Disinfo 2026 conference, formally distanced itself from the conference’s content, and asked the organisers not to include any references to the ministry in the conference materials once it became clear that certain parts of the program did not align with the government’s positions and Lithuania’s national interests,” the ministry told BNS. Speaking to LRT RADO, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said that the conference organisers “went way overboard and made a huge blunder”. He said he was “surprised and shocked” that the US was being put in the same category as Russia or China. “This does not align with our views and principles, so we decided to withdraw from the event and, in the future, ensure that the topic of combating disinformation is not twisted into an anti-American narrative that weakens our ties with our allies,” Budrys told LRT RADIO.

Lithuania plans to allocate about 4.8 billion euros to defense next year, or slightly more than 5% of gross domestic product, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Thursday. The planned allocation would be about 36 million euros higher than this year’s military budget. But because of economic growth, defence spending would account for a smaller share of GDP than this year, when the budget provided for 5.38%. “The priorities for 2027 are to maintain 5% of gross domestic product for defence. As we mentioned, being in the 5% club remains our goal and will be implemented,” Sinkevičius told reporters. He said the exact figure was still being discussed by the governing coalition and with Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, who wants defence spending to reach 5.1% of GDP. “The actual amount, compared with this year’s allocated amount, will still grow, the percentage will decrease, but the actual amount allocated for defence and security will increase,” Sinkevičius said. He stressed that increasing military spending must be accompanied by efficient and transparent use of the funds. “Is the budget growth sufficient? You can say that the more, the better probably, but I say we need efficient, transparent, meaningful spending,” he said. Among the government’s main priorities are air defence, the deployment of a German brigade in Lithuania and development of a national division, Sinkevičius said. He added that 43.92% of this year's defence appropriations had been spent so far. Lithuania has sought to maintain defence spending at 5% of GDP as it strengthens its military capabilities in response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and deepens NATO cooperation. Lithuania’s general government budget deficit is expected to reach about 3.8% of GDP next year, Sinkevičius said. “It seems that the variation is currently about 3.8%,” he said at a news conference when asked about the projected deficit. That would put Lithuania above the 3% deficit limit set under the European Union's fiscal rules. Sinkevičius said the government had already made about 1.5 billion euros in planned spending cuts after negotiations to keep the deficit from rising further. He has previously said that without allowing a larger deficit, the government would not be able to meet its commitments on military spending and other planned increases in expenditure. The EU’s Maastricht criteria generally require member states to keep their general government deficit below 3% of GDP. Remigijus Žemaitaitis, chairman of the opposition Nemunas Dawn party, criticised the decision to maintain defence funding at its current level next year. According to the lawmaker, defence acquisitions are delayed, scandals arise over the use of funds, and some purchases are made outside public procurement procedures. Žemaitaitis said some funds have already been paid in advance, but the goods will be delivered only in one or two years, so he proposed reducing the budget and completing projects already under way first. Žemaitaitis said he sees no value in being in the so-called 5-percent club, referring to countries that allocate at least 5 percent of their gross domestic product to defence. “We can leave that 5 percent club. What is the point of being in that club now if you sit in it and do not use the money? We did not use the money, we paid the advance invoices, and we will get the goods a year or two later. I ask, why throw such money into advances, better invest in education, invest in the economy, actually in raising the gross domestic product, in what boosts the economy and what will allow paying off debts in 2028, 2029,” the lawmaker said.

Lithuania will deploy up to 100 troops to help guard its border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region over the next several weeks. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the move was a precautionary measure anticipating Russian men seeking asylum from potential military mobilisation. Katelynas said he requested military assistance after assessing information from security and border agencies and concluding that the State Border Guard Service does not have enough personnel to handle all existing threats. “We can face people trying to evade mobilization and seeking to enter Lithuanian territory to request asylum,” Katelynas told reporters in parliament on Thursday. He also cited a recent incident on Latvia’s border with Belarus, where a group of migrants was reportedly accompanied by masked people who threatened Latvian soldiers and pushed migrants toward the border. “Seeing that instrumentalised migration is posing growing threats, additional forces were requested at the Lithuanian border with the Kaliningrad region,” Katelynas said. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas announced Wednesday that troops would be deployed at the border for several weeks at Katelynas’ request. Up to 100 soldiers are expected to assist border guards through October 16, according to Kaunas. Katelynas said the decision was based not only on political considerations but also on information and indications provided by security agencies. The Border Guard Service has long faced pressure along both Lithuania's borders with Belarus and Russia, Katelynas said, citing irregular migration across the border and other incidents. “Our resources are not unlimited. In fact, our border service is overloaded with work, shifts are getting longer and the number of officers is not increasing,” he said. “Assistance is needed.” Katelynas said the government was not currently considering deploying troops to the border with Belarus. He also said Lithuania’s overall threat level had not changed, and that two weeks was considered a reasonable initial deployment period that could be extended if necessary. “Of course, the threat assessment is carried out by the competent institutions,” Katelynas said. Despite the decision to deploy troops, the Border Guard Service said Thursday that the situation along the Kaliningrad border was calm. Moreover, no irregular migrants had been detected for five consecutive days on the Belarus border, according to the service. “The situation is calm. There have been no migrants for several days,” Border Guard Service adviser Giedrius Mišutis told ELTA. The troops were expected to begin assisting border guards Thursday. The Latvian incident cited by Katelynas involved at least 20 migrants who attempted to cross the Latvia-Belarus border while accompanied by masked individuals. According to Latvia’s armed forces, the escorts were armed, threatened soldiers and actively urged and pushed the migrants toward Latvia. Hours later, the masked individuals entered Latvian territory, damaged an electricity distribution box and stole CCTV cameras before returning to Belarus.

The EBU said authorities have a right to ensure compliance with the law and protect people’s rights, but argued that examining how a news organisation makes individual editorial decisions could interfere with its independence. “The decisions about whether and how to conduct an investigation are editorial decisions,” the EBU said. “The European Media Freedom Act protects media outlets from state interference in editorial policy and decisions and ensures the editorial and functional independence of public service media.” The General Prosecutor’s Office has asked LRT Director General Monika Garbačiauskaitė-Budrienė for information about the broadcaster’s rules governing secret recordings. Prosecutors say they are examining whether the rules could violate the public interest, including people’s constitutional right to privacy. The prosecutor’s office submitted 15 questions about LRT’s procedures. They include who can request permission for covert audio or video recording, what evidence must be provided, how editors assess whether covert recording is justified, whether information could be obtained by other means and how permissions are issued. Prosecutors also asked how covert recordings are supervised, how their results are reported to editors, who decides whether allegations have been substantiated and whether recordings should be destroyed or retained. The EBU said the questions could expose confidential journalistic sources or unpublished investigations by requiring information about proposed investigations, evidence and access to journalistic material. “Investigative journalism depends on journalists and sources knowing that sensitive editorial processes will remain protected,” the EBU said. “This risks chilling investigations before they even begin.” LRT’s editorial policy permits journalists to gather information covertly, eg record people without their knowledge, only in exceptional circumstances, when there is evidence that the conduct being recorded could demonstrate illegal or dishonest actions involving a clear public interest. It also requires prior authorisation from a responsible editor. The EBU called on prosecutors to ensure their investigation remains necessary and proportionate, respects LRT’s editorial independence and does not seek information that could reveal confidential sources or unpublished investigations. Reporters Without Borders, another international organisation, has also expressed concern, saying the investigation could expose confidential journalistic sources. It said covert recording can be a legitimate journalistic method when used exceptionally, proportionately and in the public interest. The General Prosecutor’s Office said the investigation was launched on a prosecutor’s initiative to determine whether LRT’s rules comply with Lithuania’s Constitution and laws governing the media and covert information gathering. Prosecutor’s Office spokeswoman Elena Martinonienė rejected the suggestion that the investigation threatens media freedom. “From the prosecutor’s office’s perspective, journalists’ freedom and the public interest are ensured precisely when editorial rules governing journalists’ activities raise no doubts about their compliance with the Constitution and laws,” Martinonienė told LRT.lt last week. She said prosecutors would decide whether there were grounds to take measures to protect the public interest only after receiving all the information necessary for their assessment. The EBU, which represents public service media organizations in Europe and beyond, said it supports LRT and is ready to help facilitate dialogue with Lithuanian authorities to protect fundamental rights and media freedom.

Lithuanian border guards have intercepted nine shipments of cigarettes smuggled from Belarus using balloons, seizing a total of 55,490 packs, the State Border Guard Service said Thursday. The shipments were discovered in the districts of Varėna, Kaišiadorys, Ukmergė and Panevėžys. Some were carried by several balloons tied together, and all packages were fitted with GPS transmitters that allowed smugglers to track their locations. The evidence collected will be added to ongoing pretrial investigations into the illegal possession of excise goods, the service said. Lithuanian border guards have intercepted 166 balloon-borne cigarette shipments from Belarus so far this year, compared with 635 cases in 2025. Smugglers also use drones to transport illegal cigarettes across the border. Border guards have brought down 61 such drones this year, following the interception of 59 last year and 54 in 2024.

Lithuania’s parliament has taken the first step toward removing a constitutional ban on weapons of mass destruction being present on its territory, a move supporters say would allow the country to participate more fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements. The Seimas voted 106-18, with six abstentions, in favour of removing Article 137 of the Constitution. The provision prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory. The change is not yet final. Under Lithuania’s constitutional amendment procedure, lawmakers must vote twice, with at least three months between votes. The proposal must receive at least 94 votes – two thirds of the total – in favour in each ballot. Supporters stress that removing the provision would not automatically lead to nuclear weapons being stationed in Lithuania. Instead, they say, it would remove a legal obstacle to participation in NATO deterrence activities, including exercises involving allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons. Why does Lithuania want to change the Constitution? Conservative Homeland Union leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, a former defence minister, said Lithuania’s current constitutional restrictions prevent it from participating fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans. He noted that Estonia, Latvia, Finland and Poland do not have the same constitutional prohibition. Under the existing provision, nuclear weapons cannot be stationed in Lithuania, and even the flight of aircraft carrying such weapons over Lithuanian territory is prohibited, Kasčiūnas said. The restriction also prevents allied vessels carrying nuclear weapons from entering the country’s territorial waters. “Given the current restriction, we cannot participate fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans,” Kasčiūnas told parliament, describing nuclear deterrence as a central element of the alliance’s broader deterrence strategy. Removing the ban would give Lithuania greater flexibility to participate in allied activities intended to deter potential adversaries, supporters argue. Former Defence Minister Arvydas Anušauskas, also a conservative, said the amendment would enable more comprehensive participation in deterrence exercises, rather than necessarily leading to the deployment of nuclear weapons. Social Democrat Remigijus Motuzas similarly argued that removing Article 137 would not turn Lithuania into a nuclear-armed state or mean that nuclear warheads would immediately appear in the country. Would nuclear weapons be stationed in Lithuania? Not automatically. Removing the constitutional prohibition would eliminate one legal barrier, but it would not itself authorize a decision to deploy nuclear weapons in Lithuania. Liberal Movement leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen said any future decisions on deploying such capabilities would require separate legislation. “What specific measures will be needed for our security is something we will decide ourselves, of course together with our allies,” she said. What about chemical and biological weapons? Kasčiūnas rejected claims that removing Article 137 would open the door to the use of chemical or biological weapons. He said Lithuania had ratified international conventions in 1997 and 1998 that have the force of law and prohibit the proliferation, production or use of those weapons. Opposition to the amendment was concentrated among lawmakers from the opposition Nemunas Dawn party. Fourteen of its members voted against the proposal and two abstained. Aidas Gedvilas of Nemunas Dawn questioned whether parliament should make such a consequential change without a public vote. He called for a referendum, arguing that alternative approaches were available. Vitalijus Šeršniovas, a member of the Seimas’ mixed parliamentary group, proposed a narrower solution that would address the need to allow aircraft carrying nuclear weapons to fly over Lithuania without removing the entire constitutional provision. He also argued that the issue should be decided by referendum. Three other members of the mixed group and one lawmaker from the Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance parliamentary group also voted against the amendment. The existing Article 137 covers both weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases. The proposal under consideration would remove the provision rather than replace it with a narrower rule.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda has criticised the country’s defence system for struggling to spend its allocated funds, citing lengthy procurement processes, a lack of flexibility and difficulties in cooperating with Ukraine. “The system is creaking under the strain and struggling to cope with the challenge of spending 5%, more than 5%, of our GDP on national defence,” Nausėda said in an interview published Friday on 15min.lt. He noted that the Defence Ministry and the armed forces had spent less than half of the funding allocated for defence this year. Lithuania’s defence budget for 2026 stands at 4.8 billion euros, equivalent to 5.38% of gross domestic product. Nausėda said he was dissatisfied with the time it takes to move from planning a project to implementing it, warning that Lithuania could not afford delays of two to two-and-a-half years. “We cannot afford the luxury of dragging this process out for two or two-and-a-half years. We certainly cannot explain to hostile countries that, you know, we need more time to prepare,” he said. The president said both the military and government institutions were contributing to the delays, with the armed forces taking too long to clearly and quickly define their needs and institutions struggling to fulfil them. He also expressed doubts about whether Lithuanian institutions were genuinely willing to learn from Ukraine’s wartime experience. Nausėda said officials sometimes feared taking risks because they could face criminal liability if oversight bodies later identified serious violations. As a result, he said, they sought to avoid personal responsibility by hiding behind collective decision-making procedures, further slowing projects. As an example, the president pointed to a stalled agreement between Lithuania and Ukraine on joint drone production. While he initially suspected that Ukraine was reluctant to share its technology or issue the necessary export licenses, he said he increasingly believed that Lithuanian institutions were failing to offer terms that Kyiv would take seriously. Nausėda said Lithuania had proposed purchasing 14 drones of one type and several of another, a proposal he suggested was too limited to justify joint production. “Why should we discuss joint production with you if your needs are so small that there is no point in manufacturing them together? You can simply buy them from us, and that is where we draw the line,” he said, describing the Ukrainian position. Lithuania and Ukraine signed a bilateral cooperation agreement in May covering joint drone production and the deployment of Ukrainian defence experts to Lithuania. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has said Lithuania would manufacture unmanned aerial vehicles using technology purchased from Ukraine, a move he said would also stimulate Lithuania’s defence industry.

Estonian border guards lie on the grass, their kit drying out beside them. After a short rest, they set off to resume patrols along Latvia’s border with Belarus. Lithuanian officers were also recently deployed here. “There is a lot of work. Just this morning, we detained eight people who crossed the border illegally," says Arturs Pupins, head of the Silene border guard post, as he drives along a forest track towards a fence built just a couple of years ago. ​ Latvia now faces the kind of migration flows Lithuania and Poland experienced in 2021. The Baltic countries, along with Brussels, have described the situation as a coordinated campaign by Minsk, carried out with Moscow’s assistance. ​ But amid the routine attempts to cross the border, something more serious happened on Monday. ​ After bringing a group of 20 migrants to the border, three people smugglers pelted Latvian soldiers who arrived at the scene with stones. One of the masked men eventually pulled out an object resembling a pistol and threatened to shoot. ​ The Latvian soldiers withdrew, and the migrants returned to Belarus. However, the incident has left officers disturbed about the potential risks. “We have warned officers to be vigilant and, above all, to prioritise their own safety. If they see people with weapons, they must withdraw to a safe place and prepare for an attack,” Pupins says. The incident happened amid warnings from intelligence agencies in NATO countries, as well as European and US officials, about potential Russian and Belarusian escalation against the Baltic states. With the Kremlin stuck in Ukraine, such incidents – whether involving drones or unidentified armed individuals at the border – could be a way to divert attention, intimidate countries supporting Kyiv or test NATO’s collective defence thresholds. “The situation at the border is always dangerous. You do not know who is on the other side of the fence – a migrant or a soldier from the other side in disguise,” Pupins says. “This may be a provocation or an escalation, but that is just my opinion,” he adds. At the border guard headquarters in nearby Daugavpils, officers show photographs retrieved from migrants’ phones. One shows Belarusian officials alongside migrants in a forest. Previously, Latvian officers shared photographs showing migrants being transported in military trucks. “We have also spotted their camps using drones,” says Vladimirs Šersts, a senior border guard, showing further video footage of Belarusian officials escorting migrants or walking alongside them. ​ Damage to infrastructure is also increasing. Latvian officers say they have recorded 10 cases of damage to electrical boxes and 11 cases involving damaged cameras this year alone. A further dozen or so cameras and sensors have been simply stolen. “We responded to every incident, but they managed to break off a pole carrying a camera in just a minute and a half. It is impossible to have a continuous line of officers standing along the border,” says Valdis Jukšs, head of the Daugavpils border guards. Videos uploaded by migrants to TikTok show the smugglers speaking Arabic and Kurdish. Officers say that at least some of these individuals are believed to have links to organised crime. However, Latvian border guards say it would be impossible to operate in a restricted border zone without the knowledge or direct assistance of Belarusian officials. ​ “I think this is being coordinated from the Belarusian side. It is not normal for people to be able to walk freely along the fence,” Pupins says. Between geopolitics and organised crime ​ Since 2021, Latvian officials have turned back 52,184 people. A further 1,143 people were admitted for so-called humanitarian reasons because they needed medical or other assistance. ​ However, officials say almost all of these cases occurred in 2023, when most people attempting to cross the border were families with children. Today, most migrants are young men, and only a few dozen people a year are admitted to the country – and detained. “The Lithuanians gave us time to prepare,’ says Jukšs, head of the Daugavpils border guards. He adds that Latvia is now facing its highest levels of illegal migration since Lithuania and Poland bore the brunt of the crisis in 2021. ​ Yet amid the geopolitics and criminal networks are people fleeing war or poverty, coming from almost every continent in the world. Some also die, but the exact number is unknown. “Yesterday [Wednesday], we found a man in Latvia who needed medical assistance. He was taken to hospital but died this morning. He was 42,” Jukšs says. ​ Human rights groups have previously criticised Latvia for largely restricting access to the border for non-governmental organisations and the media. International reports have also documented allegations of violence against migrants ​ Without independent monitoring, it is unclear whether violent incidents are isolated or systematic. “We receive various enquiries about people who may be in the border area, and we always provide responses. For example, we received a letter about the Bangladeshi man who died yesterday, and we will respond to it,” Jukšs says. ​ “When we checked the documents of the man who died, we found that he had a work visa for Belarus” he adds. The trip to the border was organised by the Latvian embassy in Vilnius, which had no influence on the content of this article.

Lithuania’s foreign population is increasingly diverse, though people from the neighbouring non-EU countries – Ukraine, Belarus – remain by far the biggest groups of foreign residents. The number of workers from the Philippines, India, Uzbekistan, Pakistan and Tajikistan have risen sharply in recent years, while the country’s economy has become more dependent on non-EU labour, official data show. Ukrainian and Belarusian citizens remain the largest groups of foreign residents, according to the Migration Department. As of September 1, about 80,300 Ukrainians and 47,900 Belarusians held residence permits in Lithuania, followed by 13,300 Russians, 12,600 Uzbeks and 9,400 Indians. Other sizeable communities include citizens of India, Tajikistan, the Philippines, Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Pakistan, Turkey, Georgia, Latvia, Bangladesh, Zimbabwe, Moldova, Germany and Morocco. More than 2,000 foreign residents were stateless. The fastest growth since January 1, 2024, has been among Filipinos, whose numbers increased by 5,100, or tenfold. The Indian population grew by 4,800, doubling in size, while the number of Uzbeks rose by 4,400, or 50%. The number of Pakistanis increased by 2,500, more than tripling, and the number of Tajiks grew by 1,800, or 30%. Data from the State Data Agency on immigrants’ previous countries of residence show that the United Kingdom was the largest source of arrivals last year, a category that may include Lithuanians returning home. However, “other countries” was the largest category in both 2023 and 2024, indicating that Lithuania is attracting people from an increasingly broad range of countries. Belarus was the leading source in 2023, Ukraine in 2022 and the United Kingdom in 2021. Foreign workers become essential to key industries The changing migration picture reflects a significant shift in Lithuania’s labour market over the past decade, according to research published in late September by the Bank of Lithuania. Linas Tarasonis, a senior research economist at the central bank’s Research Centre, and Dominykas Vaičiūnas, a student in Vilnius University’s quantitative economics program, found that the number of non-EU citizens in Lithuania increased more than twelvefold between 2010 and 2024, rising from 11,500 to 143,100. Their share of all employed people grew from 1% to 10% over the same period. By contrast, the number of employed EU citizens increased much less, from 1,900 to 4,500. Foreign workers are concentrated in a relatively small number of industries, particularly transportation and warehousing, construction and manufacturing. The transportation and warehousing sector illustrates the extent of this reliance. Non-EU citizens accounted for just a small share of its workforce in 2010, but by 2024 they made up 46%, or nearly half, the researchers said. Their share reached about 16% in construction and 11% in accommodation and food services. They also accounted for about 8% of workers in real estate and administrative services, while manufacturing employed a significant number of foreign workers. “This means that over more than a decade, parts of the Lithuanian economy have become significantly dependent on foreign labour,” Tarasonis and Vaičiūnas wrote. They said the transportation sector would probably struggle to operate at its current scale without workers from outside the EU. Dependence on foreign labour has also become important in construction, parts of manufacturing and some service industries. Drivers, construction workers and welders in demand Migration Department figures show that many foreign workers fill jobs in transport and construction, as well as skilled trades. In August, the most common occupation among immigrants was international freight truck driver, with 6,700 workers. Other leading occupations included concrete workers, with 644; welders, with 590; cooks, with 237; and plasterers, with 227. The list also included electricians, butchers, pipeline installers, bricklayers and scaffolders.

In 1993, Lithuania decriminalised consensual same-sex relations, opening the way for LGBTQ people to speak more openly about their place in a newly independent society. But as the community became more visible, so did public debate – and, at times, hostility. Three decades later, a researcher examining Lithuanian media archives from 1994 to 2004 says coverage of sexual minorities reveals a society struggling to move beyond Soviet-era attitudes while confronting new questions about human rights, European integration and social change. Rasa Navickaitė, a researcher at Vilnius University’s Institute of International Relations and Political Science, has studied how LGBTQ people were portrayed in the media during the first decade after decriminalisation. She discussed her findings while examining LRT's archives for the LRT RADIO program Buvo nebėra. During the Soviet era, LGBTQ people were largely absent from public discourse. When homosexuality was mentioned, it was often portrayed as a harmful Western influence. Same-sex relations were criminalised and could result in punishment. “Homophobia was deeply rooted in institutions,” Navickaitė said. “The KGB and police used it as a tool of blackmail and humiliation. The medical system was partly involved, venereal disease clinics and the psychiatric system were used for persecution.” As a result, she said, people could reach adulthood without ever encountering anything positive about homosexuality. Lithuania was the last of the three Baltic states to decriminalise same-sex relations, doing so in July 1993. Two years later, the Lithuanian Gay League, or LGL, the country’s first organisation representing gay people, was established. Media began reporting on homosexuality as a new phenomenon in an independent Lithuania. Early coverage was generally cautious. Some reports grouped homosexual people together with religious sects and other groups that were portrayed as unfamiliar features of the newly open society. “It is interesting that different things are placed next to each other – sects and homosexual people,” Navickaitė said. “They are treated as new phenomena in a free, independent Lithuania. Things can no longer simply be suppressed; they have to exist openly. And the question arises of how the majority of society will accept them.” The subject attracted growing attention. Television programs and newspapers sometimes used provocative approaches, while images from pride events in Western Europe became common ways of illustrating stories about LGBTQ people. According to Navickaitė, coverage became significantly more hostile around the turn of the millennium. In 2000, the tabloid Vakaro žinios (Evening News) began publishing the names of people it claimed were connected to the LGBTQ community. Articles appeared under titles referring to a “queer mafia” and in a series called “They Are Called Gays”. The reports claimed to expose homosexual people in public life, including politicians, government officials and media figures. Some of those named were not actually gay, Navickaitė said. The publications prompted a strong reaction, and the Commission of Ethics in the Provision of Information went as far as describing Vakaro žinios as “violent”, according to Navickaitė. She believes the timing may have been connected to Lithuania’s preparations to join the European Union. EU membership required Lithuania to amend some laws and strengthen protections for human rights, while European institutions and organisations supported LGBTQ rights initiatives. That created an opening for opponents of LGBTQ rights to portray homosexuality as something being imposed on Lithuania from abroad, she said. “The media began escalating the issue, suggesting that gays were sabotaging our accession to the EU,” Navickaitė said. Coverage increasingly relied on old stereotypes while also creating new conspiracy theories. One recurring narrative suggested that gay men held important positions in municipalities, government and the media and formed a powerful elite controlling public life. “It creates the image of a malicious, small elite,” Navickaitė said. “We can compare it very well with antisemitic stereotypes. It is a conspiracy theory that creates the image of an all-powerful gay elite.” She said homosexuality was also increasingly linked in public discourse with paedophilia, further reinforcing fears and stigma. Navickaitė sees the campaign as part of a broader polarisation. While some people were moving toward more respectful discussion, she said, the Respublika publishing group, one of the biggest at the time, chose to turn the issue into a scandal and a way of attracting readers. Despite the hostility, LGBTQ people were establishing their own networks and institutions. They created clubs and organisations and began publishing their own magazines. In 1993, Stasys Dimbelis, who worked at an AIDS centre, launched the magazine Naglis. Amsterdamas followed a year later. Nightclubs catering to LGBTQ people opened in Vilnius, though they remained largely invisible in mainstream public life. But distributing LGBTQ publications was not always easy. Some retailers were reluctant to stock them, while potential buyers sometimes avoided purchasing them to prevent unwanted attention. Being openly gay in public remained unusual. Navickaitė points to Dimbelis and several other figures, including Vladimir Simonko and Eduardas Platovas, the founders of the Lithuanian Gay League, as exceptional for their willingness to come out publicly and campaign for LGBTQ rights. “You could count such people on the fingers of one hand,” she said. One of the more striking examples came in 1997, when LRT TV’s flagship news program, Panorama, reported on a symbolic wedding ceremony involving gay men at Vilnius Cathedral. Obviously, the ceremony was not legally recognised. Its organisers sharply criticised the authorities, while Catholic clergy accused the television program’s staff of provoking a controversy

European Union Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said Sunday that Europe and Kyiv should consider developing an independent strategy for achieving peace in Ukraine, following US President Donald Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. “Until now the EU was the only serious financial supporter of Ukraine, but was expecting the US political leadership will help to bring peace to Ukraine,” Kubilius wrote on X. “A time comes when the EU together with Ukraine needs to elaborate and implement an independent Peace Strategy.” Until now the EU was the only serious financial supporter of Ukraine, but was expecting the US political leadership will help to bring peace to Ukraine. A time comes when the EU together with Ukraine needs to elaborate and implement an independent Peace Strategy. Kubilius’ remarks appeared to reflect his personal position rather than an official EU policy announcement. Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to “get a new leader” after Zelensky criticised Washington’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel fuel as the US president faces pressure over fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. Trump accused Zelensky of obstructing a deal with Moscow and ignoring instructions not to strike Russian oil refineries. Kyiv and its European allies have argued that easing pressure on Moscow would help finance the Kremlin’s war against Ukraine.

A dispute over how to protect Kaunas’ UNESCO-listed modernist architecture has exposed tensions between heritage conservation and urban development. City officials warn that proposed restrictions could obstruct construction projects and heritage authorities say Lithuania must honour its international commitments. Kaunas was added to UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2023 for its modernist architecture. As part of the commitments associated with the designation, Lithuania agreed to prepare a plan to protect the city’s architectural and urban heritage. Researchers at Kaunas University of Technology, commissioned by the Cultural Heritage Department, have drawn up a management plan for the city’s New Town (Naujamiestis) district. The document is now undergoing public consultation, with a public discussion held October 8. But the city administration has already signalled that it will not approve the plan in its current form, arguing that it places too much emphasis on restrictions at the expense of the city’s growth. City warns against putting development on hold Kaunas chief architect Gedeminas Barčauskas said the disagreement was not about minor details but about the plan’s underlying approach. “Kaunas is certainly not an open-air museum. It is a place where people live, with a social and economic environment. We have to balance everything – not only heritage protection but also the city’s development,” he said. Barčauskas argued that the plan should encourage development that respects historic architecture rather than become a collection of prohibitions. One of the main points of contention is the proposed regulation of building heights. The city is also concerned that the plan could affect projects outside the historic New Town district, including development on the left bank of the Nemunas River in the Žemoji Freda area, where the Nemunaičiai residential quarter is being planned. The area falls within the proposed protection zone, where the city architect believes restrictions should be more flexible. “This is not the New Town itself. It is a less sensitive area where, in our view, regulations should not be imposed in the same way,” Barčauskas said, arguing that developers had invested in land with legitimate expectations of being able to build. The plan could also complicate the municipality’s intention to auction the former Red Cross hospital complex for redevelopment, he said. Barčauskas insisted that the city was not opposed to protecting its modernist heritage. Instead, he called for an approach that would allow contemporary architecture to coexist with historic buildings. He also questioned whether the plan adequately reflected the needs of residents, the local economy and the city’s urban character. Heritage officials warn of international repercussions Cultural Heritage Department head Vidmantas Bezaras said rejecting the plan could cause an international controversy because its preparation was part of the commitments Lithuania made when Kaunas received UNESCO status. “This is not a straitjacket being imposed on the city. It is a way to preserve what has been inscribed on the World Heritage List,” Bezaras said, describing the designation as a matter of prestige for both Kaunas and Lithuania. He noted that the New Town district covers only about 2% of the city’s territory, rising to roughly 5% when its protection zone is included. The greatest disagreements, he said, concern the protection zone rather than the historic district itself. The plan takes into account observations by a World Heritage Centre expert who visited Kaunas four years ago and highlighted the importance of the valleys surrounding the modernist architecture, warning against building over them extensively. The university researchers say the plan does not change the provisions of Kaunas’ general development plan but provides more detailed rules for implementing them. Mantas Lapinskas, representing Kaunas University of Technology, said proposed building-height restrictions vary according to the characteristics of individual areas. “The aim of regulating building heights is not to stop the city’s development but to ensure that new construction does not erase the historically established scale of the New Town, its urban structure and other features,” he said. UNESCO status brings responsibilities, not a construction ban Renata Vaičekonytė Kepežinskienė, head of heritage programs at the Lithuanian National Commission for UNESCO, said the designation brought international recognition as well as long-term responsibilities. She said Kaunas’ municipal authorities had committed to preserving the urban and architectural structure of both New Town and Žaliakalnis when seeking World Heritage status. In 2025, Lithuania informed UNESCO that the concept for the New Town management plan had been approved and that the completed document was expected in November 2026. “Today, it is important to consistently fulfil the commitments the city itself undertook when it gained UNESCO status,” she said. Vaičekonytė Kepežinskienė stressed that UNESCO listing does not prohibit urban development or contemporary architecture in historic areas. Instead, new buildings must be designed so their scale, height, volume and density do not undermine the historic urban structure or overshadow protected heritage. She also warned that World Heritage status is not permanent, pointing to the removal of Germany’s Dresden Elbe Valley and Liverpool’s Maritime Mercantile City in Britain from the list after major changes to the protected areas. Lithuanian Architects Union Kaunas branch head Nerijus Stanionis also questioned the proposed expansion of the protection zone and said some provisions could conflict with existing planning documents and projects already in development.
