Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Monday that Ukraine’s allies should ask President Volodymyr Zelensky to target more data centres in Russia, suggesting such strikes could help protect European elections from foreign interference. “I think we should ask Mr Zelensky to strike more data centres in Russia, and that might help,” Sinkevičius said at the Warsaw Security Forum, responding to a question about what Lithuania, Poland and other allies should do to safeguard their elections. During a panel discussion on European security challenges amid global changes, Sinkevičius spoke alongside Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. “Nobody will offer us Europeans a seat at the decision-making table simply out of courtesy. For Europe to have a seat, it must find more strength, energy and unity within itself,” Sinkevičius said. He added that political commitments must be translated into action more quickly and defence investments into new military capabilities. Strategies and plans were necessary, he said, but “they are not what deters Russia”. Sinkevičius also called for greater cooperation among European defence industries, saying production capacity remained insufficient to meet actual needs. He urged allies to work more closely together through intelligence sharing, joint procurement, joint production and military exercises, while drawing on Ukraine’s battlefield experience and expertise.

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said Monday that a deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on diesel supplies weakens the West’s position on Russia, although he described it as less serious than other developments over the past two years. “This latest episode is not the worst we have seen in nearly two years. But it is certainly regrettable, as it does not help achieve a coordinated sanctions policy toward Russia between Europe and the United States, and slightly weakens our position as the West,” Budrys told journalists in Luxembourg ahead of a meeting of the European Union’s Foreign Affairs Council. Budrys said Washington had repeatedly made decisions without closely coordinating with Europe, despite the effectiveness of joint action. “Whenever we coordinated, we saw how effective it was, but that did not always happen,” he said, adding that the latest development was not entirely new. However, Budrys stressed that the agreement should not change the EU’s sanctions policy. “The European Union has imposed restrictions on imports of oil products into the bloc, and we will not change our position, as we believe this is one of the more effective measures to restrict financial flows to the Russian war machine,” he said. Trump announced Friday that he had reached an agreement with Putin on supplying large quantities of diesel in exchange for a temporary easing of US sanctions. The announcement drew criticism from Ukraine, the EU and some US lawmakers. Budrys said Washington’s decisions could be influenced by domestic politics, including high energy prices, as well as efforts to end the war in Ukraine. The Lithuanian minister also warned that securing funding for Ukraine would be one of Europe’s biggest challenges next year. Bilateral support from EU member states is currently at its lowest level since 2022, he said, even as Ukraine’s defence needs increase and Russian attacks continue to destroy infrastructure. Budrys said Lithuania would honour its commitments to Ukraine and urged other EU countries not to reduce their bilateral aid because of the bloc’s financial support scheme. He acknowledged, however, that maintaining European countries’ attention and support would be difficult. Asked whether the agreement could affect diesel prices or lead to Russian diesel entering the EU market, Budrys said he expected no significant impact. Lithuania would work to ensure the deal did not undermine the bloc’s sanctions policy, he added. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Monday that Lithuania continued to trust the US. “Lithuania’s trust has not wavered. We still think and firmly believe that America is our strategic partner,” he said during a visit to Warsaw. “Of course, politicians are often active, but this does not mean their statements or tweets fundamentally change bilateral relations. We welcome American initiatives to seek and find ways to achieve lasting peace, and any initiatives in this area are welcome. It is important that these initiatives actually work, as President Zelensky also said today.” Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas, meanwhile, stressed that any agreements must be consistent with Ukraine’s interests and international law. He said an energy ceasefire would be an important step but must not involve unilateral concessions to Russia. Olekas also said Lithuania would not recognise Ukrainian territories seized by Russia and supported Ukraine’s right to determine its own domestic, foreign and security policies.

Seasonal apple picking, once a popular source of extra income for hundreds of residents in northern Lithuania, is becoming increasingly difficult to staff as fewer people are willing to take the short-term jobs. At Naradava orchards in Pasvalys district, pickers can earn as much as 100 euros a day. But while the pay remains attractive to some, the number of people seeking seasonal work has steadily declined. In previous years, employers sometimes had to select workers from a pool of applicants. This year, nearly everyone who applies is being hired. Vytautas, who has been picking apples at the orchards for almost two decades, looks forward to the harvest every year. For him, the seasonal work is a valuable opportunity to earn money because finding employment in the countryside can be difficult. “It’s possible, but it’s difficult at my age,” he told LRT TV. “Here, I can manage to earn some money.” Some workers use the income to supplement their pensions, while others take vacation from their regular jobs specifically to work during the harvest. For some, the extra income is earmarked for a particular purchase or a trip. “I work and arrange my personal life – I buy something or go somewhere,” one worker said. “Maybe I’ll manage to go somewhere this weekend.” The orchards are also facing another challenge this year. A cold winter destroyed about one-third of the company’s orchards, but Naradava still expects to harvest around 4,000 metric tons of apples. Finding enough workers, however, is becoming increasingly difficult. “We really need these pickers, and this year we are using various methods to find them – ads in newspapers, asking acquaintances, and social media,” said Džiugas Palionis, director of Naradava. “We have about 150 workers at the peak this year, whereas in better years we managed to have as many as 300.” Dalia Radzivonienė, a forewoman at the company, said the change is particularly noticeable compared with previous years. Residents of surrounding districts once began asking well in advance when they could start working and often wanted to reserve places for family members. Demand was so high that the company sometimes had to hold selections. “Now we have to take whoever comes,” Radzivonienė said. “There aren’t as many people interested as there used to be. In some years, people couldn’t get in. Now we accept everyone who comes.” Naradava recruits workers from nearby villages and towns and operates its own bus to transport them from Pasvalys, Biržai and surrounding areas, Palionis said. “We manage to gather them somehow,” he said. “Every year, there are fewer workers.” The apple harvest is expected to continue until the end of October.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius on Monday called US President Donald Trump’s decision to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel supplies “shameful and dishonourable”, while Lithuania’s presidential office urged a cautious approach to broader US policy changes affecting European security. “I think it is a shameful, dishonourable act. I am not sure whether this is actually happening or whether these are just political statements. I have not seen a written agreement,” Sinkevičius told Sky News at the Warsaw Security Forum. “I think this will become clear in the coming week.” Trump said Friday that he had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement for Russia to supply large quantities of diesel to global markets. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the move, prompting Trump on Saturday to call on Ukraine to choose a new leader. On Sunday, Trump said on his Truth Social platform that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop their devastating long-range strikes on power plants and oil refineries. Zelensky said the Kremlin was unwilling to agree to a ceasefire and reported that Russia had attacked six energy facilities on Monday, after Trump’s announcement. Earlier Monday, Sinkevičius said Lithuania’s confidence in the United States remained intact and welcomed initiatives aimed at achieving peace in Ukraine. President’s office urges caution over US military presence Presidential chief foreign policy adviser Asta Skaisgirytė said Tuesday that Lithuania should remain calm and focus on strategic priorities as Washington reviews its military presence in Europe. “The presence of US troops in Lithuania is very important to us, strategically important,” she told the radio Žinių radijas. With troop deployments being reorganised, she said, Lithuania needed to avoid emotional reactions and maintain a broader strategic perspective. Skaisgirytė declined to comment directly on Sinkevičius’ criticism of the diesel sanctions decision. President Gitanas Nausėda said Monday that the move was linked to the approaching US midterm elections, created conditions for reducing Russia’s isolation and represented “a bad day”. The United States is reviewing its troop presence in Europe. Lithuanian officials have said Washington is resuming troop rotations in Lithuania after a several-month pause, with two US battalions expected to arrive in late October. Despite doubts expressed by some politicians about whether the rotations would resume, Skaisgirytė said she had no doubts and urged critics to exercise “strategic patience”. Trump intimated in early October that the United States would consider establishing a permanent military base in Lithuania. Skaisgirytė said she believed the idea was feasible and that Lithuanian officials were discussing it regularly with their US counterparts.

Amid increasing alarmism over Russia’s plans for the Baltic states, Lithuania has been preparing for that potentiality since at least the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. LRT English breaks down the key changes and initiatives taking place across the different layers of society. Lithuania’s military had to essentially be reconstructed following the deep cuts in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. What followed were years of reconstitution that included deep-pocket purchases, like tanks and armoured vehicles, and ultimately culminated in the establishment of a division that brings the country’s three main brigades into its fold. Some problems persist – at least one of the brigades is nowhere near full completion, while tank purchases were criticised for diverting hundreds of millions of euros into bulky machinery instead of cheaper, more mass-produced things like strike drones. Recently, the Armed Forces established ANBO, a military cluster bringing together the different branches of the military working on autonomous systems. The forces also worked overtime during the biggest exercise of 2026 – Strong Griffon – to showcase them adopting lessons from Ukraine, including fielding ground drones, various types of UAVs, or constructing anti-drone nets and building bunkers. This mostly rests on the civilian-paramilitary Riflemen’s Union, which brings together thousands of people in most of the country’s cities and towns ready to take up arms, or do different tasks – from civil defence and medical aid, to evacuation support and cybersecurity. Notably, the organisation is growing at pace and will now have three specialised drone battalions alone. ​ The country also has a civilian reserve, which includes professions like doctors and teachers. Until recently, the civilian reserve was just another concept on paper, but its role was recently clarified amid ongoing mobilisation scenario drills. Organisations like the Red Cross are bringing together volunteers to assist in case of a crisis, with the aim of finding a place for every person seeking to get involved in defence. Some organisations and institutions are also launching their own initiatives – examples include art students putting together a guide book on how to wage civil resistance. ​ Meanwhile, several hundred thousand people have already attended civil resistance courses at the military academy, while thousands more took drone piloting courses. Lithuania’s military reserves are made up of a 40,000-strong “active” reserve force, which are bolstered by the yearly intake of 5,000 conscripts. Fifteen years later, they are moved to the “prepared” reserve force of around 80,000 people that had prior military training. In case of war, the “active” reserve would fold into the main military force, while most of the “prepared” reserve, alongside some units of the Riflemen’s Union, would be moved to assist the Commendant’s Offices. In 2024, the military founded the Commendant’s Units (Komendantūros), which means those who have not yet served in the military or are not part of the Riflemen’s Union or the part-time, 6,000 strong Military Volunteer Defence Force (KASP), can join Komendantūros. They are ready to assist with specialised tasks to maintain law and order, like controlling checkpoints and defending key sites, and now number 1,800 troops. The whole system is arguably complicated. As another case in point, the conscription service itself is further split into multiple layers, where some professionals – like cybersecurity and IT experts – can embark on alternative service models to better bring their skills into the military. With multiple drone incidents, Lithuania’s air defences have been under a steady stream of criticism. Despite one of Lithuania's two NASAMS batteries being deployed near Vilnius, as well as the NATO air defence mission and Lithuania’s own air defence units deployed near the border, drones – and smuggling balloons – continue to enter the country’s airspace. There have been some initiatives – Lithuania will buy acoustic radars from Ukraine, as well as drone interceptors from the United States. A civilian initiative, Drone Radar, is also trying to build an alternative air monitoring system by having people around the country set up unused phones with a dedicated app to pick up on drone sounds. The app is already in operation, and it reportedly picked up on the Russian drone that entered Lithuania on September 15 that was ultimately shot down by NATO jets near Kaunas. The defensive line along the borders with Russia and Belarus has been under construction since at least 2024. The three Baltic countries are taking slightly different approaches, but the end result is largely similar. Lithuania began by constructing so-called counter-mobility parks in key locations that house fortifications and can be placed on short notice. Furthermore, bridges were prepared for demolition near the border, some swamps and forests are being restored, while the country is also stocking up on anti-tank mines and, controversially , anti-personnel mines. ​ Some areas have already been reinforced with the so-called dragon’s teeth, but critics point out that they are more for show, as they are often placed in highly visible areas – like the bridge that connects Lithuania with Russia’s Kaliningrad region. ​ The end goal will be layered defences, not a continuous line of fortifications, with prepared firing positions and defences. Lithuania has been renewing its shelter network since 2022, with it finally being put to test with the country’s first air-raid alarm in May. Problems showed themselves immediately – many shelters were locked, existed on paper only or were full of clutter, while some people simply didn’t know where to find them. ​ New legislation mandates that new apartment blocks – four floors or taller – have a shelter, with municipalities being given funds to upgrade their existing shelter networks. Dublin suggested cuts to the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) and Connecting Europe Facility. Poland’s Defence Minister on Tuesday rejected the Irish proposal to slash the defence line in the EU’s next multiannual budget by 13%, echoing similar criticism from Lithuania. “They do not see the right place for defence and security in this budget. This is unacceptable for us,” Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said during a press conference after meeting with Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius. The Irish Presidency on Saturday proposed a €113.7 billion budget for the future European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) for resilience and security, defence industry, and space, down from the €131 billion first pitched by the Commission. Warsaw has been the target of repeated hybrid incidents, from sabotage to airspace violations. Polish authorities foiled assassination attempts against Kosiniak-Kamysz and Prime Minister Donald Tusk over the weekend. “They are isolated from the rest of the Old Continent, being an island and they might not fully be aware of those threats to our security,” the minister said, pointing to Europe’s Eastern flank security landscape. Ireland is also suggesting cutting €2 billion from the €17.6 billion the Commission envisioned for military mobility in the Connecting Europe Facility. But Kosiniak-Kamysz said the future budget needed to reflect the goal of moving troops fast across the block. Criticism from countries closer to Moscow is building up, after they called for the Eastern flank to be a priority in the next seven-year budget. Lithuanian Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs Sigitas Mitkus on Tuesday morning said he regretted “considerable cuts” on defence, security and military mobility, pointing to threats Eastern European countries face. Poland is the main recipient of the €150 billion Security Action for Europe (SAFE) loans to replenish stocks and boost national production and already received a first share of its €43.7 billion envelope. And it could tap into additional funds, as some €20 billion have not been committed. The Commission is preparing a second round of applications before the end of the year. “We’re looking into the next stage of the SAFE loan,” Kubilius said, adding the sum would be used to support European countries’ industries and could include Poland. Kosiniak-Kamysz said Poland will aim to receive more EU funding, without referring to a specific programme to support European defence production. “I am actually an advocate for the war mode when it comes to the production in defence.” This story was originally published by Rapporteur, partners of LRT English.

Lithuania is investing more than €33 million to expand its military refuelling network, including fuel stations, storage facilities and vehicle wash stations, the Defence Ministry said Tuesday. The network is being expanded at military units in strategically important locations to support the Lithuanian Armed Forces and NATO allied troops, the ministry said. Some facilities have already been completed this year, while most of the newly built infrastructure is expected to be finished in 2027. “We are consistently expanding the fuel infrastructure needed to supply both the Lithuanian Armed Forces and NATO allied troops,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said. The network will help maintain reliable fuel reserves and uninterrupted supplies for combat, logistical and administrative vehicles, he said, adding that improved logistics would strengthen military readiness, operational mobility and deterrence. The new infrastructure includes modern refuelling stations with integrated fuel storage, as well as large-scale storage facilities at strategically selected locations, the ministry said. The expanded network is intended to meet the fuel needs of both Lithuanian forces and NATO allies while creating a flexible and resilient supply system. The ministry said it was also working with other state institutions to make the best use of existing fuel storage facilities and related infrastructure.

Lithuania’s parliament has taken the first step toward tightening rules for digital labour platforms – such as food delivery or ride hailing apps Wolt and Bolt – with proposed legislation aimed at improving working conditions and increasing transparency in algorithmic management. The amendments, presented to lawmakers Tuesday by Deputy Social Security and Labour Minister Aušra Putk, would make it harder for platforms to classify workers as independent contractors if they cannot freely negotiate service prices or access essential job details, such as rates and addresses, before accepting assignments. Lawmakers asked whether the changes would increase service prices. “I cannot assess the impact on prices, as that depends on business practices, but naturally, protecting workers can increase costs,” Putk said. The main amendment to the Labour Code received 85 votes in favour, with none opposed and eight abstentions. The proposals will now be reviewed by parliamentary committees before further votes in the full Seimas. The legislation has already been approved by the government and would require the president’s signature to take effect. The measures implement an EU directive intended to improve the employment status of people working through digital platforms, strengthen oversight of algorithmic management and increase transparency. Under the proposed rules, employment status would be determined primarily by the actual working relationship rather than the wording of a contract. Indicators of an employment relationship could include subordination and a lack of freedom to choose working hours, provide similar services to other clients, or accept or reject assignments without negative consequences. Platforms would also face restrictions on collecting sensitive or private information unrelated to work, such as data about workers’ emotional states or conversations outside working hours. Workers would have the right to request explanations of automated decisions affecting them. The Social Security and Labour Ministry estimates that about 28 million people work through digital platforms across the EU, with 5.5 million potentially misclassified. In Lithuania, about 141,000 people worked through platforms, including around 33,000 ride-hailing drivers and couriers, according to Vilnius University data for 2024. The number of platform workers is projected to rise to 157,000 by 2028. There are some 140 service platforms operating in the country, the most popular among them being Wolt, Bolt Food, Bolt, Uber, Ziticity, LastMile, Barbora, Trobos. The ministry says platform workers in Lithuania are generally classified as self-employed and therefore lack access to certain benefits, including unemployment and workplace accident compensation. The changes are scheduled to take effect December 2, with fines related to reclassification of employment relationships due to begin a year later, on December 2, 2027. Implementation would require about €1.1 million in additional funding for the State Labour Inspectorate to cover staffing needs.

Lithuania will seek to have Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, designated a terrorist organisation, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said Wednesday, arguing that its attacks on civilian infrastructure across Europe amount to acts of terrorism. Such a designation would have far-reaching consequences for people linked to the agency, Budrys told LRT RADIO. “It would mean that anyone who has served in or is associated with the GRU would be considered by us to be supporting or contributing to terrorism,” he said. “Such people would have no place anywhere near our companies, our banks or, ultimately, our territory.” Budrys said Lithuania first needed to establish a strong legal basis for the move, drawing on investigations and court cases that provide evidence linking attacks not only to Russia but specifically to the GRU. “On that basis, we will seek to have it designated a terrorist organisation,” he said. Lithuania wants Russia’s actions in Europe to be clearly identified and those responsible held accountable, Budrys insisted. “They are doing nothing other than carrying out acts of terror in Europe, seeking to spread fear in our societies and targeting civilian infrastructure,” he said. “If that is not terrorism, what is?” Budrys urged European Union member states to take action against the GRU at a meeting of the bloc’s Foreign Affairs Council in Luxembourg this week.

The first troops in a returning US military rotation have arrived in Lithuania, President Gitanas Nausėda said Tuesday evening, as the Baltic country seeks to strengthen its security amid Russia’s war against Ukraine. “Great news – the first returning US rotational troops have landed on Lithuanian soil. Together we are stronger!” Nausėda wrote on X, thanking US President Donald Trump for the deployment. Great news - the first returning U.S. rotation troops have landed on Lithuanian soil. Together, we are stronger! 🇱🇹🇺🇸

Many thanks to @realDonaldTrump for making this happen. US troops have rotated through Lithuania since 2014. However, amid a US review of its military presence in Europe, just over 100 American soldiers remained in the country earlier this year. In September, officials announced that two U.S. battalions, comprising more than 1,000 troops, would arrive in late October, restoring the American military presence to levels similar to those of previous years. Trump said last week that Washington would consider establishing a permanent US military base in Lithuania, an idea welcomed by Lithuanian leaders. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Lithuania was prepared to host permanently stationed US troops and cover the costs of maintaining a base if Washington decided to proceed. Up to 100 US troops have arrived in Lithuania as part of a returning rotation, with the rest expected by mid-November, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Wednesday. “The rotation started yesterday, with the first 100 or so troops arriving. There are 10 to 12 more such arrivals planned. They will continue next week, and by mid-November two battalions will be fully deployed in Lithuania,” Kaunas told LRT. The allied forces will be deployed in Pabradė, where the first troops have already arrived, he said. US military equipment is being transported to Lithuania by sea and rail, Kaunas added. Lithuania will receive two battalions: a heavy armoured battalion to strengthen regional security and provide additional response capabilities if needed, and an engineering battalion to contribute to the development of a national division and the Baltic defence line.

Lithuania expects to make progress toward restoring diplomatic representation with China by the end of the year, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Wednesday, expressing confidence in Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys’ efforts to improve ties. “The work is ongoing, it is happening,” Sinkevičius told reporters. “With Eastern countries, perhaps less background noise is needed, and quiet cooperation is required instead.” He said the government had prepared an action plan setting out specific steps and deadlines for restoring diplomatic representation, with December identified as the target for a breakthrough. “I hope it will succeed,” Sinkevičius said, adding that the outcome depended on both countries and that diplomatic matters took time. The prime minister declined to provide further details, saying Lithuania had learned from past experience and was now pursuing improved relations without public discussion. He also neither confirmed nor denied whether talks had resumed over the name of Taiwan’s representative office in Vilnius. Sinkevičius said he was not involved in negotiations with Beijing, which are being handled by Budrys. Earlier, the prime minister said he expected progress toward restoring diplomatic relations before Lithuania assumes the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027. Sinkevičius said he was satisfied with Budrys’ performance, arguing that the foreign minister’s work should be assessed more broadly than by progress on a single issue. “We are visible, heard, and new partnerships are being forged,” he said, adding that he saw potential for progress on other issues, including labour migration. The ruling coalition has increasingly voiced support for normalising relations with China to the level of diplomatic representation maintained by other EU member states. The goal is also included in the government’s program. Relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in 2021 after Vilnius allowed Taiwan to open a representation under the name “Taiwanese Representative Office”. Similar offices in other countries generally operate under the name Taipei. China responded by downgrading its diplomatic representation in Lithuania from ambassador to chargé d’affaires. Chinese diplomats have been absent from Lithuania since May 2025, after Vilnius declined to issue new accreditations to them.

Lithuania’s government on Wednesday approved national asset freezes targeting Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, after the European Union lifted sanctions against the two. The restrictions, proposed by the Foreign Ministry, will remain in force until the end of 2027. Both men were added to Lithuania’s list of undesirable persons in late September. Vilnius opposed the EU’s decision to remove Usmanov and Fridman from its sanctions lists and abstained from the vote. Once the EU sanctions were lifted, the bloc-wide freezing of their funds and economic resources no longer applied in Lithuania. “Lithuania consistently opposes any removals from the EU sanctions list on political grounds,” the Foreign Ministry said, adding that Latvia and Estonia had adopted similar measures. EU sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman were lifted following requests from several member states. French officials cited national security grounds for seeking the removal of Usmanov from the sanctions list but did not publicly provide further details. The Financial Times reported that the move may have been linked to a potential deal to secure the release of French citizens detained in Azerbaijan. Luxembourg sought the removal of Fridman, who had filed a €15 billion lawsuit against the country over the freezing of his assets. In late September, EU member states agreed to extend sanctions for three years against nearly 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s aggression.

Lithuania is seeking to extend the deployment of military personnel assisting border guards along its border with Russia until early November, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Wednesday. Katelynas said he contacted Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas on Tuesday to request an extension of the strengthened border security measures and the involvement of troops. “I believe a decision will be made soon. The agreement was for the military to be deployed until October 16, so I hope it will be extended until the beginning of November,” Katelynas told reporters. The Lithuanian military has assigned about 100 troops to help the State Border Guard Service secure the border with Russia. Katelynas said no additional troops had been requested so far, but the number could be adjusted based on the border guards’ needs. “The number is not set in stone,” he said, adding that border officials would assess whether 60, 80 or 100 troops were needed and coordinate with the Defence Ministry and military leadership. Katelynas previously described the deployment as a preventive measure prompted by publicly available, nonintelligence information suggesting Russia was planning a military mobilisation. He said the threat level along the border had not increased but that he expected people might try to seek asylum in Lithuania to avoid military service. The Lithuanian military has said cooperation between institutions to strengthen border security is routine and helps ensure that joint tasks are carried out effectively. Troops are patrolling areas around border guard stations alongside border officials. Depending on operational needs, the military may also deploy mobile patrols, mobile observation posts and military police crews.

Eight organisations representing Lithuania’s trade unions are urging politicians to reject President Gitanas Nausėda’s proposed restrictions on migrant workers, warning that the measures could increase workers’ dependence on employers and make it harder for them to defend their rights. The proposed system would allow foreign workers to stay in Lithuania on fixed-term work permits and require them to leave the country for at least six months after completing two years of employment, the Lithuanian Trade Union Confederation said Thursday. It would also not allow them to bring their families to Lithuania. “The greatest concern is that the proposed system could further tie a foreigner’s right to work and live in Lithuania to a specific employer,” the confederation said in a statement. “In such a case, it would be difficult for a worker to change jobs even if they faced unpaid wages, poor working conditions or other violations.” Trade union leaders argued that Lithuania should focus on improving working conditions and wages to attract and retain workers rather than making their residence status dependent on their employers. “If Lithuania lacks workers, we must first ask why we are unable to attract and retain them. Perhaps the problem is not a shortage of workers but the working conditions on offer?” confederation chairwoman Dalia Jakutavičė said. “Lithuanian businesses must compete on wages, working conditions and productivity, not on workers’ dependence on their employers,” she added. The eight organisations are calling on the presidential office, government and parliament to reassess the proposal and focus on measures that would help companies recruit staff while increasing employment opportunities for Lithuanian citizens. “We cannot create two labour markets, one in which people can freely choose their jobs and another in which that possibility is restricted,” Jakutavičė said. The parliament, Seimas, approved Nausėda’s proposals in principle in mid-July. The president’s office says the changes are intended to improve migration management while addressing labour shortages in the Lithuanian economy. Under the proposed model, fixed-term permits would primarily apply to foreign nationals who intend to work in Lithuania temporarily rather than settle there, including long-haul truck drivers and construction workers. The system would streamline entry and application procedures to help employers recruit workers more quickly when they cannot find suitable staff locally. After two years of employment, workers covered by the scheme would have to leave Lithuania for at least six months. Highly skilled workers from outside the European Union would not be subject to the same restrictions. The presidential office has also argued that the model would help prevent family reunification from accelerating growth in the migrant population.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has urged the Defence Ministry to improve procurement efficiency after the government spent only about half of its planned defence budget with less than three months left in the year. “I am not entirely satisfied with the situation. It is practically mid-October, and having spent half of 4.8 billion euros, to spend the other half in November and December and the rest of October does not seem very well thought out and consistent,” Sinkevičius told the radio Žinių radijas on Thursday. The prime minister said he understood that some payments under contracts already signed were scheduled for the end of the year. However, he said he had repeatedly asked Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas why spending was not distributed more evenly throughout the year. According to Sinkevičius, Kaunas assured him that everything would be fine. Sinkevičius said the previous government, led by conservative Prime Minister Ingrida Šimonytė, had operated with defence funding equivalent to 3.5% of gross domestic product. The current administrative system now has to manage a budget exceeding 5% of GDP, he said. The solution, he argued, was not to hire more staff but to accelerate procedures, make greater use of technology and, in some cases, centralise procurement. On Wednesday, Deputy Defence Minister Karolis Aleksa said more than 45% of the planned defence budget had already been spent, with spending progressing faster than at the same point last year. Lithuania’s defence budget stands at 4.8 billion euros in 2026, equivalent to 5.38% of GDP. The government plans to increase defence funding by 36 million euros next year, bringing it to a level equivalent to 5% of GDP.

After six years in which more Lithuanian citizens returned home than left the country, preliminary figures suggest the trend may be reversing, raising concerns about the country’s workforce, economic growth and ability to attract its diaspora back home. In September, 1,642 Lithuanian citizens emigrated, while 1,300 returned, according to the State Data Agency. The figures show a turning point after months in which the numbers of people leaving and returning had remained relatively close. From January through September, 12,294 Lithuanian citizens returned to the country, compared with 11,753 who emigrated – a difference of just 541. The figures are preliminary and may be revised, the agency said. Žygimantas Mauricas, chief economist at Luminor Bank, said the trend was concerning because Lithuania had hoped to attract more citizens living abroad to help develop the economy and bring back experience gained overseas. “I would view this with a certain degree of concern, because Lithuania very much hoped that a significant number of Lithuanian citizens living in other countries would return to Lithuania, contribute to the country’s economy and share the experience they have gained abroad,” Mauricas said. He warned that Lithuania could record a negative migration balance among its citizens this year for the first time in years if the trend continues. More men than women are emigrating, and most are of working age. The main destinations remain the United Kingdom, Norway and Germany, according to Vaiva Randytė, a specialist at the State Data Agency. The reasons for leaving are varied, but economic factors remain important. High housing costs, rising prices for consumer goods and services, and competition in the labour market are among the concerns facing people considering a move abroad. Mauricas said some Lithuanians see little reason to remain in the country if they can perform similar work abroad for significantly higher pay. “What difference does it make whether you work in Lithuania and speak a language other than the state language in certain sectors, or work with almost the same people in Sweden, Finland or Norway and earn twice as much?” he said. Geopolitical uncertainty is another factor, Mauricas said, with fears of war potentially influencing decisions to leave. He also warned that the longer people remain abroad, the less likely they are to return. Migrants establish social networks, start families and enrol their children in local schools, making a move back to Lithuania increasingly difficult. “Returning becomes, in a way, a second emigration,” he said. A 2024 survey found that six in 10 Lithuanians who had emigrated did not rule out returning in the future. However, many did not expect to do so within the next five years. As the government seeks to maintain connections with Lithuanians abroad, officials are promoting Lithuanian-language schools to help younger generations preserve their language and links to their ancestral country. Deputy Foreign Minister Kristupas Vaitiekūnas said the schools offer educational and practical benefits while helping children maintain ties with Lithuania. In the United States, for example, completing such a school can provide an additional point in some higher education admissions processes. Vaitiekūnas said stronger cultural connections could eventually translate into economic ties, whether through a return to Lithuania, investment or tourism. “Once that stronger connection with Lithuania is established, an economic connection follows,” he said. The government is also considering financial incentives to encourage emigrants to return. Social Security and Labour Minister Inga Ruginienė has proposed a family support package offering between 2,000 and 5,000 euros to returning emigrants. An additional 1,000 euros would be allocated for certain integration needs, recognising that returning families may include children born abroad who need to learn Lithuanian and adjust to life in the country. Mauricas said such measures would need to form part of a broader strategy to address the reasons people leave. He argued that Lithuania also needs a clear immigration policy defining how many foreign nationals the country should admit, what skills they should bring and how they should be integrated into society.

Lithuania ranks first in the European Union for the use of agentic artificial intelligence in organisations, according to a recent OpenAI study cited by the country’s Economy and Innovation Ministry. "Lithuania's leadership in agentic artificial intelligence shows that our organisations can quickly adopt cutting-edge technologies and turn them into practical solutions. We must harness this potential to boost labour productivity, strengthen corporate competitiveness and create greater added value for the Lithuanian economy," Economy and Innovation Minister Edvinas Griksas said in a press release. Ministry economist Titas Budreika said the study found that agentic AI accounted for 85 percent of all activity generated by OpenAI's enterprise AI tools among Lithuanian organisations using them. ​ "This shows that Lithuanian organisations are moving beyond testing technologies and increasingly integrating them into their everyday work processes," Budreika said. ​ The share of Lithuanian companies using AI tools has grown 2.5 times over the past year, the fastest increase among European Union member states, Budreika said. ​ Cyprus, Hungary, Poland, Sweden, Finland, Estonia, the Netherlands, Croatia and Italy followed Lithuania in the OpenAI study. ​ The study examines how European companies are moving from standard AI use to advanced AI agents capable of not only generating information but also performing tasks, analysing data and assisting with decision-making. ​ A ministry analysis of AI's impact on the Lithuanian economy found that the country's gross domestic product could grow by as much as 17 percent over a decade if Lithuania approaches the level of leading Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries in developing innovative digital businesses.

Lithuanian defence technology company Pekkla and Ukraine’s December One RND have agreed to establish a joint factory in Lithuania to produce electronic warfare systems and drone components, with production expected to begin in 2027. The plan is outlined in a letter of intent signed during Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas’ visit to Ukraine. “The goal of this agreement is to establish a joint venture in Lithuania. Production is planned to begin in 2027,” Kaunas said. “The aim is for electronic warfare equipment to be purchased primarily from Lithuanian manufacturers, as well as from Ukrainian defence industry products localized in Lithuania.” The agreement is part of efforts to implement a defence industry cooperation pact signed by Lithuania in May. Under the agreement, the two countries aim to identify Ukraine’s most urgent needs, jointly develop and improve technologies, expand production capacity and deliver the necessary equipment to Ukraine as quickly as possible. Pekkla, which was registered in Vilnius earlier this year, designs and manufactures unmanned aerial vehicles and autonomous ground vehicles. The company will contribute access to its infrastructure and business contacts in Lithuania. Ukraine’s December One RND will provide research and development expertise, technical knowledge, production capabilities and product concepts to be tested on the Lithuanian market. Kaunas has previously said Lithuania aims to produce drones for Ukraine as part of broader efforts to strengthen defence cooperation between the two countries. Elijus Civilis, head of the Invest Lithuania investment promotion agency, has said several Ukrainian defence industry investors have already received approval from the government commission responsible for screening strategic transactions to operate in Lithuania.

Lithuania’s proposed 2027 budget will further widen the government deficit and increase public debt, while ambitious revenue targets could prove difficult to meet, economists warned Friday after the government approved the draft budget. The spending plan reflects continued fiscal expansion, with expenditure growing faster than nominal gross domestic product, even when the impact of European Union structural funding is excluded, said Indrė Genytė-Pikčienė, an economist at Artea Bank. “Next year will be another year of generous fiscal expansion,” she told BNS, adding that declining EU structural support and fewer one-off economic tailwinds would make the outlook more challenging. Tadas Povilauskas, an economist at SEB Bank, said fiscal policy would again stimulate the economy through borrowing. But rising deficits and public acceptance of persistent overspending could make it more difficult to consolidate public finances in the future without slowing economic growth. The budget deficit is set to grow mainly because of higher social benefits and public-sector wages, much of which is linked to automatic indexation of pensions, benefits and salaries, Povilauskas said. He questioned the need for an additional 150 million euros earmarked for a proposed family support package, arguing that some spending increases went beyond what indexation required. He also criticised the lack of emphasis on improving public administration efficiency. However, he said higher social spending could support domestic businesses by boosting consumption among lower-income households. Genytė-Pikčienė questioned whether the government would collect all the revenue projected in the budget. Lithuania’s economy benefited this year from increased consumption following a reform of the second-pillar pension system, but that boost is expected to fade next year. Povilauskas also described several revenue forecasts as ambitious. Excise tax revenue is projected to rise by 11%, while value-added tax revenue is expected to increase by about 7.2%. He questioned whether the VAT target was realistic, particularly because 158 million euros of the expected increase is attributed to improved tax administration. Household consumption is expected to grow more slowly next year as the effect of withdrawals from second-pillar pension funds fades, he said. He also urged caution over the plan to collect 2.1 billion euros in corporate income tax, noting that the target for this year is expected to be missed. Genytė-Pikčienė said the projected deficit was significant enough to raise the possibility of an infringement procedure by the European Commission because it would exceed the EU’s Maastricht deficit limit of 3% of GDP. She noted, however, that Lithuania was not the only country exceeding the threshold. She warned that relying on borrowing to finance public spending could create serious long-term problems as debt servicing costs rise and leave less room for future policy decisions. Povilauskas said interest payments would increase by 370 million euros next year, adding the equivalent of 0.3 percentage points of GDP to budget expenditure. Public debt is expected to rise by another 6.5 billion euros in 2027, following an increase of 6.8 billion euros this year, reaching 48.2% of GDP by the end of next year. The government is financing much of the increase in defence spending – from 2% to 5% of GDP over several years – through borrowing, while also increasing other expenditure, Povilauskas said. The Finance Ministry has acknowledged the risk that public debt could approach 60% of GDP by the end of the medium-term planning period. Genytė-Pikčienė said lawmakers should carefully scrutinise any additional spending proposals during the budget process to prevent the deficit from growing further. She stressed that national defence and security must remain priorities because they are essential to economic prosperity, attracting foreign investment and supporting business stability. The draft budget maintains a strong focus on social spending and raising incomes, Genytė-Pikčienė said. The average old-age pension is set to increase at a double-digit rate, while pensions for people with the required length of service are expected to rise by 11%. Salaries for teachers, statutory officers and cultural workers are planned to increase by 7.5%, with pay for judicial assistants rising by nearly 6%. The government is seeking to offset pressure on household purchasing power from imported inflation, including higher fuel prices and heating costs, by increasing incomes, she said. Lithuania has refrained from introducing broad measures to counter energy price increases, unlike some neighbouring countries, instead relying more heavily on income growth to cushion the impact on households. Economist Romas Lazutka criticised the proposed 150 million-euro family package, saying its measures were universal rather than specifically targeted at people in the greatest need. He said much of the budget deficit was effectively predetermined by legislation and existing commitments, including social benefits, education spending and public-sector collective agreements. Reducing the deficit would likely require cuts to social spending, a politically unpopular step that would be difficult to implement, he said. Lazutka also pointed to what he described as a structural imbalance between the state budget and the Sodra social insurance fund. Sodra regularly records a surplus and builds up reserves, while the central government runs a large deficit and borrows at interest rates higher than the returns earned on those reserves. The arrangement means the government is paying more to borrow than it earns by investing money accumulated in the social insurance system, he said.

Lithuania has extended military assistance to patrol its border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region until mid-November, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said. “Assessing the potential flows of residents fleeing the Kaliningrad region and related incidents of illegal border crossings, we are extending enhanced border protection until mid-November for preventive purposes,” Kaunas said. The Defence Ministry said the decision was made at the request of Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas. Military resources will be coordinated with the needs of the State Border Guard Service. About 100 troops are currently deployed to assist border guards. Military intelligence has reported no significant changes in military activity in the Kaliningrad region, and the threat level along Lithuania’s border has not increased. The deployment is linked to public reports of a planned mobilisation in Russia following parliamentary elections. Katelynas has said he expects people might try to seek asylum in Lithuania to avoid military service. Military personnel and State Border Guard Service officers patrol areas around border checkpoints. Mobile patrols, mobile observation posts and military police units can also be deployed as needed.

Lithuania’s draft budget for 2027 allocates more than 4.8 billion euros to defence, equivalent to 5% of projected GDP, the Finance Ministry said Thursday. The government approved the proposal on Friday morning and will present the budget bill to the parliament, Seimas. The proposed allocation would increase defence spending by nearly 35 million euros from this year. It includes funding for the Defence Ministry and the State Defence Fund, which is set to receive more than 896 million euros. Although defence spending was lower in monetary terms this year, it accounted for a larger share of the economy, at 5.38% of GDP. Early last year, Lithuania’s State Defence Council, which includes the country’s political leadership and representatives of its national defence system, agreed to allocate 5% to 6% of GDP to defence annually from 2026 through 2030. The increased spending is intended to help develop an army division and prepare Lithuania to host a German brigade. The Finance Ministry on Thursday registered draft budgets for the state, municipalities and social funds for next year, projecting a general government deficit of 3.8% of GDP. State budget revenue is expected to reach nearly 22.2 billion euros, including European Union funds, while expenditure is projected at 27.9 billion euros. The projected deficit exceeds the European Union’s Maastricht criterion, which generally limits government deficits to 3% of GDP. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said in an earlier interview that most spending beyond revenue was linked to the goal of allocating 5% of GDP to defence and to increases in benefits that are indexed. The government is also proposing pay increases for statutory officers and cultural workers in 2027. Additional funding has been earmarked for a proposed package of measures to encourage families to have children. Revenue for the Sodra state social insurance fund is projected at nearly 7 billion euros next year, with expenditure expected to exceed 5.5 billion euros. The average pension is set to rise by 10.4% to 825 euros a month, increasing to 895 euros for people who meet the required length-of-service criteria. The budget allocates 715 million euros for the pension increases. The Compulsory Health Insurance Fund is expected to collect nearly 3.3 billion euros in revenue in 2027 and spend almost 3.2 billion euros. General government debt is projected to reach 48.2% of GDP next year. Sinkevičius said Lithuania would continue to devote one of Europe’s largest shares of GDP to defence. Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said the budget sought to balance stronger national security with income growth above inflation and the economy’s long-term growth potential.

Lithuania is planning to change the laws surrounding platform work. The changes aim to make the conditions better for the growing workforce who are named as “partners”, but have few – if any – possibilities to negotiate rates or even challenge automatic decisions taken by algorithms. Around 141,000 people worked for platforms like Wolt and Bolt in the country, according to data from 2024. The number is expected to rise to 157,000 by 2028. Many of them are migrants or students, often from non-EU countries. They have also been at the centre of political efforts to point at the (allegedly) runaway migration taking place in the country. Amid a flurry of anti-migration rhetoric, the interior minister proposed limiting the right of foreign, non-EU students to work on a self-employed basis. But who are the people that make up the immigrant community? Probably unsurprisingly, Belarusians and Ukrainians remain the two biggest nationalities. Meanwhile, Lithuania is at risk of increasing out-migration of its own citizens due to war fears and economic pressures . DIESEL AND YANDEX Donald Trump’s diesel-sucking deal with Russia received a bitter response even in Lithuania that normally backs Washington’s endeavours, with Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius saying the decision of the country’s strategic partner was “shameful and dishonourable”. The foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, tried to play it down, saying “this latest episode is not the worst we have seen in nearly two years”. Speaking at the Warsaw Forum earlier this week, Sinkevičius also said Ukraine should strike more data centres, wink wink. US TROOPS, BALTIC BORDERS And speaking of America, the first US troops arrived in the country earlier this week. Up to 100 US troops are now here as part of a returning rotation, with the rest of the 1,000-strong force expected by mid-November. In other defence updates, Lithuania is investing over 33 million euros into military fuel infrastructure. And if you’re feeling lost about all the different initiatives taking place in Lithuania to prepare for a potential conflict, we've got you covered . SHOOTING IN VILNIUS But it was an armed incident closer to home that proved deadly , when a former policeman shot a former kickboxing champion after an altercation outside an apartment block. In related news, a man escaped from a court hearing by pushing aside a police officer and making a run for it. Predictably, he was arrested a few hours later. EDITOR’S PICKS: – Lithuania’s rural regions are banking on religious tourism . – Lithuania is banking on mending ties with China “less publicly”. – Read what an ICC judge had to say about Trump. – Apple harvest is plentiful, but seasonal labour shortage isn’t helping. – A new TV series, The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo, will be filmed in Vilnius. – Kaunas’ UNESCO heritage is in the crosshairs . – A deep dive into archives about how the Lithuanian media used to portray gay people. Written by Benas Gerdžiūnas Edited by Justinas Šuliokas

The European Union is working on multiple fronts to limit the number of Russian citizens that can enter the bloc, including the nuclear option of a total ban on all non-essential travel into the club’s Schengen zone. ​This comes as Brussels and several EU member states have flagged that individuals using either Russian diplomatic cover or travelling on tourism visas have played key roles in various types of hybrid attacks in the bloc. ​ Most recently, German authorities revealed that the main suspect in the drone attack on Leipzig airport in August, which caused major traffic disruptions, was a Belarusian-Russian citizen who entered the EU using an Italian-issued Schengen tourist visa. ​ In a leaked EU presidency policy paper on various Russian visa options, seen by RFE/RL, it is noted that the “only long-term and effective solution would appear to be the possibility to adopt visa restrictive measures, which would ban non-essential travel for one nationality of applicants.” ​ The document notes that changes to the EU visa code would be necessary for such a move and that “these visa measures would be applied in a uniform way as EU law”. A change to the visa code would be made via qualified majority, constituting 55 percent of all member states, representing 65 percent of the total EU population. ​ A bigger overhaul of the EU visa code could come later in the year, but several EU member states, notably in southern Europe, are still reluctant to completely shut down various avenues of people-to-people contact with Russian citizens. ​ Shortly after the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the EU fully suspended the EU-Russia visa facilitation agreement that allowed for cheaper visas, multiple-entry visas and simpler procedures to obtain them. ​ Brussels also issued guidelines to EU member states on how to deal with Russian visa applications, prioritizing so-called “essential travel” requests such as applicants going for humanitarian reasons, including civil society representatives, political dissidents and independent journalists or family reunification. Patchwork approach ​ These guidelines are nonbinding, giving each EU member state wide discretion on how they would treat Russian visa applications. And the result has created a European patchwork of approaches to Russian visa requests. ​ While many countries on the EU’s eastern flank, bordering Russia, imposed very strict rules by hardly allowing any Russian nationals to enter, southern member states, keen on summer visitors, were more generous in issuing Schengen tourist visas for Russian citizens. ​ In 2025, a record since the full-scale invasion was reached, with 477,878 visas being issued to Russian nationals for tourism purposes. The vast majority of those were authorized by Greece, Italy, France, and Spain. ​ Until a potential decision on a full entry ban could be taken, the EU is working in parallel on three separate tracks on how to reduce the number of Russian visitors -- banning ex-combatants in Ukraine, reducing Russian diplomatic movement and so-called “limited territorial validity (LTV)” visas, which only allows you to stay in the country that issued the visa while prohibiting the holder from travelling to other Schengen zone countries. ​ The presidency paper notes that “LTV visas are presented as an interim measure, pending the future implementation of a full ban on travel for non-essential purposes.” Germany has argued for this approach and the paper notes that the rationale behind the push is to let the countries that still issue non-essential visas to Russian to “assume full responsibility for doing so, in a context where other Member States adopt a much stricter approach.” ​ But the paper also points out the limits with this move, noting that “this runs against one of the basic principles on which the Schengen area is based, ie mutual trust. It amounts to a re-nationalisation of short-stay visa policy”. Limited effect ​ The very fact that there hardly are any internal EU border controls also make an LTV visa have limited effect, with the document stating that “an LTV visa issued to a Russian national with malevolent intent does not seem to offer sufficient security guarantees against further movements inside the Schengen Area.” ​ Regarding ex-combatants travelling on tourist visas, movement is expected soon. ​ Various European consulates in Russia will most likely be required to check military service documents as part of the visa issuance routine. There are still some issues, however, such as the fact that many of the consulate staff are Russian citizens and that Moscow, according to European diplomats familiar with the matter, has threatened them with legal action if they ask about such documentation. ​ In a separate diplomatic note, seen by RFE/RL, the case for restricting the movement of Russian diplomats and consular staff within the EU is also being explored. ​ The common practice right now stipulates that Russian diplomatic personnel in the EU are only required to notify authorities when traveling to another member state, but there is now a push to introduce a requirement to obtain prior authorisation from the country they intend to visit. ​ Another idea gaining traction in Brussels is to limit how long Russian diplomats and officials can remain in their host countries as European counterintelligence services are keen to curb long-established spy networks, in which diplomats stationed in one place for extended periods often play a key role. This story was originally published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), partners of LRT English.

In Lithuania, children are widely seen as essential to a woman’s fulfilment and a successful marriage or partnership. Yet parents raising children often encounter a less welcoming reality, from being told not to bring children to weddings to having to breastfeed babies in airport toilets. Some everyday conflicts have little to do with a lack of public services and more to do with other people’s unwillingness to accommodate the needs of families with children. A mother may be allowed to keep flowers in her apartment building’s stairwell but forbidden to leave a child’s bicycle there, even when it does not obstruct passage. Parents may also feel unwelcome at cultural events not specifically designed for children or face criticism when a child cries in a public place. Whether such attitudes are widespread in Lithuania is difficult to establish because research into society’s acceptance of children and families in everyday public life is lacking. But researchers say the gap between the importance people attach to children in principle and their willingness to accommodate them in practice deserves closer attention. “There is a lot of talk in the public sphere about declining birth rates and the need to encourage families to have children, but we much less often consider how willing we ourselves are to accept children and their parents with understanding in everyday life,” said Aida Savicka, a senior researcher at the Lithuanian Institute for Culture Research. Giedrė Juškienė, founder and head of the nonprofit organisation Namų mama (House Mum), said it was difficult to generalise about Lithuanian society’s attitude toward children and families because experiences varied. Still, she said, parents were not always made to feel welcome. Juškienė said some parents were afraid to visit certain places because they expected to be unwelcome, adding that support from the surrounding community was essential to preventing isolation. She described a dispute with neighbours in her apartment building over whether she could leave her children’s bicycles on the second floor, despite there being enough space for people to pass. Flowers were allowed in the stairwell, but the bicycles were not. “Someone’s need to grow flowers is accommodated, but a mother’s need to shorten the distance she has to carry a bicycle is not,” Juškienė said. She also described pressure to clean the building’s stairwell, even though there was no established cleaning arrangement and other residents did not do the work. “There is this attitude that a mother with children can do the cleaning, while older people find it difficult,” she said. Her experiences abroad were mixed. During the approximately five years she lived in Germany, she received support when her child had an unexpected public tantrum. But she also encountered people who demanded that children be silenced when they cried outdoors in a park. Juškienė said parents needed to strike a balance between allowing children to learn how to behave in different settings and recognising that children could not always be expected to sit quietly or remain calm. “I am one of those mothers who takes her daughters to many places, even if it requires more effort,” she said. “Sometimes, though, you have to leave because a child cannot sit still, and you cannot force them to.” Children excluded from weddings and workplaces Gediminas Karoblis, dean of the Faculty of Humanities at Vytautas Magnus University, has raised eight children with his wife, Gitana, and now has six grandchildren. Having spent 15 years in Norway with his family, he said he had observed changes in attitudes toward children and families in Lithuania. One trend that particularly concerned him was the growing practice of asking wedding guests to attend without children. Karoblis said such requests put families in a difficult position, forcing them to find someone to look after their children so they could attend an event traditionally associated with family life and new beginnings. “It is as if the emphasis is on making sure children are absent, that nobody should see they exist at all,” he said. He also questioned why mothers sometimes had to breastfeed babies in toilets while airports provided elaborate smoking rooms with comfortable seating. “Changing a baby in a toilet is one thing, but breastfeeding there is another,” Karoblis said. He said the same lack of accommodation could be seen in workplaces, where parents taking time off to care for sick children might be accused of failing to manage their personal lives. Even when a child’s illness is a legitimate reason for absence, parents can be told to find a babysitter or otherwise ensure that childcare does not interfere with work, he said. Karoblis argued that children were often welcomed when they appeared happy and well-behaved but were treated as an inconvenience when they cried, made noise or disrupted adult routines. “People are delighted when a family with children is 100 metres away, walking nicely and smiling with balloons,” he said. “But that changes in more difficult, less picture-perfect situations.” Research suggests that Lithuanians continue to place considerable value on children as a source of emotional bonds and meaning in family life. But Savicka said positive views about children did not necessarily translate into a willingness to accommodate them in public. In a recent monograph, Generations of Change in Lithuania: A Perspective on Changing Values, co-authored with Rūta Žiliukaitė and based on European Values Study data from 1990 to 2017, Savicka found that traditional views of children as important to women’s fulfilment and successful marriages remained strong. Younger generations, however, were more likely to emphasise individual choice and less likely to regard having children as essential to a fulfilling life.
