Russia was likely behind an attempt to set fire to a Lithuanian company storing Starlink equipment at around 02:00 on Sunday, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said. He said Lithuanian authorities were monitoring the activities of hostile states “very closely” and taking measures to protect people and their property. Similar or related incidents had already occurred abroad, including in Poland and Bulgaria, Sinkevičius later told LRT RADIO, linking the incident to Russia’s hybrid war against Europe. “At around 02:00, there was an attempt to burn satellite antennas and a control unit. Incendiary liquids were found, along with containers ranging in capacity from three to 10 litres. The fact is that this was clearly an attempted act of sabotage or diversion, as we are seeing similar actions repeated across Europe. It is obvious that [...] this is part of Russia’s hybrid war, involving acts of sabotage,” the prime minister later told LRT Radio. “We will learn more about who ordered it, how everything happened and who was behind it. It is likely that it is already clear who commissioned it – it is the Russian side,” he added. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas also confirmed the information but stressed that he could not yet provide further details. “The incident has been brought under control and prevented, but it is also being investigated,” the minister told journalists on Sunday. Jolita Orentaitė, head of the Communications Division at the Fire and Rescue Department (PAGD), told BNS that a pre-trial investigation had been launched into the incident. She declined to comment further. “We cannot share that information because a pre-trial investigation has been launched,” Orentaitė said. The prime minister has called a meeting of the National Security Commission for Monday to examine the attempted arson, as well as the incident involving a drone crashing in northern Lithuania on Sunday.

A drone entered Lithuania from Poland on Sunday morning before crashing in the north of the country. “The object is preliminarily believed to have entered Lithuanian airspace from Poland. I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters. “The latest information from the police is that the debris may have damaged a civilian car,” Kaunas said. “The debris has been found, the area has been cordoned off, and the police are working to gather all the information.” National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC) head Vilmantas Vitkauskas confirmed to LRT RADIO that the object was most likely a Ukrainian drone, which could have entered the country as Kyiv carried out strikes in the St Petersburg region. The authorities later confirmed that drone debris hit and damaged a moving car in northern Lithuania, but no one was injured. “A person travelling from Biržai towards Pasvalys heard an explosion. Debris damaged their private car, denting the door. Clearly, some kind of explosion occurred. That is at least the preliminary information we have from the person who was at the scene,” Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told reporters. Defence Minister Kaunas said fighter jets were scrambled after the object was detected, but pilots couldn't see it visually because of poor weather. In response to the suspected drone threat, an air alert was issued only in northern Lithuania. Kaunas said he found the situation “strange and unacceptable”. “The military has already been tasked with gathering all the information and providing me with a detailed report. We will also look into the matter with the Fire and Rescue Department to establish why alerts were not sent out in time, if that is indeed what happened. We will analyse this, because it is absolutely unacceptable. “If the object had already been detected in one part of Lithuania, everyone should have been informed in time. This issue has therefore already been raised,” Kaunas said. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Russia’s war against Ukraine “is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU”. “What appears to be a drone exploded over the northern part of the country, posing a danger to the civilian population,” he posted on X.

Lithuania has credible evidence that a drone that crashed in the country on Sunday crossed into its airspace from Poland, President Gitanas Nausėda’s national security adviser said Monday. “We have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border,” Deividas Matulionis told BNS. He was commenting on a report by Polish news portal polsatnews.pl, which cited sources in Poland’s Defence Ministry as saying the drone had been launched from Lithuanian territory about 30 kilometres from the Polish border and had not entered Polish airspace. Matulionis cautioned against placing too much weight on the report, saying Lithuania had not yet received official information from Polish authorities. “We should not assume that something is true just because it has been published somewhere. There is so much disinformation these days,” he said. The drone entered Lithuanian airspace early Sunday, and debris was later found in the village of Juodžionys in the Pasvalys district. The aircraft exploded on impact, damaging a civilian car. No injuries were reported. Separately, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said an arson attack was attempted overnight Sunday at premises in Vilnius used by US company SpaceX. The prime minister linked the incident to Russia’s hybrid war against Europe. The attackers allegedly attempted to set fire to nine satellite antennas and a control unit on the company’s premises. Matulionis said Russia was a likely suspect but stressed that Lithuanian authorities had not yet established responsibility conclusively. “There is a high probability that Russia is behind this incident, but we do not yet have 100% confirmation and attribution,” he said. The presidential adviser said the incident bore similarities to cases in Bulgaria and Poland and suggested the suspected arson may have been intended to disrupt access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network, which is used by Ukraine. “What happened in Bulgaria, Poland and Lithuania is very similar, so it seems almost obvious that the aim was to restrict access to Starlink for Ukraine’s needs,” Matulionis said, adding that investigators could not yet disclose further details without potentially jeopardising the investigation. He said the drone incursion and the attempted arson should not be linked. Defence minister calls Polish media report ‘misunderstanding’ Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has called Polish media reports about the drone that crashed in the Pasvalys district being launched from within Lithuania a “kind of misunderstanding”. “I have been in contact with the Polish minister of defence since Sunday, and today we agreed with our intelligence officials and the military that the relevant information, the data we have, will be transmitted to our colleagues in Poland via a secure network, and we will continue to address this issue,” Kaunas told reporters on Monday after a meeting of the National Security Commission. “As for the sources, they are unofficial, so we view this as a kind of misunderstanding, because Lithuania – as I have repeated many times – has not granted and will not grant any other country access to its airspace or territory to attack another country,” he stated.

International military exercises aimed at countering hybrid threats will take place in the Baltic Sea, around the port of Klaipėda and across western Lithuania from October 19-30, the Klaipėda municipality said Monday. Lithuanian and NATO troops will train to work alongside state institutions and other organisations during the drills. The exercises will be held in the municipalities of Klaipėda city and district, Palanga and Neringa, as well as in the Baltic Sea. Soldiers and officers will wear tactical uniforms, carry firearms and other military equipment, and move on foot and in vehicles, the municipality said. Training scenarios will also involve drones, helicopters, ships and other watercraft, as well as blank ammunition and pyrotechnics. The municipality said safety requirements and fire and environmental regulations would be observed throughout the exercises.

A drone that entered Lithuanian airspace and crashed in the northern Pasvalys district on Sunday was part of a Ukrainian attack on St Petersburg, Lithuania’s defence minister said. “The attack was targeting St Petersburg, and we know that very well. Some of the drones deviated into our territory because of the electronic warfare measures used by Russia. This particular drone is a consequence of the attack on St Petersburg,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told LRT TV on Sunday night. Initial information indicated that the aircraft was a Ukrainian-made FPV-1 drone, Kaunas said, adding that Ukraine had apologised for the incident in public statements. Authorities are continuing to search for the drone’s computer equipment, the minister said. Kaunas also dismissed a connection between the drone incident and an attempted arson attack overnight Sunday at premises in Vilnius used by the US company SpaceX. “I would not link these two incidents. The drone is Ukrainian, St Petersburg was attacked, and this is part of one operation,” he said. “Meanwhile, the attempt to destroy Starlink infrastructure, which we have seen in other countries – Poland and Romania – is a separate story.” The minister said Lithuania would have a stronger air defence system in a couple of years, but acknowledged that the country faces challenges in responding to aerial threats today. “The problem is that things were not done two, three or four years ago, and today we are facing the consequences,” Kaunas said. He added that measures being implemented now should improve both detection capabilities and kinetic responses in the coming years. For now, fighter jets remain the best response to aerial threats, he said, pointing to NATO’s active air policing mission, which Lithuania relies on. Additional measures are also being implemented to strengthen the country’s defences, he added. Ukraine launched its largest drone attack on St Petersburg, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s hometown, since 2022 on Sunday. An oil refinery caught fire during the attack. Alexander Drozdenko, governor of the surrounding Leningrad region, said 126 drones had been shot down. The drone entering Lithuanian airspace prompted a red air alert in the Šiauliai and Panevėžys counties and a yellow alert in Kaunas early Sunday. The alerts were lifted in all three counties about an hour later, at around 08:00. Debris from the crashed drone was later found in the village of Juodžionys in the Pasvalys district. The aircraft exploded on impact, and its fragments damaged a civilian car. No injuries were reported.

Some are stockpiling firewood and candles. Others are buying country homes to escape from a city under bombardment. Buildings are racing to install extra power sources. Portable generators are selling briskly. Officials are considering pontoon bridges across the Dnieper River. Even a tunnel underneath. Russia's aerial campaign to pummel Ukraine into submission is increasing in intensity and ferocity; on October 14, much of Kyiv plunged into darkness as Moscow launched missiles and drones at the Ukrainian capital for a second straight night. ​ Now, Ukrainians are bracing for what many fear could be the worst winter since the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022. ​ On the front lines, Ukraine’s dogged fight has ground Russian forces to a virtual standstill; in recent months, Kyiv's forces pulled off a surprising counteroffensive that has resulted in a major, albeit localised, shift on the battlefield. ​ But its ability to fend off legions of jet-powered drones, cruise and ballistic missiles, and even slower propeller-driven drones, is increasingly stretched thin with the sheer number of Russian weapons ripping through the air – and into Ukrainian buildings and bridges. ​ And the biggest single source of weaponry for Ukraine, the United States, has slowed many of its deliveries – most crucially, interceptors for the Patriot missile system. ​ “The realistic scenario is that we could see a repeat of last winter. That means strikes on heat and utility infrastructure,” Oleh Popenko, who heads the Union of Utility Services Consumers of Ukraine, told Current Time. “We are absolutely not protected against this, and no one is.” Ukrainian officials have struggled to respond to the loss of US interceptor missiles; European allies have supplied some, but not in adequate numbers, officials say. ​ The US-built system is the only proven defence against high-speed hypersonic and ballistic missiles. US stockpiles have dropped to dangerously low levels as many of those interceptors were diverted to the Middle East to defend against Iranian attacks in the war that began in late February. ​ Officials in Kyiv also fear the loss of advance intelligence: warnings of Russian missile launches, something provided largely by the Americans. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 13 that, for a second night in a row, Kyiv had not received any warning from Western allies. ​ Adding to Kyiv’s worries: US President Donald Trump’s announcement last week of an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine, which caught Kyiv off guard and which Zelenskyy says Russia has violated repeatedly. Trump, whose approval ratings have plummeted amid soaring diesel and gasoline prices, demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian refineries and said the US would be importing Russian diesel fuel. ​ Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko and Zelenskyy’s government have traded blame over the pace of preparations in Kyiv and the surrounding region for the winter. ​ Average Ukrainians, meanwhile, are doing what they can to prepare. Vitaliy Kupchak, who heads a condominium association for an apartment building in Kyiv’s Solomyanskiy district, said the association had levied an extra charge on residents and used the funds to build a small shelter in a basement space that used to be a “dump.” ​ “Within about a month, everything was cleaned out, the walls and floor were painted, and people contributed whatever they could. Someone gave a sofa, someone gave a little bed,” he told RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service during a recent tour. ​ “When there are air raid alerts, people sometimes spend the night here. As you can see, there aren't many sleeping places, so people bring their own mats and sleeping bags and can simply lay them out on the floor here and sleep.” ​ In recent weeks, Russia has launched multiple attacks on bridges spanning the Dnieper, which splits the Ukrainian capital. The city’s main government buildings, and much of the city’s population, are on the west bank, but the east bank is home to a sizable number of residents as well: about 40 percent of the urban population. ​ Lyudmyla Petrovna, who lives in a high-rise apartment on the east bank of the Dnieper, recalled how she struggled to get through last year’s Russian barrages – and the heating outages. ​ She had already stashed away 5-litre bottles of drinking water in her hallways, and she had gotten an alcohol burner for her electric stove, in case the power is cut. She had packets of instant soup stacked up in cardboard boxes. ​ “Here's a hand warmer. Socks. A power bank,” she told Current Time during a recent visit to her home, giving only her first name and patronymic. ​ She was praying for a warmer winter, she said, citing Ukrainian village folklore that says if onions this season have no skin, the weather should not be so harsh. ​ A growing number of Kyiv residents are snapping up country homes outside the city, if they can afford it, hoping to hunker down and avoid the worst of any coming Russian onslaught. ​ Olena, who asked to be identified only by her first name, recently bought a house with a garden about 100 kilometres south of Kyiv. She doesn’t have to commute, which makes the transition easier. She said the main rooms have individual gas heaters, so she won’t be reliant on municipal heat. ​ "The first thing we did was put in firewood. Oak. 3,500 hryvnyas (€70) per cubic metre, and we bought six [cubic metres] in total," she said. ​ Others don't want to leave – or have little choice. ​ “There’s simply nowhere to go, that’s all. So, I’m not planning on it,” one man told RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service. “I suppose if I had a place to go, I’d plan for it, but as it stands – no.” Earlier this month, Russian drone strikes hit Kyiv’s Southern and Northern bridges, prompting authorities to shut or restrict traffic on those and other spans. As migrant numbers grow, anti-trafficking organisations and trade unions are raising the alarm over widespread exploitation of foreign workers in Lithuania’s labour market. “The same migrants keep coming to us – support organisations and trade unions – in droves, already exploited and seeking help,” Kristina Mišinienė, head of the Centre Against Human Trafficking and Exploitation, said at a news conference in parliament last week. Trade unions say that third-country nationals who leave their families at home in the hope of earning money in Lithuania are having their passports or residence permits taken away at work, being assigned jobs different from those agreed, and subjected to excessive overtime and fines. Contracts with foreign workers are reportedly drawn up only in Lithuanian. In some cases, employers use contracts for services rather than employment contracts, leaving migrants who decide to quit their jobs in debt. A lawmaker from the ruling Democrats “For Lithuania” party has pledged to tackle the exploitation of foreign workers. “Society has every reason to be concerned, because migration figures are indeed high. We will take very serious steps to put migration policy in order and regulate it sensibly,” said MP Tomas Tomilinas. Fines, overtime and deductions from wages Audrius Cuzanauskas, head of the Trade Union Alliance, said at the news conference that third-country nationals arriving in Lithuania faced financial pressure. He described the case of a Brazilian man employed by the logistics company Rosteka, whose contract with his employer stipulated that he would owe €10,000 if he failed to work for the company for two years. According to Cuzanauskas, another migrant owes €265,000 to a company operating in Lithuania over various alleged breaches of workplace rules imposed by the employer. “Individual cases are so brutal, and we only learn about individual cases. But there are hundreds of thousands of such cases, because when we look at the arrival of migrant workers in Lithuania and the numbers involved, we also see how frequently they leave. “Thirty to 40% of people flee the country because they cannot endure the working conditions and exploitation,” Cuzanauskas said. He added that foreign workers were also being exploited at large, well-known companies, where they were made to work undeclared overtime. “For example, they work at the poultry plants in Vilnius or Kaišiadorys. According to the documents, their work schedules involve 200–328 hours a month working in a refrigerated facility,” Cuzanauskas said. He said foreign workers who experienced exploitation often did not know where to seek help and faced language barriers. Andrius Markevičius, head of the Filipino Community in Lithuania, said migrants often did not receive payslips, making it impossible for them to check what deductions were being made from their wages and why. He added that employers frequently took away workers’ passports and temporary residence permits. “People are extremely vulnerable and intimidated,” Markevičius said. Emilis Starodubovas, head of the May 1 Trade Union (G1PS), said some employers signed contracts for services rather than employment contracts with their workers. According to him, these contracts were written only in Lithuanian, and workers were not allowed to keep a copy or take a photograph of the document. Starodubovas described a case in which an employee who had signed such a contract decided to leave the job lawfully. The employer responded by issuing what Starodubovas called an official pre-trial ultimatum. “When we read this document, we find that it is not the company that owes money to the employee, but the employee who owes money to the company and is expected to pay a fine for the losses incurred,” Starodubovas said at the news conference. “Employers can see that impunity is thriving in Lithuania,” Cuzanauskas said. He argued that the Lithuanian Transport Safety Administration, the Employment Service, the State Labour Inspectorate and other institutions were failing to provide adequate protection for foreign workers’ rights. “These violations would not happen if inspections were carried out and the violations identified,” the Trade Union Alliance chairman stressed. Representatives of the organisations said institutions overseeing labour migration should improve foreign workers’ access to legal assistance, enabling them to defend their interests more effectively against employers who can afford to hire lawyers. “Institutions need to strengthen their expertise so that cases of exploitation can be recognised and described for what they are, rather than being treated as employment relationships,” said Aurelija Baltikauskaitė, head of the Human Rights Office at the Seimas Ombudsmen’s Office. Tomilinas said migration policy “needs more order” and pledged to look for ways to prevent the exploitation of people in the labour market. “We will start working on this issue very seriously,” the MP said, but did not outline any specific proposals. According to the Migration Department, nearly 227,000 foreign nationals held residence permits in Lithuania as of September 1. About 108,000 of them had permits on the basis of employment, down from around 175,000 at the beginning of the year. Businesses, particularly in the logistics sector, have repeatedly called for an increase in the quota for bringing in unskilled foreign workers. The quota of 24,700 approved for this year was exhausted on September 7. The Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists estimates that unfilled vacancies could cost the country between €100m and €150m in lost gross domestic product (GDP) this year, rising to around €550m in 2027.

Poland’s Defence Ministry has denied a media report claiming that a drone that exploded in Lithuania on Sunday was launched from Lithuanian territory, urging the public not to spread what it called unfounded speculation. “We categorically deny information published in the media claiming that, according to sources in the Polish Ministry of National Defence, the drone found in Lithuanian territory was launched from Lithuania,” the ministry said in a statement provided to LRT. “We strongly urge people not to spread these unfounded speculations,” it added. The claim was published by Polsatnews.pl, citing an anonymous source in the Polish Defence Ministry. It said the drone had taken off from Lithuanian territory about 30 kilometres from the Polish border and flown deeper into Lithuania without entering Polish airspace. The report prompted debate in Lithuania, where initial assessments indicated that the drone had entered the country from Ukraine via Poland. Poland’s Defence Ministry said it was analysing radar data from systems operating in the relevant part of Poland and neighbouring countries in cooperation with Lithuanian authorities. The ministry said it was awaiting the results of the requested analyses after the Polish defence minister ordered a review of the incident. The ministry also said the drone that entered Lithuanian airspace early Sunday had been identified as Ukrainian and that Ukraine had officially apologised to Lithuania for the incident. Lithuanian officials have likewise rejected the report that the drone was launched from Lithuania. Deividas Matulionis, national security adviser to President Gitanas Nausėda, said Monday that Lithuania had credible evidence the drone crossed the border from Poland. “Very unequivocally, I can say that we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border,” Matulionis told BNS. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas described the Polish media report as a misunderstanding, saying Lithuania had neither allowed nor would allow another country to use its territory or airspace to attack a third country. “The sources are unofficial, so we consider this a kind of misunderstanding,” Kaunas said.

Lithuania expects to have at least part of an integrated airspace detection system operational by the end of 2027, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Monday, following a drone incursion that ended with an explosion in the country’s north. “Once everything is integrated into a single system, I hope that by late 2027 we will have at least a partial, seamless system,” Kaunas said. He cautioned that progress would depend on how quickly companies could develop the necessary software and connect existing equipment. The remarks followed Sunday’s incident, when a drone entered Lithuanian airspace from Poland and crashed in the village of Juodžioniai in the Pasvalys district. An explosion damaged a civilian car, but no injuries were reported. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said the drone was Ukrainian and carried explosives. Sinkevičius said in August that he hoped a fully integrated detection system would be in place by 2030. Kaunas said the government was working to accelerate that timeline, although equipment deliveries could take one to two years because of demand from other countries. A state procurement tender has been launched to develop software that would connect different systems used to detect airborne objects. Nineteen Lithuanian companies have submitted proposals, Kaunas said, adding that authorities would analyse them in the coming days and select those best suited to the country’s needs. The system is expected to combine radar data with information from acoustic sensors deployed along the border, as well as cameras operated by residents and border guards. Kaunas said the main problem was that existing detection tools operated separately, limiting the ability to interpret potential threats. “Everything needs to be merged into one system,” he said, explaining that radar can identify an object’s speed, altitude and direction but does not provide other information needed to assess the situation. Reports from residents who hear unusual sounds could also help identify potential threats, he added. The Defence Ministry said in September that developing a short-range air defence system was one of Lithuania’s key ongoing projects, with an estimated cost of up to 1 billion euros. The three Baltic states would need about 2 billion euros combined, the ministry said. Lithuania plans to allocate 2.03 billion euros between 2026 and 2030 to develop airspace surveillance, air defence and electronic warfare capabilities. The Baltic states have also asked the European Commission for additional European Union funding to address urgent air defence needs.

Lithuania has lost the right to host a 2027 Modern Pentathlon World Cup event in Kaunas after the sport’s international governing body withdrew its approval over the country’s restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes, the Lithuanian Modern Pentathlon Federation said. The International Union of Modern Pentathlon (UIPM) executive board decided to cancel the event, scheduled for April 13–17, at a meeting more than a week ago. The Lithuanian federation learned of the decision last Monday through a letter inviting national federations to apply to host the event. Lithuania has maintained its position against allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in events held in the country. “We were initially angry and disappointed because preparations are already underway and we have signed several contracts with service providers,” federation President Justinas Kinderis said. He added that the decision was not entirely unexpected, as UIPM officials had repeatedly asked how Lithuania planned to handle Russian and Belarusian athletes. Kinderis said the federation had hoped its experience organising international championships and winning medals would be taken into greater consideration. In a letter signed by UIPM President Rob Stull, the governing body said it must follow recommendations approved this year by the International Olympic Committee. The recommendations would allow Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under their national flags and symbols and ensure equal opportunities to qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Kinderis argued that athletes from the two countries would have other opportunities to earn Olympic qualification points, noting that the World Cup circuit is not the sport’s highest-level competition. Kaunas officials also criticised the decision, citing the city’s sports infrastructure and experience hosting international events. The Lithuanian Education, Science and Sport Ministry reiterated last month that its recommendations against inviting Russian and Belarusian athletes to competitions in Lithuania remain unchanged. To be admitted, athletes from those countries must sign a declaration condemning military action and expressing support for Ukraine, and they cannot display national flags or other symbols. Kinderis warned that the decision could also threaten Kaunas’ right to host a 2028 World Cup event and junior and youth championships. National federations have until October 25 to apply to replace Kaunas as host of the 2027 event. Four World Cup stages were originally planned for next year. If no replacement host is found, UIPM is considering holding only three.

Lithuania is seeking consultations with NATO on changing procedures to allow military aircraft to shoot down objects violating the country’s airspace even when pilots cannot identify them visually, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Monday. “I requested that we start consultations with NATO. [...] That will probably be implemented within a month, so that we can review that algorithm,” Sinkevičius told LRT. The prime minister said fighter pilots can detect objects on radar but may be unable to see them because of cloud cover or poor weather. Under current procedures, pilots cannot use force to shoot down an object if they cannot visually confirm its identity. Sinkevičius said the rules could be revised to give countries greater discretion in responding to potential airspace violations, allowing Lithuania to decide to shoot down an object detected by radar even without visual confirmation. The proposal follows an incident Sunday in which a drone entered Lithuanian airspace from Poland. NATO fighter jets were scrambled, but the pilots did not see the object and could not confirm that it was a drone, so they did not shoot it down. Debris from an explosion was later found in the village of Juodžioniai, in the Pasvalys district of northern Lithuania. Lithuanian officials said the drone was Ukrainian and carried explosives. Ukraine apologised for the incident, saying the drone may have been diverted by Russia.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed creating a European Union security protocol modelled on NATO’s Article 4 to coordinate responses to hybrid attacks, but the idea has so far received limited support and raised concerns about duplication and political divisions within the bloc. Von der Leyen raised the proposal amid a series of suspected hybrid threats across Europe, including drone incursions in several EU countries and an attempted attack at Leipzig airport. On the eve of her annual address, a drone was shot down over Lithuania. “I believe the time has come for a European Article 4 – an emergency security protocol. If one member state activates it, all the others would come together,” von der Leyen said. NATO’s Article 4 provides for consultations among allies when a member believes its security, territorial integrity or political independence is threatened. It has been invoked nine times. EU defence ministers have discussed von der Leyen’s proposal, but support appears limited. “The Commission president has raised the idea, and now we have to work on it,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said. Military officials say they will follow the political decisions made by EU leaders, while warning against unnecessary duplication of existing security arrangements. “The vast majority of EU countries are also NATO members. I think we should avoid duplication here,” Lithuanian army commander Gen. Raimundas Vaikšnoras said. “We need to find the right balance so that we do not interfere with or overshadow one another.” Experts are also divided over whether the EU needs a separate protocol. Marija Martišiūtė, an analyst at the European Policy Centre, said such a mechanism could be useful because NATO allies are not always willing to invoke Article 4. An EU protocol would give a country facing an attack another avenue to seek support, she said. Under the proposed mechanism, a member state could present its assessment of an incident, explain how it occurred and identify the perceived threat before seeking assistance or a joint decision from other EU members. The protocol could also provide for potential responses, Martišiūtė said, including an operation, increased monitoring and vigilance, sanctions or financial measures. But Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an analyst at the Bruegel think tank, called the proposal a mistake. “It is a terrible idea. It just diverts attention,” he said. Kirkegaard argued that NATO’s Article 4 consultations can already risk becoming a forum for empty talk when 32 allies cannot agree on a response. An EU version would be even more difficult, he said, given differences among member states over defence policy and spending. He pointed to four neutral EU countries and said some members, including Ireland and Malta, were reluctant to engage on defence issues. Austria, he added, was also hesitant to some extent. The EU already has a treaty provision requiring member states to provide aid and assistance if another member is the victim of armed aggression on its territory. Earlier this year, EU leaders asked the European Commission to draw up an action plan for implementing that mutual-assistance clause. So far, member states have held tabletop exercises to exchange ideas about what such assistance would mean in practice. It remains unclear when the Commission will present a concrete action plan.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said he had no reason to doubt the loyalty of the country's Orthodox community, but said believers under the Moscow Patriarchate had to "decide who they stand with". "We have a situation where, you could say, the Orthodox Church is split into two parts. One belongs to the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, the other to the Moscow Patriarchate,” Nausėda told reporters on Wednesday. “Our position is this: we currently have no reason to doubt the loyalty of the Orthodox community. The Orthodox community in Lithuania proved that loyalty both when Lithuania declared its independence in 1990 and during the bloody events of January. I want to believe that the Orthodox community consists first and foremost of citizens of the Republic of Lithuania and only then believers," he said. "So far, there are no imperative decisions from the state's side, but first of all, I repeat, what in my opinion is important: the Orthodox community has to decide who they stand with," he stressed. Nausėda also recalled that Lithuania was seeking EU sanctions against Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Moscow Patriarchate, although previous attempts had failed due to opposition from some countries. The president called the patriarch a tool of Russia's imperial policy. A national security threat assessment compiled by intelligence agencies previously stated that the Orthodox Church plays a significant role in shaping and maintaining the ideological narratives of the Russian regime. The leadership of the Lithuanian Orthodox Archdiocese has publicly condemned Russia's war against Ukraine and repeatedly stated its ambition to achieve independence from the Moscow Patriarchate. Conservative lawmakers Audronius Ažubalis and Arvydas Anušauskas are seeking to designate the Exarchate of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople as the representative of Lithuania's traditional Orthodox community. This would involve the transfer of six religious properties currently managed by the Moscow Patriarchate to the exarchate.

Russia is testing the limits of NATO’s collective defence by engaging in attacks that fall short of the alliance activating the Article 5 clause, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told LRT.lt in an interview published on Wednesday. “In political discussions, the phrase that Russia is testing us to the limits of NATO’s Article 5 is being used increasingly often. And this is not just about Lithuania, Latvia or other countries on the eastern flank. Russia is testing how far it can go without crossing a line that could prompt NATO to take collective defence action,” he said. The prime minister spoke to LRT.lt during a visit to Poland earlier this month, which followed a series of incidents involving Russian-linked attacks on infrastructure as well as a reported attempt to assassinate Polish leaders. “This poses a serious challenge for the alliance: how should we respond to and deal with such actions? These are not classic conventional attacks or straightforward border violations. Often, these actions are carried out through hired individuals, and investigations indicate that those commissioning them should be sought in the east,” he said in reference to Russia. Sinkevičius said he would work closely with his Polish counterpart to speed up responses and improve coordination in the event of future incidents. “One of the most important agreements was that we, as heads of government, would communicate directly. We exchanged personal contact details so that, if an incident occurred or we received important information, including from intelligence agencies, we could contact each other promptly rather than wait for the information to reach us through our teams. “We also agreed that, in the long term, the Lithuanian and Polish armed forces should work more closely together, particularly in the border region. This is also linked to the planned military training area in Kapčiamiestis,” he said.

A joint team from the Polish and Lithuanian defence ministries is investigating the cause of a drone explosion in the Pasvalys district, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauėda said on Wednesday. "There is additional information, but I would not like to get ahead of myself. A team has been set up by the Lithuanian Defence Ministry and the Polish Defence Ministry to investigate this incident," Nauseda, who is visiting Poland, told LRT. He said the circumstances of the incident could be discussed only after official findings had been received. The drone entered Lithuania from Poland on Sunday, crashed in the village of Juodžioniai in the northern Pasvalys district and exploded, with the debris damaging a car. Lithuanian officials said the Ukrainian drone was carrying explosives. Kyiv apologised for the incident, saying the drone might have been diverted by Russian electronic warfare measures. According to the Lithuanian Armed Forces, their Polish counterparts did not detect the drone on their radars. Polish news portal Polsatnews, citing sources in the country's defence ministry, reported that the drone had been launched from Lithuanian territory, about 30 km from the Polish border, and had not entered Polish airspace. The Polish Ministry of Defence later denied the report. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has previously said that an integrated system for detecting objects in Lithuanian airspace should be partially operational by the end of 2027. Following the incident, Lithuania also began talks with NATO on the possibility of shooting down drones without visual confirmation.​

As US President Donald Trump’s administration takes steps that critics say strengthen Russia, American troops are gradually returning to Lithuania, a frontline NATO ally seeking a permanent US military presence as a deterrent against Moscow. The contrasting developments have given Lithuanian leaders a cognitive dissonance. Washington’s reported deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin over diesel fuel, pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and revelations of Russian-American discussions about future energy deals have raised questions about US policy toward the Kremlin. At the same time, a senior American NATO commander has outlined how the alliance would respond to a possible Russian attack, including strikes against targets on Russian territory. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump confronted Zelensky in New York several weeks ago, questioning why Ukraine was attacking Russian oil facilities. As Ukraine appeared to gain momentum in its campaign against Russian targets, Trump blamed Kyiv for high diesel prices, reached an agreement with Moscow, eased sanctions and purchased some Russian diesel fuel. Zelensky has also said that the United States had temporarily suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda described the diesel agreement as “a bad day”. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius also criticized US agreements with Russia, while thanking Washington for resuming the rotation of American troops in Lithuania. For Vilnius, the challenge is to maintain support for Ukraine without directly entering a dispute with the Trump administration, said Tomas Janeliūnas, a professor at Vilnius University’s Institute of International Relations and Political Science. “Lithuania is not abandoning its support for Ukraine. We understand what it needs and want the Americans to support Ukraine as much as possible,” Janeliūnas said. But Lithuanian politicians do not want to become directly involved in the dispute, he added, seeing little practical benefit in doing so. Deividas Matulionis, the president’s chief national security adviser, said the best approach for now was to wait and see. Lithuania has already presented Washington with a proposal for a permanent US military presence. “We could do everything necessary to accommodate 1,500 to 2,000 permanently deployed American troops,” Matulionis said. Some infrastructure might need to be prepared, he added, but all political parties, both in government and in opposition, would support such a decision. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys dismissed suggestions that Lithuania’s criticism of Washington’s dealings with Moscow could jeopardise the troop deployment. “We should not assume that one issue is held hostage by another,” Budrys said. Disagreements over tariffs, trade and security, including differences over Greenland, had ultimately been resolved, he noted. Can Washington still guarantee deterrence? Lithuania’s dilemma is particularly acute because Ukraine is fighting Russia, which Vilnius considers its greatest adversary, while the United States remains the country’s principal security guarantor. The Kremlin has long been accused of efforts to undermine NATO unity. But doubts arising from Washington itself pose a different challenge, as Trump’s rhetoric toward NATO and his approach to Ukraine raise questions about the reliability of US commitments. Janeliūnas said the possibility of a secret military understanding between Trump and Putin could not be ruled out entirely, although he considered it unlikely. “The reaction would be explosive,” he said. NATO’s agreed defence plans and the powers of the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, or SACEUR, provide a significant deterrent, Janeliūnas said. The commander can take certain actions before a political decision is made to invoke NATO’s Article 5 collective defence clause. Confidence in the alliance has also been reinforced by US Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s top commander in Europe, who has publicly outlined how NATO would respond to Russian aggression. Retired Col. Vaidotas Malinionis said the American military presence remained essential, but Lithuania could not rely on it alone. “We also have other layers – the German brigade, the participation of other NATO countries on our territory, and, of course, our national capabilities, civil security and civil defence,” he said. “We need to increase our resilience.” Asked whether he would put more trust in Grynkewich or Trump, Malinionis replied: “As a retired military officer, I always trust the military.” American troops returning to Lithuania will be housed in newly built barracks at the Gen. Silvestras Žukauskas military training area. They will join Lithuanian forces and an expanding German military presence. Lithuania is also awaiting the arrival of German tanks, while the first crews are already training on German-made Leopard tanks. Brig. Gen. Nerijus Stankevičius, commander of the Lithuanian army’s land forces, said the returning US troops were coming not simply to train but to contribute to deterrence. An adversary planning an attack would have to account for Lithuanian troops as well as several battalions of allied forces, he said. That would make any operation substantially more difficult and harder to carry out without detection. “The adversary’s task becomes much more complicated, and that is deterrence,” Stankevičius said. Lithuania’s armed forces have repeatedly stressed that they would not hide behind allied troops in a war. But the presence of foreign forces would increase the costs and risks for any attacker. Still, questions remain about whether military preparations are matched by sufficient readiness at home. Dainius Gaižauskas, a member of the parliament’s National Security and Defence Committee, said preparedness should extend beyond the armed forces to the country’s internal security services and civil protection systems. Around 100 websites in Lithuania have been identified as vulnerable to a critical flaw in PHP, a programming language used by an estimated 80% to 90% of websites in the country, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre said Thursday. Antanas Aleknavičius told M1 radio that the affected sites included those operated by private businesses and state institutions. The centre is conducting further scans to determine the full extent of the vulnerability. Authorities rated the severity of the threat at 9.5 out of 10 and notified institutions in advance, he said. The National Cyber Security Centre issued a warning Wednesday following international reports of a global vulnerability in PHP code. In response, the Centre of Registers temporarily suspended some services, announcing Thursday that they were being restored. Aleknavičius warned that failure to address the flaw could leave websites and their servers exposed to attacks, potentially disrupting information systems. The extent of the damage would depend on existing security measures and the data stored on affected sites. Some websites might need only software updates, while others could require more extensive reconstruction, he said. Tools to exploit the vulnerability are being developed, but there is currently no evidence they have been used, Aleknavičius added. Antanas Raguotis, IT director at the Centre of Registers, said exploiting the flaw could enable unauthorised access to systems, allowing attackers to alter or steal data and take control of affected systems. An investigation into the incident will be conducted. Raguotis also warned of a critical vulnerability in Java, another widely used programming language, announced by Oracle. The Centre of Registers is assessing the potential impact on its systems and is awaiting international recommendations before deciding whether further precautions, including suspending services, are necessary. He said advances in artificial intelligence were making it possible to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities much faster, potentially increasing the scale of cyberattacks. When new technologies emerge, tools to exploit them are often developed before effective defensive measures become available, Raguotis said.

German federal prosecutors said Thursday they had arrested a Ukrainian man suspected of spying for Russian intelligence and gathering military-sensitive information, including details potentially relevant to NATO’s eastern flank. The magazine Der Spiegel, which first reported the arrest, said the suspect was interested in a German army brigade scheduled to be deployed in Lithuania next year. The suspect, identified as Vadym Y., allegedly collected information on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as military personnel and facilities in areas designated to protect NATO’s eastern flank, prosecutors said. He was arrested by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office in the Oder-Spree district of Brandenburg, east of Berlin, based on information provided by the domestic intelligence agency BfV, prosecutors said. “Vadym Y. had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary since at least July 2025,” prosecutors said in a statement. “Against the backdrop of the war between the Russian Federation and Ukraine, he gathered military-sensitive information in Germany for this intelligence service,” the statement added. The suspect collected publicly available information but also deliberately targeted people in Europe’s defence industry to obtain additional intelligence, prosecutors said. Martin Jäger, head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, told lawmakers this month that Russia’s “shadow war” against Germany and its allies was intensifying and had “taken on a new, more dangerous dimension”. “Germany is in danger of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia,” Jäger said at a meeting of the parliamentary committee overseeing intelligence services in Berlin.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Thursday he had received assurances from the defence minister that all allocated defence funds would be spent properly and efficiently by the end of the year, despite about half of this year’s budget remaining unspent in mid-October. Speaking to the Liberal Movement faction in the Seimas, Lithuania’s parliament, Sinkevičius said that while spending the money was important, procurement had to remain transparent and efficient rather than being rushed simply to meet a year-end deadline. He said he was personally monitoring the use of defence allocations and expected most payments to be made in the final quarter of the year. Lithuania’s 2026 defence budget stands at 4.8 billion euros, equivalent to 5.38% of GDP. “Those percentages may not be encouraging. One would like to see more even investment in defence quarter by quarter. It appears that the largest volume of payments will be executed in the last quarter,” Sinkevičius said. The government has introduced a tool to track how individual procurement organisations within the national defence system use investment funds, he added. As of last week, about half of this year’s defence funding remained unspent. Deputy Defence Minister Karolis Aleksa said, however, that spending was progressing faster than it had at the same point last year. Sinkevičius has previously said he accepted the Defence Ministry’s explanations for the delays but stressed that procurement bodies needed to work faster. He attributed some of the difficulties to the sharp increase in defence funding. The previous conservative-led government allocated 3.5% of GDP to the military, while the current budget provides more than 5%, leaving the existing administrative system to manage the larger sums. The prime minister also questioned whether efforts to centralise procurement had been fully implemented, noting that several dozen organisations were still involved in purchasing. “I think that the centralisation of procurement, which was considered and carried out through the Defence Materiel Agency, I don’t know if it has been fully realised, because there are several dozen purchasing organisations,” he said. “This means that the speed, organisation of the process, its management and monitoring face certain challenges,” he added. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has submitted proposed public procurement amendments to the parliament intended to speed up military acquisitions. The proposals include new procurement categories and shorter deadlines for the Public Procurement Office to decide whether to authorise simplified purchasing procedures. The draft government spending bill for next year allocates 5% of GDP, or more than 4.8 billion euros, to defence. The total includes funding for the Defence Ministry and more than 896 million euros for the State Defence Fund.

Two balloons carrying smuggled cigarettes exploded after striking power lines in central Lithuania on Wednesday, the Kaunas Fire and Rescue Service said Thursday. Firefighters were called to Padotnuvys village in Kėdainiai district at about 06:00 after receiving a report of something burning on Draugystės Street, possibly an exploded streetlight. When crews arrived, they found that a smuggling balloon had struck power lines and exploded. Fragments of the balloon were burning along the roadside. Later Wednesday, at about 23:00, firefighters were called to Šakniai village in Kaišiadorys district after residents reported hearing an explosion and seeing something burning in a field. Firefighters found that a balloon carrying smuggled cigarettes had hit power lines and caught fire.

Lithuania’s Environmental Protection Agency has approved an environmental impact assessment for a planned ammunition factory being built by the German defence group Rheinmetall and its local partners in Radviliskis district, concluding that the project will have no significant environmental impact. The agency said Friday that the project complies with environmental, public health, cultural heritage, fire safety and civil safety requirements. The factory is being developed by Rheinmetall Defence Lietuva, a joint venture involving Rheinmetall and state-owned investment company Epso-G Invest. Buildings and structures will cover 3.5 hectares of the 340-hectare site, according to the agency. The planned facilities include thermal processing, artillery shell filling, assembly and packaging, component manufacturing, production and storage buildings, ammunition bunkers, an administrative building and auxiliary structures. Mindaugas Keizeris, head of the state-owned Epso-G group, previously said that establishing the production lines was the project’s priority. The factory is expected to produce up to 75,000 155 mm artillery shells annually. Epso-G, through its subsidiary Epso-G Invest, holds a 48% stake in Rheinmetall Defence Lietuva. Rheinmetall owns 51%, while the remaining 1% belongs to Lithuania’s Giraitė Armament Plant. Construction officially began in early November 2025. Rheinmetall also plans to build a competence centre for artillery shell propellant charges in Lithuania, with an estimated value of about 400 million euros.

Lithuanian firms are producing anti-drone netting to shield the country’s strategic objects from potential attacks, business reps told the Verslo Žinios newspaper. Alvydas Pundzius from the Kovas company confirmed that their metal nets are already protecting some strategic objects, but declined to provide more details. Lithuania decided to increase anti-drone protection of strategic objects following the October 18 drone incursion, Verslo Žinios reported.

There was considerable pressure, including from coalition partners, to sharply reduce defence spending while preparing next year’s government spending bill, Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said, defending the 2026 budget proposal that includes a sizable deficit. “There were many temptations, including from some coalition partners, to make drastic cuts. Or to resort to certain tricks that might have been ill-considered and not coordinated with our defence partners,” Valys told LRT.lt in an interview. “There were many proposals to look at other NATO countries and tie ourselves to the minimum required by our main partners, the Americans. But we stood firm. We created expectations among our partners and, by setting an example, are already seeing certain dividends,” he said. Valys added that the government had also faced considerable pressure from the opposition. According to the minister, Lithuania’s decision to allocate more than 5% of its GDP to defence is already paying off. “We are no longer treated as a war zone. We are seen as resilient and determined, investing in defence and capable of attracting the attention of the world’s biggest market players,” he said. Lithuania has committed to maintaining defence spending at a level in excess of 5% of GDP. Valys also said that next year’s pension increases could potentially be financed using the surplus in the State Social Insurance Fund’s (Sodra) reserve, rather than drawing on the reserve itself.

A drone entered Lithuania from Poland on Sunday, before crashing in northern Lithuania. For the first time, it nearly ended tragically as debris from the explosion hit a car, but no one was hurt. Ukraine apologised for the incident, as it was one of its drones on the way to strike Russia’s St Petersburg region and was likely diverted with the use of electronic warfare means. This is prompting a risky discussion on whether the NATO air defence protocols should be changed, as jets need to identify the target visually before shooting it down. Proponents say removing this requirement would make air defences more effective. However, it could turn tragic if the object turns out to be, for example, a small Cessna plane that had suffered a communications failure, the prime minister said. We have to tread lightly, the Lithuanian president also said. There were also several peculiarities about the incident. Firstly, it crossed into Lithuania from Poland for the first time. A Polish media outlet added confusion into the mix by quoting anonymous officials who claimed that the drone had taken off in Lithuania, before this was officially denied by Warsaw and Vilnius. This narrative would have been dangerous, as Moscow continues to claim – without proof – that Ukrainian drones are being launched from the Baltic states and Poland. Secondly, another security incident happened hours before the drone crash when unidentified individuals – who are still at large – attempted to set fire to a Lithuanian firm in Vilnius hosting Starlink communication equipment that is also used by Ukraine. And amid the ongoing drone incidents and other security talks, Lithuania is forced to navigate the contrasting environment in Washington – the US arguably remains the biggest deterrent against Russia doing something really stupid. Here’s one apt example of the manoeuvring: Lithuania dropped support for an anti-disinformation conference in Vilnius that would have criticised Mr Trump. LEGAL LIMBO Even though court decisions have paved the way for same-sex couples to legalise their partnerships, the Justice Ministry is refusing to carry out the rulings. The situation is becoming awkward for the prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, with his coalition partners not stepping in line. He called on his partners to respect the rulings and the Seimas to act. DEFICIT DRAMA Lithuania’s new budget will most likely have a ballooning budget deficit, with experts and officials alike sounding alarm bells. The president and the prime minister agreed that the situation is not great, but there were few other options to finance the growing defence spending and social security needs. The political opposition is less positive, saying they will be the ones to have to deal with it following the next elections (if they win, of course). The Baltic states are turning to the EU for the SAFE instrument, as well as to request additional funding for air defences, but it’s all bearing down on the Baltic economies. The Latvian prime minister was also in Brussels, saying the so-called eastern flank countries should get more financial support to deal with the “geographical punishment” of being close to our very best neighbour. IRAN TRAVEL Two Lithuanian women were very likely detained in Iran. They were declared missing after their families lost contact with them. Speaking to LRT RADIO on Thursday morning, Lithuania’s authorities reminded people about risks associated to travelling to warzones, as well as to countries like Russia or Belarus. As one official put it, we only hear stories of those that went and came back, not the ten or so people that remain imprisoned in Belarus on nonsense charges. In related (travel) news, Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry denied reports that the country had eased visa rules for Pakistani citizens after the misinformation started viralling on social media. POPPING BALLOONS Smuggling balloons from Belarus have been less of a nuisance in recent months, but the latest incident resulted in an explosion after the balloons struck power lines. Beyond a spectacle, it caused little damage. In any case, there are a few explanations why there have been less balloons. One, rather hard to test, could be a switchup of tactics of Belarus. Another explanation, and more easily quantifiable, points at the string of arrests targeting smuggling networks inside Lithuania. W. W. An “industrial-scale” lab was discovered near Vilnius, with officers seizing almost a tonne of drugs. The pictures looked criminally impressive, to say the least. ECONOMY UPDATES: – A new laser factory has opened in Lithuania, highlighting the country’s high-tech potential. – But poverty rates in the country are rising . – Abuse of migrant workers is also growing . – Citi Group plans expansion in the Baltics, with the biggest US banking chain eyeing an office in Lithuania. – Ignitis is pausing its Baltic Sea wind farm project. – The Lithuanian president is adding fresh air to the decades-old conversation surrounding a potential Vilnius metro. EDITOR’S PICKS – Are we starting to hate children? – Don’t forget to change your clocks this weekend. – Read about Romas Šležas, a Lithuanian-born documentary filmmaker, who captured America's environmental and civil rights movements. – A post by a Lithuanian woman about communism and their youth fanbase in Italy has gone viral. – Lithuania lost the right to host a 2027 Modern Pentathlon World Cup event after refusing to readmit Belarusian and Russian athletes. – And this pretty oak.
