Politicians, military officials and industry leaders are gathering in Vilnius for a two-day conference on Baltic defence strategies and lessons from Russia's war in Ukraine, starting on Monday. Held at the National Gallery of Art, the event will focus on strengthening European air defence, addressing gaps in NATO's military capabilities and exploring the role of artificial intelligence and drone technology on the battlefield. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas will open the conference, while European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius will speak about a unified European defence shield. "Ukraine teaches us that to defend the Baltic region and the whole of Europe, we must be able to produce a lot, be fast, innovative, and resilient," Kubilius said. The programme includes presentations by practitioners from Ukraine's Defence Ministry and armed forces. Discussions will also cover societal resilience, the European defence industry's production capacity, nuclear deterrence, and military intelligence. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said insights from Ukrainian specialists would help improve understanding of what constitutes effective preparedness and what practical solutions are needed before a crisis begins. The event will be attended by top-ranking Lithuanian military officers, as well as international experts from the Institute for the Study of War, the Royal United Services Institute, the European Space Agency and other institutions.

Lithuanian defence industry companies are calling for more government support to protect against suspected sabotage, cyberattacks and intimidation, after an attempted arson attack on a facility storing Starlink communications equipment in Vilnius. Businesses producing defence and dual-use technologies say they face growing security concerns, including cars with Russian license plates parked outside their offices, employees being photographed and psychological pressure. They want the authorities to provide more training and practical advice on how to respond to potential threats. The attempted arson took place overnight Sunday at a Vilnius facility storing Starlink equipment used to provide satellite connectivity, including to Ukraine. “Incendiary liquids and Molotov cocktails were used in an attempt to start a fire,” Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said. A security guard spotted the fire and extinguished it. Only a control unit was damaged, and surveillance cameras recorded the incident. Police Commissioner General Arūnas Paulauskas said the investigation was progressing intensively but no suspects had been detained. “We treat this as sabotage,” Sinkevičius said, adding that the company had received a general warning about potential threats on Friday but that authorities had no advance information about the specific incident. The attack follows other incidents targeting Starlink infrastructure. Antennas were set on fire in Bulgaria last week, while a Starlink station was targeted in Poland a month ago. Four suspects in the Polish case were detained in Germany. Lithuanian authorities also suspect that Russian intelligence services may have been behind an earlier incident involving a drone manufacturer. Wreaths were left outside the company’s premises, and a photograph of its chief executive was marked with a black ribbon. Tomas Milašauskas, head of RSI Europe, said cyberattacks and other attempts to harm his company had become routine several years ago. The company receives security advice from Lithuanian authorities and has implemented the recommendations, he said. The National Crisis Management Centre has sent security guidelines to more than 40 companies, including advice on camera placement, perimeter surveillance, access controls and monitoring deliveries, its head, Vilmantas Vitkauskas, said. But not all companies in the defence sector say they have received sufficient guidance. Edvinas Kerza, head of ScaleWolf, called for more events and training focused on physical security, including affordable measures to prevent unauthorised access to company premises. “We need more help from intelligence services and law enforcement structures,” said Vidmantas Janulevičius, president of the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists. Smaller businesses face particular challenges because young companies tend to prioritise product development over cybersecurity and physical protection, Kerza said. He called for free or subsidised assistance to help them improve their defences. Vitkauskas said authorities assess companies according to how likely they are to become potential targets. Following last Sunday’s incident, agencies were instructed to strengthen the protection of strategic facilities, and the list of companies considered at risk is expected to expand. Public Security Service chief Gen. Viktoras Grabauskas said the alert level had been raised, although authorities had detected no specific indications of an imminent threat. The government is also considering asking companies to respond more actively to security recommendations. However, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the state could not provide physical protection to every business because it must also safeguard critical infrastructure. “The state cannot physically contribute everywhere. We have our own critical infrastructure that we must protect. Our contribution is to provide information,” Katelynas said. Vitkauskas likewise warned that businesses should not expect police officers to be stationed outside every company. “Security starts with yourself,” he said. Janulevičius warned that companies could reconsider investments in dual-use technologies if they felt abandoned by the government. “If businesses are left alone and incidents like these continue, no one will be willing to undertake the production of dual-use products,” he said. Kerza urged companies not to be intimidated into silence. “The worst thing we can do is become frightened and keep quiet, even if we are blackmailed or otherwise pressured,” he said. Estonia has determined that a fire at a defence industry company during the summer was a deliberate arson attack commissioned by Russian intelligence services. Lithuanian law enforcement also thwarted an attempted arson attack several years ago. Dozens of incidents and intimidation cases targeting European defence industry companies were recorded in seven countries during the first half of this year.

A Polish man walking along the Baltic Sea coast on the Curonian Spit is suspected of ignoring warning signs and walking into Russian territory, where he was detained, the Lithuanian State Border Guard Service (VSAT) said on Monday. Russian officials confirmed they had detained the man, VSAT said, adding that it was clarifying details to decide whether to launch a pre-trial investigation into illegal crossing of the border. The last time Lithuanian border guards recorded a similar crossing along the Baltic coast from Lithuania into Russia was in 2018. A crossing in the opposite direction, from Russia into Lithuania, was recorded in 2017.

South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace has signed memorandums of understanding with four Lithuanian companies to cooperate on producing and integrating air defence systems, the companies and the Lithuanian Defence and Security Industry Association said on Monday. The memorandums cover four areas of cooperation related to the 40mm wheeled anti-aircraft gun (WAAG) system. Potential vehicle integration will be explored with KMT, turret hull and cable production with Cosmos Construction and T&G Lithuania, and the integration of command and control systems into NATO networks with Nortal. The WAAG is a mobile air defence system designed to counter low-flying targets, including drones and other unmanned aerial vehicles. It combines automated fire control and target-tracking technologies with 40mm ammunition. Robert Park, senior vice president of Hanwha Aerospace, said in a press release the company aims to build “long-term industrial partnerships” with Lithuanian companies, focusing on technology transfer, joint solution development and system maintenance throughout their lifecycle.​ Park added that the company also aims to support Lithuania's ambition to become a regional hub for defence industry manufacturing and maintenance in the Baltic region.

Lithuania's expansion of its air force base in Šiauliai will allow it to accommodate 500 to 750 NATO troops “on a rotational basis”, the Defence Ministry said on Monday. “It is estimated that the economic impact of a 500-troop mission could reach around 65.5 million euros per year,” the ministry said. ​ The ministry estimates that a rotational deployment of 200 NATO troops currently generates an annual economic impact of around 24.6 million euros for Lithuania. ​ The ministry plans to adapt the air base to accommodate fifth-generation fighter jets by the second half of 2028. ​ "Investments in this infrastructure strengthen Lithuania's defence and at the same time create tangible benefits for our economy," Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said. ​ According to the ministry, a single NATO soldier deployed in Lithuania generates spending of around 2,000 to 2,300 euros per month. ​ Accommodation and catering account for the largest share, at more than half of total expenditure, while the remainder goes towards transport, fuel, leisure and other services. A large portion of the funds goes to Lithuanian companies and service providers. ​ The ministry added that hosting allied troops requires accommodation, catering, transport and other services. ​ Preliminary estimates suggest that every five to 10 NATO troops at the base could support one or two additional jobs related to servicing the forces.

Buying smartphones and other smart devices in instalments through mobile operators will become more complicated in Lithuania from November 20, when new European Union rules introduce stricter creditworthiness checks. Customers unable to pay the full price upfront may increasingly turn to device rental or other financing options. Under the changes, people seeking to buy phones or other telecommunications equipment in instalments through mobile operators will undergo financial assessments similar to those required when applying for other types of credit. Currently, about seven in 10 customers buy phones and other smart devices from operators using instalment plans. The new requirements are expected to affect how these purchases are financed, with licensed credit providers becoming involved in the process. “When buying a phone or other telecommunications equipment in instalments through an operator, customers will have to sign a credit agreement, which was not previously required,” said Asta Buitkutė, head of public relations at Tele2 Lithuania. “For this, we will need to work with a licensed partner that already has creditor status.” The new system will require providers to check customers’ existing financial commitments and determine whether they can afford additional payments. Jaunius Špakauskas, head of corporate communications at Bitė Lietuva, said customers could expect the purchasing process to take longer. “In practical terms, it means I will spend a little more time in the store because they will have to check my creditworthiness,” he said. “And when we feel the impact on our wallets, smartphones will become almost a luxury item for some people.” The changes have prompted concerns among consumers who rely on instalment plans to spread the cost of new devices over time. Some residents of Vilnius said they might have to save up and pay the full price upfront rather than go through the more complicated financing process. One woman said instalment plans had been particularly convenient for families buying phones for their children. Parents could purchase newer models for their children and then use the older devices themselves, sometimes financing the purchases through successive instalment agreements. Others questioned whether the changes would make smartphones less affordable, noting that the devices were essential for everyday communication and work. Customers who cannot afford their preferred model upfront may have to choose a cheaper phone or consider renting a device instead. Audrius Stasiulaitis, a spokesman for Telia Lietuva, said rental arrangements could allow customers to pay for a device for a year before switching to a new one. Another option would be a residual-value arrangement, similar to financing used for cars. “This means that you pay a certain amount in instalments for a couple of years and then decide whether to buy the device or leave it,” Stasiulaitis said. Mobile operators acknowledge that the new rules could frustrate some customers but say they will continue offering ways to access smartphones at different price points. Tele2's Buitkutė said phones would remain available at a wide range of prices, from about 200 euros to more than 1,000 euros. “There will always be good offers, and we will continue arranging those offers so that customers are not left without phones,” she said, describing smartphones as an essential means of communication. Špakauskas said smartphones had become indispensable for education, work and staying in touch with family and friends, making the changes particularly significant. Stasiulaitis said customers would still have several ways to obtain devices, even if the arrangements and terminology changed. Operators do not expect the new requirements to increase device prices. The timing is a concern for some consumers who have already planned to buy smartphones for relatives as Christmas gifts. Some residents of Vilnius said they would now try to complete their instalment purchases before the new rules take effect on November 20.

Lithuania should introduce universal military conscription from 2030, opposition Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas said Tuesday as he registered legislative amendments proposing an overhaul of the country’s draft system. Kasčiūnas and a majority of the party’s parliamentary group proposed replacing the annual conscription quota and lottery system with mandatory initial military service for nearly everyone on the annual draft list from January 1, 2030. Under the proposal, young men would be subject to mandatory conscription, while women could serve voluntarily. Exemptions would apply to people excused from service, those granted individual deferments, and certain final-year students and vocational trainees studying for professions in short supply in the armed forces. The option of alternative service would remain. The Defence Ministry’s draft list for this year included 42,556 young people, of whom 5,000 were scheduled to be called up. Kasčiūnas said the proposed changes would require a fundamental review of the conscription system to reflect the changing nature of warfare and the military’s staffing needs. “We propose to conduct a very serious review of the conscription concept, related to the fact that new warfare requires new approaches to drafting,” he said. “Take drone operators, for instance. Perhaps sometimes strong physical training is not required if a clear drone operator training program can be opened.” He added that the armed forces could adopt more flexible approaches to training personnel for different roles and assess whether everyone needed to serve in barracks under the traditional model. Kasčiūnas said the priority should be to establish a new system before determining the additional funding it would require. “We need to start primarily with the system, with the concept of how it should work, and then see how much it might cost,” he said. “I believe we can really move from talk to decisions now.” If the amendments are adopted but preparations fall behind schedule, the transition period could be extended, he said. However, he argued that lawmakers should approve the legislation and set a hard implementation deadline rather than continue debating the issue indefinitely. Kasčiūnas acknowledged that the conservatives failed to introduce universal conscription when they headed the government between 2020–2024. However, they adopted amendments allowing more conscripts to be called up and established a military commandant system, which he described as a transitional model that revealed both strengths and weaknesses in the existing system. “The times and the political situation also require it,” he said, arguing that Lithuania needed to move to a new stage of military preparedness. Lithuania’s military leadership has also outlined plans to expand conscription in the coming years. Chief of Defence Raimundas Vaikšnoras said the armed forces aimed to draft “nearly everyone who is willing and able” by 2030 and increase the number of conscripts to 7,000-8,000 through different forms of military service. Conscripts currently serve for nine months, although an option introduced this year allows mandatory service to be completed in three, six or nine months. School graduates aged 18–22 are also being called up, with their numbers expected to increase annually. Some politicians have described the measure as a step toward universal conscription. In mid-September, the National Universal Defence Coordination Council, chaired by President Gitanas Nausėda, announced that it would propose accelerating the introduction of universal conscription. Nausėda has said the transition to universal conscription is only a matter of time as Lithuania establishes a national division. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has also said the country is moving toward universal conscription but must first make the necessary preparations. Public support for the proposal appears substantial. A survey commissioned by the Universal Defence association in August found that nearly 80% of the population supported introducing universal conscription, with priority given to drafting men.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said restoring full diplomatic representation between Lithuania and China should not be directly linked to changing the name of Taiwan’s representative office in Vilnius, stressing that normalising relations is a pragmatic goal. “Such efforts are fully justified, and I do not think they should be linked very directly to the name of the Taiwanese Representative Office. We simply want neither more nor less – we want to restore relations with China to a normal level,” Nausėda told the radio Žinių Radijas on Tuesday. He said Lithuania could initially accept a lower level of diplomatic representation, with the interests of either country represented by a deputy head of mission rather than an ambassador. “This is a completely pragmatic goal to normalise diplomatic relations. That is something we should do in any case,” the president said. Nausėda said it was too early to determine whether ongoing discussions with Beijing would yield tangible results. Meetings scheduled for November could help clarify the prospects for negotiations, he added. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has previously said he hoped Lithuania and China would achieve a breakthrough by the end of the year. Lithuania’s ruling majority aims to normalise relations with China and restore diplomatic representation to the level maintained by other European Union member states. The goal is also included in the government’s program. Relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in the autumn of 2021 after Vilnius allowed Taiwan to open a representative office under the name “Taiwanese”. Similar offices in other countries generally operate under the name Taipei, which Beijing prefers because it does not imply recognition of Taiwan as a separate state. China responded by unilaterally downgrading its diplomatic representation in Lithuania from ambassador to chargé d’affaires. Lithuania subsequently stopped issuing new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, leaving China without accredited diplomats in the country since May last year.

More than 200 American troops will arrive in Lithuania starting Tuesday as Washington resumes its military troop rotations in the Baltic country, President Gitanas Nausėda said. “About 120 soldiers are here at the moment. From what I have seen, more than 200 additional soldiers will arrive starting today. This means we will probably already have almost a third of the number of troops planned to be deployed by mid-November,” Nausėda told the radio Žinių Radijas on Tuesday. The United States has rotated troops in Lithuania every nine months since 2014. However, this summer, as Washington reviewed its military presence in Europe, the number of American troops remaining in Lithuania fell to just over 100. In September, it was announced that two US Army battalions, comprising more than 1,000 troops in total, would arrive in Lithuania at the end of October. The deployment is expected to maintain a US troop presence in Lithuania at a level similar to that of recent years.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said all efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine on terms acceptable to Kyiv should be welcomed, his office said Tuesday. The statement followed a telephone conversation between Nausėda and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who briefed his Lithuanian counterpart on a recent call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Stubb said Tuesday that he and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre had held an “open and detailed” conversation with Putin. According to the Lithuanian President’s Office, Nausėda welcomes efforts to end the war on terms acceptable to Ukraine, including a meeting between Nordic leaders and US envoys in Oslo on October 20. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also attended the meeting, while Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, joined remotely. Nausėda supports European participation in negotiations on the terms of a potential peace agreement, although the question of who would represent Europe in any talks, and under what mandate, remains open, his office said. Stubb briefed Nausėda on the details of his conversation with Putin. The Finnish president and Norwegian prime minister spoke on behalf of their respective countries and not the EU or NATO.

Lithuania’s refusal to admit Russian and Belarusian athletes is costing the country international sporting events, money and opportunities for its competitors, but officials say they will not compromise on their principles despite growing pressure to reintegrate athletes from the two countries. The latest setback came when the International Modern Pentathlon Union withdrew Kaunas’ right to host a World Cup stage next year because Lithuania will not allow Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in the country. The decision has raised concerns about the future of other international competitions planned in Lithuania. Yet the government and national sports federations say they have no intention of changing their position, arguing that Russia and Belarus should remain isolated from international sport because of their countries’ actions in Ukraine. Lithuania had been building its reputation as an international centre for modern pentathlon. The country hosted the sport’s world championships for the first time about 18 months ago, followed by world junior and youth championships in Kaunas this summer. The city had increasingly been regarded as one of the world’s leading modern pentathlon venues. It was due to host a World Cup stage next year, but that event will no longer take place in Lithuania. Justinas Kinderis, president of the Lithuanian Modern Pentathlon Federation, said the loss was both a financial and a moral blow. “Organising these events requires a long process. You don’t just show up and get one,” Kinderis said, adding that the federation had already secured a number of agreements. Hosting the competition would have allowed 16 Lithuanian athletes to compete at home. Instead, the federation expects to send only a few athletes to the event elsewhere. Kinderis is also concerned about the prospects for other competitions Lithuania hopes to host, including a World Cup stage and junior and youth championships scheduled for 2028. “After this decision, getting another championship to organise is practically impossible,” he said. “The European Confederation [of Modern Pentathlon] president [Tatiana Ardabieva] will certainly not give us anything, because she’s Russia, and nor will the world federation.” The financial consequences could be significant, said Kęstutis Bartuškevičius, an adviser to Lithuania’s education, science and sports minister. International competitions bring prestige to national federations as well as revenue associated with organising major events, he said. Despite those costs, Kinderis said Lithuania’s position would remain unchanged. “We will maintain our current position, and I don’t think anything can change it,” he said. Officials reject pressure to change course Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys has also defended the policy, arguing that allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to return without restrictions weakens the international isolation imposed on their countries after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. “We had agreed that we would isolate those countries,” Budrys said. “When we admit representatives of those countries into sport, we see that this isolation is already crumbling.” He called the decision to withdraw Lithuania’s hosting rights deeply regrettable and questioned the argument that the sporting community should stop waiting for the war to end. The modern pentathlon governing body’s decision follows a broader shift in international sport, including the International Olympic Committee’s decision to permit some Russian athletes to participate in competitions under specified conditions. IOC President Kirsty Coventry has said the organisation would not hold events in Russia or invite Russian government representatives to its programs. She has also argued that athletes should not be held responsible for decisions made by their governments. The IOC has reiterated its condemnation of the war and pledged support for Ukraine. However, whether Russian athletes will be permitted to compete under their national flag and anthem at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics remains undecided. Tautvydas Vencevičius, president of the Lithuanian Sports Journalists Federation, said restrictions on Russian athletes were receiving less attention as more international sports organisations allowed them to return. Lithuania is not the only country opposing that trend. Six countries, including Lithuania, boycotted the opening ceremony of the 2026 Milan-Cortina Winter Paralympics after Russian and Belarusian athletes were permitted to compete with their national flags and anthems following the lifting of earlier suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee. Budrys said Lithuania wanted the European Union to impose sanctions preventing Russian and Belarusian athletes from competing under their national symbols. He also said Lithuania was discussing possible visa restrictions with other EU members for Russian athletes linked to the country’s armed forces. Concerns over political influence and money Lithuanian sports officials argue that decisions by international governing bodies are not always driven solely by sporting considerations. Budrys said Russia was devoting political and financial resources to changing the positions of international federations. “That is blatant corruption in some systems, and we must acknowledge it openly. Political corruption is also a form of corruption,” he said. Eimantas Skrabulis, president of the Lithuanian Athletics Federation, said the leadership of international sports organisations played a major role in determining whether Russian and Belarusian athletes could return. “The worldview and understanding of the head of an international federation matter enormously,” Skrabulis said. He cited Umar Kremlev, the Russian businessman who heads the International Boxing Association and has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s circle. Kremlev has received Russia’s Order of Friendship. Skrabulis said powerful financial inter

Lithuania’s government on Wednesday rejected a proposal by Remigijus Žemaitaitis, leader of the Nemunas Dawn party, to publish the identities of former KGB agents who have not admitted to collaborating with the Soviet security service. The government’s position, drafted by the Defence Ministry, will be submitted to parliament. In June 2025, lawmakers approved Žemaitaitis’ bill at its first reading. It proposed publishing, starting January 1, 2026, information about registered former collaborators of the Soviet security service who had not confessed to their activities. The Defence Ministry said the goal of identifying former collaborators who had not come forward was legitimate, but the proposed measures were inappropriate. Current legislation already provides for the publication of information about such individuals, the ministry said, adding that the bill would require authorities to disclose information they are not legally obligated to collect. A list of former full-time KGB personnel is available on the kgbveikla.lt website. The identities of people who confessed to collaborating with the service remain classified. A law that took effect on February 1, 2000, allowed former KGB employees and other Soviet security service personnel, as well as secret collaborators, to confess and register with a special commission. Their identities were initially kept secret for 15 years, but parliament extended the confidentiality period to 75 years in June 2015. The secrecy requirement has exceptions. If a former KGB collaborator runs for president, parliament or a municipal council, or becomes a minister, judge or prosecutor, their confession ceases to be a state secret and must be made public. Žemaitaitis and fellow lawmakers have also proposed abolishing the 75-year secrecy period for former KGB collaborators who confessed. The government has issued a negative opinion on that bill as well. Žemaitaitis has previously claimed that about 400 former KGB employees and secret collaborators work in Lithuania’s public sector, but he has not disclosed the source of that figure. People also had an opportunity to confess to collaboration with the KGB in 1991-1992 before an ad hoc commission of the Supreme Council. During a subsequent period for voluntary confessions, 1,589 people came forward to the Lustration Commission.

Lithuania is considering purchasing an artificial intelligence system developed by the US technology company Palantir for its armed forces, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Wednesday. The proposed system would help integrate large amounts of data, analyse information and support battlefield decision-making, Kaunas told TV3 News. “The purchase is being considered, and there will be further discussions, because we need a technological solution that would bring together all the data, of which we have a great deal,” the minister said. “By using artificial intelligence, it would be possible to analyse data and manage certain aspects of the battlefield. Lithuania, like other NATO countries, needs this kind of software,” he added. According to TV3 News, the first seven years of using the system would cost nearly 200 million euros, with the final price potentially even higher. Kaunas said acquiring the system could require adjustments to the Defence Ministry’s planned spending. “Some reallocation of funds may be necessary because, again, we do not yet know the final price,” he said.

Life in Lithuania’s southwestern town of Vištytis remains undisturbed. Local residents are not troubled either by the threat posed by Russia or by the Lithuanian troops deployed along the border with the Kaliningrad region, who are helping border guards patrol the area. The military has been assisting the border guards since early October. Around 100 troops are expected to continue doing so until mid-November. Government officials describe the decision as a precautionary measure in response to the possibility of a new wave of mobilisation in Russia. However, the authorities stress that the threat level along the border has not increased. “[Potential deserters] will try to cross the state border illegally, both on land and on water. That is why we have stepped up surveillance on land, on water and in the air. As we say here, along the green border, the blue border and in the air,” Rimantas Kundreckis, commander of the Vištytis border guard post, told BNS. The deployment of troops is estimated to have almost doubled the frequency of patrols along the border with the Kaliningrad region. The Lithuanian-Russian state border, including the boundary of territorial waters, stretches for almost 300km. It runs through plains, forests and bodies of water. “There’s nothing particularly scary about it, despite what I read in so many places these days,” Sandra told BNS as she hurried home carrying an armful of groceries. She is one of just a few hundred residents of Vištytis, in the Vilkaviškis district. Most locals spend the gloomier days of autumn indoors, leaving the town’s central square looking almost deserted, with only the occasional person hurrying toward a nearby shop. “Nothing has really changed here. You can just see that there are more patrols, but nothing else is happening. The only difference is that the military has arrived, and we see the occasional military vehicle,” the 31-year-old woman said. She said she was not afraid of the worsening security situation in the region. Nor was her daily life being disrupted by the soldiers recently seen alongside the border guards. “Life is normal. Everything is just as it was before. There’s no special preparation going on, with people stocking up on supplies or preparing shelters. We’re just living our lives, like everyone else in Lithuania,” Sandra said. In Vištytis, a lake separates Lithuania from the Kaliningrad region. Bright red posts protruding from the water mark the point up to which people who have provided their details to border guards are permitted to sail. Another line of yellow posts, 50 metres beyond them, marks the end of Lithuanian territory. From the pier where border guard patrol boats moor, you can see a Russian flag flying high just a few hundred metres away. The lake is monitored by cameras and patrolled by a border guard boat. According to Kundreckis, enhanced surveillance of the lake has helped reduce the number of accidental border crossings. Previously, people who went out on the water to fish or relax sometimes failed to notice that they were approaching Russian territory. Border guards can now warn them of a potential violation in advance, either by calling them using the contact details they have provided or by approaching them in an official patrol boat. Accompanying officers on a patrol of Lake Vištytis offers a practical demonstration of how border controls work. When the patrol boat spots another boat, it slows down. Officers observe the person on board and assess the distance from the marked boundary before continuing on their way without making contact. Such checks are part of the officers’ daily duties. The most recent border violation recorded by the Vištytis post occurred at the beginning of the year, when two Russian citizens entered Lithuania by walking across the frozen lake. Around 10 similar violations are typically recorded each year. Among those contributing to the border protection mission are troops from the Second Territorial Unit of the Darius and Girėnas National Defence Volunteer Forces (KASP). Company commander Leonas Ruzgas sees the deployment as an opportunity not only to contribute to the country’s security but also to help soldiers develop their skills. He was among the first to arrive at the border. “Border guards have quite a few technological innovations and systems that we do not use, [...] because our work does not require them. So it is good to see how much our border protection has improved, share experience and learn from them,” Ruzgas said. The commander of the Vištytis border guard post agreed. He said the deployment offered opportunities for professional development not only for officers and soldiers serving on the ground, but also for their commanders. “The practical experience is truly invaluable. You cannot get it anywhere else, really,” Kundreckis said. “If Day X [war] were to come and the military had to take up a position here, both ordinary soldiers and commanders would already be familiar with the specifics of the area.” Troops are rotated along the border approximately every four to five days. Different soldiers are usually sent each time, although those who wish to return can do so. According to Ruzgas, incoming troops adapt to the duty schedules of State Border Guard Service (VSAT) officers, and their powers are largely the same. Kundreckis said the soldiers assisting the border guards had also brought equipment that was “being successfully used to monitor both land areas and airspace”. The post commander said he had not noticed any signs of a potential threat, describing activity on the other side of the border as routine daily operations. “Whether it is a coincidence or not, there has been an increase in military fighter jet flights near the state border. Explosions could be heard somewhere at the training ground towards Kudirkos Naumiestis, and their helicopters have also been flying near the state border more frequently,” the commander said. Lithuania plans to introduce universal military conscription in 2032, requiring a larger number of young people to serve in the armed forces amid security concerns, President Gitanas Nausėda said Thursday. The State Defence Council, which comprises the country’s political and military leadership, agreed on the timeline at a meeting, Nausėda told reporters afterward. Women would continue to be able to perform military service on a voluntary basis, he said. Lithuania currently drafts more than 5,000 young people into the armed forces each year. Under universal conscription, the annual number would rise to about 7,500, accounting for demographic trends and the fact that some young people are deemed medically unfit for service, the president said. Nausėda said the 2032 target would give the country time to invest in adequate accommodation for the larger number of conscripts and train enough instructors. The authorities also need to balance conscript training with refresher training for reserve personnel to ensure both are carried out effectively, he said. “I think implementing conscription from 2032 is optimal,” Nausėda said. According to Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, the government wanted a quicker transition to universal conscription, but were convinced by the military to push back the date to 2032. “You could say there is political will, but at the same time, there is the question of the military’s readiness. The military has clearly stated that they would be ready by 2032,” Sinkevičius told reporters after Thursday’s State Defence Council meeting. The date for introducing universal conscription was discussed “at length and in detail, with lively debates” at the council, the PM said. “Everyone agreed that this isn’t a race, nor is it a matter of setting a specific date in stone – that we must move toward universal conscription and that it is inevitable, but needs to be done when you’re prepared,” he said. The preparations would include training some 300 instructors and building suitable facilities to house the young draftees, he added. The council also agreed to expand the range of service options available to conscripts. These could include training as drone operators or assisting the State Border Guard Service and firefighting and rescue services, the president said. After trying to switch to fully professional armed forces, Lithuania restored partial conscription in 2015, citing increased security threats following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014.

The European Commission has responded to a request by Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia for 500 million euros to develop anti-drone defences, but has offered no new funding on the scale sought by the three Baltic states. Defence ministers from the three countries sent a letter to the European Commission in late September requesting urgent financial support to strengthen defences against drones. Several stray drones have entered the Baltic airspaces this year amid air attacks between Ukraine and Russia. Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, Estonian Defence Minister Martin Herem and Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis sought the funding to develop an anti-drone system that could also serve as a model for other European Union countries. The letter was classified, but Kaunas told LRT that the Baltic states wanted to combine drone detection, artificial intelligence and interception technology into an integrated air defence system. “Air defence and anti-drone solutions are important not only for our region but for all of Europe. Lithuania has taken the lead in developing an anti-drone air defence system,” Kaunas said. The Baltic states had hoped the European Commission would approve additional funding for regional anti-drone defences before the end of this year. The commission previously told LRT.lt that it was carefully assessing the request and took member states’ concerns very seriously. However, Andrius Kubilius, the European commissioner for defence and space, told LRT on Wednesday that the commission had sent its response but could not offer the additional funding the Baltic states had sought. “One possibility now is to make use of additional funding under the SAFE instrument. We will announce a new call in the near future, because 21 billion euros remained after the first call,” Kubilius said. He added that there were few other substantial funding opportunities available through EU budget programs because the current budget period was nearing its end. Funding for anti-drone measures may also be available through the Integrated Border Management Fund, LRT understands, although the sums involved would be far below the 500 million euros requested by the Baltic states. The Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, instrument, launched last year, provides 150 billion euros in favourable loans for defence procurement across the EU. The scheme offers loans with repayment periods of up to 45 years and advance payments of up to 15%. The loans are financed through EU-level borrowing, benefiting from the bloc’s AAA credit rating. Lithuania has been allocated access to up to 6.375 billion euros in SAFE loans. The government plans to use the funds to establish a land forces division, develop the Baltic Defence Line, strengthen air defence, purchase ammunition and military equipment, and finance other military modernisation projects. In October, Lithuania’s Finance Ministry submitted its first request to the European Commission for a 1.06-billion-euro loan under the scheme. If approved, the request would bring Lithuania’s total SAFE funding, including a 800-million-euro advance received in June, to 1.86 billion euros, about 29% of the country’s total allocation.

The administration of US President Donald Trump is pressing Lithuania to allow Belarusian potash fertiliser exports through the port of Klaipeda despite European Union sanctions, Politico reported , citing European officials. US special envoy to Belarus John Coale has in recent weeks asked Lithuanian diplomats about ways to ease restrictions on the shipment of goods from Belarus, according to four European officials familiar with the discussions. The restrictions are part of EU sanctions against the government of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko. EU ports are prohibited from handling Belarusian goods, and the sanctions must be renewed annually. Trump said last month that he was working on a “big deal” with Minsk to buy potash fertiliser at prices significantly lower than those currently paid by farmers to Canadian suppliers. Such an arrangement would require a route through Klaipėda, Lithuania’s main Baltic Sea port, or other regional ports. “There has been intensified outreach to the Lithuanians by Donald Trump’s team in the last weeks,” a source familiar with the discussions told Politico. The US State Department did not respond to a request for comment. The administration’s interest in Belarusian potash, which accounts for about 20% of the global market, has grown following the collapse of US-Canadian trade negotiations in August and subsequent tariff increases, Politico reported. The push is part of Trump’s broader efforts to ease sanctions on Russia and its allies in hopes of persuading Moscow to end its war against Ukraine. However, the approach has faced strong opposition in Europe. “They are pressing politely, but we say very clearly ‘fuck no’,” one Eastern European official told Politico. Two Eastern European officials said Coale had been lobbying Lithuanian authorities at various levels for more than a year. Washington has also explored the possibility of shipping Belarusian potash through Latvia’s Riga port, which could offer a simpler route than transportation through Russia. Lithuania has repeatedly rejected the possibility of resuming transit. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys has said EU sanctions prohibit not only imports of Belarusian potash but also its transit through EU territory, regardless of the ownership of the fertiliser or the country in which the exporting company is registered. The Lithuanian president’s national security adviser Deividas Matulionis has also warned that violating the sanctions would carry legal, financial and moral consequences. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said in September that Lithuania had received no US request to allow Belarusian fertiliser transit. Former Prime Minister and opposition politician Ingrida Šimonytė has likewise argued that such shipments would be incompatible with EU sanctions and pose national security risks.

Pentagon officials have urged several NATO allies in recent weeks to tone down their public rhetoric about the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials, including in the Baltics, have undermined the continent’s security, Reuters reported Friday. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are among the countries that received the appeals for greater restraint in public statements, according to four sources who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity. One source said US officials had taken issue with statements by European leaders suggesting that Russia had been backed into a corner and was resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine made little progress. One of the US officials who conveyed the message was Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s top policy official, who is playing a key role in the ongoing review of the US military presence in Europe, the sources said. Reuters could not establish which other officials had been involved in delivering the appeals. One source told Reuters that Colby recently told an official from one of the Baltic states that Russia should not be provoked. As an example of unhelpful rhetoric, Colby reportedly cited public statements by Europeans comparing Russia to a cornered rat. Reuters said it was unclear which specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal described Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “rat in a corner” in late September, arguing that as Russia became increasingly bogged down in the war in Ukraine, its leader was resorting to sabotage across Europe. A source familiar with another recent meeting said the Pentagon had urged an Estonian delegation to exercise restraint in public statements. The source did not indicate that US officials had expressed dissatisfaction with any particular remark. “We are helping you. The Americans are there. Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise,” one European official described the message conveyed by the Pentagon during recent private discussions. The defence ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. NATO declined to comment. “Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations,” a Pentagon official said when asked about the report. The US appeals come as President Donald Trump’s administration has renewed efforts to end Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine through negotiations. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said he had no information about Pentagon officials asking Lithuanian leaders to tone down their rhetoric on Russia. “What we speak is always based on facts. If a Russian drone flew in, we say that a Russian drone flew in. If a Ukrainian drone flew in, we say that it was a Ukrainian drone, in the context of the war caused by Russia,” Kaunas said on Friday. “We do not try or wish to provoke in any other way. [...] We state the facts and will continue to do so,” he added. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda’s office said neither he nor his aides received any requests from allies regarding statements about Russia. “The President’s Office has no comment on this publication. The president and his advisers have received no calls or requests from allies to soften their rhetoric regarding Russia,” it said on Friday.

Before the Second World War, there were between 200 and 240 Jewish cemeteries in Lithuania. Most of them today stand neglected. The non-profit organisation MACEVA, the Litvak Cemetery Catalogue, has been working in Lithuania since 2011 to preserve this heritage. “Over the past 15 years, more than 70 cemeteries have been documented. It may be closer to 80 if we include this year’s work. Quite a few cemeteries have been destroyed, so there is nothing left to document. In reality, there are probably around 60 to 70 cemeteries still waiting to be documented,” says Milda Jakulytė, director of MACEVA. Working alongside volunteers, MACEVA carefully catalogues the cemeteries. It translates Hebrew epitaphs into English and makes all the information it collects available in a public online database. This year, the organisation has carried out work at cemeteries in Virbalis, Kelmė, Linkuva and Merkinė. For the second consecutive year, soldiers from Germany’s 45th Armoured Brigade, stationed in Lithuania, have helped document Jewish heritage at the cemetery in Merkinė. “Our task is to clean the gravestones, put them back upright and make the inscriptions legible. Then we document and photograph them so that these inscriptions can later help people find their relatives,” says a German captain named Lois. “I think we are doing very important work. Germany feels a sense of responsibility because there is currently no Jewish community here that can look after these and other graves. It is very important that we, the Germans, are taking care of the community’s cemeteries now,” he added. For the organisation, it is important not only to document the cemeteries and research the people buried in Jewish graveyards across Lithuania, but also to help relatives scattered around the world find the graves of their family members and ancestors. The poetic epitaphs carved into gravestones not only highlight the deceased’s good qualities but also reveal the values cherished by individual Jewish communities. “In some communities, for example, a woman’s modesty was particularly important, while in others, helping one’s neighbour was highly valued. Men’s epitaphs almost always emphasise their dedication to studying the Torah. Their professions are mentioned more often than women’s – in women’s epitaphs, a profession is mentioned only in one particular case, when the woman was a midwife,” Jakulytė says. “We recently received an [...] inscription describing a woman in an unusual way, saying that she was beautiful. We will need to investigate a little further to find out who this beauty was, but it is certainly unusual and very interesting,” she adds. Very little information, if any, has survived about the people buried in Jewish cemeteries. In its research, the organisation always seeks to involve local residents and help them better understand the history of their towns and villages. “We want this heritage to be seen not as something foreign, but as part of the community. We want people to be able to come here, point things out, take pride in them and say: ‘Look, this is where Merkinė’s very own Čiurlionis is buried, or this is where the beauty of Merkinė lies.’ “We want it to become part of the town’s history, because these cemeteries also tell the story of the town itself. We would like local communities to embrace them as part of their own heritage, to get involved, engage with it and make use of the material we collect,” Jakulytė says. The organisation plans to continue its work until all surviving Jewish cemeteries in Lithuania have been documented.

Lithuania is seeking consular access to two citizens detained in Iran, but providing assistance is proving particularly difficult. The case has drawn attention to the Foreign Ministry’s travel warnings and the challenges diplomats face when Lithuanian citizens encounter trouble in countries where Lithuania has no diplomatic representation. The Foreign Ministry confirmed that the two women, whom Vilnius police had been searching for since October 11, were detained in Iran in mid-October. The ministry is trying to arrange consular assistance but has said the process is complicated. Iran is marked in black on the ministry’s travel advisory map, meaning Lithuanian citizens are urged to leave the country immediately. The Foreign Ministry divides countries into five categories, marked in green, yellow, orange, red and black, depending on the level of risk and the recommended precautions. The Foreign Ministry publishes its full travel advisory map on its website , where travellers can check recommendations for individual destinations before departure. Lithuania seeks help from other countries Remigijus Motuzas, a diplomat who chairs the Lithuanian parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, told LRT.lt that assisting citizens detained abroad can be difficult, particularly when Lithuania lacks diplomatic representation in the country concerned. He said consular assistance has two main priorities: establishing contact with the local authorities to determine why a citizen has been detained, and reaching the detainee to assess their situation and ensure their rights are respected. “The other, even more important, task is to contact the detained citizen to establish the conditions in which they are being held, whether their rights have been violated under international conventions, whether they are receiving medical care if they have health conditions, and whether they are being tortured, among other things,” Motuzas said. Assistance can also include support for the detainees’ relatives and help obtaining legal representation, he added. The detention of the two Lithuanian women has prompted questions about their decision to travel to Iran despite the government’s strong warning against visiting the country. Motuzas said, however, that the state remains responsible for helping citizens who find themselves in danger abroad, regardless of whether they followed official travel advice. “We say that people are responsible for their own decisions when travel is not recommended. But, on the other hand, it is a diplomat’s duty not to abandon someone in distress,” he said. “Assistance is provided regardless of the circumstances in which a person arrived.” EU partners can help when Lithuania has no embassy When a Lithuanian citizen is detained in a country where Lithuania has no diplomatic mission, the government seeks assistance from other European Union member states that may be able to intervene. “That is also the case with Iran at the moment,” Motuzas said. Lithuanian authorities are seeking to arrange a consular visit to the two detained women to establish their health and detention conditions and determine whether they have access to legal assistance and other necessary services.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda on Tuesday criticised the term “hybrid threats”, saying it has become a “convenient euphemism”. Calling Russian sabotage and other operations as "hybrid threats" became “a way to avoid saying plainly what we are experiencing”, he said in a statement released by the president’s office, adding that “some of the recent attacks in essence are kinetic attacks”. The statement was released as Nausėda opened the Berlin Security Conference, which Germany is co-hosting with Lithuania. The president stressed that a strong transatlantic bond remained the foundation of collective security, and that greater European responsibility for its own defence should strengthen NATO. In his opening address, the president also highlighted the strategic partnership between Lithuania and Germany. He emphasised the significance of Germany’s decision to deploy its 45th Armoured Brigade in Lithuania and the growing defence industry co-operation between the two countries. According to the president, Germany has become Lithuania’s most important partner in this field. A Rheinmetall artillery ammunition factory is already under construction in Lithuania, while a joint project with KNDS to assemble, maintain and repair Leopard tanks has also been launched. Speaking about Lithuania’s upcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027, Nausėda said that security and defence, internal security, EU enlargement and competitiveness would be among the country’s main priorities. According to the presidential office, Lithuania will seek to ensure long-term, sustainable support for Ukraine’s security and defence, strengthen Europe’s defence readiness, including through the Eastern Flank Watch initiative, and improve military mobility.

Lithuania continues to support extending sanctions on Belarusian fertilisers, despite reported US pressure to reopen a transit route for the commodity, a senior presidential aide said on Tuesday, adding that the Politico report was several months old. ​"I am surprised by Politico's information, which probably dates back several months. Contacts took place several months ago, and the issue was discussed, but nothing happened afterwards," Deividas Matulionis, the president's chief national security aide, told Žinių Radijas. ​ Citing four European officials, Politico reported last week that US special envoy for Belarus John Coale had approached Lithuanian diplomats to discuss the possibility of easing restrictions on the transit of goods from Belarus. ​ The EU currently imposes sanctions on Belarusian fertilisers, including restrictions on their transit through the port of Klaipėda, which was halted in early 2022. ​ The extension of the sanctions is due to be considered at the end of February. Matulionis said Lithuania currently favoured extending the restrictions, although he declined to say what position Vilnius would take in February. ​ The adviser said a review of the sanctions could be considered if Belarus changed its behaviour, particularly its support for Russia's war against Ukraine, but added that Lithuania did not expect such a shift. ​ US President Donald Trump has previously said he was seeking a deal with Minsk to purchase potash fertilisers at lower prices. Such an arrangement would require securing their transportation through Klaipėda or other regional ports. ​ Eastern European officials cited by Politico said Coale had been trying for more than a year to establish a route for Belarusian fertilisers to reach global markets through Klaipėda and other Baltic ports, including Riga. ​ One European official confirmed that the US envoy had also approached Latvian officials on the issue.

Born during the presidency of Kazys Grinius, raised under Antanas Smetona, forced to flee the advancing Soviet forces under Josef Stalin and building a career under successive US presidents, Valdas Adamkus became an American citizen but never abandoned Lithuania. After returning to his homeland, he became one of the key figures in steering the country toward the West, spending a decade as president and helping raise Lithuania’s international standing and political culture. On November 3, Adamkus celebrates his 100th birthday, marking a century of a life shaped by war, exile, environmental activism and an enduring commitment to Lithuania. An impressive career in the United States Adamkus was born in Kaunas on November 3, 1926, into a family of civil servants. His father, Ignas Adamkavičius, was a volunteer in Lithuania’s independence wars and one of the first heads of the country’s aviation school. His mother worked at the Ministry of Transport. Adamkus attended Kaunas’ Aušra Gymnasium, but the outbreak of World War Two changed the course of his life. He became involved in resistance activities and fled west in 1944 as Soviet forces advanced. He initially settled in Germany, where he studied at the University of Munich, before emigrating to the United States in 1949. His first job in America was at an automobile factory. He later enrolled at the Illinois Institute of Technology, while gradually building a career in environmental protection. His professional rise began in the 1960s, and in 1971 he joined the newly established US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). He quickly advanced through the federal agency’s ranks while remaining actively involved in the Lithuanian-American community and committed to the idea of an independent Lithuania. In 1976, he opened the fifth Lithuanian Song and Dance Festival in Chicago, an event that reflected his continued involvement in preserving Lithuanian culture among the diaspora. The EPA also provided an opportunity for him to maintain contact with his homeland. As an environmental specialist, Adamkus visited the Soviet Union and occupied Lithuania almost every year. In 1981, he became administrator of the EPA’s Region 5, overseeing its work in the Midwestern United States. It was in this capacity that journalist Stasys Arnašius interviewed him in Chicago in 1989. By then, speculation was already growing that Adamkus might one day enter Lithuanian politics. “Optimistically, we can look at the recent fact that television viewers on one program suggested he become president of Lithuania. It is only a pity that Valdas Adamkus is not yet a Lithuanian citizen. But who knows?” Arnašius said in his 1989 report from the United States. Adamkus’ ties with Lithuania had never weakened. He was active in the Lithuanian diaspora and became one of the leaders of Santara-Šviesa, a liberal Lithuanian intellectual movement that sought to preserve independent thought and cultural life outside Soviet-controlled Lithuania. “Santara was born with the main goal of preserving what could not be achieved in Lithuania at the time through a free creative process. In this way, a spiritual connection with Lithuania was maintained,” Adamkus said in a 1996 television interview. Returning home, but not without disappointment As Lithuania moved toward independence, Adamkus’ environmental expertise became increasingly valuable. Environmental protection was a prominent issue during the national revival, with growing public concern about industrial pollution, the condition of the Baltic Sea and damage to natural landmarks. His frequent visits and professional experience attracted considerable media attention. On March 20, 1989, a major industrial accident occurred in Jonava, an incident that became known as the “chemical Chernobyl”. Adamkus, who happened to be visiting Lithuania, went to the site as an environmental expert. “The only thing that is reassuring is that no more lives were lost and tragic consequences were avoided. It is almost incredible that a chemical Chernobyl did not happen. [...] A factory like this should never have been built in a place like this,” he said, commenting on the accident at the Azotas chemical plant. As Lithuania prepared for its first presidential election following the restoration of independence, Adamkus became involved in the political process. In late 1992, he was appointed campaign manager for Stasys Lozoraitis, a diplomat and candidate backed by many Lithuanians abroad who challenged the election favourite, Algirdas Mykolas Brazauskas. The campaign ended in disappointment. In a television interview the following year, Adamkus spoke bitterly about the result, describing it as a defeat for democracy. “I knew the results when I entered the election campaign. It would have taken a political miracle for the outcome to be different. Mr Lozoraitis and I wanted to give people an opportunity to get acquainted with something else, and that something else was the word ‘democracy’,” he said. Meanwhile, his increasingly frequent trips to Lithuania fuelled speculation about his own political ambitions. Although he publicly emphasised environmental issues as the main purpose of his visits, his name was increasingly mentioned in political circles. Adamkus was also outspoken about the country’s difficult economic situation. “I see the economic situation as very difficult, and I do not see a particularly bright future. Whenever I meet people, I hear that the situation is hard,” he said. In a 1993 interview with journalist Laima Pangonytė in Chicago, he also criticised Lithuania’s citizenship policy, which had left many members of the Lithuanian diaspora without Lithuanian citizenship. “Those Lithuanians abroad did not accept that decision, are deeply concerned about it and will never recognise it. By stripping the entire diaspora of citizenship, the decision was made without properly considering the issue. There was only one argument: that many foreigners wanted t

For a long time, the prevailing view in Lithuania was that a portion of the electorate harboured nostalgia for the Soviet era, since supporters of the Homeland Union–Lithuanian Christian Democrats viewed the Soviet occupation of the past unequivocally negatively, while supporters of the Lithuanian left were less critical, as they saw positive aspects in that period as well; consequently, these people were considered, if not pro-Russian, then at least not sufficiently critical of Moscow. However, Ainė Ramonaitė, a professor at the Institute of International Relations and Political Science at Vilnius University, argues that the less critical attitude of some Lithuanian residents toward the Soviet past may be linked not so much to sympathy for the Soviet system as to nostalgia for the industrial past. Such trends are also observed in some other Western societies, where social resentment and nostalgia are evident in deindustrialized regions. Politically, this manifests itself in voting for more radical parties, which channel the anger of disaffected segments of society, while offering no solutions. In the US and Western Europe, deindustrialization is invoked when explaining why a portion of the population voted for Donald Trump, Brexit, or AfD. According to the researcher, this could also apply to Lithuania and be part of the explanation why some voters are drawn to political parties that position themselves in stark opposition to the mainstream. As part of her research, Ramonaitė has conducted in-depth interviews in which some people, without even being asked, speak of the hardship caused by the economic upheaval of the 1990s, of shattered lives, factories, and entire social structures. They also recall the late Soviet period as a time of industrial expansion, construction of cities and factories. This corresponds quite closely to the collective memory of people in deindustrialized areas in the US and Western Europe. Although in the West this process did not entail an economic collapse like in post-socialist Eastern Europe, people who lived through it still remember it with sadness and a sense of loss. “Now many are analysing why, for example, Donald Trump wins elections and why radical right-wing parties are gaining popularity. In the West, people have begun to talk about the phenomenon of nostalgia, even though there was no communism in the West. When you start reading scholarly works, especially in anthropology, that recount the experiences of people who lived in industrial districts, you see that they are incredibly similar to our own. “We’ve conducted a great many interviews with people who, without even being asked, share their stories and express sadness about the period after 1990. That period isn’t precisely defined, but it encompasses the economic transition. When reading the accounts of Westerners, you see how even the phrases they use echo one another. And then you think, how can this be? That’s when I began to realize that perhaps we had misinterpreted Soviet nostalgia,” Ramonaitė explains in an interview with the LRT.lt. The researcher relies primarily on biographical interviews conducted in 2021 with people over the age of 50 in the northern town of Panevėžys and its surrounding areas. Panevėžys was chosen as a place that experienced the post-Soviet transformation firsthand and most dramatically. During the Soviet era, it was home to large factories such as Ekranas, Aurida, and Lietkabelis, as well as a precision machinery plant, a glass factory, and similar industrial facilities; after 1990, the industry contracted dramatically. However, very similar stories exist in other Lithuanian cities, towns and even in rural areas, Ramonaitė notes. “In fact, no one talks about politics. It’s not that people feel nostalgia for the politics of the time. Curiously, those who feel a sense of loss over what happened after 1990 don’t talk about anything related to the political regime. It’s all about social and economic issues,” she explains. That some people long for the era of modern prosperity rather than the Soviet regime is attested to by the fact that, for many, the golden age coincided with the late 1980s and the hight of Lithuania’s independence movement. For them, resistance to the Soviet military aggression on January 13, 1991, is a sacred day. The narratives begin to diverge only after around 1992. “When we were conducting research on the era of transformation, it turned out, even unintentionally, that people were also talking about the Sąjūdis [independence movement] era. Our questions focused on the period after 1990, but people naturally felt that when we spoke of the transition, it began with the Sąjūdis era. Of course, we didn’t stop them. “My former doctoral student, now Dr Valda Budreckaitė, defended her dissertation based on that study, and she notes that people’s accounts of the 1988–1991 period are consistent. This was true of nearly all the groups we interviewed. Everyone talks about an ‘uplift’, that’s the word people use. And this ‘rallying’ is definitely associated with positive emotions,” says Ramonaitė. “Many people spoke about January 13. It was important for them to share whether they were in Vilnius or in another town. They all describe it the same way: We went, we watched, we worried, we cried, we drove to Vilnius. “In short, everyone describes that era in the same way, but after around 1992, the stories start to diverge. Some feel that things have been moving in the right direction –albeit slowly and with difficulty – while others compare it with experience after the war. Some older people even remembered the postwar period, and they drew comparison: At first, they herded us into collective farms, took away our land, everything was terrible, but then we managed to get by, started living normally, and then everything collapsed again. To them, these two transitions are similar.” People’s experiences largely fall into two big groups: for one, the Soviet time was

Lithuania has expelled three Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out assignments for “hostile” foreign intelligence services in exchange for money, the State Security Department (VSD) said Wednesday. The individuals had previously been declared threats to national security, and their temporary residence permits in Lithuania were revoked, the intelligence agency said. “The individuals posing a threat to national security have been expelled from Lithuania and banned from returning for five years,” the VSD said in a statement. According to the agency, the three Ukrainians carried out a wide range of tasks for foreign intelligence services in return for payment. The assignments were communicated through Telegram and other messaging platforms. The VSD warned that foreign intelligence services frequently use messaging apps and social media to recruit people in other countries. “This method is particularly effective because it is easy to implement, reaches a wide pool of potential agents and requires few resources,” the agency said. Intelligence officers using this recruitment method shift all risks and potential consequences of the assigned activities onto the people carrying them out, without taking responsibility for their safety, the VSD added.

Lithuania is considering establishing a state-owned drone holding company to speed up military procurement and support the development of its domestic drone industry, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has said. “I understand our procurement procedures and that we must follow them, but I would like one Lithuanian drone manufacturer to develop FPV drones, another to focus on interceptors, a third on long- or medium-range drones, and a fourth on reconnaissance drones, and so on,” Kaunas said in an interview with BNS. “The idea is to create a state-owned drone holding company,” he added. Under the proposal, the state would act as the holding company’s financial backer, while scientists and universities would contribute to technological innovation, Kaunas said. The model would allow the government to direct funding toward specific areas of development. The minister said he had recently discussed the idea with the Special Investigation Service, the Public Procurement Office and the Defence Materiel Agency. The prime minister also supports the proposal. Kaunas did not give a timeline for establishing the company, saying he planned to present the idea to representatives of the drone industry in the near future. “This is also part of their commitment. And if we have approval on all fronts, then it is a question for the lawyers of how quickly we can form everything,” he said. Establishing a defence industry holding company was among the goals of former Prime Minister Inga Ruginienė’s government. However, after she was replaced by Mindaugas Sinkevičius, the objective was dropped from the government’s programme and replaced with provisions for closer cooperation between the state and industry. Industry seeks orders, not new structures Drone manufacturers have reacted cautiously to the proposal, saying the state’s demand for their products is a more pressing concern. Industry representatives have also criticised national defence institutions for failing to buy equipment from capable Lithuanian manufacturers. Vincas Jurgutis, an adviser to the Defence and Security Industry Association, said the state could make participation in the holding company conditional on procurement contracts. However, he noted that industry representatives had yet to receive a concrete proposal. Tomas Milašauskas, CEO of drone manufacturer RSI Europe, said companies would concentrate on producing a particular type of drone if the Lithuanian government placed orders for it, making a holding company unnecessary. “The Ministry of Defence directly makes decisions on what companies should do – if it wants a manufacturer to focus on a certain area, it must buy drones from that producer, creating concentration in that specific field,” Milašauskas said. Vytenis Buzas, head of unmanned aerial vehicle developer Unmanned Defense Systems, said he had heard numerous “small initiatives and plans” similar to the proposed holding company, but they had yet to result in actual orders for Lithuanian drone makers. Milašauskas argued that the government’s role should be to organise public procurement rather than establish corporate management structures. “The state is a much less efficient decision-maker than an open market. The state’s task is to carry out defence procurement, not to create holdings and structures of uncertain purpose,” he said. He also said funding for Lithuania’s defence industry was sufficient, with capital available from venture funds operating in the country and across the Baltic region. Jurgutis said the domestic military industry wanted the Defence Ministry to set clearer priorities and provide a longer-term plan, alongside increased funding for the procurement of drones and related systems, including equipment to support Ukraine. Buzas said drone manufacturers had previously discussed the military’s requirements with the relevant authorities, invested in production and spent four to five years developing products for the Lithuanian Armed Forces. However, procurement had moved too slowly. “The buying process keeps failing to materialise, postponed year after year,” he said. “Products have been tested with the military, and everyone is satisfied. Various types of aircraft and drones have been created and combat-tested in Ukraine, where they perform well. Next, actual purchases must happen.” Jurgutis said revenue from government contracts would allow companies to reinvest in expanding their businesses and developing new products.

The Lithuanian city of Šiauliai has lost around 6,000 registered residents in six months after authorities began deregistering thousands of foreigners who had declared their place of residence at a university dormitory, exposing a demographic decline that had previously been obscured by inflated population figures. The case has revealed how the registration of third-country nationals had made the country’s fourth-largest city – with a population of a little over 111,000, according to official data from last July – appear to be growing despite a falling birth rate and a natural population decrease. Around 17,000 people had declared the dormitory, which belongs to Vilnius University’s Šiauliai Academy, as their place of residence last spring. A businessman who had rented the premises from the university had allowed them to register at the address. After learning about the arrangement, university management demanded that people who did not actually live there be deregistered. “We register only students who live here and study at Vilnius University’s Šiauliai Academy. That is our policy, and the university has asked for everyone else to be deregistered,” said Renata Bilbokaitė, head of the academy. Over the past six months, the residence declarations of more than 6,000 people who did not live in the dormitory have been cancelled. Another 2,000 or so are expected to be deregistered in the coming months. The process is taking time because of limited administrative capacity, said Diana Grigienė, head of the Šiauliai municipal administration’s customer service department. “The company submits personal data on the basis of which we deregister people. The company also confirms that the individuals do not live at this address. Since only two employees in our department handle residence declarations, we make decisions concerning approximately 100 residents a day,” she said. The mass registration of foreigners had distorted the city’s demographic statistics, making it appear that its population was increasing when the actual trend was negative.
