During the first half of this year, Šiauliai recorded just 321 births, while nearly 700 people died. Zakiras Medžidovas, a member of the Šiauliai City Council, said the inflated figures had also prevented the municipality from properly addressing the city’s demographic challenges. “Residents were repeatedly told that the city was growing, but it turns out this was fictitious accounting designed to maintain some kind of illusion. The city is not growing. It is shrinking or maintaining roughly the same population level,” he said. “This means we need a demographic policy, but we have not taken action because we had incorrect data. People say, ‘Why do we need one if the city is growing?’” According to Lithuania’s official statistics portal, Šiauliai had approximately 111,000 residents in July, including third-country nationals. That figure is expected to fall significantly by the end of the year as thousands of foreigners are removed from the population register. City authorities say the decline will not threaten Šiauliai’s status as one of Lithuania’s major cities. They also stress that foreign residents make a positive economic contribution, even if their residence registration is fictitious. “If they are registered in Šiauliai and their workplace is also registered here, they pay personal income tax, from which we subsequently finance public services, social security, health care, education, culture and sports,” said Deputy Mayor Justinas Švėgžda. He acknowledged that the city’s declining birth rate reflected a nationwide trend but said its demographic challenges would change over time. “I imagine that in four or five years we will return to the same question, but by then the problems will be different. It will not be immigration from third countries or the integration of Ukrainians, a significant number of whom have also arrived in the city. Instead, we will be looking at how we are dealing with an aging population,” he said. The practice of registering hundreds or even thousands of foreigners at a single address is becoming increasingly common across Lithuania, according to the report. Although the number of people registered at the university dormitory in Šiauliai is falling, foreigners continue to declare their residence at other addresses in the city and surrounding district.

A series of cyberattacks targeting supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe has not affected stores in Lithuania, local retailers say, although cybersecurity experts warn that poorly protected remote access to equipment could leave businesses vulnerable. The attacks, reported in at least 10 European countries, targeted systems controlling refrigerators and freezers, allowing hackers to alter their temperature settings. According to the BBC, refrigeration control systems were breached Monday at shops in Belgium, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden. Estonia also reported incidents in which temperatures were raised to as high as 50 degrees Celsius at Selver supermarkets. A similar attack took place in France in October, forcing retailers there to discard large quantities of spoiled food. It remains unclear whether the incidents are connected or who is responsible. However, European Union officials have described the attacks as a “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumer confidence in it”. Hackers linked to Russia, North Korea and China have been mentioned among possible suspects. Cybersecurity specialists warn that connected devices extend well beyond refrigeration equipment. Washing machines, dishwashers, central heating systems and other remotely controlled appliances could also be vulnerable if their systems are not properly secured. Lithuanian retailers say systems remain secure Representatives of Lithuania’s five largest supermarket chains told LRT.lt that their systems had not been affected by the attacks. Maxima spokesperson Ernesta Vareikytė said the company had carried out additional checks of its systems and security measures after learning about the incidents elsewhere in Europe. She said some of Maxima’s operations are managed remotely, making cybersecurity a significant priority. “Our IT team monitors the operation of systems every day, takes care of updates and works closely with external service providers to assess potential threats and take preventive measures in time,” she said. Although no company can guarantee absolute protection against cyberthreats, Maxima was working to minimise risks and ensure its specialists could respond quickly, Vareikytė added. Norfa spokesman Darius Ryliškis said the retailer’s security standards differed significantly from those apparently used at affected stores abroad. He suggested that the compromised systems may have allowed direct connections to refrigeration equipment without adequate safeguards, while stores may have been linked to a shared server, enabling hackers to control an entire network at once. “Our stores are separated from one another, so there is no risk of a vulnerability in a shared network affecting all of them simultaneously,” Ryliškis said. He added that all commands and remote management operations at Norfa were carried out through secure virtual private network (VPN) connections. The retailer’s refrigerators also have specialised controllers with built-in protection – safeguards that Ryliškis said would become mandatory across the EU in 2027. Representatives of Iki, Rimi and Lidl also said they were monitoring the situation and maintaining their cybersecurity measures. Expert urges businesses to check remote access Lukas Apynis, a senior cybersecurity engineer at Baltimax and an ESET expert, said the attacks had targeted not only IT infrastructure but also equipment directly essential to supermarket operations. Some of the affected refrigeration systems were reportedly older models whose settings could be changed remotely, he said. While remote access makes equipment easier to maintain, inadequate protection can allow cybercriminals to exploit the same capability. It has not been confirmed whether the reported incidents are connected, Apynis said. Similar vulnerabilities could exist at other businesses using remotely managed refrigeration, heating or industrial equipment. Outdated systems that no longer receive security updates pose a particular risk, he added. Companies sometimes continue using such equipment because replacing it is expensive or would require temporarily suspending operations. But without updates or properly secured access, known vulnerabilities can remain unaddressed for years. Apynis said businesses should first check whether their equipment management systems can be accessed remotely without adequate protection. He recommended using VPN connections and multifactor authentication for remote access, limiting permissions to employees and specialists who need them, and regularly installing security updates. Companies should also ensure that hackers who gain access to their networks cannot easily reach other systems, he said. Monitoring unusual logins, unexpected changes to equipment settings and other signs of suspicious activity is equally important. Businesses should also review how external contractors responsible for equipment maintenance access their systems. Finally, companies should have plans in place to restore systems and maintain operations if a cyberattack disables critical equipment, Apynis said.

Lithuania’s government is assessing whether to impose a windfall tax on energy companies, including fuel producer Orlen Lietuva, as the Polish-owned group’s leadership warns that abandoning a major modernisation project could force the country’s only oil refinery to close. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has instructed ministers to urgently assess excess profits across the energy sector and prepare proposals on whether they should be taxed. The review covers fuel producers as well as electricity and heat suppliers. The move comes amid growing calls from both opposition and governing-party politicians to tax what they say could be unusually high profits at Orlen Lietuva, particularly as the company is expected to benefit from a surge in fuel prices. Orlen Group CEO Ireneusz Fafara has said the company must decide whether to continue the refinery modernisation project in Mažeikiai. Although about 80% of the planned work has been completed, the remaining investment is estimated at around $600 million, or slightly more than 500 million euros. Fafara has argued that Orlen Lietuva should finance the remaining work itself rather than rely on the wider group. The refinery has not generated enough annual profit to justify the additional investment, according to the company’s leadership. The group has warned that if it decides not to complete the modernisation, the refinery would cease operations. The project has already faced difficulties, including problems with its main contractor. A large reactor needed for the reconstruction was transported from Klaipėda port to the Mažeikiai refinery, about 100 kilometres inland, in a journey described at the time as historic. Lithuanian ministers said the government had received no official notification from the Polish group that it intended to change its investment plans. “We have not received any official indications that there are plans to revise the decisions made earlier,” Energy Minister Lukas Savickas said. He noted that an agreement had been signed and a working group established to oversee the investment, adding that about 80% of the project had already been completed. Economy Minister Edvinas Grikšas said the government would examine the company’s statements before drawing conclusions about their implications. The refinery’s financial performance has fluctuated significantly in recent years. It reported a loss of 183 million euros in 2022, then returned to profit in 2023, earning 294 million euros, before recording a loss of 687 million euros in 2024. Its profit in 2025 was 25 million euros. This year, however, the fuel crisis linked to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has prompted public estimates that the company’s profit could increase at least threefold. Savickas suggested that the company’s warnings about the refinery could be a reaction to the prospect of a windfall tax. “Every company is interested in having the most favourable possible tax regime. Discussions about taxing excess profits are taking place not only in Lithuania but across Europe, and this may be one form of the company’s response,” he said. Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said a coordinated European approach to windfall taxation would reduce the risks for Lithuania. However, he cautioned against acting alone. “When we consider this from a national perspective, we have to assess various risks and circumstances. We do not want to take risks, because this is also a matter of security,” Valys said. Poland itself has introduced a windfall profit tax on Orlen, the parent company of Orlen Lietuva, intending to use the proceeds to pay for its policies of keeping fuel prices down for consumers. Economists have also warned that imposing a tax on the excess profits of a single company could be risky and difficult to calculate without taxing profits generated through normal business activity. Eglė Stonkutė, a partnership professor at Vytautas Magnus University, said the government should also consider who would ultimately bear the cost. “The question is who would actually pay it. Would it be paid out of the company’s funds, reducing shareholders’ capital, as intended, or would the cost gradually be passed on to consumers and customers?” she said. The fuel industry, meanwhile, has argued that the state could collect more revenue by cutting excise duties on gasoline and diesel, encouraging motorists who currently fill their tanks in Poland or Latvia to buy fuel in Lithuania instead.

Three Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out tasks for foreign intelligence services have left Lithuania, and the decision to expel them was made before they caused any actual damage to the state, the State Security Department (VSD) said Thursday. Asked by the BNS news agency why no pretrial investigation had been opened against the three, the VSD said it had investigated their activities and collected information indicating that they posed a threat to national security. “The VSD notes that, in order to eliminate risks to national security arising from individuals’ activities, a measure provided for by law was implemented before any actual damage to the state had been caused,” the intelligence agency said in a comment to BNS. The agency said the three had their Lithuanian residence permits revoked on the basis of its assessment of the security threat. “The activities involved carrying out various assigned tasks for payment, such as filming specific sites and interviewing certain individuals,” Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas told reporters in parliament on Thursday. He said he could not provide further details. The Migration Department has confirmed that the individuals have left Lithuania, but the VSD said it did not know which country they had gone to. The three were declared threats to national security, had their temporary residence permits revoked and were barred from returning to Lithuania for five years, BNS previously reported. According to the VSD, the Ukrainians carried out various assignments for “hostile” foreign intelligence services in exchange for payment. The tasks were communicated through Telegram and other messaging platforms.

Belarus has refused Lithuania’s request to extradite Antanas Kandrotas, known by the nickname Celofanas, who has been sentenced to prison in Lithuania, the Justice Ministry said Thursday. The ministry initiated the extradition request in August after receiving a petition from the Kaunas Regional Court. It then formally asked the Belarusian Prosecutor General’s Office to hand Kandrotas over to Lithuania. The ministry informed the Kaunas court of the Belarusian authorities’ decision. The court issued a European arrest warrant for Kandrotas on June 29. Justice Vice Minister Martynas Dobrovolskis said the warrant would allow Kandrotas to be arrested if he enters the territory of a European Union member state or one of its partner countries. “Lithuania is seeking to ensure that Kandrotas serves the prison sentence imposed on him, and all necessary measures have been taken,” Dobrovolskis said. Kandrotas fled to Belarus in early May, violating a court-imposed written undertaking not to leave Lithuania, the BNS news agency reported. In June, the Lithuanian Court of Appeal upheld his conviction in a financial crimes case and sentenced him to three years and six months in prison. A search for Kandrotas was launched after the ruling took immediate effect. He was also sentenced to four years in prison for organising riots outside the Lithuanian parliament in 2021. In a separate case, a court of first instance sentenced him to 60 days of arrest for punching Valdas Bartkevičius, a supporter of Ukraine, in the face. After the sentences were combined, Kandrotas was ordered to serve a total of four years, seven months and 10 days in prison.

Lithuania is ready to host additional US troops and provide the infrastructure needed for their deployment, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Thursday after meeting American Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker. The two met at the Berlin Security Conference. According to Lithuania’s Defence Ministry, their talks covered the continuity of the US military presence in Lithuania, strengthening NATO’s eastern flank, hybrid threats, intelligence sharing, air defence and support for Ukraine. Kaunas stressed that while Lithuania is investing in its own air defence capabilities, NATO forces are also needed. During a US review of its military presence in Europe this summer, just over 100 American troops remained in Lithuania. However, in September, it was announced that two US battalions would arrive in the country by late October, bringing the American presence back to more than 1,000 troops, a level maintained in recent years. Kaunas said the deployment was the result of Lithuania’s efforts. He added that European countries must take greater responsibility for their own security and that Lithuania must increase investment in national and regional defence. He also emphasised that cooperation between the US and Lithuanian armed forces and defence institutions remained close. In early October, US President Donald Trump said Washington would consider the possibility of establishing a permanent military base in Lithuania. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius has previously said Lithuania is prepared to host US troops permanently and cover the costs of a permanent base if Washington decides to establish one. US troops have been rotating through Lithuania on nine-month deployments, in varying numbers, since 2014.

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys has denied reports that the administration of US President Donald Trump is pressuring Lithuania to allow Belarusian potash fertiliser exports through the port of Klaipėda. “I can assure you and say responsibly that nothing of the sort is happening at the moment,” Budrys told the radio Žinių Radijas on Thursday. His comments followed a report published by Politico last Friday, citing four European officials, that US special envoy to Belarus John Coale had recently asked Lithuanian diplomats about ways to ease restrictions on goods from Belarus. Two Eastern European officials told the publication that Coale had been exerting pressure on Lithuanian authorities at all levels for more than a year, dating back to his first visit to Minsk. Budrys said he was disappointed by the report, noting that the Foreign Ministry had provided clarifications to Politico several times. “I don’t know where they got all this from. I have no idea who these sources are, but I know nothing of the sort,” he said. “I cannot rule out a 1% possibility that I am completely unaware of everything happening in the country, but, jokes aside, I can say that none of this is happening now.” The minister also said Coale had not raised the issue of Belarusian fertiliser transit during their several meetings. US President Donald Trump said in September that he was working on a “big deal” with Minsk to buy potash fertiliser at a much lower price than farmers currently pay Canadian suppliers. Such a deal would require a route to transport the fertiliser through Lithuania’s main Baltic Sea port in Klaipėda or other ports in the region. Another Eastern European official told Politico that Washington had been exploring for some time whether Belarusian potash could reach international markets through Klaipėda and other Baltic Sea ports, including Riga in Latvia. Such a route would be simpler than transporting the fertiliser through Russia, the official said. A European official also confirmed that Coale had approached counterparts in Latvia about the issue. The European Union currently imposes sanctions on Belarusian fertilisers. Lithuanian officials say the restrictions also cover transit, which previously passed through Klaipėda but was halted in early 2022. Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has also denied that Washington is pressuring Vilnius over the issue. The presidential office, meanwhile, described Politico’s report as outdated.

Hungary does not consider Ukraine’s accession to the European Union by 2030 realistic, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said Thursday during a visit to Vilnius, while reaffirming Budapest’s support for Kyiv’s membership bid. “We do not think this is realistic. [...] We strongly support a merit-based process, and I think we agree with Lithuania on this issue,” Orbán told journalists when asked whether Ukraine could join the bloc by 2030. She said all candidate countries must meet the same requirements, ruling out any accelerated accession process for Ukraine. “Every country must go through the same procedure that we went through. [...] We also do not support any fast-track entry,” she said. However, Orbán noted that Ukraine had made significant progress in its accession process, with four of the six negotiating clusters already opened. She attributed some of that progress to improved relations between Hungary and Ukraine and an agreement on protecting the rights of the Hungarian ethnic minority in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys expressed greater optimism about Ukraine’s prospects of joining the EU by 2030, saying a target date should be set. “We are more optimistic about dates. We believe that a date as a target can and should be set,” Budrys said. He said accession by 2030 was theoretically possible if Ukraine implemented the necessary reforms quickly enough and the EU completed the required steps in the process on time. “We believe it is still possible to complete all processes by 2030. [...] If we manage to do everything fast enough on the European Union’s side, and Ukraine carries out reforms, that is theoretically possible,” Budrys said.

Politico reported that the US approached Lithuanian diplomats about allowing Belarusian fertiliser transit via Klaipėda. A senior adviser to the Lithuanian president did not deny the discussion took place, but said the reporting was outdated – there was an approach, but nothing more. However, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys stepped in later to deny the discussion had taken place at all, saying “that nothing of the sort is happening at the moment”. This reporting came amid fears of Trump’s warming attitudes towards Russia. As a case in point, a report surfaced saying that the US urged some European countries, including the Baltic states, to tone down their rhetoric against Russia. That warning was largely shrugged off by Baltic officials. ADAMKUS AT 100 Lithuania’s former president, Valdas Adamkus, turned 100 on Tuesday. With congratulatory messages pouring in from inside and outside the country, we can say he seems to be universally beloved , especially for steering the country west and away from Russia. But not only that – people talked about how he engaged in dialogue and showed respect to everyone, which brought about a positive change in the post-Soviet political culture in the country. In other economic updates: – AirBaltic is reducing its fleet of planes in Lithuania and axing Vilnius–Düsseldorf flights amid the Latvian company’s restructuring. Lithuanian official said they would appeal the decision. – Lithuania’s economy has contracted 1 percent, recording the sharpest quarterly decline among 15 European Union countries that have reported data. ​ MIGRATION VS BUSINESS? ​ Lithuania has tightened the rules for non-EU nationals in seeking temporary residency permits. This came amid a surge of attention to the growing migration, which sparked several protests and is increasingly becoming a platform for populist and right-wing politicians. One of the initiatives included closing visa centres in Central Asia, which immediately sparked backlash from some business owners who are short of employees. ​ UKRAINIAN SINGLE-USE SPIES ​ Three Ukrainian nationals were sent out of Lithuania over allegations of spying for “hostile” foreign countries. The country’s intelligence service, the VSD, said they were in touch with their handlers via Telegram. Recall, Ukrainian nationals were recruited – usually on Telegram – to carry out a string of sabotage actions, including in Poland and Lithuania. Asked why they were sent out of the country rather than charged, the VSD said they had not actually done any harm – yet. ​ EDITOR’S PICKS: – Amid a looming demographics crisis, Lithuania has moved to expand access to fertility treatment beyond married couples. – Lithuania mulls establishing a state holding to produce more drones. – Lithuanian supermarket fridges survived a hacker attack unscathed. – Minsk has refused to extradite Antanas Kandrotas-Celofanas, who by now has become a propagandist in the neighbouring country. – The authorities have found plagiarism in the prime minister’s dissertation. – The population growth figures in the northern city of Šiauliai turned out to be false . – Lithuanians are basically fleeing the second-tier pension system. – Avoid these countries, Lithuanian officials say. – Revisiting the topic of Soviet nostalgia .

Lithuania’s border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region is currently calmer than the situation on the Polish side, where authorities have thwarted a potential provocation, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Friday. Speaking to the radio Žinių radijas, Kaunas said the deployment of military personnel to assist border guards was a preventive measure prompted by intelligence indicating potential threats. Lithuanian troops have been assisting the State Border Guard Service along the border with Kaliningrad since October 8. In mid-October, the minister extended their deployment until mid-November. Kaunas said a further extension was likely, although the decision would depend on the latest intelligence assessments. “Currently, the situation on the border with Kaliningrad is certainly calmer than it was in Poland, let’s say, and we are reacting accordingly,” he said. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said earlier this week that his country had thwarted a potential provocation along its border with Kaliningrad. On Tuesday, he said he had been informed shortly after midnight about suspicious activity along Poland’s northern border. Kaunas said there had been more movement near the border on the Polish side than on the Lithuanian side, prompting Warsaw to take stronger measures. “We have an aggressive neighbour and [...] it needs to be closely monitored, so we are reacting preventively at all times,” the minister said. Meanwhile, President Gitanas Nausėda declined to comment in detail on potential provocations along Lithuania’s border with Kaliningrad, saying that publicly disclosing intelligence information would benefit “hostile intelligence services”.

Two German military exercises involving more than 6,000 troops are set to begin in Lithuania on Friday and continue until December 3, the Lithuanian Armed Forces said. The exercises, dubbed Freedom Shield 26-II and Grand Eagle 26, will involve soldiers from Germany’s 45th Armoured Brigade Lietuva and 37th Mechanised Infantry Brigade Freistaat Sachsen, both part of the German Army’s 10th Armoured Division. They will be joined by troops from Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, the Czech Republic, Croatia, Belgium and Luxembourg serving in NATO’s Multinational Combat Brigade in Lithuania, as well as a Lithuanian military unit. Freedom Shield 26-II will take place at the Rūdninkai military training area, while Grand Eagle 26 will be held at the General Silvestras Žukauskas training area. The drills are aimed at strengthening combat readiness, improving command and operational planning procedures, and enhancing interoperability between Lithuanian and Polish forces and NATO allies. The Lithuanian Armed Forces said allied troops and military equipment would move along the country's roads throughout the exercises. The heaviest movement of military convoys from the Kalvarija border checkpoint to the training areas is expected on November 6-7, while convoys arriving from Klaipeda are expected to travel between November 10 and 12. From November 28 to December 3, military equipment will be transported from the training areas toward Kalvarija and Klaipėda. The military warned that the movement of military vehicles and equipment could cause temporary traffic disruptions on some roads. Drivers were advised to allow extra time for their journeys and follow instructions from Military Police officers.

An employer who delays salary payments in Lithuania may face financial penalties, while employees have several legal options to recover their money, including claiming late-payment interest, filing a labour dispute and, in certain circumstances, suspending work or terminating their employment with severance pay. The issue was recently discussed on the social media platform Reddit, where a user asked what employees should do when their employer fails to pay wages on time and what compensation they are entitled to. According to the State Labour Inspectorate, delayed or unpaid wages are not merely a financial inconvenience for employees but a violation of labour law. Here is what employees should know about their rights and the steps they can take when their employer fails to pay them on time. If an employer is responsible for delaying salary payments or other money owed to an employee, the employer must also pay late-payment interest. Interest is calculated from the first day of the delay until the employer has fully settled the outstanding amount. The interest rate is set by the Ministry of Social Security and Labour, unless labour legislation provides for a higher rate. Additional compensation, known as contractual penalties under Lithuanian labour law, may also apply when employment ends and the employer fails to settle all outstanding payments on time. The amount depends on the employee’s average monthly salary and the length of the delay. According to the Labour Inspectorate, such payments have reached as much as 10,000 euros in some cases. Employees whose employers fail to pay their wages can file a complaint with the Labour Disputes Commission. Applications can be submitted in writing or electronically. The commission’s decisions are legally binding. If an employer fails to comply, the employee can turn to a bailiff to enforce the decision. Employees can also ask the commission to impose a penalty on an employer who fails to implement its decision. The penalty can reach 500 euros for each week of noncompliance, calculated from the date of the decision until it is implemented, for a maximum period of six months. Separately, the State Labour Inspectorate warns that employers who fail to pay wages on time or in full can face administrative fines ranging from 300 to 6,000 euros. The amount depends on the nature of the violation and whether it is a repeat offense. Employees do not have to contact their employer before filing a complaint. If wages remain unpaid, they can approach the Labour Disputes Commission immediately. However, employees may choose to contact their employer first and attempt to resolve the matter amicably. Employees generally have three months from the date they became aware, or should have become aware, of a violation of their rights to file an application with the Labour Disputes Commission. The application should clearly explain what happened, specify what the employee is demanding from the employer and, if possible, state the exact amount being claimed. Employees should also provide supporting documents, where available. These may include an employment contract, payslips, bank account statements, working-time records, correspondence with the employer and other relevant evidence. Further information about the application procedure, forms and required documents is available on the State Labour Inspectorate’s website under its section on labour disputes . Employees can suspend work or terminate their contracts Lithuanian labour law also provides additional protections for employees facing prolonged nonpayment. If an employer fails to pay all of an employee’s wages for two or more consecutive months, the employee may temporarily suspend the performance of their employment contract. The employee must notify the employer in writing at least three working days in advance. The suspension can last for up to three months. During this period, the employer must pay the employee compensation of at least the minimum monthly wage for each month of suspension. Employees also have the right to terminate their employment contract if their employer has failed to pay their wages for at least two consecutive months. In such cases, the employee is entitled to severance pay. If the employee has worked for the company for more than one year, the severance payment amounts to two average monthly salaries. If the employment relationship lasted less than one year, the employee is entitled to one average monthly salary, the State Labour Inspectorate says.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Monday it was too early to discuss changing the name of the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius before planned talks with Chinese diplomats, stressing that Lithuania remained open to dialogue with Beijing without preconditions. “I think it is still too early because the talks have not yet taken place. There will be diplomatic meetings between representatives of the People’s Republic of China and the Lithuanian Foreign Ministry,” Sinkevičius told reporters. He was responding to questions about whether renaming the Taiwanese office could help restore diplomatic representation between Lithuania and China. News website Delfi reported Monday that the Foreign Ministry had asked the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius in September to change its name as part of efforts to normalise diplomatic relations with Beijing. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the report was inaccurate but declined to comment further. Chinese diplomats are expected to visit Lithuania this week for meetings with the Foreign Ministry and a parliamentary group seeking to normalise relations with Beijing. Sinkevičius said the Foreign Ministry was coordinating efforts to restore diplomatic representation, describing this as a commitment in the government’s programme. He noted that diplomatic relations between the two countries had never been formally severed, although diplomatic representation had been suspended. “I do not yet know what the talks will involve, what agreements might be reached or what either side will want. We have no preconditions and are open to a live conversation without preconditions. We are not setting any conditions for the People’s Republic of China either,” he said. Opposition politicians have reacted strongly to reports that Lithuania asked Taiwan to rename its representative office, arguing that such a move would amount to “appeasing authoritarian states” and undermine Lithuania’s interests. Remigijus Žemaitaitis, an opposition MP and leader of the Nemunas Dawn party, has proposed establishing a temporary parliamentary commission to investigate the alleged pressure on the Taiwanese representation. Asked whether Taiwan had been pressured to change the office’s name, Sinkevičius said the wording depended on how the reported proposal was interpreted. “If there is a proposal on how the work of the office in Lithuania could continue, you can say pressed, demanded, asked or proposed. As a headline element, you can say pressed,” he said. “Who pressed whom? The foreign minister probably didn’t grab anyone and start pressing them. I think there is a lot of noise here, a lot of attempts to escalate and dramatize the issue,” he added. The prime minister described the controversy as premature, saying discussions with both Beijing and Taipei were part of normal diplomatic work. “Let’s wait for the results, if there are any. Let’s not speculate about what might happen, what they will discuss, what they will decide or what preconditions exist. I think we are an open state for talks; no one is pressing us and we are not pressing anyone,” Sinkevičius said. In a statement on November 6, the Taiwanese Representative Office in Lithuania said cooperation between the two sides was based on mutual respect, shared interests, transparency and partnership. Last week, it also told news website 15min.lt that it had no intention of changing its name. Diplomatic relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in autumn 2021 after the opening of the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius. Similar missions operate under the name Taipei in other countries, reflecting Beijing’s opposition to any expressions of Taiwan’s status as a sovereign state. In response to Lithuania’s decision, China downgraded its diplomatic representation in Vilnius to the level of chargé d’affaires. Lithuania, in turn, refused to issue new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, leaving China without diplomatic personnel in the country since May last year. Sinkevičius has previously expressed hope that negotiations with China could achieve a breakthrough by the end of the year. Restoring diplomatic representation is included in the government’s programme. Meanwhile, an October review by the Economy Ministry concluded that the opening of the Taiwanese Representative Office had not resulted in a significant increase in Lithuanian exports to Taiwan.

Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry asked Taiwan’s representative office in Vilnius to change its name within a week in September, news website Delfi reported Monday. Lithuania’s government is working on restoring diplomatic ties with Beijing that have gone sour since the opening of the Taiwanese in 2021. According to the report, Deputy Foreign Minister Vidmantas Verbickas and diplomat Ričardas Šlepavičius presented an unofficial document to three representatives of the Taiwanese office, including its head, Constance Wang, during a meeting on September 24. The document requested that the office’s name be changed by October 1, China’s National Day. The Taiwanese representatives had expected to discuss economic relations and investment and were surprised by the request, Delfi reported. The document argued that the office’s current name was obstructing the development of economic ties between Lithuania and Taiwan and creating difficulties for businesses. In exchange for the proposed name change, the ministry reportedly pledged to send a vice-ministerial delegation to Taiwan to sign an agreement on investment prospects and begin negotiations on a double taxation agreement. The document also requested that its contents remain confidential. It also said public discussions about Lithuania-Taiwan relations should be based on verified facts rather than unsubstantiated assumptions or speculation. The statement did not specify which public comments or discussions it was addressing. The Foreign Ministry did not respond Friday to questions about the possible renaming of the Taiwanese office, negotiations on an economic cooperation action plan with Taiwan or efforts to restore relations with China. Meanwhile, Chinese diplomats are expected to visit Lithuania on November 11–12 for meetings with Foreign Ministry representatives and a group of lawmakers seeking to normalise diplomatic relations with Beijing. The planned visit was announced Friday by lawmaker Ignas Vėgėlė. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has said he hopes to achieve a breakthrough in talks with China by the end of the year. Restoring diplomatic representation at the ambassadorial level is included in his government’s program. Relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in the autumn of 2021 after Vilnius allowed Taiwan to open a representative office under its own name rather than using the name Taipei, as Taiwanese offices do in most other countries. China responded by unilaterally downgrading diplomatic relations to the level of chargé d’affaires. Lithuania subsequently refused to issue new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, leaving the country without Chinese diplomatic representation since May last year. Responding to the report about the Foreign Ministry’s alleged request to change the name of the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the information was “inaccurately reported” and declined to comment on it. “I will not comment on this information. First of all, it has been inaccurately reported. We have various discussions with different partners that we interact with and I certainly will not go into details,” the minister told reporters on Monday. “I can confirm that we have spoken with the Taiwanese side about various aspects of our relations,” he stated. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius wants to see the outcome of negotiations with China before commenting on the process, his spokesman said on Monday. “The Foreign Ministry’s goal, as set out in the government programme, is to restore diplomatic representation with China to the level maintained in other European Union countries. The foreign minister periodically updates the prime minister on progress. The prime minister wants to see the final result rather than comment on the process,” spokesman Gedas Salyga said. “The choice of an action plan is the responsibility of the foreign minister. Lithuania aims to maintain mutually beneficial economic and practical cooperation with Taiwan,” Salyga added.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said he was briefed on Foreign Ministry's talks with the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius about a possible change to its name.​ "All matters are coordinated with me. We no longer live under the previous government, when the foreign minister [Gabrielis Landsbergis] could open a representative office simply by exchanging letters with another state, without consulting other institutions. Such nonsense no longer happens in Lithuania," Nausėda told reporters. ​ News website Delfi reported Monday that the Foreign Ministry had asked the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius in September to change its name as part of efforts to normalise diplomatic relations with Beijing. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the report was inaccurate but declined to comment further. ​ Asked whether he supported changing the office's name, Nausėda replied: "We will wait and see." He added that Lithuania was first awaiting a meeting with Chinese diplomats scheduled for this week. ​ "What we are doing now is primarily an effort to understand why the potential talked about by the previous government was not realised, and we are ready to communicate with both Taiwan and China," Nausėda said. ​ According to Nausėda, relations with Beijing are currently "practically zero", making the restoration of diplomatic representation the first priority. ​ He stressed that Lithuania wanted to normalise relations with China while maintaining good ties with Taiwan. ​ Asked about the benefits Lithuania had gained from opening the Taiwanese Representative Office, Nausėda said he knew better than anyone about the "alleged dividends in the political arena following the opening of this office". ​ "We are talking about things that perhaps exist in the rhetoric of some Conservatives [who led the previous coalition government] and political scientists sympathetic to them, but certainly not in reality. "Therefore, I repeat, we want to restore normal relations [with China] and maintain normal relations with Taiwan. I hope that the emotions that may have surfaced at the very beginning will be set aside, allowing us to return to a normal agenda of political and economic cooperation," the president said. ​An October review by the Ministry of Economy and Innovation also concluded that the opening of the Taiwanese Representative Office had not led to a significant increase in Lithuanian exports to Taiwan. Opposition politicians have reacted strongly to reports that Lithuania asked Taiwan to rename its representative office, arguing that such a move would amount to “appeasing authoritarian states” and undermine Lithuania’s interests. ​ Remigijus Žemaitaitis, an opposition MP and leader of the Nemunas Dawn party, has proposed establishing a temporary parliamentary commission to investigate the alleged pressure on the Taiwanese representation. ​ On November 6, the Taiwanese Representative Office said cooperation with Lithuania was based on mutual respect, shared interests, transparency and partnership. It also told news portal 15min that it had no intention of changing its name. ​ Diplomatic relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in the autumn of 2021 following the opening of the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius. ​ Similar offices operate under the name Taipei in other countries, as Beijing strongly opposes any expressions of Taiwanese statehood. ​ In response to Lithuania's decision, China unilaterally downgraded its diplomatic representation to the level of charge d'affaires. Lithuania, in turn, refused to issue new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, leaving the country without Chinese diplomats since May last year.

Lithuania will introduce stricter controls on Russian and Belarusian grain shipments from November 16, requiring businesses to cover the costs of origin tests and barring cargoes from leaving the port of Klaipėda until laboratory results are received, officials said. Justas Jaskonis, a spokesman for the agriculture minister, said legislation tightening controls on food grain from Russia and Belarus had been coordinated and signed. “Every shipment of food grain from Russia and Belarus will undergo documentary and physical checks. The controls will cover wheat, barley, maize and sunflower seeds when reloaded or stored in Lithuania. Samples will be taken from every shipment for laboratory testing to establish the grain’s true origin,” Jaskonis said. Under an order issued by Kęstutis Mažeika in early September, the State Food and Veterinary Service was instructed to verify the origin of all grain, both for animal feed and human consumption, transported from Russia and Belarus. The measure is intended to prevent grain allegedly stolen from occupied Ukrainian territories from being shipped through Lithuania. Until the new inspection system formally takes effect, the State Food and Veterinary Service has been covering the costs of sending samples to foreign laboratories. Shipments have also been allowed to leave Klaipėda port before final test results were available. From November 16, however, cargoes will be held until laboratory results confirm their origin. Customs authorities will clear shipments only after receiving authorisation from the State Food and Veterinary Service. If a discrepancy in the declared origin is established, the shipment will be returned or destroyed. Businesses will be responsible for the costs of inspections, laboratory tests and related procedures. Since September, the State Food and Veterinary Service has taken five samples from two shipments whose origins were unclear. The samples are currently being tested at foreign laboratories. Service spokeswoman Aiste Prielgauskaitė said the results were not yet available and no additional samples had been taken. Jaskonis said laboratory testing could take two months or longer. In early October, the Lithuanian president and the prime ministers of Latvia and Estonia urged European Union leaders to ban the transit of Russian grain. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius also said he would propose prohibiting Russian food grain transit through EU territory and imposing sanctions on certain Russian agricultural oligarchs. The debate over grain shipments intensified after Lithuanian grain growers said Russian grain exported from the Kaliningrad region through Baltic ports was being offered at significantly lower prices than locally produced grain. As a result, Lithuanian grain has remained in storage, prompting farmers to call on the authorities to stop Russian grain transit through Lithuania.

Lithuania would reject any agreement on a new European security architecture that gave Russia the power to restrict NATO troop deployments in the region, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said Tuesday. His comments came as negotiations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia were taking place in Abu Dhabi, where long-term European security issues were reportedly also under discussion. “Lithuania finds any consideration of a return to the era of the Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe, or to any other arrangements under which Russia would have leverage to dictate what forces can be deployed in our region while doing whatever it wants on its own territory, fundamentally unacceptable,” Budrys told the news website 15min in an interview. Moscow is seeking agreements of this kind, Budrys said, warning that restrictions on the deployment of allied forces would have existential consequences for Lithuania. He noted that the Lithuanian government’s programme includes a commitment not to accept restrictions on the deployment of weapons in Lithuania or the wider region. Budrys stressed that no agreements on European security could be concluded without the involvement of European countries. “There can be no discussion about European security without Europe, and ultimately, it is for no one else to decide but Europe,” he said. Lithuania must be directly involved in any negotiations, he added, because their outcome would primarily affect the country and the wider region along NATO’s eastern border. “Lithuania’s position is clear: no such agreements can be considered without us, because they will primarily be about us, about our region, right on the NATO border, and we must be there,” Budrys said. He said European Union institutions should represent Europe in the negotiations, although the bloc has yet to agree on a specific model for doing so. Discussions on new European security arrangements should only begin after a ceasefire in Ukraine and an agreement on the terms of peace and security guarantees for Kyiv, Budrys insisted. “Now is not the time to talk. First, there must be a ceasefire. We must first agree on the terms of peace in Ukraine, and then on security guarantees for Ukraine,” he said. Budrys also stressed the importance of maintaining military, energy and financial support for Ukraine through the winter.

Lithuania plans to build at least 10 new power plants and establish seven “energy islands” by 2033 as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s electricity system against natural disasters, sabotage and other emergencies. The islands would be able to operate independently of one another and maintain electricity supplies to consumers if the main regional transmission network becomes unavailable. Andrius Šemeškevičius, CEO of Lithuania’s electricity transmission system operator Litgrid, said the initiative was prompted by an increase in extreme weather events causing power outages, as well as growing geopolitical threats. “Energy islands are electricity system regions capable of operating independently when the main 330-kilovolt electricity transmission network is unavailable. This can happen because of natural disasters, sabotage or other emergency situations,” Šemeškevičius said. “We want to ensure that electricity supplies to consumers continue even in the most difficult circumstances. To implement this model, we have drawn up a plan for upgrading existing power plants, incorporating battery storage and installing new flexible electricity generation capacity where needed,” he added. The seven planned energy islands will cover the Vilnius, Kaunas, Klaipėda-Mažeikiai, Panevėžys-Šiauliai, Alytus, Jurbarkas and Utena regions. During isolated operation, electricity would be distributed according to priority. Emergency services and hospitals would receive supplies first, followed by households, with businesses given the lowest priority. “We estimate that households would be able to receive electricity for at least eight hours a day. However, that is the worst-case scenario. If the sun is shining and the wind is blowing, electricity supplies within an energy island could be maintained around the clock,” Šemeškevičius said. Litgrid has prepared an interactive map showing the planned energy islands and potential locations for new flexible generation capacity. The energy island project envisages the construction of about 10 new power plants across Lithuania by 2033, with a combined capacity of 800 megawatts. The facilities will have to meet specific technical requirements, including the ability to start operating within 30 minutes. Their minimum capacity is expected to be 50 megawatts, while the maximum will be 100 megawatts. Litgrid plans to organise competitive tenders under a technology-neutral approach. Companies winning the auctions will have five years to install the new flexible generation capacity and will subsequently provide regional isolated-operation services for 15 years. The plants will be built by private investors, while Litgrid will purchase their capacity to provide isolated-operation services. If the necessary legislative and regulatory changes are approved, the first auctions are expected to take place in 2027. The energy island model should be fully operational by 2033. “We are talking about power plants that can start operating quickly. This means that gas-fired plants would probably be the most popular option at present. However, we are technologically neutral. These could also be hydrogen, biomethane or liquid-fuel power plants,” Šemeškevičius said. Under normal operating conditions, the plants will be able to sell the electricity they generate on the market if it is commercially viable. “We will purchase isolated-operation services from the market, but there will be no restrictions on how they provide other services. They will be able to offer electricity balancing, power generation and heat production services,” he said. Litgrid estimates that the new services will add 0.67 cent per kilowatt-hour to electricity transmission tariffs after 2033. However, the additional flexible generation capacity is expected to help reduce peak electricity prices and lower average wholesale market prices. The private sector is expected to invest about €880 million in building the 10 new power plants. First four energy islands expected by 2028 Although all seven energy islands are scheduled to become fully operational by 2033, Lithuania wants the first four to start operating as early as 2028. They will cover the Vilnius, Kaunas, Panevėžys-Šiauliai and Klaipėda regions. To achieve this, some existing power plants will need to be upgraded to improve their ability to maintain electricity supplies during emergencies. This would allow the four islands to operate independently, although not yet at full capacity. Šemeškevičius identified several risks to the project’s implementation, including potential opposition from communities concerned about new power plants being built near their homes. “The legislation will have to be amended, everything will need to be coordinated with the National Energy Regulatory Council, and there will need to be interest from market participants. Of course, building power plants can also pose challenges. Some communities may not want these facilities in their immediate vicinity,” he said. Other challenges include securing regulatory approval and attracting enough private-sector investment to deliver the planned generation capacity. On Tuesday, Litgrid is launching a public consultation on its concept for isolated-operation services, inviting market participants to review the proposed service conditions and technical requirements and submit suggestions. The consultation will run until December 10. A public presentation of the concept to market participants is scheduled for November 25, with an updated version provisionally expected to be published in mid-January.

Taiwan has no plans to change the name of its representative office in Lithuania, the island’s Foreign Ministry said Tuesday, describing media reports suggesting otherwise as potentially damaging to relations between Vilnius and Taipei. “Currently, there are no plans to change the name,” Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi told reporters in Taipei. His comments followed a report by Delfi.lt on Monday that Lithuania had asked the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius in September to change its name as part of efforts to restore full diplomatic representation with China. Chen declined to comment on what he described as rumours, saying media reports were not necessarily accurate. However, he did not directly confirm whether the Delfi report was false. He said Taiwan and Lithuania had developed closer relations based on mutual benefits and shared values, which had provided the foundation for their agreement to establish representative offices, including the decision on the name of Taiwan’s mission in Vilnius. Taiwan urges democratic partners to stand together Taiwanese Foreign Ministry spokesman Hsiao Kuang-wei said at a separate news conference that the two sides had continued to develop substantive cooperation since establishing their representative offices. Areas of cooperation include trade and investment, industry and technology, education and culture, and humanitarian assistance, based on mutual respect, openness, transparency and mutual benefit, he said. Hsiao also highlighted cooperation between Taiwan and Lithuania in supporting Ukraine, saying it demonstrated how democracies on the front lines could work together to defend freedom and democratic values in the face of authoritarian expansion and threats. “Democratic partners must firmly adhere to shared convictions and principles, support each other, and jointly counter pressure and challenges from authoritarian countries,” he said. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Monday that discussions with Taiwan over a possible name change had been coordinated with him. The proposal was submitted to Taiwan by Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry. Chinese diplomats are expected to visit Lithuania this week for meetings with Foreign Ministry officials and a group of lawmakers seeking to normalise relations with Beijing. Diplomatic relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in autumn 2021 following the opening of the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius. Similar Taiwanese missions in other countries operate under the name Taipei, while Beijing strongly opposes moves it considers expressions of Taiwanese statehood. In response to the office’s opening, China downgraded its diplomatic representation in Lithuania from ambassadorial level to chargé d’affaires. Lithuania, in turn, refused to issue new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, leaving the country without Chinese diplomatic personnel since May last year. Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has previously expressed hope for a breakthrough in talks with China by the end of the year. Restoring full diplomatic representation is included in the government’s program. However, an October review by Lithuania’s Ministry of Economy and Innovation found that the opening of the Taiwanese Representative Office had not significantly increased Lithuanian exports to Taiwan.

Lithuania’s authorities issued an air alert warning (code yellow), on Tuesday evening at around 23:00, urging people to locate their nearest shelter and wait for updates. The warning was issued in the counties of Vilnius and Utena. It was called off before midnight. “The Lithuanian Armed Forces inform: POSSIBLE AIR RAID ALERT (YELLOW). Find a safe place. If you see a suspicious object, keep away, call 112. Wait for the all-clear,” the authorities said in an emergency message. An object was detected in Belarus travelling toward Lithuania, the authorities said, adding that it was still unclear whether it was a drone. Code yellow does not mean there is an imminent danger, but people should be prepared to seek shelter in case the authorities declare an air alert warning (code red). Find more information about your nearest shelter or safe premises on the government’s crisis response website, LT72.lt. The object has not yet been identified and was moving through the Ignalina area, National Crisis Management Centre head Vilmantas Vitkauskas told LRT. “It is difficult to say at this point whether it is a drone or some other object. Our air force continues to monitor it,” Vitkauskas said. According to Vitkauskas, when alert messages were sent to residents shortly before 23:00, the object was approximately 30 to 50 kilometres from the Lithuanian border. Fighter jets participating in an air defence mission are on standby, he added. “If a decision is made to scramble the jets and neutralise the target, that is what will be done,” Vitkauskas said. He could not specify the exact number of objects detected but said authorities were currently dealing with one. Lithuanian Airports announced that operations at Vilnius Airport and the surrounding airspace had been temporarily restricted because of the potential air threat. At around 23:45, the authorities called off the air alert warning in Vilnius County, followed by Utena County about 10 minutes later. Vilnius Airport also announced it was resuming operations, although cancelations and delays were likely.

Former foreign minister Gabrielius Landsbergis is credited with steering Lithuania toward Taiwan, which ultimately led to the breakdown of relations with China. In an interview with LRT.lt, he said Lithuania has backed itself into a corner after leaked information suggested Vilnius asked Taipei to rename its de facto embassy. Earlier this week, President Gitanas Nausėda criticised Landsbergis, claiming that the former minister had agreed with another state to establish a de facto embassy after merely exchanging several letters. Nausėda added that such “nonsense” was not happening under the current government; Landsbergis declined to respond directly to the president's remarks. “We are in a difficult position. I do not know what nonsense the president is talking about, but I think the same description could be applied to what is happening now,” he said. The current foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, has found himself in a particularly difficult position, having been tasked with restoring relations with Beijing. “If China refuses to restore relations, it would mean that the minister would almost have to resign. And if China sets some incredibly high demands, we will simply put so much pressure on Taiwan that it meets those demands,” Landsbergis said. According to the former minister, it was “clearly” China that had initiated the request for Taiwan to rename its office in Vilnius. “This is China’s demands being passed on to Taiwan. We are acting as an intermediary in this situation. Instead of being a country that shapes its own foreign policy, we are, at least in this context, becoming a country that implements the foreign policy demands of a state that is hostile to us. That is regrettable. “This undermines our standing, first and foremost in the eyes of Taiwan, given the friendly ties and partnership we had established there, and the opportunities to develop those relations in a positive direction. It also undermines our standing in the eyes of our partners and, frankly, our adversaries, who will want to remind us in the future that we are ‘a country that broke’,” he said. However, Lithuanian officials say that the promised economic ties with Taiwan had failed to materialise. Nausėda also said that countries that have no relations, or lower-level contacts, with Taiwan are still maintaining a closer cooperation with Taipei than Lithuania. Meanwhile, Landsbergis said he had “received signals” that China was calling for the outright closure of the Taiwanese Representative Office. In the past, China had stepped up its demands whenever it believed a country had done something wrong, Landsbergis said, adding that Lithuania could face a similar situation. “And if we were talking about some kind of normalisation and the restoration of diplomatic representation, say, at the level of a chargé d'affaires, the question of ambassadors would then arise. China would come up with new demands, and so on,” he said. With Lithuania's wavering support for the Belarusian opposition and the ongoing discussions surrounding Taiwan, the country risks losing its international standing. “Lithuania has managed to carve out a niche for itself in a highly competitive international environment. This has allowed us to draw attention to our security concerns, our security situation and the threats to our democracy and sovereignty by pointing to what we do for others. “Lithuania needs help, but it also provides help to the Belarusian opposition, supports Ukraine, helps Taiwan and assists others in similar situations. It is then clear that our argument carries much greater weight when we ourselves need to ask for that help. And we have deprived ourselves of that argument,” Landsbergis said.

French President Emmanuel Macron has promised to explore ways to accelerate the delivery of Caesar self-propelled howitzers to Lithuania, President Gitanas Nausėda said Tuesday. “Military cooperation between Lithuania and France is intense. We discussed the delivery schedules for the Caesar artillery systems. In some respects, we would like them to be implemented faster, as this is a very important element in building our national division,” Nausėda said. “Both the president and his team promised to look for ways to shorten these delivery schedules,” he added. Lithuania signed a 252-million-euro contract with the French defence company KNDS France last December to acquire a second batch of Caesar Mk II howitzers. The deal marked the country’s second purchase of the artillery systems and its largest arms procurement from France. Under an initial agreement signed in 2022, Lithuania ordered 18 howitzers, with deliveries scheduled for 2027. Following the acquisition of the second batch, Lithuania will become the second-largest operator of Caesar systems after France. In September, the Lithuanian Defence Ministry also announced an agreement with KNDS France to invest 12 million euros in establishing and equipping a specialised maintenance workshop for the artillery systems in Lithuania. The Caesar is one of the few 155 mm wheeled self-propelled artillery systems manufactured in NATO and European Union countries. The system has also been combat-tested in Ukraine.

Airspace restrictions and an overnight air alert disrupted three flights carrying a total of 465 passengers at Vilnius Airport on Tuesday evening, while operations at Kaunas Airport were unaffected, Lithuanian Airports said. After flights to Vilnius were suspended because of suspected smuggler balloons launched from Belarus, a private aircraft was diverted to Kaunas Airport and an incoming flight from Nice was delayed. The disruptions affected 225 passengers. A subsequent air alert caused a further delay to a flight from Vilnius to Hurghada, Egypt, affecting another 240 passengers. Kaunas Airport experienced no flight disruptions despite temporarily suspending operations twice on Tuesday evening and overnight into Wednesday because of risks posed by contraband balloons and a suspected drone. Both restrictions were lifted within two hours. Operations at Vilnius Airport were initially restricted at around 19:20 Tuesday and suspended again later following the declaration of an air alert. Full operations at the airport resumed after midnight.

Drone incursions prompted yellow and red air alerts across large parts of Lithuania overnight, with NATO fighter jets scrambled on both occasions, but the drones were not shot down and flew into Latvian airspace, Lithuanian officials said Wednesday. The first yellow alert was declared in the Vilnius and Utena regions at around 23:00 Tuesday and lifted shortly after midnight. Almost immediately, a second alert was issued, initially in the Alytus region before being expanded to much of central and northern Lithuania. The warning was subsequently upgraded from yellow to red, meaning that residents in the regions were to take shelter. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the National Crisis Management Centre, said three drones had initially been detected in Belarus, but none entered Lithuanian airspace. “They were in Belarusian territory but did not enter Lithuania. One of them entered Latvia and later flew toward northern Russia. During the first episode, residents of the Utena and Vilnius regions were alerted,” Vitkauskas told LRT RADIO. During the second incident, one drone is believed to have entered Lithuania from Belarus in the south, near Druskininkai. It may have briefly crossed into Poland before turning north and flying through the Marijampolė, Kaunas and Panevėžys regions. It left Lithuanian airspace near Pasvalys. Air alerts were issued for Druskininkai, Lazdijai, Marijampolė and Kaunas, as well as the districts of Panevėžys, Radviliškis, Pasvalys and Biržai. Vitkauskas said fighter jets had detected the object but did not shoot it down. “The fighter jets came quite close to making contact. But why they failed to shoot it down [...] it could have been due to poor weather conditions, or perhaps it was an area where shooting down a drone would have been unsafe,” he said. Before the air alerts were issued, the National Crisis Management Centre had also received a warning about possible weather balloons that could disrupt air traffic. “At around 21:30, we received a warning about possible balloons and potential disruptions to airspace. The initial airport closure took place in Vilnius, followed by Kaunas. As the situation escalated and the drones entered, the airspace was closed again,” Vitkauskas said. Preliminary information indicated that only three flights at Vilnius Airport were affected, involving more than 400 passengers, he added. After 03:00 Wednesday, Latvia’s National Armed Forces issued an airspace threat warning for the municipalities of Cesis, Smiltene and Gulbene. The Latvian military said drone interceptors, air defence units and NATO air policing fighter jets had been activated in the Baltic airspace. It remains unclear how many drones were involved in the incidents or whether any crashed or were shot down. Similar warnings were also issued in some areas of Estonia and Lithuania, according to the Latvian military. Debris from a missile fired by a NATO fighter jet was found near the northern Lithuanian town of Biržai on Wednesday, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said. Earlier reports said fighter jets deployed for air defence had failed to shoot down a drone flying over Lithuania overnight. He said service data showed that four unmanned aerial vehicles and dozens of radar tracks associated with smuggled balloons had been recorded in the region overnight. One drone had crossed Lithuanian territory. Air raid warnings were issued in several regions of the country on Tuesday evening and overnight into Wednesday due to the potential drone threat. Sinkevičius urged residents who find suspicious objects not to approach or touch them, but to report them to the authorities. He also said the overnight events would be thoroughly investigated. The National Crisis Management Centre and the military are expected to provide further details on the situation later on Wednesday. Belarus warned Lithuania about possible drone incursions Belarus warned Lithuania on Tuesday evening about unidentified objects potentially flying toward its territory, prompting an air alert in two Lithuanian counties, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Wednesday. “At 22:47, information was received from the Belarusian side via a technical line that unidentified objects were flying toward Lithuania, which Belarus was trying to neutralise. [...[ The objects did not enter Lithuanian airspace; they turned toward Latvia and Russia,” Kaunas told LRT. The warning prompted a yellow-level air alert in the Vilnius and Utena counties. After midnight, another drone entered Lithuanian airspace. It briefly crossed into Poland before returning to Lithuania and eventually flying into Latvia. Yellow- and red-level air alerts were issued in all areas over which the object passed, Kaunas said. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said earlier Wednesday that four drones had disrupted airspace in the region overnight. Kaunas said the drones were most likely Ukrainian and had been intended to target the Russian port of Ust-Luga and other locations in Russia but had drifted off course. Lithuania is cooperating with Poland, Latvia and Estonia to investigate the circumstances of the incidents, the minister added. A drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday was targeted twice in attempts to shoot it down and was also tracked in Latvia, but no further information about it is available, officials said. “Flying north towards Panevėžys, air defence aircraft made two attempts to destroy this unmanned aerial vehicle. The attempts were unsuccessful due to various conditions,” Rear Admiral Giedrius Premeneckas, Chief of the Defence Staff of the Lithuanian Armed Forces, told reporters. According to Premeneckas, after leaving Lithuania, the drone flew across Latvia and entered the neighbouring country’s military area of responsibility. “The drone then left Latvian territory, entered Estonian territory and, according to our information, later flew into Russian territory,” the military official said.
