More than 125 million text messages leaked over four years have been found in a publicly accessible database belonging to the Latvian branch of telecommunications company CSCTelecom, including sensitive data belonging to Lithuanian businesses and their customers, the technology and cybersecurity news website Cybernews reported. Cybernews researchers discovered leaked data associated with Lithuanian companies and organisations including EuroCash1, Akropolis, Depo, Iki, Perlas Go, Autoplius, Šypsenos akademija, Denticija, airBaltic and Porsche. The exposed information included personal and internal business phone numbers, order numbers, two-factor authentication (2FA) codes, flight details, surnames and other sensitive data. “The leaked information makes it possible to build extremely detailed profiles of individual users. Even without seeing the contents of messages, knowing which services a person uses opens the door to highly targeted data fraud attacks,” Voldemaras Kadys, head of security and platform engineering at Mediatech, the digital publishing company that operates Cybernews, said in a statement. According to Kadys, messages associated with EuroCash1 exposed phone numbers and security alerts concerning protected premises and ATMs. Data linked to Depo included phone numbers, order IDs and status updates, while messages associated with Akropolis revealed internal phone numbers and visitor traffic statistics. Messages linked to Iki contained phone numbers and authentication codes. Those associated with airBaltic exposed customers’ phone numbers, flight information and surnames. The incident also raises questions about compliance with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Kadys said. Under the regulation, companies must retain personal data only for as long as necessary to fulfil the purposes for which it was collected. “The publicly accessible archive contained data dating back four years, raising serious security concerns,” he said. According to the researchers, the exposed records covered the period from October 2022 to September 2026, and the database was continuously updated. This meant that criminals could potentially intercept authentication codes, password-reset links and private information before the intended recipients even saw the messages, Cybernews said. The company was notified of the security vulnerability on September 29, according to the news outlet. The database was closed on October 27 and is currently inaccessible. The breach affected organisations across the Baltic states. In Latvia, researchers also found SMS messages associated with Swedbank, SEB, medical institutions, online stores, government organizations and the country's emergency number, 112. In Estonia, the affected businesses included local operations of airBaltic and Depo.

Lithuanian lawmaker Ignas Vėgėlė has expressed hope that diplomatic relations between Lithuania and China can be restored following a meeting with visiting Chinese diplomats, but declined to disclose details of their discussions. “In my view, we should define what tasks we set ourselves and whether we want to restore relations and diplomatic representation with China,” Vėgėlė told reporters Wednesday when asked about Beijing’s conditions for improving ties with Vilnius. “The content of the discussion, including what the Chinese diplomats and Foreign Ministry representatives would like, is confidential, and we do not wish to disclose it. This is a matter for the Foreign Ministry,” he added. A Chinese delegation has arrived in Lithuania as Vilnius explores ways to restore diplomatic representation between the two countries. A meeting with the Lithuanian Foreign Ministry is scheduled for Thursday, although Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys will not attend. Vėgėlė, who chairs a temporary parliamentary group seeking to restore diplomatic relations with China to the level maintained by other European Union member states, said he had not heard of the conditions reportedly being imposed by Beijing. “I have not heard any of the messages you are mentioning today, suggesting that there are numerous conditions and that they have been laid out,” he said. Lawmakers Rimas Jonas Jankūnas, Vitalijus Šeršniovas and Karolis Neimantas also attended Wednesday’s meeting. The Chinese delegation included Zheng Huiyu, deputy director general of the Department of European Affairs at China’s Foreign Ministry, and Fang Mei, a counsellor at China’s Mission to the European Union and representative to Lithuania, along with other diplomats. Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Lithuanian parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, said the meeting had been organised on the initiative of the parliamentary group and was not part of the Chinese delegation’s official programme. “Today, we believe it is not expedient for parliamentary politicians to meet. On the other hand, a member of parliament, a politician, has the right to meet anyone. Therefore, we do not consider this meeting official. It is an initiative of that group and is not included in the official programme of the visit,” Motuzas said earlier Wednesday. He stressed that the objective was to restore diplomatic representation rather than political relations, adding that Lithuania had not forgotten the “threat” posed by China. The government led by Social Democrat Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has included the restoration of diplomatic representation with China in its programme. The Foreign Ministry said Thursday’s meeting would form part of regular consultations with China on the conditions for accrediting diplomats in Vilnius and Beijing. The ministry said it had submitted specific proposals for restoring the operations of diplomatic missions and remained open to dialogue based on Lithuania’s interests, international law and national legislation. Budrys said he expected neither a major breakthrough nor disappointment from the meeting. Relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in 2021 after Vilnius allowed Taipei to open a Taiwanese Representative Office in the Lithuanian capital. Similar offices in other countries generally operate under the name of Taipei, rather than Taiwan. Beijing strongly objected to the decision, and Chinese state media have previously reported that changing the office’s name alone would not be sufficient to restore relations. News website Delfi reported this week that the Lithuanian Foreign Ministry had suggested in September that the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius change its name. In return, Lithuania reportedly offered several bilateral economic agreements and the appointment of a special envoy for Taiwan at the ministry. Budrys confirmed that the possibility of changing the office’s name had been discussed with Taiwan but stressed that it had not been presented as an ultimatum. Following the office’s opening in 2021, Beijing unilaterally downgraded diplomatic representation with Lithuania from ambassadorial to chargé d'affaires level. Lithuania subsequently refused to issue new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, leaving China without diplomats stationed in the country since May last year.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda has warned that Russia is unlikely to agree to a ceasefire in Ukraine in the near future, saying Moscow could use ongoing peace negotiations to buy time while continuing its aggression. Speaking to LRT in Dublin on Wednesday evening after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Nausėda said he remained sceptical that the diplomatic efforts would bring an immediate end to the fighting. His comments came as Dublin prepared to host the ninth European Political Community (EPC) summit on Thursday, bringing together leaders of around 50 countries and international organisations. The meeting coincides with renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including talks involving Ukrainian, Russian and US representatives. US President Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were expected to travel to Moscow after two days of negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the United States in Abu Dhabi, before heading to Dublin to meet Zelensky. All sides described the Abu Dhabi talks as cautiously positive. “These are only the initial stages of negotiations. I remain of the opinion that Russia will still use the coming winter to torment the people of Ukraine,” Nausėda said. He suggested Moscow might seek to prolong the process, possibly agreeing to minor issues while avoiding a ceasefire. “They will try to buy time and pretend to negotiate, perhaps even reach agreements on some nonessential matters. But expecting a ceasefire – which, in my view, should be the main condition of peace negotiations – would be difficult at this point,” he said. Nausėda noted, however, that the sides had agreed on the release of prisoners. The negotiations have also seen Russia call for a review of Europe’s security architecture, reviving demands that NATO withdraw its forces from eastern European countries. Nausėda firmly rejected the possibility of accepting Moscow’s demands. “In my view, the European security architecture, shaped primarily by NATO as a transatlantic and collective security organisation, must remain in place. There should be no spheres of influence,” he said. Russia issued a demand in late 2021 to withdraw NATO forces from eastern European countries, Nausėda noted. “This must not happen. I believe all European leaders understand this perfectly well, and nobody will ever agree to such conditions,” he said. The issue is expected to feature prominently at the EPC summit on Thursday and an informal European Council meeting scheduled for Friday in Dublin. Another question gaining prominence in discussions about a possible peace settlement is who should represent Europe if it is included in negotiations. Some European Union countries have recently called for the bloc to have a stronger role in the process, a position also raised by the United States. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Kushner said Wednesday after the Abu Dhabi talks. Several names have been mentioned in diplomatic circles, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who recently spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, Norway is not an EU member, while Stubb does not attend European Council meetings, which are attended by Finland’s prime minister. Their conversation with Putin has also drawn criticism. Nausėda said European Council President António Costa would be the most appropriate candidate to represent the bloc. “The simplest legal option, and perhaps the person who already has a mandate from the members of the European Council, is António Costa,” he told LRT. “But I know there are other views and opinions, so I do not want to speculate before the issue has even been discussed.” Costa’s candidacy is also being promoted in Brussels. “When issues concern the EU and require collective decision-making within the European Union, the treaties stipulate that the institutions should represent those issues,” a senior EU official told reporters in Brussels on Wednesday. However, the official expressed little hope that EU leaders would agree on appointing a special representative during the Dublin meetings. “If you asked me whether I expect an agreement on a special envoy, my answer would be no. I do not believe so,” the official said.

Lithuanian and Chinese officials held working-level talks Thursday on restoring diplomatic representation in Vilnius and Beijing, but both sides agreed not to disclose details of the meeting. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that the meeting took place November 12, saying the discussions focused on possible ways to restore diplomatic representation. The two sides agreed to continue consultations. The Chinese delegation’s visit comes as Lithuania seeks to repair relations with Beijing, which deteriorated after Vilnius allowed Taiwan to open a representative office in its capital under the name Taiwanese Representative Office. Similar offices in other countries operate under the name Taipei. In response, Beijing unilaterally downgraded its diplomatic representation in Lithuania from ambassadorial to chargé d’affaires level. Lithuania subsequently declined to issue new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, leaving China without diplomatic representatives in the country since May 2025. Ahead of Thursday’s meeting, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said no concrete decisions should be expected. He described the talks as part of an ongoing diplomatic process and said further steps would depend on their outcome. The delegation also met Lithuanian lawmakers Ignas Vėgėlė, Rimas Jonas Jankūnas, Vitalijus Sersniovas and Karolis Neimantas on Wednesday. It includes Zheng Huiyu, deputy director general of the European Affairs Department at China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and Fang Mei, a counsellor at the Chinese Mission to the European Union and representative to Lithuania. The Delfi news portal reported this week that Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry proposed in September that the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius change its name in exchange for several bilateral economic agreements and the appointment of a special envoy for Taiwan at the ministry. According to the report, Taiwan was asked to make a decision by October 1. Budrys confirmed that the diplomatic discussions had addressed possible timelines, taking into account the political circumstances in both countries, but declined to provide specific dates. He also cautioned that changing the office’s name would not, by itself, guarantee increased investment from Taiwan, saying that investment decisions depend on business interests and operating conditions.

Last week, NATO fighter jets tried twice to shoot down a stray drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, unsuccessfully. While human lives put at risk by such incursions are invaluable, how sound is the rationale of using missiles worth hundreds of thousands of euros to shoot down relatively cheap drones? The suspected Ukrainian drone entered Lithuania from Belarus, briefly crossed into Poland and then returned to Lithuanian airspace. NATO fighter jets identified it over Kaunas, Lithuania’s second-largest city, but could not fire at it because it was flying over an urban area, where falling debris could cause damage, Rear Adm. Giedrius Premeneckas, head of the Lithuanian military’s Defence Staff, said. Two subsequent attempts to neutralise the drone failed. Debris from one missile fell in the Biržai district, while the other apparently failed to fire. “The aircraft, together with the missile, landed safely on the ground, and it is now up to the country that was carrying out the air policing mission to determine what happened to it,” army commander Raimundas Vaikšnoras said. Italy and Belgium are currently conducting NATO’s air policing mission in Lithuania. Retired Maj. Darius Antanaitis told LRT that Italian pilots flying Eurofighter Typhoon jets were likely responsible for the attempts. The aircraft can use several types of weapons, including short-range IRIS-T and AIM-9 missiles. Antanaitis said one of these was likely used. An IRIS-T missile costs about 400,000 euros, while an AIM-9 Sidewinder can cost between 500,000 and 900,000 euros. A Eurofighter Typhoon’s flight hour costs about 50,000 euros, he estimated, excluding ground crews, maintenance and other expenses. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said the cost of a missile launch amounts to several hundred thousand euros, not millions. NATO mission participants currently cover the expenses, but Lithuania is seeking an agreement on sharing the financial burden. Some social media users have questioned the use of expensive missiles against drones worth only tens of thousands of euros. Antanaitis argued that the comparison overlooks the potential damage a drone could cause and the military’s purpose of protecting the population. Arūnas Kumpis, a drone operator and volunteer who fought in Ukraine, raised another concern: Lithuania has limited stocks of missiles designed to destroy more dangerous targets, including aircraft and missiles carrying large explosive payloads. Using those weapons against cheap drones could leave the country less prepared for more serious attacks, he told LRT. He suggested using electronic warfare equipment and interceptor drones instead, as Ukraine does, but said Lithuania lacks an advanced system to track and classify drones. Kaunas said Lithuania began developing an integrated counter-drone defence system this year and hopes it will be operational by the end of 2027. The system is intended to combine data from radars, acoustic sensors, cameras and electronic intelligence equipment. Three or four companies have been shortlisted for a government procurement project, and the minister hopes to sign a contract by the end of this year, with prototypes available for military testing in March or April 2027.

The demands put forward by Russian negotiators during talks on ending the war in Ukraine include bans on setting up NATO military bases in the Baltic states and Finland withdrawing from NATO, the German newspaper Bild reported Friday. The unofficial proposals, presented to European representatives in Abu Dhabi, are part of Russia’s stated aim of negotiating a new security order in Europe. Russia is reportedly seeking a ban on NATO military bases in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Finland, which joined the alliance in 2023, would be required to withdraw and return to its neutral status. In return, Russia is offering to withdraw its nuclear weapons from Belarus and refrain from deploying intermediate-range missiles there, according to the report. Under the Kremlin’s reported proposals, Russia would retain all Ukrainian territories currently under its occupation and take control of the entire Donbas region, including parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions still under Ukrainian control. The ports of Odesa and Mykolaiv would be demilitarised and prohibited from being used as naval bases. Separate agreements would guarantee freedom of navigation in the Black and Baltic seas, Bild reported. The proposals would also require Ukraine to remain permanently outside military alliances, ruling out NATO membership while leaving open the possibility of joining the European Union. Regarding Moldova, the plan envisages the creation of a federal republic comprising the country’s main territory, the breakaway region of Transnistria and the autonomous region of Gagauzia. If Moldova joined the EU, Transnistria and Gagauzia would be allowed to hold referendums on independence. The Bild report follows an earlier account by US news outlet Axios, which cited two sources familiar with the negotiations as saying that President Donald Trump’s administration had asked Russia to present proposals for a future security agreement with Europe.

Lithuanian Airports sees no indications that Latvian carrier airBaltic plans to discontinue its flights between Vilnius and Lisbon or Hamburg, despite the airline’s decision to drop another route and significantly scale back its operations in Lithuania. Diana Bankauskienė, interim head of Lithuanian Airports, said the Lisbon and Hamburg routes, which have operated since May 2024 under risk-sharing agreements, remained attractive, with strong passenger load factors and further growth potential. Despite airBaltic’s plans to discontinue its Vilnius-Düsseldorf route, reduce the number of aircraft based in Vilnius, halve the number of destinations served from Lithuania next summer and lay off some employees, Bankauskienė said the situation remained under control. Transport Minister Juras Taminskas has said a contingency plan is being prepared in case the airline further reduces its operations in Lithuania or withdraws from the country altogether, urging the public not to panic prematurely. AirBaltic announced last week that it would suspend flights between Vilnius and Düsseldorf from November 23 because the route had performed below expectations. Lithuanian Airports said it would challenge the decision and seek to recover the money invested in the route through the airline’s restructuring proceedings in a US court. If necessary, it would also contest the termination of the agreement in Lithuanian courts. “In our assessment, the route can become profitable in the future and has potential, which is why our strategy is to challenge airBaltic’s decision and seek to prevent the agreement from being terminated altogether,” Bankauskienė said. She noted that proceedings in a US bankruptcy court involved a different legal jurisdiction, procedures and rules, making the process relatively unfamiliar to Lithuanian Airports. “We are preparing the documents, there will be hearings as part of the proceedings, and then we will see what the outcome might be,” she said. The airport operator is also considering legal action in Lithuania because the agreement was concluded under Lithuanian law. “Our main goal, of course, is to preserve the agreement, as funds have been invested,” Bankauskienė said. She declined to disclose the value of the agreement, saying it was based on a business plan that included projected returns on investment and an assessment of both parties’ costs under the risk-sharing arrangement. Lithuanian Airports is also negotiating with other airlines in an effort to maintain the Düsseldorf connection. Bankauskienė declined to identify the carriers involved, citing commercial confidentiality. She neither confirmed nor denied reports that Lithuanian Airports was in talks with Eurowings, part of Germany’s Lufthansa Group. Eurowings said it was “closely monitoring the situation at Vilnius Airport and constantly evaluating opportunities regarding its route network”. Lithuanian Airports received a 3.2-million-euro capital injection in April to ensure the continuity of flights to Hamburg, Lisbon and Düsseldorf, as well as to support the launch of a new route to one of London’s main airports. The airport operator launched a tender in April for flights from Vilnius to Gatwick, Heathrow or London City but suspended it in June after receiving only one bid. The bidder’s business plan for Gatwick did not “ensure the economic sustainability of the route”. In early September, the Transport Ministry, which is Lithuanian Airports’ shareholder, said a new tender was expected to be launched shortly. However, Bankauskienė said the airport operator was currently focusing on commercial negotiations with airlines and did not plan to launch another tender under the risk-sharing model in the near future. Its aim is to establish a London connection on a commercial basis. She added that air connectivity between Vilnius and London remained good, with passengers able to choose direct flights or connections through other European capitals. Direct flights between Vilnius and London City were discontinued at the end of March by Lithuanian Airports and LOT Polish Airlines because the route was unprofitable. It had also operated under a risk-sharing agreement.

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said Thursday that if all European countries cannot participate directly in negotiations on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine, they should be represented by European Union institutions. Speaking to LRT TV, Budrys said Lithuania, which borders Russia and Belarus, must have a voice in the negotiations. However, if there is insufficient room for every European country at the negotiating table, EU institutions would be best placed to represent their interests. He said the bloc already had established procedures for member states to submit their positions, which are then consolidated by EU institutions while ensuring accountability. Budrys also questioned whether individual political figures had a mandate to represent Europe, stressing that efforts to establish a common European position should continue. EU member states have yet to agree on who should represent the bloc in potential peace negotiations on Ukraine. Some countries believe current EU leaders could take on the role, while others favour appointing a dedicated envoy or forming a group of representatives from several member states. Meanwhile, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda did not rule out Thursday the possibility of European Council President António Costa representing Europe in the negotiations.

Palantir, a controversial AI software company, is entering Lithuania, where the country’s military is eyeing procurement of a tool already used in combat. But enabling algorithmic decision-making carries its own risks. AI-powered autonomous weapons platforms that can kill people at their own choosing – something like in sci-fi Hollywood movies – are still some time away, if at all possible. But algorithmic targeting – where a machine collects data and presents options to the commander on where and what to strike – is already being used in combat. Thus the system is already helping make life-or-death decisions, confirmed Peter Andrysiak, a retired US general and former chief of staff at US European Command, now a senior counsellor at Palantir. ​Having an algorithm gather and process data speeds up laborious tasks, like checking different drone footage or analysing intelligence data, Palantir reps told LRT.lt in interviews on the sidelines of the Defending Baltics event in Vilnius last month. “If you understood the pace of what a [military] headquarters does on a daily basis, most of that time gets spent not thinking,” said Andrysiak. He joined the company after retiring from the military, where he took part in efforts to bring Palantir’s technologies to use in the American military. ​Cognitive surrender and military AI agents During a side event at the Defending Baltics event, Palantir representatives demonstrated the workings of one of its main military-grade softwares, Maven Smart System (MSS). ​Although the presentation was introduced as a look inside AI in combat, the actual footage showed little – if any – use of AI in the software. Only after questions from the audience, Palantir reps explained – not showed – the AI potential when coupled with this software. “AI can work on top of sensors and find the target you're looking for; it's a huge cognitive load on staff. AI can say: ‘I found the target you're looking for– here's a range of options and effectors [weapons],” said Andrysiak. ​But it doesn't automatically destroy targets, he added. The company is now introducing agentic AI models, whereby the system takes upon a role normally occupied by a member of staff at the military headquarters. This is already in use in the US, he confirmed. “I know that even in NATO, because NATO's purchased Maven Smart System, they're getting to the point where they're actually able to start building agents and using those agents to do work for them as well,” Andrysiak added. The platform also has a version of a large-language model (LLM), where users can ask the platform questions like you would do on a civilian AI platform – but, again, in a military context. “What it can do is then bring all of that into much like a typical query that you would do on a desktop, but it's working on the data that's on your platform,” he said. ​The AI-led targeting process is what researchers and human rights activists are most concerned about – the so-called cognitive surrender, which leads people to accept algorithmic-presented answers as the truth. “There are absolutely risks,” said Andrysiak, adding that human oversight was necessary. But that’s only possible if humans retain “meaningful control”, according to analysts and campaigners for AI safety, with time and capacity to analyse and verify algorithmic data. There have already been dangerous precedents. ​A past investigation into AI-targeting tools used by Israel in its Gaza operation showed disproportionate civilian casualties. Whistleblowers in the Israeli security forces told reporters about being presented with targeting options without knowing how the system arrived at the conclusion or what the implications were, because they either didn't have the time to confirm the data or were under pressure to act. The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) denied the allegations, saying “information systems are merely tools for analysts in the target identification process and that analysts “must conduct independent examinations”. Another incident is also under scrutiny amid the US-Israel war against Iran. In February, a system using Palantir technology misidentified a girls’ school in Iran as a military target, leading to widespread child deaths. ​A Palantir representative responsible for civil liberties, Richard Evens, refused to answer a question regarding the incident to the audience in Vilnius, citing the ongoing investigation.​ Evans stressed that a human maintains oversight and control of the algorithmic data analysis in the software. “The image of AI finding and executing targets is not a reflection of reality,” he said. “Fundamentally, targeting is a human-driven, regulated, and governed process.” ​But AI could still make independent decisions. As an example, the platform could decide to send a drone to “collect additional data”, Evans said. In late October, Lithuanian Defence Minister Kaunas announced that the country’s military is considering buying Palantir technology. “It is being considered, and there will be further discussions, as we need a technological solution that would bring together all the data, of which there is certainly a great deal,” the minister told TV3 Žinios on Wednesday. According to Lithuania’s TV3 news, the technology would cost Lithuania some 200 million euros over a seven-year period.​ The country’s defence budget for 2026 was 4.7 billion euros. “Artificial intelligence could be used to analyse the data and manage certain aspects of the battlefield, for example. So Lithuania, like other NATO member states, needs this kind of software,” he said. In an interview with the Baltic News Service published on November 4, Kaunas said Palantir technology could help process data. “A soldier or an individual can do that, but artificial intelligence can also do it by providing recommendations,” he said. In a written answer to LRT.lt, the Lithuanian Defence Ministry said it signed a memorandum of understanding with Palantir Technologies on April 25, 2023

The Taiwan question was blown wide open when news surfaced of Vilnius asking Taipei to rename its office. Delfi broke the news earlier this week, citing sources who said a document was given to Taiwanese representatives back in September. In it, Vilnius calls for the request to rename the office to remain confidential . Several MPs welcomed Chinese representatives into the parliament this week, who have also met with Foreign Ministry reps. So far everyone is tight-lipped about the contents of the discussions. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda did not confirm whether Vilnius really asked Taiwan to rename its de facto embassy in an effort to mend ties with Beijing that ruptured in 2021. Nausėda did say that all moves are coordinated with him, unlike “the nonsense” that took place under the previous government. Gabrielius Landsbergis, the former foreign minister who spearheaded the Taiwan pivot, was critical , saying Lithuania risked being branded “a country that broke”. He also threw the “nonsense” jab back at the president, saying what was happening now could be called the same. MORE DRONES So we had another drone incident . First, three unidentified objects approached from Belarus, but then moved north into Russia. Then, likely a Ukrainian stray drone entered Lithuania from Belarus via Poland. This happened as Kyiv launched drone attacks on Russia’s St Petersburg region. Here’s the problematic part: the drone moved across the whole country before entering Estonia and Latvia where local authorities also declared air alerts. At first, it couldn’t be shot down as it flew over urban centres. Then, two attempts by NATO fighter jets to shoot it down failed, with one of the missiles missing and exploding in rural Lithuania. Not great. NO WAY The Russian ultimatum for NATO to pull back its forces to the 1997 borders is back on the agenda? Instead of writing it off as a nonstarter which it had always been, the US side keeps referring to a “European security” structure that Moscow is pushing for. Vilnius officials are not happy, with Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys saying Russia cannot have a veto over NATO activities in Eastern Europe and the Baltics. ENERGY ISLANDS Lithuania announced an ambitious plan to subdivide the country’s energy grid into seven independent “islands” that could function autonomously. This would involve building 10 additional power plants, with the private sector expected to invest some 880 million euros. More details here . RUNNING ON FUMES? Swedbank announced the end of the economic boom, cutting Lithuania’s growth forecast. The country is also hearing alarm bells over a projected budget deficit amid accelerating defence and social security spending, with the shortage of cash leaving politicians to eye new taxes. This, of course, received an immediate rebuke from business leaders. One option to fill coffers is introducing a tax on windfall profits of energy companies, with Poland’s Orlen being seen as the biggest dish on the table. For its part, Orlen said it might shut the refinery entirely. But despite the doom and gloom, food prices in Lithuania continued to fall even amid the spiking inflation. Economists are not sure why. DEMOGRAPHIC CRISIS Unmarried couples and single women will now have access to assisted reproduction services, according to a new law adopted on Thursday. This comes amid Lithuania grappling with a demographic crisis and seeking ways to increase child births. One politician in favour of the changes said it could lead to 500 to 600 additional births annually. And amid rising cases of abuse, here are some ways you can recover unpaid wages. – Vilnius is entering a new phase of growth (and it’s not all good news). – And please pay for your online content. In September, 68-year-old Russian citizen Igor Odintsov fled across the Nemunas River from Russia’s Kaliningrad region to Lithuania, but was handed over to Russian border guards five hours later. He was subsequently sentenced in Russia to six years in prison for condemning the war in Ukraine. Odintsov is a surveyor from the town of Sovetsk in the Kaliningrad region. According to his friend Boris, who spoke to journalists from the Sever.Realii news outlet, Odintsov had consistently opposed Soviet rule. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had also spoken out against Vladimir Putin and the Russian authorities. “He held anti-communist and anti-Soviet views, and now takes an anti-Russian position,” Boris said. Alyona Dergacheva, a former journalist with the now-defunct independent news outlet Mediazona, reported receiving a letter from him while he was being held in a temporary detention centre. In the letter, he described the circumstances of his detention on the Lithuanian side of the border and said he had explained to border guards why he did not want to return to Russia. “Barefoot and wearing only swimming trunks, I walked 4–5km before meeting a border patrol vehicle coming from Rambynas. I explained to the officers that I was seeking political asylum. I told them that I had crossed the border to avoid punishment under Article 205.2, Part 2 of the Russian Criminal Code,” Odintsov wrote. The sentence against Odintsov was handed down because he had, “holding radical views and harbouring negative attitudes towards the Russian Federation’s state authorities, as well as being an opponent of the special military operation, published information in one of the online messaging applications in which the ideology and practice of terrorism were presented as justified”. According to Odintsov, the officers took him to a border post, where they gave him a blanket, clothes and shoes. He was questioned for several hours but, he claims, was never offered the opportunity to submit a written application for asylum. “I was questioned (apparently as part of the standard procedure). They took a long time to establish when I had crossed the border, but gave me no answer at all. Later, as 18:00 approached, I was taken to Panemunė and handed over to Russian border guards on the bridge. The Lithuanian officers told them that no criminal proceedings had been initiated against me in Lithuania. “Throughout my time at the border post, I was not given the opportunity to submit a written application,” Odintsov told the independent journalist. At the same time, he stressed that he had no negative feelings towards the Lithuanian authorities. “In my opinion, an independent country, whether Lithuania or China, has the right to determine its own migration policy. However, looking back at my actions, I am disappointed and angry with myself for taking such a dangerous step (I nearly died while sailing – I am no longer young) without even bothering to check or look up online what that country's migration policy was,” the journalist quoted Odintsov as saying. State Border Guard Service: no legal grounds The State Border Guard Service (VSAT) said that, following an individual assessment of the circumstances, it had decided not to allow the man to enter the country and to return him to Russia. Its representatives said they could not regard his words as a clear request for international protection. VSAT adviser Giedrius Mišutis told LRT.lt that the border guards had noticed indications that the man might intend to seek asylum. According to Mišutis, Odintsov was detained after crossing the border. At the time, he was attempting to avoid contact with border guards. Following his detention, as in other similar cases, an individual assessment of his situation was carried out. “First of all, his health was assessed, of course. He was in good health. Border guards provided him with dry clothes and footwear. His circumstances, legal status, situation, potential threats and all other factors relevant to assessing his position in Lithuania were then established,” the VSAT representative said. He said the assessment took more than five hours, from the moment of Odintsov’s detention until his return to Russia. During that time, border guards not only questioned the man but also examined the information he provided, as well as intelligence obtained from other agencies. Mišutis explained that the initial conversation had revealed indications that the man might wish to apply for international protection, in other words, seek asylum. However, border guards had doubts about whether his words could be considered a clearly expressed intention to request asylum. According to the VSAT, the assessment found no circumstances that would have prevented the man from returning to Russia. “It should be emphasised that, from the moment of his detention until his return to Russia, the foreign national never once reported that his life or freedom would be at risk in his country of origin,” Mišutis said. Interior Ministry: no questions on border guard conduct On the day of the incident, Lithuanian media initially quoted Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas as saying that the man who had arrived in Lithuania had requested asylum. ​LRT.lt contacted the ministry to ask for clarification of the minister’s statement but received no response. Commenting on other aspects of the incident, the Lithuanian Interior Ministry stressed that it trusted the professionalism of the border guards and had no intention of taking any action against them. “The ministry trusts the professionalism and competence of VSAT staff,” Mindaugas Bajarūnas, head of the Interior Ministry’s Strategic Communications Department, said in a comment provided to LRT.lt. The ministry said it did not assess the information published by Russian media outlets. The ministry later expanded its comment, explaining why the foreign national’s actions had been assessed as an attempt to enter Lithu

False bomb threats on planes and sabotage create a new pressure scenario on European societies. Russia appears in numerous investigations of these hybrid threats and disposable agents, but it is not the only one. France attributes the attack against hundreds of supermarkets to Iran; China develops influence and coercion operations, and the border pressure in southern Europe by Morocco also falls under that array of hybrid threats, which constitute the challenge of autocratic regimes against democratic and free societies. The latest bomb threats, all false, against commercial planes triggered alarms and initiated emergency protocols, flight diversions, and passenger evacuations while security teams inspected the airplanes. This wave of false threats disrupted European air traffic. Although no explosives were found, each message activated a security device, mobilized resources, and sowed uncertainty among thousands of travelers. The operation managed to produce real effects without placing a single bomb. The same has happened this week with threats in more than 6,000 Italian schools. These false threats are not the only alarm signal in European skies. Interferences in satellite navigation systems, false GPS signals, and drone incursions have forced a review of procedures and increased surveillance. On land, there are fires, sabotage, cyberattacks, and disinformation operations. At sea, the target is the underwater cables. And, increasingly, people recruited via the internet appear to carry out tasks that can range from placing stickers or gathering information to starting a fire or participating in a cyberattack. Not all these episodes have the same origin nor can they be automatically attributed to the same actor. But they share a common scenario: a Europe under increasing pressure in that gray area between peace and war. Sometimes the objective is to destroy; other times, it is enough to interrupt a service, force the deployment of resources, test a response, or convince the population that nothing is safe and that their governments are ineffective. From the sabotage attributed to Russia in Central and Eastern Europe and the recruitment of collaborators, the map of this shadow war is broader than a confrontation between Moscow and the West. It also includes influence campaigns linked to China and forms of geopolitical and border pressure exercised by other states, such as Morocco in Ceuta. In addition to causing fear and chaos among passengers, the threats allow for observing how airports react, how long it takes to activate protocols, and what resources the authorities mobilize. They are an attempt at hybrid aggression and psychological warfare. However, a bomb threat is not the same as interference in navigation systems or a drone incursion. They are distinct phenomena, with different mechanisms and risk levels. That they occur in the same context of tension does not prove that they respond to a single operation nor that they necessarily have the same perpetrator. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) has detected a significant increase in interferences in navigation systems. The episodes are especially concentrated in areas close to conflicts and strategic zones: the Baltic, the Black Sea, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and the Arctic. Their consequences can include positioning errors, alterations in navigation systems, and abnormal alerts, which require crews and controllers to apply alternative procedures. In this area, there is indeed a formal international attribution. In October 2025, the Assembly of the International Civil Aviation Organization condemned Russia for harmful interferences in systems that affect air operations in Europe, based on evidence presented by Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, and Sweden. This condemnation, however, does not allow attributing to Russia any GPS incident that occurs in Europe. Caution in attribution is essential: in hybrid warfare, confusion can be part of the objective. The interferences are compounded by recurrent drone incursions. Their unauthorized flights or sightings near airports, military facilities, and critical infrastructure can force temporary closure of airspace, interrupt operations, and test surveillance systems. A commercial drone can be cheap and relatively easy to acquire, but its use for observing, provoking an alarm, or interfering with strategic activity can result in disproportionate consequences. The shadow war also unfolds underwater. Undersea telecommunications and energy cables are essential for the functioning of European economies. They carry communications, data, and electricity between countries. Their strategic importance contrasts with their physical vulnerability. There have been incidents in the Baltic Sea where vessels have damaged cables and other underwater infrastructures. In some cases, anchor drags and shipping routes have raised suspicions. Concern extends to the protection of energy infrastructure, ports, communication networks, and the systems that allow the everyday functioning of countries. The problem is that these infrastructures are extensive, difficult to monitor, and, in many cases, privately owned. Their protection requires cooperation between governments, businesses, armed forces, and security agencies. It also requires the ability to detect anomalies and share information quickly. Hybrid threats are not new. They combine known instruments -espionage, sabotage, propaganda, economic pressure, or the instrumentalization of social conflicts- with technologies and forms of action that multiply their reach. The novelty lies in the combination, speed, and difficulty in identifying those behind them. Hybrid warfare develops in the context of armed conflict, while hybrid threats can also operate in peacetime, in that gray area where there is no declaration of war, but there is sustained confrontation. With increasing exploitation of foreign workers, a Cameroonian student found himself facing appalling working conditions. He was threatened with a 1,500-euro fine for disclosing information about his contract, while the company refused to pay his wage when he decided to leave the job. Emmanuel is a student from Cameroon who came to Lithuania to pursue a master’s degree in social sciences. He already holds a bachelor’s degree in sociology and anthropology. “I decided to pursue a master’s degree to improve my skills in dealing with social problems in my community. Cameroon has been experiencing a social and political crisis for the past 10 years. “This crisis has caused widespread trauma, claimed many lives and resulted in the loss of property. There is no longer any stability in people’s lives. I could not continue my studies in Cameroon, so I decided to pursue them abroad,” Emmanuel told LRT.lt. The student arrived in Lithuania a year ago. He attended lectures for several months without working before finding a job at a construction company. However, Emmanuel said he had concerns about the company’s operations from the outset. “The recruitment process seemed strange to me, but I had arrived in a new country and did not know how the system worked. I had never worked in Europe before,” the Cameroonian said. According to the student, the construction company told him to register as self-employed. There was no proper recruitment process and no employment contract. Fearing that he would not be covered by health insurance in the event of an accident without an employment contract, Emmanuel soon demanded one. Some time later, he was offered a document which he described as a mockery. “The document was in Lithuanian. I asked how I was supposed to sign something I could not understand, but they told me I did not need to understand it – I just had to sign. I refused, and later translated the document myself,” Emmanuel said. According to him, the document provided no rights for the employee and stipulated financial penalties for various breaches. Emmanuel was also surprised to discover that, when working as a self-employed person, his wages were not transferred automatically – he had to issue an invoice. As he did not speak Lithuanian, he was unable to do this. The company offered to prepare an invoice on his behalf in exchange for a fee, which it deducted from his wages. Emmanuel was also unhappy with the working conditions and eventually decided to quit. Although his contract stipulated that he had to give two weeks’ notice, his employers demanded that he stay for an entire month. According to Emmanuel, a month passed, but he still had not received his final wages. “I said I would contact lawyers, and then my employers sent me documents claiming that I had failed to show up for work. I was scared. I think that was probably their intention – to intimidate me,” Emmanuel recalled. The company demanded that he pay compensation for alleged losses and warned that he would receive a court summons. Frightened, the student asked his employers to keep the money they owed him and let him continue his studies without pursuing legal proceedings. Eventually, Emmanuel managed to contact a trade union, which helped him with the subsequent proceedings. Emilis Starodubovas, head of the May 1st Trade Union (G1PS), recalls that Emmanuel was hired under a contract for services, even though his work had all the characteristics of an employment relationship: subordination, fixed working hours and a stable monthly salary. He says this was how the company concealed the actual nature of the working relationship. Emmanuel’s contract also included various deductions and financial penalties. For example, it stipulated a €50 fee for assistance with issuing an invoice, a €12 fine for an incorrectly issued invoice and an €80 penalty for arriving late to work. Fines of up to €1,500 were also in place for disclosing information about the contract or providing services to other contractors. Starodubovas also notes that the contract included a clause stipulating that, if the employee approached the Labour Disputes Commission or a court seeking recognition of an employment relationship, he would have to cover various costs if the decision went against him. The Labour Disputes Commission later confirmed that the company had failed to fulfil its tax obligations related to the employment relationship, the trade union leader said. Starodubovas points out that migrants are generally more vulnerable in the labour market because they do not speak Lithuanian and lack information about the law and other procedures. “Foreign nationals are often afraid to seek help because they have been seriously misinformed. For example, they may be told that simply initiating legal proceedings will automatically result in them losing their temporary residence permit in Lithuania. “Our experience shows that there are a great many cases of exploitation, and their number is growing. The scale of harm suffered by workers is also increasing,” Starodubovas said. According to the trade union leader, companies often give migrants documents written in Lithuanian without providing them with a separate copy. They are also intimidated with threats that, if illegal employment is discovered, they will face hefty fines or even imprisonment. “In reality, the employer bears full responsibility for illegal employment, but there are many misconceptions,” Starodubovas said. “People often do not even realise that their rights are being violated or that this is not normal practice in Lithuania.” In the first half of this year, labour disputes involving foreign nationals accounted for around 19% of all cases examined, the majority of them involving citizens of non-EU countries, according to the State Labour Inspectorate (VDI). Citizens of non-EU countries most frequently bring claims concerning unpaid wages. Such complaints account for around 78% of all cases involving this group

Vilnius’ Halė Market, the Old and National drama theatres, and Kaunas Mosque are among the best-known buildings designed by Lithuanian architect Wacław Michniewicz (or Vaclovas Michnevičius). Yet the man behind these landmarks remains relatively unknown – a modest, exceptionally productive architect who preferred the quiet of his country estate to the fame and social life of Lithuania’s largest cities. Despite his professional success, Michniewicz spent the final years of his life dispossessed and impoverished after the Soviet authorities seized his estate. Following his death, his wife and daughter were deported, and his family was scattered across Europe. A roadside shrine in Strebeikiai, in the Jonava district, is one of the few reminders of the life that once flourished there. The village was home to the Michniewicz estate, surrounded by tobacco plantations, with lilacs and jasmine growing in the yard. After returning from work in Vilnius or Kaunas, the celebrated architect would put aside his drawings and suit and sit down to eat with farmworkers. Despite having access to the finest restaurants, he preferred simple home cooking, particularly potatoes and sour milk. “He went to church dressed simply. People would tell him: ‘Sir, perhaps you could dress more elegantly, stand out from the grey crowd.’ He would reply that clothes could be simple – what mattered was having a good head,” folk artist and local historian Artūras Narkevičius says. Michniewicz designed at least 30 churches across Lithuania, including those in Birštonas, Žiežmariai, Vievis, Ukmergė, Ramygala, Perloja, Barzdai and Nemunaitis. The actual number may have been considerably higher. “He was not particularly interested in documenting his work. He simply kept working and did not worry much about putting his name on every project,” ethnologist Libertas Klimka said. In 1925, when Michniewicz sought the position of chief architect of Kaunas, he compiled a list of his projects from memory. Some architectural historians believe the number of churches he designed could have been twice as high as the documented figure. Michniewicz was one of the most prolific Lithuanian architects of the early 20th century, but his name was largely absent from public life throughout the Soviet occupation. His religious architecture and biography attracted little interest from the authorities, although much of his architectural legacy survived. One of his most recognisable buildings is the Halė Market in Vilnius, completed in 1906. Its distinctive metal structures have survived largely unchanged. He also designed the former Liutnia Theatre, now the Lithuanian National Drama Theatre, and the building that houses the Old Theatre of Vilnius (formerly the Russian Drama Theatre). He contributed to the interior reconstruction of the present-day National Philharmonic following a fire. His work extended far beyond theatres and churches. Michniewicz designed hospitals, military barracks, warehouses and apartment buildings. He was also involved in the development of the Montvila housing colonies, considered an innovative urban planning concept at the time. As Vilnius’ population grew, he designed spacious apartments for its residents and helped expand the city’s public infrastructure. “Michniewicz was a modern architect of his time,” Klimka said. In 1919, however, Michniewicz left Vilnius, which was then under Polish administration, and moved to Kaunas, Lithuania’s provisional capital. Although he identified as a Pole in Lithuania, he chose to continue his career in the newly established Lithuanian state. There, his work included an unusual commission: the Kaunas Mosque. In 1930, the Lithuanian government decided to build a mosque in recognition of the Tatar Muslim community’s historical contribution to the country. Although the community in Kaunas numbered only about 100 people, the project was entrusted to Michniewicz. Completed in 1931, it was the first brick mosque in the Baltic states. He also worked for the Roads and Highways Board of the Ministry of Transport, contributing to infrastructure projects including the Žemaičių Highway in Kaunas. Despite his professional achievements and invitations to official receptions, Michniewicz remained attached to his estate in Strebeikiai. One of his favourite pastimes was admiring the church he had designed in nearby Žeimiai. According to Narkevičius, the architect considered the church his finest work and often showed it to visitors. “People who knew him and workers who had worked for him said he called this church his calling card. When guests arrived, he would take them to the church or lead them onto the balcony, extend his hand and show how the church stood on his palm,” Narkevičius said. Michniewicz designed the church free of charge. The building was severely damaged during World War One. In 1915, retreating Russian troops mined it to prevent it from being used as an observation post. One tower was partially destroyed, while the organ and stained-glass windows were ruined and the bells were taken away. When Michniewicz returned from the war, he was devastated by the damage. However, rather than demolish the damaged tower and rebuild it, he devised a way to restore the existing structure. Today, the reconstructed tower can still be distinguished by its lighter-coloured bricks. Michniewicz’ attachment to Strebeikiai was rooted in a complicated family history. His mother initially owned the estate and was reportedly unhappy when her son returned from studies in St Petersburg with a German wife. His wife was well-educated, worked as a teacher and spoke several languages, but the relationship between mother and daughter-in-law was strained. According to Klimka, Michniewicz’ mother eventually transferred the estate to another relative rather than her son. The architect later bought it back, apparently because of his deep attachment to the property, although he had little enthusiasm for farming. His final ye

Lithuania plans to opt out of accepting migrants under the European Union’s migration solidarity mechanism and instead make a financial contribution, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Monday. The proposal has been approved by a commission, but the final decision must still be endorsed by the government. “I want to announce that the commission has approved my proposal to contribute to the fund differently, namely by not accepting a single migrant,” Katelynas told reporters. The EU solidarity mechanism requires member states to share responsibility for migrants arriving in countries that serve as their first point of entry into the bloc. Countries can choose whether to accept relocated migrants or make financial contributions instead. In December last year, the Lithuanian government decided that, under the EU Migration and Asylum Pact approved by the Council of the European Union in May 2024, Lithuania would accept half of its allocated migrants and pay a financial contribution for the other half. In May, Lithuania decided to accept 58 migrants from Cyprus and pay 1.4 million euros. However, Katelynas said it was not yet clear how much Lithuania would have to pay if it chose not to accept any migrants. The EU migration and asylum pact aims to establish a common framework for managing migration and sharing responsibility among member states, particularly easing pressure on countries facing the largest numbers of arrivals.

The naming of Taiwan’s representative office in Vilnius is an internal political matter for Lithuania, while the European Union faces broader challenges in its economic relations with China, EU Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Síkela said. The Czech member of the European Commission said he had regularly visited Taiwan, China and Hong Kong during his career as a banker, adding that Prague maintained close ties with Taipei. “Perhaps it is easier for a banker than for a politician. [...] On the other hand, I observed Lithuania’s difficult situation after it was removed from China’s customs system, as well as perhaps greater pressure from some member states, but I will leave the discussion about the office’s name to Lithuanian politicians,” Síkela said in an interview. He said the EU needed to address imbalances in its economic cooperation with China and ensure greater reciprocity for European businesses. “De-risking must not mean decoupling, but we must find the right approach because the current strategy is unbalanced. In Europe, we have 5G vendors from China, but European vendors in China are not considered trusted. This is an issue we must address; there should be a certain level of reciprocity,” the commissioner said. “Anyone from Europe knows how difficult it is to develop a business in China. Perhaps there are a few exceptions. De-risking is necessary, but it should not lead to complete decoupling,” he added. Síkela’s comments come after Lithuanian media reported that the Foreign Ministry had asked the Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius in September to change its name. According to news website Delfi, several bilateral economic agreements and the creation of a special envoy position for Taiwan at the ministry were offered in return. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys confirmed that the terms had been discussed during diplomatic talks, taking into account the political circumstances in both countries, but did not provide specific dates. Meanwhile, Lithuanian and Chinese delegations have discussed the possibility of restoring diplomatic representation in Beijing and Vilnius. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said the talks had created the preconditions for such a move. Diplomatic relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in autumn 2021 after Vilnius allowed Taiwan to open a representative office in the capital under its own name. Similar offices in other countries generally operate under the name Taipei, which Beijing considers less politically sensitive. China subsequently downgraded diplomatic relations with Lithuania and imposed trade restrictions, including removing the country from its customs system.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda on Monday backed Estonia’s decision to close all border crossings with Russia from December, calling it an appropriate response to an alleged sabotage plot linked to Russian military intelligence. “Estonia’s decision is appropriate. Estonia is facing very brazen attempts that can be described as acts of sabotage. These are essentially kinetic acts that create a very dangerous precedent. This is nothing new in the region, so Estonia’s decision seems entirely understandable to me,” Nausėda told reporters. Estonia announced it would close all border crossing points with Russia from December after thwarting an alleged attempt to set fire to a drone factory it linked to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. Nausėda said he did not rule out Lithuania taking similar measures if efforts to destabilise the region continued. “Lithuania could also make such decisions, but we must take all circumstances into account, first and foremost the fact that we are a transit country to Kaliningrad,” he said, referring to Russia’s exclave bordering Lithuania and Poland. “However, if efforts to destabilise the situation in the region continue, there must be a response. Russia does not understand when we fail to react to its actions. It sees that as a sign of weakness. If similar incidents occurred, we would certainly consider measures to prevent them,” the president added. Nausėda said he had been informed about Estonia’s decision by Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. Michal said the GRU had attempted to carry out an act of sabotage Saturday evening at Threod Systems, an Estonian defence industry company that manufactures reconnaissance and combat drones. The alleged plot was uncovered in Viimsi, north of the capital, Tallinn. Security forces have detained eight Latvian residents in connection with the case. Michal described the incident as part of “Russia’s broader hybrid war against Europe” aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and weakening pressure on Moscow.

Lithuania on Monday welcomed two new US Army battalions at the General Silvestras Žukauskas Training Area in Pabradė, strengthening the American military presence on NATO’s eastern flank. The incoming units from the US Army’s 1st Infantry Division include a heavy battalion and an engineering battalion. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said the continued presence of American troops alongside other allied forces was an important deterrent. While Lithuania was strengthening its own defence capabilities, credible deterrence also required allied troops, equipment and readiness to act, he said. US Army troops have been rotating through the Baltic states and Eastern Europe since the spring of 2014 as part of Operation Atlantic Resolve, aimed at reinforcing NATO’s eastern flank. US heavy battalions have been rotating to Lithuania since 2019. This summer, as Washington reviewed its military presence in Europe, just over 100 American troops remained in Lithuania. Plans to deploy two battalions to the country were announced in September. The heavy battalion will conduct armoured reconnaissance, surveillance and security operations. The engineering battalion will focus on ensuring the mobility of allied forces, restricting enemy movement and protecting personnel and military equipment. According to the Ministry of National Defence, the engineering unit’s capabilities will also support joint exercises with the Lithuanian Armed Forces, improve procedures for establishing defensive obstacles and contribute to the implementation of the Baltic Defence Line. The incoming troops will be stationed at the General Silvestras Žukauskas Training Area. More than 55 million euros in additional funding is planned for the site’s infrastructure and host nation support package through 2030.

Lithuania has submitted proposals to the United States on establishing a permanent American military base in the country, with discussions between the two sides ongoing, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Monday. “The proposal package has been discussed and handed over. Again, we should not oversimplify the issue by thinking we just send a letter and get a yes or no answer. This is a long process, long negotiations,” Kaunas told LRT. Lithuania has already begun negotiations with Washington on securing a permanent presence of US troops in the country, he said, noting that Poland had also faced a lengthy wait for a decision on a similar deployment. Kaunas said the decision would depend not only on military infrastructure and capabilities but also on whether Lithuania could provide suitable living conditions for troops and their families, including the necessary civilian infrastructure. He cited the German brigade stationed in Lithuania as an example of the infrastructure and arrangements needed to accommodate a permanent foreign military presence. In early November, Kaunas said he had discussed the possibility of a permanent US troop deployment with US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker. In early October, President Donald Trump suggested Washington would consider establishing a permanent military base in Lithuania. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has previously said Lithuania was prepared to host US troops permanently and cover the costs of a military base.

Lithuania’s Chief of Defence Raimundas Vaikšnoras has suggested installing physical barriers along vulnerable sections of the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region, saying continuous troop patrols are costly and divert soldiers from military training. Vaikšnoras said the military should consider alternatives to maintaining a constant presence along the border, including barriers similar to those installed along Lithuania’s border with Belarus. It was announced Monday that enhanced security measures along the Kaliningrad border had been extended until the end of November. “There is a request from the Ministry of the Interior to extend joint patrolling with border guards to reinforce border security in areas, I stress, in areas that are potentially at highest risk,” Vaikšnoras said. He said the heightened security measures were intended to counter potential activities by hostile saboteurs, draft evaders and smugglers. Although the number of troops deployed along the border remains relatively small, security has been reinforced in specific sectors in cooperation with the State Border Guard Service. Vaikšnoras said army patrols required significant resources and took personnel away from military training, making physical barriers a possible longer-term solution in the most vulnerable areas. Lithuanian military personnel have been assisting the State Border Guard Service along the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region since October 8. In mid-October, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas extended the assistance until mid-November. The armed forces have deployed around 100 troops to patrol areas under the jurisdiction of border checkpoints alongside border guard officers. Mobile patrols, mobile surveillance posts and Military Police units can also be deployed as needed. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas previously described the military deployment as a preventive measure prompted by public reports – rather than intelligence assessments – suggesting that Russia planned to mobilise forces after its State Duma elections. Officials have stressed that the threat level along the border has not increased.

Lithuania continues to have the highest intentional homicide rate in the European Union, but it has also recorded the bloc’s most significant improvement over the past decade, according to Eurostat data. The country recorded 2.63 intentional homicides per 100,000 inhabitants annually, the highest rate in the EU, followed by Latvia, Estonia and Finland, Eurostat reported Wednesday. Although Lithuania has traditionally topped the bloc’s homicide statistics throughout much of its post-independence history, the longer-term trend offers some grounds for optimism. A decade ago, the rate stood at 5.27 homicides per 100,000 inhabitants, meaning it has halved – the largest decline among EU member states. The change is even more striking when measured in absolute numbers. In 2024, 74 people were intentionally killed in Lithuania, compared with 560 in 1994. However, the country’s persistently high ranking reflects deeper social and cultural problems, according to Gintautas Sakalauskas, a criminologist and associate professor at Vilnius University. Sakalauskas said Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia had historically recorded the highest homicide rates in Europe, pointing to a culture of violence, aggression and disrespect. Some of the underlying causes, he said, can be traced back to childhood, infancy and upbringing. “Statistics show that there is a great deal of aggression. Other indicators point to the same thing: domestic violence and bullying in schools,” Sakalauskas said. Lithuania also stands out for its number of serious bodily injury cases. Violent incidents in the country are more likely to result in death or severe injuries than in many other European countries, he said. “There are quite a lot of cases in which a person is struck repeatedly with various objects and seriously injured – 50 or 60 blows,” the criminologist said, describing the brutality sometimes involved in violent crimes. At the same time, Sakalauskas urged caution when comparing homicide statistics between countries, as legal definitions and criminal classifications differ. Lithuania applies a relatively broad definition of intentional homicide, including cases involving indirect intent. “For example, if someone punches another person in the face, the victim falls, hits their head on the edge of a sidewalk and dies, this is classified as intentional homicide with indirect intent,” he said. In Germany, the same incident would probably be classified as serious bodily injury resulting in death rather than intentional homicide, he added. The typical circumstances surrounding homicides in Lithuania often involve people from the same social environment and gatherings where alcohol is consumed. Men most frequently kill other men to whom they are not related, while women are more likely to kill men close to them, Sakalauskas said. Lithuania also has one of the EU’s highest suicide rates. According to the criminologist, the two phenomena share some underlying causes. “Some people direct their anger outward, for example, immediately reaching for a knife or striking someone, while another person slams the door and walks away or takes their own life. It all comes from the same root,” he said. Despite the substantial decline in homicides, Sakalauskas warned that the pace of improvement could slow in the coming years. He attributes the progress so far largely to cultural changes and improvements in social relationships. “Relationships are changing, attitudes toward other people are changing, and there is less aggression,” he said. He rejected suggestions that tougher criminal penalties were responsible for the decline, noting that homicide rates had fallen even without the repeated calls for harsher punishment that often follow particularly brutal crimes. Nor should alcohol consumption be treated as the sole explanation for violence, he said. “Many people drink alcohol. A few percent of the population drink heavily and intensively, but they don’t kill anyone. It is just one factor in a complex combination of causes,” Sakalauskas said. Homicide rates have declined in most European countries over the past decade, although some have recorded increases, including France, Croatia, Austria and Germany. Sakalauskas said the increases were relatively small and that their causes were difficult to establish. He also cautioned against linking them to migration. “This is a long-term trend, not just a matter of the past 10 years. On the other hand, homicides account for a very small share of overall crime in any country,” he said. Lithuania records approximately 50,000 criminal offenses annually, of which about 75 are homicides, he noted. “That tells us something, but far from everything,” he said. The criminologist also pointed to the problem of unreported or undetected killings, which account for a small but persistent share of homicides. These can include cases of missing people whose deaths are never discovered, as well as potential abuses by medical professionals that may remain undetected for years. Sometimes unidentified bodies are found in forests, with no one reporting the person missing. “An examination is carried out, but if nobody has reported the person missing, there is no further difference. The person is buried at municipal expense, and that is it,” Sakalauskas said.

The deployment of two US rotational battalions in Lithuania was officially completed on Monday. “I think the entire Lithuanian nation breathed a sigh of relief,” Lithuanian Armed Forces Chief General Raimundas Vaikšnoras told LRT in an interview. General, did you breathe a sigh of relief when the American flag was raised again at the Pabradė base? Yes. And I would say I was not the only one. I think the entire Lithuanian nation breathed a sigh of relief. You will remember how much anticipation there was and how the deadlines kept getting pushed back: first to midsummer, then to the end of summer, and finally to the beginning of autumn. By early autumn, we more or less knew the date. It was clear because certain things, which I do not want to discuss now, indicated that we were on the right track and heading in the right direction. Perhaps, for operational security reasons, this was not communicated very clearly or precisely. Today is the big day: the Americans, the rotational forces, have returned to Pabradė, and we will begin training together. For nine months? These are still rotational battalions. Do you have any indications or news suggesting that this arrangement will continue? We believe this will not be a one-off rotation and that it will continue, but we will see how things develop over time. What matters to us now is having them here. We have provided accommodation and good training conditions. The Lithuanian Armed Forces' Land Force is taking them under its wing and integrating them into its overall military training cycle. I think we have plenty of things we can work on together. The time will come, and we will find out. The previous rotation involved an armoured and artillery battalion, while this time it is an engineering battalion. Is this what Lithuania asked for, or are we simply making do with what the Americans have offered? The engineers who have replaced the artillery troops bring a different level of capability, allowing other units to train alongside them. We have worked quite extensively with the artillery troops, gained a good understanding of their capabilities and what they can do, and learned how to exchange expertise. Now we have the engineers – another new level. Other units can train alongside them, building various fortifications. By the way, I saw today that they had brought some heavy, highly sophisticated equipment. We would also like to acquire similar equipment. I would say this is a very good preparation process, helping us understand exactly what we need and how to use this kind of equipment and machinery on the battlefield. Despite political statements that Vladimir Putin is demanding the withdrawal of military bases from what he calls the new NATO member states, Lithuania is seeking a permanent US military base. Politicians have already signalled that Lithuania would even cover the costs of such a project. How prepared are the armed forces if such a political decision is made? This is ultimately a political decision, and various criteria will probably be assessed. Of course, Lithuania has done a great deal of groundwork and demonstrated to our allies that we are a reliable partner. This applies to the amount of money we allocate to defence, the infrastructure we provide, training and accommodation facilities, as well as the share of the costs we cover to make it cheaper for American taxpayers to maintain rotational forces here. I think this is a good model for everyone else, particularly when discussing how to keep American troops on the European continent in general. I would say that Europe is still one of the wealthiest continents, and we can afford to pay for our own security. That would be both fair and honourable. As for the Lithuanian Armed Forces, we have effectively handed over Pabradė and the infrastructure built there – the barracks and training grounds – to the Americans for almost two years now. Of course, another factor that needs to be considered – and this will ultimately be a political decision – is that if it is eventually decided that we will have permanent military bases here, families may start moving in as well. We would then have to think about other things: kindergartens, schools and additional infrastructure. All these challenges are natural developments, similar to those involved in bringing the German brigade to Lithuania. The advantage is that Pabradė is not far from Vilnius, a city with an international school and international kindergartens, as we already have a foreign community here. I think the logistical costs could actually be very low. Another priority for both politicians and the armed forces is air defence.
