[...] Can we say that the Lithuanian Armed Forces can now detect more objects, but neutralising them remains a problem? It was only last year that we seriously began considering what capabilities might be needed. Procurement processes are under way, certain contracts have been signed, and we are waiting for the equipment to arrive and be integrated into our systems. Radars are a simpler matter. As you mentioned, we are covering some of the gaps and blind spots that previously existed. With relatively modern radars, we now have a much clearer picture. Detection is taking place, but we also need to understand that, in peacetime, there is another requirement: before neutralising a target, we need to identify it visually. Visual identification is difficult, particularly at night or when objects are obscured by clouds. Radar data may indicate that an object is very likely to be a particular type of target. Of course, there are other criteria, such as sound, speed and so on. However, we know there are quite a few airports in the surrounding area. Particularly in summer and early autumn, light and ultralight aircraft are flying around, and they are not necessarily equipped with transponders, as these were not mandatory. We are now looking at how to improve these processes in cooperation with air navigation services.

Lithuania’s Chief of Defence Raimundas Vaikšnoras has warned that military radar systems could again mistake drones for flocks of birds, saying the armed forces must rely on visual identification before deciding whether to engage suspicious flying objects. Vaikšnoras also revealed that Lithuanian forces nearly opened fire on an ultralight aircraft last spring after it appeared in the country’s airspace. “Let’s be realistic, this is physics, and we will probably mistake one for the other again, perhaps more than once,” Vaikšnoras told LRT RADIO on Tuesday, referring to the possibility of confusing drones with birds. He said the military needed reliable means of visual identification, including cameras or scrambling fighter jets. The latter, he said, was currently the most flexible and straightforward way to quickly reach different parts of Lithuania and establish whether an unidentified object was a flock of birds or a human-controlled aircraft. “There were several incidents that perhaps were not widely discussed. Last spring, we were almost at the point of having our finger on the trigger, but it turned out to be an ultralight aircraft that had somehow entered our airspace,” Vaikšnoras said. He added that the military had since improved its procedures in cooperation with air navigation authorities, including measures to quickly close restricted airspace in specific areas to prevent similar incidents or potentially catastrophic consequences. Vaikšnoras said firing a fighter jet’s missile at a drone entering Lithuanian airspace was currently the most effective and fastest way to destroy it. However, he stressed that Lithuania could not afford to protect its entire territory with an impenetrable air defence system. “People and our citizens need to understand that we could not cover the entire territory of Lithuania with an iron dome, and we will probably not be able to do so in the near future, because it would cost billions,” he said. He also emphasised that peacetime rules of engagement require visual confirmation before a target can be destroyed. The military must establish that an unidentified object is not a civilian aircraft or another vehicle operated by someone who has accidentally entered restricted airspace, such as an ultralight plane, hot air balloon or paraglider. Otherwise, an attempt to eliminate what appears to be a threat could itself result in a catastrophe, Vaikšnoras said. An air alert was declared in parts of Lithuania on the night of November 11 after a drone entered the country’s airspace from Belarus. NATO fighter jets identified the object but failed to shoot it down. NATO’s Baltic air policing mission operates from bases in Lithuania and Estonia.

Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas has rejected accusations of xenophobia and racism after announcing that Lithuania would accept no migrants under the European Union’s solidarity mechanism next year, opting instead to pay to the bloc’s migration fund. “Such regulation is established by the European Commission, allowing member states to contribute to the solidarity fund in various ways, including by accepting migrants or paying for their maintenance in other countries, which is what we chose,” Katelynas told reporters near the government building Wednesday. The minister dismissed accusations of xenophobia and racism, describing the decision as a political and financial choice. According to Katelynas, making a financial contribution would be cheaper for Lithuania over an estimated five-year period than accepting relocated migrants. The minister announced Monday that Lithuania was changing its position on participation in the EU solidarity mechanism and would not accept any migrants next year. The amount of its planned financial contribution has not yet been determined. The EU solidarity mechanism requires member states to share responsibility for migration with countries that serve as the main entry points for migrants arriving in the bloc. Each member state is assigned a quota of migrants to be relocated, but the government can decide whether to accept them all or pay instead. This year, Lithuania agreed to accept 58 migrants from Cyprus and contribute 1.4 million euros to the mechanism. Some countries facing significant migration pressure, including Poland and Estonia, are exempt from the arrangement.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has urged Lithuania to develop a credible medium-term fiscal strategy to curb rising public debt, set clear spending priorities and ensure the sustainable use of public funds. The strategy should identify sustainable sources of budget revenue, improve the targeting of social benefits and make public spending more efficient, the Bank of Lithuania said Wednesday, following the conclusion of an IMF staff mission to the country. “When discussing growing public borrowing, it is important to assess not only today’s needs but also their long-term costs. Higher defence spending is undoubtedly necessary, but we must also plan other budget expenditures responsibly,” Gediminas Šimkus, chairman of the board of the Bank of Lithuania, said. The IMF highlighted long-term challenges facing Lithuania’s public finances, warning that planned spending increases in 2027-29 would further widen the budget deficit and increase public debt, raising the risk of breaching European Union fiscal rules. The fund forecasts Lithuania's economy will grow by 2.7% this year, slow to 2.1% in 2027 and accelerate again in 2028. Economic activity this year has been supported by rising wages, increased borrowing, withdrawals from second-pillar pension funds, public spending and investment from the European Union. Growth is expected to moderate slightly next year as the factors driving domestic demand weaken, before picking up again in 2028. The IMF identified persistent geopolitical tensions, volatile energy prices and weak external demand as the main risks to the economic outlook. Inflation is expected to gradually ease as energy price pressures subside. However, the fund warned that public sector spending and continued rapid wage growth could prolong inflationary pressures. It also cautioned that wage increases outpacing productivity gains could undermine Lithuania’s competitiveness. The IMF also pointed to the significant decline in second-pillar pension fund assets as highlighting the need to strengthen the pension system. It called for a comprehensive plan to ensure its long-term sustainability and adequate pension levels amid growing demographic challenges. The IMF staff mission visited Lithuania from November 11 to 17. In October, the fund lowered its forecast for Lithuania's economic growth this year to 2.7% from the 2.8% projected in August. Its forecast for 2027 was raised to 2.1% from 2%. The IMF also expects average annual inflation in Lithuania to reach 5.4% this year, up from its previous forecast of 5.2%, and 3.5% in 2027, compared with the earlier projection of 3.1%.

Lithuania is offering US defence technology startup Mach Industries expedited administrative procedures and other incentives to attract investment, Economy and Innovation Minister Edvinas Grikšas said, following the company’s establishment of a subsidiary in Vilnius. The government is proposing a so-called green corridor, designed to speed up the launch of major and strategic investment projects, allowing companies to begin construction while completing certain building permit procedures. The initiative has already been applied to German defence giant Rheinmetall’s planned ammunition factory in Baisogala, Radviliškis district, and could also be extended to Mach Industries, Grikšas told BNS. “We have presented all the terms of our value proposition, because Lithuania is certainly one of the most competitive countries for establishing operations, especially in the defence innovation industry,” the minister said. He added that Mach Industries was being offered the same conditions available to other domestic and foreign investors whose projects qualify as large-scale or strategic investments. Grikšas described the establishment of Mach Industries Lithuania as a positive development, although negotiations over the company’s potential investment remain ongoing. “It is very encouraging that there has been progress – they have opened their own representative office here. They are seriously considering Lithuania, and we are also doing our best to persuade them to choose our country,” he said. The minister called Mach Industries one of the fastest-growing startups in the United States, saying Lithuania wanted the company to invest and manufacture defence systems locally. However, he declined to disclose what products the company might manufacture in Lithuania or where a potential factory could be built. “There are discussions, but there are no details yet about what exactly could be produced in Lithuania,” Grikšas said, adding that the company had agreed to explore investment opportunities in the country. Mach Industries has not publicly commented on its plans. Its marketing and communications director, Tamara Diller, did not respond to BNS questions about whether the company intends to build a factory in Lithuania or how much it might invest. The company recently established a subsidiary, Mach Industries Lithuania, in Vilnius. Mach Industries founder and CEO Ethan Thornton has been appointed as its head. The foreign investment promotion agency Invest Lithuania confirmed Monday that it was holding consultations and meetings with the company about potential investment. In late September, Grikšas said an agreement with Mach Industries could lead to the production of defence systems in Lithuania, creating opportunities for local engineers and suppliers while strengthening NATO’s eastern flank and helping Ukraine defend itself. Grikšas and Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas signed a cooperation agreement with the company in the United States that month concerning its expansion into Lithuania. Kaunas said at the time that Mach Industries was developing drone and reconnaissance capabilities and that Lithuania would seek to facilitate the production of drone systems in the country. Mach Industries develops advanced unmanned aviation, aerospace and defence systems, as well as infrastructure for their mass production. One of its products, the Viper autonomous vertical takeoff and landing platform, has already been demonstrated during exercises at the Rūdninkai military training area in Lithuania. The company announced in September that it had raised $600 million in an extension of its Series C funding round, doubling its valuation to $3.7 billion. Mach Industries said last year that it was considering Lithuania as a potential location for its European expansion and a manufacturing facility.

Phillippe Perchoc, head of the Brussels bureau of France’s Strategic Research Institute of the Military Academy (IRSEM), has been analysing the Baltic states for over two decades. Bringing the expertise to France, he often has to explain “very basic things”. In an interview with LRT.lt, Perchoc talks about France's relations with the Baltic states, the changing approach in Lithuania toward European security, and how France's military footprint shifted its centre of gravity from Africa to Eastern Europe. You wrote that interest in the Baltic states has never been so high in France since 1991. Why? When I started working on the Baltics 20 years ago, the topic looked very exotic in Paris. It was difficult to find a supervisor for a PhD, and now it's not the case anymore. I think that everyone understands how key the region is for the security of all of Europe. Nowadays the issue is about not overstepping – sometimes you hear people in Paris saying that the Russians are about to attack the Baltic states. Now it's the other way around – so [the Baltics] are now telling them to calm down. In the expert community, I see that there is a difference between people who read things published by the Baltic experts themselves and sometimes by the secret services of Estonia or Lithuania, and people who just look at Russia and really don't have a real interest in the societies here. For example, there have been a number of studies published in France about a possible attack on Estonia, for example, but they completely overlook the fact that the Estonians will defend themselves. So, either it's a very large attack, and you see that coming, or it’s something more localised and the Estonians – with the support of Brits and the French – can repel them and it's not a big deal. How about this question of the agency of the Baltics themselves: how is it viewed in Paris, the Defence Ministry? The defence community has good knowledge of the real situation on the ground because we have troops in Estonia, so they can really assess what the situation is. Now the question is how they convey the message to the wider public. ​ Very often I have to tell people super basic things. For example, that Latvia is twice the size of Belgium, or the Baltic states together being twice the size of Portugal. And when you put real numbers in the equation, then people start thinking, “Okay, it's not possible to invade [a country] twice the size of Belgium within one week – people will resist.” The interest in Central and Eastern Europe has been tremendous in the past five years. I think most French people didn't know where Ukraine was on the map when the war started. At the same time, it's clear that France is a country that is also looking into the South for obvious reasons. ​Sometimes it's difficult for French people, and especially young people, when they watch TV, they see the images of Mariupol; it's clear we should do something about that. But then they see the images of Gaza, and they ask themselves: “Why is the EU doing nothing about it? Why is the UN doing nothing about it?” So there's interest in both [regions], but there is this questioning, especially among the young people, why do we have double standards when it comes to the situation in the Middle East? I understand that there is a demand in the French public that if we are fighting for the rule of law and principles, then we should fight for the rule of law and principles everywhere. Previously, you wrote that the relations between the Baltics and France have never been straightforward or easy. How will they look if Le Pen or Mélenchon wins the election next year? So first of all, this is an election with 40 candidates, so the threshold to go to the second round is very low: 15 or 16 percent. It's very difficult to know who it will be, but it will most likely be Marine Le Pen in the second round. But I think what most people outside of France don't really get is that we will have parliamentary elections after that. For the past three years, the French Parliament has been very divided, and the parliament will stay, I think, very divided. It will be very difficult to have a total shift in foreign policy because of this. At the same time, the rising question is the public debt, and I see a storm coming there. You also wrote that the Baltic states must face the need to rethink their defence mode that is largely based on NATO and their relationship with the United States, in the context of American disengagement. Do you think this is happening? It's a fact of life that the Atlantic Ocean is widening two centimetres every year. And it's a fact of life that the sociological impact of the Baltic community in Washington will decrease. I think that it was exceptional that, 20 years ago, the three countries had such importance in the debate in Congress; only Israel had a better connection with Congress. But this generation is fading away. The US is also changing. So there is still interest, even from President Trump, in the region, but I think that will slowly fade. The European pillar within NATO is much more important for this region than it was even 10 years ago. There is also a discussion in Brussels about preparedness and willingness. Were the Ukrainians prepared to defend themselves? No. But when it happened, the Ukrainians had the will to fight. So if something happens in this region and NATO is lost in discussions in Brussels, first, regional players will enter the game. I don't see Poland, Finland, or Sweden doing nothing about it. There is also the JEF model [the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force], which is interesting. It's not a plan B [to NATO and the Americans], but it's a fact of life – and one of the lessons from the Second World War and from Ukraine – that you have to defend yourself. If NATO is lost in meetings, it's not like no defence happens. Will it be as efficient as having American troops with tanks and nukes in the debate? Surely not. But still. If someth

Lithuania’s Liberal Movement party will initiate a no-confidence procedure against Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys if he continues pushing to change the name of Taiwan’s representative office in Vilnius, party leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen said Thursday. “If the minister continues to seek the renaming of the Taiwanese Representative Office or forces it to leave Lithuania, we will definitely initiate a no-confidence motion, because that would be a huge mistake,” she told reporters. Čmilytė-Nielsen said the move could attract support from members of the ruling coalition, making the threat a serious problem for Budrys. She added that the liberals consider Budrys one of the strongest ministers in the current government but cannot ignore what they regard as a mistake in his policy toward Taiwan. Opposition Conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, however, said it was too early to consider a no-confidence motion. “Let's wait for a decision. Today we learned in our parliamentary group that the minister wants to refer the issue of the Taiwanese Representative Office to the State Defence Council. Given the context, we cannot make an assessment before a decision is made,” he told BNS. Budrys confirmed at a meeting with the Conservative parliamentary group Thursday that the State Defence Council, which comprises the country’s top political and defence officials, should decide on questions related to restoring diplomatic relations with China. The minister said he was not concerned about the prospect of a no-confidence motion, describing it as a normal part of democratic oversight. “All the things provided for in our constitution to make democracy work well are good. The same applies to a no-confidence motion – if there is a desire to test confidence, then let’s do it. It is one of the celebrations of democracy,” he said. Budrys argued that parliamentary oversight was essential to prevent costly political mistakes, pointing to decisions made in 2021. “If parliamentary oversight had been working as it does today, that would not have happened, because it would not have been allowed,” he said. Lithuania’s current government is seeking to repair relations with China that went sour in 2021 when the Conservative-led government invited Taiwan to open a representative office and agreed it be named “Taiwanese”. Similar offices in other countries use the name Taipei to avoid tensions with Beijing which regards the island as part of China. Beijing responded by unilaterally downgrading diplomatic ties, reducing representation from the ambassadorial to the chargé d’affaires level. Lithuania later refused to issue new accreditation documents to Chinese diplomats and no Chinese diplomats have been present in the country since May last year. Lithuanian and Chinese diplomats discussed prospects for restoring relations in Vilnius last week.

A Vilnius regional court on Thursday convicted border guard Karolis Ilgevičius of murder and abuse of office for fatally shooting a suspected cigarette smuggler who failed to stop his vehicle during a police pursuit. The court sentenced Ilgevičius to one year of restricted freedom without intensive supervision. It also ordered him to work or register with the Employment Service and pay 1,000 euros to the Crime Victims Fund. At an earlier hearing, Ilgevičius pleaded for acquittal, saying he had fired his weapon to protect other people’s lives and health and to stop a person committing a crime. His lawyer, Vidas Vilkas, argued that the Law on the State Border and Its Protection contradicted Lithuania’s Constitution and asked the court to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. After the request was rejected, he sought the termination of the proceedings. Under the law, an officer may use a firearm against a driver only when the officer’s or another person’s life is in danger, rather than when their health is at risk. Prosecutor Darius Šneideris had requested a two-year sentence of restricted freedom without intensive supervision, as well as compensation for property damage and a 2,500-euro payment to the Crime Victims Fund. Although Lithuania’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of seven to 15 years for murder, the prosecutor argued that imprisonment would not be an appropriate punishment in this case. The man who was shot, identified as A. Aleksiukas, had previous convictions for smuggling, resisting officers, illegal possession of excise goods and other offenses. The incident took place on the evening of June 1, 2024, in the Šalčininkai district near the border with Belarus. Border guards received a report from the Padvarionys border post about drones carrying packages entering Lithuanian airspace. Officers began searching the area and soon spotted a Volkswagen Passat traveling along a road. The driver ignored orders to stop, as well as the sirens and flashing lights of the pursuing border guards’ vehicle. He also failed to stop when confronted by an armed officer standing in his path. The border guard says he fired at the car’s wheel, but the bullet struck the driver, killing him. The vehicle was subsequently found to be carrying boxes of smuggled cigarettes.

Lithuania’s national defence system is failing to keep pace with military needs, putting at risk plans to establish a fully equipped army division by 2030, Auditor General Irena Segalovičienė warned Wednesday. She made the remarks after presenting a classified audit of military equipment and weapons procurement to the parliamentary National Security and Defence Committee. According to Segalovičienė, the main risk identified by the audit concerns the development of the division, although the review also covered procurement for air defence and other military capabilities. She said both external and internal factors were contributing to the problems, with significant shortcomings stemming from inefficiencies within the defence system itself. “Essentially, there are external and internal factors. External ones relate to market developments, such as military equipment acquisitions. Internal factors include funding and broader management issues: procurement, personnel, competencies, cash procedures, IT, artificial intelligence and all other aspects,” Segalovičienė said. “A significant portion of the reasons lies precisely in these internal elements of system inefficiency,” she added. The National Audit Office has previously warned that Lithuania’s planned defence spending of 5% of GDP next year might not be sufficient to achieve its military objectives. According to the office, spending would need to reach 5.44% of GDP to meet the targets. Lithuania aims to fully develop a military division by 2030 as part of efforts to strengthen deterrence against Russia. However, next year’s defence budget is expected to remain largely unchanged, potentially forcing the military to equip the division with less advanced equipment than originally planned. Around 4.8 billion euros has been allocated for the military next year, a few tens of millions of euros more than this year. Lithuania is not abandoning its goal of developing a military division by 2030 despite potential equipment shortages, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Thursday, adding that existing military hardware would be used to fill capability gaps. “We are not moving away from the 2030 date,” Kaunas told BNS. However, he acknowledged that the timely delivery of Swedish-made CV90 infantry fighting vehicles, one of the division’s key acquisitions, would largely determine the level of capability the formation could achieve by that deadline. “If most of the CV90s arrive before 2030, I believe we will be able to call it an optimal level of capability. Whether we can call it fully or partially developed, I do not want to speculate,” the minister said. Lithuania is currently negotiating a contract for the vehicles, leaving approximately four years for the manufacturer to fulfil the order. “We are signing the contract now, so there are effectively four years. I believe the manufacturer should certainly be able to deliver within that period, and this is precisely what we are discussing with them,” Kaunas said. Lithuania plans to purchase 100 infantry fighting vehicles from Swedish manufacturer BAE Systems Hägglunds. The contract is expected to be signed next week, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2028. Following the audit findings, Rimantas Sinkevičius, chairman of parliament’s National Security and Defence Committee, said he considers it impossible for Lithuania to fully develop the division by 2030, although he argued that the deadline should not be postponed by too long.

Nearly half of Lithuanians believe NATO allies would be capable of defending the country in the event of a Russian attack, while confidence in Germany’s military presence is considerably higher than in US troops, according to a new survey. The poll, commissioned by communications agency Bosanova and conducted by Norstat in September 2025 and September 2026, found that 48% of respondents believe NATO allies could defend Lithuania against an attack. Confidence in the German brigade stationed in Lithuania stood at 68%, compared with 43% for US forces. The findings suggest that concerns about Russian aggression remain widespread, although confidence in Lithuania’s defence capabilities and NATO has increased, according to Bosanova head Vytautas Matulevičius, who presented the research. Some 62% of respondents believe Russia could attack the Baltic states, a slight decrease from last year. Meanwhile, 56% said they were worried that Russia could stage a provocation against Lithuania in the near future. Concern about the threat posed by drone incidents also increased slightly. Confidence in the authorities’ response to drone incidents nearly doubled compared with 2025, although only 31% of respondents considered it good. The survey also found that 39% said they followed instructions after receiving emergency alerts on their phones, including considering or seeking shelter. Three-quarters of respondents said they were aware that Russia conducts disinformation and propaganda campaigns. Matulevičius said 96% of Lithuanians agreed with at least one statement that the researchers associated with “Russian narratives”. These included, for example, assertions that Russia has enough resources to continue the war in Ukraine, that Ukraine has a widespread corruption problem, or that Lithuania's autonomy is limited by its dependence on the West. However, Matulevičius stressed that this did not mean those respondents supported Russia. “Belief in Russian narratives does not mean that a person is pro-Russian. The overwhelming majority of the population view [President Vladimir] Putin negatively and consider Russia a threat. Russian disinformation does not seek to make us like Russia; it seeks to divide us and undermine trust in institutions,” he said. He added that Russia’s efforts to persuade Lithuanians that their country would be unable to defend itself against aggression had not been successful, pointing to growing confidence in the military and NATO. The survey found that about 30% of respondents in both years agreed with the claim that NATO expansion was a factor in Russia’s attack on Ukraine. Meanwhile, 48% agreed that traditional values were withering away in Lithuania and other Western countries, while 16% said Lithuania was culturally and historically closer to Russia than to the West. Economic pessimism and attitudes toward Ukraine The research also highlighted growing economic pessimism. Nearly half of respondents, or 49%, said Lithuania’s economic situation was constantly deteriorating, up from 38% in 2025. The share of people who believe Lithuania should improve relations with Belarus also increased slightly, reaching 28%. Almost one in five respondents, or 18%, said they had considered leaving Lithuania because of the threat posed by Russia. About half supported increasing defence spending to between 5% and 6% of GDP. Attitudes toward Ukrainian refugees have become somewhat less favourable. The proportion of respondents who believe Lithuania should accept refugees from Ukraine fell by several percentage points, although 52% still supported doing so. Matulevičius warned that Russia could exploit declining support for Ukrainian refugees to turn Lithuanian society against them. Another finding was that 29% of respondents believe the war in Ukraine should end as soon as possible, even if that means Ukraine giving up some of its territory. The survey also found a slight decline in the number of people who believe Russia can sustain its war against Ukraine for a long time. Matulevičius said such perceptions could be exploited to discourage continued support for Kyiv by suggesting that Russia would ultimately prevail. The survey also examined how Lithuanians consume information. While the overwhelming majority read news in Lithuanian, about one in 10 also read news in Russian, and a quarter in English. About one-third said they get their news from Facebook and Instagram, while TikTok and Telegram were somewhat less popular sources. Nearly half said they had encountered misleading information, although a similar proportion found it difficult to identify whether information they had seen was misleading. The survey’s margin of error was 3.1 percentage points. Matulevičius said economic pessimism was a particular warning sign for Lithuanian politicians, as Russia could use dissatisfaction with living conditions to promote the “narrative” that life in Lithuania was deteriorating. Around 4% of respondents said they viewed Russian President Vladimir Putin positively, while 11% expressed a neutral opinion of him.

Lithuania’s Ministry of Social Security and Labour has proposed reducing the annual quota for foreign workers by several hundred, allowing companies to recruit up to 24,400 workers from third countries in 2027. The proposal was submitted for coordination with other institutions on Thursday, Ignas Algirdas Dobrovolskas, spokesman for Social Security and Labour Minister Inga Ruginienė, confirmed. “The Ministry of Social Security and Labour has submitted a proposal for coordination to set the foreign employment quota at 24,400 for 2027. The draft is being coordinated with the relevant institutions, which have five working days to submit comments and proposals,” Dobrovolskas said. The quota currently stands at 24,706, meaning it would be reduced for the second consecutive year. The ministry said the proposed limit followed an assessment of labour market conditions and forecasts. Its aim is to balance employers’ demand for workers with the employment interests of Lithuania’s population while avoiding incentives for the immigration of low-cost labour. The annual employment quota is set by the social security and labour minister in coordination with the interior minister. It cannot exceed 1.4% of Lithuania’s permanent population. This year’s quota was exhausted on September 7, prompting businesses to argue that the limit was insufficient to meet their labour needs. According to November data from the Migration Department, nearly 234,000 foreign nationals hold valid residence permits in Lithuania, the majority of them Ukrainian citizens. Almost half, or around 110,000, have residence permits based on employment, while just over 4,600 hold permits as highly qualified workers. Belarusian citizens make up the largest group in the latter category.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Thursday that the country could still establish a military division by 2030 by reallocating defence funding from other areas. Establishing a national division by the end of the decade remains Lithuania’s top defence priority, and the necessary funds could be secured by cutting spending on areas not directly related to the division’s development, Nausėda said. He also stressed the need to accelerate defence procurement to ensure the project stays on schedule. The president expressed hope that proposals submitted to parliament by the Defence Ministry to streamline procurement procedures would receive serious consideration and be adopted. Nausėda was speaking after the National Audit Office presented an assessment concluding that Lithuania’s current national defence system was failing to meet military needs, casting doubt on the country's ability to develop a fully operational division by 2030. Lithuania is unlikely to receive all the Swedish CV90 infantry fighting vehicles it has ordered by that deadline. However, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said the shortfall could be offset with other equipment and capabilities available to the armed forces. Kaunas stressed that Lithuania was not abandoning its 2030 target. The country plans to purchase 100 CV90 infantry fighting vehicles from Swedish manufacturer BAE Systems Hägglunds. The contract is scheduled to be signed November 27, with deliveries expected to begin in 2028. Rimantas Sinkevičius, chairman of the parliamentary Committee on National Security and Defence, has also acknowledged that the division would not be fully developed by 2030, estimating that it would be about 80% complete by then.

The word “admin” is the most commonly used password in Lithuania, while “123456” remains the world’s most popular choice, according to the eighth annual ranking of the 200 most common passwords published by cybersecurity company NordPass. Lithuania’s top 20 list is dominated by easily guessed words, number sequences and keyboard patterns. Six of the 20 most popular passwords consist entirely of numbers. Some choices reflect local history and language, including “vytautas” and “lietuva123”, while “nezinau123” (“I don’t know”) may be among the more candid password choices, the company said. The 10 most popular passwords in Lithuania are: Globally, “123456” retained the top spot, followed by “admin” and “12345678”. The top four passwords remained unchanged from last year. The report also highlighted the risks of using simple passwords, citing a recent cyberattack in which a hacker accessed Denmark’s Central Person Register using “123456”, exposing the personal data of about 8.8 million people. Researchers found a further increase in the use of special characters, which appeared in 39 passwords in this year’s global ranking, compared with 32 last year. However, many combinations remained predictable, including “Admin@123” and “P@ssw0rd”. “If you need to create a non-random password, for example, a master password, it is better to choose a long passphrase consisting of two or three words rather than a short and commonly used password with special characters,” said Karolis Arbačiauskas, head of product at NordPass and Nord Security. The researchers also identified several default router passwords in the global ranking, including “ALC#FGU” and “adminHW”, which ranked 116th and 118th, respectively. Their presence suggests that numerous routers and internet-connected devices remain vulnerable to cyber threats because users do not change default credentials. This year’s study also examined how popular culture has influenced password choices over the decades, finding that music, films, video games, sports stars and internet trends all leave traces in people's login credentials. “Passwords are rarely random. When people need something memorable, they choose what they know well – a game they have played hundreds of hours, a musician they liked, an athlete they admired or a show they watched until the end,” Arbačiauskas said. Before the turn of the century, rock and heavy metal dominated culturally inspired passwords, with choices such as “metallica” and “Slayer007”. Classic films also provided inspiration, producing passwords such as “corleone13” and “Rambo017”. The 2000s brought Japanese animation and video games into the mix, with passwords including “Narutofoda2”, “Sasuke”, “Bleach15”, “kingdomhearts3” and “Windwaker1”. Music remained influential, with “eminem2004” among the examples. During the 2010s, video games such as Minecraft and Temple Run inspired passwords including “Minecraft” and “Templerun303”. Social media platforms and sports stars also left their mark, with choices such as “insta123”, “telegram”, “Lewandowski1234!” and “neymar10”. The current decade has brought internet culture into passwords almost in real time. Examples include “skibiditoilet”, “squidgamethebest” and “roblox.com1”. The Covid-19 pandemic also inspired choices such as “Covid@19” and “corona2020”. Researchers cautioned that culturally inspired passwords do not necessarily indicate when they were created. For example, “metallica” could belong to a longtime fan who grew up listening to the band in the 1980s or 1990s, or to a teenager who discovered it during the recent revival of vinyl records. An earlier NordPass study also found that many adults continue using passwords they created as teenagers or even earlier. “Pop culture passwords are a reminder that what you like becomes a code for your predictability. Hackers do not need to know you personally – they only need to know your interests,” Arbačiauskas warned, adding that combining the name of a childhood favourite band with a birth year could produce a password that hackers can crack in less than a second.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Thursday that US President Donald Trump expects Europe to take a more active role in efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, adding that the conflict was discussed extensively at a recent summit involving the United States, China and Russia. “We had the opportunity to speak directly with the US president by phone, and perhaps the most important message that the Lithuanian people would like to hear was that, yes, Ukraine was discussed in China, and discussed extensively,” Nausėda said. “I got the impression that the US president hopes to reach an agreement and is even suggesting that Europe could play a more active and proactive role in finding a solution,” he added. Nausėda was speaking after a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin, initiated by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The talks focused on diplomatic efforts to achieve peace and continued support for Ukraine. In a statement issued by the Lithuanian President’s Office after the meeting, Nausėda said meaningful peace negotiations could begin only after a ceasefire and the provision of security guarantees to Ukraine. He also expressed Lithuania’s support for Ukraine’s energy sector, which is facing serious challenges as winter approaches. The Berlin meeting brought together about 40 heads of state and government, along with representatives of the European Union and NATO, as well as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Nausėda said the gathering demonstrated unity among Ukraine’s allies and close coordination with Washington. He described the meeting as a “good introduction” to efforts to find a solution, noting that Trump had said Russian President Vladimir Putin was tired of the war and wanted to end it. However, the Lithuanian president expressed scepticism about Putin’s willingness to negotiate. “I have some doubts about that, because war fatigue or a genuine desire for negotiations and peace would be reflected in more realistic demands. Unfortunately, so far I see Russia sticking to the same demands it presented to Europe in the form of an ultimatum back in 2021,” Nausėda said.

Lithuania begins four days of celebrations Friday to mark the 108th anniversary of its armed forces, with military parades, ceremonial formations, equipment displays and aircraft flyovers planned in six towns. According to the Lithuanian military, events will take place in Klaipėda and Jonava on Friday, Šiauliai on Saturday, Kaunas on Sunday, and Alytus and Vilnius on Monday. In Klaipėda, the programme includes a military parade, a ceremonial formation and an oath-taking ceremony for conscripts beginning their mandatory initial military service. An exhibition of military equipment and weaponry will also be held. Jonava will host a formation of troops from the Rukla garrison and a military equipment exhibition. On Saturday, troops in Šiauliai will march along the town boulevard toward the shore of Lake Talksa, where a ceremonial formation will take place. Fighter jets participating in NATO’s Baltic air policing mission are also scheduled to fly over the city. On Sunday, Armed Forces Day will be commemorated in the garden of the Vytautas the Great War Museum in Kaunas. The main celebrations will take place Monday in Vilnius’ Cathedral Square. At noon, President Gitanas Nausėda, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas and Chief of Defence Raimundas Vaikšnoras will greet troops and members of the public. Italian fighter jets participating in NATO’s air policing mission are scheduled to fly over the capital. Lithuanian troops, NATO allied forces and members of the Lithuanian Riflemen’s Union will march along Gedimino Avenue. Military equipment belonging to Lithuania’s armed forces and allied forces will also be displayed in Cathedral Square. Meanwhile, Alytus will host a military formation at the Angel of Freedom monument, ceremonial volleys and an exhibition of military equipment. Lithuanian Armed Forces Day is observed annually on November 23, commemorating the first order issued in 1918 to re-establish the country’s military following the restoration of independence.

Thousands of troops from European countries, including Lithuania, are taking part in unprecedented military exercises in southeastern Poland to prepare for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at stabilising the country and rebuilding its armed forces. The multinational force, led by France and the United Kingdom, is a non-NATO military initiative of the Coalition of the Willing, a group of 37 countries supporting Ukraine. The two-week exercises, which began November 9, are the first test of the coalition’s readiness to deploy forces to Ukraine after the war. They are intended both to test deployment plans and to signal to Russia and US President Donald Trump’s administration that European countries are strengthening their military role in efforts to secure Ukraine’s future. The drills are taking place as Ukrainian and nearly 40 other delegations meet in Berlin to demonstrate support for Kyiv and discuss postwar security arrangements. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is seeking guarantees to prevent another Russian invasion, while Moscow wants to prevent NATO from moving closer to its borders. US envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday that he believed Russia could accept NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine after the war. Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff travelled to Berlin to reassure European leaders amid Trump’s discussions on ending the nearly five-year war following a historic trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Kushner said Trump joined the Berlin discussions by phone after his meeting with Putin. Ukraine has long sought NATO membership, particularly because of the collective defence guarantee under Article 5 of the alliance’s treaty, which considers an attack against one member an attack against all. However, the precise form of any alternative security guarantees remains unclear, as does whether Russia and Ukraine would ultimately accept them. Following Thursday’s meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the military exercises in Poland demonstrated that the Coalition of the Willing was prepared to contribute to securing peace alongside the United States. About 2,800 troops from Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and the UK are participating in the two-week exercises. Poland is providing logistical support, while Turkey is involved indirectly through command centres in Istanbul. The exercises in Poland follow a year of planning by the Multinational Force Ukraine, or MNF-U, said British Brig Gen Campbell Close, deputy commander for operations of the French army’s 1st Division, which is responsible for the land component of the Coalition exercise in Poland. If deployed after a ceasefire, the multinational force would help rebuild and strengthen Ukraine’s armed forces, provide security guarantees needed to reopen the country’s airspace and assist with clearing mines in the Black Sea, MNF-U commander Lt Gen Tom Bateman said earlier this month. The force would not carry out peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring duties. Coalition troops arrived in Poland by sea, air and land before continuing by rail and road to Nowa Deba, according to a statement from the Polish government. The exercises have included rehearsals for moving personnel and equipment across Poland, joint command-and-control drills, fighter jet operations and aerial refuelling missions in preparation for helping Ukraine reopen its airspace. Troops have also operated reconnaissance drones, practiced responding to drone attacks and trained in trench warfare in wooded areas. The Coalition of the Willing was initially established to provide Ukraine with security guarantees resembling those under NATO’s Article 5. Without a NATO commitment to fulfil that role, France and the UK decided to pursue a separate European proposal bringing together countries willing to assist Ukraine if necessary. Last year, Putin warned that any foreign troops deployed on Ukrainian territory would be considered “legitimate targets”.

When retired Vilnius resident Romualdas Petruškevičius hears forecasts of a storm along Lithuania’s Baltic coast, he gets excited. Rough seas could mean one thing: amber washed ashore by the waves. He is willing to drop everything, travel to the coast and spend a sleepless night wading through cold autumn waters in search of the golden stones. He makes no money from his unusual hobby, although he could, but says the excitement of finding amber is reward enough. “I check the weather forecasts constantly. When I hear there has been a storm, I know there might be amber on the shore,” Petruškevičius told LRT.lt. A former forester, he has been collecting amber – officially known in Lithuania as amber fishing – for more than a decade. It all began by accident. Once, while walking along the coast near the Latvian border, he spotted a handful of yellow stones on a pile of rocks. He collected them and asked kiosk vendors whether they were really amber, finding it difficult to believe. Another discovery came during a winter walk with his wife near the Palanga bridge, when a wave deposited a sizeable piece of amber right at their feet. “Those experiences hooked me and made me want to take amber fishing more seriously,” he recalled. These days, Petruškevičius does not leave his discoveries to chance. He closely follows weather forecasts and wave conditions, using an app originally designed for surfers that provides information on wave heights and intervals. He has invested in the necessary equipment: a long-handled net, waist-high rubber boots, a waterproof jacket and a special ultraviolet flashlight. Under its light, amber glows at night, easy to distinguish from ordinary stones. During the day, he uses his net to pull piles of seaweed, driftwood and other debris onto the beach, then searches through them for amber. The best opportunities usually come a day or several days after a storm, when the sea remains unsettled and produces waves capable of bringing treasures from the seabed. The ideal waves are between half a meter and a meter high, with several seconds between them. Autumn and spring are particularly promising seasons, he says, because the chances of finding amber can be greater than in summer. Petruškevičius has found amber along much of the Lithuanian coast, from Palanga to Karklė, Šventoji and Klaipėda, as well as near Pape in Latvia. But trips are not always successful. Sometimes he travels all the way from Vilnius only to return empty-handed. Two months ago, he bought an apartment in Šventoji to avoid constantly spending money on accommodation. He also purchased an electric bicycle to reach promising stretches of coastline. One of his most memorable experiences happened in Šventoji at about 2 o’clock at night. “I saw that the sea was washing amber ashore along a stretch of a couple of hundred metres. The water was practically yellow. I collected it all alone until six in the morning and ended up with about a kilogram,” he said. “That night was an especially beautiful experience.” His passion has occasionally brought him into disagreements with lifeguards, particularly when he searches in cold weather. He argues that amber fishing is recognised as part of Lithuania’s intangible cultural heritage and should be allowed to continue as a traditional activity. Unlike commercial collectors, Petruškevičius has little interest in selling his finds. He keeps them at home in vases and small dishes, occasionally giving individual pieces to people who appreciate them. Every time he arrives at the coast, he greets the sea. When he leaves, he says goodbye and thanks it for its gifts. “Amber fishing is an incurable disease, but I don’t want to recover,” he said. “What makes me happy is the process itself: finding amber among the seaweed and rubbish, picking it up and holding it in my hands. Then, when I get home, I examine it under a microscope to see whether it contains any inclusions. It is food for the soul. And it becomes addictive – you always want to find more.” His collection includes about 10 pieces containing inclusions – tiny prehistoric organisms preserved in amber. Every spring, he also visits the Amber Trip exhibition, where he particularly enjoys looking at creations made from natural, unprocessed amber. His largest find so far weighs 143 grams, an unusually large piece by Lithuanian standards. He discovered it this summer between Palanga and Karklė, even though there had been no major storm. But he is still dreaming of something bigger or more unusual. “I once asked an experienced jeweller who works with amber what the most valuable find could be. He said perhaps a piece containing an inclusion with a little lizard. I don’t even know whether such amber exists, but that is how my dream began,” he said. “People talk about wanting to catch the fish of their lifetime. I want to find the amber of my lifetime.” People often ask him how they can find amber themselves. His advice is simple: Go to the sea. Others ask when he will have enough amber to build his own Amber Room. His answer is characteristically modest: He already has enough to make an amber-covered stool. Petruškevičius always carries several pieces of amber in his pocket. He enjoys feeling their warmth and what he calls their aura, knowing that the stones are about 50 million years old.

People in Lithuania increasingly rely on paid AI services, and institutions are quickly following suit. Experts warn that redundancies are becoming more likely. “People understand the value of time. Anyone who has tried these tools knows that they can save many hours of work or simply improve the quality of their output,” says Tadas Povilauskas, an economist at SEB bank. SEB data show that the number of people regularly paying for artificial intelligence tools is growing rapidly. There are now more than 16,000 such customers. “They are already using a package that requires greater computing capacity and paying for it. We can see how much each person spends on average. In the case of ChatGPT, for example, the figure is around €25. This is likely to be the monthly subscription price. For some people, that is a lot; for others, not so much,” Povilauskas says. In September alone, SEB customers spent €320,000 on ChatGPT, a service developed by OpenAI. This figure has doubled over the past year. Spending on Claude, an artificial intelligence assistant developed by Anthropic, reached €130,000 – 16 times more than a year earlier. These figures cover spending by private individuals only. “One possible vision is that every civil servant has their own virtual assistant to help them carry out some of their tasks,” says Rytis Valūnas, a board member of Silensis, a Lithuanian tech company providing AI services. According to Valūnas, around 20% of public sector institutions currently use digital tools. Lithuania’s goal is to increase that figure to at least 50% within four years. “To put it slightly jokingly, the first goal could be to get rid of boring or unnecessary work by essentially delegating it to artificial intelligence agents,” Valūnas says. AI could help the public sector identify unnecessary tasks and eliminate them, while automating those that are needed. This could, for example, help reduce waiting lists for medical treatment. Experts say artificial intelligence can be used wherever data are available and need to be analysed. “The public sector probably should not set itself the goal – however it may sound – of simply cutting jobs or reducing costs. Those would be one-off achievements. We need to think about how to generate more income and become a stronger economy,” Valūnas says. However, job losses caused by artificial intelligence are inevitable. Young people, those without work experience and lower-skilled employees are likely to be particularly affected. “The threat of workers being directly replaced already exists today. This raises the question of how we will train and develop a new generation of employees,” Valūnas says. “Not every company will find ways to increase its revenue. So the first step may still be to cut costs. Tensions in the labour market are likely to increase as a result,” says Povilauskas from SEB. AI is also expected to widen income inequality. Those at the forefront of this technological wave will earn more. “The question of progressive taxation may arise increasingly often in the future,” Povilauskas says. The State Tax Inspectorate (VMI), which is also seeking to expand its use of artificial intelligence, already anticipates that the widespread adoption of the technology could eventually reduce the amount of personal income tax collected by the state. Meanwhile, economists warn that artificial intelligence tools will become more expensive in the future. The companies developing them will sooner or later want to recoup the money they have invested in these technologies.

Lithuania, Poland, Germany, and Bulgaria are planning to set up a joint investigation team to investigate arson attacks targeting Starlink satellite communications infrastructure, Polish radio station RMF24 and Ukrainian news outlet The Kyiv Independent reported on Monday. Starshield – the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system – has become a crucial communications tool for Ukrainian forces, helping them coordinate operations on the battlefield and control drone missions. Attacks on the system's infrastructure in Europe therefore pose a threat to networks carrying internet traffic to Ukraine. According to RMF24, prosecutors from the four countries are expected to meet in early December to discuss setting up a joint investigation team. The team will seek to establish whether the attacks were coordinated by a single group, who carried them out and who commissioned them. On September 23, two masked individuals allegedly set fire to a Starlink ground station in the Polish village of Wola Krobowska. Polish prosecutors suspect the attack was carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence services in an attempt to disrupt satellite internet traffic in Central and Eastern Europe. Poland's Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the day after the attack that the Wola Krobowska station, operated by state-owned telecommunications company Exatel, served as an internet hub routing traffic through Poland, including to Ukraine. Polish authorities have charged two Turkish nationals living in Germany with acting on behalf of a foreign intelligence service and carrying out sabotage. Both suspects were arrested in Germany on October 10 at the request of Polish authorities, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in a post on social media platform X. He described the attack as "another act of hybrid warfare". The Associated Press reported that Poland's minister responsible for coordinating special services, Tomasz Siemoniak, held Russia responsible for the attack. "We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage," the minister was quoted by AP as saying. On October 9, an arson attack targeted SpaceX Starlink antennas at the Plana Teleport facility, south of the Bulgarian capital, Sofia. Meanwhile, on October 18, Lithuanian authorities thwarted an attempt to set fire to Starlink equipment in Vilnius. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius linked the incident to Russia's hybrid warfare campaign.

After an air-raid alert was declared in Russia’s Kaliningrad on November 21, Russian state media and English-language accounts on X needed three hours to turn it into a claim that Ukraine or NATO was attacking Russia from Lithuanian territory, the Repsense media monitoring firm said in a press release on Monday. In an analysis shared with the media, Repsense looked into 2,875 publications in 31 languages and traced, hour by hour, how the alleged operation unfolded. ​ Chronology of events ​ At 19:31 on November 21, Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh wrote two sentences on Telegram: the warning system had “reacted to a suspicious object from the Lithuanian side”, and “specialists have carried out all necessary checks; there is no threat”. ​ Russian news agencies and Telegram channels relayed only the first sentence. ​ In the first three hours, 48 Russian-language headlines mentioned Lithuania, but only two of them kept the words “there is no threat”. ​ This redacted version was spread by TASS, RT, and Russia’s largest Telegram channels. ​ Russia’s foreign and defence ministries did not comment on the alert. The regional governor remained the only official Russian source. ​ On November 18, the Polish daily Rzeczpospolita reported that Polish services had foiled a Russian plan to stage an attack near the Kaliningrad border and blame Ukraine. The next day, Moscow-based commentator Andrew Korybko published a piece claiming that Ukraine was preparing a provocation in Kaliningrad. Within a day, the text appeared in Italian, Slovak, Spanish, and Lithuanian. ​ On the morning of November 21, drones struck the vessel Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland as it sailed towards Kaliningrad. At 18:12, Russian war correspondent Alexander Kots called the attack a “rehearsal for a Kaliningrad blockade”. ​ Sixty-eight minutes later, sirens sounded in Kaliningrad. ​ By the following evening, military commentators quoted by Russian outlets were already treating the two events as one: a Western rehearsal for a blockade. ​ “It does not suit Russia to admit that Ukrainian drones could reach a Baltic Fleet base. An object from the Lithuanian side moves the story into a frame prepared long ago: ‘Kaliningrad is encircled’, ‘NATO is preparing a blockade’, ‘Lithuania is the staging ground’,” said Mykolas Katkus, CEO of Repsense. ​ “Moscow’s officials kept their distance this time, which leaves it free to say they never claimed anything,” he added. ​ Three X accounts create the ‘NATO attack’ narrative English-language accounts on X then sharpened the story. At 19:47, the account Global Surveillance wrote that Ukrainian drones were “using Lithuanian airspace”. ​ At 20:30, the news account Russian Market added that “it was Lithuania that attacked Russia first”. ​ At 20:54, Norwegian professor Glenn Diesen, a regular contributor to Russian state broadcaster RT, posted a map and wrote that “Russia may be under attack from NATO”, arguing that since Kaliningrad does not border Ukraine, the attack must have come from NATO territory. The post gathered 7,757 likes. ​ Of 450 posts about a “NATO attack”, 355 came from just three accounts (Glenn Diesen, Russian Market and IntelSphere): their own posts and reposts of them. Diesen’s post alone was shared 229 times. According to X, the IntelSphere post was sent from Moscow. ​ Lithuania’s first statement came 4 hours and 32 minutes after the governor’s post. In that time, X's chatbot Grok repeated the governor's version in 87 of its 94 replies to users asking about the incident. The denial gave Russian headlines the word ‘attack’ ​ Until midnight, Russian media reported only what the governor had said: an object from the Lithuanian side. None of 150 Russian headlines mentioned a drone launch, an attack or Lithuanian airspace, with only the English-language accounts on X using these words. ​ At 00:40 on November 22, Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry responded directly to the claims that spread on X: it rejected claims that Lithuania had taken part in a “drone attack” and that its “airspace” had been used for attacks. This was the first time the words “attack” and “airspace” came from an official source. ​ Russian outlets seized on this. Reporting on Lithuania’s denial, Russian media began writing about a launch and an attack for the first time. ​ “Lithuania was debunking false claims from social media, but to deny them, it had to repeat them. That let Russian newsrooms quote ‘attack’ and ‘airspace’ from Lithuania itself,” said Katkus. ​ In Lithuania, a third of commenters blamed their government or allies; 12% of posts were copied texts ​ In Lithuania, 2,299 posts and comments about the incident appeared, mostly under Facebook posts by media websites. Roughly a third of commenters wrote that the government, NATO or Ukraine was “dragging Lithuania into war”. ​ Not all of it spread organically: 12% of Lithuanian posts and comments were copy-pasted texts. A question by Giedrė Gorienė, editor of an alternative media portal, “Does NATO want to sacrifice us?”, was posted ten times in 82 minutes across three accounts and five Facebook groups. ​ The post about a “NATO attack” by Diesen, the Norwegian commentator for Russian state media, reached Lithuanian Facebook at 23:15 and had been translated into Lithuanian by 00:23. ​ That was before the Lithuanian foreign minister’s first post appeared. A claim made in English on X for pro-Russian audiences in the West became Lithuanian-language content in Facebook groups within a few hours. ​ These themes had already been circulating in the Lithuanian information space for a while. ​ In the two weeks before the incident, Kaliningrad and Lithuania were mentioned together in 3,232 sentences: mostly about “closing border checkpoints” and “Kaliningrad as a possible flashpoint”, and less often that “a Ukrainian drone flew into Poland from Lithuania” and that “Poland and Lithuania are threatening a blockade”. ​ Two days before the sirens, a fringe Lithuanian

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled that deporting foreigners to countries that use migration as a political tool does not, in itself, violate the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment under the European Convention on Human Rights. The court’s Grand Chamber issued the ruling Tuesday after examining cases brought by several applicants against Lithuania, Latvia and Poland. “In the context of the instrumentalisation of migration, the expulsion of a foreigner to the state carrying out the instrumentalisation does not in itself mean a violation of Article 3 [of the Convention], which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment,” the court said. However, the Strasbourg-based court stressed that national authorities must identify, before carrying out expulsions in such circumstances, individuals who would face an exceptionally high risk of torture or other ill-treatment. It identified two categories of people requiring such an assessment: those with evident personal vulnerabilities, such as advanced age, poor health or disability, and those with specific grounds to believe that returning them to the country using migration as a political weapon would pose a real threat to their lives or a serious risk of ill-treatment. The court also said national authorities were not required to assess whether individuals would have access to an adequate asylum procedure in the country instrumentalising migration. In Lithuania’s case, the Grand Chamber found that the applicants did not belong to either of the vulnerable categories. The ruling was adopted by 11 votes to six, with the court finding no violation of the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. In the case against Lithuania, four applicants complained that Lithuanian border guards detained them and returned them to Belarus in March and April 2022. They said they had requested asylum in Lithuania but their applications were not considered. According to the Strasbourg court, Lithuanian border guards established the identity and country of origin of all four applicants. “Even if the applicants expressed a wish to seek asylum, the court did not consider this, in itself, sufficient evidence that their immediate removal to Belarus would expose them to a real and imminent threat to their lives or a real risk of ill-treatment,” the ECHR said. As the applicants could not be classified in either of the two vulnerable categories identified by the court, it found that their removal to Belarus did not violate the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Grand Chamber also examined complaints against Latvia from 19 applicants, including three families of four, and complaints against Poland from two applicants. In the case against Latvia, the court found that the child applicants belonged to the first category of vulnerability and that their adequate protection could not have been ensured without the presence and support of close family members. The court ruled that Latvia had violated the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment by returning the children and their accompanying relatives to Belarus on separate occasions. However, it found no violation in the cases of the other adult applicants who were not considered vulnerable. In the case against Poland, the court found a violation concerning one applicant because an interim measure prohibiting his return to Belarus was in force on the day he was expelled while he was on Polish territory. The rulings against Latvia and Poland were adopted unanimously. The influx of migrants into eastern European Union member states from Belarus began in 2021. Western countries have accused the government of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko of organising the migration in an attempt to pressure the bloc. Lithuania has so far prevented pushed back 26,500 migrants on the Belarus border. Nearly 2,000 were pushed back this year, compared with more than 1,600 last year and 1,002 in 2024.

NATO should respond to Russian hybrid attacks and provocations by stopping vessels belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow oil fleet in the Baltic Sea, says Lithuanian opposition conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas. “NATO should find a way to respond, not necessarily kinetically, but in a way that makes Russia pay a price for such actions. I have said this many times and will say it again: the Baltic Sea and the shadow oil fleet,” Kasčiūnas told LRT TV television evening. He said several dozen percent of Russia’s shadow fleet passes through the Baltic Sea, which he described as an area NATO has called its “internal sea”. “Let’s start effectively stopping these ships, slowing them down. Every day that one ship is held up already costs the Russians millions. But we are not even doing that,” he said. Kasčiūnas, a former defence minister who now leads Lithuania’s second-biggest parliamentary party, reiterated his call for NATO to become a more active defensive alliance, arguing that the bloc should exploit Russia’s vulnerabilities and apply pressure through asymmetric measures. “We know where Russia hurts, where its sensitive points are, and we should apply pressure there. Unfortunately, we are unable to do that,” he said. The remarks follow an incident Friday in which three Russian cruise missiles fell in three locations in eastern and southeastern Poland. No one was injured, although one of the incidents caused an explosion and a fire. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident as a deliberate provocation by Moscow, while NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the alliance had scrambled fighter jets in response to airspace violations. Rutte said NATO stood in solidarity with Poland and would continue strengthening its deterrence and defence capabilities. Warsaw plans to request additional NATO aircraft to reinforce its air defences and improve airspace surveillance along the alliance’s eastern flank. The requests are expected to include the deployment of an additional Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft.

Recent events in Russia’s Kaliningrad region likely reflect Moscow’s fears of a possible Ukrainian attack on the exclave rather than an attempt to provoke NATO, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda’s chief national security adviser Deividas Matulionis said Tuesday. “I think this reflects the state of paranoia that has existed in Kaliningrad since May. They imagine there could be some kind of Ukrainian attack against facilities in Kaliningrad,” Matulionis told the radio Žinių radijas. Over the weekend, unverified reports of possible attacks on military facilities in the region circulated on Russian social media. A drone threat warning was issued, air raid sirens sounded and operations at Khrabrovo airport were temporarily restricted. Lithuanian officials confirmed that the incidents were likely related. Kaliningrad region Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said the warning system had been activated after a suspicious object allegedly approaching from the Lithuanian side was detected. However, an inspection found no threat. Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Monday that he believed both the reports on Russian social media channels and the actions of Kaliningrad officials were attempts to provoke a reaction from Lithuanian authorities. Matulionis, however, said Russia’s behaviour was more indicative of anxiety over the region’s vulnerable geographical position. “Russia perfectly understands the situation of the Kaliningrad region. It is a geographically isolated region and therefore [their anxiety] is quite understandable,” he said. As for a possible provocation against Lithuania, Matulionis added: “If they wanted to do it, it would be done much more subtly.” Discussions in Russian media about access to Kaliningrad have also been fuelled by Estonia’s decision to close all border checkpoints with Russia from December. The move followed an Estonian operation to thwart an attempted arson attack on a drone factory linked to Russian military intelligence. Matulionis stressed that Lithuania had no plans to restrict access to Kaliningrad and urged Lithuanian officials not to escalate tensions. “Escalation will certainly not help and will only create a pretext for a disinformation attack or more serious actions by Russia,” he said. He added that Lithuania consistently meets its obligations regarding the transit of Russian passengers and cargo to Kaliningrad and has never questioned the uninterrupted continuation of these operations. “Let us not create a pretext for escalation ourselves. We should react calmly and fulfil our previous commitments. Today, Russia is so bogged down in the war in Ukraine that opening a second front with NATO countries is, in my view, simply unrealistic,” Matulionis said.

Taiwan should acknowledge its “mistake” and change the Chinese name of its representative office in Vilnius, Lithuanian presidential national security adviser Deividas Matulionis said Tuesday, as Lithuania seeks to ease tensions with Beijing. The office, established in 2021, is called the “Taiwanese Representative Office in Lithuania” in English and Lithuanian, but uses the name “Taiwan” in Chinese. Beijing views Lithuania’s decision to allow the office to open as support for the island’s pursuit of greater autonomy and international recognition. “The Foreign Ministry is in contact with Chinese representatives and is also trying to maintain contacts with Taiwan’s representatives in order to resolve this naming issue fundamentally in good faith. I think the ball is not in our court here, but in Taiwan’s court, and Taiwan should admit a certain mistake was made,” Matulionis told the radio Žinių radijas on Tuesday. He said the “mistake” was using different names for the office in different languages and expressed hope that the Lithuanian Foreign Ministry would find an “elegant” solution. According to Matulionis, the naming dispute could be resolved without confrontation, although it remains unclear whether a compromise would satisfy China. The Foreign Ministry has proposed that Taiwan change the name of its representative office in Vilnius and is also seeking to restore diplomatic relations with Beijing. In response to the office’s opening in 2021, China unilaterally downgraded its diplomatic representation in Lithuania from ambassadorial level to that of chargé d’affaires. After Lithuania refused to issue new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, no Chinese diplomats have remained in the country since May 2025. The Social Democrat government, which took office in 2024, has made restoring diplomatic relations with China one of its goals. A delegation of Chinese diplomats visited Vilnius for talks in November.

Lithuanian prepaid SIM cards were found in Russian drones used in attacks on Ukraine in 2025, Lithuanian news portal 15min.lt reported Tuesday, citing Ukrainian military intelligence data. According to the report, eight Pildyk prepaid SIM cards issued by mobile operator Tele2 were recovered from drones used by Russian forces. Ukrainian intelligence documents also mention Ežys SIM cards managed by Telia, but journalists were unable to obtain further information about them. Tele2 confirmed that the identified cards had been purchased and activated in 2024, before Lithuania introduced mandatory registration for prepaid SIM card users. Company representative Linas Marcinkevičius told 15min.lt that such cards could end up in the wrong hands through groups that purchase, activate and resell them. The European Commission, responding to information provided by journalists, urged European Union member states to investigate possible cases of European SIM cards being used in Russian military operations. The investigation, conducted by 15min.lt in cooperation with international media partners, also found that electronic components manufactured by Western companies are being used in Russian drones and missiles, with some components produced just months before the weapons were deployed. Nearly 100 electronic components were identified in a Russian Geran-4 drone shot down in Ukraine in August. Of those, 76 were manufactured by US companies. According to Ukraine’s Prosecutor General’s Office, more than 16,000 foreign-made components have been identified in Russian weapons in total. The investigation was coordinated by Belgian news portal De Tijd, with 15min.lt and other international media partners.

German tanks taking part in the German-organised military exercises Grand Eagle 26 and Freedom Shield II in Lithuania have arrived in the country largely unnoticed, sparing a propaganda gift for the Kremlin and keeping tensions down. The plan had initially been for the military convoy to travel along roads through Poland and Lithuania. However, at the last minute, the German authorities decided to transport the tanks and other vehicles by ferry and rail instead. ​ The decision, taken by the Bundeswehr in coordination with NATO, was first reported on Sunday by Bild am Sonntag, the Sunday edition of Germany's largest-circulation daily newspaper, Bild. ​ "Pictures of German tanks heading towards the Baltic states near the border with Belarus would have been a perfect propaganda gift for Putin," the newspaper quoted a source in military circles as saying.​ There were concerns that publicly visible columns of German tanks travelling to NATO's eastern flank could unnecessarily provoke Russia. ​ It was also reported that, in the run-up to major military manoeuvres, plans are constantly reviewed to determine whether adjustments are needed to avoid unnecessary provocations. ​ Sources in the Bundeswehr also confirmed to the German political weekly Der Spiegel that the military abandoned plans to send a convoy from the 10th Panzer Division through Poland to Lithuania. ​ Alongside the arguments already mentioned, the magazine cited another factor: "An important role was also played by the fact that there have recently been isolated protests by right-wing MPs in Poland against the German armed forces, and there was therefore a reluctance to further fuel anti-German sentiment." ​ The German Defence Ministry gave the newspaper the following official explanation: "Changing the mode of transport for vehicles is nothing unusual, and it is something that needs to be practised, as it may also have to be done in an emergency."
