From ferry to railway tracks ​ For many years, the rapid deployment of military forces to NATO's eastern flank has been identified as one of the biggest challenges in the event of a real military threat. ​ The Bundeswehr's website makes no mention of the last-minute change of plans, but provides a detailed account of how heavy military equipment from the Bundeswehr's 10th Panzer Division was transported to Lithuania for the two German-led exercises, Grand Eagle 26 and Freedom Shield II. ​ It explains that transporting the equipment is itself part of the exercises. All the vehicles arrive in Lithuania by ferry across the Baltic Sea, including infantry fighting vehicles and main battle tanks, as well as lorries and off-road vehicles. ​ Their routes diverge at the port of Klaipėda. Wheeled vehicles continue by road to the exercise areas. Fuchs armoured personnel carriers, off-road vehicles and a convoy of lorries travel along rural roads in Lithuania. ​ Tracked vehicles, such as Puma infantry fighting vehicles, are transferred from the ship directly onto railway tracks. A special train then transports them to Pabradė. ​ More than 6,000 troops from the German 10th Panzer Division's 45th Armoured Brigade Lithuania and 37th Mechanised Infantry Brigade Saxony are expected to take part. ​ Troops from NATO's Multinational Brigade Lithuania will also participate in the exercises. They include personnel from Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, the Czech Republic, Croatia and Belgium, as well as Luxembourg and a unit of the Lithuanian Armed Forces.

A Lithuanian man has been charged with assisting Russia in activities against Lithuania by gathering intelligence on strategically important infrastructure and support for Ukraine, the Kaunas Regional Prosecutor’s Office said Wednesday. The man is also accused of illegally possessing firearms, ammunition and explosives, including hand grenades, as well as violating public order. According to prosecutors, the suspect began collecting information in August 2021 while carrying out assignments for Russian intelligence services. The information reportedly concerned infrastructure important to Lithuania’s national security and assistance provided to Ukraine. Investigators believe the man received money several times from Russian citizens in exchange for his activities. Prosecutors said the available evidence provides reasonable grounds to believe the information was gathered for Russia’s benefit. The investigation initially began following an incident in March last year, when the suspect allegedly entered the premises of a private company and secretly photographed, using his phone, aid collected there for Ukrainian soldiers. He also photographed the company’s grounds and surrounding areas. The man was wearing a medical mask while taking the pictures, prosecutors said. A company employee noticed the suspicious behaviour and approached him to ask what he was doing. In response, the suspect allegedly sprayed the employee in the face with tear gas before fleeing the scene. The incident was subsequently reported to police. An investigation led authorities to identify and detain the suspect. Further investigative measures uncovered information suggesting that he may have been involved in a broader intelligence-gathering operation dating back to 2021. During the investigation, authorities also obtained evidence concerning the suspect’s alleged illegal possession of firearms, ammunition and a large quantity of explosives, including hand grenades. The case has been referred to the Kaunas Regional Court. If convicted of the offenses, the man faces up to eight years in prison.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda has called for closer scrutiny of Lithuanian politicians’ trips to Taiwan and the circumstances surrounding them, saying this could help establish who was involved in the decision to open the island's representative office in Vilnius. Nausėda made the remarks in view of resistance from some politicians to seeking better relations with China and possibly changing the name of Taiwan’s representative office, suggesting there might be vested interests. “There are certainly more than a few names. And the best way to answer the question about those names would be to look into the matter itself – who travelled to Taiwan, under what circumstances, and how long they stayed there. Then you would see very clearly what the real situation is,” Nausėda told LNK News on Monday. However, he stepped back when asked to clarify whether he meant that Lithuanian politicians were influenced by material benefits offered by Taiwan. “It’s not necessary to label everything with terms like ‘bribery’, ‘corruption’ or something like that. Yes, I won’t deny that those people may have gone to Taiwan because they had a certain prior political positions, a desire to develop relations with Taiwan more broadly and deeply,” Nausėda said. The president’s remarks have drawn criticism from politicians who have visited Taiwan, with several saying such comments were inappropriate for the country’s head of state. The Taiwanese Representative Office, opened in Vilnius in 2021, continues to be a source of controversy as Lithuania seeks to restore diplomatic relations with China. Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen, leader of the Liberal Movement, said Nausėda’s comments cast an unfair shadow over parliament. “Such a statement by the president, casting a shadow over the entire parliament, is of a low standard because it creates the impression that members of parliament’s opinions, views or even values can be bought with a plane ticket,” she said. Čmilytė-Nielsen visited Taiwan while serving as parliamentary speaker. Her trip was funded from the state budget allocation for the parliament’s leadership. In early 2023, a parliamentary delegation led by Laurynas Kasčiūnas, then leader of the National Security and Defence Committee, travelled to Taiwan in business class, with the island covering travel and accommodation expenses. Kasčiūnas, who now leads the conservative Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats, also criticised the president’s remarks, saying the head of state should first examine his own conduct. “It is not becoming of our head of state to talk about such things, because one should always look in the mirror first and assess whether one has ever aligned or failed to align state interests with, for example, family circumstances,” he said. Matas Baltrukevičius, an associate analyst at the Vilnius Institute for Policy Analysis, said the president’s comments risked fuelling speculation without providing concrete evidence. “As long as everything remains at the level of generalities, it simply looks like an artificial attempt to fuel speculation. The country’s highest-ranking officials should not engage in such things,” he said. More than 40 Lithuanian members of parliament have visited Taiwan at the island’s invitation since 2021, most of them from the conservatives and Social Democrats. Social Democratic lawmaker Algirdas Sysas noted that the president’s office also sometimes travels at the invitation of foreign governments. “Of course, one can make accusations, but I think the Presidential Office also sometimes travels not only at the expense of Lithuanian taxpayers but also at the invitation of other countries,” he said. Dovilė Šakalienė, another Social Democratic lawmaker who has visited Taiwan several times, said foreign partners often cover at least part of the expenses of official visits. “It would be quite interesting to say, for example, that I cannot travel somewhere as a speaker at the expense of the United States, or that our parliamentarians cannot go on study visits. But when Taiwan does it, we cannot? As far as I know, democratic partnerships should be more acceptable in our country,” she said. Linas Kontrimas, head of Vilnius University’s Political Communication Research Centre, said politicians should provide facts and arguments rather than engage in speculation. “The Taiwan issue has never been a clean game – neither in the campaign launched by the Homeland Union nor in the one currently being pursued by the president. Nevertheless, we must tell politicians, and perhaps even demand of them: put forward the facts, put forward the arguments,” he said. Kontrimas added that such controversies could be avoided if Lithuania pursued a consistent foreign policy and had clearly defined strategic objectives. “When there are no such objectives, when we do not know what they are and they change like the seasons, society is trapped in these fragmented political tug-of-wars,” he said. Lithuania seeks to restore ties with China The current Lithuanian government is seeking to restore relations with Beijing, and a Chinese delegation has already visited Vilnius for talks. Relations with Beijing soured in 2021 when Lithuania, then under the conservative-liberal leadership, pursued policies hostile to China and, among other things, invited Taiwan to open a representative office in Vilnius. Its name includes the word “Taiwanese” as opposed to “Taipei”, the appellation used in most other European countries. In response, Beijing accused Lithuania in violating the so-called One China principle and downgraded diplomatic relations with Lithuania. It also imposed undeclared trade sanctions that have since been lifted. However, China still has no diplomatic representation in Lithuania. The current Social Democrat-led government is seeking to repair ties with Beijing, a goal that has attracted some criticism, particularly from conservative and liberal lawmakers. Lithuania and six other European Union countries have urged the bloc’s leaders to restrict nonessential travel by Russian citizens to the EU and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes from competing in European sporting events. A letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa was signed by Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda and the prime ministers of Latvia, Estonia, Poland, Denmark, Finland and Sweden. The leaders called on the European Commission to propose measures preventing nonessential travel by Russian citizens to the EU. They also urged member states to stop issuing visas to Russian and Belarusian athletes to prevent their participation in European sporting competitions. “Sport and geopolitics cannot be separated. This principle is already embedded in EU policy,” the letter said. It cited a European Council statement that “until a just and lasting peace is ensured in Ukraine, the participation of Russia and Belarus in international sporting and cultural events should not be normalised, especially with the display of national symbols.” “It is time to put this provision into practice,” the leaders added. According to the letter, the EU must demonstrate that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine will bring no benefits by maintaining firm support for Kyiv and increasing the costs of Moscow’s military aggression. The signatories also warned that recent developments in international sport risk sending the opposite message by contributing to the normalisation of Russia’s aggression. Allowing Russian teams and athletes to participate in European sporting events would be perceived by the Kremlin as a victory, the leaders said.

Lithuanian social media is increasingly filled with opponents accusing each other of belonging to the real or imaginary extreme right- or left-wing camp. In a new book, researchers trace the country’s biggest dividing lines. Following the shooting in Poland in November, Lithuania’s social media space was overtaken with arguments over which radical left or right-wing camp the attacker allegedly represented. At times, the discourse overshadowed the tragedy itself. Ieva Petronytė-Urbonavičienė, a political scientist at Vilnius University, says that social media users splitting into fierce camps and trying to pin an ideology they dislike on the perpetrator is a typical symptom of a polarised society. "The first explanation that comes to mind is that only an opponent could have done this. Group psychology kicks in. We believe our like-minded allies certainly could not have behaved this way," says Petronytė-Urbonavičienė. She is one of the authors of the book The Test of Togetherness: (Dis)trust in the State and Societal Polarisation in Lithuania (Bendrystės išbandymas. (Ne)pasitikėjimas valstybe ir visuomenės poliarizacija Lietuvoje). "Because we now see the opponent mostly in the context of political division, people on the left think it was the work of the right, and people on the right think it was the left," she adds. Polarisation has become a very commonly used word in recent years, seen as being harmful to democracy. Research cited in the book suggests that division is still less of an issue in Lithuania than in Western Europe, but topics such as the pandemic and LGBTQ+ rights have set people against each other also in Lithuania. Drawing on sociological surveys, the authors found that since the 2024 parliamentary election the most polarised voters in Lithuania are those of the Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats (TS-LKD) and the Nemunas Dawn party. "Other parties are also viewed negatively. For example, voters of the Social Democrats and the Farmers are rather distrustful and negative towards the TS-LKD, while liberal voters view Nemunas Dawn negatively. "But when we talk about dislike of the other party's voters, the tension between these two camps was, and probably still is, the greatest," says Petronytė-Urbonavičienė. However, there are currently no truly radical or extremist parties in Lithuania, she points out. This can be linked to the consensus among parties on Russia and security issues that has prevailed since independence. Meanwhile, Lithuania has no shortage of political forces that favour traditional values, such as the Farmers and the Electoral Action of Poles in Lithuania. "The ideas of the National Alliance could be seen as reflecting the views of the more radical right. But we probably cannot identify such a clear, large force at the very edge of the spectrum, especially among the main parliamentary parties. "The situation is somewhat different from Germany or France, whose radical right-wing forces are sometimes regarded in public debate as a kind of benchmark," says the political scientist. Petronytė-Urbonavičienė notes that in a polarised society there is a prevailing belief that the opponent also considers you worse than they are. This is how the cycle of division is set in motion. According to Petronytė-Urbonavičienė, it is easy to get drawn into division and very hard to climb out of it: by defining who "we" are, we also define who "they" are. "Labels circulate in society, such as 'leftists' and 'radicals', and, if we think back over the past few years, 'vatniks' and 'vaxxers'. Such labels stick very quickly. "Sometimes the labelling becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. A person may not be particularly sympathetic to a camp, but after being given such a label by its opponents, they are effectively pushed into its ranks. If the process gathers pace, the camps expand. More moderate people sometimes join them because they are rejected," she says. Radicalism in Lithuania: from Valančius to Kedys According to Justinas Dementavičius, a political scientist at Vilnius University, accusing someone of political radicalism is a relatively new phenomenon. It emerged more than 200 years ago in the French National Assembly, where supporters of the monarchy sat on the right and reformers, who would later overthrow the king, sat on the left. "Let's agree that neither left nor right are philosophical concepts. They are more like metaphors," he says. He says the hurling of epithets accusing opponents of being radicals reached Lithuania as early as the 19th Century. For example, Motiejus Valančius, a bishop and an important figure in the national revival and the liberation from the Russian Empire, criticised the 1863–64 uprising, Polish nationalism and anti-religious republicanism. "From his perspective, these were radical movements. Russian imperial policy was undoubtedly considered no less radical, wanting to tear out the roots of tradition and often tolerating various extremist attacks," says Dementavičius. The search for radicals also marked the interwar period. Dementavičius cites the distinction between moderate and radical members of the Varpas group, writers for the banned Lithuanian-language newspaper published in the Russian Empire, in the memoirs of the country's third president, Kazys Grinius. Some were democrats, while the more radical leaned towards revolutionary ideas. In the interwar years, political opponents defended their ideas with attacks and brawls even before the coup of 1926. "I would say that, compared with what has gone before, we live in a fairly calm political system, perhaps because in a certain sense we live in a post-ideological world," says Dementavičius, comparing today’s struggles with the interwar period. But he warns that even though traditional political ideologies are being distorted today, parties are not being formed along ideological lines. Five people have been detained on suspicion of “working against” Lithuania in exchange for payment and cooperating with Russian state media, the Prosecutor General’s Office said Wednesday. According to the prosecutors, the investigation was launched after authorities received initial information suggesting that a group of Lithuanian citizens had been in contact with representatives of the state-controlled Russian Television and Radio Broadcasting Company since autumn 2024. The detainees are Kazimieras Juraitis, Vaida Juozapaitytė, Dmitrijus Glazkovas, Laurynas Ragelskis, and Mindaugas Ramoška, the Prosecutor General’s Office confirmed to LRT, The suspects allegedly carried out various assignments related to collecting and transmitting information in exchange for financial compensation. Investigators also suspect that the group produced and distributed information in Lithuania that served Russian interests and repeated Kremlin propaganda narratives, the prosecutor’s office said. The five have been formally suspected of assisting another state in acting against Lithuania, a criminal offense under the country’s Criminal Code. More than 10 searches have been conducted at various locations as part of the investigation, along with other planned procedural measures. Lithuanian intelligence agencies are also cooperating with investigators. The identities of those detained have not been disclosed. Prosecutors said decisions on precautionary measures would be made in the coming days and declined to provide further details, citing the need to protect the investigation. The investigation is being led and supervised by the Vilnius Regional Prosecutor’s Office and carried out by the organised crime investigation unit of the Vilnius County Police Headquarters. The investigation is linked to the organisation Tėvynės konduktoriai (Conductors of the Homeland), whose associates have been submitting large numbers of inquiries to Lithuanian state institutions, creating additional administrative burdens. The organisation and people associated with it have reportedly inundated government agencies with hundreds of requests on various sensitive issues, including matters that could be of interest to the Kremlin. When their requests are not answered, they allegedly involve the institutions in legal disputes. News portal 15min reported last week that Tėvynės konduktoriai had been using a legal loophole by registering in Lithuania’s Information System of Producers and Disseminators of Public Information, which is intended for media outlets. According to the portal, the organisation is linked to Audrius Nakas, head of the Ekspertai.eu website, and Kazimieras Juraitis. Its director is Dmitrijus Glazkovas.

Lithuanian prosecutors have detained five people suspected of cooperating with Russian state media in exchange for money, allegedly spreading Kremlin propaganda and collecting and passing information of interest to a hostile foreign state. The Prosecutor General’s Office announced the detentions on Wednesday, naming the suspects as Dmitrijus Glazkovas, Kazimieras Juraitis, Laurynas Ragelskis, Mindaugas Ramoška and Vaida Juozapaitytė. The pretrial investigation concerns suspected assistance to another state in acting against Lithuania, an offense covered by Article 118 of the country’s Criminal Code. More than 10 searches have also been conducted at various locations. Investigators say the probe began after receiving information that a group of Lithuanian citizens had allegedly maintained contacts with representatives of Russia’s state-controlled television and radio broadcasting company since the autumn of 2024. In exchange for financial compensation, they allegedly carried out various assignments, including collecting and transmitting information. Prosecutors also suspect that the individuals prepared and disseminated material in Lithuania that served Russian interests and repeated Kremlin “propaganda narratives”. The investigation is being conducted in cooperation with the State Security Department, Lithuania’s intelligence agency. Several of the detainees have previously been associated with organisations and activities that have attracted the attention of Lithuanian authorities over alleged links to Russian or Belarusian interests. Dmitrijus Glazkovas heads the association Tėvynės konduktoriai (Conductors of the Homeland) and is also linked to the International Forum for Good Neighbourhood, an organisation associated with Algirdas Paleckis, who is serving a prison sentence for attempted espionage. Glazkovas and several other people signed an appeal to the Supreme Court of Lithuania on behalf of the forum, challenging a decision to dissolve the organisation. Lithuanian courts have previously ruled that the forum’s objective was to act against the country. Kazimieras Juraitis was also a member of the forum. He is currently standing trial at the Vilnius Regional Court alongside Erika Švenčionienė on charges of assisting another state in acting against Lithuania. The two have visited Belarus and appeared on its TV programs. According to evidence in that case, Lithuanian intelligence recorded their contacts with the Belarusian KGB. Juraitis ran for parliament in 2016 on the Lithuanian People’s Party ticket. Laurynas Ragelskis is known for his Russian-language livestreams, in which he promotes anti-Western arguments and confronts participants at various public events in Lithuania. He has been convicted of inciting hatred against Jews and Belarusians and desecrating a place of public respect. Among the restrictions imposed on him was a ban on livestreaming, creating new websites or online accounts, and using other people’s accounts or profiles. Ragelskis has also been mentioned in the State Security Department’s national security threat assessments. The intelligence agency has described him as managing a Lithuanian-language platform featuring anti-Western and pro-Russian articles from various websites and characterised him as a political fringe figure who actively cooperates with Belarusian propagandists. Vaida Juozapaitytė, Juraitis’ wife, also ran for parliament on the Lithuanian People’s Party ticket in 2016. In her biography at the time, she said she and her husband produced reports, documentary films and political and educational programmes. Mindaugas Ramoška hosts programmes on the Ekspertai.eu online platform.

Europe and Canada have always been natural allies, through both good times and bad, and are growing even closer. It’s not only politics, trade and security, but culture, sports and way of life that joins us. Next year will mark a historic milestone when Canada will compete at the Eurovision Song Contest for the first time. May the best song win! For Europe, Canada is a trusted democratic partner. As Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney said when addressing the European Parliament: “Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom, and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication.” And those shared values are translating into concrete cooperation. Trade is obvious area where the partnership has delivered tangible results. Since the provisional application of Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), bilateral trade in goods and services has grown by around 80%, rising from €72.1 billion in 2016 to €130 billion in 2025. And more opportunities lie ahead. For example, Europe is seeking to reduce its dependence on China, particularly in the supply of critical raw materials. Fortunately, Canada is one of the few democratic partners with the resources and capacity to supply the EU with minerals essential to batteries, semiconductors, defence, aerospace, renewable energy and telecommunications. Canada is also a major producer of uranium, cobalt, nickel and zinc, as well as the world’s leading producer of potash. During this time of Russian aggression, defence and security are of the utmost importance. Europe must build a circle of trusted friends around our continent and, here, Canada plays a vital role. Canada has stood firmly with Ukraine and contributes directly to European security through its leadership of NATO operations in Latvia. Canada’s defence spending reached 2.0% of GDP this year, and its new federal budget sets out a path towards more than 4% by the end of the decade. This is an ambitious commitment, bringing Canada closer to the level of investment pursued by frontline allies like Poland. Earlier this year, Canada also became the first non-European country to join the €150 billion defence procurement instrument, SAFE, though more remains to be done to better integrate Canada into European defence markets and defence industry development. Education offers another chance for mutual benefits. Canada consistently performs well in international education, remaining among the strongest OECD countries. According to PISA 2025, it outperforms most EU member states in science and reading. We can deepen this relationship by welcoming Canada into the Erasmus+ exchange scheme, one of the most tangible benefits of European integration for young people. Following the launch of formal negotiations at the recent Canada-EU Summit in Montréal, Canada is poised to become the first non-European country associated with the programme, which funds people and organisations to study and train abroad. Research cooperation is also moving forward. In 2024, Canada became associated with Pillar II of Horizon Europe, which supports collaborative research across a wide scientific and technological fields. Although this is an important milestone, there is still room to strengthen Canada’s participation. Negotiations on deeper participation have now begun and we fully support Canada’s closer integration into Horizon Europe. The case for a stronger EU–Canada partnership is clear. From critical minerals and trade to defence, education and research, there is considerable scope to work closer together. Great partnerships, like great oaks, do not grow overnight. But with the right foundations, they can weather even the roughest political storms. We must make full use of the opportunities available under our existing treaties and agreements. Whether we describe this relationship as an alliance or an association matters less than what we achieve together. As the strongest political force in the EU political system with majorities in the main institutions, the Commission, the Council and the Parliament, the EPP is an effective broker. We are determined to drive the renewed political momentum between the EU and Canada forward. In an increasingly uncertain world, Europe and Canada have every reason to stand together, whatever the political weather. The timing of our visit couldn’t be better. Lithuania is seeking ways to maintain relations with both China and Taiwan and has no plans to close the Taiwanese representative office in Vilnius, says MP Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the parliamentary Foreign Affairs Committee. “There is certainly no goal to abolish it. The goal is to maintain very good relations between two countries, Lithuania and Taiwan,” Motuzas told LRT RADIO Thursday. His comments come after President Gitanas Nausėda said Wednesday that if Taiwan refused to change the name of its representative office, Lithuania could use the right to “make unilateral decisions” regarding its status. The name of the office – which uses the word “Taiwanese” instead of “Taipei” – has been a sticking point between Lithuania and China. Changing the name appears to be a key condition for normalising Vilnius-Beijing relations. A spokesperson for Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius earlier stressed that, under the law, the foreign minister has the authority to decide on the establishment of “other representations”, the category under which the Taiwanese office is accredited. MP Motuzas said the president and other state leaders had merely recalled the existing procedure: the Taiwanese office was accredited by an order of the foreign minister, meaning its accreditation could also be amended by a ministerial decision. He added that the experience of other European Union and NATO countries showed that relations could be maintained with both China and Taiwan. Lithuania has asked the Taiwanese representative office in Vilnius to change its name as a condition for restoring diplomatic relations with China, but Taipei says it has no intention of doing so. Former Prime Minister Ingrida Šimonytė criticised the government’s position, saying Lithuania had backed itself into a corner and that its approach to China amounted to “premature appeasement” of Beijing. According to Šimonytė, allowing Taiwan to open a representative office under its own name was beneficial not only for relations with Taipei but also for ties with other Indo-Pacific countries and the United States. Lithuania’s relations with Taiwan should therefore not be viewed solely through the prism of economic cooperation, she said. The government argues that the partnership with Taiwan has not delivered tangible benefits to Lithuania and that efforts to restore relations with China are important for the country’s security, economic and other interests, as well as its upcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union, which begins in January. China views Lithuania’s decision to allow Taipei to open a representative office in Vilnius under the Taiwanese name (Taiwan in Chinese) as support for the island’s pursuit of greater autonomy and international recognition. Following the opening of the office in 2021, Beijing unilaterally downgraded its diplomatic representation in Lithuania from ambassadorial to chargé d’affaires level. After Lithuania refused to issue new accreditations, no Chinese diplomats had remained in the country since May last year. The Social Democrat government, which took office in 2024, has declared restoring diplomatic relations with China one of its goals. A delegation of Chinese diplomats visited Vilnius for talks in November.

Lithuania currently sees no reason to close its border crossing points with Russia, the country’s newly appointed border guard chief Donatas Škarnulis said Wednesday, following Estonia’s decision to shut its crossings with Russia from December over a suspected sabotage plot linked to Russian military intelligence. “I don’t think the situation has reached a point where border crossing points need to be closed,” Škarnulis told LRT TV Estonia announced the planned closures after thwarting an alleged attempt to set fire to a drone manufacturing facility linked to its defence industry. Estonian authorities have attributed the suspected operation to Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU. Škarnulis said Lithuania’s border with Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave nevertheless required close attention, adding that authorities were monitoring potential security threats along the entire frontier. Lithuanian troops have been assisting border guards in the Kaliningrad region since October. Their deployment has been extended through the end of November. “Provocations are possible, I would say, to a similar extent on the border with Belarus and on the border with the Russian Federation. We understand what kind of neighbours we have. Various situations could arise. We assess the threat equally in both cases,” Škarnulis said. His comments come amid differing assessments among Baltic leaders of how to respond to the latest security concerns. Last week, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda described Estonia’s decision as an appropriate response to the planned attack and said he did not rule out Lithuania adopting similar measures if “efforts” to destabilise the region continued. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the GRU had organised an attempted act of sabotage against Threod Systems, a defence industry company that manufactures reconnaissance and combat drones. Estonia’s decision has not received unanimous support across the region. Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs described the move as a mistake, arguing that closing the border would be unwise unless all three Baltic states took the same action.

Lithuania plans to refuse the relocation of asylum-seekers from other European Union countries next year and instead contribute to the bloc’s migration solidarity fund, a decision that could cost the country up to 4 million euros and has sparked criticism from opposition politicians. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the government had changed its approach after difficulties encountered in implementing this year’s relocation commitments, arguing that accepting some asylum-seekers had proved more challenging than anticipated. The decision has prompted a debate over Lithuania’s obligations to European partners, the cost of migration management and whether the country should spend the money on domestic priorities instead. At a refugee reception centre in Lithuania, the corridors are relatively quiet. About half of its 250 places are occupied, including by asylum-seekers recently relocated from Cyprus. One of them, a man from Nigeria, said he hoped life in Lithuania would be better than in Cyprus, where he had struggled to support himself. “I didn’t have any support. I had to survive on my own. It was difficult to pay bills and buy food,” he said. He arrived in Lithuania this week with 21 other asylum-seekers transferred from Cyprus. Among them is a young man from war-torn Sudan who said he had spent three years in Cyprus. “I am seeking asylum because of the situation in my country. There is a war, and I want security and stability,” he said. Lithuania agreed to accept 58 migrants under the EU’s solidarity mechanism this year, but only 28 have arrived so far. Another group is expected in December. “Single men predominate, mostly from African countries,” said Gediminas Pocius, head of the Reception and Integration Agency. He said the total number was manageable given the migration flows Lithuania faces during the migration season. “Fifty-eight people, considering the flows we deal with during the migration season, would not be a major problem,” Pocius said. However, Interior Minister Katelynas said the government had concluded that the relocation process involved difficulties related to the profiles of the people being transferred. “We see the difficulties involved in relocation and the types of people being transferred,” he said. This year’s relocation program involved asylum-seekers from Cyprus. Lithuanian lawmaker Ruslanas Baranovas, a member of the ruling Social Democratic parliamentary group, said Cyprus had offered Lithuania a list of particularly problematic cases. “The country we worked with selected the most problematic migrants it had. It gave us a list, and we had to relocate them. These were people with mental disorders or who had experienced radical torture and similar things. Integrating them in Lithuania afterward would have been very, very difficult,” Baranovas said. European Parliament member Dainius Žalimas criticised such descriptions, saying they risked discriminating against people with disabilities. “Obviously, there may be people with disabilities among migrants,” he said. The asylum-seekers were selected by Lithuania itself, following interviews and assessments conducted by officials from the Migration Department and the State Security Department. One man from Turkey said he had waited two months before Lithuanian officials travelled to Cyprus to interview him. “They came to Cyprus. I had an interview lasting several hours,” he said. A Sudanese asylum-seeker also described a lengthy interview process. “They asked about many things. It was a long interview, several hours,” he said. Under the EU solidarity mechanism, member states can contribute by accepting asylum-seekers relocated from countries facing particularly heavy migration pressure or by making financial payments to the bloc’s solidarity fund, a fine of sorts. Lithuania initially chose a combination of the two options, agreeing to accept half of its allocated number of asylum-seekers and pay nearly 1.5 million euros for the remainder. Next year, however, the government intends to accept none and pay instead. The exact amount has yet to be determined, but Katelynas estimates it could reach 4 million euros. The proposal has received support from the parliamentary committees on foreign affairs and European affairs. Baranovas said the decision reflected lessons learned from this year’s experience. “Some countries actually prefer money rather than the relocation of migrants. It seems that this money also helps them cover other budget lines,” he said. Opposition politicians, however, argue that Lithuania should use the money to address domestic needs, particularly as the country faces a substantial budget deficit and public-sector employees are demanding higher salaries. Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen, leader of the Liberal Movement’s parliamentary group, said the government was too willing to spend public money abroad. “It is easy to spend a million euros that could, for example, be used to increase the salaries of Migration Department employees,” she said. MEP Žalimas also questioned the decision, arguing that the government was spending millions while looking for ways to reduce the budget deficit. The financial argument is further complicated by the fact that the EU covers the integration costs of relocated asylum-seekers. According to Pocius, a country accepting a relocated person receives 10,000 euros in EU funding. However, the Reception and Integration Agency estimates that integrating one person over a period of 18 months costs about 5,000 euros. Some relocated asylum-seekers may also fail to qualify for refugee status following assessments by the Migration Department and could eventually be deported. The EU also covers the costs of such returns. Football is simple game with some classic ground rules that is played and enjoyed all around the world by millions of people. However, only a few players and managers will succeed to leave a lasting mark in football, and even fewer manage to change the game with revolutionary new playing styles or tactics. Among them is the visionary Austrian-Jewish coach Otto ‘Schloime’ Fischer (1901-1941) whose tactical acumen and unyielding spirit redefined Latvian football in the 1930s and brought it to a completely different level. “He was the Pep Guardiola or Jürgen Klopp of his day – a visionary coach with revolutionary new methods who brought beautiful football to the Baltics and unprecedented, unexpected sporting success to his club," writes British author Vincent Hunt, full of admiration for Fischer, who has left behind an important, but sometimes overlooked legacy, although his training methods are still felt in the modern football game. The then 35-year-old Fischer arrived from Vienna in Latvia in 1936 to train FK Olimpija Liepāja and completely transformed the game of the club from the third largest city in the Baltic country. Under the leadership of the former Austrian national player, Olimpija won the championships of Latvia in 1936, 1938 and 1939. Due to an offensive playing style and tactical masterplay, historians and football experts refer to Olimpija as the 'Barcelona of the Baltics' – an analogy with the modern and technically high quality football played by the Spanish club. Many coaches have applied the philosophy of possession and passing that made Barcelona famous under their captain and later coach Pep Guardiola, but the idea of playing this way can already be traced back to Fischer. While the methods and tactics of the Austrian trainer have lived on and are still recognisable today, the person behind them is hardly known nowadays – both in his home country and in Latvia. Not least because Fischer’s life was cut short in 1941 during the German occupation of Latvia and his story slipped from history. He died in the Holocaust and was shot just a few kilometers from the site of his footballing triumphs. Following the long years of Soviet occupation when any public discussion about the tragedy and fate of the Jewish population was suppressed for ideological reasons and deliberately excluded from the historiography, Fischer remained also largely forgotten in the once again independent Latvia. But now finally some commemoration initiatives have paid homage to one of the brightest personalities in the history of both Liepāja and Latvian football. “For me as an Austrian ambassador, it is a privilege and pleasure to be here today“, envoy Bernadette Klösch told the audience in April 2025 in her speech at the beginning of two-day long memorial event in Liepāja that started off with the unveiling of a commemorative plaque at the Olimpija stadium and was followed by an international conference and a football tournament. Photo: Alexander Welscher Commemorative plaque for Otto Fischer at the Olimpija stadium in Liepāja Organised by the Austrian embassy, the Liepaja Jewish Heritage Foundation and other partners, it brought together city officials, residents, members of the Jewish community, historians, football enthusiasts and guests from Austria – among them even descendents of Otto Fischer. “I am very grateful that we have this memory plate there that will stay here for a few generations, reminding young football players and the population of the Liepāja about the great achievements of Otto Fischer. And what he has achieved for the city in the field of football and also for the football community“, Klösch said at the ceremony, before pulling the curtain together with Liepāja mayor Gunārs Ansiņš to the tunes of “We are the champions“ and the applause of the attendees. Calling him “a very special person”, Ansiņš thanked all people involved in what he called a “historical investigation“ about Otto Fischer. The city head admitted in his speech that he had not heard the name of the Austrian footballer and coach before Ilana Ivanova from the Liepāja Jewish Heritage Foundation approached him several years ago. Ivanova back then told him about Fischer and her reseach project, aiming to restore the memory of the legendary trainer of the strongest football teams in pre-war Latvia. The plaque has been installed at one concrete stand resting on an old fortification structure of the strategic military port that used to protect the coast of Liepāja Fortress south of the Trade Canal and in the early 1920s was included in the construction of the Olimpija Stadium. Being once the epicenter of Liepāja’s sporting life, it was home to the Olimpija football club and the Maccabi athletics club. Nowadays the stadium is primarly used by reserve and junior teams of FK Liepāja and serves also as venue for other sport events. “This is not the most obvious place for a memorial plaque. Usually we would unveil it at a house or something like that but here we unveil a plaque at a place where somebody actually worked,“ the Director of the Museum Jews in Latvia, Ilja Lensky, commented on the location of the monument that he nevertheless considers a suitable and very fitting place. “It is important that the plaque will be seen by those for whom his work means the most – for football players or for sportsmen.” Fischer's name is inseperately linked to the golden age of football both in Austria and Latvia. Born in Vienna in 1901 as the youngest of five children of a Moravian Jewish family, the talented footballer rose to prominence in his home country during in the 1920s and early 1930s and became a national player. “During his active football career, Otto Fischer was one of the most popular and successful footballers in Austria,“ explains the Austrian author Alexander Juraske, who wrote the 2024 published biography “Otto 'Schloime' Fischer – Ein jüdischer Fußballstar aus Wien“ [Otto 'Schloime' Fischer – A Jewish Football Star f

The ‘HADES GEKON M2’ unmanned platform is demonstrating its capabilities at the University of Latvia’s Academic Centre. It can operate in areas where it is dangerous for humans to be present. It can be used for reconnaissance, the evacuation of the wounded, and engineering work. It can also be adapted for the use of combat and air defence weapons. This land-based drone can carry a payload of 300 kilograms and reach a speed of 50 kilometres per hour. “Using a radio-controlled remote, it can operate within a range of up to two kilometres; alternatively, by using either satellite navigation or a ‘Starlink’ satellite connection, this robotic platform can essentially be controlled remotely from the other side of the globe, without any restrictions. It all depends on the connectivity systems,” said Armands Sakne, Business Development Manager at SIA “LV-Teh”. The “HADES GEKON M2” unmanned platform has been developed for the Latvian Armed Forces. In April this year, a contract was signed with the National Armed Forces (NBS) for the supply of the platform. It differs from the robotic systems used in Ukraine. “Entirely developed in Latvia. Latvian engineers have developed it entirely themselves. It is essentially built using as many European components as possible. This vehicle is free of Chinese components, which is very important from a supply chain perspective. It has been specially designed for Latvian conditions – Latvian vegetation, that is, marshes, wetlands and dense, dense forests. The Latvian Army has conducted extensive comparative tests on various platforms and is still continuing these tests. “And so everything has been specifically designed to ensure that this platform will, more or less as we hope, serve as the Baltic region’s national unmanned ground platform – not only for Latvia, but also, as is our aim, for the armed forces of Lithuania and Estonia,” emphasised Sakne. The University of Latvia and the company ‘LV-Teh’ have signed a long-term cooperation agreement to promote the development of defence technology, robotics, artificial intelligence and electronics, and to transform research into practical and competitive products. “This is very, very important. Consequently, artificial intelligence infrastructure is being deployed, which is capable of recognising what is happening on the battlefield from this volume of data,” explained the Head of Business Development at SIA “LV-Teh”. Such collaboration helps to create high-value-added products for international markets, promotes economic development and enhances national defence. Meanwhile, students and young researchers have the opportunity to work with technologies on which future security will largely depend.

This vulnerability was discovered two years ago by the cyber incident response organisation ‘Cert.lv’. They informed LVM of this and asked them to rectify it, but this did not happen. “Yes, it should have been fixed. We misunderstood the information,” says Māris Kuzmins, Director of IT Infrastructure and Development at LVM. “We were also keen to understand where exactly the communication problem had been. For the time being, we have realised that on the ‘Latvian State Forests’ side, the mathematical symbol “≥” (greater than or equal to) appears to have been misinterpreted, and conclusions were consequently drawn regarding whether a specific version of the software was affected or not,” explains Varis Teivāns, deputy head of “Cert.lv”. LVM had received an email from “Cert.lv” containing technical information about the affected software and which specific parts of it were affected. It is reportedly standard practice to use such a mathematical symbol when describing the ranges of affected software versions. LVM is not seeking to hold any specific individual responsible. At present, the organisation is paying heightened attention to any indications of potential system security vulnerabilities. “From now on, we’re not talking about four pairs of eyes, but six or eight. We are paying much closer attention to any emails or any information that contains details of a vulnerability,” says LVM spokesperson Kuzmins. “Security tests must be carried out by a third party. You cannot simply take your own team and carry out the security tests. They will simply be blind to the obvious,” explains Kirils Solovjovs, head of the IT security group “Possible Security”. The cybercriminal stole 44 gigabytes of data stored by LVM. Following the data breach, “Cert.lv” contacted several critical infrastructure operators, as the leaked information could potentially affect them as well. “A further investigation specifically into the content of the leaked data was carried out, and it was found that it does indeed contain sensitive details, both from the perspective of technical infrastructure maintenance – various access keys, authentication data, correspondence details – as well as employee information and details regarding the infrastructure and documents of the Latvian State Forests themselves,” reveals Teivāns. The specific attacker or group targeted several organisations in European countries this summer. It is expected that this trend will continue due to artificial intelligence. “I wouldn’t say that artificial intelligence models can detect something that a human cannot; they simply can do so much faster in certain cases,” says Solovjovs. Given that artificial intelligence will make it possible to identify system vulnerabilities much more quickly, the intensity of cyber-attacks could increase significantly. “Of course, there are various speculations that, if these artificial intelligence tools continue to develop at the same rapid pace, a situation known as the ‘vulnerability apocalypse’ could arise. As it is often referred to in this industry, there will be so many vulnerabilities, and they will be discovered so rapidly, that the industry will be unable to fix them quickly enough,” says Teivāns.

https://eng.lsm.lv/article/society/defen: "Given the current geopolitical security situation and recent drone incidents in Latvian airspace, it is necessary to introduce a mechanism that would allow for the rapid deployment of air defence systems anywhere in Latvia. The amendments will strengthen comprehensive national defence, allowing the armed forces to respond as quickly as possible in the event of a military threat," said Defense Minister Raivis Melnis explaining the need for the change. The amendments provide that in the event of a military threat, the Commander of the National Armed Forces (NBS) or a person authorized by him or her has the right to make a decision on the temporary takeover of real estate for a period of up to 14 days with the right to extend this period for another 14 days. "A decision to take over property by the National Armed Forces will be made only if, in a specific situation, the use of the property is necessary to prevent a military threat or implement protective measures," said a Defence Ministry statement. "It will be possible to deploy air defence systems, radars, communications equipment, military equipment or, if necessary, military units on temporarily occupied lands and parts thereof, as well as to carry out activities related to the fulfillment of defence tasks," it added. Legally, the new regulation could be applied anywhere in Latvia, not only along the borders. In addition, such temporary land requisitions could take place even if the threat is not necessarily directed against Latvia itself, provided they are deemed to pose a threat to the security of the state and society of Latvia. Thus the amendments give considerable leeway to the NBS to requisition land for what is effectively a month. The ability of the Commander to delegate responsibility – any military is in a sense an organization with delegation at all levels in the form of ranks – further broadens the power of the NBS with regard to private property. For the duration of the NBS' presence, the real estate taken over will acquire the status of a military facility. Therefore, the security restrictions imposed on military facilities will apply. This will, among other things, mean restrictions on unauthorized photography and filming and if necessary, military personnel will also be able to restrict the presence of the landowner. No compensation will be payable, except in cases where property is damaged as a result of the actions of the National Armed Forces. The procedure for compensation for losses, transfer and return of property, the procedure for challenging decisions, as well as other related issues all remain to be decided. It should be noted that in order for the amendments to the law to enter into force, they must still be reviewed and adopted by the Saeima, where they are likely to come under scrutiny. The NBS can currently agree with landowners on the use of real estate for national defence purposes. However, such a solution requires an agreement process and is not regarded as suitable for situations where a decision must be made in a very short time to prevent a military threat. The new amendments are intended for such a scenario and particularly the necessity of putting air defence systems in place rapidly at locations that may be far from state-owned land plots. The intention of the amendments is therefore not to generally expand the NAF's right to use private property (though this is certainly one result), but rather to create a legal mechanism for specific situations of urgent military threat. Finding themselves thousands of kilometres from home, Ukrainians have come to realise that independence is not merely a territory with borders on a map. Independence is the people, their values and their inner freedom – things that cannot be occupied. For many war refugees, the first few months in exile were spent in a state of shock, pain and disorientation. Longing for their homeland had paralysed their will. It seemed that, along with the flat, job and familiar circle of friends we’d left behind, some of us had lost a part of ourselves. “I thought I’d coped quite well with this forced move to Latvia. I didn’t have any panic attacks or anything like that. But only now, more than four years on, do I realise – the stress was there, and it was quite severe. I simply bottled it up inside and am only now gradually letting it go. At the time, I was as if frozen – there were no emotions, no desires, no colour." However, the support of Latvian society and the inner strength of the Ukrainian community set the process of change in motion. The Ukrainians’ longing for their homeland gradually began to turn into pride in their own country. It was precisely whilst living abroad that many Ukrainians realised what Ukraine meant to them. “I realised that Ukraine is a character,” says Maria from Kyiv. “It’s a will, it’s warmth, it’s self-sacrifice. I remember 24 February well – the first day of the great war – when our men – usually builders, drivers, managers, IT specialists – set off to defend Ukraine and its independence. I am deeply moved by the hearts of those Ukrainians who, for the fifth year running, have been tirelessly supporting the front line; by the strength of our soldiers’ mothers; and by the strength of the soldiers themselves in captivity. That, you see, is Ukrainian independence. That is exactly how I see it.” Watching how Ukraine is fighting, how it refuses to give in against all the odds, many Ukrainians realise: ‘I am part of this great, proud and indomitable nation.’ And this realisation gives them the strength to hold their heads high even when things are at their hardest. “For four and a half years I’ve been living in Latvia, keeping up with how things are going in Ukraine. Is it hard for me? Yes, it is hard. I have no one here apart from my children and the responsibility for them. But it’s even harder over there (in Ukraine – O.P.). Because every day and every night under Russian shelling is a threat to life. If people are living in such conditions and continuing to fight for freedom, then how can I give up?” says Svitlana from Reny in the Odessa region. The Latvian people understand the pain of the Ukrainians like no other, having themselves endured Soviet occupation, deportations and a long struggle to restore independence. Ukrainian flags on the streets of Latvian towns, words of support from locals – it’s inspiring. The people of Latvia have shown that you may lose your land for a time, but if you’ve kept your spirit alive, you will certainly regain everything else. The fact that Ukrainians abroad are celebrating Independence Day is like a special test of maturity. There is no need for ‘tick-box’ gestures – creating the impression of patriotism, making sure to wear a vyshyvanka or singing the national anthem. Yet every such choice is voluntary and conscious. And it is a way of declaring that the Russian occupiers have not succeeded in forcing us to forget where we come from. “We’ve always had vyshyvankas; every family had their own even before the war. Yet the feeling with which we wear it here in Latvia is quite different. It is not a formality, nor is it simply a beautiful garment. It is – without exaggeration – the nation’s code; it is what is now close to my heart,” says Ludmila from the Kirovohrad region. What does it mean to be a Ukrainian patriot in Latvia? It is a daily endeavour. For example, learning the Latvian language out of respect for the country that has taken in Ukrainians, whilst at the same time speaking Ukrainian with the children at home so that they do not lose their connection with their homeland. It involves sending money to the Ukrainian Armed Forces. It involves weaving camouflage nets at volunteer centres in Riga after the working day. It means remaining a worthy representative of one’s country, shaping its image in the eyes of Europeans. Ukraine’s independence depends on each and every one of us – the soldiers are holding the front line, but they need reliable support from the home front, including from abroad. Our independence lies within us. It lies in our thoughts, our principles, our love for one another and for our land. And as long as this fire burns in our hearts here in Latvia, Ukraine will remain unconquerable. Happy holidays, my dear compatriots! Glory to Ukraine!

The initial investment is estimated at around 50 million euros, but the total could reach 200 million euros. AI will tell you what each party says it stands for and what it says it will do, but AI is also notoriously credulous and dispassionate. https://eng.lsm.lv/article/features/comm: Borrowing has not become costless; rather, governments are reassessing the cost of not investing. Germany illustrates the shift clearly. In March 2025, it amended its fiscal framework to allow defence and specified security-related expenditure above 1% of GDP to be financed outside the regular borrowing limit. It also established a €500 billion special fund for infrastructure and climate-neutrality investments over 12 years. (Source: German Federal Ministry of Finance, Financing package for security and investment, April 2025; Special Fund for Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality, June 2026.) Poland is making a similar calculation under tighter fiscal conditions. The European Commission expects public debt to rise from 59.7% of GDP in 2025 to 64.5% in 2026 and 68.3% in 2027, with the deficit remaining at 6.5% in 2026, defence investment being among the contributing factors. (Source: European Commission, Economic Forecast for Poland, 21 May 2026.) These decisions are being taken in a euro area where government debt already stands at 88.9% of GDP, up from 87.7% at the end of 2025. (Source: Eurostat, 21 July 2026.) The consequence of simultaneous fiscal expansion across a currency union deserves more attention than it receives. When many governments increase borrowing and spending at once, the effect on prices is shared by all members of the union, whether or not they took part. In this sense, inflation in a monetary union is a common resource: no single small member's restraint can meaningfully reduce it. Local conditions still matter, as the Baltic experience of 2022 showed, but the monetary component of the price level that Latvian households and pensioners will face over the next decade is being set as much in Berlin and Paris as in Rīga. The scale of the debt also shapes how the coming decade is likely to be managed. Euro area government bonds are held overwhelmingly by banks, insurers and pension funds, which is to say, by citizens' own savings. A government carrying debt of this size faces, in the end, a choice between two paths: defend the real value of the bonds, which means years of restrained spending and stagnant or falling incomes, or allow inflation to run ahead of interest rates, eroding the debt while incomes, at least in nominal terms, keep growing. Wherever democracies have held that choice in their own hands, at the level of a currency they control, they have resolved it the second way, because no electorate will accept prolonged income stagnation to protect the value of paper it holds through its pension statements. The European Central Bank can lean against this with higher interest rates, but at a debt ratio near 90% of GDP, each percentage point of rates eventually adds close to a percentage point of GDP to governments' annual interest bills, and the governments feeling that pain are the same ones who write the central bank's mandate and appoint its leadership. That is the environment in which Latvia's investment decisions are now being made. For Latvia, this is not an abstract question. The country is building the largest infrastructure project in its modern history, connecting the Baltic states to the European standard-gauge railway network. Hesitation in a project such as Rail Baltica rarely means deciding to stop. It is more gradual: funding the project incrementally, waiting for successive European funding cycles, postponing decisions on financing beyond grants, and allowing the delivery schedule to slip one individually reasonable decision at a time. Each decision may be defensible on its own, while the cumulative effect can still be expensive. Cost escalation has damaged confidence in Rail Baltica, and the state has every reason to challenge specifications, remove unnecessary scope and demand credible estimates. Bringing the project down to a rational minimum technical specification is part of responsible management. But cost discipline and delivery speed should not be confused. https://eng.lsm.lv/article/politics/elec: But while the process of a Latvian parliamentary election is an excellent example of transparent democracy in action, there are a few unusual and particularly Latvian variations on how 100 deputies are actually chosen for a four-year term in Latvia's unicameral parliament, the Saeima. Here's a summary of how the whole process works. Candidates for Saeima elections must be members of a registered political party or alliance of parties. Many of the main 'parties' are in fact groups of smaller sub-parties, though this makes little practical difference beyond some very long party names on ballot papers. For example, what's usually called the 'National Alliance' should correctly be referred to as the "National Alliance 'All for Latvia!' – 'For Fatherland and Freedom/LNNK'" and will appear as such on ballot papers. For the 15th Saeima elections, the submission of lists of candidates took place from 20 June to 5 July, at the Central Election Commission (CVK), the body which oversees all elections in the country. Candidates have to be Latvian citizens (dual citizens are also eligible) aged 21 or over. There are restrictions on allowing former Communist Party members, Soviet functionaries, prisoners and mentally ill persons to stand. Parties have to pay a security deposit of €4,680 along with the submission of their electoral list. The list can be submitted electronically or in paper form in person. If the party fails to win at least 2% of the vote, it loses its deposit. If it does get 2% or more, it gets its deposit back. The move is designed to discourage 'vanity' runs for office, and the deposit required has risen from €1,400 at the 2022 elections. After submission, the lists are checked, and any ineligible candidates are barred from standing. Parties can field a maximum of 125 candidates. All citizens of Latvia aged 18 and over are entitled to vote on election day. They need to take a valid Latvian citizen's passport or eID card. You cannot vote without a valid identity document. Latvia's "non-citizens" – a legacy of the Soviet occupation years – are not entitled to vote in parliamentary elections, even if they have permanent resident status. However, they can gain the right to vote if they undergo a process of naturalisation and become citizens. An interactive map shows all the polling stations here . https://eng.lsm.lv/article/politics/elec: While everyone likes to be talked about, such coverage can sometimes lead to Latvians pulling their hair out as correspondents sent to cover the election repeat a variety of misconceptions or fall into traps of assumption based upon a brief wander around the streets of central Rīga. With that in mind, we've drawn up a brief list of some of the more common booby-traps that might be encountered, in the hope that it might help our international colleagues to sidestep them. Latvia's multi-party system means voters have plenty of different options from which to choose – at least on paper. Even if one party turns out to do much better than all the others, that does not necessarily mean it has 'won' the election or that it will necessarily even be part of the next government. Just look at the example of the Harmony Centre party, which 'won' the elections of 2014 with 23% of the vote and again in 2018 with 20% of the vote. It has never been in power, as other parties with smaller shares of the vote consistently refused to join it in coalition. The 2018 results also demonstrate another similar item of interest: the Prime Minister does not necessarily come from the dominant party in a coalition. In that year, the PM ended up being Krišjānis Kariņš from the 'Unity' party, which was actually the smallest party in the entire parliament, after PM candidates from both the New Conservatives and KPV LV failed to find support. Magnifying this is a certain reluctance to take up the role of Prime Minister among many Latvian politicians. While being PM is viewed as the pinnacle of political achievement in many countries, in Latvia it is sometimes seen as a bit of a poisoned chalice. In general, political types seem much happier to be a Minister with responsibility for just one area than a Prime Minister, who has to reconcile opposing parties, soothe the egos of everyone involved and do a lot more work under a lot more scrutiny. Several recent Prime Ministers, such as Māris Kučinskis and Laimdota Straujuma, essentially got the jobs because better-known and higher-profile politicians didn't want to touch the PM's chair with a bargepole. A happy side effect is that these more modest politicians who are uninterested in being famous and yet have the premiership thrust upon them tend to be quite competent because they are largely uninterested in ambition and in-fighting. The notions of 'left' and 'right' politics are in flux throughout the world, not least because of the rise of various forms of populism and an increasing tendency to use American political discourse and definitions in a non-American political environment such as Europe. In Latvia's case, "left" and "right" have long been problematic and sometimes fairly irrelevant terms, though in the 2026 elections it is notable that several parties are much more open about describing themselves as parties of the right and even of the 'Christian' right, despite Latvia's secular state. It could be argued that 10 of the 14 parties participating would describe themselves as right of centre to a greater or lesser extent. Yet even a party as overtly 'nationalist' as the National Alliance favours large-scale state intervention in the economy – not a usual 'right' position. Conversely, Harmony does its best to depict itself as a modern social democratic party of the left, but everyone still perceives it as essentially an ethnic Russian party rather than one with a left-wing ideology. Until 2017 – well after the illegal occupation of Crimea by Russia in 2014 – it still had ties to Vladimir Putin's United Russia party, and its position on social policy was often considerably more conservative than social democrats would expect. For example, it did not support attempts to establish a same-sex civil partnership law and some of its members voted against Latvia ratifying the Istanbul Convention. Conservative offerings range from soft-right liberals to far-right demagogues. The Progressives are probably the only unambiguously left-of-centre party, and in fact the closest thing to a 'green' party in this election, which brings us neatly to the problematic status of 'green' politics in Latvia. Two parties in the election lists contain the word 'green' in their names: the Greens and Farmers' Union (ZZS) and the Latvian Green Party, which is part of the United List political ticket. Now, ZZS doesn't actually have any green politics to speak of, being essentially an agrarian farming lobby with a long history. The Latvian Green Party used to be part of it but split away, along with quite a few other ZZS politicians who were sick of its links to oligarch Aivars Lembergs, to form the United List. Nevertheless, the name remains unchanged. https://eng.lsm.lv/article/economy/emplo: Forecasts from the Ministry of Economics indicate that by 2040 the working-age population in Latvia could decline by approximately 9.4 per cent. Opportunities to significantly increase the supply of local labour will be limited. At the start of the year, 15,177 third-country citizens were residing in Latvia on the basis of employment, representing 16 per cent of all third-country nationals with the right to work in Latvia. However, it is not clear to the state in which sectors, occupations and to what extent Latvia will require foreign labour. Nor have any mechanisms been established for the targeted recruitment of labour from specific countries, such as bilateral migration agreements, target country programmes or simplified procedures for nationals of certain countries. As a result, the flow of foreign labour is determined primarily by individual employer demand rather than by a coordinated national policy. Although policy planning documents emphasise the attraction of highly skilled professionals, from the start of 2024 to mid-2025, only 14 per cent of work permits were issued for highly skilled occupations. 57 per cent of work permits were granted for medium-skilled occupations and 29 per cent for low-skilled occupations. Furthermore, approximately 40 per cent of all work permits were issued to lorry and tractor unit drivers. This indicates that the actual labour force requirements are much broader than those set out in policy documents. The audit concluded that the process of obtaining a work permit is lengthy and difficult to predict for employers and foreign workers. Although the decision-making deadlines set out in legislation are not significantly longer than in other European Union countries, the overall process is significantly prolonged by various intermediate stages, the duration of which is not systematically managed or monitored. Obtaining a work visa takes approximately three months, whilst obtaining a work residence permit, if the application is submitted from outside Latvia, takes an average of six months, according to the audit. The capacity of Latvia’s diplomatic missions abroad, the availability of appointments for document submission, and the speed of document processing have a significant impact on these timeframes. Another major problem is the repeated submission of the same documents and data to different authorities. Although several institutions are involved in the decision-making process, they do not have access to the full set of previously submitted documents and the results of checks carried out; consequently, the same circumstances sometimes have to be assessed repeatedly. This creates an additional administrative burden for employers, foreign workers and the public authorities themselves. The State Audit Office has also concluded that a complex work permit process, including certain disproportionate and unjustified conditions, may encourage employers to opt for other labour recruitment models. The number of third-country citizens posted to Latvia from other European Union countries has risen from 972 to 1,863 in the space of a year. The more the recruitment of foreign labour shifts towards other models regulated by the European Union, the less practical significance Latvia’s work permit system has, and the less influence the state has over the recruitment of foreign labour. Furthermore, the auditors’ estimates indicate that, as a result of such short-term postings, the Latvian budget may have lost approximately five million euros in labour tax revenue in 2025. The audit also identified cases in which a work residence permit may have been used as a simpler route to obtaining the right of residence. Upon examining 60 work residence permit cases, it was found in 12 instances that a foreign national had, through a company in Latvia owned by themselves or related persons, invited themselves or family members to work. A total of 160 companies were identified in which a third-country national was simultaneously the company’s beneficial owner and an employee. Of these, 101 companies paid only payroll taxes, whilst in 50 companies the beneficial owner was also the sole employee. Although European Union regulations allow Member States to set a waiting period of up to two years before family reunification, in Latvia family members may join a foreign national immediately after a work residence permit has been granted. This means that residence rights are granted to family members even before there is certainty regarding the stability of the person’s employment and residence in Latvia.

https://eng.lsm.lv/article/features/feat: Apart from the politicians themselves, who clearly have a vested interest, prominent among the encouraging voices are earnest journalists – or sneaky members of the global media conspiracy, if you prefer to think in those terms. Whether their motivation is an idealistic vision of the benefits of democracy, a sinister desire to bend you to the will of their overlords or just a lazy intellectual arrogance that leads them to assume they know the political landscape better than you do, is a matter for conjecture. The point is that not only do they want you to vote, but they will also even provide pointers to help you choose where to place your 'X'. These pointers usually take the form of a series of questions, to which you are expected to provide honest answers – itself something of a tall order. At the end of this process you receive the name of the party which most closely matches the preferences you expressed, and probably a couple of other parties who are in the same ballpark as you but fielding right out near the fence. Incidentally the LSM version of this gizmo is now available here (in Latvian) if you want to give it a go. These selection processes – which are really just glorified flowcharts, whether they are described as questionnaires, quizzes or the supposed insights of (yawn) Artificial Intelligence – have a couple of major drawbacks. First, they always come across as patronising, relishing their own cleverness and their ability to reveal hidden tendencies deep within you, of which you have been unaware until the revelatory verdict is delivered. It feels as if you are getting voting advice from Sigmund Freud based upon vague childhood memories. The second, and more serious, drawback of this selection process is that it takes the political parties and their promises at face value. Their track records on delivering previous promises are not taken into account at all. The percentage of a party's leading members who have previously been members of other parties that collapsed immediately after an election is not considered. And then there are the false dichotomies: party X favours stricter immigration controls, but party Y favours bringing in more guest workers. Which option do you select in the questionnaire? Possibly the one that brings in more guest workers who are also subject to stricter immigration controls? All this is by way of preamble, and we Latvians love a preamble, particularly when it's pointless. So let's get down to it. Below, you will find a few alternative ways to select which political party deserves your backing on October 3rd. Some of them may not be entirely serious, but they might cause a pause for thought for a few nanoseconds, and none have been generated by AI, for which you have our 'ironclad' (to use a popular buzzword of the moment) guarantee. We should admit this also has a secondary purpose, and it is not even to advance the pan-galactic media conspiracy.
