European Union (EU) member states are due to extend sanctions against more than 3,000 individuals in connection with Russia's invasion of Ukraine this week. The sanctions list also includes Pyotr (or Petr) ​​Aven, who lives in Latvia and was added to the list four years ago as one of Vladimir Putin's closest oligarchs. He holds Latvian and Russian citizenship. Aven has been a Latvian citizen since 2016, having apparently completed necessary citizenship procedures including a language test. As previously reported by LSM, the manner in which Aven obtained his Latvian passport has been a long-running controversy. He was also in the headlines in connection with a controversial exhibition in Ogre of his porcelain collection, which was backed by the local mayor . Way back in 2017 he said he was mulling opening a personal museum in Rīga. No such museum ever opened, and his official website appears to be sorely in need of an update, as it says he will "open the venue to the public by 2025". Despite calls for Aven to be stripped of his Latvian citizenship, he can be fairly certain about retaining his Latvian citizenship, reported De Facto. Even with a self-styled hardliner now in charge of the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry sees no reason to deprive him of citizenship, reports De Facto. Billionaire Aven, was met by De Facto by chance in a park in central Riga a week ago, when negotiations were taking place between EU member states on extending sanctions. "Now I can't, I can't, I can't, I'm not ready," Aven repeated several times in Latvian when asked if he would agree to be interviewed. Aven was among the businessmen who were gathered in the Kremlin at the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Notoriously, when asked by President Putin if anyone had objections to such a course of action, none of the meek oligarchs, including Aven, said a word. He then moved to his grandfather's homeland, Latvia. Aven can stay here because he had already acquired Latvian citizenship, in contrast to other Russian emigres who have been shown the door. The Corruption Prevention and Combating Bureau investigated the arrangement whereby Aven obtained his passport, but the case was closed without any evidence found of a crime being committed. The tabloid press occasionally records Aven attending sporting or cultural events. "I will live in Latvia all my life, and there will be time [to talk], but now I can't," Avens replied when asked what he plans to do in Latvia – a sentiment with an echo of his silence in 2022. He asked De Facto to contact his office for interview opportunities, despite the fact that Aven has always refused De Facto's previous interview requests. His assets are currently frozen. Aven has challenged the imposition of sanctions in the Court of Justice of the EU. The final decision in neither case has entered into force. He has also been sanctioned by the US and the UK. Latvian security authorities have been assessing whether there are any reasons to revoke Aven's citizenship in recent years. But so far, they have found none. Some of the most active critics of Aven's citizenship have been politicians from the National Alliance (NA). At the beginning of the year, while working in the Saeima opposition, Edvīns Šnore, who recently became the parliamentary secretary of the Ministry of the Interior, called it "quite strange" for the billionaire to retain Latvian citizenship. "This is also something we wanted to find out more about when we took office, and what we also received from the services is that, yes, this is the current situation. It is not static. It is developing with some, let's say, activities that Aven is carrying out," said Šnore. Amendments to the Citizenship Law adopted in the spring of 2022 provide for the deprivation of Latvian citizenship for those who have provided support to countries that have committed war crimes and undermine the independence of democratic states. It must be concluded that in the case of Aven, the state security authorities have not presented such evidence. "I would personally support this issue being finally resolved and making it impossible for this person to maintain dual citizenship. But it is not possible for the Minister of Internal Affairs to make that decision directly with his signature," said Minister of Internal Affairs Jānis Dombrava (NA). He mentions as a theoretical possibility the article of the law under which Avens obtained a Latvian passport could be clarified so that he would not be able to retain dual citizenship. However, even Šnore, a member of the same party, doubts whether such amendments could be applied retroactively to Aven. Despite De Facto's subsequent request, Aven did not agree to an interview and declined even to provide written answers to questions that were sent to him. "Considering that currently some politicians are actively using my name in Saeima pre-election communication and political rhetoric, I do not want to get involved in pre-election discussions or become a tool in the political struggle," Aven wrote in reply to De Facto. He is currently in appeal proceedings with Latvia regarding the sanctions imposed until the spring of 2023. The EU court granted Aven's initial claim, but Latvia contested the decision . It is not known when a final decision is expected in this case.

Back in 2016 a wargaming simulation by the RAND Corporation led to the Defence Minister seeking to reassure the public , and a BBC television simulation show called World War Three: Inside The War Room used a strikingly similar "they are all in a bunker while events escalate in Latgale" set-up. It led to widespread criticism from Latvian politicians with then-Foreign Minister and now-President Edgars Rinkēvičs describing the scenario as "rubbish" but "with many lessons to learn". Anyway, returning to the 2026 edition (which is stretched over three shows rather than the 2016's mercifully brief one-off), the parties in the Dr Strangelove war room are the Greens and Farmers Union (ZZS), For the Development of Latvia, Progressives, For Stability!, United List, New Unity, National Alliance, Sovereign Power/New Latvians, and Latvia First. Police are called and the pensioner dies in the incident, which sparks controversy on social media. The second scenario sees the atmosphere in Silgale becoming more tense and polarised between its Russian and Latvian populations. There are demonstrations and counter-demonstrations, not all of them official. How should politicians react? The third scenario sees Russian propaganda seizing upon the Silgale situation and buzzing the nearby border with drones. The atmosphere becomes more febrile still and the politicians must mull whether to declare a state of emergency.

https://eng.lsm.lv/article/society/educa: In 2025, “Cert.lv” carried out 16 phishing simulation campaigns to assess the vigilance of company employees against cyber security threats and to identify areas where further training is required. Following the tests carried out, ‘Cert.lv’ concludes that it is possible within the company’s e-service to alter user data and create an account for another person, thereby granting unauthenticated access to protected user information; it is possible to create multiple applications for a single user, to approve an incomplete application, and to select files from the ‘MS IIS’ web service using the ‘~’ symbol. “Cert.lv” is a unit of the Institute of Mathematics and Computer Science at the University of Latvia, whose tasks are to maintain a unified overview of activities taking place in the electronic information space, to provide support in preventing information technology security incidents, and to coordinate the prevention of such incidents within Latvian IP address ranges and the ‘.lv’ domain name zone.

https://eng.lsm.lv/article/society/defen: Industrially manufactured shelters could be either above-ground or underground, and could be purchased by local authorities and other institutions in places where there are no suitable cellars or where adapting them would be too complicated. The Ministry of Economics (EM) has promised to draw up standardised documentation for the procurement of such shelters by the start of October. Olga Feldmane, Director of the Ministry of Economics’s Construction Policy Department, explained that, based on the example of Ukraine, installing an above-ground shelter could be cheaper than creating a shelter within existing premises. Standardised procurement documentation will enable local authorities to compare different options and select the one best suited to a specific location. Feldmane cited the example of a school where, for instance, the cellar can provide shelter for 200 children, but 300 are needed. “In that case, we can install a freestanding shelter to ensure that all the children have a place to take shelter.” Why is it only now that industrially manufactured shelters are being given serious consideration in Latvia, even though it hsa been clear for a long time that the existing basement capacity will not be sufficient for the entire population? Elīna Egle-Ločmele, Chair of the Board of the Latvian Security and Defence Industry Federation, emphasised that the problem does not lie in the industry’s ability to produce them. Although the State Fire and Rescue Service (VUGD) has been raising this issue for several years, there has so far been a lack of clear demand, uniform requirements and a long-term procurement programme. The Federation is currently assessing the standard specifications prepared by the Ministry of the Environment and submitting its proposals. Overall, the assessment is positive, but there will be recommendations, noted Egle-Ločmele: “The work is, of course, long overdue. It is currently quite challenging for companies to invest in production, as there is still no clear demand for such products.” Egle-Ločmele emphasised that Latvian companies have both the expertise and the potential to manufacture industrially produced shelters.Foreign solutions are also available on the Latvian market, but local companies can offer both large-scale structures and shelter solutions, as well as specialised materials. When asked by Latvian Radio whether the sector would be ready for larger-scale state and local authority procurement in the near future, Egle-Ločmele replied in the affirmative: “Our members working in the construction sector are certainly ready for this. But, to be honest, in order to produce such large-scale, mass-produced items, it would be necessary to place orders for much larger volumes, so that companies can, in turn, place orders in the supply chain in good time and mobilise their production.” At the same time, she emphasised that the strength of Latvian companies currently lies not in mass production, but in their extensive expertise in construction, ventilation, energy supply, communications and security solutions. This provides flexibility in a situation where the scale of demand is not yet clear. However, the first signs of demand are already visible. For example, procurement has taken place for “Augstsprieguma tīkls”, and local authorities are also beginning to procure shelter equipment. Egle-Ločmele emphasised that mobile shelters will not replace all cellars. If suitable premises are already available, it makes more sense to adapt them; if not, a factory-built shelter may be quicker to install. However, it is not always cheaper, as the cost of foundations, transport, assembly and utility connections must also be taken into account. “That is why the state should consider both of these solutions. Using a standardised methodology, taking into account how much it costs to create a shelter for one person, and how quickly it can be provided,” she said. Looking at the bigger picture, shelter coverage is currently particularly poor in residential areas: both in the vicinity of blocks of flats and private homes. Uldis Ķevers, Head of the Civil Protection Administration at the State Fire and Rescue Service (VUGD), explained that residents in areas with private homes need to consider either building their own basement or constructing another structure that would provide protection. One such solution in the future could be mobile shelters. “In future, owners of such private homes may also be able to purchase a 60-square-metre shelter to install on their property, subject to simplified building and registration requirements, and place it on their own land,” explained Ķevers. This was confirmed by Feldmane from the Ministry of Economics, who pointed out that there would be no obstacles for private individuals to install such shelters: “Anyone can purchase such a shelter. The market offers both small shelters suitable for a single family and large shelters, which we can also assemble later in a modular fashion to create very large shelters.” To make it easier to install them, the Ministry of the Environment is proposing amendments that would allow for deviations from certain zoning regulations when installing shelters, as safety considerations would take precedence in such cases.

https://eng.lsm.lv/article/features/comm: The fundamental question facing us before the 15th Saeima elections is clear: can Latvia be entrusted to this or that party and its leaders in the event of war? Will they be able to lead the country under dire circumstances? Will they flee at the first opportunity or, worse yet, work for the enemy? We are each burdened by our own daily worries, and it is highly likely that we are deeply disappointed that the state has failed to help us deal with some of them. Every day we witness some absurdity, and perhaps we feel we have even experienced injustice. We have reason to be angry about many things that the politicians who have led the country did or did not do. It is depressing to look at comparative tables of European Union countries where Latvia often languishes near the bottom. A grip on the Rail Baltica project has eluded several successive governments. Inequality and declining demographics remain as apressing as ever. One could cite countless other examples. Yet, getting bogged down in these issues risks obscuring the bigger picture. On a global scale, Latvia belongs to the bloc of the wealthiest and most successful nations, and it continues to grow and develop even in unfavorable conditions. It is hard to predict how events will unfold in the coming years, but one thing is certain: a brutal war is taking place in Ukraine, and we live next to an aggressor state—Russia—that has never been well-disposed toward us. We are already experiencing a form of warfare ourselves: European countries are being targeted through sabotage, terrorist acts, information and influence operations, drones, and migrants who are helped to cut barbed wire or tunnel beneath our borders. LSM is not neutral regarding the war in Ukraine. We have clearly taken Ukraine’s side, and this stance serves as a significant catalyst in politics as well. It is unacceptable for parties to come to power if they fail to distinguish between the aggressor and the victim in the Ukraine war or refuse to support Ukraine—regardless of the excuses used, such as "not wanting to fuel a bloody conflict" or "putting the interests of Latvia's residents first." I have noticed that whenever we publish a post on LSM’s social media platforms about aid to Ukraine, a swarm of trolls appears with condemnatory comments, claiming we are squandering money on Ukrainians while we ourselves lack this or that. I believe that, unfortunately, there are people who really think this way; however, it is well known that this is also a Kremlin-inspired narrative circulated across Europe’s political landscape. There is never enough money, of course, but let us remember what is truly fundamental right now. It would be suicidal to hand the country over to individuals who maintain ties—whether familial, artistic, or financial—with Putin’s regime and Russia’s military-industrial complex. During the election campaign, we learned that such people are indeed vying for seats in parliament. I also wish to emphasize the importance of honesty—in every respect. Corruption stifles national progress. Latvia lived in the grip of oligarchs for far too long. Voting for politicians who use politics to build their own businesses—or who operate on the principle of "stealing but sharing the spoils"—is akin to sawing off the very branch one is sitting upon. There are no simple solutions to our challenges; if someone offers a magic wand that will fix everything with a wave, it is merely a ploy to garner your votes. Populists the world over rely on the same set of tricks. Sometimes these are bogeymen conjured out of thin air, and sometimes they stem from real problems; yet, merely stoking emotions offers no salvation and no progress. One trigger for outrage will simply replace another. Calm, credible journalism remains an indispensable source of information about candidates. While it is good that candidates communicate directly with voters via social media platforms, no candidate will voluntarily disclose details about expensive gifts they have received, business ties to Russian oligarchs, schemes large and small, big lies, small evasions, or even the feasibility of their election promises. Take a look at how the media portrays the candidates—whether via Latvian Public Media or any other independent outlet with a longstanding, trustworthy reputation. And here's one thing to consider: if candidates say they don't like being asked certain questions, wonder why.

https://eng.lsm.lv/article/culture/food-: The art of making sandwiches without butter was taught to Latvian housewives during World War II. In 1941, the newspaper "Tālavietis" reported on cooking courses where you could learn how to feed four people with 120 grammes of meat and how to make bread spreads to replace butter. It sounds like ingenious housekeeping. But behind these recipes lies a much more serious story – about how the war changed both the menu and the notion of good food. When Latvia was occupied by Nazi Germany, food and raw materials were systematically exported and used to supply the German army. The population of Latvia was left with strictly rationed food. For example, in April 1942, the weekly ration for one person was 250 grammes of meat, 180 grammes of butter or other fats, and 150 grammes of sugar. Housewives now had to figure out how to prepare meals for the whole family from a very small amount of ingredients. However, this situation was not a surprise to the Reich. It had been preparing for food shortages even before the war and encouraged its citizens to consume more local products, grow their own vegetables, abandon imported coffee in favor of German-made ersatz coffee, and reduce meat consumption. A peculiar example was the so-called "stew Sundays". During these times, the usual Sunday roast had to be replaced with a more modest dish that could be cooked in one pot - pea soup, beans or stew. The money saved - and this amount was calculated by the state - had to be donated, and on Sundays, collection workers went from house to house. Even family dinners had to become a declaration of loyalty to the regime. Printed materials for such food propaganda had been prepared even before the war. When World War II began when Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, the materials could be distributed immediately in Germany. During the Nazi occupation, seven cookbooks dedicated to wartime thrift were published in Latvia, including publications translated from German with titles such as "The Thrifty Mistress" and "Wartime Kitchen". They immediately differed from pre-war publications. Instead of meat dishes and desserts, now vegetables, cereals, and fermented milk products came to the fore in cookbooks. "Fake bull's eye" was a thick layer of minced potatoes mixed with buttermilk or cabbage juice spread on bread. A hole was made in the middle, filled with stewed carrots and tomatoes, which visually resembled an egg yolk. "Fake fish soup" made from carrots, potatoes and skimmed milk was given a 'fishy' taste by onion. Even the meaning of the word "cutlet" changed – in the past it was the best piece of rib, but now it meant anything that could be ground and fried in a pan: cottage cheese, semolina, mushrooms, oatmeal – hence today's Latvian ' kotlete ' which is a meatball rather than a chop. And what about sandwiches? Cookbooks had a special group of recipes – "bread spreads". For example, basic spreads were recommended to be made from flour, a very small amount of fat and broth, adding herbs, onions, tomato puree or mushrooms to the mass. Leftover sauce from lunch could also become a bread spread if you whipped a little butter into it. It was called "sandwich thrift butter." Cookbooks even taught how to use potato peelings, the water in which vegetables were cooked, and the flour that was swept into the pan after baking bread. Wartime cookbooks were not just practical guides. They were also propaganda publications. The Nazi occupation authorities tried to convince the population that abandoning their usual diet was not simply a consequence of deprivation. It was a patriotic act – it was the duty of civilians to save so that there would be enough food for the soldiers. Cookbooks claimed that before the war people ate too much meat, fat, and sweets, and that the current, modest menu was in fact healthier. However, behind the thrift calculations of wartime cookbooks, one can also see a completely human desire to preserve the usual order of life – at least in the appearance and names of familiar dishes. If you couldn't bake a cake like before, you could bake a cake from beans. If you couldn't spread real butter on bread, you could make something that resembled it and still call it a sandwich with a bit of imagination. These recipes remind us that cuisine is not just calories and nutrients. It stores habits, memories, and even a sense of security. Therefore, a sandwich without butter is a very accurate symbol of wartime cuisine. It tells both about scarcity, the ingenuity of housewives and the attempts of power to determine people's daily lives, plus the desire to preserve the sense of life as it was before the war, even in the most difficult circumstances.

PHP is one of the most widely used programming languages in the world, supporting everything from public sector websites and online stores to a wide range of digital services. This means that a single significant vulnerability in this technology can simultaneously affect a large number of organisations across different countries. Similar preventive measures are also being implemented elsewhere in Europe, including Finland, Germany, France and the Netherlands, where access to certain digital resources is being restricted or services are being temporarily suspended to reduce potential risks and allow the necessary security updates to be implemented. The current situation should therefore not automatically be interpreted as evidence of shortcomings in Latvia's information systems. Critical vulnerabilities can be discovered in any software, including technologies that are widely used and well established. No system is completely immune to such risks, whether in the public or private sector. The decision to restrict access to potentially vulnerable systems as a preventive measure is understandable and justified. If there is a risk that a vulnerability could be exploited to gain unauthorised access to a system, temporarily restricting its availability may be necessary to allow time for security updates. At the same time, restricting access solely from abroad does not, in itself, guarantee adequate protection. Today, cybercriminals do not necessarily have to be physically located in the country from which an attack appears to originate. By using various technological solutions and proxy servers, attackers can make it appear as though requests are coming from Latvia, even when they are operating from elsewhere in the world. This means that geographical access restrictions may reduce certain risks, but they cannot be considered a comprehensive security solution. If a vulnerability is critical and its exploitation could have serious consequences, the safest temporary approach may be to completely isolate the affected system from the public internet until the necessary updates have been implemented. However, any such restriction should remain a temporary measure. The primary objective must be to address the vulnerability and restore access to services as quickly as possible. We must recognise that situations like this may become increasingly common in the future. One reason is the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), which is fundamentally changing both software development and security testing. AI already helps developers write code faster, analyse complex systems and identify potential errors. However, the same capabilities can also be exploited for malicious purposes. While identifying vulnerabilities previously required considerable time and specialised technical expertise, AI tools can now significantly accelerate certain stages of this process. This does not necessarily mean that software is becoming less secure, but vulnerabilities can be identified and potentially exploited much faster than before. As a result, the time available for organisations to respond to emerging threats is also shrinking. Under these circumstances, simply implementing security solutions is no longer sufficient. Last week, in Latvia and in many parts of the world, a large number of government, local authority and private sector websites were taken offline due to cyber security risks . Website administrators had to update them urgently. Around five websites of public importance are still down, such as “rindapiearsta.lv”, which lists medical facilities providing state-funded healthcare services and indicates where these can be accessed most quickly. The “Rīgas siltums” website is also down, as is the Latvian Radio website, according to CERT.lv, which concluded that the vast majority of websites important to the public that had been taken offline are now accessible again. However, the organisation states that a large proportion of websites are still inaccessible from abroad, but it is likely that on Monday, 26 October, they will gradually become accessible again. Varis Teivāns, Deputy Head of CERT.lv, emphasised that no website has been hacked so far. Teivāns said: “There is noticeable activity, but it is not on an extraordinary scale. This could be explained by the fact that, in order to successfully exploit this vulnerability, an attacker still needs quite specific knowledge both of the process itself – how to exploit the vulnerability – and of the target system.” “If we choose to attack, for example, ‘Likumi.lv’, then we need to know the specifics of the system maintained by ‘Likumi.lv’ in order to successfully exploit its vulnerability. This actually works in favour of infrastructure defenders at the moment, as the attackers who are now visible on a large scale are most likely opportunists rather than professionals,” explained Teivāns. In Teivāns’ view, state authorities have coped very well, although they are still in the process of restoring their systems. The risk was high – critical data could have been lost. Teivāns said: “I don’t want to say that money is the solution to everything. Undoubtedly, there are situations where a lack of financial resources, or an inability to secure them, is the reason why something has become outdated or why there are other problems with the systems. A great deal can be resolved simply by planning the work properly and taking the right action. There are certain systems where, of course, we can now conclude that they were not maintained to the standard required by today’s cyber security challenges. But this incident… In fact, it isn’t really an incident, but our process of preventing an incident has spurred a great many people into action, and that is a good thing.” Last week, CERT.lv reported that around 6,000 websites could be vulnerable due to software issues. CERT.lv says that, to date, dozens of private-sector website operators have also approached them for assistance.
https://eng.lsm.lv/article/society/defen: KNDS Deutschland is ramping up production of Patria 6x6 armoured wheeled vehicles for the Bundeswehr at its facility in Freisen. The defence company plans to deliver the first vehicles at the end of 2026. Initially, they will be produced in Finland and Latvia, equipped with specialised components for the German army and undergo final assembly at the plant in Saarland. Serial deliveries to the Bundeswehr are scheduled to begin in early 2027, while German production will increase gradually and at the end of the same year the first of the vehicles built entirely in Freisen will be delivered. Patria is working with KNDS and other German industrial partners to establish the necessary local manufacturing capacity by combining German and Finnish engineering and expertise. The initial Bundeswehr order comprises almost 900 armoured 6x6 vehicles in four different configurations, with a total value of around €2 billion. It is the largest single deal in Patria’s history and was placed under the multinational Common Armoured Vehicle System (CAVS) programme. The first pre-series Patria 6x6 vehicles have already been delivered and are being used for testing, operator training, maintenance familiarisation and technical verification. Arhīva foto. Pievienots 30.05.2025. Miks Kuncevičs/LTV Bruņutransportieris "Patria". Adopting the Patria platform is intended to support Germany’s military objective of achieving full combat readiness by 2029. The robust three-axle vehicles will replace the long-serving German made Fuchs armoured personnel carriers, which have been in service since the early 1980s. The CAVS programme was launched in 2020 as a result of cooperation between Finland and Latvia, with the aim of developing a unified and modern 6x6 armoured vehicle system based on the Patria platform. It has since expanded to include Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Germany and the United Kingdom. Vehicles produced under the programme are also already operational in Ukraine through Latvian military assistance. A key focus of the project is the standardisation of components to meet common requirements and create synergies. The German programme will therefore follow a model similar to the one already established in Latvia, where Patria 6x6 vehicles are produced at a state-of-the-art facility in Valmiera opened in May 2024. “We call it a battlefield taxi,” says Uģis Romanovs, CEO of Patria Latvia and Defence Partnership Latvia, standing in the production hall next to Patria 6x6 vehicles being manufactured for the Latvian Armed Forces and National Guard. Latvian companies have been involved in the CAVS programme’s supply chain since its inception, contributing to the development of the Patria 6x6 vehicle that will be on display at the military parade in Riga on 18 November – and soon afterwards will also be produced in Germany. This story appears in the Autumn/Winter edition of Baltic Business Quarterly magazine, which is produced by the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania (AHK), and is reproduced by kind permission. The ban applies to all carriers, regardless of the carrier’s legal entity or the country of registration of the vehicle. Regular passenger transport services are not currently restricted; however, the Ministry of Transport has drafted amendments to the Road Transport Act, which provide for a ban on regular and occasional passenger bus services to Russia and Belarus from 10 January 2027, as well as a ban on such transit journeys through Latvia.

https://eng.lsm.lv/article/society/defen: These are among the conclusions of the study Baltic Defence Industry: United We Stand, Divided We Fall? by the Latvian Strategy and Economic Research Institute (LaSER). “Five years ago, there was a widespread belief in Europe that the Green Deal would provide an impetus to sluggish economic growth. Today, we hear similar expectations about the defence industry – that it can strengthen military capabilities neglected for decades while simultaneously becoming a source of economic growth,” says LaSER researcher Robert Kits. The potential is considerable, he adds, but success is by no means guaranteed. All three Baltic states have set strategic goals for developing their defence industries. By 2030, Estonia aims to achieve defence-industry exports of at least €1.4 billion, total sector revenues of €2 billion and a contribution equivalent to 2% of GDP. Lithuania intends to triple defence-industry exports compared with 2025 and increase the sector’s added value to more than €1 billion. Latvia has set targets for 2036: the defence industry should account for 5% of GDP, while 30% of defence procurement should come from domestic producers. However, LaSER researchers identify a fundamental problem: there is no common definition of what constitutes the defence industry, while reliable and comparable data for measuring progress are not collected consistently. Across the Baltic sample analysed by LaSER, the number of defence industry companies increased by 30% in six years, from 232 in 2019 to 300 at the end of 2024. Their combined turnover rose from €1.96 billion in 2019 to more than €3 billion in 2024 – equivalent to approximately 1.9% of the Baltic states’ combined GDP. Lithuania recorded the fastest turnover growth. In 2024, turnover among Lithuanian companies in the sample was 79% higher than in 2019, compared with increases of 51% in Latvia and 48% in Estonia. Lithuania also led in the growth of added value, which increased by 122% between 2019 and 2024. Latvia recorded growth of 64% and Estonia 47%. In absolute terms, however, Estonia remained the leader, with companies in its sample generating €616 million in added value in 2024. Employment is expanding too. The number of people employed by companies in the LaSER sample increased from just under 19,000 in 2019 to more than 21,000 in 2024. Latvia recorded the fastest employment growth at 36% over five years. Human capital could nevertheless become a major constraint. Leading industry representatives estimate that Latvia alone could require an additional 5,000 specialists in the short term. For small countries, domestic demand alone cannot sustain a large defence industry. Export competitiveness is therefore critical. Between 2019 and 2024, exports of goods and services accounted for 29–38% of turnover among Estonian companies in the LaSER sample, 27–36% among Latvian companies and 51–57% among Lithuanian companies. Lithuania was also the only Baltic country in which defence-industry exports continued to increase in 2024. Export volumes declined year-on-year in both Latvia and Estonia, allowing the Lithuanian companies in the sample to overtake Estonia for the first time. For Kits, this is close to the central question facing the industry. “Whether the defence industry becomes a competitive sector of the economy in the long term will largely depend on how successfully we can create high added value and export it,” he says. Achieving this requires more than increased defence spending. Companies must produce reliable products, have access to testing infrastructure and receive regular feedback from military end users. They also need predictable long-term orders if they are to invest in production capacity. Manufacturers must be capable of supporting their products throughout their lifecycle – from maintenance and repairs to modernisation and personnel training. At the same time, Baltic countries need to become better at promoting their companies internationally. Competition is intensifying as almost every European country now sees defence manufacturing as both a security priority and a potential source of economic growth. Kits argues that Latvia currently lags behind Lithuania and Estonia in presenting its defence industry internationally. Both neighbouring countries have publicly available industry portfolios identifying companies and their areas of specialisation. “By citing security considerations, we are reluctant to disclose what actually constitutes Latvia’s defence industry. As a result, an image of Latvia as a regional defence-industry hub cannot develop,” Kits says. Human capital represents another structural challenge, making Baltic cooperation increasingly important. Kits sees opportunities to coordinate priorities already at the higher-education level, where the next generation of specialists is being trained. Better data are equally important. Without a clear definition of which companies constitute the defence industry, strategic targets risk remaining political rhetoric rather than measurable economic objectives. Finally, the sector will need considerably more private capital. Public financing instruments have expanded, but governments cannot finance defence-industry growth indefinitely. The challenge is particularly acute for start-ups, where investment risks are inherently higher. The Baltic defence industry has already demonstrated that it can grow. The more difficult test comes next: turning that expansion into a sustainable, innovative and internationally competitive industry. Rather than straightforward information briefings, the videos are presented as a "mini-series" or micro-dramas featuring different people in different situations. For example, in the first of the series we meet a busy woman living in a rather grand residence who has a large dog. While preparing a meal for a dinner party and listening to some rather baleful music, she receives a yellow alert on her mobile phone about strong winds which are expected. Luckily, she manages to finish cooking dinner before the power goes off, and winds up spending the evening enjoying a heart-to-heart with her hound by candlelight at the dinner table. This turns out to be a fortunate development for the dog in particular who not only gets an uncommonly good dinner but avoids being crushed by a tree which has fallen overnight on its kennel. Her no-show guests call to explain why they didn't or couldn't come the previous night and despite a somewhat disappointed and vacant air, the hostess expresses her understanding. It seems possible that her invited guests also thought they had a narrow escape. Episode 2 centres on that most Latvian of things, a mushroom-picking expedition in the forest. Sitting in a leather-upholstered car in the city, two men discuss the best locations for finding mushrooms. As always in such situations, there is some dissent about where to go, probably because neither man wants to reveal to the other where the best location really is. Inevitably, the senior forager, Toms, pulls rank. The car appears to be in need of a service despite its obvious newness by ordinary Latvian mushroom wagon standards as it is reluctant to start. There is some mention of having to pick a woman called Zane up from the airport later, and postponed flights, but obviously, this is a secondary consideration when there are mushrooms to be had. The fungal foragers depart for the forest to the strains of some Mississippi delta style music and go about their business. They have barely covered the bottoms of their baskets when an orange alert for forest fires pops up on one of their mobile phones, which happily still has a connection in the middle of the forest massif. What to do when in the middle of the forest and told that there is a dangerous forest fire in the vicinity? Leave? Or continue to pick mushrooms? Tricky one. A small argument ensues as they are engulfed in smoke. This fact serves to resolve matters more swiftly than might otherwise have been the case and they return to the car which, inevitably, fails to start, in a marvellous example of the 'Chekhov's gun' dramatic principle. However, rather than being incinerated in their vehicle, eventually the engine does turn over and they speed away past fire trucks which have materialised to tackle the spreading conflagration. They decide to go to the alternative mushrooming location rather than give up entirely. In episode 3 we meet a man who gives off the vibe of being an enthusiastic 'prepper'. He is dressed in outdoor gear with multiple layers and many pockets. He has a gasoline generator ready to activate at a moment's notice. It fires up first time. He gets a supply of fresh water from the well. He seems to have a fireman's jacket in his van, so he's either a real fireman or someone who likes to dress up as a fireman. In a nice callback to the previous episodes, we learn that poor old Zane is still waiting for her delayed flight and a tree fell and destroyed the dog kennel from episode 1. They discuss the meanings of various different warning alerts, rather than whose turn it is to do the washing-upy, which would be the case in less well-prepared families. https://eng.lsm.lv/article/society/crime: Estonia's domestic intellegence service has attributed the arson plot to Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU. Estonia is planning to close its eastern border in response. Prosecutor General Astrid Asi said at a press conference on Sunday that there was an attempt to break into Threod Systems' property in Viimsi, near Tallinn, to start a fire at 3.06 a.m. on Saturday, November 14th. The incident was thwarted thanks to the intervention of Threod's security team, Asi added. Estonian Internal Security Service (KAPO) Director General Margo Palloson said counterintelligence had confirmed that Russia was behind the attempted attack and that it was coordinated by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU. "This was yet another attempt by Russia to carry out an act of sabotage in Estonia," he told the assembled media. The attackers are believed to have attempted to break the building's windows and pour flammable liquids inside to set the building on fire and cause an explosion, Palloson said. "We assess that if this attack had succeeded in the way the attackers planned, it would have caused very significant damage to the company," he said. Palloson said no one was injured in the incident and the company did not suffer any significant damage. Eight people have been detained, all residents of Latvia. "The Prosecutor's Office submitted an application to the court for the arrest of five suspects. The task of the criminal proceedings now is to establish the circumstances surrounding the organization of the attack, the roles of those involved and possible links to other individuals," Asi added. Palloson said Latvia's State Security Service (VDD) and Prosecutor's Office have helped significantly with the case. For its part, the VDD said in a press release: "On 13 and 14 November 2026, Latvian State Security Service (VDD) provided support to Estonian Internal Security Service (KAPO) in preventing an act of sabotage, namely arson, against the defence industry company "Threod Systems" in Estonia, which manufactures unmanned aerial vehicles. "VDD obtained and provided risk information to Estonian partner service KAPO regarding possible plans to carry out sabotage in Estonia, and the services immediately launched jointly coordinated activities to prevent the potential criminal offence. As a result of the close cooperation between the two services, a total of eight Latvian nationals were detained on Estonian territory on the night of 14 November, and an attempted act of sabotage against the aforementioned company was thwarted. "At the same time, on 14 November, VDD carried out criminal proceedings at nine sites in Latvia linked to the suspects. During the searches, explosive devices, pyrotechnic articles and ammunition were seized, as well as a large amount of mobile phones and other data storage devices," VDD said, adding that "the goals of Russia-organised sabotage acts are aimed at escalating tensions and fear in the public, and delaying support to Ukraine." This is the second known attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company this year, ERR said. In August, a fire was reported at defence contractor Milrem's office in Tallinn's Lasnamäe district, which KAPO also attributed to the Russian special services. Several Latvian citizens were also arrested in connection with that case.

https://eng.lsm.lv/article/society/defen: Three months have passed since Latvia was hit by one of the strongest summer storms in the last 60 years. As it swept through, it spared nothing – forests were devastated and the electricity supply was disrupted. Communications were also cut off in parts of the country. One of the regions particularly hard hit was the Ogre municipality. Shops and petrol stations in the town were closed, and residents were charging their phones in their cars. Uncertainty reigned in the town’s streets. It was precisely the experience gained in August that prompted the search for solutions to ensure communications even when the usual infrastructure ceases to function. In Ogre District, the procurement of additional generators and the adaptation of buildings for backup power supply have already begun. The local authority aims to ensure that every parish has a place where residents can turn to for help in the event of a crisis. “Uncertainty is usually what causes the most anxiety. The storm in August also showed that uncertainty was what caused additional stress both for us as a local authority and for residents,” commented Andris Krauja (National Alliance), Chair of the Ogre Municipal Council. To ensure that people do not lose contact in such situations, “Latvijas Mobilais telefons” (LMT) plans to supplement its usual mobile network with satellite communications. On a day-to-day basis, when making a call from a mobile phone, the connection is provided by the nearest base station. However, if that stops working, calls could in future be facilitated via satellite. To this end, a satellite dish located outside the home is connected to the internet router. All the resident would need to do is connect to the wireless internet on their phone, and they would be able to both make and receive calls in the usual way – without any special apps or additional equipment for the phone itself. On Tuesday in Ogre, a test was carried out to see how this would work by artificially putting a phone into flight mode, during which no connections are possible. As LMT’s Technical Director Aigars Benders emphasised, the user will not even notice that the phone is switching to satellite connectivity, as this will happen automatically. The technology required to implement this solution is already available, and discussions have already taken place with local authorities regarding the establishment of shared communication points. For the time being, however, the solution has only been tested on the LMT network. It also remains to be assessed how large an influx of users the satellite communications network could handle at any one time. At the same time, the company is also testing other technologies, including those that would, in future, allow a mobile phone to connect directly to a satellite without the need to search for a wireless internet connection.

https://eng.lsm.lv/article/society/socie: The mobile push notification was issued as a ‘yellow-level’ alert. Around 10.00, several social media users reported that they had received the notification on their phones, but without any specific audible alert. LSM.lv contacted the State Fire and Rescue Service (VUGD) to clarify in which circumstances a mobile broadcast alert can ‘break through’ a phone’s silent mode. In Latvia, mobile broadcast alerts are sent at two levels – yellow and orange. Each level requires specific action from the person who has received the alert, whilst mobile operating systems also have special provisions designed to override the settings chosen by the phone’s owner. Residents of several Latvian municipalities have been receiving these alerts at night over the past year, warning of an airspace threat or a potential threat. Similarly, cell broadcast alerts have been sent out to help locate missing persons. A yellow-level ( Severe Alert on iOS phones) cell broadcast alert is for information purposes only and does not require immediate action. “A Yellow-level alert generally does not override a person’s personalised sound and vibration settings. For example, if the phone is in silent mode, the alert will only trigger a vibration,” explained Viktorija Gribuste, Head of the Public Education and Information Division at the State Fire and Rescue Service’s Prevention Directorate. Similarly to a potential airspace threat, a yellow-level alert merely warns of what is yet to come. In contrast, orange-level ( Extreme Alert on iOS phones) cell broadcast alerts require people within the active cell broadcast zone to take action. A cell broadcast alert should be accompanied by a distinctive audible signal, alerting the recipient and prompting them to take action. However, there may be exceptions on certain phone models where the manufacturer has either not provided for such a system or where the orange-level alert is not prioritised, allowing it to override the user’s chosen settings.
